Uniform Title: Kulamuktikallolinī Author: Navamīsiṃha (also known as Ādyānanda)
Manuscript: NGMCP Manuscript No.: 1-1675 Reel No.: B 120/6 Description: Description by Mark S.G. Dyczkowski:
The author of the *Kulamuktikallolinī* is Navamīsiṃha.
Also known as Ādyānanda, he introduces himself at the beginning of his *Tantracintāmaṇi* (Asiatic Society of Bengal MSS no.
6217–8) as the minister of King Bhūpālendra of Nepal, who is described as being pious and...
A learned man; he was likely King Mahīndra Malla or Bhūpālendra Malla of Kathmandu, who reigned for approximately five years between 1689 and 1694 CE.

The *Kulamuktikallolinī* deals with Śākta Tantra ritual and practice, particularly the worship of Kālī. Extending over 9,000 verses in twenty-two chapters, it is a compendium that draws from a vast array of sources.
The number of sources includes the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*, *Rudrayāmala*, *Kumārītantra*, *Mahākālasaṃhitā*, *Phetkāriṇītantra*,
*Kālitantra*, *Svatantratantra*, *Merutantra*, *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*, and *Piṅgalāmata*.
The Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi, Kulārṇava, Mahākapilapañcarātra, Tattvasāra, Ṣoḍaśārṇava, Somaśambhupaddhati, Vīrāgama, Śivapaddhati,
Devīmata, Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra, Śivasadbhāva, and Yoginītantra.

The *Candrayāmala*, *Siddhayāmala*, *Mohaśūrāntara*, *Nāradapañcarātra*, *Matsyasūkta*, *Vaiśampāyanasaṃhitā*, and many others. Although the Navamīsiṃha writes little of his own, it is clear from the sheer...
The breadth of the sources from which he draws indicates that he was profoundly learned.
He draws from tantras of all schools, including the Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra and the Śaiva Siddhānta, yet he demonstrates a clear preference for [the latter].

The Kaula and Śākta Tantras are mostly of the later period. His primary concern is with ritual. He begins with the rites of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and proceeds systematically, chapter by chapter, with the rites that follow.
These constitute the worship (*pūjā*) of the deity. They include the fashioning and purification of the fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*),
the consecration of the sacrificial fire (*agni-saṃskāra*), the consecration of the mantras, and the daily worship.
The daily rites (*nityavidhi*), the rituals and mantras for those embarking on a journey,
the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), and the consecration of the vessel for the arghya water (*arghyasthāpana*).
and so forth. Although not original, the work contains interesting and important source materials, frequently drawn from unpublished sources.
Such compendiums, which became very popular from around the twelfth century...
The period of a given century can often be roughly dated based on the date of its compiler;
thus, this may substantially contribute to future research into the development of tantric literature after the eleventh century.

It is the singular essence of all systems, saluted by all the gods;

O child, it is worthy of being struck by the single arrow of both sin and merit; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; it consists of every wonder, and it deludes even the wise.
It gives rise to various meanings for the wise, yet it is crowded and agitated by various meanings;

This conduct, which is praised by all speakers and censured by all speakers, was spoken by me to Viṣṇu; it was not told to Dhātṛ nor to Gaṇapa.
O child, protect this tantra with effort within your heart, like a yogi;
for without it, O child, nothing brings happiness to the Kula.
2a) O child, this secret and marvelous [teaching] must be protected from the profane;
it should not be disclosed to anyone, nor should it be practiced in any way whatsoever.
Now, O Omniscient One, you who are skilled in all things—
O Maheśvara, you alone are the speaker of the scriptures, and no one else.
You are the guru of all tantras; neither I nor Hari am the master, even though I have attained the state of being the cause and possess the form of the Kula.
There is neither an effect nor anything whatsoever; I am the radiant Lord, Brahman itself.
When I, whose form is the universe, have attained the state of being the very substance of the effect, that is my nature.
"At that time, you alone were the speaker of the tantras, and I was not, O Maheśvara.
Now, O omniscient Maheśvara, speak the knowledge of the tantras."
"O Lord, enter Viśvāmitra’s body and become united with me;
for without me, no other woman should ever be conceived as his progenitor."
Therefore, since you have attained the state of being an effect, sonship resides in you;
apart from you, there is no father whatsoever who can manifest that effect.
Therefore, you alone are Janaka; there is no other whatsoever.
At times you are my husband, and at other times you are my guru.
Sometimes assuming the state of a son and sometimes remaining merely as thought,
the conceptualization of creation arises from the union of Śiva and Śakti.
From the union of Śiva and Śakti arises the conceptualization of Kula and the rest;
everything whatsoever that exists within the world is composed of Śiva and Śakti.
Therefore, I am indeed everywhere and you are everywhere; of this there is no doubt.
O Lord of Gods, you alone are everything, and I, the eternal one, am everything.
If you are the Guru, then I am the disciple; thus there shall be an investigation of the scriptures.
Therefore, O Lord, be the Guru; O Supreme Ishvara, I am the disciple.
In the Śrī Rudrayāmala, the venerable Mahādeva said:
O beloved of Hara, tell me what more is to be said after this in the Kumārī-tantra.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, skilled in the meaning of all treatises:
by what means do men in the Kali age attain a good rebirth?
Tell me that, O Mahādeva, if you have compassion for me.
Bhairava said:
For this, O Ānanda, is the most secret and eternal truth; it must be kept strictly hidden and cannot be spoken at all.
Although I say that you are exceedingly dear to me, nevertheless,
this world— both gross and subtle— is composed of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman).
Without primordial nature (prakṛti), however, cyclic existence and the like are simply not possible;
therefore, no further root cause for primordial nature is ever observed.
O beautiful lady, there are many forms belonging to Prakṛti;
among them, however, the form of Kālī is the most preeminent and captivating.
Especially in the Kali age, it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men;
thus it is stated in the Mahākālasaṃhitā.
In the Kali age, Kālī is the Great Vidyā; in the Kali age, Kālī indeed bestows accomplishment;
in the Kali age, Kālī is perfectly perfected; and in the Kali age, Kālī grants boons.
In the Kali age, Kālī is prepared to appear before the practitioner;
in the Kali age, Kālī alone exists—there is no need for deliberation on this point.
In the Kali age, there can be no bliss of knowledge other than the knowledge of Kālī; indeed, in the Kali age, whoever desires spiritual perfection must do so by means of Kālī alone.
O Goddess, without Śakti, one desires sexual enjoyment;
O Goddess, in the Kali age, whoever desires to accomplish any task [must do so] without Kālī.
Having abandoned the practice of Nīrasādhana, he wanders everywhere;
for in the Kali age, whoever seeks liberation must first leave behind Kālī.
If a practitioner desires success while abandoning meditation on the Guru, he is like one who,
in the Kali age, wishes to run away after leaving behind Kālī.
He abandons food, desiring only the cessation of hunger;
for there is no worship equal to Kālī, nor is there any praise equal to Kālī.
Indeed, within this cosmic egg, there is no mantra equal to the Kālī-soma-mantra,
even with thousands of millions of mouths or hundreds of millions of hymns of praise.
O beautiful one, I am not able to describe it even in a hundred years;
it cannot be described even in a thousand lifetimes.
Who indeed are her worshippers? They are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others;
as well as Candra, Sūrya, Varuṇa, Kuvera, Agni, and yet another.
Durvāsas, Vasiṣṭha, Dattātreya, and Bṛhaspati—what need is there to say more? All the gods are his devotees.
"By the grace of Kālikā, [practitioners] become partakers of worldly enjoyment, liberation, and so forth," as stated in the Mahākālasaṃhitā.
Now I shall extract the mantra of Dakṣiṇakālī;
by remembering it even once, what is there that would not be accomplished?
In the Phetkāriṇī Tantra.
I shall proclaim its mantra, which bestows the fulfillment of all desires:
the first letter of the first class, joined with fire (the letter *ra*), and endowed with Rati and the Bindu (*ī*).
Then the *kūrca* mantra repeated three times, followed by the pair of *lajjā* mantras;
then "Kālikā" in the south, and thereafter again as before.
The wise know this mantra to be joined with two *ṭha*s; thus it is stated in the Kālitantra.
I shall proclaim its mantra, by which the three worlds are brought under control:
the letter *ka* conjoined with fire (*ra*), and endowed with the essence of passion (*i*) and the bindu.
Then one should utter the three qualities (guṇa), followed by the pair of *kurca* mantras joined with *lajjā*,
and then "O Kālikā" on the right, pronouncing the preceding seed-syllables as well.
3a) The great mantra of Kālikā is said to end with the wife of Vahni (the fire-god).
In the independent tantra.
One should write Krodhīśa joined with Vahni (Ra), conjoined with Trimūrti (Ū) and Indu (the moon-dot); O Goddess, one should write this three times, followed by two Huṃkāras.
Having drawn the two *māyās*, Atri, joined with the subtle *saṃvarta*,
[places] the seven syllables beginning with *ṇe kālike* as before, O Supreme Goddess.
At the end of "svāhā," there is the supreme twenty-two-syllable Great Vidyā beginning with "yaṃ."
In the Kumārī Tantra:
The three *kāmas* (KĀM) situated upon fire (RA), conjoined with *rati* (I) and *bindu* (M);
likewise, the pair of *kūrca*s (HŪM HŪM), followed thereafter by the pair of *lajjā*s (HRĪḤ HRĪḤ).
One should utter the seed-syllables as before, ending with "Kāli" on the right;
at the end, one should give "Vahnivadhū"—this is proclaimed as the Queen of Vidyās.
In the awakening to reality.
Brahmā is mounted upon fire (Ra) and conjoined with the fourth vowel (Ī);
joined with Nāda and Bindu, his form is tripled.
The pair of *kūrca* syllables, the pair of *śiva* syllables, and then "O Kālikā" on the right;
the seed-syllable as before, ending with the wife of fire (*svāhā*), constitutes the twenty-two [syllables] of the Southern [Kali].
In the Meru Tantra:
Now I shall fully describe another goddess, Dakṣiṇakālikā:
having uttered *krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ huṃ*, one should then utter *huṃ* and the two *lajjās*.
To the south is Kālikā; thereafter, one should again recite the seed-syllables. In due order, the mantra of Agnigṛhiṇī consists of twenty-two syllables.
In the Kumārī Tantra:
In this [practice], there is no concern for the attainment of supernatural powers (siddhi) and the like, nor are there characteristics such as enemies or friends;
furthermore, there is neither excessive travel abroad nor the occurrence of physical hardship.
Indeed, by the mere recollection of this, the eight supernatural powers (siddhis) are attained.
In the Kālitantra:
Thus, it is impossible to praise the Queen of all vidyās,
even with thousands of millions of mouths or hundreds of millions of tongues.
O Goddess, Aniruddha-Sarasvatī is the bestower of all accomplishments;
therefore, indeed, all siddhis arise from her mantra of knowledge.
By the mere knowledge of Aniruddha-Sarasvatī,
the practitioner shall attain mastery over learning and poetic composition, reaching the level of the Goddess of Speech herself.
His scholarship is indeed pitiable due to his fabrication of various phrases;
even the gods are ashamed of it, let alone humans and others.
Furthermore, if there were a woman equal to you, or a man equal to me,
then I would be the equal of Aniruddha Sarasvatī.
In the Phetkāriṇī Tantra.
Whoever should contemplate this lute, which grants the fulfillment of all desires, in his hand always resides every accomplishment; of this there is no doubt.
3b) His speech in the assembly becomes composed of both prose and verse;
[he is freed from] the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, and likewise sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached.
One should indeed rely on everything, but one should contemplate only the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
in speech, he is equal to Vāgīśvara, and in wealth, he is like Kubera.
"Having become equal to the moon and sun, one shall dwell in heaven for ten thousand kalpas. Why say more? Such passages as these are numerous.
Nothing is difficult to obtain for him who remembers Ghorakālikā;
[as stated] in the Kumārītantra.
By means of horse-sacrifices, cow-sacrifices, human-sacrifices, and others as well;
by various other gifts and also by manifold kinds of fire-offerings (homa).
By means of other assemblies of merit,
this supreme Vidyārājñī Ghorakālī, who is indeed Aniruddha Sarasvatī, is attained.
One attains liberation simply by knowing this; what more need be said of the supreme?

by its mere light, the disputants are rendered lusterless.

[He brought about] the freezing of fire's army and the immobilization of the sun's movement.

Likewise.
Merely by knowing this, one becomes liberated while living;
eloquent like Bṛhaspati and as patient as the earth.
In valor and form he is remembered as equal to Śrī Rāma; in beauty he is considered like Kāmadeva; in depth he is like the ocean, and in splendor he is comparable to the sun.
In matters such as cursing, he was like Durvāsas; in matters such as anger, he was comparable to Yama; in creation, he was Prajāpati himself; and likewise, in preservation, he was Viṣṇu.
For he who truly knows this [teaching] is equal to the dissolution of the world; what need is there for much speaking here? There is no one on earth equal to him.
In the Kālitantra:
The recitation of this [mantra] is the recitation of Brahman; meditation upon it is reflection on the Self.
Its perfect concentration is undoubtedly the true practice of Yoga.
In great calamity, in great sin, in warding off the influence of great planets;
in great fear, in great portents, in great sorrow, and in great disease.
In the great delusion, in the great caravan, in the peril of great poverty,
in the great battle, in the great void, in the great ignorance, and in the great conflict.
On a long journey, in a difficult dwelling, during famine, or when faced with ill omens—
in the midst of all such heaps of suffering— one shall destroy them merely by recollection.
For her, ignorance itself is knowledge; for her, meditation is the contemplation of the Self.
For her, there is no doubt that even ignorance is perfect wisdom through this mantra.
The abode of Brahmā and the other gods belongs to him; how could anyone else be his equal?

he is like Tumbaru himself in song and equal to Karṇa in generosity.

In the Vīracūḍāmaṇi.
Now I shall proclaim another [mantra], the Śāraṅgī, which bestows all accomplishments;
by the mere knowledge of which one becomes a bestower of all sovereignty.

by the mere remembrance of her, knowledge of the body arises.

In the Phetkāriṇī Tantra.

now I shall duly describe the goddess known as Dakṣiṇā.
The origin of the mantra verses is stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*:
Because it brings about the perfect accomplishment of contemplation, universal knowledge, and protection from the bonds of saṃsāra, it is therefore called "mantra."
Also elsewhere.
Through secret instruction, it is a mantra because it bestows reflection;
it is a mantra because it protects through honor; for practitioners, it is a wish-fulfilling tree.
Thus says the statement of another tantra.
In the Meru-tantra.
Neither in heaven, nor at sacred fords, nor in medicinal herbs, nor in the stars do the sages and deities exist; rather, the mantras themselves are the deities.
The gods assumed the form of the *talatru* in order to bestow the fruit upon practitioners;
however, their primary essential nature consists solely of mantras and nothing else.
In the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
One should not speak after merely looking at the scripture, nor recite it without practicing;
one should not look [at it] without teaching, nor act without accomplishing.
Having obtained the recitation, ritual placement, worship, and so forth from the instruction of the Guru,
one should thereafter accomplish all of that, always permeated by the state of being absorbed in that [divine reality].
In the Meru Tantra:
If one should mutter a mantra heard by chance, or even one obtained through deception or force, or one prompted by others, or a mere verse, it will bring about misfortune.

4b) Therefore, there is dependence upon a teacher. Now, the characteristics of a teacher:
In the Kulacūḍāmaṇi.
One who is of noble birth is proclaimed to be qualified for all sciences;
he alone, and no other, is the master of initiation and of every mantra here.
But one who is disciplined should take a noble person from a noble family as a teacher.
He who knows the reality of the Kula, is proficient in the Kula-āśrama, and is devoted to the worship of the Kula, shall be a true Kaulika; any other is merely a hypocrite.

He who becomes joyful upon seeing those devoted to the family, those who follow the family conduct, those who possess family knowledge, and those who observe the family vows— he, the Kaulika, is dear to me.
By accepting the three realities, knowing the reality of the meaning of the root mantra,

In the Meru-tantra.
Akula is said to be Śiva, while Kula is proclaimed to be Śakti;

But the animal has no entitlement [to the Vedic rites].
O God Bhairava, there are two kinds of *paśu* (bound souls), including those mentioned previously;

The characteristics of the Guru, according to the Merutantra.
One should look upon the Guru as endowed with twenty times twenty single qualities;
he is of noble birth, possesses well-proportioned limbs, is pure in appearance, and is captivating.
He knew the true meaning of all scriptures and was conversant with the application of all mantras;
through his gestures, facial expressions, and movements, he perceived from afar those who were wicked.
Inward-turned yet with outward vision, omniscient and knowing place and time,
endowed with the arising of perfected command, peaceful and a knower of the Vedas and their auxiliary limbs.
One who is devoted to obligatory, occasional,
and optional rites that are beyond reproach, who is free from greed, non-violent, and impartial, is considered a Guru.
A mantra that is not such as this leads either to death or to happiness.
In the Kulārṇava:
O Supreme Goddess, the glorious Guru is elegantly dressed and captivating;
he is endowed with all auspicious marks and his every limb is beautiful.
He knew the true meaning of all scriptures and was conversant with the procedures of all mantras;
he appeared to delude the world, yet his appearance was as pleasing as that of a god.
One who is pleasant-faced, like a moth [entering the flame], transparent, and pure within, undoubtedly cuts through [the enemy];
having discerned their gestures, facial expressions, and movements, he keeps the wicked at a distance.
Inward-turned yet with outward vision, omniscient, and knowing place and time;
one who has attained mastery through command, knowing the three times, and capable of both restraint and grace.
5a) One who is learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas), who is tranquil, devoted to compassion for all living beings,
who has mastery over the movement of his senses, and is capable of conquering the group of six internal enemies.
Foremost among the assembly, profound, and discerning between those who are worthy vessels and those who are not;
stainless, eternally contented, free from dualities, and ever-powerful.
He is a true devotee, affectionate, steadfast, compassionate, and one whose speech is preceded by a smile;
he is fond of his devotees, impartial toward all, merciful, and a teacher of disciples.
He should have his own chosen deity as his preceptor, be wise, be eager to honor women, and be devoted to blameless ritual actions— whether daily, occasional, or performed for specific desires.
Free from disease, hatred, fear, anger, hypocrisy, and egoism,
he does not disclose his own learning, spiritual practices, or the performance of austerities.
Content with whatever is obtained by chance, discerning between virtues and faults,
unattached to women, wealth, and the like, and free from the calamities of evil associations.
One who is free from greed, non-violent, impartial, and discerning;
one who does not sell mantras, yantras, tantras, and the like for the sake of wealth, learning, or other such things.
Free from intention and free from conceptual construction, he is one who has realized the Self and is most righteous;
equal toward blame and praise, silent, indifferent, and self-restrained.
O Dear One, the Śrī Guru is said to be endowed with such characteristics as these:
he is pure-hearted, compassionate, a Brāhmaṇa, and one who has mastered the Vedas.
Always devoted to the conduct of his lineage, he applies himself to the scriptures of his family;
he is peaceful, self-controlled, all-knowing, and free from greed and delusion.
Having abandoned anger and delusion, he is free from passion and honored by heroes;
he is a knower of the Nigamas and Āgamas, and his mind is exceedingly serene.
One who has abandoned all supports and is intent upon the worship of the *lalanā*—
one endowed with such characteristics as these should worship the Guru with reverence.
In the Mahākapila Pañcarātra.
Neither too young nor old, neither lame nor emaciated;
neither with extra limbs nor deficient in limbs, neither bald nor with protruding teeth.
One who is grateful, eloquent, brave, well-established, a master of the scriptures,
trained in the science of architecture (vāstu-vidyā), and capable of discerning the extraction of arrows (śalyoddhāra).
To one who knows the sequence of ritual actions and discerns the tantras of mudrās.
In the *Tattvasāra*:
One who eats excessively, is procrastinating, and is greedy for sense objects and the like;
one who delights in sophistry, is corrupt, is a talker, and is a reviler of virtues.
Aroma and Bahuroma were censurers of those who serve the hermitage;
Kāladata had oversized lips, and Durgandha emitted a foul-smelling breath.
Even if he is himself a lord, an Ācārya who is endowed with wicked characteristics and is addicted to accepting many gifts brings about the destruction of prosperity.
5b) The ocean of sixteen syllables.
One who is childless, one whose children have died, a *kuṇḍa*, as well as a dwarf,
one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one conquered by women, and one with an extra limb.
One who has missing limbs, is deceitful, diseased, talkative, or hunchbacked—
only he who is free from these defects is a teacher fit to be a vessel for disciples.
In the Vārāhī Tantra:
One should not adopt a teacher who bears one's own name, nor a wife whose name is that of one's mother.
Somaśambhu.
One who is endowed with knowledge of place and time, scriptural learning, proper conduct, behavior, and virtuous qualities,
and who is further perfected by his own nature, shall be a guru appointed by a guru.
In the Vīrāgama.
A learned man born in a region situated between the Kumārī and Hīman mountains, which is naturally endowed with black antelopes, is indeed worthy of the status of an Ācārya.
In the Śivapaddhati.
Those born in the Middle Country, Kurukṣetra, Nābhīka, and Pīni; those established in Antarvedī, and the Āvantyas—these are the most excellent gurus.
The Gauḍas, Sākhodbhavas, Sauras, Māgadhas,
Keralas, Kośalas, and Daśārṇas are the seven middle Gurus.
Those born in Karṇāṭa, Narmadārāṣṭra, Kachchha, and Ābhīra,
as well as the Kāliṅgas, Kāmarūpas, and Kāmbojas, are considered the lowest.
In the Devīmata.
The preceptor should be a knower of the Śaiva scriptures, born in a land designated as excellent,
and either a celibate student or a householder who is solely devoted to devotion for Śiva.
An astrologer who is born under a constellation favorable to the patron of the sacrifice is called a Janmādeśika.
In the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*.
One should always appoint as a guru a householder established in celibacy, who avoids the eight syllables beginning with 'ka', and who is devoted to the vow of fasting.
Belonging to Śiva.
In the Śaiva Āgama.

The Great Goddess does not bestow the initiation of mantra upon monks, forest-dwellers, or those still in the stages of life (varṇins); nor should one who is a householder seeking both worldly enjoyment and liberation perform it [on others].

Those who have abandoned the sacred fires, those devoid of ritual acts, those born of improper wombs, those who have taken wives, forest-dwellers of such a nature, and those belonging to a lower stage of life— [these are excluded].
Therefore, O Maheśvarī, they have no authority in the bestowing of initiation.
In the true nature of Śiva.
O beloved, a householder seeking worldly enjoyment and liberation should not choose ascetics or forest-dwellers as his gurus during initiation; this has been described accordingly.
In the Yoginītantra.
But for one who, having taken the initiation of an ascetic, is ever deluded,
there is either one cow as penance or a three-night vow.
6a) Having then performed the expiation, one should undergo initiation once again.
In the Candrayāmala:
The initiation of one devoted to his father, the initiation of forest-dwellers,
and the initiation of those in secluded hermitages— all such initiations destroy sons, longevity, and wealth.
In the Siddhayāmala:
O beloved, if one should obtain a perfected vidyā solely by the power of fortune,
then at that very moment one should initiate her, setting aside all consideration of a guru.
But in the bestowing of one's own chosen vidyā, one should not entertain thoughts of a guru.
Within the brave ones who are deluded.

A teacher should be one who maintains the conduct and vows of his social class, is proficient in mantra, possesses knowledge, is well-composed, constantly devoted to practice, renowned, and may even be a *yati* or a *hautika*.
In this context, the statement regarding the gravity of the offense for an ascetic refers to cases other than those involving a householder.
In the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*.
He who possesses supreme devotion toward Viṣṇu as he does toward his guru—he alone is to be known as a true teacher; I speak this truth.
In the Nārada-pañcarātra.
A Brāhmaṇa who knows all times should bestow favor upon all;
in his absence, the best of the twice-born—tranquil in soul and absorbed in the Blessed One—should do so.
Among the castes of Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra, the Kṣatriya is capable of bestowing favor;
for even in the case of a Kṣatriya, [the initiation] occurs if there is the sight of the four [Vedas] or the absence thereof.
O high-minded one, a Vaiśya should perform his duties with a Śūdra who is of the same caste as himself; this is the favor shown toward the twice-born.
The *anugraha* and *abhiṣeka* initiations should always be performed for a Śūdra,
even when there is a member of a superior caste present, whether that person is eminent or renowned.
One who desires auspiciousness should not perform this rite in one's own country or elsewhere;
however, if it is already established, one may do so wherever there is a reversal [of fortune].
One may suffer ruin in this world and the next; therefore, one should practice what is declared in the scriptures.
One should not initiate those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes in the reverse order of classes.
In the Meru Tantra:
A Brahmin alone should be made such a guru, provided he is not otherwise;
one born of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes should not initiate [a disciple] in the reverse order of classes.
In the Tantra:
The preceptor, the maternal uncle, the officiating priest, the paternal uncle, the father-in-law, and the king—
these six are declared here to be gurus for one who is proficient in mantras.
In the Jñānonnayana and Yoginītantra.
For one must indeed disregard the counsel of a father, as well as that of a maternal grandfather,
of a younger uterine brother, and of one who has taken the side of an enemy.
In the Yoginītantra.
Either through grace or through such knowledge, one should perform the initiation of the ancestors;
having then performed an expiation, one should undergo initiation once again.

6b) Here, the genitive case in the word *pituh* (of the father) is used in the sense of disregard (*anādara*). Therefore, the meaning is that if there is disregard toward the father and others in the form of a lack of devotion due to excessive familiarity and so forth, then the mantra should not be received from the son or others.

In this regard, it appears to me that [the mantra] should be given to a devoted son who bestows wealth, according to the statement in the *Prayogasāra*: "It should be bestowed upon a devoted son," and according to the statements in the *Phetkāriṇī* and other texts: "It should be released and given even to the eldest, provided he is disciplined. However, some maintain that it should be given to the eldest son who is the ornament of his own family, based on the statement in the *Phetkāriṇī* and other texts: "One should give it to the eldest son, the ornament of his lineage."

They say that the right to receive the mantra from the father belongs only to the eldest son who is devoted, and not to the younger sons, nor to grandsons and others from the side of the maternal grandfather and so forth.
But others, however, [say]:

However, they say that because of the statement in the *Bhairava Tantra*— "One should not entertain thoughts of [other] gurus regarding the instruction of one's own mantra"— there is a prohibition against receiving a mantra from an uninitiated father or other relative.
But in the Matsyasūkta, however:
For it has been stated that a father’s mantra, being devoid of potency, is rendered defective by a Śākta [mantra] within the Śaiva [tradition].
In the Merutantra:
The path of the right hand (dakṣamārga) is devoid of potency for the father, the maternal grandfather, and the brother who is a householder;
the path of the left hand (vāmamārga), however, is potent.
In the Rudrayāmala.
A husband shall not initiate his wife; a father shall not initiate his daughter;
likewise, a brother shall not initiate a son, nor shall he initiate a brother.

This [teaching] also pertains exclusively to those who are not devotees; for this very reason, it accords with the words of the *Matsya-sūkta*: "In the past, this was told by Brahmā to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, and Vasiṣṭha, in turn, gave it to his own grandson, my father."
Receiving mantras from a woman is praised; initiation from a woman is declared auspicious, and that from one's mother is remembered as being eight times more so.
According to this statement from the Yoginītantra, she too—a widow—is prohibited.
She was virtuous, of good conduct, devoted to her guru, and had conquered her senses;
she knew the true meaning of all mantras, possessed excellent character, and delighted in worship.
She alone is fit to be the Guru’s consort, for she must be free from widowhood.
For it is stated in that very same [text]: "Thus."
And [the mantra] Hayaśīrṣa at night.
But that twice-born man who perceives the Self as distinct from everything, even if he lacks all auspicious marks, is a guru; of this there is no doubt.
One who is awakened to the Pañcarātra and knows the reality of its established tenets is declared to be an Ācārya, even if he is devoid of all [other] auspicious characteristics.
In the Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā.
That which is obtained in a dream or given by a woman is purified by the rite of consecration alone.
And the formative forces (saṃskāra) are in that very same [place].
And one should cause the life-force of the Guru to enter the jar obtained in a dream;
having written [the mantra] with saffron on a banyan leaf, the seizing is performed.
From that, one attains success; otherwise, it would be fruitless.
On the lunar seat.
Even mantras obtained in a dream, given by a woman, or bestowed by anyone else without being properly mastered, must nevertheless be received from a true guru in order to yield their fruit.
Thus ends the definition of the guru. Now, the definition of the disciple, as stated in the Kulārṇava:
O Mistress of the Kula, he should be accompanied by a disciple, endowed with all the auspicious marks,
possessed of the hundredfold means of accomplishment, and gifted with virtue and good character.
One should approach a virtuous person who possesses a pure body, a pure mind,
firm vows, and righteous conduct, and who is endowed with faith and devotion.
One who is grateful, fearful of evil, associated with the virtuous and the noble,
a believer, generous by nature, and devoted to the welfare of all living beings.
Endowed with trustworthiness and discipline, free from stinginess regarding wealth,
capable of accomplishing what is difficult to achieve, heroic, and possessed of strength and splendor.
One who acts with favor, is diligent, and discerning; who speaks words that are beneficial, truthful, measured, and affectionate, and who is free from fault-finding.
One who grasps the meaning upon being told once, who is clever and possesses an expansive intellect, who remains unchanging on the floor, on a seat, or in one's lap, and who requires no attendant;
A hero who acts with deliberation, free from the poverty of mind,
highly skilled in all undertakings, steadfast, and helpful to all.
O beloved, [I seek] one who is averse to censuring others for their own sake, who has a pleasant countenance,
who has conquered the senses, who is happy, contented, wise, and a celibate student.
Free from excessive attachment and the like, devoid of fickleness, ill-will, fear, and anxiety,
it is eager for the service, worship, and devotion consisting of meditation upon the Guru, praise, and listening to his discourses.
O Goddess, [one who is] devoted to the Guru as a deity, desirous of the beloved, eager for worship,
an observer of the Guru’s command, and a praiser of the Guru’s glory.
O Mistress of the Clan, [one should choose] a Guru who knows the authority of the Guru’s words, who is devoted to serving the Guru,
who acts in accordance with [the disciple's] mind, and who performs [his duties] with foresight.
Free from shame, pride, arrogance, and the like in the presence of the guru;
indifferent toward the guru’s property, yet longing for his grace.

The teacher should accept as a disciple one who is devoted to the meditation on the guru and other such practices, who proceeds along the path to liberation, and who possesses these and other such characteristics.
In the Meru Tantra:
The Guru should examine the disciple for twelve years, or half of that, or even a quarter of that, to see if he is endowed with the twenty characteristics; only then should he initiate him.
One who recognizes the authority of the guru’s words, is devoted to the service of the guru,
is free from shame, pride, arrogance, and the like, and is a leader of his lineage.
7b) One who is indifferent toward the teacher's property, who desires his favor,
who is devoted to recitation, meditation, and so forth, and who proceeds along the path to liberation.
One who is endowed with the means of practice such as tranquility, possesses a pure body,
is righteous, firm in his vows, of good conduct, and is filled with faith and devotion.
Speech that is beneficial, truthful, measured, and affectionate, which is esteemed by the virtuous,
agreeable, pleasant, steady, and helpful to all.
One should always maintain a pleasant countenance toward the disciple for the satisfaction of the deity.
Now, the characteristics of the wicked, as stated in the Kulārṇava:
One born of a wicked lineage, who is corrupt, devoid of virtues, deformed,
a disciple of another, a heretic, a rogue, and one who merely fancies himself a scholar— [these should not be taught].
Possessing limbs that are deficient or deformed due to inferiority or excess,
one is lame, blind, deaf, filthy, and afflicted by disease.
Uchiṣṭa, Durmukha, and Viṭa, who assumes whatever guise he pleases; as well as Durvidagdha, Kuceṣṭa, Kuṭila, and Bhīmavīkṣaṇa.
It is always possessed of sleep and laziness, afflicted by lethargy and the like, and its body is constantly obstructed by doors, walls, pillars, and so forth.
What is the use of one who is devoid of power and capability, base, lacking in faith and devotion,
a mere talker, arrogant, a mere messenger, fickle, and deceitful?
One who is devoid of purity regarding wealth and wife, who disregards prohibitions and injunctions,
who reveals secrets, and who destroys for the sake of performing rites for the gods.
One who behaves like a cat or a crow, intent on seeking out vulnerabilities;
one who is deceitful, ungrateful, and a giver whose inner heart is concealed.

One who betrays trust, O Lord, one who is hostile to the gods, a doer of evil, one devoid of faith, one lacking knowledge, and one who desires the failure of his undertakings— [these are to be avoided].

O Goddess, [one should avoid] one who seeks to kill, one who desires to seize property, one who is contemptible, a false witness, one who cooks for all [castes], and one who goes to women by force or through seduction.
One who is devoted to untruth, incompetent, vulgar, and a talkative chatterer; one who engages in wicked deliberations and fallacious reasoning, and who is fond of quarreling.
One who acts in vain to cause distraction, or who is a deceiver, a mere talker,
one who finds fault behind one's back, yet speaks kindly to one's face.
One should know that a person who speaks harsh words, who praises himself like a thief,
who cannot endure the virtues of others, who is fearful of the virtuous, and who is possessed by excessive anger [is not to be trusted].
The Cārvāka is the mouth of the wicked, despised by all the world;
it is treacherous, causing distress to others, and terrifying to all living beings.
O Goddess, one who speaks without affliction [of truth], yet betrays friends, deceives his brother,
is devoted solely to the tongue and the genitals, is a thief, and acts like a beast.
One who causes hatred, laughter, afflictions, anger, and the like without cause; one who initiates mockery and derides others within their delusion.
8a) He is lustful, utterly shameless, indicative of false and wicked conduct,
and possessed of envy, intoxication, malice, hypocrisy, and egoism.
One who is envious, slanderous, harsh, malicious, angry, and proud;
one who is inferior, miserable, hateful, incompetent, and devoid of reality.
One whose mind is unrefined, who is deluded, whose heart is agitated by anxiety,
who is possessed by craving and greed, who is wretched, discontented, and performs sacrifices for everyone;
O beloved, [one should avoid] one who eats from fire, a rogue, a deceiver, a crooked person,
and one who is devoid of devotion, faith, compassion, tranquility, and righteous conduct.
It causes laughter among parents, teachers, the wise, and great beings;
it is loathsome regarding family property and the like, and it treats service to the guru with pride.

O Mistress of the Family, the Guru should abandon a disciple who is a woman, who is wicked, who has fallen from his commitments, who is suspicious of his teacher, or who is possessed of such other defects as these.
If, out of affection or even greed, he should accept [a disciple] or initiate him,
then a curse from the deity will fall upon that guru and his disciple.
In the Meru Tantra.
Having bestowed initiation out of greed, one indeed incurs the curse of the deities;
likewise:

Initiation is indeed fruitless for one who is a disciple of another, belongs to a wicked lineage, is a rogue, fancies himself a scholar, hates women, has fallen from his observances, or is physically deformed.
In the Kulārṇava:
Therefore, one should never accept such a disciple under any circumstances;
if one accepts him out of delusion, the preceptor becomes tainted by that person's sins.
Just as a minister [is affected by] the sin of a king, and a wife by that committed by her husband,
so too does the sin committed by a disciple generally affect the teacher as well.
The teacher should examine the disciple through either knowledge or action for a year, or half of that, or half of that again, or half of that once more.

He should cause those of superior status to perform inferior tasks and those of low status to perform superior tasks, by means of bestowing life or wealth, and through commands given equally to both superiors and inferiors.
By means of words that pierce his vital points, by deceptions, by family intrigues,
by partialities and by indifference, and by many other such means, he assailed him again and again.
Whether drawn out or even tormented, he who does not succumb to despair,
always reflecting with joy, "The Guru shows compassion," [is one who attains success].
O beloved, [this applies] also during the remembrance of the glorious Guru, as well as in his glorification, salutation, service, invocation, sending forth, seeking, and searching.
O Īśvarī, those for whom there is supreme bliss, as well as transformations of the voice, eyes, and so forth,
shall possess knowledge of the three and also attain perfection in mantra.
And having understood this capacity to convey [the meaning], the disciple shall become [a teacher] and not otherwise;
those who are fit at the beginning, middle, and end are those who have attained power.
O Goddess, disciples are proclaimed to be of three types: inferior, middling, and superior.
O Goddess, those who speak for the sake of initiation must first possess devotion.
Furthermore, those whose [spiritual] states have been lost are said to be "beginners" (ādiyogya);
they have received initiation and the observances (samaya), yet they are devoid of knowledge and realization (jñāna-vijñāna).
Therefore, those whose vigor has been destroyed are known as "intermediately fit" (madhyayogya);
at first they are devoid of devotion, and in the middle stage devotion may or may not exist.
In the beginning there may be abundant devotion, but from this [practice], one becomes fit in the end.
In the Nārāyaṇīya [section].
One who performs service to the teacher through the actions of mind, speech, and body,
being pure in disposition and possessed of great enthusiasm, is known as a Buddhist disciple.
The son is one who acts contrary to the instruction, as is Vasuda;
likewise, the minister is one who, having given a different counsel, adopts another counsel.
And it is said elsewhere:
"Knowledge is acquired through service to the teacher, or by means of abundant wealth, or else through knowledge;
it is not attained in a fourth way."
In the Prapañcasāra.
He who is constantly attentive with body, speech, and mind for a period of three, two, or one year, being self-restrained in thought, should be accepted along with his family.
In the Meru Tantra.
If both the teacher and the disciple, out of delusion, give and receive instruction without examining one another, they shall attain the state of a piśāca.
In the Maṇtramuktāvalī:
Within just three years, there will be mutual understanding of their knowledge;
whether one is a teacher or a disciple, it shall not be otherwise—this is the certain conclusion.
In the Meru Tantra.
When both disciple and teacher are endowed with devotion and faith and possess all the requisite characteristics,
then every path bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation at that very moment.
And a disciple, having received the mantra from a true guru, should not abandon it.
"According to the statement in the Liṅgāgama: 'A disciple who abandons his guru shall certainly be subject to penance.'"
Obtaining a mantra from an unworthy teacher and even its subsequent abandonment is the meaning of the scriptures.
This has been stated in the Merutantra:
How can a false guru, who is himself lost, deliver another?
In the meantime.
If, by chance, knowledge is obtained from a person of noble birth who is a master of the horse,
one should nevertheless seek knowledge again from a Kaulika Brahmin.
In the Devyāgama.
Whoever undertakes the initiation of a sacrificial animal will certainly experience physical suffering;
of this there is no doubt, and it may even happen to his kinsmen.
Having written that mantra on a banyan leaf, one should cast it into a stream;
or, having taken refuge in a true guru, one should receive the consecrated mantra.
In the Śrīkulārṇava:

O Goddess, having obtained a glorious Guru endowed with the proper characteristics— who is the cause for cutting through doubt— one should not seek another guru once the joy of knowledge has been attained.
Having approached a teacher who is ignorant and unable to sever one's doubts, a disciple who goes to another teacher is not defiled by the faults of that [first] teacher.
Also in the Śaiva Āgama:
There are many gurus who know the practice of evil mantras; however, one who knows the mantras declared in the Vedas, Āgamas, and Śāstras is rare on this earth.
One who knows the world may uplift a fool, but a fool cannot uplift another fool;
for can a boat that is itself crossing a stone ever cause that stone to cross?
Also in the Merutantra and in the Shaiva Agama.
Just as a bee, greedy for honey, goes from flower to another flower,
so too a disciple, greedy for knowledge, should go from one teacher to another teacher.
Thus, when there is a mutual contradiction among the statements of mantras, the method taught by one's own guru alone should be adopted.
That has been stated in that very same place.
Many paths have been proclaimed by the wise in the scriptures of mantra;
having taken recourse to the opinion of one's own guru, the auspicious work should be performed, and not otherwise.
In the Meru Tantra.
One should never interrupt the Kaula tradition;
as long as the tradition exists, so long shall the state of a Yoginī endure—this is the characteristic of a disciple.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Kulamuktikallolinī composed by Śrī Ādyānanda.
Now follows the procedure for initiation (*dīkṣā*), according to the *Merutantra*.
The Veda does not exist apart from the Praṇava, and a mantra is that which is endowed with the Veda;
therefore, the mantra is considered superior to the Veda, while the Āgama is known as the limb (aṅga) of the Veda.
Rites such as subjugation and attraction, which bestow both visible and invisible fruits,
are all accomplished through the Veda by means of planetary sacrifices and other rituals.
There is no sacrifice without the Veda, nor are the Vedas devoid of sacrifice;
therefore, the mantra is superior to the Veda, yet the mantra does not exist apart from the Veda.
According to this statement, Śūdras have no entitlement to the use of mantras.
In the Mahākapila Pañcarātra.
Śūdras have no entitlement to mantras; for them, there is only the supreme discipline.
Due to the absence of mantras, every ritual act is indeed performed without a mantra.
In the Śātātapasaṃhitā:
For as many syllables as one might cause a mantra to be imparted to a woman or a Śūdra, for that many instances of killing a Brahmin would they incur; so Prajāpati himself has declared.
In the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa: "Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are pure and stainless— to them indeed the mantras should be given, but not to those of mixed caste."
In the Meru Tantra:
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those born of the Paulastya lineage—
these are known as the five kinds of men, and they may be given [in marriage] in the direct order of castes (anuloma).
9b) In the Devīyāmala:
If a twice-born man imparts a mantra joined with the *svāhā* and the *praṇava* to a Śūdra,
the Śūdra shall go to hell and the Brāhmaṇa shall attain the state of a Śūdra.
In the Brahmapurāṇa.
The Vedic or the mixed [path] is prescribed for the Brahmins and others;
the Tantric path is proclaimed even for a Śūdra who is devoted to a Brahmin.
Women and even Śūdras should perform the worship of Viṣṇu with faith according to the path taught in their own scriptures, keeping their husband in their hearts.
For women who are devoted to the pleasure of their husbands, there exists an even greater [merit] in the worship of Viṣṇu and other such acts; this is the eternal Vedic tradition.
A woman who is separated from her husband, yet auspicious and endowed with virtuous conduct,
may receive these mantras, provided she has the permission of her husband.
In the Maruta-tantra.
Śūdras have no entitlement to mantras; for them, there is only the supreme discipline.
One may impart mantras to a Śūdra only as far as [the syllables] belonging to their own caste.
For them, there would be the sin of killing a Brahmin; therefore, one should perform the consecration for him.
One should give [the offering] devoid of the word "svāhā" and the syllable "oṃ," and afterwards, the Tantric [rite].
Worship should be performed even by women and Śūdras according to the path taught in their own scriptures,
and they should perform it with those [mantras] praised therein, following the way prescribed by the Āgamas.
The son of a widow [may go] from his country [by his mother's will], and a maiden by her father’s command;
a woman has no independent authority, and a wife [goes] by her husband’s command.
The husband alone should initiate his wife, since he is always her guru;
for him as well, she is the object of worship and the means for all spiritual accomplishment through the intellect of the Divine.
In the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa:
Without one's own dharma, whatever [practice] there may be, such as the propitiation of deities and so forth,
will fall away in an instant like a palace built of sand.
In the Kulārṇava:
The son of a widow [may leave] the country, and the daughter by her father’s command;
for women and Śūdras, this mantra ending in "namaḥ" brings happiness.
Knowing this, O Mahāsena, one may initiate even Cāṇḍālas;
however, a Śūdra or women should never recite Vedic mantras.
"Or a Śaiva mantra ending in *namaḥ*, or a Vaiṣṇava one, is desired by the wise," so it is stated in the Yājñavalkya Saṃhitā.
And in the Merutantra:
Whether one is a Śaiva or a Vaiṣṇava, for women and Śūdras, the mantra should end with "namaḥ";
knowing it to be a name-mantra (nāma-mantra), one may initiate even a Caṇḍāla.
In the Śāradā [Tīkā]:
A Brāhmaṇa becomes qualified in one year; a Kṣatriya, O King, in two years;
a Vaiśya in three years; and a Śūdra in four years under a Guru.
One who is desirous of hearing is worthy of being accepted through initiation, sacrifice, vows, and so forth.
10a) In the *Tantrarāja*:
Having observed the fitness [of the candidates] for one, two, three, four, or five years,
according to their devotion, virtues, and [status within] the caste system or mixed castes, in due order.
In the Kulārṇava:
Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those born of Paulastya—
thus they are joined with five divisions.
In the Sautrāmaṇī Tantra and in the Meru Tantra.
The Māyā-bīja is for the Brāhmaṇa; the Śrī-bīja is remembered as being for the Kṣatriya;
the Kāma-bīja should belong to the Vaiśya; and the Vāgbhava is declared for the Śūdra.
The mantra known as Paulastya consists of four seed-syllables when [the prefix] is omitted;
for Brahmins it has four seed-syllables, while for Kṣatriyas it has three.
For Vaiśyas there are two seed-syllables, but for Śūdras there is only one seed-syllable.
In the Meru Tantra:
One of lower caste or lineage should bestow the mantra upon one of higher caste.
In the *Kulamūlāvatāra*.
The Goddess said:
Among the Śākta, Śāmbhava, and Saura [traditions], as well as among the Gāṇeśa and Vaiṣṇava [sects],
and especially for the Śaṅkaras belonging to the castes of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and so forth.
I wish to hear about the ritual procedure for the benefit of practitioners;
O Śaṅkara, tell me the specific mantras associated with each of those [procedures] and their respective divisions.
The Lord said:
Umāmaheśvara, Dakṣiṇāmūrti, Aghoraka,
Hayagrīva, Vārāha, and then the eight-syllable [mantra].
I wish to hear about the process of practice for the benefit of practitioners,
as well as which mantras belong to which specific categories.
Vāsudeva preceded by the Praṇava, as well as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa,
should be given to those of the three [twice-born] castes, but never to any other caste.
The Pāśupata, the Nārasiṃha, and likewise the Sudarśana [mantras] should be given to those of two castes, and never to any others whatsoever.
Whatever mantras of Agni there may be, as well as those of Sūrya,
and the mantras of Ghṛṇi beginning with "Tārā," these should be bestowed upon one who possesses the three castes.
The Śakti-mantras are in the Ānuṣṭubh meter, as is Vindhyavāsinī. Likewise...
Nīlasarasvatī should be bestowed upon the first letter;
likewise Mātaṅginī, Ugratārā, Kālikā, and Śyāmalā.
Chinnamastā and Vālā should be given in every painting;
likewise Tārā and the others, Gaṇeśa, and the one known as Haridrā.
It should not be disclosed among the three castes, and especially not among women;
[one should not disclose] the Praṇava, Māyā, Lakṣmī, Vāgbhava, or any other seed-syllable.
Combined with this seed-syllable, it should be given at the beginning of the coloring;
likewise, for the Kṣatriyas, one should utter Māyā, Lakṣmī, and Vāgbhava.
10b) Lakṣmī and Vāgbhava are indeed taught for the Vaiśya caste;
Vāgbhava and another seed-syllable are proclaimed for the Śūdras.
For the *saṃkaras*, it is praised [to recite] starting with the heart-mantra and ending with *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*.
In the Meru Tantra:
O Brahmin dwelling in the Vindhyas, those prescribed in the Kalpas and the Vedic ones should be given;
likewise, those known as Pāśupata should be given to both Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas.
The *Saudarśana* and *Nārasiṃha* [mantras] belong to Kārtavīrya and not to anyone else;
the *Dakṣiṇāmūrti* and *Aghora* [mantras] should be given even to those of the three [higher] castes.
The eight-syllable Hayagrīva, likewise Umāmāheśvara,
Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa, Astra, Devatāra, and Varāhaka.
The rays of Agni and Sūrya, the stars and other such lords of the hosts,
as well as Kālikā and Śyāmalā, should be assigned among all the castes.
Chinnamastā, Vālā, Mātaṅginī, Ugratārī, as well as the Yoginīs, Yakṣiṇīs, Traipura, Vaṭuka, and the others.
The Śāvaras and Pulastyas are not to be recited during the birth of a twice-born.
Now, the times for initiation (dīkṣā).
Among those, first are the months.
That has been stated in the Merutantra:
From Caitra onwards, the results are: initiation, suffering, consecration, the attainment of jewels, inferiority, death, destruction of kinsmen, and wickedness, respectively.
In sequence, [the results are]: increase of bliss, suffering, envy, destruction, and censure;
as well as poverty, accomplishment, knowledge, excellence, and happiness.

The destruction of knowledge and intellect, the attainment of gold, the increase of wisdom, prosperity, success, and excellence—these occur; one should avoid the intercalary month (malamāsa) and the waning period (kṣaya).
In the Śrīkaṇṭhasaṃhitā.
Initiation in the autumn season and in Vaiśākha yields the most excellent fruit;
it is also excellent in Mārgaśīrṣa and Phālguna, while in Jyeṣṭha it is merely mediocre.
In the month of Māgha it bestows auspiciousness, but in the month of Āṣāḍha it is malevolent;
in the month of Śrāvaṇa it is blissful, while in the months of Pauṣa and Bhādrapada it is censured.
In the Āgamakalpadruma.
In Caitra, initiation leads to suffering; in Vaiśākha, there is an accumulation of jewels;
in Jyeṣṭha, death occurs; and in Āṣāḍha, there is the destruction of kinsmen.
Prosperity will surely occur in Śrāvaṇa, while loss will occur in Bhādrapada; furthermore, there will be the destruction of subjects in Āśvina, as well as total inauspiciousness.
In Kārttika there shall be knowledge; indeed, in Mārgaśīrṣa there shall be happiness.
In Pauṣa there is the loss of knowledge, while in Māgha there is the increase of intelligence.
In Phālguna, there shall be complete success; one should avoid the intercalary month (malamāsa). Āṣāḍha is also stated by some to be suitable.
For example:
Beginning the recitation of mantras in the first month of Vaiśākha is extremely difficult to endure;
in Vaiśākha it bestows wealth, but in Jyeṣṭha it would bring about death.
In Āṣāḍha, it is for the attainment of a son; in Śrāvaṇa, it is considered to bestow auspiciousness;
in Bhādrapada, there is loss of knowledge, while likewise in [Āśvina], success is proclaimed.
In Āśvina there is the attainment of all perfections; in Kārttika it bestows the perfection of knowledge;
Mārgaśīrṣa shall be the bringer of auspiciousness; and Pauṣa is the producer of suffering.
In Māgha there is increase of intelligence, and in Phālguna there is subjugation of all.
In the Siddhāntaśekhara.
Initiation in the autumn season and in Vaiśākha yields the most excellent fruit;
initiation in Phālguna, Mārgaśīrṣa, and Jyeṣṭha is middling.
The months of Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, and Māgha are declared by the virtuous to be the least [auspicious];
while the month of Caitra, as well as Pauṣa and Bhādrapada, are censured.
Even during months that are censured.
The initiation prescribed for the time of [planetary] eclipse is auspicious.
In the Gautamīya Tantra.
The commencement of mantra practice in Caitra bestows all human goals;
in Vaiśākha there is the acquisition of jewels, but in Jyeṣṭha death is certain.
In Āṣāḍha there will be the loss of kinsmen; in Śrāvaṇa one will attain a full lifespan;
in Bhādrapada there will be the destruction of offspring; and in Āśvina there will be an accumulation of jewels.
In Kārttika there shall be success in mantra; likewise it shall be so in Mārgaśīrṣa.
In Pauṣa there shall be affliction from enemies, while in Māgha there is an increase in intelligence.

In the month of Phālguna, all desires shall be fulfilled; one should avoid the intercalary month (mala-māsa). Herein lies the procedure for Caitra, which is devoted to initiation into the Gopāla mantra.
In the Kālottara [Tantra].
The conjunction of autumn and winter is prescribed for the ritual procedure of initiation;
in their absence, the rainy season—excluding the month of Āṣāḍha—is likewise commended.
In the *Kriyākāṇḍaśeṣara*.
There should be no initiation on a festival day during the rainy season, nor in the months of Madhu and Pauṣa.
In the case of a cause.
A wise person should not perform initiation during the first half of the month of Āṣāḍha, nor in the months of Āṣāḍha or Mārgaśīrṣa; however, one may perform it in other months.
Thus concludes the determination of the months. Now follows the determination of the fortnights (pakṣa). In the Agastisaṃhitā:
Whether in the bright fortnight or the dark, initiation brings all auspiciousness;
as stated in the Kālottara:
It is said that those desiring liberation should worship during the dark fortnight, while those desiring devotion should do so constantly during the bright fortnight.
In the Maruta-tantra.
Kṛṣṇa bestows worldly enjoyment and liberation, while Śukla is remembered as the bestower of liberation alone;
for those who follow the Vāmācāra path, even the excellent Kṛṣṇa is not honored, and Śukla is considered mediocre.
11b) In the Gautamīya Tantra:
In the bright fortnight, the auspicious initiation (śubhadīkṣā) should take place; in the dark fortnight, it may occur until the fifth lunar day.
Thus it is stated in another Tantra.
In the bright fortnight there shall be the attainment of desired goals, while in the dark fortnight it bestows inauspicious results.
Likewise.
The dark fortnight becomes bright until the day of the eighth lunar day (kṛṣṇāṣṭamī).
Now follows the determination of the lunar days (tithi-nirṇaya).
In the Tantra:
On the first, second, and third lunar days one should remain pure;
on the fourth there would be loss of wealth, while on the fifth there is an increase of intelligence.
On the sixth day, one obtains the happiness of the destruction of ignorance; on the seventh day, [one obtains] wisdom;
on the eighth day, there may be a loss of intellect; and on the ninth day, there is the decay of the body.
On the tenth day there is royal fortune; on the eleventh one becomes pure;
on the twelfth all success shall be attained; on the thirteenth there is poverty.
On the fourteenth day of the waning moon, there is birth as an animal; on the new moon, there is loss of one's flesh and fat.
In the Meru Tantra:
The fruit of the tenth house is the destruction of intellect; the excellent accomplishments are to be known [in the others] in sequence.
Those who have fallen from their mothers, those who are not Gaurī, and those who have lost their lords of the year are miserable.
All mantras may be accomplished, yet they may never be accomplished;
there is prosperity and swift success, as well as foolishness and the destruction of the guru.
The destruction of dullness and the attainment of all-perfection shall be the fruit;
for the Lord of Men, Hari, the bright fortnight is best, never the dark.
There shall be success for all mantras, but for those who are not devotees of Śiva, there is great danger;
though it grants success especially, there is the loss of sons for one who deceives his father.
In the Vaiṣṇava [tradition].
At the end of a fortnight, there shall be an increase in merit; one should avoid recitation during a thunderstorm at twilight, an earthquake, or the falling of meteors.
One should avoid these and other days mentioned in the Śruti,
according to the *Sārasaṃgraha*.
The full moon day, the fifth, the second, the seventh,
as well as the thirteenth and the tenth, are praised for all ritual acts.
In the Vijayamālinī Tantra.
Furthermore, the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, the seventh, the thirteenth, the tenth,
and especially the twelfth of the bright fortnight [are auspicious].
In the *Maṃtrasārasaṃgraha*:
It may be performed on the third, the fifth, or especially the sixth;
it may also be performed on the twelfth or even on the thirteenth day.
In the Rudrayāmala:
On that fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, the initiatory rite (dīkṣākarma) bestows auspiciousness.
In the *Ratnāvalī*:
Excluding the fourth, ninth, sixth, eighth, fourteenth,
and full moon days, the remaining days are beneficial for those seeking liberation and those already liberated.
In the *Tattvasārasaṃhitā*:
Having carefully considered each respective lunar day (tithi), he should initiate those who are devoted to it on that very day.
12a) Likewise.
The full moon day is prescribed for Brahmā; the twelfth day for the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu);
the fourteenth day is prescribed for Śiva; and the thirteenth day is declared for Vāc.
The second is declared to belong to Śrī, the third to Pārvatī,
the fourth to Gaṇanātha, and the seventh is declared to belong to Bhānu.
Among the regular paths, O Pārvatī, the eighth and fourteenth lunar days are preeminent.
In the Nārada Pañcarātra.
Likewise, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, as well as during the transit of the sun.
In the Gautamīya Tantra.
On the twelfth day, which is entirely pure and auspicious, one must perform the rite;
that Dvādaśī is beloved by Kṛṣṇa and is the initiator of the initiation into Kṛṣṇa.
In the Kālottara [Tantra].
And those [days] which are free from the gaps of the day are known as the three days.
In another tantra:
The new moon day on a Monday, the fourteenth day on a Tuesday,
and the seventh day on a Sunday are equal to hundreds of solar eclipses.
Or rather, the determination of the [proper] time.
This has been stated in the Merutantra:
In sequence, the results of the doors are: intelligence, dullness, death, likewise appointment, loss of status, sons, acquisition of wealth, and death by drowning.
In the Gautamīya Tantra.
It should be performed on Sunday, Thursday, Saturday, or Monday, and under the auspices of Mercury or Venus;
Monday is recommended during the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), but it is prohibited during the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa).
This has been stated in the *Mantrasadbhāva*:
At the commencement of a mantra, [the results are] auspicious on Sundays and Fridays, especially on Mondays and Thursdays;
there is death on Saturdays, loss on Tuesdays, and everything is fruitless on Mondays.
In the Ratnāvalī:
For the sake of prosperity, one should avoid the days of Āditya (Sunday), Maṅgala (Tuesday), and Sauri (Saturday).
Now follows the determination of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras).
In the Gautamīya Tantra.
The three Uttaras, Rohiṇī, Revatī, Puṣya, Vāsava (Jyeṣṭhā),
Dhaniṣṭhā, Vāyu (Svātī), Mitra (Anurādhā), Aśvinī, Pitrya (Maghā), Tvāṣṭra (Citrā), and Nairṛta (Mūlā).
The asterisms Āiśa (Ārdrā), Vaiṣṇava (Śravaṇa), and Hastā are auspicious for initiation (dīkṣā).
Vāsava (Dhaniṣṭhā), Jyeṣṭhā, Vāyu (Svātī), Mitra (Anurādhā), Pitrya (Maghā), Tvāṣṭra (Citrā), Nairṛta (Mūla), Āiśa (Ārdrā), Vaiṣṇava (Śravaṇa), and [Hastā] are likewise favorable.
In the case of the cause.
Pauṣṇa, Rohiṇī, Āditya, Śravaṇa, and likewise Aśvinī;
Sāvitra, Svāṣṭra, Vāyavya, Maitra, and also Nairṛta.
Tiṣya, the three Uttarās, Ārdrā, and Saumya— these are the auspicious lunar mansions for the rite of initiation, O observer of excellent vows, provided they are the birth-stars of the disciple.
Revatī is for Pūṣan, Punarvasu for Āditya, Hasta for Savitṛ, and Mṛgaśiras for Soma.
In the Nīrataṃtra:
Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, Ārdrā, Dhaniṣṭhā, the three Uttarās,
Puṣya, and Śatabhiṣaj are declared to be the asterisms for initiation.
12b) In the Tantra:
In the third and the seventh, as well as in the sixteenth and the eighteenth,
and likewise in the nineteenth, the twenty-first, and the twenty-third.
One should avoid performing auspicious rites under twenty-five lunar mansions.
In the Meru Tantra:
In sequence, there will be the fruit of initiation, equanimity, as well as adversity,
mental distress, happiness from loved ones, worldly pleasure, and the accomplishments of mantra.
The success of cruel mantras, the accomplishments of the Śakti mantra,
all mantras, and the accomplishments of the serpent mantra are attained.
There shall be an end to [misfortune], royal punishment, mastery, and all perfections;
through the deity Rudra, there is complete accomplishment, swift success, and an auspicious mind.
Friendship with gods, total loss, quarrels, and great fear;
prosperity, disease, success through recitation, agitation, torment, and lordship.
The fruit of all accomplishments is attained through the sequence of the right or the left;
however, when the square is at the bottom, with the foot burnt, embraced, and smoked.
Thus.
In the Śaiva Āgama.
When the zodiac sign is facing downward and is auspicious, and especially when the moon is pure,
one should perform the contemplation of one's own name and so forth during the strength of the stars in the dark fortnight.
In the *Ratnāvalī*:
The first lunar day is Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and likewise the fifth is Kṛttikā;
the sixth is Pūrvabhādrapadā, and likewise the tenth is Rohiṇī.
When the Sarpa (Āśleṣā) constellation falls on the twelfth lunar day, and when the Trayodaśī (thirteenth) lunar day falls on the Aryaman (Pūrvaphalgunī) constellation—
these are known as Nakṣatra-luptās, and they bring destruction even to the gods.
Now follows the determination of yoga.
In the Meru Tantra.
Of the yogas beginning with Viṣkumbha.
The fruit shall be equal to the name.
The fruit of all yogas, beginning with Ānanda, is everywhere complete and unimpaired.
In the *Ratnāvalī*:
And the yogas are Prīti, Āyuṣmān, Saubhāgya, Sobhana, Śubha,
Sukarman, Dhṛti, Vṛddhi, Dhruva, Siddhi, and Harṣaṇa.
And Varīyas, Śiva, Siddha, Brahmā, and Indra are the sixteen.
In the Gautamīya Tantra.
In all auspicious conjunctions, initiation bestows every kind of merit.
Now follows the determination of the Karaṇas.
In the Gautamīya Tantra.
They declare the auspicious moments to be favorable for initiation, especially so;
however, one should specifically avoid those times marked by the Śakuni and other such omens.
And so it is stated in the Merutantra:
One should perform actions during the Karaṇa while avoiding Viṣṭi; success will then be swift.
All accomplishments are attained during the tail of Viṣṭi, and stability is achieved when it is fixed.
Now follows the determination of the ascendant (lagna).
In the *Sārasaṃgraha*:
The commencement of mantras and other rites in Aries bestows wealth and grain;
in Taurus, one meets death; and in Gemini, there is the loss of offspring.
In Cancer, there shall be success in all things; in Leo, the destruction of intelligence;
in Virgo, the constant bestowing of fortune; and in Libra, success in all endeavors.
In Scorpio, there shall be the accomplishment of all goals; in Sagittarius, there is the destruction of knowledge;
Capricorn is said to bestow sons; and Aquarius grants the abundance of wealth.
Pisces always bestows suffering; such, O beloved, is the fruit of the zodiac signs.
In the Meru Tantra.
Now, regarding the results of the ascendant (lagna): there will be wealth from the gods, grain, and prosperity;
or else there may be death, loss, and the destruction of cattle and offspring.
Sovereignty, divine beings, spiritual accomplishment, loss, intelligence, destruction,
jewels and the like, the attainment of fortune, wealth, grain, and various successes.
Complete success, majesty, loss, the destruction of wisdom,
the birth of a son, mastery of mantras, livestock, and abundant wealth.
For those born under the Vāmin [sign], there is constant suffering as well as loss;
for the Yavanas, the dual sign is auspicious, yet it is in many ways unfavorable for the Vāminas.
In the Śaiva Āgama.
The gift of Dharma at dawn brings [merit]; the *saṃgava* period bestows sovereignty;
at midday there shall be the attainment of all perfections; and in the evening it becomes middling.
However, the best of teachers have prohibited the imparting of mantras during the night.
In the Mṛta-tantra:

The [period] at dawn bestows dharma, the midday bestows sovereignty, the middle [period] bestows siddhi, and the afternoon brings about destruction; these are dawn, forenoon, midday, afternoon, and evening.
In the Gautamīya Tantra.

Every movable sign (cara-rāśi) should be avoided; in fixed signs (sthira-rāśi), it bestows happiness. A fixed ascendant (lagna) is auspicious for the Viṣṇu-mantra, while a movable one is auspicious for the Śiva-mantra.
An ascendant situated in two signs is praised in the Śakti-mantra.
Now begins the consideration of the strength of the planets.
By the followers of Gautama.

Malefic planets situated in the third, sixth, and eleventh houses, and benefic planets situated in the quadrants and trines, are auspicious for initiation; however, all [planets] occupying the mouth [the first house] cause total destruction.
In the Tantra.
The Moon situated in the third, eleventh, sixth, or tenth house is auspicious;
the Moon of birth is also declared to be auspicious, provided it is free from its natal asterism.
In the bright fortnight, the second, fifth, and likewise the ninth lunar days are auspicious;
even if joined with planets that are pure in their course, the Moon is favorable.
Even when situated in a neutral position, the Moon may become a giver of inauspicious results.
In the Merutantra:
Malefic planets situated in the three *ṣaḍāyas* (the sixth, eighth, and twelfth houses) and benefics situated in the angles (*kendras*) and trines (*trikoṇas*) [are auspicious].
All [planets] in the eighth house bestow death; [planets] in the twelfth cause loss of wealth, and in the sixth, disease.
Mantras should be received during the strength of the moon; otherwise, there may be excessive obstacles. Through accordance with the strength of the stars, the grace of the deity will arise.
In the Gautamīya [Vinaya].
The consecration of mantras is recommended on a day pure in its five limbs, during the rising of the moon and the sun, and likewise during the rising of Jupiter and Venus.
In the Vārāhī Tantra.
If Venus is increased by water during the day and Jupiter and the Sun are present,
then initiation is not permitted when [Venus] is in Aries, Scorpio, or Leo.
Likewise.
For a disciple, [this should be performed] on the birth-star, during a solar transit (saṃkrānti), at the equinoxes (viṣuva) or solstices (ayana),
on other auspicious conjunctions (puṇyayoga), or during lunar and solar eclipses.
On the five parvan days, on the Yugādi days, during the Su-vyatīpāta yoga, and on such days, initiation is declared to be auspicious; no further deliberation is required in this matter.
In the Yoginītantra.
Indeed, that purification of the month, lunar day, weekday,
and so forth which has been taught should be understood by the best of practitioners as pertaining specifically to mantra initiation (mantradīkṣā).
In the case of the initiation into knowledge (vidyā-dīkṣā), there is no purification of the lunar day, month, or other such factors;
whenever there is a desire, then the initiation occurs according to the command of the Guru.
Now follows the refutation.
In the *Kriyākāṇḍaśekhara*.
The rules regarding time and other factors for one desiring liberation have been prescribed;
all those [other times] are censured, while these are praised for the sake of liberation.
In the Tantra:
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, at the birth of the disciple, during the transit of Capricorn,
and at the time of the Guru’s compassion— by these [occasions], the constellations and other such factors are not required for initiation.
In the Rudrayāmala.

When performing a mantra-initiation during the eclipses of the sun or moon at the seven sacred fords (saptatīrtha), or on the festivals of Tantudāma and Parvaṇi, one need not purify the month, the lunar mansion, or the day.
In the Yoginītantra.
During the sun's transit (saṃkrānti) and likewise during a solar eclipse,
one should never consider any [inauspicious] factor such as the ascendant (lagna) or the like.
Especially on the Mahāṣṭamī day, for the sake of attaining the fulfillment of one's desires for wealth.
In the Agastisaṃhitā:
At the time of a solar eclipse, however, nothing else should be sought;
there is nothing whatsoever equal to the time of a solar eclipse.
In that regard, whatever is performed there shall all yield infinite fruit;
on the occasion of a solar eclipse, there is no need for purification based on the month, lunar day, or weekday.

Those who were born facing the enemy in battle and were thus oppressed and repeatedly defeated in combat— he alone was the lord of creatures (Prajāpati).
At the end of a thousand divine years, the gods came for refuge to Viṣṇu, to me, and to Pārvatī; that was also heard by the lord of the Daityas.
Desirous of fighting and urged by Nārada, he rushed forward and said:
"A war has been waged by me against you for five years."
Then the Daitya, intoxicated with pride and deluded by Viṣṇu’s Māyā, being pleased, spoke these words: "Choose, choose!"
Neither by Indra nor by Kuvera was this feat of water-making performed for me;
rather, that battle was fought by you alone, even while wearing matted locks, together with your army.
This has been accomplished by him who has Viṣṇu as his companion and who bears Pārvatī as half of his body;
therefore, I, the Supreme Lord of the three worlds, have attained satisfaction.
"I have nothing that cannot be given; let all three of you go as you wish.
Having heard these words of his, Śiva and Pārvatī were urged by the Earth.
Hari said: "O most fortunate lord of the Daityas, there is no one equal to you. Make your threefold promise true; then a boon shall be granted by me."
"Even for Śiva and Pārvatī there is but one [consort], never another.
Thus the Daitya spoke three times, and then Viṣṇu questioned him.
"Tell me that means by which death may come to you quickly.
Having understood this to be a ruse of Viṣṇu, the lord of the Daityas replied:
All must inevitably go into the mouth of Death;
nevertheless, he who goes for the sake of his own vow lives.
However, there is one person for whom I have not yet performed such service;
having shown him the path, let this body be cast down.
And at that time, O gods, an incorporeal voice spoke:
"O Lord of Daityas, do not grieve; your birth from the earth shall come to pass."
Dissolve yourself right there; listen to a boon for the sake of your satisfaction:
those castes who shall build new houses for their own enjoyment [shall prosper].
There, however, except for Utsava, those beginning with Kālakarṇī— the female servants— and those beginning with Vināyaka were afflicted by various miseries.
"The servants shall cause him pain"—such is the command of the Supreme Lord.
Having heard these words, he too dug a pit, a great cavern.
Then he entered [the cave], which had been filled with earth and stones by the gods who,
fearing his resurgence, had previously been defeated by him.
Above that, however, fifty-three [deities] are striving to establish their abodes;
therefore, they must certainly be worshipped by those who desire the happiness of domestic life.
That has been stated in that very same place:
When the pavilion has been thus prepared, one should commence the worship of Vāstu;
this must also be done for a new house, otherwise there will be a great calamity.
That is declared to be of two kinds: Smārta and Tāntrika;
O gods, listen to its procedure according to the Vāma and Dakṣiṇa paths.
One should perform the invocation and worship of Vāstoṣpati with the Vedic mantra: "In a stone or in an image, I recognize Vāstoṣpati."
Somaśambhu.
In acts of worship, one should remember [the deity] with hands folded or extended upward;
