The knees and elbows are in the direction of Vāyu, the feet in the direction of Agni,
the two soles of the feet in the direction of the Ancestors (Pitṛs), the head in the direction of Rudra, and the heart in the direction of Añjali.
Thus ends the section on meditative concentration.
Having performed the worship of others with their respective name-mantras, one should complete [the rite];
in the southwest corner of the house, one should fashion an auspicious square shape.
Having made the ground level and the altar free from husks,
the wise one should draw [the design] there, measuring one cubit in width and length.
The wheel consists of eighty-one squares; the deities of the Veda reside therein.
One should first worship Brahmā in the nine central cells.
One should place Apavatsa in the northeast, Prāgartryastra in the three compartments, Savitṛ in the southeast, and Vivasvat in the western rows.
One should place Indra in the southwestern quarter, Mitra in the three western directions,
Rājayakṣmāṇa in the northwest, and Sumeru in the three northern directions.
In the Vedic squares (vedakoṣṭhas), starting from Vaiśānī and the Īśa corner, the deities are Śikhin, Parjanya, and Āpa; then Diti is in the two squares to the east of Prākeṣṭha.
These five deities are to be known in succession from the right-hand path:
Jayanta, Indra, Sūrya, Satya, and Bhṛśa, located in the southeast corner (āgneya-koṇaka).
Likewise, Antarikṣa, Vāta, Pūṣan, and Sāvitṛ—these four gods belong to Īśāna; thereafter, in the southern pentad, [are the others].
In the pair [of directions], Vitatha, Vṛhatkṣata, Yama, Gandharva, and Bhṛṅgarāja are situated in the four squares starting from the southwest (Nairṛtī). 17a)
From Īśānī [the northeast] come Jayanṛpa, Pitṛda, and Vārika;
thereafter, O Vika, there are five: Sugrīva and Puṣpadantaka.
Varuṇa, Asura, and Śeṣa are in the northwest;
Īśa and Ahi are in the northeast; and Rudra, Pāpayakṣmī, and Roga are in the five [directions] of the north.
Mukhya, Bhallāṭa, Soma, Bhujaga, and likewise Āditi—
these forty-five deities should be worshipped with devotion using arghya.
Now, according to the Tantric path, likewise on the sixty-four squares,
one should worship Brahmā in the center after drawing two lines across the two corners.
In the four squares, beginning with the one to the east of that, in each pair of squares,
[one should place] Āryaka, Vivasvat, Mitra, and the other, Mahīdhara.
Sāvitra, Savitṛ, Śakra, Indrajit, Rudra, Tatjaya,
Apāya, and Vatsaka— these are the Śaivyas in the two half-cells of the southeast corner.
Śarva, Guha, Āryamāṇa, Jaṃbhaka, Pilipicchaka,
Carakī, Vidārī, and Pūtanā— these two groups are in the east.
Īśāna, Parjanya, Jayanta, Śakra, Bhāskara, Satya, Vṛṣa, and Antarikṣa are, in order, those who reside in the chambers of the eastern quarter.
Agni, Pūṣan, Vitatha, Yama, Gṛharakṣaka,
Gandharva, and Bhṛṅgarāja are situated in the southern direction.
And likewise, at the beginning, Nirṛti, Vārika, Sugrīvaka, Varuṇa,
Puṣpadanta, Asura, and the two known as Soṣa and Rogaka.
Then, in the west or the north, Vāyu and the Nāga are the principal deities; beyond them are those named Soma, Bhalla, Gargala, Aditi, and Diti in the north.
The Brahmā-place [is marked] with red colors, the cardinal directions with yellow, and the intermediate directions with white;
then the cardinal directions with green and the intermediate directions with black colors.
A reddish enclosure should be made so that the mandala becomes beautiful;
it should be prepared with rice, mung beans, and barley, sequentially soaked in honey, ghee, and milk.
One should offer one hundred and eight, or twenty-one,
oblations for each of those substances with their respective mantras, and likewise with milk-rice (pāyasa).
And one should offer them an oblation consisting of milk-rice accompanied by various side dishes, mixed with sugar and combined with milk,
plantains, honey-cakes, and other such items.
Thus, when the sun has entered Leo, on the full moon day of every year,
whoever performs the worship of Vāstu in pavilions within his own home;
There shall be no untimely death, disease, or afflictions caused by *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and the like;
nor shall there be suffering from snakes, mutual strife, or other such inauspicious things.
17b) Possessing abundance of sons, grandsons, wealth, health, cattle, and female slaves,
he lives long in that house, free from disease, victorious, and renowned.
Everywhere in the royal palaces, as well as in the house of the queen,
in the dwellings of the ministers and the commanders of the army, and likewise in the city;
The preceptor should perform this every year for the sake of the aforementioned accomplishment;
otherwise, if it is not done, there will be constant suffering as a result of the contrary forms [of obstacles].
For the Bhairavas, the Kṣetrapālas, and especially for the Yoginīs,
an offering (bali) should be made by those of the left-hand path (vāmācāra) using buffaloes or even cocks.
When propitiated with offerings on the left, the deities become hungry;
they desire the bali offering, and if it is deficient, it destroys the practitioner.
Intoxicated by liquor and meat, they are impelled by their past karma;
they may occasionally desire what is auspicious, and therefore the virtuous do not turn away from them.
Their worship is performed because they fall nearby;
whether it be auspicious or otherwise, it is as stated in the scriptures and among the people.
As long as a person does not consume liquor and meat, they remain free from greed;
once that has been consumed, their mind becomes intent upon it—where then is recitation, and where is the deity?
He who, through the renunciation of liquor, meat, and so forth, or through their consumption, appears identical in form [to others], is a perfected one (siddha); otherwise, he is a sinner.

Priyaṅgu, śyāmāka, sesame, mustard, and śāli rice; or mudga, āḍhakī, suriṣya, or khalva beans—these are proclaimed as the varieties of māṣa.
One should scatter the offerings first in the vessel of Brahmā, then in that of Viṣṇu,
and then in that of Śiva, accompanied by the five musical instruments and preceded by the chanting of the Vedas.
Then, having sprinkled [the image] with turmeric water, one should cover it with cloths;
furthermore, one should offer an oblation at both twilights and at midnight.
Following the path instructed by the guru, one who is foremost among the three [classes] should duly offer oblations for nine days, dedicating each to its respective deity.
On the first day, rice mixed with saliva and barley flour,
combined with turmeric powder, is considered this offering for the spirits (bhūtas).
Thus, on the second day, [offerings] of sesame and rice are for the ancestors;
on the third, parched grain flour and parched rice mixed with curd are for the yakṣas.
One should joyfully offer to the Nāgas a libation of parched grain mixed with coconut water, and on the fifth day, an offering of lotuses and unbroken rice grains (akṣata) to Brahmā.
On the sixth day, rice mixed with cakes is recommended for Śiva;
on the seventh day, one should offer rice with jaggery to Viṣṇu.
On the eighth day for Viṣṇu, an offering of milk is prescribed;
on the ninth day, an offering of kṛśara-rice is highly commended for Viṣṇu alone.
On the left-hand path, one should offer oblations (bali) to the mandala in the four directions;
O gods, at the station of Brahmā, a Vetāla is present, and a ram is his offering.
In the place of Viṣṇu, Bhairavī should be present; her offering (bali) is considered to be a goat.
But Bhairava, in the place of Śiva, desires an offering of buffalo.
In that context, liquor made from molasses, honey, and flour are considered *surā* in their respective order;
fish, meat, and intoxicants are prescribed as an offering (*bali*) for the spirits (*bhūtas*).
To the ancestors, an offering of meat with liquor; to the yakṣas, chicken and honey;
and to the nāgas, frogs and mice—this is the offering on the left-hand path.
When nine days have passed in this manner, one should examine:
from what has [the result] properly arisen, what has been lost, and what is intermediate?
If the [mantra] rises perfectly, success is attained; if it is blunted, one encounters obstacles.
If it has been eaten by insects or is decayed by fruit, its placement results in total destruction.

Success is to be known through *priyaṅgu* flowers; through *śyāmāka* grains, there shall be happiness with women; through sesame seeds, the delight of honored people; and through mustard seeds, imprisonment.
O Lord, through *śālī* rice there is superiority over all; may there be grace toward *mudga* beans.
Through *āḍhakī* there are four quarters, as are *niṣpāva* beans in the field or the house.
Success in virtuous deeds comes from *khalva* [beans], and peace from enemies through *māṣa* [beans];
all results are achieved when they rise evenly on the left side, but otherwise, there is a fall.
Thus concludes the section on the conjunctions of the site.
Now, the means for knowing the directions, such as the east, for the purpose of constructing the mandala, is stated in the *Tantrarāja*:
Having ascertained the directions by the movement of the sun, the preceptor should perform his rites;
for due to irregularities in the site, the cardinal points may not be correctly known.
Having fixed a stake there, one should determine the position of Indra’s direction;
listen as I explain, according to the rule, how to fully understand its movement and so forth.
Having fashioned a circle on a level ground by means of circumambulation,
one should place a twelve-finger-long gnomon upon a point at its center.
Due to the two [shadow] tips at the eastern and western circles,
one should mark them on both sides of that [point], having done so from the forenoon and afternoon.
19a) Having again drawn two circles with their own equal radii,
[one] situated in the middle and [the other] in the south and north, produced by the junction of those two;
One should place a thread in the middle of the two junctions, facing east and west;
then, using the tips of those [threads], one should determine the directions starting from the east, extending to the south and north.
Also in the Kriyāsāra:
Having leveled the ground there,
one should place a gnomon made of khadira wood, twelve finger-breadths in height and one cubit in circumference.
In the absence of that, the wise man should install a sacrificial tree there;
the point where its shadow touches is considered the middle point between them.
One should extend the thread transversely; the center is known as south-north.
From the extension of four threads, the other four corners of the city are formed.
Thus has the thorough knowledge of the directions been clearly explained;
having understood this, the wise practitioner should properly construct the pavilions and other structures.
But in the Merutantra, however:
When the ground has been leveled in this manner, one should perform the preliminary ritual for the site;
having taken the measuring lines, the compass, and the stakes, one should proceed during the night.
A tube joined at both ends with two plummets is used for piercing the pole star;
one should draw a circle from the center between the southern and northern directions.
Within the circle, using that compass (karkaṭaka), one should draw a line between the two points;
from that, one should form a bow, and then one should stretch the bow-string once more.
In this manner, there are six bows there, and the lotus becomes six finger-breadths [in width].
Having made three [bends] each in the north and south from the middle of the petals—
That long line which is drawn shall be designated as east-west;
[it is established] between the south and west, and between the north and east, situated above.
The string occupying the half of one bow would be the Īśānī (northeast) and the Rākṣasī (southeast);
likewise, for the other two bows, they would be the Āgneyī (southeast) and the Vāyavī (northwest).
The threads situated at the intermediate directions are equal and extend outward;
having drawn them outward as desired, one should drive stakes into the ground there.
Now, the pavilion: it is of three kinds.
Due to the distinction between superior, inferior, and middling.
In the Meru Tantra:
Having first worshipped Gaṇeśa, the wise man should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited;
thereafter, he should construct an auspicious pavilion with the five sounds.
In the rite of family initiation (kuladīkṣā), one should construct a pavilion measuring twenty cubits,
so that there may be the full immersion (samāveśa) of wine, meat, and women.
In the Siddhānta and the Vāmamārga, the sacrificial pavilion (maṇḍapa) has eight pillars and ten doors;
because the fire-pits (kuṇḍas) there are few, even though there are five [pits], that [pavilion] remains the same.
In the Vedic tradition, when there is an abundance of ritual materials, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be sixteen cubits; however,
when the materials are few, it should be one cubit in size.
To the south, in the *bahusāmagrī* configuration, the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) should be ten cubits;
in the *alpā* configuration, it should be nine cubits, which is always suitable for Vaiśyas.
For Śūdras it should be seven cubits, but for those of mixed castes (saṃkara) it should be five;
this measurement of pavilions (maṇḍapa), hidden in all the Tantras, has thus been declared.
This has been stated in the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṃgraha*:
This [first] is very small, measuring twelve thousand; from there, it increases successively by two [thousand] each time.
Or one who is honored by Soma, or one who has made a mandala.
The remaining pavilions should be auspicious, increasing by two cubits each.
Also in the Mahākapila Pañcarātra:
Starting from twelve cubits and increasing by two cubits at a time,
one should thus perform the purification of the ground and construct the sacrificial pavilion as follows.
"Nine cubits, five cubits, or three cubits, according to one's inclination," because it is stated thus in the Gautamīya Tantra.
By the phrase "nine cubits or five cubits," a fourteen-cubit pavilion is indicated; and by the phrase "nine cubits or three cubits," a twelve-cubit pavilion is indicated. Likewise:
"The distance between the left [shoulders] is five, seven, or nine cubits," as stated also in the Śāradā-tantra.
By the phrase "with five and seven," a maṇḍala of twelve cubits is described; by "with five and nine," one of fourteen cubits; and by "with seven and nine," one of sixteen cubits.
The measurement in finger-breadths is as stated in the Merutantra.
In whatever place and at whatever time barley grows, according to that [measurement],
one *aṅgula* for those twice-born men shall be defined as the measure of eight grains of that [barley].
For Śūdras, it should be equal to their own stomachs; likewise for those beginning with Karāla, it should be measured by liquids.
For non-Vedic Brāhmaṇas and others, it should consist of that same number of śāli rice grains.
Where the agent himself is present, this is the authority; otherwise, it is different:
[the measurement] is the middle phalanx of the middle finger of the teacher’s right hand.
The long interval between two joints (parvan) is declared to be one mātrā-aṅgula;
by this measure, the height of the image as well as that of the temple and so forth is constructed.
The altar, the pedestal, the palanquin, the chariot, and so forth, should be made according to those same proportions.
Thus it has been stated in that very [work]:
One should know that the measure called "finger-breadth obtained from the body" (dehalabdha-aṅgula) is that very same [unit];
furthermore, twenty-four of these finger-breadths shall constitute one cubit (hasta).
By this [method], one should fashion the limbs and the measurement of the image for both men and women; thus it has been revealed.
Likewise.

"Then one should construct a pavilion with a smooth altar measuring exactly seven immovable [units] in length and two arms [in width]," as stated in the *Kramadīpikā*. Here, "seven immovables" refers to seven [units], and "two arms" refers to two; thus, [the total length is] fourteen.

The meaning is that it should be measured by those [nine] cubits; for according to the literal sense of the scripture, eight sacrificial pits and an altar would be impossible for the officiating priests to perform their duties and so forth. As for the statement from the *Tantrarāja*: "One should construct a pavilion for the performance of the King's fire-oblations, consecrations, and other rites, measuring nine cubits in both width and length."
That [term] refers to the pavilion used for rituals other than initiation; it is stated in that same sense in the first verse of both the Siddhāntaśekhara and the Merutantra.
The ground for the pavilion is said to be one cubit high from the level of the earth.
In the Mahākapila-pañcarātra, however:
It is stated that the height should be one cubit, perfectly level, and very beautiful.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
It should be provided with sixteen pillars, four of which are to be placed in the center;
they should be eight cubits in height, with twelve positioned around them.
Those auspicious officiating priests (ṛtvij) should be five cubits in height and free from defects;
the most proficient knower of the tantras should mark out a fifth part of that on the ground by means of drawing lines.
One should cover it on all sides with coconut leaves or bamboo.
In the Meru Tantra.
One should further cover it with coconut leaves and bamboo mats,
so that the wind, the rustling sound, the trees, and so forth do not reach the interior of the house.
Regarding the phrase "eight cubits" and so forth: this refers specifically to the sixteen-cubit pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).

According to the *Pañcarātra* scripture, "one should likewise extend them, provided with crests and raised above the pavilion by the number of the Vedas," the placement of the pillars—whether in the center or on the outside—should be performed in the order starting from the southeast (*āgneya*) and so on.

"Because of the scriptural statement: 'The commencement [of the rite] consists of the raising of the pillar, the laying of the foundation stone, the application of the measuring line, the ritual peg, the digging, and the consecration of the pit; this is the domain of the fire.'"
From the Siddhāntaśekhara.
In the center there should be a group of four pillars, and in their midst, an excellent altar.
In the Merutantra:
The pillars at the corners of the altar-platform (vedikā) should be raised to half the height of the pavilion (maṇḍapa) on the outside;
one should place the fifth part upon the ground according to the thread-measurements for the sake of fullness.
One should fashion the shape of a water-pot (kalaśa) at the summit;
the altar (vedī) should be equal in length and height to that [base], with joints formed by nine compartments.
One should place the pillars at one-third of the length of the pavilion.
In that interval.
One should place pillars representing the Vedas at the corners of the altar.
In the *Pañcarātra*.
One should make the pillars firm, straight, and equal, fashioned from heartwood.
In the Kriyāsāra:
For the work of erecting pillars, one should use sacrificial wood, bamboo, or betel-nut trees;
or other pure trees may be used, but never any other species of plant.
20b) A house-post that is itself dry, crooked, ancient,
and produced from inauspicious ground must be abandoned in the work of erecting pillars.
In the case of the middle and lowest [types of] buildings, the measurement of the twelve pillars should not be calculated by the rule of three;
for it is stated in the *Merutantra* of the *Vāstuśāstra*: "Five-fifths [of the height] should be placed on the ground; this is the rule common to all."

Furthermore, according to the statement in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, "The digging for all [pillars] is declared by Śiva to be at the fifth part," the excavation for all pillars of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) is indeed at the fifth part. The phrase "with coconut leaves" and so forth is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); [the area] should be well-covered with mats, while the Vijayā and other [pillars] are [treated accordingly].
Or rather, they are called *maṇḍapas* because of the statement in the *Vāstuśāstra*.
In the Meru Tantra:
One should construct four doors for the pavilion in the directions previously established;
the threshold should indeed measure five parts, and there, O Brahmin, the door-panels and frames should be of equal height.
In the *Mantramuktāvalī*:
One should provide four doors in the cardinal directions, each occupying one-fifth [of the width].
In the *Pañcarātra*.
In the smallest [temple], the door should be two cubits; from there, it increases by four finger-breadths for the medium and the best [sizes]. One should thus install the beautiful door.
One should construct four archways (toraṇas) at the gates outside the pavilion according to the measurement of a cubit; as it is said:
"And outside the gates of the pavilion, one should [construct them] in the sequence of the directions according to the measurement of the altar."
One should install an archway made from Plakṣa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, or Vaṭa wood.
In the Meru Tantra:
One should construct a beautiful threshold measuring two hands of eight finger-breadths each;
in the central pavilion, one should construct it measuring two hands of the [specific] finger-breadths required for the ritual.
In the Hīna [yoga], its height is two cubits, and its height is considered to be double that in the [subsequent] ones.
Somaśambhu.
Toranas made of Plakṣa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa wood should be constructed in order starting from the east; alternatively, there may be a reversal of the sequence at the beginning and end.
If one does not obtain [the desired result] from one, one should place it in all directions.
In the Siddhāntaśekhara.
If none of these are available, there should be a *śamī* tree;
in its absence, the heartwood of *jambu*, *khadira*, *sāra*, *tāla*, or *vaṭa* is prescribed for the archway (*toraṇa*).
In the Meru Tantra:
Having left a space of one cubit outside the eastern door from there,
[the area] for the best, middling, and lowest [types of temples] shall be seven, six, and five cubits respectively.
One should make the plank elevated, ten finger-breadths wide,
five finger-breadths thick, and of an irregular quadrangular shape.
On both sides of the door,
one should place two wooden planks, one *vitasti* high from the top of the lintel, in superior, middling, or inferior sizes as appropriate.
In the Mahākapila-pañcarātra.
21a) The gods are stationed in the form of archways within the sacrificial pavilion,
for the purpose of destroying obstacles and for the protection of the sacrifice.
One should place a Nyagrodha tree in the east, likewise an Udumbara in the south,
a Pippala in the west, and a Plakṣa in the north.
One should place the very beautiful Ṛgveda-mantras and so forth in the east;
and in the south, the one called Subhadra, with the mantra beginning "iṣe tvā."
One should place the one called Sukarma in the west with the Sāmaveda and so forth, using the mantra "śanno devī"; and one should place Suhotra in the north.
In the Meru-tantra:
In the two pavilions, according to their length, there are respectively two practitioners;
on the ground, they are two feet and two cubits [in width], totaling fifty [units].
One should bury it with the verse "Agnim īle" in the two side-chambers using Gāyatrī meters;
its interior cavity should have an extent equal to that [of the main chamber] and be constructed from wood of the same species.
One should drive stakes into the two uneven corners of the square and tie a garland of *darbha* grass; this is the procedure for the eastern gate.
Thus, at the southern gate, one should place a garland made of Plakṣa wood at that door with the mantra "iṣe tvā" and fasten it as previously described.
One should make this [seat] out of udumbara wood from the western door;
however, in a Vedic sacrifice, it should be made of plakṣa wood with the mantra "agna āyāhi."
One should perform it in this manner as previously described; likewise, one should place [the image] made of the vaṭa tree from the door in the northern direction with the mantra "śanno devī".
In the Śāradā-tantra: "At the gates, there should be archways (toraṇas) in sequence."
The height of the trunks of milk-exuding trees is recorded as being seven cubits each.
Its circumference is said to be ten finger-breadths in measure;
the measurement of the horizontal plank should be half the measurement of the pillar.
One should fashion tridents in the middle of the archway measuring one cubit;
according to the Vāstuśāstra, this is for the best type of pavilion, which measures seven cubits.
Their height is five cubits and their width is two cubits;
by increasing six finger-breadths and so forth, they reach seven cubits in the highest grade.

"Six finger-breadths, etc. means that by this, the measurement of the horizontal plank for the lower and upper types of pavilions is also stated according to the distinction of the pavilions: the space between the two pillars of the lower pavilion gate is two cubits; for the middle type, it is one cubit plus six finger-breadths; and for the superior type, it is two cubits plus twelve finger-breadths.
How is it that for those of medium size, whose height is stated to be five or seven cubits, a height of eight cubits is mentioned?
In the Meru Tantra:
Having made a hole in the middle of those upright wooden posts standing above and across,
one should fashion a beautiful archway from wood of the *jāti* species.
That has been stated in that very same place.
Other unblemished, straight timbers of a single species should be placed upon the pillars;
one should join them at the neck of the pillar.
In the absence of [specific] woods, woods of a single species are to be taken.
In the Piṅgalāmata:
It should be marked with a trident, and there should be twelve spokes at the top;
the central prong should be straight, while those on the two sides should be slightly curved.
When both of those have been declared equal, one should then plant a finger-breadth (aṅgula).
In the Meru Tantra.
In the Śaiva sacrifice, the trident [is placed] among the superior, middling, and inferior [vessels].
In the Kriyāsāra:
Having thus constructed the archway (toraṇa), one should install three upward-pointing spikes (ūrdhva-śūla);
the length of each spike shall be five aṅgulas, and its width shall be one-fourth of that.
For the remaining [deities], the increase is indeed two finger-breadths, starting from an increase of five finger-breadths.
In the Meru-tantra:
The central prong is indeed straight, while those on the two sides are slightly curved;
thus is Śūla-Gaṇapati, and Śivā and the others are considered to be like Śiva.
And this arrangement of the trident is used in the Gaṇapati, Śaiva, Śākta, and other systems; however, there is a specific variation for the Vaiṣṇava system in the Vāstu-śāstra.
On the head, with a twelfth part [of the measurement], one should place the conch, discus, mace, and lotus in sequence starting from the east; for these, the material should be excellent wood.
In the Meru Tantra:
A Vaiṣṇava, or even a Saura, should also install the conch, discus, mace, and lotus using one-twelfth part of the Vaiṣṇava [measure], placing them in sequence starting from the east.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
One should fasten banners in the various directions that possess a radiance equal to that of the world-protectors,
and one should adorn the pavilion with canopies, garlands of darbha grass, and other such ornaments.
In the *Pratiṣṭhāsārasaṃgraha*:
The colors, beginning with yellow (pitta) and red (rakta), are prescribed for banners five cubits in length;
they are considered to be joined with bamboo staffs measuring ten cubits.
With ten cubits [measuring] five times two; also elsewhere.
The banners should be made five cubits long, or optionally two cubits;
they may also be six or ten cubits, and one should place them in the eight directions.
In the Meru Tantra.
Then, in front of the pavilion, a bamboo pole ten cubits long above the ground and two cubits long along the ground shall be covered with a clean cloth.
The banner should be one cubit wide and five cubits long;
thereupon, one should draw the deity of the mantra, together with his weapons and his vehicle.
Having established the banner, which is equipped with a bell and a fly-whisk and adorned with the colors of the deities, one should subsequently arrange it throughout the ten directions.
The banners of the lords of the directions shall be half the measure of the flagstaff;
they should be of their respective colors and offered in their respective directions with the specific mantras prescribed in the Vedas.
And [the mantra] "trātāram indram" is yellow in color, located in the direction of Hari (the East).
In the south-eastern direction (Āgneyī), the goddess Piṅgalā is known by the mantra "agne varuṇa";
she is dark-complexioned and is remembered as being accompanied by Gaṇu and the mantra "paṃthām".
With the mantra "anutvaṃta," there is a smoke-colored [deity] in the southwest according to Manu;
with the mantra "tatvāyāmi brahmaṇā," there is a white-colored [deity] in the west.
The mantra "ā no miyudbhiḥ" is yellow in the north-western direction;
"vayaṃ soma vrata" is moon-colored in the northern direction.
One should worship him as Īśāna with the *śānti* mantra; he has a white banner.
Between Īśāna and the East, one should worship Śeṣa, who possesses a red banner.
In the southwest, in the middle, one should worship Vidhi, who bears a red banner.
In the Hayashirsha Pancaratra.
O Brahmin, in a pavilion devoid of a banner,
all worship, fire-offerings, and other rites— even those rich with recitation performed by the wise— would be in vain.
Just as the property of a landowner perishes without a protector,
and a temple perishes entirely without its banner, so too do the cruel ones known as the Viṣṇuthārīs,
the Kūṣmāṇḍas, and others [perish].
The gods accept the offerings and other gifts when they see that they have not been protected;
likewise, they do so upon seeing the banners of the god blazing with light within the pavilions.
All of them perish, just as darkness is dispelled when struck by the rays of the sun.
But in the Mruta-tantra:
On the path of the left (vāmamārga), a Vedic mantra is considered equal to the fall of a thunderbolt;
for Brahmins, the path of the left leads only to hell.
In the absence of mantras, one should recite name-mantras preceded by the Praṇava (Om) and ending with the word "Hṛd" on the southern path;
however, on the left path, they are to be recited without the Praṇava.
One should fasten a white canopy above the pavilion;
one should decorate it with flower garlands and the like, and encircle it with the [sacred] thread.
Having encircled the pillars with long garlands made from mango and *aśvattha* leaves, one should construct an altar in the center.
In the Siddhāntaśekhara.
It was adorned with canopies known as garlands of mango sprouts,
covered with various bamboo lattices, and embellished with pillars supporting the beams.
With fruitful plantain trunks, betel nuts, and coconuts;
with various kinds of fruits and foods, as well as mirrors and chowries.
One should cause the pavilion to be adorned, radiant with jewels and flowers.
In the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*.
One should decorate the pillars with mirrors, chowries, and bells, as well as with cloths,
water-pots, small jars, and stone bases provided with stands.

22b) In that regard, one water-pot (kalaśa) should be placed at each gateway arch (pratitoraṇa); two at each side of every door, and one at each corner. It is said regarding those [pots]: "The jars, provided with perfumes, flowers, and garments, should be placed upon them."
One should cast it out.
Upon those archways.
One should worship Dhruva, Dharā, Vāk, and Vighneśa among them; these [deities] are to be worshipped in order within the pitchers situated at the corners of the pavilion.
Amṛta, Durjaya, Siddhārtha, and likewise Maṅgala— these,
beginning with Śakra, are to be worshipped in the jars stationed at the gates with their respective supreme mantras.
Elsewhere as well.
One should place two jars each in the pavilion, at every door;
they should be filled with strained water and adorned with mango sprouts.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
In a field measuring one *taṇtrī* in extent, one should prepare a square altar (*vedi*) one *aratni* high for the sake of the mandala.
Also elsewhere.
Then, one should determine the cord for the pavilion as threefold;
from east and so forth in sequence, the altar in its center shall consist of one part.
In the Meru-tantra.
Having divided the pavilion into nine parts, there is an altar in its central portion.
Also in the Siddhāntaśekhara:
Having constructed a pavilion divided into nine sections, a central altar is prescribed;
it should be one cubit (*aratni*) in height at its center and one hand (*hasta*) high at its four corners. Prosperity is attained through three times the measure of two spans (*vitasti*).
O Śivā, two *aratnis* make one *hasta*, and two of those [make one *vyāma*].
Thus, by this statement from the *Tantrarāja*, the words "aratni" and "hasta" are declared to be synonyms.
In that very place, according to one part out of three parts.
And because it is stated: "One should construct an altar in the middle, measuring exactly one cubit."
In the Meru Tantra:
A lump made of unburnt bricks is one span in width.
Also in the Maṇtramuktāvalī:
A wise person desiring success should construct an altar resembling a mirror, either with bricks or with clay, having a height of one royal cubit (rājahasta).
Also in the Kriyāsāra:
Having divided the mandala into three parts, the middle part shall be the altar (vedikā);
its height should be one cubit, and it should be square and level.
In the Meru Tantra.
In the initiation of the left-hand path (vāmamārga), it has three edges; in the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice, it is conch-white.
A square altar with four corners bestows all fruits.

In the consecration of tanks and similar works, the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala, which resembles a lotus-leaf, is for kings; it is used for the consecration of those who possess the four auspicious qualities.
In the marriage rite, the altar of Śrīdhara is endowed with twenty corners;
however, in initiation according to the Vāmamārga, the concealed altar is triangular.
23a) Regarding the dimensions of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), the statement from the *Meru* text— "nine, seven, or five [parts] by means of hair-threads"— refers to the twice-born (*dvija*) and others.
Likewise, it is stated in the *Kriyāsāra*:
A woman whose ribs are prominent, whose waist is moist, whose eyes are harsh and unattractive, and who is either deficient or excessive in stature, destroys the work of the man who marries her.
It has been stated that there is a fault if the pavilions (maṇḍapas) are not otherwise [properly] situated.
In the *Kriyāsāra*:
If a pavilion is constructed with unmentioned proportions, or if it is crooked in shape,
or if it exceeds or falls short of the prescribed measurements, it brings about the destruction of the patron.
This beautiful, well-constructed, and harmonious pavilion, fashioned by the means of verbal roots, is pleasing to the mind and brings auspiciousness to the agent of the action.
In the Meru Tantra.
Or, having observed that the nose-arch is elevated by its constituent parts,
the pavilion is constructed so that there may be a complete integration of the materials and other elements.
Thus ends the examination of the pavilion.
Thus ends the second chapter in the Kulamuktikallolinī composed by Śrī Ādyānanda.
Now, regarding the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) on both the right and the left, it is stated in the Merutantra:
A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit is prescribed for up to one million recitations;
for every ten million recitations, one should increase the size by one cubit.
For Vedic rites, it is stated that the sacrificial pit for a crore-fold oblation should measure ten cubits.
It has also been stated in that very same place regarding those who possess [the breath].
The oblation of liquor, meat, and so forth is prescribed specifically in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa);
when the oblation measures fifty [units], it is performed with the forearm closed into a fist.
The measurement of the pit (kuṇḍa) should be one hundred cubits for a sacrifice of one hundred [oblations], it should be equal [to that] for a thousand;
it should be one cubit for ten thousand, and two cubits is prescribed for one hundred thousand.
It has also been stated in that very same place regarding those who possess [the breath] (vāmin).
The oblation of liquor, meat, and so forth is prescribed specifically in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa);
when the oblation amounts to fifty [units], the measure is a forearm with the fist closed.
The measurement of the pit (kuṇḍa) should be one hundred cubits for [the rite of] a hundred thousand;
it should be one thousand cubits for a million, and two thousand cubits is considered appropriate for ten million.

A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring four cubits is prescribed for one hundred thousand oblations, six cubits for one million, and eight cubits for ten million homas; such is the rule established by the wise.
Also in the tantra known as the Kirana:
In a homa of fifty [oblations], the measure should be one muṣṭi;
in a homa of a thousand or ten thousand, it should be one cubit or two cubits respectively.
For a homa of one hundred thousand oblations, Śaṅkara should be four cubits; for ten million oblations, he should be eight cubits; beyond that, one should not cause him to be made larger.
Likewise.
In the ritual procedure for a single pit (kuṇḍa), a square shape is prescribed;
this is especially for Brāhmaṇas, and it is also used for the rite of immobilization (stambhana) when facing the east.
23b) In the ritual procedure for nine pits, however, there is a vulva-shaped [pit] in the portion of the fire;
for the sake of enjoyment, or for the sake of leaves, it is like a square for the residents.
For Vaiśyas, in all rites, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should resemble a half-moon in the south;
for others, it is prescribed for the rite of killing, and is likewise desired in the four pits.
A triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the southwest is known to cause the destruction of enemies;
it brings about enmity and is especially prescribed for Śūdras.
One should have this performed in the northwestern direction, especially for the Śaṅkaras;
ghee is the primary substance for all Kṣatriyas in rites for peace.
In the west, however, that same rite grants success even for Buddhists and others;
it effects eradication in a hexagon and is especially distinguished for acts of destruction.
One should have this constructed in the northwest, especially for those of mixed caste;
in the north, for rites of nourishment, a lotus [mandala] which bestows joy as well as contentment.
In all ritual applications, this is considered to bring joy to others;
an eight-cornered [mandala] that grants liberation is thus prescribed in the northeast.
One shall obtain liberation from prison, as well as from disease, anxiety, and the like;
however, this procedure for the nine-pit arrangement applies specifically to the case of a ruined pit.
The ninth [square] should be a quadrangle in the interval between the east and the northeast.
In the great tantra known as the *Kiraṇa*.
The square, the womb-shape (triangle), the half-moon, the triangle, the circle, the hexagon, the lotus, and the octagon— these are situated in order starting from the east.
In the Gautamīya [Vinaya].
For a thousand oblations, one should indeed offer into a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit;
for ten thousand, it should be two cubits, and for a hundred thousand oblations, four cubits.
With six hands, there is one hundred thousand recitations; with eight hands, one million;
and with ten hands, indeed ten million—the number of recitations is thus established according to the count of hands.
On the earth for performing *homa*, there is no sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) larger than ten cubits;
for a *koṭi*-homa, it is prescribed as eight cubits—this should be understood according to the weightiness or lightness of the materials on the left and right sides.
A pit measuring one cubit is ordained for a *lakṣa*-homa.

In this case as well, it should be understood that even when the *ājya* oblation consists of ten lakhs as stated for Meru, it applies to the *vīra* and other types of oblations which produce minor or wicked results.
Likewise.
This sacrificial pit is said to be one fist in size for fifty oblations;
it is one cubit in size for a hundred oblations, and one span in size for a thousand oblations.
For ten thousand [handspans], it is said to be two cubits; for one hundred thousand, four cubits are prescribed;
for one million, six cubits; and for ten million, eight cubits are traditionally taught.
In a fire-pit measuring one cubit, one hundred thousand oblations are prescribed;
up to ten lakhs, one should increase the size by one cubit for each lakh.
In the Meru-tantra.
Furthermore, for one who is incapable, a fire sacrifice of ten thousand oblations (ayutāhuti) should be performed upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) on the right side.
Now, its characteristics [are described] in the Śāradā:
In the previously described pavilion, the learned one, having divided the area outside the altar into three parts,
should designate the central portion starting from the east.
In the eight directions, sacrificial pits of beautiful form should be arranged in sequence:
square, yoni-shaped, crescent-moon, triangular, and perfectly circular.
These [fire-pits] are hexagonal, lotus-shaped, and octagonal by name;
the fire-pit for the Preceptor (Ācārya) should be in the center, between Gaurīpati and Mahendra.
In the Kriyāsāra:
The central area of the one who lies with Vṛṣa (the Bull) may be circular or square;
between the lords of Indra (Purandara) and Īśa (Īśāna), it is both circular and square.
And because of the statement in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "That has been pointed out by the Teacher."
Now, regarding the square sacrificial pit (*caturasrakuṇḍa*), it is stated in the *Tantrarāja*:
Having stretched a cord from east to west, one should mark the center;
then, from that point, twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas) to the east or to the west.
Having projected [the line] further, one should also place a pair of marks there; using the measurement of the marks from east to west, one should rely on those two [lines].
Having placed two *haṃsapada* marks to the south and north,
one should then extend a thread between those two and erase them according to the stated measurement.
Then, having fixed those tips according to the measurement of the central mark,
he should make a half-measure on each side and drop them down at those corners.
The four [primary] lines should form a symmetrical square;
within that, I shall describe to you the other sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) according to their measurements.
In the Gautamīya Tantra.
Having stretched out a cord one cubit in length from east to west,
one should clearly form a pair of fish at its two ends so that they are distinct.
Having divided that cord into two parts, one should drop it from south to north;
then, one should clearly form a pair of fish-marks at its two ends.
One should cast four lines in the four directions according to that measurement;
thus it shall become a square with four compartments, exceedingly beautiful.
One should apply two diagonal threads; by means of that, one should mark the measurement.
Thus the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) shall become square, endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
Likewise.
By means of this, the best of mantra-knowers should produce all the sacrificial pits.
In the Sāradā [Tantra]:
Those who know the cubit (hasta) understand it to be four fingers plus one satya;
this is measured by the joints of the middle finger of the right hand of the maker.
The measurement of the middle [part] by its length is declared to be in standard finger-breadths (mānāṅguli).
The measurement of a cubit has also been stated previously.
The area of a pit measuring one cubit is [one square]; for those measuring two cubits and so forth, it is double that, and so on.
In the Gautamīya Tantra.

One should excavate a pit measuring two cubits according to the measurement of the ear-ornament (karṇasūtra); thus, one should increase the size in all pits everywhere according to the prescribed rule.
Thus is the characteristic of the square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
24b) Now,
the characteristics of the *yoni* and the *kuṇḍa*, as stated in the *Tantrarāja*:
In the middle of that, having expanded the Brahma-thread by one-fifth part from the center of the pair of eastern and western squares, [one should proceed].
O Dear One, one should rotate [the cord] from the western tip toward the north and likewise toward the south, using the measurement of that corner.
From that center, supported by the two tips of the transverse lines,
there should likewise be two lines extending outward as far as the Brahma-line.
O auspicious lady, this sacrificial pit (yoni-kuṇḍa) consists of four parts.
In the Meru Tantra:
The sacrificial pit for the womb (yonikuṇḍa) should resemble an aśvattha leaf and face north;
here, the altars shaped like wombs should be constructed with beautiful girdles.
Thus ends the description of the *yonikuṇḍa*. Now follows the description of the *ardhacandrakuṇḍa*, as stated in the *Merutantra*:
The wise knower of the system should divide the square field into ten parts;
he should omit one part each from the east and from the north.
One should drop the bowstring at the front and then rotate it according to that measurement;
thus, this pit, resembling a half-moon, becomes beautiful.
In a quadrangular field, having left two units above and as many below, one should place the Jina-fraction in the middle of the side.
The portion diminished by a sixteenth part [of the circumference] is increased by three times its width for the purpose of rotation; from that measurement, the pit (kuṇḍa) is indeed half the moon.
Also in the great tantra known as the *Kiraṇa*:
One should set aside half of the southern fifth-part of the field;
likewise, having set aside half of the northern third-part, one should again leave an equal portion.
Having done so, a thread-rotation should be performed there, shaped like a half-moon.
Thus ends the description of the half-moon-shaped sacrificial pit (*ardhacandrakuṇḍa*). Now follows the description of the triangular sacrificial pit (*trikoṇakuṇḍa*), as stated in the *Tantrarāja*:
One should expand that very [area] by one-sixth on both sides; O Lord, the western thread for each [side] shall be of that same measure as the two threads.
One should lay down the Brahma-sūtra from the end [of the cord] up to the tip of its two ends by means of suspension.
Also in the great tantra called Kirana:
The field should be divided into five parts; one should set aside two parts on the outside, leaving those two sides and discarding the middle from that [remaining area].
By that measurement, using the mark on both pegs as well, one should draw three lines there; thus, a triangle is clearly manifested.
Thus ends the description of the triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
25a) Now, the characteristics of the circular *kuṇḍa*, according to the *Merutantra*:
One should conceive of the desired square as having twenty-four parts;
then, from its center, one should mark a solar portion with a karkoṭaka.
"One should make it circular. Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the circular *kuṇḍa*. Now follows the description of the characteristics of the hexagonal *kuṇḍa*.
In the Kriyāśāra:
Having divided the field into nine parts, one should place two shoulder-lines on the outside of both sides;
by that measurement, one should lay out the central square as it is.
One should lay down six lines: the other four corners and two each on the two sides;
from these [lines], that hexagonal sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) shall be formed.
In the great tantra known as the *Kiraṇa*.
Having divided the field into eight parts, one should lead out each single part from the outside;
having likewise grasped the middle from both sides, [one proceeds].
One should mark all the corners there by laying down six lines;
having done so, a hexagonal fire-pit (kuṇḍa) with clear characteristics will be formed.
Thus ends the description of the hexagonal sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Now follows the description of the lotus-shaped sacrificial pit, from the *Lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*.
One should divide the square field into eight parts, O Ambika;
then, with a compass set to the measure of one-eighth part, [one should draw] from the center.
One should rotate this circle from the pericarp and the filaments;
by means of two eighths [of the diameter] from the center, the circle shall be formed.
The middle of the petals is considered to be three-eighths [of the diameter];
in the fourth [circle], the field of the serpent (nāga) is equal to the width [of the petals] through rotation.
O fair-faced one, the Brahma-sūtra is said to consist of twenty-four parts;
taking one part of that, it is further divided into sixteen parts with devotion.
Having taken the fifth and eighth parts, each diminished by five sixteenths,
one should place them outside that fifth mandala, O Śivā.
One should rotate [the thread] from the center; the tips of all the petals are considered to be the ground.
O Goddess, one should then draw the lotus according to the procedure taught in the Śāka.

The space between the outer edge and the interior is the measurement from the tip of the filaments; having made that measurement as the *karkaṭa* (compass) and having placed it at the tip of the filament.
Having written sixteen half-moons along the path instructed by the guru, one should draw the tips of the petals with the hand.
Having set aside the height of the pericarp according to the measurement of Vyāsa, one should bury the remainder; this is the mandala of the filaments.
One who digs here, while digging the earth elsewhere, makes it take on that same form.
O Supreme Goddess, just as it arises in the form of a leaf when properly purified.
In the Meru Tantra.
Furthermore, the second [section] consists of three and a half parts.
25b) One should cast eight threads in the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, and the spaces between them.
Then, from the northern circular line, [one should draw] a thread from the tip of the thread at the northeast (īśa).
One should draw a line from the top of the eastern sūtra of the outer circle to the top of the southern line of the inner circle.
With that [line], one should bring forth the petal-base; thus indeed are the petals formed.
Furthermore, the circle drawn with a radius equal to half the diagonal of the sectors is the pericarp (karṇikā).
Then, on a circle whose diameter is half of that [mandala], one should draw its filaments;
the height of both the pericarp and the filaments should be measured as one-sixth of the diameter.
One should dig according to the instructions of the guru so that it takes the form of a lotus.
One should fashion the form of a lotus.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the lotus-shaped sacrificial pit.
Now, the characteristics of the eight-cornered sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
In the *kuṇḍeṣṭāmra* (the desired copper vessel), one should divide the middle line into twenty-four parts;
then, by increasing the circle by two parts starting from the first, third, and tenth parts, [one forms the shape].
In the center of that, by laying down eight lines in the cardinal directions, one forms a regular octagon.
In the Meru Tantra:
Now, for the desired square, its diagonal increased by one-twelfth of itself is used;
with that very measure, one should describe a circle and mark points in the eight directions.
One should extend the lines in sequence and draw arms above them;
thus an eight-sided (octagonal) pit is formed, and its neck and girdle are likewise.
Thus ends the description of the eight-cornered sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
The specific distinction regarding those who vomit [the seed] will be explained.
In that Tantra, the procedure for the nine sacrificial pits at the beginning of initiation and so forth is the same.

One who is capable of constructing these sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should, in all cases, make them either square or circular; for it is the traditional teaching of Hara that the sacrificial pits may be square, circular, or of various other shapes.
Those [altars] are praised as being either circular or square at all times, according to the statement of Somaśambhu as well.

It is also stated at the beginning of the Merutantra: "The middle [method] is the system of five sacrificial pits (pañcakuṇḍī), while the system of constructing a single pit is the lowest. Nine, five, or even one [pit] should be made, provided it possesses the required characteristics"—this is the secret traditional teaching (āmnāya). The arrangement of those [pits] is also described in that very same work.
Also in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*: "In the directions, there are squares of four [units], five [units] for the northeast."
But in the Nāradīya [Purāṇa]:
In whatever ritual action a set of four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) is prescribed, they should be square,
crescent-shaped, circular, and lotus-like.
The wise one should construct four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in the directions starting from the east;
it is said, O twice-born, that he should cause a fifth pit to be made in the region of the northeast.
In the Meru Tantra.
These sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) are renowned for use in Tantric and Smārta rituals;
they are not deficient, nor are they neckless, according to the Śruti which declares them to be "not of low origin" (viyoni).

If one lacks the capacity for eight, there should be four fire-pits (kuṇḍas) in the cardinal directions according to the Tantra; if one lacks even that capacity, one should arrange only a single square pit.
In the ritual arrangement of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), that which is the fifth should be in the northeast (īśāna).
And likewise, in the *Ratnāvalī* itself, the venerable Ārya [Nāgārjuna] has stated that the placement of the wings should be in a single pit;
or else, one should establish a single square pit in the north for the remaining [deities].
Also in the Merutantra:
"The ninth, the Ācāryakuṇḍa, is square in the Vaidika [rite]"; thus it is stated in the Meru regarding the Vaidika.
"Navamam" refers to the position of the ninth [pit] in the system of nine pits; however, according to the Merutantra, it is on the left.
Or, according to one's capacity, for the worship on the left path, there is a single fire-pit (kuṇḍa).

But Somaśambhu has stated: "A wise man should cause one [pit] to be made in the western direction, which is the quarter of Śiva. Furthermore, this pit (kuṇḍa) should be made either square or circular. This has been stated in the *Kriyāsāra*:
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) may be square or it may even be circular.
In the worship of the fixed [liṅga], the moving preceptor [is required]; in the daily fire-sacrifice rite, it is the same.
Also in the Piṅgalāmata:
The pit is one cubit in size and circular; the girdle is at the level of the neck and the navel.
In daily rites, initiation, pacification, and nourishment, this [system] is considered auspicious.
If capable, it should be square on the right; or, if unable to do so at all, it should be a *yoni* altar-pit on the left.
Now, the prohibited sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) are described.
This has been stated in the Merutantra:
If the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) possesses many defects due to its measurement being either deficient or excessive,
then one who desires auspiciousness must examine it thoroughly before proceeding.
If the pit is too deep, there will be disease; if it is too shallow, there is loss of cattle and wealth.
In the Brahma-kunda, there is suffering, and if the rim is broken, death occurs.
If the girdle is missing, there is grief; if it is excessive, there is loss of wealth. A *kuṇḍa* made without a womb is said to cause the destruction of one's wife.
A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) that is devoid of a neck is said to cause the destruction of one's offspring;
likewise, a pit that lacks ornamentation or has a frayed boundary (mekhalā) is defective.
If the [measuring] line bursts, there will be the eradication of the patron;
if the line is excessive, there is enmity toward friends; if the line is deficient, there is poverty.
If the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) is too narrow, there will be disease in the stomach; if it has a hole, there will be infamy.
Even if the pit is constructed exactly as prescribed, this is the fruit that arises when the deity is invoked.
Now, regarding the excavation of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
In the Meru-tantra.
The excavation of the pit should indeed be exactly as wide as the pit itself;
once the measurement for the desired dimensions of the pit has been made in all directions, [the digging follows].
Also in the Śāradā [Tantra].
The depth of the excavation is said to be equal to the width of the pit.
26b) In the Meru-tantra:
Having first drawn a square with four compartments using threads as before,
one should dig a pit in its center, measuring one cubit in depth and length.
O Lord of the Gaṇas, for those who possess discernment.
It should be twenty-four finger-breadths in length and provided with a pit of the same depth.
In the Māheśvara Tantra.
One should dig one cubit deep, both horizontally and vertically, together with the girdle.
And yet:
In the *Viśvakarmīya*, it is stated that the other [type] is taught by Vyāsa as being lower by the measure of the lunar days (tithi) in finger-breadths;
while in the *Prathama-tantra*, it is said that the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is nine finger-breadths across and upwards, together with its girdle (*mekhalā*).
Also in the Siddhāntaśekhara:

The pit should be of the measure of a *kuṇḍa*, including the girdle (*mekhalā*) above; this should be understood as pertaining to very small-scale *homa* rites, or specifically to *homa* rites involving delicate flowers such as *mālatī*.
In the Gautamīya [Vinaya].
Then the mantra-practitioner should dig a pit according to the injunctions of the scriptures,
carefully avoiding the body and especially the head region of the serpent.
It is like the knowledge of a snake's head.
According to the measurement of the site, he indeed always lies on his left side;
after three months, having turned over upon the ground, the perfected ones call that site a *nāga*.

In the months beginning with Bhādrapada, that serpent has its head facing north; in the three months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, its head faces south; indeed, in the months beginning with Phālguna, its head faces west; and in those beginning with Jyeṣṭha, that serpent has its head facing north.
Death occurs at the head-joint; the joining of the body-parts occurs in the lumps;
suffering arises in the tail; and in the chest, there is the accomplishment of all aims.
Now, the measurement of the neck.
In the Mahākapila Pañcarātra.
The neck is proclaimed to be one twenty-fourth part;
the excavation of the neck is two finger-breadths wide—this is the rule for all sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
One should calculate the finger-breadth (aṅgula) as consisting of twenty-four parts.
In the Meru Tantra:
The ear of a one-cubit [image] should be two *varas*;
for a two-cubit [image], the ear should be [one *vara*], and for a three-cubit [image], it should be equal to the length of the arm.
In this same manner, even for [mandalas] of four cubits and so forth, the neck is everywhere level with the ground.
Now, regarding the girdle (*mekhalā*), according to the *Piṅgalāmata*:
Leaving a space of one finger-breadth from the edge of the pit, the placement of the girdles (mekhalās) should take place.
In the Meru Tantra:
The girdles (mekhalās) should be made outside the entire portion belonging to the Jina.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
Whatever is the form of the sacrificial pits, such is the form of the girdles.
27a) In the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā.
Or there may be three girdles, or two, or even one.
In the Meru-tantra:
Now, first, the procedure for the exterior of the square is stated:
the excellent sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), provided with a navel and a womb and possessing three girdles, is described.
The Śūdras have two girdles, while those of mixed caste have a single girdle.
In the Kriyāsāra:
A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) joined with the navel and the womb, provided with three ridges (mekhalā), is excellent;
one with two ridges is middling; and one with a single ridge is inferior.
The specific detail is stated in the Merutantra:
Indeed, there should be six arrows, three fires, and two eyes [in measure] for the five girdles;
this applies when there is a difference in dharma or a difference in caste between the preceptor and the sacrificer.
Two girdles are prescribed, measuring one-sixth and one-eighth [of the total height],
in the Kaulika, Vāmamārga, Buddhist, Jaina, and Śavara traditions.
Thus it has been stated quite clearly in the Somaśambhu [Tantra].
It is stated that for a Brāhmaṇa there should be a sacrificial pit with three girdles (*mekhalā*), for a Kṣatriya two girdles,
and for a Vaiśya one girdle; nevertheless,

because of the censure heard in the words "there is grief in being devoid of a girdle" and the term "bad girdle" (*kumekhalam*) used for those of mixed caste (*saṃkara*), it follows that [the absence of] girdles constitutes a lack of qualification (*anadhikāryatva*).
Because it is stated in the Śruti, "The necks are of different origins," it shines forth as "with a girdle" (samekhalam) in that very same place.
The twenty-fourth part of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) is designated as one finger (aṅgula);
by means of this division, the girdles (mekhalā), the neck (kaṇṭha), and the navel (nābhi) are to be constructed.
In the Mahākapila Pañcarātra.
The *kuṇḍa* is said to be one-sixth [of the altar], while the second is remembered as one-eighth.
"The third [note] shall be its twelfth."
In the Meru Tantra:
Twelve finger-breadths in width and four finger-breadths in height from the base,
the other [part] should be longer than that, eight finger-breadths in length and of the same height.
It is four finger-breadths long and as high as that, and more than that above.
In the *Yoginīhṛdaya*.
O Goddess, listen to me regarding the girdles, especially concerning the hands and other parts;
they should be measured in sixths, twelfths, and eighths, well-concealed and auspicious.
In another tantra:
Whichever girdle was worn previously, that is declared to be the corresponding region of the earth.
In this context, priority (pūrvatva) is to be understood with reference to the external.
In the *Kriyāsāra*:
In this context, the height of the principal girdle is stated to be nine finger-breadths;
the height of the outer girdle is traditionally recorded as five finger-breadths.
Outside of that, the three girdles (mekhalā) should be two finger-breadths (aṅgula) in height respectively;
the widths of these three girdles, however, are four, three, and two finger-breadths.
27b) Here, the statement regarding height is made with reference to the fundamental level (*mūlabhūmi*). [This concludes] the summary of characteristics (*lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*).
The first [lid] is two finger-breadths in length and elevated by nine finger-breadths;
the middle one is three finger-breadths wide externally, while the third is four finger-breadths.

As for that which was stated by the teachers— "The girdles (*mekhalā*), preceded by sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and decreasing successively by twelve, eight, and four finger-breadths in height,

and having a width of four finger-breadths on all sides, are said to grant all perfections (*siddhi*)"— that is intended for specific results; therefore, the first girdle there has a width of twelve finger-breadths.
Its height is four finger-breadths, and it is equal all around;
its surrounding wall (parivapra) should be four finger-breadths according to the measurement of the cord.
It should be properly extended eight finger-breadths wide and equal on all sides;
above that, moreover, the third body should be fashioned.
"Four finger-breadths wide and likewise elevated"—it is stated exactly thus in the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā as well.
And that which is divided into twenty-four parts by Vyāsa consists of three [sections] each extending over four and three [verses] respectively.

Then, the neck, the exterior, the girdle, and the nine-fold seasonal garment are considered to be equal [in height]. However, some have stated that these are equal in width and height; others have said they are in the proportion of twelve parts. Regarding the first, its height is stated [as twelve], while for the other two, it is established in sequence according to the measure of eight and four parts respectively; this is what has been declared by the Vājapeyins.

Due to the absence of authoritative evidence, this should be disregarded; however, that measurement is stated in the *Lakṣaṇasaṃgraha* regarding the fifth enclosure (*pañcamekhala*) and also in the *Merutantra*.
Five girdles should indeed be made with [strings] consisting of six, five, four, three, and two-and-a-half [units].
Also in the Siddhāntaśekhara:
The five girdles should measure six, four, four, three, and two [finger-breadths] respectively.
According to another system, there are two girdles.
The two girdles are considered to be [respectively] one-sixth and one-eighth [of the total height].
According to the Piṅgalāmata, there is one girdle in the alternative view.
The girdles (mekhalā) are considered to be one, six, and eight finger-breadths in height and width respectively.
Also in the Mahākapila-pañcarātra:
And that single girdle is recorded as having a width equal to one-fourth [of the base]; this is also stated in the *Prathamatantre*.
A single girdle (mekhalā) six finger-breadths wide should be made outside the neck-line (guṇa); this is also stated in the Siddhāntaśeṣara.
One should fashion a single girdle for the sacrificial pits measuring six finger-breadths; thus it is stated in the great tantra known as the Kiraṇa.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) may have three girdles (mekhalā), or even just one;
for a pit measuring one fist (muṣṭi), there should be two palas [of earth] for the girdle.
Two girdles should be made, measuring half a finger and one finger respectively;
for a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) of one cubit (ratni), the rim should be three fingers wide.
For a sacrificial pit measuring one cubit, its two eastern sides shall be two finger-breadths each,
and the circumference shall be four finger-breadths, increasing sequentially by one finger-breadth for each subsequent side.
For this two-cubit sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), two rims should be made, measuring three finger-breadths and two finger-breadths respectively;
the eastern rim of this pit is six finger-breadths [in width].
With four other fingers and three fingers of the third [hand],
the bricks for the eastern circumference of a four-cubit sacrificial pit are determined.
The first girdle should be made with six finger-breadths and the other with four finger-breadths;
it should be six cubits long and ten finger-breadths wide.
The second girdle is eight finger-breadths wide, and the third is six finger-breadths;
of the eight-cubit [stūpa], the first girdle is twelve finger-breadths [in height].
The second [girdle] is considered to be ten fingers wide, and the third eight fingers;
the girdles should have the same form as that of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Now, regarding the fruit of the girdle, according to the Gautamīya:
The first girdle is said to be *sāttvika*, the second is remembered as *rājasa*, and the third is to be known as *tāmasa*; thus has the description of the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) been stated.
Now, regarding the *yoni*, it is said in the *Śāradā*:
Their source is the cause at the beginning, like the leaf of the *aśvattha* tree above; [this is stated] in the *Somaśambhu*.
Above those, there should be the *yoni*, shaped like an *aśvattha* leaf in the center; thus it is stated in the *Gautamīya*.
In the *Merutantra*: "At the first boundary, one should fashion the vulva-shaped sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in front of the Hotṛ priest."
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) of the womb, resembling an aśvattha leaf, faces north; [this is stated] in the Svāyaṃbhuvatantra.
The sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) located in the east and south are said to have their openings facing north;
the remaining ones are traditionally held to face east, arranged according to what is aesthetically pleasing.
In the Meru Tantra:
To the east of the fires and the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), the altar (yoni) is said to face northward.
"The remaining [deities] face east," as it is said in the *Trailokyasāra*.
The *yoni* of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is situated in the south-eastern corner, while that of the water-pitcher is in the north-western corner;
the *yoni* of the ninth [pit] is likewise located on the southern petal.
In the Svāyambhuva [Manvantara].
The girdle is at the center; the womb (yoni) is half the size of the pit (kuṇḍa) and three parts wide;
it should be made with a rim one thumb-breadth high and shaped like the petal of an ashvattha leaf.
In the Meru-tantra.
The vulva (yoni) is twelve finger-breadths (sūryāṅgula) in length; its width is one-third less than that.
It is one finger-breadth in height and likewise enters inwardly [to the same depth].
Also in the Siddhāntaśekhara:
The womb is eight finger-breadths in width, its length being [measured] by long sun-fingers, and its height is two finger-breadths.
Also in the *Prayogasāra*:
One should fashion the womb (yoni) from the center, measuring twelve finger-breadths in length;
it should be raised by one-twelfth of that measure and be slightly inclined toward the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
And thus:
The source of the kuṇḍas, which have a single jewel in their hands and are shaped like fists, has been declared.
28b) In the autumn.
It is characterized by a length, width, and height of six, four, and two *aṅgulas* respectively; this is also stated in the *Kriyāsāra*.
Regarding this, Rāghavabhaṭṭa states that the two statements— "six finger-breadths in height" and "four finger-breadths in width"— apply to the view of having a single girdle.
In reality, the phrase "six, four, and two finger-breadths" applies collectively to the width and other dimensions. As it is said in the Pañcarātra:
One should fashion the womb (yoni) with a height of twelve finger-breadths and a length of the same measure. Also elsewhere:
The yoni should be twelve finger-breadths in height and width;
this refers to the method of the thick girdle (mekhalā) as taught in the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā and other texts.
But in the Nāradīya [Purāṇa], however:

The *yoni* is one-third the width of the pit (*kuṇḍa*) and one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) in height; its length is half that of the pit, and its elevation is stated to be one finger-breadth. This is also stated in the *Piṅgalāmata*.
The width of the vulva is eight fingers, and its height is measured at one finger;
it has a width of eight fingers because it is contracted at the initial part.
In the Meru Tantra:
It is one finger-breadth high and likewise enters within;
it is joined to two bulbous parts (kumbhas) and is considered to be like a leaf of the holy fig tree (aśvattha).
Thus it is also stated in the *Trailokyasāra*, and likewise in the *Vāyavīyasaṃhitā*.
One should fashion a girdle at the center, either toward the west or the south;
it should be beautiful in the middle, slightly depressed, and gradually tapering like the edge of a lotus stalk.
Facing the sacrificial pit with her girdle slightly loosened, she stood at the forefront.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
One should make the tip of the yoni one finger-breadth in size, slightly turned downwards;
here, by one part, a rim (nemi) should also be made around the top of the yoni, characterized by both width and height.
This has been stated by Rāmavājapeyin:
The *yoni* [of the fire-pit] is as wide as half the diameter of the pit and as long as that [diameter]; it is one-third [of the length] in height and has a circumference equal to that [height].
It is radiant all around and enters into the interior of the pit by its own tip to that same extent;
below, it is beautiful with two circular halves like the leaf of a *aśvattha* tree.
The word *kṛti* means "having a cavity within," just as a vessel has a cavity for the purpose of holding ghee; thus, the meaning is that it possesses such a cavity.
"Round at the bottom" means that in its lower portion, it is joined with two half-circles shaped like a water-pot (*kumbha*). As stated in the *Merutantra*:
"In the *yoni*-shaped sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should avoid [the central] *yoni*."
In the Gautamīya [Vinaya].
One should make the tip of the yoni one finger-breadth wide and slightly downturned;
in other sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), one should increase the width of the yoni by one finger-breadth for each successive size.
One should also increase the tip of the vulva by a measure of two barley-corns.
For the fist-shaped, jewel-shaped, and single-pit [vulvas], the length and width should be increased respectively by six, four, and two finger-breadths.
