29a) Starting from the base, there should be a stalk in the middle of the yoni, provided with a cavity.
Also in the *Pañcarātra*:
Starting from the base, the stalk should be equal in height to the outer girdle.
In the Gautamīya [Vinaya].
Starting from the base, the stalk should have a hole extending to the center of the womb.
A tube is desired that has a fine tip, a thick base, and is perforated;
one should make an opening in the middle of the womb, and that is known as the "grasper."
"From the middle" means up to the end of the middle.
In the Meru Tantra:
One should lead the stalk from the middle of that [pedestal] to such a length and such a height;
by "to such," it is meant to be equal to the girdle (*mekhalā*). However, in the *Prayogasāra*:
To the west of the vulva, the stalk of my *māyā* is four finger-breadths [in length];
its width is desired to be three, two, and one finger-breadth respectively, decreasing in sequence, as it has been stated.

According to the tradition, an altar at the base of the square stalk should be constructed, four finger-breadths in height and width, joined externally to the girdle (*mekhalā*). Now, the characteristics of the *nābhi* (navel): as stated in the *Śāradā*:
One should fashion the navel of these pits (kuṇḍas) resembling a lotus;
its measurement is declared to be either conforming to that pit or otherwise.
For sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) measuring one, three, or four cubits, the depth is considered to be equal to the navel [of the pit], provided with four or three finger-breadths;
in other pits, one should increase this accordingly.
The wise one of noble intellect should calculate the navel by the sequence of two *yava*s;
however, when [the measurement] has reached the twelfth part of the pit (*kuṇḍa*), it should be doubled by the intelligent one for the left and right sides.
In the *Śāradā-tantra*, however, it is stated from the perspective of the gross view because of its proximity [to the subtle].
In the Tantra known as the Kirāṇa.
The navel, situated in the middle of the pit, should be made following the lines of the girdle;
it should be fashioned like an aśvattha leaf, and its width is considered to be eight aṅgulas.
It should be twelve finger-breadths in length and eight finger-breadths in width;
for the remaining [categories], an increase of one finger-breadth is beneficial for both the width and the length.
In the *Śāradā-tantra*: "One should avoid the navel in the *ajvakuṇḍa* [fire-pit], as follows:"
One should perform the daily and occasional fire-oblation (homa) either on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
which should be square, level, and equal in height to the thumb.
But on the lunar seat (candrapīṭha), however...
A sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring one cubit in extent should be prepared with sand and other materials, being either triangular or square and one span in height.
The first rampart is proclaimed to be two finger-breadths in height;
then, above that, the ground for the rampart is likewise endowed with a height of two finger-breadths.
The width of all [the channels] therein is stated by the wise to be two finger-breadths; this applies even when there is an increase in the oblation.
The cord (karaṇī) is said to be either one and a half times or double [the length], and by it the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) is measured.
Now, the characteristics of the sacrificial ladle (*śrugh*). In the *Śāradā*:
The Guru should fashion the *sruva* ladle for the yoga that is about to be described, not according to the [usual] method;
it should be made from one of these: *śrīparṇī*, *śiṃśapā*, or *kṣīravṛkṣa*.
Having taken [the measurement], one should divide it by thirty-six to obtain a span (hasta);
with twenty parts there shall be the staff (daṇḍa), and with eight of those parts the altar (vedi) shall be formed.
The neck is measured as one part, and the face is seven parts;
the width of the neck is proclaimed to be three parts of the altar-base (vedī).
In this case, one should fashion a passage at the mouth equal in size to the throat,
measuring the width of the little finger, for the purpose of the exit of the clarified butter.
In the center of the altar, the pericarp (karṇikā) should be fashioned with one part;
one should then fashion a pit (avaṭa) all around it with one part on the outside.
Its pit should be circular with three parts, and with half a part outside;
one should fashion petals all around with a single part.
The rim (nemī) of both the Mekhalā and the Mukhavedī should be one and a half parts in measure;
at the base and tip of the staff (daṇḍa), there should be two pots (kuṃbha) measuring three and four finger-breadths respectively.

The pair of staffs (daṇḍa) should consist of the portions of Yama; this is declared to be the circumference (anāha) of the staff. The rear portion of the altar (vedi) should consist of six parts, and it should be shaped like a tortoise (kūrma).
One should carve the face of a swan, an elephant, or even a vessel; the characteristics of the *sruc* ladle are said to be on the back part of the face.
The śrīparṇī, gambhārī, and milk-exuding trees; the aśvattha, udumbara, vaṭa, and plakṣa.
In the Phetkāriṇī Tantra.
One may have it made from *kāraskara*, *āmalakī*, *palāśa*, or *khadira* wood;
or one may have it fashioned from gold, silver, copper, or even iron.
In the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā.
The *sruc* and *sruva* ladles should be made of metal, not of bell-metal or mixed with lead;
alternatively, they may be made of sacrificial wood, as approved by craftsmen for the purpose of the Tantric ritual.
Or on a leaf of a sacred tree (*brahmavṛkṣa*) and the like, which is undamaged, elevated in the center, and made of iron;
herein, the injunctions and prohibitions pertain respectively to fierce and gentle rites.
This has been stated in another [text]:
The *sruc* and *sruva* ladles should be made of gold for all rites pertaining to Soma;
these two should be made of iron for rites such as *stambhana* (paralysis) and the like.
Also elsewhere.
In the absence of that, the oblation is offered with two leaves of the Palāśa tree.
Also the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā.
The *sruc* and *sruva* ladles are considered to be made from a beautiful, flawless leaf of the *palāśa* tree;
or, for a concise fire-offering (*homakarma*), one may fashion them from a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree.
"A cubit's length" means "the length of an arm."
One should indeed fashion the *srūva* ladle with the length of one's own arms for the purpose of the fire-oblation.
This is because of the statement in the *Agastisaṃhitā*, and also because of the statement in the *Phetkāriṇī*: "The sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) should be thirty-six finger-breadths in length."

The altar (vedī) is made with one-third [of the measurement]; by bending it with a third part, otherwise there would be the contingency of the lamp-stand being useless. Here, there is no digging out of petals, due to the absence of authoritative evidence (pramāṇa). One should fashion two very beautiful jars at the base and the tip, according to the statement in the *Mantramuktāvalī*: "Having taken hold of the *śruci*..."
In the Maṃtramuktāvalī:
The wise one should cause a channel below the throat for the exit of the clarified butter,
and he should perform the piercing at the mouth with a heated iron probe.
In the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā:
There should be a hollow in the region of the throat through which the little finger can enter.
Now, the characteristics of the sacrificial ladle (*śruva*), according to the *Śāradā*:
One should fashion the *sruva* ladle with twenty-four parts;
its handle measurement is declared to be twenty-two parts.
The swelling (ānāha) is situated at a distance of four parts from the point where the probe (karṣa) is grasped;
one should insert [the instrument] two parts deep, as it takes the shape of a deer's footprint at the edge.
At the base and the tip of the handle, there should be a knob adorned with a ring; thus is the rule for the *sruva* ladle declared.
Now, the procedure for initiation (*dīkṣā-vidhi*). In the *Merutantra*:
The Goddess said:
How does initiation occur in the left path, and how does it occur in the right?
What is essential therein for whom? Tell me your definitive conclusion on this.
The illustrious Lord said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the fivefold procedure for initiation, which is concealed in all the tantras and is the most excellent among those intended for kings.
For those who are great and wealthy, it is said to be excellent; for ordinary people, it is middling; for Brahmins, it is not small; and for ascetics, it is exceedingly subtle.
Therefore, I shall first declare to you that which is the most supreme among the supreme,
wherein there exists no further distinction of categories such as "most supreme" and so forth.
In that regard, one should first construct a pavilion for the most excellent of rites.
The characteristics of the pavilion have been described.
In the Sāradā [Tantra]:
That [initiation] is of four kinds, distinguished as sāsaṃdiṣṭā, kriyāvatī, and so forth;
it consists of kriyāvatī, varṇamayī, kalātmā, and also āvedhamayī.
These [mantras], which bring about prosperity, are not explained here in this tantra in their sequential order.
The preceptor, having bathed according to the rules and performed his morning rites, [should proceed].
Having thus prepared himself, remaining silent, he should proceed to the sacrificial pavilion for the sake of the sacrifice.
In the Meru Tantra:
On the day preceding the initiation (dīkṣā),
having performed the morning rites and having well-adorned one's own body, one should perform worship in one's own home.
Then, according to the ritual procedure for Gaṇeśa, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited;
having offered libations to the Nāndīmukha ancestors, accompanied by the fivefold musical instruments.
Having completed the equipment as described, one should proceed toward the teacher's house.
In the Gautamīya [Vinaya].
The disciple, having bathed and being well-attired, and provided with all necessary materials,
should choose the preceptor with devotion, honoring him with garments, ornaments, and decorations.
One should perform the Nāndīmukha Śrāddha and satisfy the Brāhmaṇas;
one should gratify one's own preceptor with gifts such as cows, land, gold, and clothing.
30a) Just as one who is contented and pleased bestows a mantra that grants boons.
Likewise.
There, one should choose fifteen, ten, or two officiating priests (ṛtvij).
In the Yāmala:
Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), the disciple, with his senses subdued,
should offer sesame seeds and gold for the sake of destroying the sins committed since birth.
In the Meru Tantra:
The selection of the preceptor and the officiating priests, and the collection of materials—these are considered the tenfold preliminary requirements.
The seats made from *śrīparṇī* wood should be one cubit in measurement according to the prescribed dimensions.
Twenty-seven blades of *darbha* grass, equal in length and each eight finger-breadths in height, are joined together at their tips and adorned with a knot.
The characteristics of the seats for all sacrifices have been fully proclaimed;
for the purpose of the water for the feet, copper basins filled with cool or warm water should be used.
Conch shells, accompanied by water, fragrance, and flowers, are for the offering of *arghya*;
and vessels of fine copper, filled with water, are for sipping (*ācamana*).
They brought vessels made of bell-metal filled with curds and other ingredients for the madhuparka offering,
as well as costly garments and fine ornaments such as finger-rings.
One should collect peacock-feather umbrellas and turbans;
one should also bring sandals there, adorned with leather ornaments.
By performing this, one obtains a fruit equal to the honor accorded at a great sacrifice;
the honoring of other Brahmins with the madhuparka is thus prescribed.
One who is full of devotion should give twice that amount to the preceptor with great devotion;
for in such a case, the worship of the teacher is equal to that of other twice-born brahmins.
In that sacrifice, the fruit is meager, just as there is no rain for a parched field;
likewise, having gone to the house of the Guru and prostrated before the Guru’s sandals.
Having presented the materials for the formal request and having made the resolve, he should choose a guru, saying:
"O best of the twice-born, for the sake of receiving such-and-such a mantra."
"Having addressed you with the words 'Because of your weightiness,' I therefore choose you as my teacher";
having spoken thus, the disciple should choose [the teacher], and then the teacher should say, "I am chosen."
The child should say, "Perform the service for the guru as is appropriate," and having uttered,
"I shall do so," he should then call out to the guru.
One should select eight Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas,
as well as those devoted to the specific deity [of the rite], or otherwise, when acting through an officiating priest (ṛtvij).
Then four sacrificial pits are prescribed and four officiating priests are appointed;
thereafter, the Guru, accompanied by his disciple, should proceed to the sacrificial hall.
And having sat down at its door, one should then begin the examination.
This procedure is praised; as stated in the Śāradā-tilaka, beginning with the preceptor:
Having sipped water according to the rule and having prepared the general offering (sāmānyārgha) there,
one should sprinkle the door with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra) and perform the worship of the door.

The procedures for bathing, the twilight rites (saṃdhyā), libations (tarpaṇa), the worship of the door, and so forth, as well as the daily worship, will be explained in the chapter on daily ritual (nityārcana-paṭala).
31a) Likewise.
Touching the left branch slightly, the Guru should step over the threshold;
contracting his limbs, he should enter within, keeping his right side toward the interior.
In the Meru-tantra:
Having slightly contracted his limbs while touching the topknot with his left hand,
he clears away the obstacles and grants them passage on the right.
O Lord, one should enter the sacrificial pavilion with the right foot;
or else, in the Śākta path, one should proceed with the left foot foremost.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
One should worship Vāstveśa and Brahmā in the southwest,
and sprinkle the sacrificial pavilion with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and water for the arghya offering.
In the Meru Tantra.
One should worship Brahmā and Vāstvadhīśa in the south-western direction at the well-sprinkled sacrificial site with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and products of the cow (gavya).
In the *Śāradā*:
One should perform that purification up to the crossroads by means of inspection and other rites;
inspection with the root mantra and sprinkling with the Smara-mantra are prescribed.
With that very [mantra], one should perform the striking; sprinkling with the armor-mantra (*varma*) is prescribed.
The wise one should fumigate the interior with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor.
There, one should scatter the *vikīra* seeds, consecrated seven times with the weapon-mantra (*śarānu*).
[The substances are: saliva, sandalwood, white mustard, ashes, sprouts of *durvā* grass, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*).
Commanding them with the word "Vikirā," which destroys the entire multitude of obstacles,
one should sweep them away with handfuls of darbha grass consecrated by the Astra-mantra.
One should prepare a seat for the Vardhanī in the direction of Īśa (the northeast).
In the Meru Tantra:
Then one should perform the purification of the four doors through inspection and other rites;
having inspected them with the root mantra, one should then sprinkle them with the weapon mantra.

One should perform the striking with the Astra-mantra and sprinkle [the disciple] with the Kavaca-mantra; having fumigated him seven times with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, using the Astra-mantra.
Having recited the mantra over sandalwood paste, white mustard seeds, dūrvā grass, ashes, unbroken rice, and kuśa grass,
the practitioner should scatter them along with parched grain in the pavilion on the day that destroys obstacles.
The mantra-knower should sweep those [impurities] with a handful of *darbha* grass while reciting the *daṇḍa-mantra*;
then, he should place them for the sake of a seat upon the *vardhanī* vessel in the northeast.
Then, having caused the Brahmins to pronounce "an auspicious day" (puṇyāha), he should diligently satisfy them.
But in the case of the *somasaṃbhava*, however...
One should scatter either parched grains or pure fried rice, consecrated seven times with the Astra-mantra, sprinkled with water empowered by the Astra-mantra, and enveloped by the Kavaca-mantra.
These various forms of weapons, which ward off floods of obstacles,
are fashioned from *darbha* grass thirty-six *tāla*-lengths long and consisting of thirty-six blades.
"O best of beings, it is said that one should empower the fist with the Astra-mantra recited seven times."
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
Having caused the auspicious day to be proclaimed and having satisfied the brahmins,
one should draw [the deity] upon a pedestal in one of the pavilions already described.
The mandala is the Sarvatobhadra and so forth.
It is stated in the *Mera* that one should perform the examination while standing at the door prior to entering the pavilion; therefore, that procedure is now set forth.
In the Meru-tantra:
Having sat down at its door, he should then begin the examination;
he should give the disciple a tooth-stick consecrated with the root-mantra.
Having cleansed his teeth, the Guru should examine the site on a square plot of ground one cubit in size situated before him, and then cause the candidate to relinquish [his attachments].
That which is situated at the tip of the direction—therein lies this result from the east:
prosperity, heartache, the destruction of kinsmen, and likewise memory.
Grief, agitation, happiness, and the attainment of knowledge are the results in successive order.
If one falls upon an inauspicious place, one should perform expiation.
Or one may offer one thousand eight hundred and twenty oblations to the deities,
using their names conjoined with the Astra-mantra and suffixed with "svāhā."

If there are defects in this [rite], then one should offer oblations with clarified butter alone, reciting the verse beginning with "tadīty evam padam," while wearing the sacrificial garment; indeed, one should act in this very same way during bad dreams.
The tooth-stick should be offered again; if it is still defective, it should be offered four times over.
If it remains defective even on the third attempt, that particular deity should not be accepted.
On the left-hand path, even once, [the practice] may destroy both the teacher and the disciple.
Having thus examined, one should cause [the disciple] to enter.
This procedure is indeed possible, for there is no contingency that would render its constituent materials useless;
furthermore, this procedure, though established by tradition, is here explicitly set forth.
In that regard, the Sarvatobhadra mandala is as follows.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
In a square divided into four compartments and provided with diagonal threads,
one should likewise place four threads at the corners within each of the four compartments.
In such a way that there may be fish-shaped spaces at regular intervals,
the practitioner should drop [the lines] two each, extending from east to west and from south to north.
One should drop four equal threads upon those fish;
as before, one should drop the diagonal threads (karṇasūtra) in the corner squares.
The practitioner of mantra should cast the lines there according to the prescribed rite, up to two hundred and fifty-six steps.
One should draw a lotus with its characteristic features in the center using thirty-six squares;
the pedestal (pīṭha) should consist of one outer row, and the pathways (vīthīkāḥ) should consist of two rows.

The practitioner of mantras should fashion the deities named Śobhās for the beauty of the gates using the two remaining [deities] according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures; thereafter, he should draw a lotus.
Having abandoned the twelve-fold outer perimeter of the lotus-field,
the wise one should divide its center into three equal parts by means of circular lines.
The first [circle] should be the location of the pericarp (karṇikā), the second that of the filaments (keśara),
and the third that of the petals; the tips of the petals are formed by a portion of the pearls.
Having measured the space between the outer and inner perimeters according to the prescribed rule,
the wise one should place half-finger-breadths all around at the tips of the filaments.
Having marked the joints and established the positions, one should drop the lines there;
and with the same measurement as that of the tips of the petals, one should draw the circle.
Then, in that interval, in the middle of it, the wise one should draw the tips of the petals evenly on both sides of the thread using the outer hand.
One should arrange the filaments in pairs at the bases of the petals;
this is declared by those learned in the tantras to be the common lotus design.
One should sweep three squares for the purpose of the pedestal at the corners of the platform;
with the remaining squares, the wise one should fashion the limbs of the pedestal.
When one has swept the paths according to their arrangement,
one should then construct doors in the cardinal directions using two or four squares.
Then, on the two sides of the door, there should be *śobhās* consisting of three and one square respectively;
immediately thereafter, the *upaśobhās* should consist of one and three squares.
With the remaining six squares, one should form the four corners;
one should color that captivating mandala with five colors.
Yellow powder should be made from turmeric, white from rice,
red from safflower, and black from burnt husks.
That which is produced from leaves such as those of the bilva tree is called "śyāma" (dark-colored), and it is said to consist of five colors.
Now, the Sarvatobhadra-cakra as taught in the Meru-tantra.
Thereafter, one should draw the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala upon the altar;
listen to its procedure, for that which is heard is called auspicious.
One should construct square grids for the Dhṛtivargas;
one should fill the khadga, the crescent moon, and the three hexagons with the color white.
A black-colored chain is formed by five squares located at the corners;
on both sides of the chain, the squares of the creeper-stalks are blue.

The Śṛṅkhala [yantra] is auspicious for warding off fear; it consists of nine squares with Aruṇa at the center. The Vāpī [yantra], having white squares at the feet of the Jina, should have yellow boundary lines within.
In the center, one should encircle a beautiful sixteen-petaled lotus with white, red, and black [lines] on the outside; thus is the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala.
Now, [here is] the Sarvatobhadra mandala for the practitioners of Tantra.
In the Meru Tantra:
Now I shall further explain another matter which one should perform in Tantric rites:
square enclosures should be constructed, equal in size to the king’s [own] quarters.
In the center, one should erase six square compartments;
there, having excluded the outer portion which constitutes one-twelfth of the total length, one should then draw [the lines] from the middle.
Then, one should draw three equal circles in the center according to the rule:
the pericarp by the central circle, and the filaments by the second.
The petals are formed by the inner curve; from the abandoned portion, the petal-lobes are to be placed at the tips of the filaments, and half-moons are to be positioned on the sides.
In front of that, one should place the feet in three squares at the corners;
the remaining parts of the pedestal are formed by six squares thereafter, arranged in pairs.
Having swept the ground, one should construct the pathways in the four directions and in the center;
at the four gates, there should be two and four squares respectively.
By means of three compartments on each side of the door,
and likewise by three compartments on one side, the *śobhās* (ornamental projections) are formed.
Then, one should arrange the decorative borders (upaśobhās) filled with six compartments;
the white powder should consist of rice flour, and it should be equal in height and length.
The boundary lines, the petals, the body-parts of the pedestal, and the fourfold door should be made equal by means of a finger-measure; one should complete [the design] with that.
The petals should not be filled with red at all;
rather, they should be filled with safflower powder that is reddened.
The door-decorations and the feet of the pedestal should be determined by all colors;
the turmeric powder should be yellow, as should the interior of the pedestal and the pericarp.
O Brahmins, one should fill the decorative borders and the interior of the pedestal with green powder produced from the grinding of bilva leaves.
One should fill the junctions with *kalpavallī* creepers, the filaments with yellow and red,
and the *kalpavallī* creepers within the fourfold pathways in the center.
Adorned with the forms of leaves, roots, and fruits, and reaching to the heart,
the skillful Guru should conquer the stars with powders of various colors.
The corners [should be] black in color; then, one should decorate the three outer lines in sequence with powders known as white, reddish, and black.
This Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala is proclaimed in all tantras;
however, in this [text], the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala for the divine progenitors and others has been omitted due to a lack of necessity.

Now, according to other tantras, he states the distinction regarding colors: "Likewise, dust mixed with impurities and alkali is called 'red' (rakta). Another type of black [pigment] is mentioned in the *Prayogasāra*: "Black [pigment] is said to be the dust produced from the leaves of the *śyāma* tree, for auspicious rites. There are further particulars in other tantras.
If one is capable, however, and desires fierce accomplishment, then one should construct mandalas here with gems of that same color.
One should adorn it with pearls, topaz, emeralds, sapphires, and gold—these precious gems.
In the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*, its necessity is stated:
"The yellow ground is to be known [as the first], while the white is proclaimed as the initial one."
Fire is indeed red in color, while wind is proclaimed to be dark blue;
space, O great sage, is black in color as the fifth.
In white, Rudra is the presiding deity; in red, Brahmā and the other deities;
in yellow, Viṣṇu is the presiding deity; and in black, Acyuta is traditionally remembered as such.
O sinless one, I have declared that the presiding deity of the Śyāma [mantra] is the Nāga;
it destroys the affliction caused by the planets when it is white, and that arising from malefic groups when it is red.

The black [quality] destroys the enthusiasm of all the asuras; likewise, the blue [quality] destroys the Vaināyikī, Paiśācī, and Rākṣasī [energies], while the green [quality] destroys the quality of passion (rajas).
Therefore, during the fire-oblation, the consecration, and especially the sacrifice,
one should indeed fashion a maṇḍala, O God, for it brings about the satisfaction of the deity.
In the Sāradā [Tantra]:
The auspicious white boundary lines should be one finger-breadth in height and width;
the pericarp is yellow in color, and the filaments are orange.
The practitioner of mantra should color the petals with white pigment and their joints with black,
or else the pericarp itself may be yellow.
The filaments should be yellowish-red, and the petals likewise;
the joints should be black in color, or alternatively, white with a yellow center.
One should color the interiors of the pedestals; the lotuses should have the luster of red coral, and its limbs should be white in all four pathways.
One should draw wish-fulfilling creepers endowed with leaves and flowers,
variegated with various colors and captivating to the sight of all.
But in the Gautamīya [Vinaya], however:
Outside that, one should fashion four beautiful wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas),
graceful, covered in blossoms, and adorned with fruits and sprouts.
They were filled with aquatic and terrestrial flowers,
and abounded with swans, cranes, kāraṇḍava ducks, sūka birds, bees, and cuckoos.
It is said that the spaces between the branches are occupied by peacocks, ruddy geese, and other birds.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
The doors are red in color; the ornaments (śobhā) are said to be red;
the secondary ornaments (upaśobhā) are yellow in color; and the corners (koṇa) have a black luster.
One should draw three lines on the outside, white, red, and black in sequence;
this is known as the Sarvatobhadra mandala, which is common to all.
But in the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā, it is stated specifically:
Yellow should be placed in the east, white in the west, and likewise in the north;
red in the south, black, and pale-red (pātala) situated in the southeast (vahni).
In the southwest it is blue in color, in the northwest it is smoky-colored, and in the northeast it is designated as fair (gaura);
this is the sequence for the eight petals.

Then, having sat upon the seat and performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the placement of the letters (*mātṛkānyāsa*), the specific placements (*viśeṣanyāsa*), the internal worship, the preparation of the *argha* water, and so forth,
[he should place] the *ādhāra-śakti* and the others upon the lotus of the *sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala.
Having performed worship up to the *pīṭha-mantra*, one should perform the installation of the water-pot (*kalaśa*); such is the procedure common to all Tantras.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
The pitcher, fashioned by Hemādri, its interior washed with water consecrated by mantras,
fumigated with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, and possessing a beautiful form;
Its body is completely enveloped by a triple-stranded thread without any gaps;
it is adorned with perfumes, flowers, and the like, and provided with a *kūrca* grass-bundle and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
The practitioner, reciting the syllable *tāra*, should place [the vessel] whose interior contains the nine gems.
In the Meru Tantra.
There, a water-pot made of gold or other precious materials, free from any cracks,
should be wrapped on all sides externally with a triple-stranded thread.

The most excellent preceptor, having properly perfumed the center with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, should certainly install [the deity] while reciting the mantra according to the prescribed rite.
Having placed the nine gems and the pitcher with its wick-brush on top, one should set it down together with dūrvā grass, sandalwood paste, and unbroken grains of rice.
The nine gems are in that very place.
Blue flower-gem, lapis lazuli, coral, and likewise pearl;
then emerald, diamond, hessonite, and ruby.
In the *Tantrarāja*:
One should wrap twenty-seven blades of darbha grass, adorned with a braid and a knot;
that is proclaimed as the *kūrca* for all sacrifices.
In the Meru Tantra:
Twenty-seven long blades of Kuśa grass with their roots cut off,
joined at their tips with a Brahma-granthi, are here called a *kūrca*.
In the Sāradā [Tantra]:
The knower of the ritual procedure, having conceived the unity of the water-pot and the pedestal,
[should perform this] with a decoction of milk-tree bark or with that derived from the bark of the *palāśa* tree.
Or, with water from sacred fords, scented with camphor and fragrant flowers, one should ritually purify oneself according to the rules,
reciting the *mātṛkā* in reverse order while maintaining a sense of non-duality.
In the same manner, one should recite the root mantra and fill [the vessel] with the thought that it is the deity;
it should be completely filled with conch-water decoction, perfumed with the eight fragrances and the eight sweets.
Having beheld it, one should worship therein.
In the Meru Tantra.
Having recited the mantra from the beginning to the end in sequence, and having recited the Mātṛkā-mantra,
he should then recite the root mantra (mūlamantra) at the conclusion, contemplating the non-duality of his own self.
The best of practitioners should contemplate the breaking of the jar's pedestal;
immediately thereafter, he should fill it with decoctions of fifty-five medicinal herbs.
Just as with the medicinal herbs in that very same place.
These medicinal plants of various colors are accompanied by one [other];
they are sandalwood, that which is called red sandalwood, and likewise black sandalwood.
Camphor, milk, kuṣṭha, vālaka, and also keśara; kaṅkolaka, nutmeg, jaṭāmāṃsī, and likewise urā.
Granthika, rocanā, jātipatra, pippalī, bilvaka,
pṛṣṭiparṇī, citraka, and likewise lavaṅga and tṛṇa.
Kadūphala, guñjā, udumbara,
kāśmarī, padmaka-wood, śaṅkhapuṣpī, and likewise the crest of a peacock.
Plakṣa, agni, mantha, as well as mudgaparṇī, kuśa, pāṣāṇabheda, kṛṣṇa-śaṅkhapuṣpī, and rohiṇa.
Syonāka, bṛhatī, pāṭalī, mukhakarikā,
tulasī, śikharī, indravallī, and the one called bhṛṅgī, O King.
Then Aparājitā, Tālamūlī with palms joined in reverence,
Dūrvā, the maiden known as Śrīdevikā, Bhārgava, and Bhadramuṣṭaka.
And these fifty are devoid of the latent tendencies (anuśaya).
And furthermore, in that very same place:
With decoctions of the bark of milk-exuding trees such as the *brahmabhūru* (udumbara) and *kṛmighna* (nimba),
or with auspicious waters scented with fragrant pastes, musk, and the like.
Having filled the conch with water such as decoctions and the like, one should stir it within that vessel.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]: "Having invoked all the kalās..."
First, there are the ten digits (kalās) of Fire, then the twelve of each of the twelve Ātman-s, and also the sixteen of Soma; thereafter are the fifty digits.
Having recited the root mantra in reverse order,
the knower of mantras should meditate upon the deity of the mantra with a concentrated mind.
The wise practitioner should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of vital breath) therein;
he should then pour the decoction, which consists of the *kalās* and is situated within the conch, into the pitcher.
In the Meru-tantra:
Having recited the verse beginning with "haṃsaḥ śuciṣat," one should perform worship;
having performed the installation of the vital breaths (prāṇa), one should worship those [deities] of the kalās.
In the Śāradā-tantra, he states the eightfold offering of perfumes (gandhāṣṭaka).
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, coraka, saffron, gorocana,
jaṭāmāṃsī, and kapi— these eight, when combined with śakti, are known as the eight fragrances (gandhāṣṭaka).
In the Meru-tantra:
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, coraka, saffron, gorocana,
jaṭāmāṃsī, and musk— these are known as the eight fragrances of Śakti.
Thus [it is said].
"Gold and so forth"—by the word "and so forth," silver and the like are included; "thief" refers to what is commonly known as *bheda* or *ura*.
The "Kapi-grantha" is well known as the *Mana*; [it is found] in the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra*.
A beautiful vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even earthenware,
provided it is free from defects and smeared with sandalwood paste.
The measurement of the water-pot, however, is [given] in the Mantrarāja.
The width [of the base] of the jars shall be fifty finger-breadths, their height sixteen finger-breadths,
and the mouth shall be eight finger-breadths.
And also the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā.
34b) It may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay;
it should be strewn with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), and honored with blades of kuśa grass and sprouts of dūrvā grass.
There is a specific distinction in another tantra-sutra.
With a triple-stranded thread made from the fibers of the *kanyā-kartika* plant,
one should wrap it evenly all around with the armor-mantra (*varman*), which consists of the three qualities (*guṇatraya*).
In the Meru Tantra.
Then, one should firmly tie shoots of the Aśvattha, Panasa,
and Cūta trees to the mouth of that jar with an Indu-vāruṇī creeper.
And one should visualize the presiding Kalpavṛkṣa tree above the flask;
[and] that vessel, filled with rice and accompanied by a coconut fruit.
For this is indeed the fruit of the wish-fulfilling tree; the presiding deity should establish it there.
Then, one should wrap the jar with a pair of silk cloths.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
Afterwards, the Guru [honored him] with tender sprouts of the *aśvattha*, *panasa*, and *cūta* trees,
entwined with *indravallī*, regarding them as if they were the essence of all trees.
Having fashioned a pot-mouthed vessel, he should place upon it a cup containing fruit and unbroken rice,
according to the ritual rules for the wish-fulfilling trees, with the intention that it be fruitful.
Then, one should wrap the pitcher with a pair of stainless linen cloths;
having worshipped the form [of the deity] with the root mantra, [one should place it] upon this branch of the wish-fulfilling trees.
Having invoked [the deity], the practitioner of mantras should worship the deity of that mantra within it.
Likewise.
One should extend the limbs up to the world-protectors (lokapālas), as well as the enclosures (āvaraṇas).
In the Meru Tantra:
This is proclaimed as the installation of the principal pitcher;
now, in the directions beginning with the east, near the archways (toraṇas).
One may construct mandalas according to one's desire, including those with eight petals; above each, one should place a heap of rice at every door.
Above that, one should worship the Full Vase (pūrṇakalaśa) and there the conscious principles:
Dhruva in the east, Dharā on the right, Vāk in the west, and Utatya in the north.
Then, one should properly place the jars for Vighneśa in the directions starting from the southeast (Agneya),
and worship Amṛta, Durjaya, Siddhārthaka, and Maṅgala.

Furthermore, one should worship Indra and the other guardians of the world (lokapālas) in order within the directions starting from the east, both in the mandalas and upon the water-pots (kumbhas), with their respective mantras.
Airāvata, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Kumuda, Añjana, Puṣpadanta, Sārvabhauma, and Supratīka were positioned at its front.
In the case of the *pañcāyatana* initiation, one should establish five pitchers (*kalaśas*), invoke the deities therein, and worship them;
for it is stated in the *Prapañcasāra*: "The rite of the pitcher is performed either by this single method as described, or by means of multiple jars."
In the *Jñānamālā*, a specific rule for the installation of deities is stated:
"But when one should worship Śaṅkara in the center and Śrīpati in the northeast."
35a) O Haṃsa,
likewise Bhavānī,
who is compassionate toward her devotees, is always to be worshipped in the southeast, the southwest [as] the son of Pārvatī, and in the northwest.
But when one worships Govinda in the center, Śaṅkara in the northeast,
Gaṇanātha in the southeast, and likewise Tapana in the southwest;
The practitioner, with a concentrated mind, should worship Ambikā in the northwest,
the thousand-rayed sun in the center, and the Lord of Pārvatī in the northeast.
One should worship Ekadanta in the southeast and Acyuta in the southwest;
one should worship the Goddess, the sole ground for enjoyment and liberation, in the northwest.
When Bhavānī is in the center, one should worship Mādhava in the northeast,
Pārvatīnātha in the southeast, and Gaṇanāyaka in the southwest.
The preceptor should worship Pradyotana in the northwest;
when Heramba is in the center, one should worship Acyuta in the northeast.
The practitioner, indeed unwearied, should worship the five-faced one in the southeast, Jagadambikā in the southwest,
and Dyumaṇi in the northwest.
Devas who have been deprived of their own stations bring about grief, suffering, and fear;
consequently, the king and the practitioner situated within that mandala perish.
In another tantra:

When Śambhu is situated in the center, Hari, Hara, Bhūdevī, Harī, Śakra, Bhāsya, Nāgasutā, Arava, Haragaṇeśa, Ajā, Ambikā, Viṣṇu, Devī, Hari, Ekadanta, Rava, Yau, Lambodara, Jaiśvara, Arya, and Inā are established starting from the portion of Śaṅkara. When Devī is in the center, Viṣṇu, Hari, Ekadanta, Rava, Yau, Lambodara, Jaiśvara, Arya, Inā, Śaṅkara, Bhāga, and so forth are established starting from the portion of Śaṅkara.
These, when stated in reverse order, are said to be the causes of loss.
In the Meru Tantra:
Then the Guru, having gone to his own altar, should sit upon his seat;
the most excellent Guru, having meditated upon the Form [of the deity] therein with the root mantra.
The sequence of worship, however, is found in another tantra.
Having offered a handful of flowers to the principal deity, there should be worship of Gaṇeśa and the others;
however, if Gaṇeśa alone is the principal deity, then the sequence beginning with Sūrya should be followed.
In the Cāmuṇḍā Tantra:
In the case of Śyāmā, Bhairavī, Tārā, Chinnamastā,
Subhairavī, Mañjughoṣa, and likewise Raudrī, the five-limbed [nyāsa] is not prescribed by the wise.
The five-limbed sacrifice consists of the initiation into the fivefold sanctuary.
In the Meru Tantra.
Having prepared an excellent sacrificial mound on the southern side of the altar,
and having established and consecrated the fire, one should commence the Vaiśvadeva rite.
Then, according to the prescribed rule, one should worship the deity there with perfumes and other offerings;
having first offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by the *praṇava*.
One should offer oblations with the root mantra using milk-rice and clarified butter;
thereafter, one should again offer twenty-five oblations with the *avyāhṛti* formulas.
One should worship [the deity] with sandalwood and other offerings and install it in the form of the pedestal (pīṭhamūrti).
Having dismissed the fire, one should offer a bali-oblation with the remaining milk-rice (pāyasa).
To the attendants, [offer] sandalwood paste and so forth, together with flowers and unbroken rice grains.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to the south and having placed the invited deity upon it,
the wise one, having performed the purificatory rites according to rule, should worship the deity.
There, having worshipped the deity whose form has been released with perfumes and other offerings,
the knower of mantras should offer oblations with the Tāra and the Vyāhṛtis, and with the root mantra.
Having offered twenty-five oblations of milk-rice mixed with clarified butter while reciting the *avyāhṛti* formulas, one should again worship [the deity] with perfumes and other offerings.
Having joined that [mantra] to the image placed upon the pedestal, one should dismiss the fire;
with the remaining oblation, one should scatter the bali offering all around.
To the attendants of the deity, [one should offer] accompanied by scents, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
Here, by the term *vaiśvadeva*, only the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*) is intended; this is according to the etymological interpretation established in the *Kaumudī* regarding all deities.
This consecration of the fire (*vahnisaṃskāra*) is indeed distinct from the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*), because of the scriptural injunction;

for it is stated in the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā* that "rites such as the formal establishment of the fire (*agnyādhāna*) do not exist in the daily fire-oblation," and thus there is an absence of fire-consecration in the *nityahoma*. Furthermore, after this oblation, [the rite is performed] in the common (*laukika*) fire.
In the Jñānārṇava.
Then, O Goddess, having sprinkled [the area], one should perform the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma).
O Mistress of the Gods, one should offer five oblations in sequence with the root mantra.
One should know that the nature of the five āhūtis consists of prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna.

Rāghavabhaṭṭa has stated that the oblation (homa) must be performed based on the scriptural injunction: "Six oblations [are offered] in the six limbs; this is declared to be the daily homa. However, this is to be considered doubtful, because in no other tantra is the Vaiśvadeva ritual ever heard of as being an integral part of that procedure.
In the Agastyasaṃhitā:
"It is recorded that for the obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya) rites, this [fire] is the mouth;

for even in the case of the obligatory fire-oblation (nityahoma), the consecration of the fire (vahnisaṃskāra) is prescribed. Therefore, the truth is that regarding the obligatory fire-oblation, there is indeed an option between the *Śāradā* and the *Jñānārṇava*.
In the Meru Tantra.
The practitioner, with a concentrated mind, should recite the root mantra one thousand times;
then, having offered that recitation to the deity, he should dedicate it for the sake of prosperity.
In the northeastern direction, that which was previously established as a scattering-offering (vikira) should be joined with gold and cloth, and filled with water-pots and *karaja* flowers.
One should install and worship here the deity of the Astra-mantra, who is of a terrible form,
holding a bow and a shield with her two rear hands, and seated upon a lion.
Standing there and having worshipped him, one should then take hold of him and circumambulate him;
then one should recite, "May the Lords of the World protect this."
Then, making the command of the deity heard with water poured from the mouth of the vessel,
one should place it in its own place and thereafter worship it with the *tatutphaṭ* mantra.
Having sat down, the best of those who know mantras should again worship with perfumes and other offerings;
then, having properly consecrated the fire, he should cook the sacrificial oblation (caru).
Having washed a vessel made of new copper or other materials with the *śara* mantra,
and then consecrated it with the root mantra, one should take rice grains produced from the *śāli* variety.
Chanting the *śaraṇu* mantra according to the measure of the expansion of the lunar day (*tithi*),
one should cast [the water] while covering the mouth with a washed vessel.
Then, with the mantra *hūṃ* and the root mantra, the preceptor, the best of teachers, facing eastward, should cook it; once cooked, he should sprinkle this [liquid] over [the disciple].
Then, one should pour [the remainder] using the *mūla-mantra* with the clarified butter situated in the *śruva* ladle;
it should be cast upon the *kuśa* grass spread out over which the *astra-mantra* has been recited with the syllable *huṃ*.
One portion from the three parts should be offered to the deity, and another should be presented into the fire;
the preceptor, who knows the mantras, should then eat the remainder together with the disciple.
Having consecrated with mantras a tooth-stick of the prescribed length, one should give it to the disciple; after cleaning his teeth with it, he should discard it after rinsing.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
Having recited the root mantra one thousand times with undistracted mind,
he should offer that recitation to the deity for the sake of all prosperity.
Then, in the direction of Śambhu, the preceptor should scatter [the grains] from a water-pot filled with water and joined with gold, cloth, and other items, using those previously collected.
Having established upon her [the goddess] who is seated on a lion, bearing a sword and a shield,
of terrible form and facing west, one should worship the deity of the weapon (astra-devatā).
One should worship the deity of the weapon with a moving seat.
Having honored the preceptor once again with the *calāsana* rite,
he should [protect him] with water joined with the mantras of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), beginning with "rakṣa" (protect).
Having caused the command of the deity to be heard, turning inward and circumambulating to the right,
one should recite the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra) and install [the deity] as before.
Having worshipped him again with perfumes and other offerings, he, remaining steady in his posture,
should cook the sacrificial porridge (caru) with cow's milk in the consecrated fire.
In a vessel made of silver, copper, or other materials, which has been cleansed with a weapon-mantra,
one should place rice grains produced from the *śāli* variety, consecrated with the root mantra.
Having cast fifteen handfuls [of water] with the Astra mantra, one should recite the Astra mantra;
then, having washed the mouth of the vessel, one should cover it with the Kavaca mantra.
Facing east, the preeminent teacher should cook the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the root mantra;
once it is prepared, he should pour hot clarified butter over it using the *śruva* ladle.

Afterwards, with the *mūla-mantra*, the preceptor should lower that vessel with the *kavaca-mantra* onto the mandala which has been strewn with *kuśa* grass and consecrated with the *astra-mantra*, according to the prescribed rite.
Having divided that into three parts, one should assign one portion to the deity,
offer another into the fire, and the preceptor himself should consume the remaining portion.

One should eat together with the disciple once the mind has been thus prepared; and this refinement is called "saṃskṛta" (refined), because it is a consecration performed by the preceptor within the preceptor’s own sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), as it is the duty of the preceptor to perform it.
This has been stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
Having sprinkled the sacrificial pit with the mantra and placed the fire there,
one should then duly worship the deity, beginning with the rite of placing the firewood (sāmnādhāna).
"Having prepared the husked rice, one should cook the *caru* in that milk.

"Another [priest] should offer oblations into the fire"—the remainder [of the sentence] is "the teacher (*ācārya*) and the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*"); the sequence for that is given in that very same [text].
Having described the fire-purification (agni-saṃskāra) to be performed by the preceptor (ācārya) in the preceptor’s sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Then, in other consecrated pits as well, according to the prescribed rite.
The preceptor, being composed, should place the fire in the eastern and other directions.

The officiating priests, having worshipped him along with the limbs (aṅgas) and the surrounding deities (āvaraṇas) as prescribed in the Tantra, using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, twenty-five times;
It is stated that they should offer oblations with clarified butter using the root mantra, and likewise with the sacrificial porridge (caru) mixed with clarified butter.

Regarding the consecration of the other fire-pits (kuṇḍas), the specific distinction here is that while the officiating priests perform it, the disciple also participates; furthermore, in the *Somasaṃbhava*, one should take a third part of the caru, measured by three mouthfuls.
Or it should be the measure of eight morsels, avoiding contact with the teeth.
Having placed [the food] in a cup made of *pālāśa* wood for the sake of liberation, or on a leaf of the *pippala* tree for the sake of enjoyment,
the practitioner, feeding [the deity] with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, should cause [him] to sip pure water.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
Having brought the disciple who has sipped water and performed the ritual purification (sakalīkṛta),
the preceptor [should take] a staff of the height of a palm tree, made from a milk-tree or similar wood, over which the heart-mantra has been recited.
Then he should give a tooth-stick to the disciple whose mind is humble;
having carefully cleansed his teeth and rinsed [the stick], he should dismiss it.
In the Nārāyaṇīya [section].
Having consecrated a tooth-stick produced from a milk-tree or similar source with the *hṛdaya-mantra*,
one should rub the teeth with it, bite off [the end], rinse it, and cast it upon the ground.
In the directions starting from the east, including the zenith and nadir, its falling upon the tip [of the needle] occurs in sequence, resulting respectively in:
prosperity, suffering, death, loss of wealth, peace, disease, and gain.
It has been stated previously as well, according to the opinion of Meru, that happiness is supreme growth while suffering is the opposite; these are the fruits that exist incessantly.
In another tantra:
Then, a tooth-stick of the mango tree measuring twelve finger-breadths should be provided here; it should be chewed by the tips of the teeth.
One should cast the upward-marked [line] there into that mandala and raise the pedestal;
if the auspicious fall occurs in the northeast of Rudra, it is auspicious, otherwise it is inauspicious.
One should perform a hundred oblations with the mantra for the destruction of evil omens.
37a) In the Meru Tantra:
Thereafter, one should perform the examination of dreams; the procedure for that is now stated:
[it applies] to those of the Vedic tradition, the Dakṣiṇas, the Vaiṣṇavas, and the Vāmas.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules, protected by the binding of the topknot (śikhābandha),
and having prepared the altar with a layer of darbha grass together with the mantra, the Guru [proceeds].
One should sleep on that [bed] for that night; this is declared to be the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa).
In the Nārāyaṇīya [section].

Then, having caused that disciple— who has performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and is protected by the binding of the topknot (śikhābandha)— to lie down upon a bed of darbha grass on the altar together with him, the Guru should sleep there.
In the Meru Tantra:
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) according to the rules and having bound that well-protected mantra upon his crest-lock (*śikhā*),
the practitioner should lie down upon the altar on a bed of *kuśa* grass together with this disciple; thus is described the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*).
In the Piṅgalāmata:
Relying upon the dream-man, one should cause [the patient] to sleep with the head facing eastward.
Somaśambhu also [says]:
He should place the householders on a bed of *darbha* grass with their heads to the east, protected by the *astra-mantra*;
and the ascetics (*yatīs*) on a bed of ashes with their heads to the south, using the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
In the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā.
On the right side of the deity, the pure disciple should be made to dwell upon a bed covered with a fresh spread and strewn with grass.
Having consecrated it with mantras and meditating on Śiva, he should sleep at night with his head toward the east;
then, the Guru, having tied the thread around the disciple's crest-lock, should fasten that crest-lock with the [thread].
Having wrapped it with a new cloth and covered it with armor,
one should draw three lines all around with ashes, sesame seeds, and mustard seeds.
Having performed the recitation of the weapon-mantra, one should offer oblations to the lords of the directions outside of that.
In the Mahākapila-pañcarātra.
Having performed the worship of the Guru’s feet, fasting and with senses subdued, one should lie upon a bed of darbha grass at night; having seen a dream, one should report it.
In the Meru-tantra, and also in the Yoginī-tantra.

That which rises far from one while awake, the deity, the ritual action, the mantra, and the three-fold oblation— these the practitioner, being restrained, should observe during sleep, eating light food and lying on his right side, according to the instruction.
In the Meru-tantra:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, wielder of the trident, whose vehicle is the bull:
declare to me, as I sleep, that which is eternally desired and undesired.
Thus, having slept upon a bed strewn with kusha grass with a disciplined mind,
he beholds at the end of the night a dream, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
Also in the Merutantra, in the section revealing the Mantra-tantra:
Oṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu, the all-pervading lord, the source of all worlds, the universe itself, whose form is the universe, and the sovereign of dreams.
37b) This mantra of the Dream-Manava has been taught by Nārada and others; [one should recite it] while fasting and with senses subdued— this is the variant reading.
Having gone to a bed of darbha grass at night, one shall see a dream exactly as it will be.
The Nāradīya.
O Lord, you who are the very nature of the Supreme Brahman, you move within the universe as its sustainer;
O God, reveal to me the auspicious and inauspicious course of my dream.
Having uttered this, one should pay homage while kneeling upon the ground;
being pleased and restrained in speech, one should lie down and contemplate the desired object.
In the Meru Tantra.
Having eaten, one should sleep on a very clean bed or upon the surface of the earth;
then, having risen at midnight and performed the cleansing of the feet.
Having sipped water (ācamana), recollected the deity, and worshipped Him with the five offerings (pañcaka),
he should contemplate the oneness of Śiva and the deity, and recite this [mantra].
Homage to the unborn, the three-eyed, the tawny-hued, the Great Soul;
homage to the left-handed one, to the one whose form is the universe, to the Lord of Dreams!
"O Maheśvara, tell me daily in my dreams everything regarding all matters without exception; by your grace, O Great Lord, I shall accomplish the success of my undertakings."
Listen attentively, O gods and goddesses, to the procedure by which dreams arise for both those who have been initiated and those who have not.
On an auspicious day, at the conclusion of the worship of the Sun, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
one should then perform oblations with bilva leaves soaked in ghee, numbering one-tenth of that amount.
Having performed the libation and the ritual sprinkling, one should provide a meal for the Brahmins;
then his mantra becomes perfected, and it reveals in a dream whatever he desires.
In the Merutantra and also in the Piṅgalāmata.
*Tāra*, *hili* twice, *śūlapāṇaye*, and *dviṭha* (svāhā) is proclaimed;
this twelve-syllable mantra is said to be for the human [aspirant] in a dream.
Now, auspicious dreams, according to the Yoginītantra.
Their vision is of three kinds: that which is according to reality, that which is not according to reality, and the vision of those who are self-restrained, well-established, and free from passion.
That which arises from the transformation of those who are ill-situated is according to reality.
That which is not born of the senses and is mental is said to have a result that corresponds to reality.
In the established doctrine of the Āgamas.
From the first year, digestion occurs in the second watch after half a year; in the third watch, it occurs after a quarter of a year;
in the fourth watch of the night, it occurs immediately; and that which is seen in the emissions [of semen] occurs instantly.
In the Meru Tantra:
A dream occurring in the first watch of the night bears fruit within one year;
one arising in the second watch bears fruit in six months; and one from the third watch bears fruit in three months.
If, however, within only the fourth month, there is quickly, at the time of dawn,
a slight and long-lasting pain of anxiety, that result does not exist at all.
38a) Due to a predominance of wind (vāta), there occurs a dream preceded by rashness and flight;
due to bile (pitta), [dreams of] fire, light, yellow and so forth, as well as anger and the like.

One afflicted by Vāta should consume a meal beginning with milk-porridge; one afflicted by Valā should do so in the morning; and one afflicted by Pitta should take it at midday, as it soothes the eyes.
From phlegm (kapha) you always have urinary disorders; why then, when two [humors] are combined, do you not have [disorders] for each pair, even among the three?
In the established doctrine of the Āgama.
In the Krūra, Dhamā, Madhyamā, Adṛṣṭa, Anuttama, and Uttama [breaths],
one indeed beholds in a dream the deity of one's own choice, who faces in all directions.
I bow to the Guru, who is gracious, with a serene countenance, and as pure as the orb of the moon;
to Gāṃ, Gāṃ, Gāṃ, the goddess Bhāratī; and to the Sun, the wearer of the Liṅga, the divine Liṅga itself.
One should know that success is attained there when [the deity] appears clearly in a dream.
In the Nāradapañcarātra.
The acquisition of land, the crossing of the ocean of blood, the worship of fire,
the performance of oblations in a blazing fire, and likewise victory in battle.
And the mounting of chariots by swans, cuckoos, and peacocks.
In the Mahākapila-pañcarātra.
A maiden, an umbrella, a chariot, a lamp, a palace,
a lotus, a river, an elephant, a bull, a garland, the ocean, and a fruit-bearing tree.
Upon seeing a mountain, a sacrificial horse, raw meat, wine, spirits, and all such things as these, one shall attain success.
In the Meru-tantra:
To the Siddha, one's own father-in-law, the God, the pleased one,
the maiden, Gaṃ Gāṃ Gāṃ, Bhāratī, the Sun, the wearer of the Liṅga, and the Īśvara-liṅga.
A tail-feather, an umbrella, a chariot, a lamp, a palace,
a lotus, a river, an elephant, a bull, a garland, the ocean, and a fruit-bearing tree.
He shines like a blazing mountain, like raw flesh and liquor,
like the planets, the moon, the sun, jewels, and ornaments.
A lion-throne, a celestial chariot, a banner, a royal consecration,
white sandalwood, garments, śāli rice, saffron, and honey.
The king, Siddhārthaka, women, and neither the vessel nor the milk-rice;
the horse, fruits, prepared food, curd, and a beautiful courtesan.
Milk, musical instruments, a blue jay, a peacock, a mongoose, a deer,
a single bound animal, flowers, virtuous speech, and collyrium for the eyes.
A full water-pot, a mirror, a fish, yellow pigment (rocanā),
a corpse devoid of weeping, weapons, and small banners.
O Bhāradvāja, he [perceived] the Vedic sounds of the kings, their singing,
the auspicious songs of the whip, the goad, and whatever was dear to their hearts.
If the practitioner sees these in a dream, he shall attain accomplishment.
For one afflicted by disease or poverty, there is no suffering; he shall attain ordinary happiness when,
in dreams, he beholds a woman during rites performed for desired ends.
He beheld one desiring to cross the river Sindhu, wandering about,
the rising of the sun, and the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
Ascending a palace, a temple, an elephant, a mountain, or fire;
eating food with curd and boiled rice, and the consumption of raw meat.
Smearing oneself with worms and excrement, sprinkling oneself with blood,
chewing betel, drinking liquor, and saluting curd— these are [prohibited].
The fierce rays of the sun are a sign of the successful accomplishment of one's own purpose;
likewise, a woman wearing black garments and anointed with black perfumes and unguents [is a favorable omen].
If one embraces someone in a dream during the final watch of the night,
there will be illness through blood and sorrow through that which is similar to the dawn.
If she is stained with blood, there will be strife and slaughter; if she is yellow, there will be quarrels. A woman wearing white garments, white garlands, and white unguents [indicates prosperity].
In his dreams, prosperity embraces him from every side—
whether upon his seat, his bed, his vehicle, his carriage, or his house.
If one awakens while it is blazing, his prosperity will be manifest in every direction;
if a bite from a white serpent occurs on the right hand, [the same result follows].
Within ten days there will be gain; the sick person is freed from disease;
or one may be bound by fetters or arm-cords, or a son may be born.
His stability increases by drinking milk, while the loss of wealth occurs from drinking liquor;
by drinking blood, a Brahmin may obtain knowledge, and another may obtain great wealth.

Seeing curd, there will be joy; with wheat, the arrival of wealth; one should know that with *siddhā* (a type of grain), there is the arrival of a messenger; and likewise, with white mustard seeds (*siddhārthaka*), there is gain.
From obtaining curd there will be wealth; from obtaining ghee, certain victory;
from eating ghee, distress regarding wealth; but from eating curd, victory.
Having seen the worship of the *liṅga* and other [emblems], one shall attain victory in worldly affairs;
moreover, he who eats ghee and iron in the midst of a pond or similar body of water [shall likewise succeed].
One should know that he who remains unshaken upon a lotus leaf is a lord of the earth;
for deities, Liṅgas, cows, ancestors, Brahmins, and kings [all depend] on him.
One who sees five tusks in a dream will find it to be exactly so;
likewise, one who sees intestines encircling a village or a city [will experience the same].
In a village there shall be a mandala kingdom; in a city one shall become a sovereign.
There will also be the eclipsing of the moon, stars, and sun, as well as extensive searching.
On earth, there shall be the seizing of wealth, the slaying of enemies,
victory in marriages and at dice, and likewise triumph over one's foes.
The milking of mares, buffaloes, lionesses, cows, female elephants, and so forth;
and the favor of gurus, the most excellent brahmins, gods, siddhas, and others, which is auspicious.
Bathing, royal consecration, the severing of one's own head, death,
crossing over waters at sacred fords (tīrtha), and likewise leaping over a precipice;
The birth of a cow, a bull, or a mare, as well as the acquisition of fire;
the embrace of another man by her, and likewise the acquisition of that [embrace], and even weeping.
Anointing with poison, the sight of the *kunda*, *jātī*, *vakula*, and *kṣmeśa* flowers,
victory in battles, gambling, and conflicts, and imprisonment in fetters.
Today there will be the acquisition of livestock and wild animals, as well as overeating;
one will possess the luster of a peacock's crest, wear white garments, and apply flowers and sandalwood paste.
When the practitioner sees food in a vessel made of jewels, pearls, gold, and so forth, then it should be known that accomplishment is at hand.
For those distressed by their tasks, there shall be the accomplishment of their business; for those with lines of the feet, there shall be the arrival of wealth.
Now, the inauspicious dreams.
The skin of a barren woman, chaff-fire, and so forth; salt, charcoal, and fuel; excrement, a eunuch, a madman, oils, matted hair, and medicinal herbs.

A renunciant [is auspicious] when he has cast off diseases like grass; one afflicted by hunger when he has abandoned his attachment; one with disheveled hair when he has fallen from his station; and a lizard or a sneeze when blood flows from the limbs.
A fight between cats, cotton, a pregnant woman,
a female donkey, molasses, buttermilk, a saffron-robed ascetic, and a quarrel among five men in the house.
[The results are] the burning of one's own clothing and so forth, as well as conflict with a buffalo; likewise, blindness, being humpbacked, foul speech, deafness, and being both lame and humpbacked.
A person vomiting, one who has just emerged from a water-pot, a washerwoman, and one wearing soiled garments—if these are seen, no purpose will be achieved; the sick man shall meet with death.
Having seen the Aśoka, the Karavīra, or even the flowering Pālāśa tree,
or having seen water even in a dream, a man shall encounter sorrow.
Entering another form, as well as traveling toward the southern direction,
and sinking into mud and bathing— these bring about the destruction of one's son and wife.
It is not auspicious for a cowherd, a householder, a twice-born, a brahmin, or others to wear black [garments];
nor is it auspicious for one who is wearing red perfumes and garments and adorned with garlands to face the south while dressed in black.
If one sees a house-camel mounted by a buffalo, he shall not live for three months;
or if a dog enters his house through the door, his life is likewise closed.
And for him who does not rise from that state, his life has reached its end;
he vomits urine and feces, and there is the cessation of the continuity of rebirth.
He who sees white [objects] in a dream has a lifespan of ten months;
he is assailed by deformed, black men with raised weapons.
Or if he is struck with stones, his death is certain, without a doubt;
likewise for one mounted upon a buffalo, a bull, or a donkey, who is smeared with oil and shaven-headed.
39b) For one who sets out on a journey, there is no doubt that death will come;
he shall see the collapse of a palace or the falling of the moon and sun from the sky.
There shall be a displacement from their positions for both mountains and trees,
as well as the wasting away of one's own limbs and being overcome by disease.
The house was swept and smeared with either cow dung or clay;
having crossed the river, he arrived at the bank and put on another garment.
