And upon all the girdles, one should arrange a garland of lamps.
In the Tripurāsārasamuccaya.
In a pit with a single girdle, the sharpened intelligence [is placed] below the girdle;
in a pit with two girdles, it is on top of the second girdle.
Then, one should place [the syllable] upon the intermediate girdle above the triple-girdled [seat].
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
One should place the enclosing sticks (paridhis) in the various directions, excluding the east, with the heaviest one [placed] in the north.
Likewise, in the Merutantra:
In a pit with a single girdle, one should spread [the grass] below the girdle;
in a pit with two girdles, on the second [girdle]; or in a pit with three girdles, on the middle one.
Kātyāyana says:
They place the enclosing sticks around [the fire], which are fresh, from a single tree or from various trees, reaching the height of the arms, and made of palāśa, vaikaṅkata, kāśmarya, or bilva wood.
In the Meru Tantra.
They say that the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) should be made from the Palāśa, Kāśmarī, Bilva,
and Vikaṅkata trees, or from a single tree, and they should be fresh.
In that interval.
One should carry forth the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), provided with three enclosures and strewn with darbha grass whose tips point toward the east.
Also in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*: "Then, on a mound of sand, one should place the three enclosing stones (paridhis) outside."
In the Meru-tantra.
One should spread sand upon a sacrificial mound or over the ground of the site.
In that very same [text], 44a).
Having performed breath control according to the rules and having strewn it with intermediate kuśa grasses,
one should proceed according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra, starting from the east of the wind-point.
The *sruk* and *srūva* ladles, the *praṇītā* vessel, the pair of *prokṣaṇī* vessels,
the clarified butter pot (*ājyasthālī*), the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), the fuel (*idhma*), and handfuls of *kuśa* grass.

Then, one should arrange all the vessels with their openings facing downward, as well as the materials for the oblation, the sacrificial offering (bali), and the perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth.
Having sprinkled those [grains] with water and placed them face upwards with a strainer,
one should fill the pair of *prokṣaṇī* vessels with auspicious water.

Having offered the unbroken grains (akṣata) and the purifier (pavitra), one should place that vessel containing the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) in the northern direction; that vessel is called *praṇītā* by the wise.
Then, having placed a small amount of consecrated water in the *prokṣaṇī* vessel,
one should sprinkle the collection of sacrificial implements with that water while reciting the root mantra.
One should choose a peaceful Brāhmaṇa who has been initiated into the deity-mantras and seat him upon a cushion of Kuśa grass on the southern side of the sacrificial pit.
"I, belonging to such-and-such a lineage and being the son of such-and-such a lineage,
choose you as Brahmā for this homa which is a constituent part of the initiation."
One should honor him by clothing him with garments, ornaments, and so forth;
or one may employ a *kuśa*-grass boy if no Brāhmaṇa is available.
In the center of the pit (kuṇḍa), there is a lotus containing a hexagon, with golden filaments,
endowed with various stamens, and surrounded by four gates.
One should visualize an eight-petaled lotus surrounded by three squares;
that is the worship pedestal of Fire, wherein one should [place] Maṇḍūkaka and the others.
Having worshipped the Yoga-pīṭha ending with Jñānātman, one should worship on the eight petals,
proceeding clockwise toward the center, the yellow, white, and likewise red [energies].
One should worship Kṛṣṇā, Dhūmrā, Tīvrā, Visphuliṅginī,
Rucirā, and Jvālinī, and thus worship the entire pīṭha.
"Omnipotent one, to the lotus-seated one"— this twelve-syllable mantra of the heart is proclaimed as the mantra of Fire for the worship of all sacred seats (pīṭhas).
Then one should meditate upon the Fire-god (Hutāśana), who is perfectly resplendent with arms joined by the Varada, Svastika, Śakti, and Abhaya mudrās.
The color of vermilion, seated upon a lotus, adorned with golden ornaments,
three-eyed, with matted hair and a crown, and wearing red garlands and saffron-colored garments.
The intermediate dhyāna is described in the Śāradā [Tantra].

One should meditate upon the Fire-god, who is the color of hibiscus, adorned with golden ornaments, seated upon a lotus, possessing three eyes, and wearing his matted locks bound in a crown; he holds aloft the sacrificial ladle (śakti), the svastika, and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) in his long arms.
Also in the Rudrayāmala:
Resembling the bandhūka flower and possessing the luster of well-refined gold,
seated upon a lotus for the sake of the patron, and adorned with two faces.
O King, this [palace] situated atop the celestial mansion consists of the seven meters;
it has three necks, four feet, and is the destroyer of the offerings to gods and ancestors.
Adorned with the four horns of the Brahman, Adhvaryu, Udgātṛ, and Hotṛ,
[it consists of] the Pañcarātra, Pāśupata, Kāpila, and Mahāmata systems.
This [work], consisting of six chapters on Buddhist and Vedic topics, has Piṅgala as its eye;
it contains the meaning of the Vedas and the resonance of the four Śrauta scriptures.
Resplendent with a crest-jewel bound in matted locks tinged with pale red,
he was adorned with golden ornaments and embellished with golden earrings.
Seated upon a red lotus in the svastika posture,
with his third lotus-foot resting against the region of his back.
Always bestowing [boons] and shining with his own splendor,
he held a spear, a thunderbolt, and the *sruc* and *sruva* ladles in his four right arms.
He held a spear, a palm-leaf fan, and a vessel of ghee made of gold,
while wearing red garments and supporting them with his three equal arms.
Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, and Kṛṣṇā are situated on the face of Dakṣa;
Suprabhāvati, Raktā, Bahurūpā, and Jihvikā [are likewise].
These knowers of taste are eternally situated in His mouth;
He possesses these seven tongues and has a split face.
Thus ends the section on meditative concentration.
One should worship the fire of meditation in the center with perfumes and other offerings using this mantra.
In the Meru-tantra:
Having meditated thus, one should worship with the ritual offerings using this mantra:
"O Vaiśvānara, Jātavedas, bring [the gods] here, O red-eyed one!"
Accompanied by *svāhā* at the end and preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ),
this twenty-seven-syllable mantra, used for the worship of the fire, accomplishes all rites.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
One should worship the tongues, radiant with flames, in the center and in all six corners;
here, the sequence of worship is in the center and within the six corners.
And in the corners, the sequence begins with Īśāna; as it is stated by Somaśambhu:
In the directions of Rudra, Indra, Vahni, Māṃsāda, Varuṇa, Anila, and Gocara,
the tongues of fire beginning with Hiraṇyā are situated in sequence.
"From the middle, it is multiform," so [it is said].
In the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā.
Hiraṇyā has her tongue directed toward the northeast; Kanakā is situated in the east;
Raktā is in the southeast; Kṛṣṇā is in the southwest; and the other is considered to be Suprabhā.
Their tongues are exceedingly red like the coral tree, and they possess a beautiful luster.
The middle tongue is called Triśikhā, while the one with many forms is known as Samāhvayā;
one stands blazing on the right side, and the other on the left.
"Immediately after their own seeds is Vāyavyā," as it is stated in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarṣiṇī* as well.
Then, one should worship the tongues in the six corners and in the center:
Hiraṇyottakā is situated in the eastern direction, Hemābhā in the south, and Āruṇī in the southern direction.
The sky-colored tongue of Vaiḍūrya is situated in the eastern intermediate direction;
resembling the rising sun, the red tongue is situated in the [southeastern] direction.
Kṛṣṇā, resembling a blue lotus, is situated in the south-western direction;
Suprabhā, possessing the luster of a ruby, is situated in the western direction.
Exceedingly red and glowing like the hibiscus flower, she is situated in the northern direction;
multiform and appearing according to her true nature, she is stationed in the south and the north.
These [deities], radiant with flames, are surrounded and likewise grant the boons of the Varada and Abhaya mudrās.
Also in the Tripurāsārasamuccaya:
Possessing the beautiful color of well-refined gold, she stands in the eastern direction of the Trident-bearer;
possessing the color of lapis lazuli, she named Kanaka stands in the southern direction of Vāsava.
That tongue which is red, with a color like the rising sun, is well-situated in the southeast of the fire.

That which is black, with the luster of a blooming blue lotus, clinging to the quarter of the Lord of the Rakshasas, is the flame Suprabha, resembling a ruby, situated in the direction of Varuna. That which resembles the Maharañjana flower in the direction of the wind is Atiraktika; she is truly named Bahurūpikā.
She is situated to the south of the north of the tongue.
The specific details regarding the domestic rite are also stated in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarṣiṇī*:
"For these [deities], there should be oblations of gold and the like, and a sacrificial pap (caru) with clarified butter for Gaganā."
For the sake of accomplishing one's purpose, one should offer barley into the red Vahurūpā fire;
into the black fire, one should offer goats; and into the Suprabhā fire, one should offer parched grain flour (saktu).
The practitioner should always offer sesame seeds into the Atiraktā fire, and into the Kanakā fire,
he should offer all substances in all rites.
In another tantra, however, the fruit is proclaimed according to the distinction of desires in successive order:
the first [direction] is considered for subjugation and attraction, while the western direction is intended for paralyzing.

Raktā is intended for acts of hatred and delusion, Kṛṣṇā for rites of subjugation; Suprabhā is considered suitable for pacification and nourishment, while Suraktā is held to be for the rite of eradication.
Though she is but one, she possesses many forms and bestows the fruits of all desires.
In the Meru-tantra:
Then, in the center of the hexagon, one should perform the meditation on and worship of the tongues;
all the tongues possess the luster of flames and likewise hold both [the boon-granting gesture] and the protection-gesture.
In the northeast is Hiraṇyā, golden-hued, which bestows the accomplishments of pacification and nourishment;
in the east is Kanakā, the color of lapis lazuli, which effects the rite of immobilization.
45b) For the rite of causing enmity, she resides in the southeast corner, red like the rising sun;
for the rite of killing, she is capable [of accomplishment] in the southwest, resembling a heap of black collyrium.

Suprabhā, possessing the luster of a ruby, bestows wealth when situated in the western direction; she who is intensely red with the brilliance of the hibiscus flower, having gone to the northern direction, effects eradication.
Vahūrūpā, however, is situated in the center of a hexagon and is joined with six syllables;
she is considered the accomplisher of manifold tasks and the destroyer [of obstacles].
Just as the task [is], so the tongue is seen extending toward the various directions;
when it has the form of a flame, then there is success, but in the opposite case, the reverse.
Regarding the Vaiṣṇava tradition, it states a specific detail concerning the tongue in that very same source:
"Prabhā, Dīpti, Prakāśā, Marīci, and likewise Tāpanī."
Karālā and Ālelihā are the two tongues for the Vaiṣṇava rite;
[they are located] in the east, southeast, southwest, west, northwest, and in the center.
All the tongues are stationed together, their excellent hands shining on both sides.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
One should worship the deities of the limbs (aṅgadevatās) by the path traced upon the filaments;
on the petals, one should worship the forms (mūrtis) who bear the power (śakti) and the svastika.
Then one should worship the world-protectors in the directions according to the prescribed characteristics.
In the Meru Tantra:

One should worship the six limbs in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, Vāyu, and in front of the deities, as well as in the intermediate directions; and one should worship the presiding deities upon the petals.
Afterwards, having worshipped Indra and the other deities along with their weapons, one should worship Agni again;
here, the worship of the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) should be performed upon the darbha grass situated on the girdle (mekhalā).
Also in another tantra:
In the six corners and in the center, as well as on the filaments with the tongues, one should then [place] the limb-mantras; outside of that, in sequence, with the eight forms.
One should worship the lords of the directions, starting from the east, upon the darbha grass resting on the girdle.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
Thereafter, taking the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with both hands and turning them downward,
the preceptor should take *darbha* grass and heat them three times in the fire.
One should purify their tips, middles, and bases respectively with those [blades];
having taken them with the left hand, one should sprinkle them with the right.
Having heated them again, one should cast the *darbha* grasses into the fire;
one should then place those two *kuśa* mats on one's own right side.
Having taken up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles from another tantra, [one should hold them] respectively with their openings facing upward and downward.
Having heated the roots, middle, and tips of the *darbha* grass in the fire three times, one should touch them;
then, having heated them again three times, one should cast the *kuśa* blades into the fire with their tips downward.
One should place the powers beginning with Ikṣā in sequence at the base, middle, and tip;
one should install Śakti in the *sruc* ladle and Śambhu in the *sruva* spoon using the Heart-mantra (*hṛdayāṇu*).
"Icchādikā" means will, knowledge, and action.
In the Meru Tantra:
Then, having turned the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles face downwards, one should heat them;
one should wipe their tips with the tips of *kuśa* grass, and their middles with the middle parts.
Having thus slain the root with the roots in three ways, one should heat it;
holding it with the left hand, one should sprinkle it with the waters of the *prokṣaṇī* vessel.
Again, he should heat those two with the tip of his right hand;
then, having cast kuśa grass into the fire, he should place them upon a bed of kuśa grass to his right.
Having set down the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles behind [the fire], one should then perform the consecration of the clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
This has been stated in the Śāradā:
Then, having taken the oblation vessel, one should sprinkle it with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra;
having poured clarified butter into it, it should be purified by the rites of inspection and so forth.
In the Śaiva Āgama.
Having taken up cow-dung and consecrated it with the root mantra,
one should heat it over the fire while meditating upon one's own form as consisting of Brahman.
This was stated according to the intention of the *Gavyamṛtyuttamakalpa*.
In the Meru Tantra:
Having taken up a vessel of ghee, one should sprinkle it with mantras;
having filled it there with ghee, it should be consecrated by the rites of inspection (vīkṣaṇa) and so forth.
This has also been stated in the Piṅgalāmata:
Cow’s ghee is declared to be the best, that produced from a buffalo is middling, and that born from a goat is the lowest; therefore, cow’s ghee is praised.
Also in the Merutantra:
Cow's ghee is declared to be the best; that from a buffalo-cow is middling;
that produced from a goat is inferior; while that originating from a sheep and so forth is forbidden.
When the sacrificial butter has been purchased at the stake, let the Udgātṛs consume it as they please.
In the absence of those who are praiseworthy, [it is said] in the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā:
Having recited the mantra over the ghee, one should display the mudrā known as the dhenu-mudrā.
In the Meru Tantra:
Having constructed small mounds (gārā) outside in the northwest, one should place [the substances] upon them with the Heart-mantra;
this is declared to be the "heating" (tāpana), after which one should throw two blades of kuśa grass.
One should place that clarified butter, mixed with ghee, into the blazing fire.
"One should deposit" means one should cast it into the fire.
One should perform the purification with two *darbha* blades over the blazing fire while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*;
then, having offered clarified butter while reciting the *varma-mantra* and performed the lustration (*nīrājana*), one should cast the two *darbha* blades into the fire.
That which is for me illumination shall be called "lighting up";
having shown the kusha grass set ablaze externally, one should draw it from the heart.
Having offered clarified butter into the fires with the *vrahnā* and *buddha* mantras,
the knower of mantras should touch water and then perform the *utpracaṇa*.
The practitioner of mantra should recite the weapon-mantra (astramantra) while holding two kuśa blades, each ten finger-breadths long,
with the thumb and ring finger, and should stir the clarified butter.
Then, one should firmly immerse [the head] facing oneself with two blades of kuśa grass;
that immersion shall be with clarified butter. These are declared to be the six purificatory rites (saṃskāras).
"By means of the thumb and the little finger" should be understood as referring to both hands; "it should leap up" means it should face toward the fire.
This has been stated in the Śaiva Āgama:

With two *darbha* blades the size of a span, held between the tips of the thumb and ring finger and smeared with clarified butter, one should perform the act of "casting away" (*utpavana*) in front of the fire while reciting the *astra-mantra*.
In the Śāradā [Tīkā]:
Having placed a span-long knot of two darbha blades within the clarified butter,
he should divide it into two parts and contemplate the two wings as white and black.
Having meditated upon the *iḍā* channel on the left side, the *piṅgalā* on the right,
and the *suṣumnā* in the middle, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) according to the prescribed rule.
In the Meru Tantra:

Having placed two blades of *kuśa* grass in the clarified butter, one should then fashion them to the measure of a span, making a knot at the base; one should then contemplate the two tips as being white and black respectively.
The practitioner of mantra should visualize Iḍā on the left in the row, Piṅgalā on the right, and Suṣumṇā in the middle; thereafter, he should perform the fire oblation (homa).
The method for holding the *sruva* ladle is as described in the *Nāradīya*:
The sacrificer indeed suffers loss from the sight of the base of the *sruva* ladle;
therefore, one should conceal the base of the *sruva* at the time of the oblation.
It is said that [a vessel] at the tip causes disease, it is remembered as causing grief in the middle, and it is said to cause ruin at the base; how then can such a *sruva* ladle be held?
Having left four finger-breadths at the front and likewise sixteen [finger-breadths] at the end,
one should hold it in the middle with four finger-breadths using the conch-mudrā.
In the Homasāra:
Leaving six finger-breadths from the base, or four finger-breadths,
one should cover the base of the forearm and wear it with the śaṅkha-mudrā.
In the Meru-tantra:
One should take clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle from the right side while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*;
one should offer it into the fire for the right eye of Agni, saying "Svāhā to Agni."

Having taken clarified butter from the left side and placed it in the left eye of the fire, one should offer it with the mantra "Svāhā to Soma"; the renunciation (tyāga) of this is for me in all matters.
Having taken clarified butter with the heart-mantra, O Madhyalocanā, one should offer it into the center;
and for the third [offering], one should sacrifice with "To Agni and Soma, Svāhā!"
Then, one should take clarified butter from the right side with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and offer it into the fire with the mantra:
"To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, who is the mouth of Agni, svāhā! Thus one should perform the oblation.
"Having struck [the fire] with the *heti* [mantra], one should offer oblations of clarified butter into the parts in sequence;
thus the Guru should perform the piercing (*ghāṭana*) of the eyes and faces of the Fire-god," so it is stated in the *Śāradā*.

The meaning of "he should pour the residue" (*saṃpātayet*) is that one should pour the remnant of the oblation (*huta-śeṣam*) back into that portion from which it was taken when the offering was made. Regarding the statement "the renunciation (*tyāga*) is considered to be everywhere," the remainder of the sense is that one should pour the residue from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel over the name of whichever deity the subsequent oblation (*anvāhuti*) was offered to, according to the sequence.
This has been stated in the Śaiva Āgama:
Having taken [the substance] with the *sruva* ladle, one should perform the oblation.
In the Svāti, Agni, and Heti asterisms, one should sequentially add the remainder to that respective portion.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
One should again offer oblations with clarified butter using the seven *vyāhṛtis*:
here, *oṃ svāhā*, *oṃ bhuḥ svāhā*, *oṃ bhuvaḥ svāhā*, *oṃ svaḥ svāhā*, *oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ*... [svāhā].
"One should offer five oblations with the five mantras, both individually and collectively, using the formulas 'svaḥ' and 'svāhā'," according to the statement in the Nārāyaṇīya Tantra.
Also in the Merutantra:
One should again offer oblations of clarified butter with the *vyāhṛtis* accompanied by the *saptarṣis*.
But in the Uḍḍīśa [Tantra]:
One should perform the *avyāhṛti-homa* for the Goddess and offer four oblations with the mantra beginning with *Tārā*.
"Bhūḥ! To Agni, to Pṛthivī, and to Mahat—this is dear to Vahni."

The mantras beginning with "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," "padādvāra," and "antarīkṣāya," as well as those ending with the word "śabda" and extending up to "divyāya mahate" and "vahnijāyā" (svāhā), are traditionally prescribed.
The words *svaḥ*, *āditya*, and *candramas* [are followed by *namaḥ*] when preceded by *ṅ*, *e*, *o*, *na*, *kṣa*, or at the end of a word (*padānta*).
After these three, the word *svāhā* is used when at the end of a word; then follow the words *bhūḥ bhuvaḥ svaḥ*.
Agni, Āditya, Candramas, Aṅgiras, Nakṣatra, Tvaṣṭṛ, Soma, and Diti—
these are the beloved wives of the great Vahni.
In the Meru-tantra:
The most excellent preceptor should offer oblations three times with the fire-mantra;
[these rites] for the fire begin with conception (garbhādhāna) and end with marriage (samudvāha).
In auspicious rites, the ritual actions should be performed with eight oblations of clarified butter;
having first uttered the *praṇava*, one should then pronounce the name of the rite.
"I accomplish [this], svāhā"—this is the rule for all rites oneself.
One should perform the *garbhādhāna*, *puṃsavana*, and *sīmantonnayana* ceremonies.
One should first meditate upon the Fire born from the womb of Vāgīśvarī as before;
then, having performed the birth-rite, one should carry out the cutting of the umbilical cord.
Then, having purified the birth-impurity (sūtaka), one should perform the naming ceremony according to the prescribed rule;
for the sake of his satisfaction, the name of whichever deity he belongs to should be preceded by the word "Agni."
The Caulopanayana for Agni, likewise the Mahānāmī-vrata,
the Mahāvrata, the Upaniṣad-vrata, and the Godāna itself.

The rites beginning with the return home (samāvartana) and marriage are preceded by the Śakti and Vāgbhava [syllables] in auspicious acts; those rites ending with marriage are performed in connection with cruel deeds.
"Those who do not know the fire are declared to end in death," according to the specific statement in the Śāradā-tilaka.
But in the case of *uḍḍīsa*, however...
Saying, "O Agni, I perform here the rite of conception (garbhādhāna)," one should first utter the Praṇava and then, for the remainder, speak the names "Vahni" and "Vadhū" in sequence.
Having thus offered seven oblations, there is likewise the casting of fuel-sticks;
in this same sequence follow the Puṃsavana and the Sīmantonnayana rites.
Then, having completed the birth-rites, for the sake of dispelling fatigue,
[he should offer] a fuel-stick of the size of a span, its base and tip smeared with clarified butter.
One should cast [the oblation] with the mantra: "Oṃ, svāhā to Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśī.
Then the practitioner, having performed the fire-ritual, should unite the two parents within his own body.
One should perform the naming of the fire using the name of one's chosen deity; specifically,
for Śrīvidyā, it is "by Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśvarī," whereas elsewhere it is "by Vāgīśvara and Vāgīśvarī."
This is to be known. A specific rule is stated in the *Merutantra*: "In the Śaiva, Śākta, and Gāṇeśa [tantras], [the worship is] with the two goddesses;
but in the Saura and Vaiṣṇava [tantras], it is with Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa."
In the *turṇāyāga* (the swift sacrifice).
Having offered eight oblations of clarified butter, one should perform the naming ceremony;
the preceptor should designate [the child] with the words "You are so-and-so" using the root mantra.
In the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā.
Having meditated upon the newborn as possessing form, one should perform the birth-rites (jātakarman);
then, having removed the umbilical cord, one should purify the birth-impurity (sūtaka).
Having given her the name Śivāgni, preceded by oblations,
and having performed the dismissal of the parents, as well as the tonsure, initiation, and other rites;
Then, having performed the concluding rite of the marriage ceremony for him,
the rite of removing the bamboo tube is performed according to the Śaiva Āgama.
Then, for the removal of the stalk, one should offer five fuel-sticks (samidh) smeared with ghee at the base and the tip of the fire using the Astra-mantra.
In the Meru Tantra.

Then, having worshipped the parents of the fire as well as the gods and goddesses and so forth, and having dismissed them, one should offer oblations soaked in ghee at the base and the tip of the root-mantra.
Then, one should cast the fuel-sticks into the five fires as before.
In the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā:
Those sacrificial twigs, even if far away, should be made of *pālāśa* wood, twelve finger-breadths in length,
straight, naturally dried, of the same species as the tree, free from blemishes, and uniform.
Alternatively, they are prescribed as being ten finger-breadths long, or equal in measure to the little finger;
or, if available, they may all be given even if they are only a span (prādeśa) in length.

And thus, when all the funeral rites had been completed, the five-faced one, whose form was like that of Śaradā, wandered as if in a secluded place while leading the two parents to Nālāyana. Here, after the *godāna* ceremony, the *samāvartana* (the rite of returning home) must also be performed. This is stated in the *Gaṇeśvaravimarṣiṇī*: "The *samāvartana*, marriage, and the establishment of the sacred fire..."
"And after that," it says; "he should offer oblations at both the *samāvartana* and the marriage" is also stated in the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya*.
In the Meru-tantra, as before.
He should offer the oblation of desire with the seed-mantra known as *rasanā*.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
The best of those who know mantras should offer one oblation for each of the mantras of the tongue, limbs, and forms of Fire, in due order and according to the prescribed rule.
In the Gaṇeśvaravimarṣiṇī.
One of clear intellect should offer oblations at those locations, one by one, with the limb-mantras and others beginning with *Tārā*, ending each with *svāhā* in due order. 48a)
Here, by the word "today" (adya), there is the inclusion of everything from the world-protectors (lokapālas) up to their weapons (tadastras).
In the Meru Tantra:
Then one should offer oblations to the limbs [of the deity], as well as to the eight forms (mūrtis) of Fire,
followed by Indra and the other world-protectors (lokapālas), and thereafter to their weapons.
The wise one, meditating upon the deity of the mantra, should offer oblations with a mantra preceded by *oṃ* and ending with *svāhā*,
concluding each offering with *svāhā*.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
Having purified the *sruva* ladle, the preceptor, with a restrained mind, should pour clarified butter four times into the *sruk* while holding it over the fire,
standing still throughout the process.
One should perform the oblation with the fire-mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ" for the sake of prosperity.
In the Meru Tantra:
Having taken clarified butter four times with the *sruva* ladle, he should pour it into the *sruc*;
having performed that [offering] with that very [ladle], the Guru himself, standing, should offer it into the fire.
Then, for the sake of prosperity, the practitioner should [worship] the mantra of Agni ending with *vauṣaṭ* upon the tongue situated in the center, which has a body of garlands of flames.
Having placed the *sruva* ladle with its opening facing downward into the *sruc* which is filled with clarified butter (*ghṛta*),
and having fixed a flower upon the tip of its prong, [he should hold it] afterwards with his left hand.
Again, holding those two with the left hand in the conch-like mudrā,
he stands arisen with his body upright and his feet even.
Having placed its root at the navel, with eyes fixed on the tips of the horns,
and having brought [the other horn] between the left breast and the navel— this is the specific instruction regarding their root, as stated in the Śaiva Āgama.
In the Gaṇeśvaravimarṣiṇī.
With the mantra of Mahāgaṇeśa joined with each preceding one,
and with the six seed-syllables beginning with *Tāra* (Om), [the worship] is performed on the hands with the syllables of the mountain (seven).
O Goddess of the gods, having offered [the oblation] tenfold when [the mantra] is divided, one should offer it with the whole [mantra] together.
Also in the Prapañcasāra:
One should offer ten oblations with the Gāṇapatya mantra, preceded by the tenfold divisions beginning with Tārā, each combined with the preceding one.
And one should perform oblations four times with that very [substance] in its entirety.
In the Meru Tantra:
One should first offer ten oblations with the Gāṇapatya mantra, accompanied by the ten variations beginning with Tārā, each preceded by its respective preceding element.
The Guru should then perform oblations four times with that entire [mixture];
having properly worshipped the deity and the seat within the fire, he should proceed accordingly.
There, one should worship the most beloved deity in the form of Agni.
Also in the Vīracūḍāmaṇi:
Afterwards, there is one oblation of clarified butter for each of the deities of the seats (pīṭhadevatās).
One should worship [the deity] ending with the form of fire.
"With perfumes, flowers, and so forth, in due order."

Having worshipped [the deities] beginning with Ādhāraśakti and ending with the Pīṭhamantra by offering one oblation to each, one should invoke the chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) there, worship them with the ritual services (upacāras), and [worship] the presiding deities (āvaraṇadevatās).
"One should also worship"— this is established in the Uḍḍīśa.
Then, having performed the protective rites for the deities, one should offer individual oblations for each desired object;
thereafter, having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should perform the optional homa.
Having recited the root mantra ending with "svāhā" and saying "this [is for] the deity," one should offer oblations into the blazing fire and perform the prescribed number of circumambulations.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
The practitioner of mantra should offer oblations into its mouth twenty-five times with clarified butter while reciting the root mantra; this is the rite of unifying the faces.
Thus, the inclusion of the faces within the desired face occurs through their unity;
or else, one should contemplate the measurement of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) as being present in the face.
In the Śaiva Āgama, it is taught that the unification with That consists in internalizing one's own faces [of consciousness].
In the Meru Tantra.
The mantra-practitioner should offer oblations twenty-five times into the mouth of the fire with clarified butter while reciting the sādhya-mantra; this indeed is the unification of the faces.
The knower of the Self, contemplating the unity of the self, the fire, and the deities,
should then offer eleven oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra.
This is indeed declared by the best of teachers to be the "joining of the channels" (nāḍī-saṃdhāna).
One should offer one oblation for each [deity], beginning with the limbs and continuing through the enclosures (āvṛtis).
In all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) located in the directions beginning with the east, according to the prescribed ritual.

In the *Tripurāsārasamuccaya* and the *Śāradātilaka*, it is stated that at the end, one should offer a single oblation for each member of the retinue and ten oblations to the Goddess; this is the procedure for the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*).
Now follows the ritual procedure for the day of initiation.
In the Meru Tantra:
Having risen at dawn, one should perform the morning bath, the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), and other rites;
then the preceptor, the disciple, and the officiating priests should proceed toward the sacrificial hall.
All of them should offer oblations in their respective fire-pits with sesame seeds mixed with ghee,
reciting the mantra one thousand and eight times, plus a half [thousand].
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
Having risen in the morning, they should again offer oblations with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter,
or with materials prescribed by the ritual manuals, one thousand and eight times for each separately.
The clarified butter is to be offered with the *srūva* ladle, the fuel-stick with the hand, and the remnants either with the *sruk* ladle or with the hand;
in that case, it should likewise be offered at a divine or a human *tīrtha*.

Since it is stated in both the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā and the Meru-tantra that "the rising of sesame seeds" (tilodaya) should be offered with either a sacrificial ladle (sruk) or by hand, they are to be offered in that manner.
In the Mahākapila Pañcarātra.
One should offer oblations into a fire that is not yet blazing, nor into one that is merely smoldering;
rather, oblations should be offered into a fire that is fully kindled and licking with flames for the successful accomplishment of rites.
And much more is also found in the *Pariśiṣṭa*.
If the planet Mercury is in Aṅga, one should offer oblations into the fire during the smoke;
the sacrificer, along with his sons, shall become fuel— so says the Śruti.
The man who offers oblations into a sacrificial fire that has flames but lacks glowing embers becomes one with weak digestion, afflicted by disease, and born into poverty.
Thus it is stated in both the Merutantra and the Chandogapariśiṣṭa.
In the Tripurāsāra:
From an oblation into the ear of the fire, disease and affliction arise; from the eye, blindness; from the nose, mental distress;
and from the head, the loss of wealth. Therefore, a wise man should always perform the oblation within the mouth.
In the Navadurgākalpa.
Where there is wood, there is the ear; where there is smoke, however, that is the nose;
where there is a small flame, that is the eye; and where there is ash, that is the head.
And where the fire blazes, there the tongue is proclaimed to be.
In another tantra:
Where there is wood, from that [direction] is the ear; where there is smoke, here is the nose;
where there is a small flame, that is the eye; and where there are embers, from that [direction] is the head.
There, the blazing flame became the tongue of the Veda.
Also elsewhere.
Fire with smoke is to be known as the head; smokeless fire as the razor (kṣura);
blazing but thin fire as the ear; and fire clinging to wood as the nose.
There, within that which resembles pure crystal, fire flickers;
its opening should be known there as being four finger-breadths in measure.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
The preceptor should meditate on Vaiśvānara as standing during the offerings of fuel-sticks;
as reclining during the offerings of clarified butter; and as seated during all remaining rites.
Likewise.
Resembling gold, vermilion, the morning sun, saffron, and honey,
the Suvarṇa type is proclaimed as beautiful, possessing a golden hue.

The sound of fire that resembles a kettledrum, the roar of water, or the trumpeting of a lordly elephant brings auspiciousness; it is like the fragrance of the nāga, campaka, punnāga, pāṭala, and yūthikā flowers.
That which resembles a lotus, a blue water-lily, a white lily, clarified butter,
or molasses is said by those learned in the Tantras to be the auspicious fragrance of fire.
Cocks whose crests move clockwise, are free from trembling, and resemble the luster of an umbrella bestow auspiciousness upon the sacrificer,
and especially upon his kingdom.
Smoke as white as a jasmine flower or the moon is said to bring auspiciousness for the fire;
however, black smoke, which is the color of a dark destination, shall destroy the sacrificer.
A white horse quickly destroys the kingdom; one with a voice resembling that of a crow brings misfortune;
and a sound like the braying of a donkey causes total destruction.
If it has a foul odor, it becomes a consumer of fire that brings about suffering;
if its base and crest are severed, it causes death rather than total destruction.
Smoke resembling the color of a parrot's wing, or possessing a luster like that of a pigeon,
soon brings about the loss of breeds of horses and cattle.
When such defects have occurred, the preceptor should offer twenty-five oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra as an act of atonement.
Also in the Tripurāsārasamuccaya:
One should offer more than a hundred oblations of clarified butter with the *śāntika* [mantra] during times of misfortune or defects;
then, as it is said, the lord of practitioners should perform the worship of the wheel (*cakrapūjā*) by means of the *astra* [mantra].
"The worship of the wheel (cakrapūjā) is to be seen in the remaining chapter," [it is said] regarding the left; on the right, there are only oblations of clarified butter (ājyāhuti).
In the Meru Tantra:
With the previously mentioned substances or procedures, one hundred and eight [offerings] are made with the arms;
this also pertains to the ritual application for both the left and right [sides].
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
Then, having made the disciple— who has thoroughly cleansed his teeth and other parts and is composed—
drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he should lead him to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
In the Meru-tantra:
The best of mantra-knowers should cause the bathed disciple to drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
having brought him near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), he should gaze upon him with divine vision.
In the *Prayogasāra*:
Having drunk the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) as prescribed and having completed the ritual according to the rules,
O Lord, he should cause him to enter the sacrificial ground by the southern door.

"Having perceived that consciousness with divine vision from the heart-lotus and having united it with his own self, the Guru should perform the purification of the substrate (adhyaviśodhana)," so it is stated in the *Śāradā*.
In the Meru-tantra:
The teacher should project the consciousness from the heart-lotus into that [disciple’s] self;
there, he should purify the sixfold path in due order.
In another tantra:
Taking that consciousness residing in the heart, which is throbbing and star-like in form,
one should establish it by means of the Heart-Angle Hook (hṛdayāṅkuśa) mudrā.
In the great jewel of the six lineages.
Purification consists of contemplating the unity of the causes of the principles (tattvas),
and within that, contemplating the oneness of consciousness (cidaikya) regarding the phonemes (varṇas) and the digits (kalās).
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
It has been stated that there are three paths: the path of the *kalās*, the path of the *tattvas*, and the path of the worlds (*bhuvanas*);
and another triad consisting of the path of the phonemes (*varṇas*), the path of the words (*padas*), and the path of the mantras.
In the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā.
In that regard, three sounds are proclaimed as paths, while three are said to be meanings.
In another tantra:
The path of mantras, the path of words, and the path of phonemes are [designated] by name;
likewise, the path of worlds, the path of principles, and the path of energies are [designated] by their meaning.

50a) However, it should be understood that here the description follows the order of withdrawal (*saṃhāra-krama*), whereas in the *Śāradā-tilaka* and regarding Meru, it follows the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭi-krama*).
The five kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, are proclaimed as the path of time (kāla-adhvan).
The path of principles (tattva-adhvan) is divided in many ways according to the different Śaiva Āgamas.
There are thirty-six principles (tattvas) of the Śaivas, thirty-two of the Vaiṣṇavas,
and twenty-four principles belonging to Prakṛti in the Maitra system.
The ten principles (tattvas) have been stated, as well as the seven principles belonging to the three-fold nature;
from these Śaiva principles one is liberated: Śiva, Śakti, and Sadāśiva.
The Lord, for the sake of the purpose of knowledge, indeed [established] the five pure principles:
Māyā, Kāla, Niyati, Kalā, and Vidyā; furthermore, Smṛti.

Passion (rāga), the person (puruṣa), these seven pure and impure [categories], as well as primordial nature (prakṛti), the intellect (buddhi), the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the mind (manas), and the organs of knowledge (jñānendriya).
The organs of action, the subtle elements (tanmātras), and the five gross elements—
these, O Teacher, are declared in the Āgama to be the twenty-four impure principles.
Thus, the classification of the principles (*tattva*) of the Śaivas is demonstrated here.
"Pure" (*śuddha*) refers to the state of being free from the three impurities (*mala*): the atomic (*āṇava*), the karmic (*kārmaṇa*), and the māyic (*māyīya*).
Among these, the atomic (*āṇava*) consists in the non-endurance of one's own nature as Sadāśiva. The karmic (*kārmaṇa*) consists in merit and demerit.

The cognition "I am" is [the notion of self]. That which is called "illusory" (māyīya) is the conception of the Self with respect to the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra) and so forth. "Pure" (śuddha) means being free from the three impurities (mala) by virtue of being the cause; "pure through effect" (kārya-śuddha) means being endowed with those [impurities] by virtue of being the effect—just as a staff is pure because it is a staff; such is the meaning.
Likewise.
The individual soul, the vital breaths, the intellect, the mind, the organs of knowledge and action,
the five subtle elements, the five gross elements, the heart-lotus, and the triad of luminaries.
Vāsudeva and the others—these are the principles (tattvas) of Śaṅkara:
the five gross elements, the subtle elements, the sense organs, and likewise the mind.
The wise know that pride, increase, and the primary element are the [first] five kalās, beginning with Maitrāṇī; from that, the bindu has five kalās again, beginning with Nirvṛtti.
Nāda is Śakti, eternally prior to Śiva and beyond Prakṛti;
Śiva is the Ātman-avidyā, and thereafter Śiva is Vidyā himself once again.
All reality and the principles (tattvas) have been declared to be the source of fear for the self;
indeed, this path of principles (tattvādhvan) has been described by those who distinguish between various scriptures.

50b) "The path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvā) is called *īrita* by the wise," according to the *Śāradā*. And the fourteen worlds are called the "path of the worlds," based on the statement in the *Gautamīya Tantra*: "The fourteen worlds are the path of the worlds."
In the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā:
It has been stated that "the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan) is proclaimed as extending from the Foundation (ādhāra) up to the Transmental (unmanī). Likewise:
The wise declare that the path of letters (varṇādhvan) consists of the phonemes beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa'.
The collection of words constitutes the path of words (padādhvan), while the multitudes of mantras constitute the path of mantras (maṃtrādhvan).
But in the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, however:
The path of words, which is a collection of words divided into many varieties,
exists as the constituent parts of great mantras and sub-mantras.
Having ascended by means of the Pradhāna, he consists of five parts.
It is also stated in the *Gautamīya*.
It has been stated that "the path of the foot" (padādhvan) would be the "foot-investigation" (padamūha); thus, "the collection of mantras" refers to the aggregate of Vedic and Tantric mantras.
"The path of mantra" (maṃtrādhvan) would be the "collection of mantras," for those are indeed both Vedic and Tantric.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
The most excellent guru should gradually purify these six paths;
he should meditate upon them in the disciple's feet, genitals, navel, heart, forehead, and head.
Then, touching him according to the rule with a bundle of kuśa grass,
the preceptor should perform the oblation in the teacher’s sacrificial pit using purified sesame seeds soaked in clarified butter.
Saying "I purify this path,
svāhā," one should offer eight oblations for each of the paths beginning with Tāra in sequence, and thereby lead it to dissolution.
In this regard, it is stated in the Merutantra:
It is stated with a different sequence.
The Guru should contemplate these kalās, preceded by the tattvas, worlds, syllables, words, and mantras,
at the feet of the disciple.
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and likewise Śāntyatītā—these are the five; now the sequence of purification is described.

And the Guru, touching the disciple with the *kūrca* [grass-bundle], should offer oblations in his own sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with sesame seeds soaked in ghee, reciting "Tārādyam amukādhvanam atra" (The path of such-and-such, beginning with Tārā, here).
One should perform eight oblations with the mantra ending in *dviṭha* (phaṭ) for purification;
then, one should contemplate the meditation on the *kalās*, which dissolve into the resonance of reality (*tattva-dhvani*).
Then, one should contemplate these principles in the region of the *liṅga*:
those pertaining to Gaṇeśa and those pertaining to Śiva; therein, [the elements] are six and three.
Namely: Śiva and Śakti, Sadāśiva and Maheśvara, and Vidya—these are the five pure [tattvas]; and there are seven pure-pure [tattvas].
Māyā, avidyā, kalā, rāga, kāla, niyati, and puruṣa—these are the impure [evolutes]; so too are prakṛti, buddhi, and ahaṃkāra.
51a) The mind, the ten sense organs, the five subtle elements (tanmātras), and the five gross elements—
thus, indeed, the thirty-two Vaiṣṇava principles are established.
The individual soul, the vital breath, the mind, the intellect, the subtle elements, the five gross elements,
the ten sense organs, the heart-lotus, and likewise the sun, moon, and fire.
Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha;
the solar [lights], the elements, the subtle elements, the mind, the ego, and the senses.
Nature (prakṛti) and intellect (buddhi), numbering twenty-four;
the ten principles of power (śakti-tattva); and the Self (ātman), knowledge (vidyā), and Śiva.
"Śiva, Vidyā, and likewise Ātman—these are the auspicious [deities] of the Self-knowledge (ātmavidyā).
Furthermore, 'all the principles' (sarvatattva)—one should again perform the oblation as before by means of inference."
Having dissolved into that chapter on reality, one should contemplate the sound of the worlds;
the fourteen worlds are to be contemplated by the disciple at the navel.
These are, in order: Pātāla, Rasātala, Mahātala, Talātala, Sutala, Vitala, Atala, and Bhūḥ.
Bhuvaḥ, svaḥ, mahaḥ, as well as janaḥ, tapaḥ, and in sequence satyam—these are the worlds (bhuvanāni). Meditation, oblation, and so forth are to be inferred as before.
One should contemplate the path of the worlds as dissolved within the path of phonemes;
one should gather the phonemes from 'a' to 'kṣa' within the heart.
Having dissolved [the deity] into the chapter on phonemes (varṇādhyāya), one should contemplate it within the path of the words;
the oblation (homa) and the offering (oha) are as before, and thereafter one should contemplate [it] in the forehead.
The meditation on the words consists of the root mantra and the nature of the syllables of those words;
one should perform the meditation on the words, as well as the fire-offerings (homa) and other rites, exactly as previously described.
Once the path of mantra has dissolved, one should contemplate the meditation on the word (pada);
one should then contemplate the complete path of mantra upon the head of the disciple.

The oblation of fire (homoha) dissolves here, as before, into this supreme Śiva situated at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra); one should meditate upon this, for it constitutes the purification of the paths (adhva-śodhana).
"The Supreme Guru creates those who have been created and causes them to dissolve back into Śiva; this should be noted by the wise. Hereafter, [the sequence] is equal."
In the Meru Tantra:
And the supreme teacher, having beheld that disciple again and again with his divine vision,
should unite that consciousness which resides within himself with that [consciousness] in the disciple.
In the Kulārṇava:
For those born of the Śūdra and Śaṅkara castes, purification through the path is not prescribed;
one should effect their liberation from bonds by means such as the offering of water for the feet.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
Having offered the full oblation with the *sruc* ladle using the root mantra, the preceptor—
51b) In the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā:
Then, having filled the *sruva* ladle with the clarified butter remaining from the oblation and placed a flower upon its tip, one should hold it with the *sruc* spoon facing downwards.
Having covered [the vessel] with a bunch of Darbha grass, standing with palms joined at the base [of the vessel],
one should offer a continuous stream of water mixed with barley, ending with the syllable *vauṣaṭ*.
In the Meru Tantra:
Having filled the *sruva* ladle with clarified butter, with flowers placed both above and below it,
and having placed the *sruk* spoon over the *sruva*, one should cause the flowers to fall therein.
In the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*.
And having offered with the oblation, one should present three full oblations with the *sruc* ladle.
"By means of the mantra ending with vauṣaṭ."
In the Nārada-pañcarātra.
In the absence of ghee, however, one should fill [the vessel] with the substance for the oblation;
one should place ghee upon that, and above that, saffron and other such items.
In the sacrifice for the restless one.
Then, having uttered the root mantra ending with "namaḥ," the practitioner of mantras should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the left foot foremost, perceiving it as supreme nectar.
In this case, it is appropriate that they offer one oblation to each of the deities chosen for the sacrifice.

As for what was stated regarding the root-mantra ending in *namaḥ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *svāhā* in the context of the *bhūrṇi*-sacrifice and others—that must be considered as pertaining to the left-hand (*dakṣetara*) tradition. It is stated specifically in the *Merutantra* as follows:
Placing the right foot forward, the adept should perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti);
he should offer three such final oblations which fulfill all desires.
The Vedic practitioner, well-composed, should perform the rite with the mantra "pūrṇādarvi" at the root,
using fruit and clarified butter, ending with the word "svāhā."
In the Śaktihoma, one should place the left foot forward, step by step.
And the follower of the left-hand path is everywhere.

The fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with effort using the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* and *svāhā*, along with wine and meat, as well as water from a sacred ford and clarified butter; for it has been stated that [the rite] reaches completion through these—this is the truth.
And also something else.

One should state the specific positions for each of the constellations, the days of the week, and the zodiac signs, as well as their presiding deities, and likewise declare whether it is day or night.
Then, having performed the ritual conduct, one should utter "Salutation to all beings.
O gods, thus has this Tantric procedure for the fire-oblation been declared by me.
In the Gautamīya [Vinaya].
Having taken up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and filled them with clarified butter,
he should then place the oblation materials within them and position them at his navel.
One should again offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the mantra "brahmārpaṇam."
In the Meru Tantra:
The wise knower of mantras, for the sake of severing all karmic bonds, should offer eight oblations of pure clarified butter with the mantra known as "brahmārpaṇam."

Whatever has been thought by the mind, spoken by speech, or performed by action—with the vital breath, the intellect, and the functions of the body; whatever was done while awake, dreaming, or in deep sleep; whatever was done with the hands, feet, belly, or genitals; whatever was remembered or uttered—all that becomes an offering to Brahman, svāhā!
The mantra *brahmārpaṇam* is prescribed for the evening rite in the ritual of *brahmārpaṇa*.
Having thus performed the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homa*), [one should dismiss] the deities residing in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the altar (*sthaṇḍila*).

The Guru should also bring the guardians of the directions (dikpālas), the deities, and the deities of the placement of the limbs (aṅgulārpaṇa) into the water-pot (kalaśa), and meditate upon their oneness with Kṛṣṇa.
"Kṛṣṇa" is used with reference to the subject at hand.
In the Meru Tantra:

Having worshipped again with perfumes and other offerings using the root mantra, the preceptor, skilled in mantras, should transfer the deity born of the fire from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and install her in the water-pot (kalaśa).

The Guru, having dismissed the deity along with its limbs and retinue into the water-pot (kumbha), [proceeds].
In the Meru Tantra.
Having extracted the seven vyāhṛtis, the fire-syllable (agnibīja), the [seven] tongues, and one from each of the [seven] forms (mūrtis).
Having sprinkled with milk.

Having caused the fire to sacrifice for himself, the practitioner of mantra should burn these—namely the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the surrounding grass-beds (*paristaraṇa*)—in an occasional rite (*naimittika*); however, in a regular rite (*nitya*), he should not burn them.

Then, one should not throw the enclosing sticks (paridhis) into the fire;

With the *vyāhṛtis*.

"Bhuvo vāyave cāntarikṣāya mahate svāhā" (Bhuvas! To Vāyu and the great intermediate space, Svāhā!); then "svaścandramase digbhyaśca nakṣatrebhyaśca svāhā" (Svaḥ! To the moon, the directions, and the constellations, Svāhā!); "Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaścandramase nakṣatrebhyo digbhyaśca mahate svāhā" (Oṃ Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ! To the moon, the constellations, the directions, and the great [space], Svāhā!). Having thus prepared the fire, that procedure is performed on Mount Meru; then one should pray to Agni.
The Guru.

Even when this interval between rites has arrived, please remain present with due respect.

One should bind [the eyes] with the eye-cloth using the Netra-mantra.

Taking [the water] from the vessel into his hand while reciting the *jaya* mantra in the presence [of the deity],

O auspicious one, the Puṣya constellation is auspicious when conjoined with the asterisms Rudra (Ārdrā), Indra (Jyeṣṭhā), and Uttara (Uttarā-phalgunī).

Having removed this blindfold, one should cause him to enter upon a bed of kuśa grass.

In the Meru Tantra.
Then the supreme guru should cause the disciple to pierce [the eye] with this mantra,

Salutation to that illustrious Guru by whom the eye was opened.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
Having worshipped the chosen deity residing in the water-pot with the five-fold offerings (pañcopacāra),
one who has performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa should perform [the rite] for her according to the path taught in the Tantra.
In the Meru Tantra.
Having worshipped the desired deity residing in the water-pot with the five-fold offerings (pañcopacāra),
one should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa there according to the path taught in the Tantra.
Immediately following this, the teachers have stated the request for boons from the presence of the deity.
O Goddess, abode of compassion, refuge for all who approach; O Mother, affectionate toward those who seek shelter, bestow Your grace upon this child.

"May this person increase even through shares of both this world and the next;
let all devotion, both with parts and partless, be given to him as his refuge."
In the *Prayogasāra*:
Then, in the northeast direction, according to the mantra,
he whose form was thus disposed should be seated upon a square pedestal on the altar, with the tips of darbha grass in his hands.
One should consecrate one's own disciple who follows the reality of the Self (ātmatattva).
In the Meru-tantra:
Then one should seat the disciple upon the ground within the mandala;
then one should quickly consecrate the disciple for the swift attainment of prosperity.
In the Somaśambhu [Tantra].
In a bathing pavilion constructed in the direction of the sacrificial hall,
one should prepare [the ground] measuring two cubits in width and eight fingers in height.

Having placed an āsana made of śrīparṇa and other materials there, and having seated the disciple facing east upon that seat which has Ananta as its foundation, one should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and worship him.
In that very same [text].
For liberation, one should face north during bathing; for enjoyment, one should face east.
Also elsewhere.
Having established the mandala with its entrance toward the northeast for those seeking liberation through the unsurpassed [vehicle],
one should seat the disciples there facing east for the sake of worldly enjoyment.
In the Meru Tantra.
Then, one should cause the disciple, who is adorned, to sit within the mandala.
The teacher should place the *kuṃbhāsyas*, *sthvasuras*, and *adrūs* upon the head of the disciple.
Then, accompanied by the fivefold sounds and the benedictions of the Brahmins,
they sprinkled the self-restrained and well-established [prince] with water from the jars and flowers.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
While the five musical instruments resounded, the preceptor, together with the brahmins and the śikhās,
duly excavated the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and [removed] the celestial trees situated at its opening.
Having placed the Mātṛkā on the child’s head while mentally reciting it,
the knower of the Self should sprinkle him with water consecrated by the root mantra.
The Mātṛkā and the reverse Mātṛkā.
Filled with the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*.
Placing his hand upon the head of the disciple while reciting the *mātṛkā* in reverse order.
And because of the statement in the *Gautamīya*: "Having likewise recited the root mantra, one should perform the consecration of the deity. Likewise:
Having taken up again the *vardhanī* vessel, which has been worshipped and is the embodiment of mantra,
one should immediately sprinkle [the disciple] with its well-prepared waters for the sake of protection.
With the remaining water, the Guru should cause the disciple to sip;
then, the knower of the Self, having performed the ritual integration (sakalīkaraṇa) of him, regards him as identical with the deity.
Having risen, the disciple, wearing clean garments or with his upper cloth tucked in,
and having sipped water and become silent, should sit in the presence of the teacher.
The supreme teacher, contemplating the identity of those two, should worship the deity who has been infused into the disciple with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Then he should impart the knowledge to that disciplined disciple with due reverence.
In the Meru Tantra:
Then, for the sake of swiftly attaining perfection, he should consecrate the disciple,
having taken up the previously worshipped water-pot which is of the nature of the weapon-mantra.
The best of preceptors should sprinkle him with those waters for protection;
then, with the water remaining, the Guru should have the disciple rinse his mouth.

Then, at the command of the Guru, he should perform the ritual of sakalīkṛti (the infusion of the deity's limbs) upon the form of the deity, having put on two beautiful garments with their borders turned inward.
Having sipped water (ācamana) nearby him, the learned man should correctly recite the mantra three times into the right ear of the Brahmin, preceded by the offering of water.
In the Gautamīya [Vinaya].
Having diligently performed the web of nyāsa upon his body, the Guru,
with a full heart, should whisper the mantra three times into the right ear.
In the Kulāmṛta.
One should recite the Vidyā three times into the ear, or as many times as one’s knowledge permits.
In the Dīpikā.
Then the Guru, being priceless, should duly recite that supreme mantra— endowed with the Ṛṣi and other elements— thrice into the left ear.
Also elsewhere.
One should recite the Vidyā three times into the right ear with a single utterance;
such is the rule for the twice-born, while for women and Śūdras it is done from the left.
In that interval.
"O bulls among sages, with a gracious countenance, he then spoke to that disciple, saying, 'May it bear fruit for both of us.'"
Then the Guru should visualize her as proceeding toward the Vidyā consisting of light.
"One should contemplate the disciple as having arrived."

The Guru should contemplate [the disciple] as going toward the self-luminous Vidyā;
the disciple should contemplate her as having arrived, [thinking], "I am not that," for she bestows the distinction.
The disciple should recite one hundred and eight times what is uttered by the Guru,
or twenty-eight times, or eight times.
The disciple, contemplating the identity of the Guru, the Deity, and the Mantra as one, [should practice].
In the Gautamīya [Vinaya].
Having recited the mantras of Gaṇeśa and the others, the Guru should explain them according to the tradition;
this, however, is in the case of the initiation for the five-shrine (pañcāyatana) system.
Having properly and diligently worshipped the Wheel-King (cakrarāja) nearby,
one should fashion a beautiful name joined with the first syllable [of the deity's name].
Having thus united oneself with the human gurus,
one should then properly remember all the gurus preceded by a full prostration.
Having written the vidyā on the ground, one should worship it properly with flowers and other offerings;
O Dear One, one should then show the vidyā, which has been recited a hundred times, to the disciple.
"If there should be great devotion in the disciple and in the giver of life,
then one should mutter the *parā* [mantra] into the right ear with a single utterance," so it is said in the *Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā*.
The King of Tantras.
The disciple, endowed with the aforementioned characteristics and adorned by his conduct,
has been purified for many days through the two vidyās consisting of five and six kūṭas.
Having consecrated him with water-pots and seated him within the Śrīcakra,
one should contemplate the Cakra in the center, at the base, the heart, and the head.
Having invoked [the deity] from his own heart, established [him], and worshipped him together with the ritual placement (nyāsa),
the divine-souled one, with a fulfilled mind, should whisper the thirty-fold Vidyā into the ear.

Constantly contemplating the oneness of the deity, the guru, the mantra, and one's own self, one should recite [the mantra] a hundred times while standing before it; one should dwell in its proximity for three days.
If the mobile power (saṃcāriṇī śakti) does not reach the Guru, there is no doubt;
therefore, one should dwell in his presence, performing worship, prostrations, and other such acts.
In the Gautamīya [Vinaya].
One should dwell with devotion for three days in the presence of the Guru for the sake of attaining perfection;
otherwise, there is no doubt that the spiritual luster residing therein will return to the Guru.
In the *Maṇtratantraprakāśa*.
A mantra that has not been received from a teacher, or one that has been received but for which the ritual fee (dakṣiṇā) was not given,
will not grant success even if it is recited constantly.

Having given the teacher a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of one's entire property, half of it, or a quarter less than that, the reception of the mantra (*mantragraha*) is then considered appropriate.
In the Meru Tantra:
One should respectfully offer ornaments and garments to those worthy of honor,
perceiving them as the Lord himself, and be gladdened by the blessings of the twice-born.
The disciple should give half of his own wealth to the guru, or half of that,
or even a tenth part, provided he is free from stinginess regarding his possessions.

as well as food, clothing, and other necessities without hardship, according to one's wealth.
In the Gautamīya [Vinaya].
Devoted to devotion, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru that is half of one's wealth,
or else one should give half of that, according to one's capacity and with devotion.

rather, one should offer cows, land, gold, clothing, and other such things to the preceptor.
One should also give clothing and ornaments to the preceptor’s son and his wife, as well as to his disciple, according to one's ability, along with desired food according to their taste.
One should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests, accompanied by garments and ornaments.
In another tantra:
Cows, land, abundant gold, houses, fields, and so forth—much of it;
or if not that, half of it, or half of that, or even a tenth part of it.
One should give food, clothing, and so forth, without distress, according to one's wealth.
In the Meru Tantra.
Resorting to another method, one should diligently awaken the Guru,
with a mind perpetually dependent on him and intent upon his contemplation.
Adorned with the dust of his lotus feet, he shall become the most excellent of practitioners.
In the Brahma-saṃhitā:
"O Nārada, it is certain that an action performed without a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is in vain;

Therefore, O great sage, receive the mantra from me according to the prescribed rite;
for an action performed devoid of the proper rite never bestows success.
Likewise.
Having performed the ritual sprinkling with consecrated water, one should give a sacrificial fee (brahmadakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins according to one's own means, free from greed and delusion.

In the Meru Tantra:
Then, having dismissed Brahmā, one should cause it to be given to a Brāhmaṇa;

Having filled it with rice grains, he should give that [vessel], along with gold and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), to a Brahmin; for his satisfaction, [he should recite] "pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idam."

Here, having performed the pouring of the consecrated water (praṇītā), the sprinkling (mārjana), and the dismissal of Brahmā (brahmodvāsana), they conclude with "the initiation" (dīkṣām iti) in the Melapa ritual.
Many [teachers] maintain that this occurs immediately after initiation (dīkṣā).
In the Meru Tantra:
Then, one should properly feed the Brahmins with various kinds of foods— both solid and liquid— and should bestow abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
The construction [of the term] applies to both paths: "with things to be licked and things to be sucked."
In the Brahmasaṃhitā:
Then, having consumed the remainder of the oblation in a quantity the size of a hen's egg, one should proceed.

55a) In the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā:
One should give the pavilion, along with the implements of sacrifice, to the preceptor;
having imparted the mantra, the teacher should recite it one thousand times for the sake of his own perfection— so it is stated in the Nārāyaṇīya and Mahākapila Pañcarātras.
One should recite it one thousand and eight times, or according to one's own capacity, even in other instances as well.
In the Kulāmṛta.
One should instruct the disciple, who is prostrate like a staff, in all the rules of conduct.

The Guru should instruct the disciple regarding bathing, the twilight prayers, right conduct, as well as the obligatory and optional rites, and the methods for attaining mastery over mantras.
And the conduct of the observance (samayācāra) will be explained further on.
On the day of initiation, fasting is prohibited.
This has been stated in the Yoginītantra:
Having given even a mere morsel, if you, O Guru, should observe a fast, you will become a worm in the hell of great darkness; it cannot be otherwise.
When a practitioner, having performed the initiation, observes a fast,
the deity always becomes enraged and, having pronounced a curse, departs for his own city.
Now, there is a specific detail in the Vīradīpikā.
As it is stated in the Merutantra:
Having worshipped the Kula-cakra according to the prescribed rite with the Kula substances, one should properly show it to the disciple; this is considered the Kaulika initiation.

Therein, the Guru, having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the deposition of the *mātṛkās* (*mātṛkānyāsa*), the sixfold deposition (*ṣoḍhānyāsa*), and all else upon his own body and the body of the Śakti, and having performed the installation of the ritual jar (*kalaśasthāpana*), produces and consecrates the substance arising from the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* according to the sequence of the *dūtīyāga*, as well as the consecration of fish, meat, and so forth.

Having performed the worship of the deity according to the sequence of the upcoming Vīrapūjā, O Maheśānī, at the time of imparting the mantra to the disciple, one should place the vessel in the disciple’s hand; this is the Vīrapātra as described in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*: "O Kuleśvarī, drink this pure nectar, which is the medicine for existence [in this world]. [It severs] the bonds of the bound soul..."
One should place [the substance] in the hand of the disciple with the mantra declared in the *Kulārṇava* as "The cause of total eradication has been uttered by Bhairava."

The disciple also, with the same mantra, should say "Let it be drunk" (*pīyatām*); here too, having recited "Vāmī," he should drink with the mantra to be mentioned later, beginning with "Oblation of dharma and adharma, O blazing one" (*dīpta*).
Then the Guru should impart the mantra; regarding this, it is said in the Yāmala:
Having written this [mantra] together with the ṛṣis and other [components], placed it within the ground,
and worshipped it with flowers and other offerings, one should then show it to the disciple.
If the teacher feels great affection for the disciple, then he should speak into his ear;
even more so if the disciple is an object of the teacher's exceeding love.
Then the most excellent guru should first give her [the water] for rinsing the mouth;
even if the disciple is free from conceptual constructs, he should receive it with a focused mind.
If it is accomplished without that [initiation], one shall incur the curse of the deity.
In the Meru Tantra:

Having filled the mouth with the perfected substance (siddhadravya) accompanied by the five *vyoma* mantras and the *mātṛkā*, one should consecrate the beloved disciple; this is declared to be known as the "mouthful" (*gaṇḍuṣa*) consecration.
In the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā:
One should sprinkle the auspicious [image] three times with sprouts placed in the water-pot;
once thus consecrated, he becomes a preeminent leader among teachers.
O Pārvatī, when one is endowed with the knowledge of reality (tattva), then he is worthy of the worship of Śiva;
otherwise, there can be no success for one who possesses conceptual doubt.
If a doubt arises in the disciple regarding the offering of the mouthful of water (gaṇḍūṣa), there is no accomplishment for him anywhere; even Śrīvidyā turns her face away from him.
The remainder is the same as for the animal sacrifice.
Now, there is a specific distinction regarding the initiation of Tārā.
Having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) one thousand and eight times, or one hundred and eight times, or twenty-eight times with *bilva* leaves,
and having offered milk-rice (*pāyasa*), gold dust (*kṛśana*), sweetmeats (*modaka*), sugar, and a goat-sacrifice,
one should offer the meat of a monitor lizard (*godhā*), plantain flowers (*raṃbhāpuṣpa*), and *sāla* fish. Then, [offer] rice cooked with *śāli* grains.
Having offered barley and milk, one should undergo initiation; "cows, land, gold, and so forth are the sacrificial fees"—so states the *Nīlatantra*.
In the Cāmuṇḍa Tantra:

In all the minor sciences (*upavidyās*), such as the accomplishment of the six rites (*ṣatkarma*) and so forth, there is no initiation (*dīkṣā*) here, nor is there the worship of the limbs (*aṅga*) and other such rituals. Regarding the minor sciences, such as the *iṇya* [mantras] and others— the specific mantras used in the application of spells for the six rites, subjugation (*vaśya*), and so on— if a mantra has been written in a book by someone, O beautiful one...
It is recited.
For him, no success arises; there is only loss at every step.
All rites performed through the mouth of the Guru bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Since all ritual actions not instructed by the guru will certainly be fruitless.

If it be asked how this can be so on account of various such statements, we say no; for although there is a prohibition against initiation preceded by the selection of the *kuṇḍapāyin* priests and the performance of the *varaṇa-homa*, there is no prohibition against the instruction [of the doctrine].
In another tantra:
The mere recitation of a mantra at a time of lunar or solar eclipse, at a sacred ford (tīrtha), at a place of spiritual accomplishment (siddhikṣetra), or in a temple of Śiva—
that is called "instruction" (upadeśa).
Because, by such statements as these, even instruction is prescribed.

And because of the statement, "One should not accomplish the mantra after having learned it from a treatise," it should not be said here that knowledge of the mantra even from a book produces success; for the procedures to be performed [are those] prescribed by the treatise.
Because of the injunction regarding knowledge, the word "mantra" is construed with the phrase "one should accomplish."
In the Meru-tantra:

Thus has been described the initiation consisting of ritual action (kriyāmaya-dīkṣā), which bestows [spiritual] form upon kings, as well as upon Vaiśyas, Brahmins, and those engaged in worldly occupations, through the granting of wealth and other such means.
This sequence of initiation has been proclaimed for those who desire success accompanied by worldly enjoyment.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the initiation involving physical action.
Now, the initiation consisting of the phonemes (varṇamayī-dīkṣā), according to the Merutantra.
Now, listen to the initiation consisting of the phonemes (varṇadīkṣā), which bestows knowledge;
it has been proclaimed that the phonemes consist of the nature of both the Person (puruṣa) and Primordial Matter (prakṛti).
And such a thing regarding the body has been declared by the teachers.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
The phonemes consist of both Spirit (puṃs) and Nature (prakṛti), and the body is likewise composed of them;
therefore, the preceptor should project the phonemes onto the body of the disciple.
In the Meru Tantra.
Then, having placed the letters upon the body of the child, the best of preceptors should withdraw those letters situated in their respective locations in reverse order.
By his own power and by the command of the deity’s self,
the lord of teachers makes the disciple become the deity’s self, with all his constituent principles then completely dissolved.
Then, one should unite the consciousness of the disciple with the Supreme Self;
having produced those vowels from that [Self], one should place them within the body of the disciple.
And in that [disciple], one should again deposit that consciousness according to the sequence of emanation;
thus the disciple becomes the very self of the deity, Śiva, whose nature is eternal bliss.
Initiation consisting of the mirror of knowledge has been described; it bestows all accomplishments.
"Also in the Śāradā [Tantra] it is said thus. This concludes the procedure for initiation consisting of the phonemes (varṇamayī-dīkṣā).
Now, as for the initiation into Kalāvati, it is as follows: in that very same [text].
Now I shall describe the initiation of the Kalās, which bestows the eightfold supernatural powers beginning with the power of becoming small as a gem;
I shall speak of the five-fold Kalā-initiation, while the right-hand tradition considers it to be three-fold.
The fifty-four *kalās* are on the left; from the Guru, that perfected mantra should be received swiftly as it brings about success, whereas in the opposite case, the reverse occurs.
The wise one should pierce, in sequence, those five movements of the elements— headed by the withdrawal of the digits (kalānivṛtti)— into the body of the disciple, which is composed of the elements.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
Since the powers of the five elements, beginning with *nivṛtti*, are time itself,
one should therefore meditate upon them within the body composed of the elements and pierce [the heart] of the disciple.
56b) In the Meru Tantra:
The *nivṛtti* kalā is established from the feet up to the knees;
the kalā called *pratiṣṭhā* is situated from there up to the navel, extending from the region of the sun.
The kalā known as Vidyā is situated from the navel up to the throat;
the kalā known as Śānti is situated from the throat up to the forehead.
The Śāntyatītā Kalā is said to extend as far as the eye on the forehead;
the wise one should pierce it from that location according to the sequence of withdrawal.
In this manner, initiation consisting of five kalās is prescribed for one’s own station by one’s own command;
O deities, now hear the method for initiation consisting of thirty-eight kalās.
In due order, the letters beginning with *ka* are situated on the petals;
where those beginning with *ha* follow in reverse order, there are the *kalās* in those two places.
The sixteen digits of the Sun and likewise those of the Moon are to be meditated upon;
in the place beginning with the letter *ya*, the ten digits of Fire are to be meditated upon.
Then follows the withdrawal of the phonemes and their constituent parts, as well as from their respective positions;
thereafter, one should generate the disciple once more—this is the ritual procedure for initiation by means of the kalās.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for initiation into Kalāvatī.
