Now follows the procedure for initiation consisting of piercing (vedha).
This is clear in the Merutantra.
In the Kaulika and Vāmamārga traditions, the initiation by piercing (vedhadīkṣā) bestows its fruit;
those other [initiations] exist in the Dakṣiṇamārga, while otherwise they may occur everywhere.
In that very same [text].
I shall describe the initiation consisting of piercing (vedha), by obtaining which the radiant one,
at that very moment, becomes liberated while living within saṃsāra.
One should meditate on a four-petalled lotus at the disciple’s mūlādhāra;
in its center is a triangle, and in the middle of that is Kuṇḍalinī.
The Goddess who consists of three revolutions, whose form is like a mass of lightning,
who is identical with Mahādeva, and whose body is composed of pure consciousness alone.
One should [meditate upon] the Goddess, subtler than the subtlest, who pierces the six chakras,
the divine Yoginī, by way of the Suṣumnā path toward the abode of Śiva.
One should collect the letters beginning with *sa* (the sibilants) located in the *sāntavādi* group into the position of the lotus;
likewise, the pair of letters beginning with *la* (the semi-vowels) should be placed upon the six-petalled lotus.
Having properly joined [the disciple] at the Svādhiṣṭhāna, the Guru should pierce him;
he should lead those syllables into Viṣṇu, and Viṣṇu into that lotus of the navel.
One should oneself place [the letters] beginning with *pha* and *ṭa* joined with vowels upon the petals of the directions;
one should join those letters to Rudra, and place that Rudra within the lotus of the heart.
57a) One should oneself pierce the petals of the lotus [of the heart] starting from the letter *ka* up to *ṭha*,
and likewise extract those ending with the final letter (*kṣa*) into this lotus of the throat.
Having diligently joined the vowels within a lotus consisting of sixteen petals,
one should then join them to Sadāśiva in the lotus at the center of that [body].
Then, having pierced the two petals joined at the eye, the Guru should lead the self,
together with Śakti, up to Paraśiva.
By the power of the teacher's command, the disciple’s ignorance is burnt away;
once that [ignorance] has been destroyed, he falls [into the state of realization], and having attained higher knowledge (vijñāna), he then becomes omniscient.
May Sadāśiva himself become [one with you]; this is indeed the truth, there is no doubt.
This auspicious initiation, consisting of piercing (*vedha*), is said to bestow knowledge.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
He becomes Śiva directly; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
This initiation, consisting of penetration (āveśa), has been declared as that which bestows pure consciousness.
Thus ends the procedure for initiation consisting of piercing.
Now, the various types of initiation.
In the *Kularatnodyota*.
Initiation (dīkṣā) is considered to be threefold: Śāmbhavī, Śāktī, and Āṇavī.
The Śāktī [initiation] brings about splendor; one should conceive it as non-different from Śakti.
That which is a mixture of the Śākta, Śāmbhava, and Āṇava [methods] is proclaimed as such;
thus, O Goddess, initiation shall take place through these three modes.
In the great jewel of the six lineages.
The wise, proficient in the scriptures, declare that initiation is manifold as *āṇavī*, *śākteyī*, and again *śāṃbhavī*, or else it is simply one.
Having stated that the *āṇavī* [power] is manifold, its divisions are now described:
the *smārtī*, the *mānasikī*, the *yaugī*, the *cākṣuṣī*, and likewise the *spārśanī*.
The vocal, the mantra-based, the sacrificial, the scriptural, and the consecratory [initiations]—
having remembered the Guru who resides in another land, [the disciple] should [purify] the three bonds for the disciple in their proper order.
This is called the *smārta* initiation, which consists of the proper unification with the supreme Śiva through the procedure of dissolving the bonds of worldly enjoyment.
Having perceived with the mind one who is pure and seated in one's own presence,
that which liberates from the three impurities by means of the [three] means is the mental [liberation].
Following the sequence taught in Yoga, the yogi enters the body of the disciple,
seizes his soul, and unites it with his own self.
This is declared to be the initiation for yoga, which destroys the three impurities;
it consists of gazing with a heart melting with compassion, having resolved, "I am Śiva."
This initiation through the gaze is the Cākṣuṣī initiation, which destroys all sins;
having become this supreme Śiva, the Guru possesses a mind free from doubt.
With the hand of Śiva, he should touch the disciple’s head while reciting the mantra;
this is declared to be the initiation by touch (sparśadīkṣā), which effects the manifestation of Śiva.
Having visualized his own mouth as the mouth of the Guru, the Guru, with reverence,
[bestows] the divine mantras and so forth upon the disciple through the application of the Guru’s mouth.
This is indeed the supreme oral initiation (vācikī-dīkṣā), which should be given together with the placement of mudrās (mudrā-nyāsa) and other rites;
likewise, it consists of the mantra joined with the placement upon the body (vigraha).
Having herself become the embodiment of the mantra, she respectfully bestowed the Sakra-mantra upon her disciple; that initiation is the "Mantric" (māntrī), which destroys impurity and ignorance.
Having deposited the fire according to the prescribed rite either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
[one should perform the ritual] through the sequence of dissolution and enjoyment, proceeding step by step along each path (adhvan).
One should perform oblations for the purification of the mantra-syllables, the kalās, the tattvas, and the pīṭhas; this is considered the *hautrī* initiation.
Initiation by means of the words of the scriptures, bestowed upon a worthy disciple who is devoted and intent on service and worship, is called *śāstrī-dīkṣā*.
Having reverently worshipped Śiva and the consort of Śiva within the pitcher,
the initiation that occurs through the consecration from the pitcher of Śiva is known as the *ābhiṣecikī* initiation.

"Of the enjoyment of absorption" (layabhogasya) means: by way of the sequence of piercing initiation (vedhadīkṣākrama), it consists of the withdrawal (saṃhāra) of the deities of the phonemes (varṇadevatā) residing in the mūlādhāra and other centers.
With the hand of Śiva, one should fashion a small mandala on one's own right hand with meditative concentration.
One should worship the Lord here according to the prescribed rite; "thus it shall be Śivahastaka" means in the form described by Sāmaśambhu.
In the Meru Tantra.
The Guru should meditate upon his own Guru in the form of Śiva within his own hand,
while reciting the root mantra, the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), the Mātṛkā, and other mantras.
Having placed his right hand upon the head of the disciple out of compassion, he should then utter the secret name; this is called the initiation by touch, which bestows spiritual accomplishments.
The Guru should cause the disciple’s mind to rest upon Sadāśiva, who is of the nature of consciousness;
meditating on all mantras as having arisen from Him, he himself then becomes identical with that.
By the grace of my Guru, I alone am born as Sadāśiva.
Meditating thus, one should instruct; this is declared to be the initiation of speech (vāgdīkṣā).
Having closed one's eyes and meditated upon the deity within the Supreme Self, [one should proceed].
With eyes filled with the bliss of seeing him, the Guru should look upon the disciple with a serene mind and, being composed, should instruct him as follows.
58a) For one who has already achieved success through mantras, such an initiation will grant the fruit;
[it is attained] by the mere sight of the guru, by his speech, or even by his touch.
Knowledge arises immediately; that is remembered as the Śāmbhavī initiation.
For the sake of attaining worldly enjoyment and liberation, the Guru should examine [the disciple] according to the prescribed rule.
One should teach the mantra afterwards; otherwise, it will be fruitless.
He who gives [the mantra] through improper means, and he who receives it improperly—[both are at fault].
Whether giving or receiving, there will be a breach of family tradition;
for the teacher and disciple are like earth and water, which must examine one another before coming together.
One who gives instruction or receives it [in such a manner] shall become a Piśāca;
likewise for one who gives or receives instruction that is contrary to the scriptures.
Both of them shall experience twenty-one streams of hells,
that fool who imparts instruction without having performed the purificatory rites.
And those mantras perish like rice seeds sown in sand;
the knowledge of mantras never remains in one who is unworthy.
Therefore, one should speak only after careful examination; otherwise, it would be fruitless.
Knowledge is bestowed upon a worthy disciple who has been properly distinguished and prepared.
The observer of the vow constantly attains that [result], just as one obtains ghee from cow's milk;
however, if one should initiate an unworthy person out of desire for wealth, fear, gain, or the like, [the result is lost].
One incurs the curse of the deities, and what has been done becomes undone.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka).
That has been stated in that very same place.
Having thus bestowed initiation, the Guru should perform the final consecration (pūrṇābhiṣecana);
for without this consecration, the practitioner cannot attain full awakening.
He attains the status of a teacher and the desired higher state;
therefore, the guru, having instructed his beloved disciple, should perform the consecration.
Having fashioned a vast and beautiful pavilion,
one should place a jar filled with a khārī measure or more in the center of the mandala.
There, upon the petals, various jars adorned with cloth and gold should be placed; therein, one should install the external tutelary deity.
Having worshipped the deities of the limbs and the surrounding retinue in the center and in the other [vessels],
the preceptor, touching the central jar, should recite as follows:
Then, with that water, the preceptor consecrated the disciple along with the four Vedas and their auxiliary branches; this is known as the "Full Consecration" (pūrṇābhiṣecana).
From the Vedas all the Tantras arose, and from those Tantras likewise the Mantras;
since they were born from them, the disciple is the sole vessel for all mantras.
One who bears the name of an Ācārya, or whom the Guru has given another name—
if one receives initiation from such a person, he shall possess spiritual accomplishment (siddhi).
He becomes capable in all these acts of giving;
he is under the control of all the gods, and his recitation of the Vedas is indeed virtuous.
This very same procedure should be followed on that path, with the intention of making a sacrificial gift (dakṣiṇā).
From there, the wise man should collect whatever sacred bathing places (tīrthas) exist.
From the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Sarasvatī, and the great ocean; from the Sindhu, Godāvarī, Revā, Kāverī, and other rivers of vast waters.
The waters of the Mahendrī, Sarayū, Carmaṇvatī, Puṣkara,
the great river Vedikā, Kṣiprā, and Vetravatī [are present].
At Kurukṣetra, at the Gaṅgā, at Pūrṇā, and at Mānasa,
one should offer oblations into a jar and recite mantras even from various tantras.
Having been consecrated by those [mantras] for that purpose, those mantras of his become perfected;
thus, the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) is for the sake of proceeding to Prayāga and likewise for the sake of giving gifts.
Alternatively, there is the procedure for the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) of the disciples.
That has been stated in that very same place.
Or else, in the Vāmaka [tradition]:
A pitcher for the Tīrthas should be placed in the center; the remaining pitchers are for water.
Whatever deities were invited by the Guru into the excellent pitcher of the gods, [those are to be honored].
Those very mantras, assuming form, establish their presence within his mouth;
his speech becomes spontaneously perfected, and he shall never bow his head to another.
For one for whose sake the head is bowed, death will come without a doubt;
such is the case when one who follows the left-hand path becomes a perfected master (siddha).
And the disciple should be free from egoism, always devoted to the deity;
for the sake of the deity, he should have no attachment to his three debts nor any mind set on worldly enjoyment.
He alone is successful; anyone other than he is a vessel for the left-hand path and for hell, impoverished, miserable, and foolish both in this world and the next.
One should perform the ritual procedure of initiation according to one's capacity, following the instructions of the Guru.
Now follows another method.
With a conch or a water-pot filled with live fish, filled with wine,
and completely filled with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Then one should perform the consecration with sprouts from trees growing on the riverbank;
this is proclaimed as the "Full Consecration" (pūrṇābhiṣeka) in the path of the Ugra-kula.
Likewise, its greatness is described in that very same place.

This initiation, performed by a preceptor according to the prescribed rite, burns away hundreds of thousands of minor offenses (upapātaka) and tens of millions of major sins (mahāpātaka) in an instant.
Just as iron, when pierced by the essence of mercury (rasendra), attains the state of gold,
so too the self, pierced by initiation, certainly attains the state of Śiva.
The status of a Śūdra has departed, and the Brahminhood of the Brahmin has departed.
In one who is perfected by the purificatory rite of initiation (dīkṣā), no distinction of caste exists;
for the signs of caste are established only in wood, stone, metal, clay, and gems.
Just as Mahādeva is described, so too are the initiated members of the castes.
In the *Sārasaṃgraha*:
This is the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), which bestows success upon practitioners;
it is known as the "twofold" (ubhaya) Kaulika, and this full consecration is that which brings subjugation.
This has been stated in the Kulārṇava and the Merutantra.
If a Kaulika who is devoid of the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) dies,
he attains the state of a Piśāca until the dissolution of the universe at the end of the kalpa.
The measure of a *khārī* is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
Two *pala*s are considered a *prasṛti*; a *kuḍava* is held to be double that.
Four *kuḍava*s make a *prasṛti*, and four times those [make] an *āḍhaka*.
Four guṇas make one droṇa; two of those are known as a kumbha.
Eight of those *kuṃbhas* constitute a *khārī*.
Thus ends the full consecration on the left.
In the Meru Tantra:
I shall speak another most secret [teaching], hidden in all tantras;
I proclaim this mantra, which one should bestow only as a deity would.
Know that the letters recited in the traditional sequence beginning with 'ca' and ending with 'ra' are denoters of the moon and other objects,
joined respectively with the four vowels in increasing numerical order.
The convention regarding the deities of the previous [system] has been declared along with its defects;
furthermore, in this case, the letters beginning with *anāmā* (the letter *na*) are to be taken, as well as those joined with numerical figures.
In the Dakṣiṇāmnāya, however, the syllables are devoid of the first letter of their names;
two, two, one, and again two—these are the groups that constitute the secret convention.
The castes are determined by the traditional transmission and by purchase; likewise, the vowels and so forth follow their respective order.
In that sequence, the vowels and consonants belong to the deities of the West and the North.
According to the conventions of the four traditions (āmnāyas), one should apply the combination of letters and numbers in each syllable;
however, in the Vaidika tradition, the Upper Tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya) is to be performed, and nothing else.
In whatever order and in whatever location those letters have been proclaimed,
those letters, numbering one and so forth, should be grasped in that same order.
When the conjunction of the numerical signs of the mantra syllables is combined with the numerical sign of one's own name and reaches its root, then a dream arises.
In the absence of a root mantra, one should again apply the name of the deity marked with its seed-syllable;
when a root mantra cannot be obtained, the application of the name of the sacred seat (pīṭha) should be used.
When the root no longer proceeds through the sequence of the names of the seats (pīṭha),
and when the root no longer proceeds, then dreams do not arise.
Even if received from a teacher, it would be ineffective if it lacks the mantra.
[One should draw] squares marked with the root-syllables, extending north-south and east-west.

Having written down the numbers starting from one, one should write them so that there is a sequence of counting; the method for making all [the rows] have an equal number of items is now being explained.
In an uneven [number of squares], the first [line] should be drawn facing north in the middle, and likewise the last;
the second should follow the movement of a horse, and thereafter the movement of a minister.
One should first write the initial letter, and thereafter proceed with the movement of the horse as before;
then, following the movement of the minister, one should perform the king's movement upon its obstruction.
Again, the practitioner should perform the movement as before, and again the horse-like movement;
thus it should be done repeatedly according to the path shown by the Guru.
The completion of the numbers occurs, as well as their equality in every respect;
thus is described the extraction of the three uneven [numbers].
From Indra (14), Bāṇa (5), Veda (4), Indu (1), Vasu (8), Diś (10), Tithi (15), Bhāskara (12),
Viśva (13), Trayas (3), Ṣaṭ (6), Sapta (7), Dvi (2), and Ṣoḍaśāṅka (16), [the numbers] are obtained in sequence.
One should write equal numbers in the four compartments of the square;
having designated this as the center, one should then place the final number in the northeast (māheśī) corner.
One should place the penultimate [syllable] in the southeast, the first in the southwest, and the second in the northwest; thereafter, the sequence should proceed according to the numerical order.
In the same manner, O Ambikā, the full [digits] should be maintained in the cardinal directions (kāṣṭhā), one by one;
those that rival them should be established in the intermediate directions (diś) that rival them.
In this way, the completion of the three times is proclaimed;
or else, one should cause the sequence of the vessels, the distributor, and the machines to be written down.
Without a preceptor, nothing is known, just as the entire world is not perceived without the sun;
therefore, having bathed on a Sunday before the rising of the sun, one [attains knowledge].
At sunrise, having offered those gifts, one should enter the house;
one should not look at anyone lower than oneself, nor should one utter even a word [of contempt].
One should write the foremost [mantra] on birch bark, palm leaf, or a small wooden tablet;
or one may write it on a leaf or a circular plate using the eight fragrances appropriate to each respective deity.
Having first worshipped Gaṇeśa, and then the lords of the directions,
one should draw the yantra in a secluded place and observe silence for those days.
The celibate student (brahmacārī), while consuming sacrificial food (haviṣya), should not look at censurable objects;
he should recite the mantra while scratching the area above his navel with both hands.
One should write two *ṭha*s at the end of this [mantra] on the right side;
likewise, [the cloth may be] saffron-colored, yellow, red, black, or white.
One should well-wrap the yantra there— blue in color, measuring one span (prādeśa), and dedicated to the deities of the Āmnāyas beginning with the East— using one kuḍava measure of oil.
One should arrange the desired offerings starting from the east: sesame oil, buffalo ghee, fish, one's own sister, cow's ghee, and fat.
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus on the ground with unhusked grains;
then, one should worship Gaṇeśa, who is free from obstacles, in the pericarp to the north.
Having worshipped one’s chosen deity in the center, Kṣetrapāla in the south,
and the eight lords of the directions upon the petals, one should dismiss them.
Thereafter, one should place a beautiful lamp on the pericarp;
having established the lamp there, one should light it and then perform worship.
One should sleep there attentively, with the head toward the northeast according to the tradition;
on that day, one becomes free from sin and shall attain the assembly of the gods.
One should meditate upon that mantra in whatever form the deity bestows it, as being truly the guru himself, and one should honor those who have mastered it.
On the second solar day, one becomes middling; on the third, a great sinner;
and on the third solar day, a mortal who is free from sin shall attain the mantra.
In the fourth [house], there is middling sin; in the fifth, one who commits many transgressions;
in the fifth, there is the ruin of a Rākṣasa; in the sixth, that [ruin] is middling; and in the sixth, it is sinful.
One certainly attains the mantra on the seventh day of the sun;
this most secret [instruction] has been declared, hidden throughout all tantras.
Now follows the initiation apart from the Guru.
In the Meru-tantra:
Because greed and other defects reside in the preceptor, the mind recoils from him;
therefore, having established a preceptor according to the scriptures, they fled out of fear of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
"It is to be grasped."
Likewise.
Now, listen to the initiation into the Tantric mantras without a guru:
on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, when it is endowed with the strength of the moon and the stars.
Having gone into the presence of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, one should worship the Guru.
Having performed the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa), one should place it before him;
having written the mantra on a palm leaf, one should worship both the mantra and the deity.
Having meditated upon the deity as the Guru, one should clearly recite the mantra.
This is called the undertaking of the mantra one hundred and eight times;
this reality has been declared by me, and it must be kept secret like a lover is from his mother.
Thus concludes the procedure for initiation characterized by the excellence of the Guru.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Kulamuktikallolinī composed by Śrī Ādyānanda.
60b) Now, the ten purificatory rites for mantras.
In the *Tantraśekhara*.
Mantras are proclaimed to be defiled by defects such as being "chinned" (cut);
yet, when constantly practiced, they indeed become bestowers of fruit.
Therefore, we shall describe ten purificatory rites for the destruction of those defects.
In the Meru-tantra.
Now, for the purpose of neutralizing verbal curses and the like, it is said:
[one should perform this] upon a seat made of *śrīparṇī*, sandalwood, or mango wood, and so forth.
One should draw the diagram of the five elements using musk, saffron, and lotuses.
In the *Tantrasekhara*:
The wise one should divide the triangle into seven equal parts;
likewise, one should do so starting from the northeast corner and from the southeast corner.
Thus, there would be forty-nine *yoni*s there on all sides;
the practitioner of mantra should write the syllables in sequence, starting from Īśāna and ending with Varuṇa.
In the Gautamīya [Vinaya].
O observer of noble vows, one should inscribe the supreme Mātṛkā-yantra upon a vessel made of gold or other precious materials, or else with saffron, sandalwood paste, or even sacred ash.
Saffron is prescribed for the consecration of the Śakti, sandalwood for a Vaiṣṇava gem,
and ashes are declared for the Śaiva [tradition], while the Mātṛkās are used for the drawing of the yantra.
In the Meru Tantra.
One should invoke there the goddess Sarasvatī, known as Mātṛkā;
having performed worship according to the prescribed rule, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
Having recited the Mātṛkā, one should [extract] from its midst the mantra desired by oneself,
as well as the vowels, consonants, bindus, visargas, and the letters of the Yoga.
Having extracted each individual syllable and unified them according to the instructions of the Guru, one should grasp the mantra; this is declared to be "saṃjanana" (the generation).
Having placed that first *praṇava* at the beginning, one should recite the letters of the mantra with a *praṇava* interspersed between them;
one hundred and eight times—this is the "life-sustenance" (*bhūjīvana*) of the mantra.
One should write the mantra on a birch-bark leaf with yellow pigment (rocanā) and saffron (kuṅkuma),
and strike it one hundred times for each syllable with sandalwood water.
Uttering this seed-syllable of Vāyu (Yam), it is called "striking" (tāḍana). Śāvara mantras that have become blunted become effective when struck.
Having drawn [the diagram] on the previously mentioned seat according to the number of syllables in its mantra,
and then taking karavīra flowers while reciting [the mantra].
One should offer oblations with those flowers one hundred times for each syllable while reciting the fire-seed (vahnibīja); this is called "awakening" (vodhana).
As before, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus on the pedestal with the prescribed substances;
in its pericarp, one should smear it with a single bud of *māla*.
Reciting the mantra in this manner, one should take [earth] from the sprouts of the Bodhi tree syllable by syllable, according to the number of syllables in that mantra.
One should consecrate him with the mantra "namaḥ," sprinkling [him] with various fragrant substances using a single sprout while reciting the syllables.
One should consecrate it one hundred and eight times; this is remembered as the consecration which, like water, effects the purification of the mantras of men.
The Jyotir-mantra should be meditated upon in the fire-mandala at the mūlādhāra; one should thus contemplate the mantra as being consecrated within that very [fire].

The impurity of the individual soul (āṇava) is considered innate; that of action (kārmaṇa) is adventitious; and that which is called the impurity of yoga (yogākhya), pertaining to illusion (māyika), resides in one's own mantra. Thus, the three impurities are located within one's own mantra.
One should contemplate each [element] as being individually incinerated by the *jyotis* mantra;
thus, one should think, "I have become pure through my own mantra."
The Jyotirmantra, beginning with the Veda and consisting of the two syllables "Hraum," is considered [the essence];
one should perform this purification at the conclusion of its application as well.
As before, one should inscribe the mantra upon the pedestal using substances such as saffron;
then, [one should prepare] a vessel of copper or the like with camphor and scented water.
Having filled [the vessel] with pure [water], one should write [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
then, having consecrated the water with that mantra, one should sprinkle it with drops from kusha grass.

They should sprinkle [the water] syllable by syllable; this is considered to be the nourishment (āpyāyana) for those who have completed the preliminary rites (puraścaryā), as well as the ritual of returning home (samāvartana).
One should inscribe the mantra within a copper vessel using musk and other substances,
and in another vessel, there should be pure water scented with camphor and similar ingredients.

Having taken [the water] with the noble vessel (āryapātra) and reciting this mantra, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) by saying "I satisfy [you], obeisance" (tarpayāmi namaḥ). Thus is the libation.
One should recite the mantra preceded by *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ* one hundred and eight times;
this is the "kindling" (*dīpana*), which is desired for all mantras as well.
The concealment and non-disclosure of the mantra being recited— these ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras) have been proclaimed and kept secret in all Tantras.
Thus, eleven consecrations have been declared, as well as five others; for each mantra, the recitation, the fire-oblation, and the libation are to be performed as they will be described.
Sweeping and eating—these two for each [of the four] make sixteen.
61b) One should recite the mantra one thousand times, purified by the *haṃsa* mantra. This is called "illumination" (*dīpana*), according to the *Maṃtraśeṣara*.
In the Gautamīya [Vinaya].
One should recite the mantra while encased within the white moon, the favoring moon, and the crescent moon;
this is declared as "nourishment" (āpyāyana) by those expert in the science of mantras.
The letter *ṣa* is white; the letter *sa* is the moon; the letter *bho* is grace.
In that very place.

The libation with honey is prescribed for the Śakti-mantra; for the Vaiṣṇava-mantra, it is with water mixed with camphor; and for the Śaiva-mantra, it is with clarified butter—thus it has been correctly declared by the masters of mantra.
Having first performed the mantra-consecration himself, the guru should subsequently instruct the disciple.
This has been stated in the Merutantra:
"Since it is stated that 'one who is liberated from an unspoken curse should thereafter instruct him,' these are the purificatory rites for mantras (mantra-saṃskāras).
Now, the procedure for the abandonment of a mantra that yields undesirable results is described."
In that regard:
Now, the ritual procedure for the complete renunciation of mantras is clearly elucidated.
The definition of a sacrificial post (yūpa) is as follows.
Or it should be understood as having undesirable results.
Likewise.
Having become pure and composed, on an auspicious day,
the preceptor should commence the excellent rite for the destruction of all suffering.
There, first, in a beautiful pavilion within the mandapa, the wise one should place the water-pot according to the sequence of the initiation rite and fill it with auspicious waters.
By reciting the mantra in reverse order, one should cause the deity there to descend;
having performed the ritual integration (sakalīkaraṇa) and worshipped [the deity], one should worship the [protective] enclosures.
Having thus worshipped the deity of the mantra along with its protective coverings,
the twice-born practitioner, having offered oblations of clarified butter with the mantra in reverse order, should likewise offer a cow.
Then, just as one would offer an oblation to the deities with various kinds of food,
so too should one offer it in the intermediate and cardinal directions with the supreme mantras that are about to be described.
O Indra, Lord of the Āyus, Sovereign of the Suras, Śatamanyu, Lord of Śacī!
Salutations to you; accept this offering of flowers, incense, and other oblations.
O Agni, mass of splendors, bestower of boons,
accept these flowers, incense, and other offerings, along with this well-honored sacrificial gift.
O King of Pretas, come hither, you who possess a luster like crushed collyrium;
having accepted this offered oblation, be well-pleased and grant boons.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the Rakshasas, O Nirṛti; you have come here.
Accept this offering, worship, and other gifts presented by me with devotion.
Come, O Guardian of the Western Quarter, Lord of the Waters; salutations to you!
Having accepted this worship offered with devotion, may you indeed attain delight.
O Wind-god, protector of life, together with your retinue,
accept this offering respectfully as it is duly presented by me.
May Kuvera and the Lord of the Stars (the Moon), those two best of gods, come;
being pleased by flowers, incense, and other offerings, may they grant me boons.
O Lord, O Master who is the refuge of all knowledge, you alone are the sovereign;
when worshipped with flowers, incense, and other offerings, you become pleased for the sake of prosperity.
Come, O Lord of all worlds, O Brahmā;
accept this worship and turn back all my obstacles—homage be to you!
Come, O bestower of boons, unmanifest Viṣṇu, leader of the universe;
worshipped with supreme devotion, may you be the giver of happiness to me.
Then one should worship the mantra-deity together with his retinue;
[this was done] by me, whose intellect was unsteady, without having observed [the deity's] favor.
O Lord, by that very nature of the mantra which has been received and honored by me,
may you completely dispel every agitation of my mind.
May evil be repelled, and may worship bring eternal well-being;
salutations to me, and may there be auspiciousness—O Revatī, devotion is purifying.
Having thus offered this prayer, one should write the mantra of Devaśī in reverse order upon a leaf and worship it with nutmeg, camphor, and sandalwood.
Having established the water-pot with supreme devotion,
the wise man should then place that leaf upon his own head.
One should bathe with the auspicious waters contained in the consecrated pitcher, which are permeated by mantras;
then, having restrained oneself, one should fill the pitcher again with other water.
Having placed the mantra-leaf in the middle of that,
one should then worship that pitcher on the bank of a river or in another pure reservoir of water.
Then one should cast [the mantra] into the brahmins and feed them according to one's ability;
for one who has performed the rite in this manner, the diseases arising from enemy mantras [shall be destroyed].
There is no doubt that as these [defilements] perish, a clarity of mind gradually arises;
once it has become fully perfected, it increases through the lineage of the family.
Now, devotion to the guru.
In the Meru Tantra.
This path, inherited through the lineage, has been fully revealed by the Guru;
when practiced correctly, it shall become the means for accomplishing both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Even a Brahmin, though endowed with virtues, is not praised if he is not devoted;
even a Mleccha, though devoid of virtues, is called a disciple if he possesses devotion.
Likewise.
For one devoid of devotion to the guru, austerity, knowledge, vows,
and noble lineage are all as futile as various ornaments adorning a corpse.
In the Kulārṇava [Tantra] (62b).
O Goddess, just as devotion is shown toward Nārāyaṇa, Mahādeva, one’s mother and father, and the king, so too should it be directed toward one’s own guru.
In the Merutantra and the Kulārṇava.
A disciple residing in the same village should prostrate to the guru at the three junctions of the day;
even one residing only a krośa away should bow to the guru every day.
A disciple who travels half a yojana should recite the *praṇava* during the five parvan days;
starting from one yojana, this extends up to twelve yojanas.
Having traveled on the path for a distance measured in various yojanas,
the disciple, though situated in a distant land, approached the presence of his beloved guru with devotion.
Month by month, for as many yojanas [the distance] has been calculated, the disciple should bow to the Guru;
when he is situated at a great distance, he should go [to him] whenever the desire arises.
One should not approach a king, a deity, or a teacher with empty hands;
one should offer fruits, flowers, garments, and so forth according to one's ability.
Likewise.

One should perform austerity for the sake of one's guru, but should not bathe for the sake of personal purification; one should not give instructions to the guru, nor should one address him by the pronoun "you."
Likewise.
A disciple who desires prosperity should never, at any time, engage in lending money, giving away material goods, or buying and selling with his teachers.
O Ambikā, he who worships another while the Guru is present shall go to a terrible hell; that worship becomes fruitless.
If the Guru has a desire for a particular object, one should not experience it;
however, if there is a necessity, one may experience it only by his command.
For he who takes even a very small amount of another's property without it being given, O beloved teacher, enters the womb of a beast and is devoured by carnivorous animals.
One who covets the property of the guru and is eager to have sexual intercourse with the guru’s wife becomes fallen; of this there is no doubt, and no expiation exists for such a person.
One should not obstruct the status of the guru, the tradition, its dharma, or its source;
such a sinner should be cast out by the gurus, punished, and even executed.
Upon seeing the Pāṇḍukāmāśana seat, a vehicle, an umbrella, or chowries belonging to a guru, one should pay homage; one should not employ them for one's own enjoyment.
O beloved, one should not practice indifference toward tasks, whether they have been explicitly mentioned or left unsaid;
whatever the guru declares as good or bad, that task should be carried out without hesitation.
Even after committing a hundred murders of Brahmins, one should obey the command of the Guru;
for in both punishment and favor, the Guru is the cause of everything for all beings.
Whatever has emerged from the mouth of the Guru is called all the scriptures.
Likewise.
To disobey the command, to steal from the guru, and to act unfavorably toward him—they say this is treachery against the guru; whoever commits such acts is a sinner.
O Goddess, one should not sit on a seat in the presence of a deity or a guru;
whether one is noble by birth, learned, or wealthy, upon seeing the guru from afar, one should approach with joy.
One should not harbor pride on account of birth, learning, wealth, and so forth;
one incurs that same sin by speaking falsehood in the presence of the Guru.
Even after committing the slaughter of a cow or a Brahmin,
one shall not incur that sin if one performs a single prostration with the staff-like body and circumambulates three times.
Likewise.
O Dear One, in the sacrifice for that Guru and his Guru, one should salute the *praguru*;
then one should bow to the Guru, and he too should prevent [the salutation] in the presence of his own Guru.
In the presence of his preceptor’s preceptor, the disciple should mentally bow to his own guru.
Likewise.
One should perform three prostrations before the guru, one for those who are senior, and likewise join the palms (añjali) for other venerable persons; for others, a verbal salutation suffices.

One should always bow down to the gods, teachers, family preceptors, those advanced in knowledge, those whose wealth is austerity, those eminent in learning, those established in their own duties, and those well-versed in the Vedas.
One should never abandon the glorious Guru; when commanded by him, one should proceed with joy. When the Guru is below, one should never stand above him.
If the Naga were not present before them while the Guru remained there.
The word "seated" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense after "tuṣṭi" (satisfaction).
Wherever there may be slander of the venerable Guru, one should immediately cover one's own ears and depart from that place far away, so as not to hear it.

Afterward, he should recite [the mantra] with his guru; that is the remedy for hearing it [otherwise]. One should not show disrespect toward the guru, friends, well-wishers, residents, servants, and so forth.
The Guru’s consort, his two sons, the elder brother who is equal to the Guru,
the younger brothers who are like one’s own self, and the protectors of the lineage who are like one’s own children.
The word "should be practiced" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
In the Meru Tantra.
Thus, a Brahmin who worships in a womb shall become a Brahma-rākṣasa.
The term "vipra" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) that includes kṣatriyas and others as well.
Now, the rules of conduct (*ācāra*) [are described] in the *Merutantra*, the *Kālitantra*, and the *Yāmala*.
Now I shall proclaim the conduct by practicing which one partakes of immortality:
one who is devoted to the welfare of all beings and is a protector of the conduct of the samaya.
Abandoning impermanent actions, intent upon eternal practice,
he offers all his deeds to the Supreme Deity.
The word "syāt" (might be) is to be understood as the ellipsis. One who desires liberation should not perform any action out of desire for things such as the impermanent fruits of ritual acts;
rather, being devoted to obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) duties, one should contemplate during the propitiation of the mantra: "May there be only my auspiciousness (*śiva*).
Whatever action has been performed, one should offer it to the Deity—this is the meaning of the section.
To have faith in and worship mantras other than one's own,
to revile noble women and heroes, and to steal their property.
A wise person should always avoid anger toward women and physical assault;
for the entire world consists of women, and one should oneself likewise become so.

One who strives with a disciplined mind should contemplate the drink, the chewed, the sucked, the eaten, the licked, the home, happiness, and the beauty of every young woman as being [of the nature of] the deity.
Upon seeing a young woman of noble birth, one should offer salutation with a concentrated mind,
provided that the sight of such a person occurs through the power of one's fortune.
At that very time, one should perform mental worship for them—
whether they be a girl, one intoxicated with youth, or likewise an old woman or a beautiful lady.
Or, having paid homage to one who is contemptible or greatly wicked, one should meditate upon their blows,
their insults, as well as their deceit and unpleasantness.
Under no circumstances should one act otherwise, for it creates an obstacle to success:
women are gods, women are life-breaths, and women alone are the ornament.
One should always avoid association with women, even those who are great ascetics;
likewise, food placed in their hands, sleeping while one's teacher is asleep, sleeping while an elder is asleep, and nakedness.
If, by chance, she is seen, the wise man should have a Śrīcakra constructed for her.
The term "asleep" is an elliptical expression; the meaning is that one should not look upon these people while they are naked due to a lack of attention.
In the Kulārṇava:
O Goddess of the gods, one should not speak of the sandals of the glorious Guru, the root mantra, or the pādukā-mantra to anyone other than the disciple.
In the Merutantra and the Kulārṇava.

O beloved, the lineage transmission received through successive succession, as well as the mantras, tantras, and so forth—all of these become fruitful when obtained from the Guru; it is not otherwise.
O Pārvatī, one should employ the weapons of the Kuśalas as if they were one's own wife;
one should avoid all the scriptures of the Paśus as if they were the wives of another.
Just as milk situated in its own hide should not be drunk by the best of the twice-born,
so too the unrighteousness of those with the faces of beasts should not be heard by the Kaulikas.
Young maidens, restless in their play, [passed by] a wine-jar on their heads, a perfected ascetic at the end of the road, a mango tree, and an aśoka tree.
Upon seeing a solitary tree, a cremation ground, a gathering of women,
or a woman dressed in red garments, one should pay homage with devotion.
The gurus, the Śaktis, the sons, the elder and younger ones, the teachers of the Kula,
the scriptures of the Kula-darśana, the Kula-substances, and the Kaulikas.
O Yoginī, [I seek] those who incite, those who indicate, as well as those who speak,
those who beg, teachers, enlighteners, and perfected beings (siddhapuruṣa).
One should not dance with, nor feel disgust toward, nor laugh at, nor treat with contempt girls, young maidens, naked women, those who are insane, or those whose breasts are exposed.
One should not speak untruth or anything unpleasant to any member of a family of yogins; nor should one say "Do this" or address a female yogini as "O Kṛṣṇā."
And also in mercury.
One should not address a woman of noble family as "black" or "ugly," nor should one examine the devotion of heroes or what has been done or left undone by them.
Likewise.
The Kula-yoginīs always grind [substances] upon the Kula-trees;
one must not eat from their leaves, and especially not from the leaves of the Arka tree.
One should not sleep at the foot of a family tree, nor should one commit any act of violence there;
having seen it or eaten from it, one should offer salutations, but one should never cut it down.
One should not look at a woman who has fallen from her status, one who is naked, one who is insane, or one whose breasts are exposed;
nor should one frequent a woman during the day, nor gaze upon her private parts.
Whatever woman there may be in the world born of a mother’s family,
women of noble birth become enraged when their lineage is insulted.
In the Rudrayāmala and in the Merutantra.
He who drinks unfermented liquor, engages in sexual intercourse by force,
or kills an animal with his own hand, shall go to the Raurava hell.
In the Meru-tantra:
One should avoid these five in the Kaula tradition: expiation, falling from one's status, renunciation, the observance of vows, and pilgrimage to sacred fords.
Killing a hero, drinking intoxicants in vain, seizing the property of a hero,
sexual intercourse with the wife of a hero, and association with those who commit these acts— these are the five.

What is called a "mahāpātaka" (great sin) in the *Kulāgama* of the Kaulikas has a penance prescribed in the Tantras that is distinct even from the observance of vows; likewise, the undertaking of a pilgrimage to sacred sites (*tīrthayātrā*) according to the Smṛti tradition is not prescribed in the Tantras, as is the case with the pilgrimage to the *pīṭhas*. Furthermore, sexual intercourse with another's wife [is likewise forbidden].
Then, with the permission of the owner, it is not prohibited.
O Goddess of the Gods, he who should bestow his sister, daughter, or wife upon a yogin of noble family who is intoxicated with honey— his merit cannot be calculated.
And because of this statement from the Kulārṇava:
Likewise.
One who perceives the teacher as a mere human being, the mantra as a mere collection of syllables,
and the images as mere stone shall go to hell.
From abandoning the guru, death occurs; from abandoning the mantra, poverty results;
by abandoning both the guru and the mantra, one goes to the Raurava hell.
When both previous faults are present, there is this additional fault in abandoning both:
he who performs his duty while possessed by the suspicion that it is excrement, urine, or leavings.
O beloved, all that—penance, worship, and so forth—would become impure.
Likewise.
Desiring to enter the abode of the Teacher, one who is peaceful in mind and full of devotion [should set aside] the fan,
sandals, umbrella, clothing, vehicles, and so forth.
Having discarded her attire characterized by an abundance of betel-leaf, she should enter slowly;
[she should perform] the washing of the feet, bathing, anointing the limbs, and cleaning the teeth.
Spitting, shaving, lying down, indulging in women,
the hero’s posture (vīrāsana), harsh speech, excessive laughter, and twisting the limbs— these [are forbidden].
O beloved, loosening the hair, wearing a turban, wearing a bodice, being naked,
stretching out the feet, as well as quarreling and finding fault— these are [prohibited].
O Ambikā, [these include] playing musical instruments with the limbs or breaking the limbs, touching or shaking the hands,
gambling, and fighting cocks, wrestlers, and so forth.

One should not practice [the transgression] at the seats, sacred fields, hermitages, and so forth of the Guru-yogis and Mahāsiddhas; if one should practice it out of delusion, one will incur the curse of the deity.
In the Kālī-kalpa.
O Īśāna, how can one who is my devotee become a Kaulika without wandering at night and worshipping the Śakti at night?
In the *Kulāmṛtadīpikā*.
Indeed, that [time] should not be missed by practitioners except at the time of worship.
And this conduct must always be kept secret.
For it is said thus in the Kulārṇava:
The Vedas, Shastras, and Puranas are as clear as courtesans;
but this Shaiva knowledge is hidden like a woman of noble family.
The deities favor the practice of the Kaulas when it is well-guarded;
they grant the fulfillment of desires, but destroy those who reveal [the secrets].
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*.
O you of excellent vows, that which is called the family custom and the sacrificial fee has been explained to you.
In the conduct of the samaya.
O Goddess Vāmadevī, conduct is of two kinds, distinguished as the Left-hand (Vāma) and the Right-hand (Dakṣiṇa).
That which is joined with the five mudrās and so forth is proclaimed as the left-hand practice (vāmācāra);
that which is devoid of the five mudrās and so forth is designated as the right-hand practice (dakṣiṇācāra).
And in this tradition, there is a necessity even for the fivefold division; [as stated] in the Merutantra:
The deities proclaimed in the Uttarāmnāya are pleased by the five [offerings];
however, if even one essential item is lacking, they chastise the practitioner.
In the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya), the drinking of wine has been performed by the gods whether it was done or not; they desire my satisfaction, and without it, they curse that very [wine].
The meat of the deities mentioned in the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya), whether prepared or unprepared, as well as the mantra for inducing possession— they do not accept these without that [meat].
Those gods mentioned in the Ūrdhvāmnāya, as well as the fish, perform that [rite] at every creation;
they enter into that state even without the two obligatory [daily rites].
The fourfold prohibited conduct (macatuṣṭaya) of the deities of the Dakṣiṇāmnāya— though they are [normally] forbidden—
indeed grant their grace to the practitioner even without the unification of the mind (manaika).
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*.
One who desires their own welfare must not disclose it to anyone:
the family flower, the family substance, the family worship, the family [lineage], and the recitation.
One should never, under any circumstances, reveal the Guru, the head of the family, the lineage of the family, the family circle, or the family meditation.
From disclosure comes the loss of accomplishment; from disclosure comes bondage and the like;
from disclosure comes the loss of power; indeed, O God, from disclosure comes injury to the deity.
O Maheśānī, at the time of worship, if anyone should enter here, there will be the attainment of death through exposure; therefore, it must never be made known.
Displaying the Vaiṣṇavī mudrā, as well as the Viṣṇu-nyāsa and the hymn of praise,
there may at times be a loss of limbs, yet never a loss of manifestation.
One should never perform worship externally, nor should one ever reveal [one's inner state];
internally Śākta, externally Śaiva, and in the assembly considered Vaiṣṇava.
Assuming various forms, these heroes roam upon the surface of the earth.
In the Meru Tantra:
Internally Kaula, externally Śaiva, and among the people Vaiṣṇava;
one should conceal the Kaula, O Goddess, like the water within a coconut fruit.
The wise man should reveal the Guru, but he should guard the mantra with great effort;
for through revealing what is not to be revealed, one's prosperity and lifespan are diminished.
It should be understood that even the manifestation of the Guru occurs only at certain times.
In the Phetkāriṇī Tantra.
In the Śrītārāprakaraṇa.
One should always protect both this mantra and the guru;
for by that, the vidyā becomes powerful, whereas it would become powerless through disclosure.
In the Tantra:
One should not sit down during a very intense [fever], nor should one lie down in the midst of darkness.
65b) Or one should not revile the beautiful-eyed woman.
One should always perform the ash-bath while observing one's own capacity;
one should worship the yantra marked with vajra-flowers using a vajra-flower.
Especially at the time of worship, one should not fail to remember the name of Hari;
and having set aside other perfumes, one should use sandalwood and red sandalwood.
One should worship with red flowers and also worship with bilva leaves;
one should not worship with tulasī, mālatī, dhātrī, or aru-vaka.
O Goddess of gods, even without the *śakti*, all practices such as recitation (*japa*), fire-offerings (*homa*),
libations (*tarpaṇa*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and worship (*pūjā*) result in the obstruction of spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*).

O Maheśānī, one should abandon other substances for the sake of the flour-based offering (paiṣṭī) used for nourishment and other purposes; the worship of the Vīras takes place when one watch of the night has passed.
One should not perform a fast nor observe any other vow;
having constructed a pavilion according to the rules, adorned with blue banners and archways.
O Goddess, one should fashion a triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) marked with the emblem of a serpent-pestle (nāgaśūla).
Now, regarding the states of being (*bhāva*). In the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*, the venerable Goddess said:
O Mahādeva, hear how the state of the Hero (vīrabhāva) is described, O Bhairava:
having become free from all mental agitation, one’s body is the form of the digit of desire (kāmakalā) within the heart.
At night, worship is most excellent; for that is indeed the cause joined with destiny.
Having assumed a form without earrings, he himself bears the appearance of Bhairava.
The family is the form of Bhairavī;
one should perform the extensive placement (nyāsa) upon her limbs, having likewise performed the entire placement consisting of the nine wombs (navayoni).
"Consisting of nine wombs" refers to the Śrīvidyā.
In the center of a pedestal made of flowers,
strewn with heaps of blossoms and filled with various fragrances, one should arrange the yantra using the kula-substance.
Having written it, one should worship it if one has the capacity, preceded by the ritual installation of a water-pot (ghaṭa-sthāpana);
on one's left side is a hexagon, and in its center, at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Having written [the mantras] there, one should indeed place a golden or silver pitcher.
It may also be made of copper or earth, provided it is devoid of any base metal.
One should place the jar’s base, a vessel perfumed with fragrant scents,
and fill it with the causal substances according to the distinctions of the Brāhmaṇa and other classes.

The phrase "according to the distinction of Brāhmaṇas and so forth" means that milk, clarified butter, honey, and liquor should be filled [into the vessels] by the Brāhmaṇas and others respectively; and thus it should be understood that for a Brāhmaṇa hero, milk alone is the cause in the place of the [standard] substance, whereas for another, even that is not permitted.
Having first drawn the yantra there, one should meditate upon whichever deity arises from one's own lineage as the desired deity, and then recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
Then, having displayed the source of meditation (dhyanu-yoni), one should contemplate that which has issued forth;
indeed, seeing the nectar received, the hosts of Yoginīs dance.
All the Bhairavas dance, and the Mothers dance as well;
all the gods, beginning with Indra, dance, longing for the honey.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others dance, intent on joy;
having divided the vessel of the *arghya* offering into three parts, one part is given to the Guru.
Having given one portion to his family and satisfied the gods with another,
he drinks the essence of the clan, adorned with various garments and ornaments.
If the Guru is not personally present, then one should offer [the offering] into water;
having become one whose form is bliss, one should worship the Supreme Goddess.
One should worship each [deity] according to its respective ritual procedure and with the appropriate effort;
then, having performed the dismissal (visarjana), one should unite [the deity] within the bud.
By traveling upon that very moon, nectar is consumed by me;
from tasting its flavor as a cakora bird, great joy arises within me.
By grasping that fruit, one descends from the peak of Mount Meru;
by the mere embrace of the creeper, one's body becomes washed with nectar.
When the root-yoga has been performed there, one should recite eight thousand [times];
and in both daily recitation and fire-offerings (homa), wherever no specific number has been prescribed.
In this regard, the following counting is prescribed: one should take one thousand and eight units of purified water and sacrificial substances, and then perform the libation (tarpaṇa).
Having performed the libation (tarpaṇa), O Lord, one should proceed clockwise around [the deity];
then, having offered praise and prostrated, one should gratify [the deity] with the hymn prescribed in the Kalpa.
Thus, O God, the Vīrakula is worthy of divine worship and captivating;
O Bhairava, wherever a hero exists in a land, that land—or even that family—is likewise [worthy of honor].
There is no fear of pestilence there, nor fear of dust and the like;
it is always highly auspicious, increasing wealth and progeny.
O Mahādeva, prosperity remains there certainly and steadfastly;
one must necessarily recite the Svapnaprabodhinī mantra at the foot of a tree.
It must be applied with great effort so that no obstacle arises;
it is not suitable for another hero to grasp, even by the gods.
And that which is distinct from the Yoginīs and free [from worldly bonds] is not joined with sin,
even when one goes here or there, to a family, on a day of the week, or to a cremation ground.
There, the fruit of worship shall be equal to that of seven times [repetition];
when the fourteenth day of the fortnight has passed, the fruit of worship there shall be [equal to] a fortnight.
One who does not proceed from ignobility to a noble state is undoubtedly like a mere beast;
he is solely intent on the thought, "There is no god superior to this one."
Through intoxication, the consumer of the substance shall become devoted to the Kula;
when the practitioner falls into agitation, my own agitation arises.
One who does not proceed toward noble conduct will undoubtedly remain a mere beast;
he is solely intent on the thought, "O God, there is nothing superior to this."
But when one who is devoted to your family becomes a consumer of substances out of intoxication,
and falls into agitation toward the practitioner, my own agitation arises.
Therefore, Vīravara, becoming diligent, endowed with enjoyments, and happy, he attains liberation through enjoyment; through enjoyment, he accomplishes the Kula practice.
Without a cause, Maheśvara, becoming agitated while tasting [the world],
performs neither worship nor circumambulation of me, nor meditation nor reflection.
Therefore, having eaten and drunk, one should worship the Supreme Lord;
herein there is no fault of transgression, nor is there any calamity, for faults are themselves ornaments here.
Whatever one speaks, even sleep, whatever one does,
and whatever one worships— all that, having meditated upon as being of the nature of the Kula, the wise person should perform.
Alone in a secluded place— in a cremation ground, on a mountain, in a forest,
in an empty house, or on a riverbank— one should wander joyfully, free from attachment.
For heroes, the time for recitation is praised as being at all times;
it should be performed in any place or on any sacred seat, without a doubt.
If a Brahmin, terrified of worldly existence and devoted to the ancestral heritage,
should desire to satisfy his lineage, he must perform this rite according to the following procedure.
The Brahmin is indeed a hero; thus also in the Merutantra.
Furthermore, within the interior of the flower is a captivating place of the Kula;
there is the bliss of all the gods, consisting of the arts of great desire.
O Lord, Sadāśiva himself is present as the flower that is the enemy of horses (the *hayāri*);
taking a small portion from its midst, one should place sandalwood in the middle of the flower.
Or, having offered a red flower and meditated upon oneself as being of the nature of Śiva,
one should unite [the offering] with the power of Śiva (śiva-śakti), contemplating with the intellect their essential oneness.
Having reflected for a moment and having worshipped the Supreme Goddess right there,
he should recite the mantra over that very substance called *kuṇḍa*, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain.
Likewise.
O Bhairava, where the Aparājita flower, the javā flower,
the red and white karavīra, and the droṇa flower remain.
There, one should always worship me in that yantra where the Goddess resides;
and by offering hibiscus flowers, one shall obtain the fruit of silk cloth.
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are certainly destroyed in an instant;
yet, O Maheśvara, it is impossible to fully describe the majesty of Aparā.
The practice of *vīrasādhana* must be performed by heroic men;
it may also be performed by divine beings, but not by commoners or those who are like cattle.
It is certain that the work of a commoner is better than that of a beast;
whatever has not been declared by the True Guru in the presence [of the disciple] regarding the convention for mantra-attainment is [not to be followed].
The powerful Vīra may prepare collyrium, pills, and so forth;
however, there is a distinction between him and the divine Vīra, which is now being explained.
The Śānta (peaceful) hero is calm, disciplined, sweet, and endowed with refined grace;
the Divya (divine) hero is mostly like a celestial being; and the Vīra (heroic) hero possesses a haughty mind.
Whether adorned with magnificent ornaments, or smeared with sandalwood paste,
whether his form is concealed or abandoned— O Kulabhairava!
Whether anointed with red sandalwood paste or not, whether a Vaiṣṇava or even a non-Vaiṣṇava,
he shall always remain joyful and well-nourished during both insult and worship.
Whether one is intent on censuring the deity or else intent upon various forms of worship,
provided that the essence of worship is performed and one abides by the Kulākula doctrine,
being endowed with one's own true nature, one may move about on earth like a god.
The preliminary practice (puraścaryā) must be performed at night within one's own family lineage, and not otherwise;
O divine twice-born, it is just as the story of the Vedas is not heard by one devoid of the Vedas.
Just as devotion to the Goddess does not flourish without devotion to Viṣṇu,
so liberation leads only to ridicule without the knowledge of Śākta.
Just as one has no entitlement whatsoever to the Tantra without a guru,
so too is a woman devoid of all ritual efficacy when she is without a husband.

O follower of the Kaula path, one who lacks [the prescribed] family lineage (kula) never possesses the qualification for my practice regarding the rite of the deities; therefore, be devoted to the inner state (bhāva).
How can one whose family is undisciplined be my worshiper?
Therefore, one must act with such effort that [the family] becomes endowed with discipline.
In this scripture of the Kula, there is no qualification whatsoever for one who is characterized by existence or non-existence;
therefore, a practitioner who is purified of such states becomes a true Kaulika.
The Goddess said:
I shall explain the state of the sacrificial animal (paśubhāva); listen with a concentrated mind, my son.
Having received the knowledge of the animal according to the rule, one should be intent upon that state.
First, one should diligently perform the preliminary service and then practice purification;
one should avoid eating fish and should not even mentally recall women.
One should not covet the property of others, nor should one indulge in pride regarding enjoyments;
whether on the shore of the ocean, on a mountain, in a forest, or in a temple of the gods.
At the root of a bilva tree, in a secluded place, and in a beautiful, holy field, one should not allow a Śūdra to see [the ritual]; one should diligently avoid all crookedness.
The deity of auspicious complexion should be meditated upon by those who are well-composed;
one should perform the worship of the deity at the three junctions of the day and practice recitation at the three junctions of the day.
One should never touch the mantra or the rosary at night;
one should not recite the mantra after eating, and one should remain silent during all ritual actions.
The best of practitioners should never approach a woman during the sacred festival days (parva-kāla);
instead, he should perform worship by personally bringing flowers, incense, and water.
One should completely avoid sexual intercourse, talk about it, and socializing with those intent on it; and one should not approach a woman with passion except during her fertile period.
O Supreme Lord, one who has faith in hearing the Purāṇas and is devoted to the meaning of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas should not eat at night, O Wise One, nor consume betel leaf.
O Bhairava, one should diligently perform everything that has been prescribed by the Guru; likewise, O Bhairava, one should employ flowers born of one's own kind as the causal substance.
Having touched [such a person] and likewise composed himself, he becomes pure by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Devoted to the Goddess, he should not accept red garments.
In the Viṣṇu Tantras, the ritual procedures and their performance are prescribed;
however, O Hero, one who honors heroes should not engage in worldly conversation.
One who is devoted to righteousness should perform the daily *śrāddha*, the *gayā-śrāddha*, the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā-vandana*),
bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha*), and visiting the seats of power (*pīṭha*).
O God Bhairava, the *paśu* is of two kinds; together with the former, [the latter] has authority in worship, but never in the state of being a Guru.
The one from the former [tradition] has no authority regarding worship performed within or outside his own country;
however, the one from the former [tradition], who is worthy of all Kaula rites, must be excluded from his own country.
O Lord, it is better to commit the sin of killing a Brahmin than to practice the observance of the Kula merely by having previously seen [the teacher]. It is the truth.
O Lord of Gods, O Master, I tell you the truth, the absolute truth: even this soul of mine is indeed all-pervading.
Nevertheless, a doubt arises in me at every step regarding that;
it would be better to abandon one's family, and even better to destroy one's own lineage.
Better is the ruin of one's own family, better is the loss of one's own family’s vision;
better is the downfall of one's own family through body, mind, or speech.
One should not form an attachment to a beast, for it causes the destruction of one's own path;
in the Kula scripture, these two are the gravest sins that bring about the ruin of the lineage.
There is great infamy within one's own family, and the Lord of the Family is alienated;
even greater than that, a great sin arises from association with the uninitiated (paśu).
O Lord of the Kula, in every respect, two states are not to be manifested there:
existence and non-existence; it is from the abandonment of these that the bound soul (paśu) is born.
A hero is recognized through destiny, and a hero is born from destiny;
O Lord of the Family, in every respect, two states in that regard must not be disclosed.
When there is doubt regarding the divine hero, it is designated as "sāmya" (similarity).
For emotion (*bhāva*) is a mental property; how indeed could it be verbal?
Therefore, existence should not be spoken of; only a mere indication has been given.
O Lord, just as the sweetness of sugarcane gradually arises [in the form of] jaggery.
In that way, however, the manifestation of existence is thoroughly contemplated by the mind.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Kulamuktikallolinī* composed by the venerable Ādyānanda.
Now the daily ritual (nityavidhi) is written down. In the Merutantra, the Goddess said:
For the wealthy and the middling classes, for the poor who dwell in their homes,
for those residing in foreign lands, and for those dwelling in prisons and the like.

O Ocean of Compassion, for those who have turned away from their duties at the outset of a task, or for those engaged in work who are impeded by birth-impurities and the like, or for those who are left-handed (vāmakas) regarding the components of the ritual or its inherent nature— [for all these, you provide protection].

O Lord, tell me of the daily practice (*dinacaryā*): how can the daily ritual (*nityakriyā*) be performed within the secret tradition of the Sixfold Transmission (*ṣaḍāmnāya*), even if it should lead to public shame?
The illustrious Śiva said:
That which was proclaimed by Mahākāla and heard by me through the power of great illusion—
that most secret of secrets is concealed within all mantras.
I shall now proclaim that daily ritual, the secret of the sacred traditions;
listen all of you, O gods, for it bestows success upon practitioners.
Therein, the eternal is said to be threefold, according to the distinction of the three qualities.
That too would be of three kinds.
Whether pure, mixed, or dissolved, it yields fruit in exactly that same way;
the pure bestows complete fruit, while the mixed bestows some fruit.
If the self is devoid of egoism and preceded by right knowledge, there is neither the incurrence of sin from what is not done, nor the failure to obtain the fruit of what is well-done.
That which is performed by an ascetic with a healthy mind is said to be pure;
the same applies if it is performed by a householder or one who is destitute of wealth.
Whether on the road, or having gone to a prison or a house,
or out of devotion, or mixed with that [alms-food], according to the rules for external worship.

Or, due to fear of cold and the like, from the exhaustion of the mind, from having few duties, or from the command of women and others, the pride of a householder may fall away; this is what is recognized by the wise.
Whatever external worship and so forth is performed by a householder with devotion, in solitude, and according to fixed rules, that is considered pure and characterized by passion (rājasa).
Whether it be performed for the sake of worship after having established faith and devotion,
or that which is done out of fear of people or fear of the gods— that is mixed with worldly motives, O King.
O Lord, for the purpose of deceiving the world, that substance was cast down by name;
it was made by the region, and that indeed belongs to the Rajas quality.
Having resorted to the left-hand path and having reflected upon the Kaula doctrine,
and because of a lack of aversion toward other doctrines, that which was performed is indeed pure, yet characterized by tamas.
Whatever action is performed out of desire, whether pertaining to this world or the next,
by resorting to the left-hand path (vāmamārga), that is indeed mixed and characterized by darkness (tāmasa).
That which is eaten out of greed by the tongue, that which is drunk out of desire, or that which is consumed for the sake of killing and so forth— that is the *tāmasa* state of the throat.
From pure sattva there would be liberation; from mixed sattva, heaven;
from sattva that has diminished, there would be mundane accomplishments and human birth.
O King, from pure [rajas] there would be heaven; from mixed [rajas] there would be the fulfillment of desire;
and when the suffering of rajas has dissolved, there would even be happiness in the animal realm.
O Lord, from a *sāttvika* [state] or a *tāmasa* one, men may attain birth among the gods;
from a mixed *tāmasa* state, they become miserable; and from an extremely *tāmasa* state, they become hell-beings.
Action is said to be fivefold, bestowing liberation in five ways:
spreading, appropriation, sacrifice, study, and union.
Sweeping, plastering, and other consecratory rites performed in the temple of the Lord,
as well as devotion, straightforwardness, and prostration, bring about residence in the same world as the Lord (sālokya).
The cleansing with the collection of materials for worship and the sprinkling with water of devotion constitute the "appropriation" (upādāna),
which brings about delight in that [deity] and bestows the form of the deity.

The worship of the seat (pīṭhapūjana) performed previously with the sixteen and other subordinate offerings constitutes the worship of the deity in either the image or the yantra; this worship brings about proximity [to the divine].
Having properly studied that scripture and having contemplated the meaning of the mantra, one should perform recitation; such self-study, O God, brings about union with the Divine.
The perfect contemplation of the identity of the Guru, the Deity, and one's own Self is Yoga;
it is the destroyer of the subtle body (liṅgadeha) and brings about union with Kāla.
Now, as for the morning ritual (*prātaḥkṛtya*), it is stated in that very same [text]:
In the latter part of the night, one should remember one's chosen deity.
In the Kulacūḍāmaṇi:
The practitioner, having risen at dawn and bowed to the family tree (kulavṛkṣa),
should meditate upon the Kula from the base to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) and then remember the Guru.
The family trees [are described] in the Rudrayāmala and the Merutantra.
The śleṣmātaka, karañja, nimba, aśvattha, kadambaka, bilva, paṭa, śāla, tāla, śākhāṭa, and likewise the kharjūra;
The family trees have thus been fully described.
In truth, those who know the secret say that a courtesan is the family tree.
In the middle of the ocean.
69a) Having arisen during the Brahma-watch of the night, one should contemplate Kulakuṇḍalī,
who consists of the root mantra and is the very embodiment of nectar and bliss.
By means of the great fire-rituals of karma.
One should contemplate within that [lotus] the Śakti known as Kuṇḍalinī, who is designated as Ādamas, intent upon creation,
resembling a shimmering lightning flash, like the curling of a conch shell, having the form of a sleeping serpent, and enchanting the world;
she has the appearance of a slender vine and the form of a lotus stalk.

In the *Kramakallolinī*: At the hour of Brahmā (*brāhma-muhūrta*), the wise one, having risen from his own bed and performed the ritual procedures beginning with yoga, visualizes within the calyx of the lotus of his head the lotus-feet of the lineage of masters beginning with Śiva.

One should then meditate upon Kubjeśvarī, whose nature is Kuṇḍalinī, who proceeds from the center of the Ādhāra to Akula; she is intoxicated by drinking the nectar of the Kākāśa-Soma, and she is joined with the drinking of the Unstruck Sound (Anāhata). This is the descent of the five jewels of the root of the Kula.
In the thousand-spoked [lotus], one should meditate on the Guru, resembling pure crystal,
with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, peaceful, and adorned with white ornaments.
Embracing the red Śakti, he is a festival of the essence of the bliss of desire;
his face is serene and pure, bestowing the fruits of all actions.
In the Bhairava Tantra.
Then, having risen in the morning from his bed, being well-composed,
he should meditate upon his own guru in the form of Śiva within the lotus situated at the crown of his head.
One should remember the name of one's own Guru, preceded by that [name], ending with "asukānandanātha";
one should worship the Guru with mental offerings.
There is a specific distinction in the Meru-tantra.
Having risen, one should place the left foot on the ground on the right side of the body;
then, having gone outside the house, one should perform the rite of subjugation with devotion.
Having discarded the night-garment and put on two [fresh] garments,
and having sipped water (ācamana) so as to be pure of body, one should go to the temple of yoga dedicated to the gods.
Having performed the purification, one should then sit upon a prescribed seat in a clean place, facing east, endowed with devotion according to one's capacity.
Having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas) and having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the rules,
one should then remove the remains of the previous offering (nirmālya) and likewise offer a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali).
Having first presented the arghya vessel, one should indeed give the tooth-stick;
having performed the washing of the mouth, one should give the water for sipping (ācamanīya).
Then, for the wiping of his hands, one should give a clean and auspicious cloth.
Now, the meditation on the Guru.
Then, one should visualize a thousand-petaled lotus upon one's own head,
radiant as camphor, and there, one should remember one’s own Guru in his true form.
69b) [He is] very serene, adorned with shining ornaments, and white sandalwood;
his hands are occupied with the Varada, Abhaya, and Jñāna mudrās, as well as with books.
He is clad in white garments, peaceful, and adorned with white flowers;
he is embraced by his Śakti of red complexion, who rests upon his left lap.
Clad in red garments and ornaments, wearing garlands of red sandalwood,
she held a playful lotus in her left hand, while her right hand was placed upon the linga.
One should meditate upon the tranquil yogin, whose form is Śiva, with his face turned inward;
[one should bathe him] with the stream of nectar flowing from his pair of lotus feet.
The disciple should thus contemplate his own body as having been consecrated;
he should worship it with external offerings such as perfumes and flowers, or with mental ones.
Having thus prostrated with the heart-mantra using his names— which are conventionally established and proclaimed by the Guru— one should meditate upon his absorption into one's own heart.
In this regard, the *Tattvacintāmaṇi* also states the *gurumantra-jaya*:
"Alternatively, one should extract the *vāgbhava*, *māyā*, and the seed-syllable of *lakṣmī*."

One should meditate upon *hasakhaphreṃ*, as well as the one named Nandabhairava, *sahakhaphreṃ*, the name of the Guru, and the name of the Śakti, [and meditate upon] the Śrīpādukā. The wise one should recite [the mantra] ten times, or seven times, or even three times. Afterwards, one should offer the recitation (*japa*) into the right hand of the venerable Guru. Thus it is stated in the Bhairavatantra.
Then, having meditated upon Kālī as described in the visualization within the heart-lotus, one should worship her with perfumes and other offerings, reciting the Gāyatrī twenty-eight times.
Or one should recite it ten times; hear that [mantra], O Bhairavī:
it consists of the syllables *kāmo*, *llā*, *kṣi*, and *nādānta*, joined with the letter on the right side (*dakṣiṇa*).
We know the seed-syllable *kūrca* (huṃ), and then *cāmuṇḍā* joined with *ṅeṃ*;
then saying "we meditate upon," [one says] "may Kākālī impel us."
This Gāyatrī-Ṣāmayā has been proclaimed; it is concealed in all the Tantras.
Without it, no sacred knowledge (vidyā) ever attains perfection.
In the Kumārītantra, however, the Gāyatrī is described quite differently.
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O cause of the dissolution of the universe!
O Lord, how can perfection be attained through these [means] according to the Kula practice?
For this is indeed the cause of unrighteousness; O Lord, sever my doubt.
