The illustrious Bhairava said:
"Excellent, O Goddess of gods! You have asked well; I shall tell you, listen, my dear.
Long ago, in the delightful Dāruvana forest, sages were afflicted by disease."
They constantly commit adultery with the wives of others and consume wealth;
seeing that improper conduct, Viṣṇu appeared in the form of meat.
O God of gods, Mahādeva, you whose nature consists of creation, preservation, and dissolution!
Those women who were devoted to the forest of wood, as well as those devoted to [the consumption of] substances and drinks— [they have all attained this state].
Even sages, deluded by passion, violate the wives of others;
and out of delusion they go about naked—what will be the fate of such people?
Having heard these words of Viṣṇu, O beloved, he spoke to Rūha:
"The great vidyā of Kālikā is Aniruddha-Sarasvatī."
She is proclaimed as the Queen of Knowledge (Vidyārājñī), the progenitor of this mantra;
those who recite her Gāyatrī will become supremely liberated.
And by her power all the gods have been utterly deluded;
I shall declare that secret to you, which, once heard, must always be kept hidden by the wise.
Having uttered the word "kālikāyai," one should say "vidmahe" immediately after that;
then one should say "śmaśānavāsinīm" ending in the feminine nominative case (ṅe), followed by "dhīmahi."
In that Tantra, having uttered the word "ghore," one should then recite "pracodayāt.
By the mere grace of this [mantra], millions of great sins [are destroyed].
They undergo immediate dissolution for the practitioner; it is not otherwise.
Indeed, by the slaying of Rāvaṇa, Rāmacandra was liberated.
By her grace, Paraśurāma was liberated from the sin of matricide;
likewise, Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Dattātreya were freed from the drinking of liquor.
And by the severing of Brahmā’s head, I, Rudra, was liberated;
thus, O beautiful goddess, is this Gāyatrī the Great Vidyā.
Even if one is joined with a great sin, O Great Goddess, if one should recite [the mantra] ten times,
truly, truly, one becomes liberated at that very moment.
Indeed, sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are shattered into fragments by this;
there is no knowledge equal to this, nor is there a recitation equal to this.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a knowledge equal to this.
The Śrī Devī said:
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, regarding that Gāyatrī which was previously mentioned: who are her seers and so forth, and what are her meditations, recitations, modes of worship, and the like?
O Mahādeva, you yourself should also explain the means of accomplishment (sādhana) and its power.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
I shall speak, O Great Goddess; listen, O beloved of my life!
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the seer (ṛṣi) of that [mantra], and Gāyatrī is indeed its meter (chanda).
The deity is indeed proclaimed to have the nature of Śiva and Śakti;
O Goddess, listen with devotion as I describe the meditation upon them here.
And in the cremation ground, one should meditate upon the goddess Mahākālī,
naked, with a face made terrifying by her fangs, and adorned with a garland of severed heads.
In the upper right hand he holds a bow, and likewise arrows in the left;
below those, a noose and a sword are proclaimed in that same sequence.
Having meditated thus upon Mahākālī, one should recite her mantra four hundred thousand times;
one should then perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with bilva leaves smeared with blood, using a tenth part of that number.
And the means of accomplishment, O Great Goddess, one should perform as before.
In the Meru Tantra:
Then, [one should meditate upon] a column of light rising from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *brahmarandhra*,
situated within the *suṣumnā* and resembling a thousand suns.
Having meditated upon the root mantra as being of that same nature and having contemplated one's own body as enveloped by its splendor, one should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the sage and other elements of the mantra using the root mantra;
then, having performed the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa), one should meditate upon the deity in the heart.
Having worshipped with mental offerings and physical movements, one should mutter the mantra according to one's capacity; then, one should offer that recitation to the Deity.
Having praised and bowed to the god, one should pray for his command with these verses:
In the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*.
The wise man should perform the ritual visualization (saṃkalpa) for the Great Vidyā known as Vīrahaṃsa.
Out of a desire for the welfare of practitioners, I shall now describe the practice (sādhana) called Haṃsa.
By the mere knowledge of whom one becomes omniscient on earth—
the Blessed Lady whose essence is the *haṃsa*, which the individual soul chants at all times.
By the mere remembrance of this, a person becomes liberated while living.
The seer is proclaimed to be Haṃsa, the deity is Paramahaṃsa,
the meter is Avyakta Gāyatrī, and the application is the bestower of perfection.
In the Surendra-saṃhitā:
The seer is Haṃsa, preceded by the Unmanifest; Gāyatrī is said to be the meter.
The deity is the Supreme Beginning; "I am Haṃsa" is said to be the seed-syllable.
"Aḥ" is the Śakti, "So'haṃ" is the Kīlaka, and the Praṇava is indeed the Tattva;
thus is the Udātta-svara proclaimed as the Manorama.
This application is for the sake of liberation; thus a person should always act.
In the Vīracūḍāmaṇi.

O Dear One, the goddess is the Heart belonging to the nature of the Sun, the Head likewise belongs to the nature of the Moon; Nirañjana is the Light of the Crest, and Nirābhāsā is likewise [the Topknot].
Having placed the syllable *avyakta* on the eyes, one should mutter *phaṭ* on the two shoulders;
having thus performed the rite of placement (*nyāsa*), one should offer it to Gaṇeśa and the others.
But in the Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā, however:
O Goddess, the two wings of this swan are the Vedas and the Āgamas;
furthermore, Agni and Soma are its two wings, and the Tāraka-mantra shall be its head.
The three *bindus* are established in the crest, the eyes, and the mouth; *nāda* is established in the face.
Śiva and Śakti are the two feet, and Kālāgni is the pair of flanks.
But this Paramahaṃsa is all-pervading and luminous.
In the Surendrasaṃhitā:
The individual soul always recites this mantra consisting of the syllable *haṃsa*, which is the Blessed Lady herself;
by the sound *ha* it goes out, and by the sound *sa* it enters again.
By the mere awakening of this [knowledge], a person becomes liberated while living;
and through the power of *prāṇāyāma*, one becomes liberated while living.
A living being should recite daily twenty-one thousand six hundred times the supreme mantra consisting of the bliss of Brahman.
Its origin is the commencement of recitation, and its death is the offering;
even without formal recitation, it is always considered a constant recitation at all times.
When the recitation has been performed in this manner, one should offer it to Gaṇeśa and the other deities.
In the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*.
Six hundred for Gaṇeśa, six thousand for Prajāpati,
six thousand for the wielder of the mace (Viṣṇu), and six thousand for the wielder of the Pināka bow (Śiva).
One thousand [repetitions] for oneself, one thousand for the Supreme Self (Paramātman),
and one thousand for the Guru, according to the rule for the formal resolve (saṃkalpa).
One should worship the red-colored Gaṇeśa at the four-petalled Mūlādhāra,
which is endowed with the four Vedas, six hundred times.
One should offer the Svādhiṣṭhāna, which is like the water of a coral tree and possesses six corners and six petals,
together with Sāvitrī and Vāsudeva, to Brahmā.
I salute Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, who possess the radiance of a mass of lightning; one should offer the ten-syllable mantra beginning with "dalaṃḍā" six thousand times.
And in the Mahānīla [mandala], upon the twelve petals beginning with 'ka',
one should worship Umā and Maheśvara and offer six thousand [oblations].

Bhairava said:

Having thus resolved in your mind, tell me with respect:
how is it that practitioners achieve success through mere meditation?
The Goddess said:
The Lord of the Gods beholds that man endowed with this meditation,

In such a way that meditation arises for her perfectly,
so does the Lord of Gods act when the powerful Vajradhara is present.
It kills the practitioner himself, or that madman makes him go insane.
Bhairava said:
O Goddess of gods, by what means does one destroy thousands of obstacles?

May Tuṣṭi, the bestower of contentment, protect; may Śānti, the bestower of peace, protect;

May the pair of *māyās* protect the region of the waist;

Tāriṇī shall protect all that, and Tripurasundarī shall protect the Dharma;
one should always recite this meritorious armor (*kavaca*), which provides protection from fear.
It directly brings about great accomplishment and destroys even the most heinous sins;
whoever recites it even once shall obtain the fruit of worship.
One who seeks liberation attains liberation; one who seeks wealth shall obtain wealth.
One who seeks liberation attains liberation; one who seeks wealth shall obtain wealth.

Now follows the Mātṛkā-kavaca.
The illustrious Lord said:

Having prostrated before her who is without vowels yet ends with a vowel,
who consists eternally of the letter 'Sa', who is perpetual, and who is established upon the lotus of Yoga, I shall describe her.
Subtler than the subtlest, the supreme pinnacle, with moon-like radiance and most excellent,
four-armed and three-eyed, she holds the Vidyā and a book.
She who holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness and supports the earth, who stands upon the four Vedas,
who is bowed to by Brahmā and Viṣṇu, and who is the supreme mother of the cosmic egg.
Having thus meditated upon the Goddess Mātṛkā— who is composed of the Śabdabrahman, who is the very nature of Brahman, and who is the syllable "Ai"— one should recite the Mātṛkā-kavaca.
O Goddess, O fair-faced one, if one performs the ritual placement (nyāsa) without the armor (kavaca),

having drawn it forth from the *kulastha* by means of the *kulamudrā-aṅkuśa*.
Having brought together the sacred sites (tīrthas) of one's lineage right there,
one should drink that water belonging to the lineage three times and perform the sprinkling of the body three times.
To whichever family he belongs and by whichever mantra he has been initiated.
Just as with the *kuladarbha* grass.
In the Rudrayāmala.
Three blades of darbha grass are prescribed, made of gold, silver, or kuśa;
among these, two are for the Śākta, while for others, three are considered appropriate.
Gold and silver are indeed prescribed for rites such as recitation (japa) and worship;
they are said to perform the functions of kuśa grass, but wild kuśa grasses are not true kuśas.
Silver should be worn on the index finger, and gold should be worn by me on the ring finger;
this alone is declared to be *kuśa*, not that which is produced from the *darbha* grass.

There is no worship of the Goddess here that is ever performed without lapis lazuli;
therefore, one should take auspicious dūrvā grass, which embodies all flowers.
Having placed a bundle of *durvā* grass in his hand, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) according to the prescribed rule.

*Kulapuṣpa* refers to the *javā* flower and the like. *Kulapātra* refers to a vessel such as one made of gold. Regarding the *kulacakra*—the triangular wheel (*trikoṇacakra*)—of the *kuladeva*, that is, the chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), the method for drawing it is found in the *Mālinītantra*.
O Goddess, with a concentrated mind, one should draw a triangle using the root seed-syllable while reciting the *Sāvitra-haṃsaka* mantra, proceeding in a clockwise direction.
"By the root-seed" refers to another mantra; in the Sāvitra, which is the Sūrya-mantra, "haṃsakaṃ" means the mantra "haṃsaḥ."
In the Meru Tantra:
Having performed the Vedic bath as well as the removal of its scent, [he should proceed].
As for the *aṅkuśa* mudrā, it is described in that very same place as follows:
Then, having formed the right fist with the index finger in the shape of a kusha blade,
this great mudrā called the "Goad" is capable of attracting the three worlds.
O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī,
Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, please be present in these waters!
Thus, it is stated on Mount Meru in the Śrīkramasaṃhitā.

Reciting the root mantra, the leader among practitioners should pour water upon his head with the mudrā known as the "pitcher" (kumbha); after performing this three times, he should then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Self-knowledge [is attained] through the auspicious principles (tattvas).
I purify the gross body through the reality of the Self, svāhā!
I purify the subtle body through the reality of knowledge, svāhā!
The meaning is that one should take three handfuls of water with the mantra "I purify the supreme body as Śiva, svāhā," using these three mantras.

Having thus sipped water three times with the *vidyā* mantra, she then did so accordingly.

Then, for the ritual bath according to the Tantras,

Having removed [the water] with only the *śikhā-mantra*, one should consecrate it three times with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*).
Having smeared [it] from the head down to the feet, one should offer the water.
I bow down to those waters, which are the support of Viṣṇu of incomparable splendor— the source of all beings— and from which all things of that same nature are born.
Having formed the *saṃmukhīkaraṇī* mudrā and restrained the vital breaths (*prāṇa*),
one should submerge oneself in silence and then rise, standing in water reaching up to the navel.
Having performed the ritual resolve (saṃkalpa) for the Tantric bath, preceded by the mention of the month and other details,
one should then perform three breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra.
Having performed the assignment of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa), one should fashion a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) in front,
within a square measuring one cubit, prepared in water.
The sacred fords within the belly of the cosmic egg have been touched by your rays;
by that truth, O Lord of Gods, O Maker of Day, grant me a sacred ford.
Having thus prayed to the Sun, and having pierced the solar orb with the *krom* syllable and the *kuśa*-mudrā,
one should cause the sacred bathing places (*tīrthas*) to descend from there into this [place].
And [the word] "Ganges."
Having spoken thus, one should direct the sacred fords (*tīrthas*) into that water;
then, with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), one should invoke the power of the sacred ford (*tīrthaśakti*) there.
Having meditated upon the orb of the sun, one should worship it with its mantra;
the origin of the Gaṅgā as an ancillary part of this context is stated in the *Lalitā-svacchanda*.
The Goddess said:
O best of gods, please graciously explain in brief how the Gaṅgā, who is saluted by the Suras and Siddhas, came into being.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O lady of excellent vows, I shall indeed tell you of the origin of Gaṅgā;
she was formerly my wife, the Great Goddess, the Mother of the World.
The tears from my eyes were wiped away by you with your fingernails;
yet, O Mother of the World, those very eyes were opened again by you in the past.
The tears flowing from my eyes were wiped away by your ten fingers; thus the Gaṅgā emerged from the ten directions, and Varuṇa became my protector.
Seven indeed are established there: one resides in the city of Viṣṇu, the second in the world of Brahmā, and the third pervades the seven worlds.
And she indeed remained again in heaven within the orb of the moon;
and having issued forth from the moon, she was once more established in the ether.
Then, O Lord, the swan [was addressed] by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others, for the sake of the welfare of mortals: "The river Gaṅgā is exceedingly meritorious."
Having brought her down to the mortal world, Mahādeva would dismiss her;
she who was previously mentioned by you, O Queen, is Aparājitā.
"Come for the sake of the welfare of the worlds, O beautiful goddess;
having come to my side, you previously went to the center of Meru."
Emerging from that, O Goddess, she flows toward the four directions:
the Śītā is indicated in the east, and Suvakṣā in the south.
Sunandā is in the western part, while Bhadra and Somā are in the north.
As with meditative absorption (dhyāna).
I meditate upon Gaṅgā, who is composed of all bliss, the destroyer of every sin, radiant as the moon, and three-eyed;
she holds in her two upper hands a noose and a goad on the left side,
and within [her other hands] a golden pitcher filled with nectar, a rosary of pearls, and the boon-granting gesture, accompanied by Sindhu, the best of rivers.
I worship the power of the sacred ford (Śrītīrthaśakti). Hrāṃ Hrīṃ Hrūṃ Hraiṃ Hrauṃ Hraḥ—this is the station within that which consists of all-bliss.
Likewise, Tīrthaśakti and Vahni with his wife form a couple;
this great mantra of Tīrthaśakti is said to consist of twenty-one syllables.
One should consecrate that water eight times with the Gāṅga mantra:
"Tāro namo bhagavate bhūyād aṃ vedatoṃ vike."
O Ambālikā, O Mahāmālinī, come indeed, O Blessed One;
as [prescribed], one should utter the seed-syllable of Māyā-Śrī within the basin of all sacred fords without exception.
The Gaṅgā resides upon the matted locks of Śiva; the Gaṅgā is the mistress of the Gaṅgā. This is declared to be the Gaṅgā-vidyā, consisting of fifty-three syllables.
Having worshipped Bhuvaneśī and rendered her nectarine with a particle of nectar,
the knower of mantras should then envelop her with the armor-mantra and protect her with the weapon-mantra.
Having invoked the deity there along with the limbs and the retinue by means of the root mantra,
and having visualized her emerging from between the two feet [of the deity] into the water;
Having meditated upon the sacred ford (*tīrtha*), one should bathe three times in the water while reciting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
Afterwards, remembering the deity within the heart, one should sprinkle [the water] with the *kaṅkumudrā*.
In three verses, the root here is the *tāra* (OM) preceded by the seed-syllables;
for one desiring to emit the universe, which is repeatedly dissolved, it is born again as white.
The Mothers, the goddesses who are the source of all beings, protect me once again;
Lakṣmī, whose form is stainless, resides within all beings.
May the waters, those goddesses, purify me again through their own touch,
[cleansing] that misfortune which resides in my hair-ends, in the parting of my hair, and on the crown of my head.
On the forehead and the two ears, one should say: "rakṣorāpastaṃghnastuvo namaḥ.
Then, one should perform the *trirucamana* (threefold sipping of water) with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*.
Having thus gratified the deity three times, one should then depart from the midst of the water.

In this manner, when these methods are not in conflict, they are to be combined; when there is a conflict, there is an option (*vikalpa*). That which is common to all regarding Mount Meru has been stated in the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā*, but it is not written here because it is identical [to what has already been said]. [This concludes] that which was stated in the *Tripurārṇava*.
They also know that the method is indeed that of Tripura; however, there is a specific distinction regarding the meditation on the Gaṅgā-mantra in the Vāma tradition.

The mantra, ending with "svāhā" and consisting of the syllables of the Star (Tāraka), is the destroyer of sin.
Meditative absorption.

Clad in red garments and red in complexion, she holds a trident, a jar, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in her hands; smiling, she stands upon a tortoise and is worshipped by the gods and others.
[She] who is well-practiced for the destruction of the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) by means of those very forms.
Thus concludes the procedure for bathing. Now follows the mantra-bath. In that same [text]:

Having washed his feet and sipped water with water drawn up [from a vessel],
he should then sit down after purifying his place and the ten directions as before.

Having placed water upon the palm of the hand, one should then perform the sequential placements (nyāsa) of the Mātṛkā and others, as well as the root mantra, according to the established rule for ritual bathing.
O constant yogi, one should perform the weapon-mantra within the heart by means of one's own vidyā.
Also in the Nārada-pañcarātra and the Meru-tantra:
Now I shall describe the bath of meditation, which surpasses even the two [preceding baths].
One should meditate upon the Lord, the lotus-eyed one, who abides in the sky and whose form is the mantra.
Meditating upon the stream of water from His feet falling upon his own head,
he visualized it entering his own body through the subtle aperture (brahmarandhra).
Therefore, one should wash away all that impurity residing within my body;
at that very moment, the practitioner becomes free from dust and is like a crystal.
This excellent bath is considered to possess a hundred times the merit of a mantra-bath;
he whose mind is pure is pure in all ritual actions.
The phrase "the lotus-eyed one" (*puṇḍarīkākṣa*) is an illustration; one should instead remember whichever deity is one's own object of worship. This authority was stated on Mount Meru.

for since that yields the fruit with little effort, it is superior to both [the external and the intermediate]. It should be understood that for one who possesses that [mental practice], the former is primary. As for the black [thread] and so forth, there is the *mahācīna* and so on.
Because it is to be practiced in sequence, mental [worship] alone is primary here. Thus ends the mental bath.
Now, the ritual bathing of Śiva; in that same [text]:
Alternatively, having rendered the sacred water (tīrtha) identical with Śiva by means of mantras whose essence is Śiva,
the act of sprinkling [the body] with the mantras of the Saṃhitās is declared to be the "Bath of Śiva" (śivasnāna).
"With the *saṃhitā* mantras" means with the mantras for sprinkling (*mārjana*) and so forth. Likewise:
All rituals preceded by bathing attain purity and success;
therefore, one should first perform at least one bath according to the strength of one's body.
Now follows the wearing of the washed garment. That has been stated in that very same place:
Having put on a pair of washed garments, one should likewise wash them for the sake of Hari.
In that case, one should perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth with earth and water.
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*.

Having risen and put on two garments of noble lineage, and having applied a sectarian mark (tilaka) of noble form according to one's family tradition, and having completed the rite of subjugation (vaśya), [one should proceed].

Regarding "family attire": one should also wear excellent red or white garments; furthermore, by means of the family root-mantra (*mūlamantra*), one should constantly apply the *tilaka* in the form of the family, namely, the wearing of the triple horizontal mark (*tripuṇḍra*).
That *vīratilaka* [is made] with earth from a cremation ground, as stated in the *Sudhīritimatsyasūkta*; [it is described] in the *Nārada Pañcarātra*.
Then, having put on a pair of well-washed garments that provide relief from fatigue,
or in their absence, he should wear a single cloth (śāṭī) together with a yogapaṭṭa.
And one must never be clad in only a single garment.
In the Svatantra Tantra.
One seeking liberation should wear two red garments, while one seeking wealth should wear two white ones; having dressed thus, the wise man should then enter the ground of yoga.
In the Yāmala:
O radiant one, she should apply a sectarian mark (tilaka) on her forehead according to the distinction of her caste.
In the Meru Tantra.
Then one should apply a sectarian mark (tilaka) belonging either to one's birth-constellation or to one's tutelary deity;
whatever auspicious fruit is obtained at the sacred ford through clay or water, that is attained through a state of devotion.
"The division of castes" is stated in the *Yāmala*.
The vertical *ūrddhvapuṇḍra* mark should belong to the Brāhmaṇa, the *tripuṇḍra* to the Kṣatriya,

78b) In the Meru-tantra:
The vertical *puṇḍra* belongs to the Brāhmaṇa; the triple *puṇḍra* (*tripuṇḍraka*) to the Kṣatriya;
the half-moon to the Vaiśya; and the circular shape to the Śūdras.
One should make the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* with clay and the *tripuṇḍra* with ashes;

the half-moon to a devotee of Gaṇeśa, and the circle to a devotee of the Goddess.
He who is devoted to Nārāyaṇa, who bears a trident-mark of sandalwood on his forehead and an application of sacred ash, is the very embodiment of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
Now, the fruit and non-fruit of wearing the *vibhūti*: likewise.

In this context, the procedure for the preparation of the ash and the procedure for its wearing are also recorded here, as they are essential for the followers of the Śaiva and Śākta traditions.
That has been stated in that very same [work].
The ash of the Śiva-fire should be collected, whether it originates from a fire-oblation or even from an ordinary external fire;
it must be thoroughly cooked, pure, and fragrant.
Once taken from a tawny cow and cast into the sky,
it falls down neither wet nor hard, neither foul-smelling nor parched.
If it should fall, one should discard what is above and below and take up what has fallen;
having reduced it to ashes, one should cast it into the Śiva-fire while reciting the root mantra.
Having discarded the immature intellect as well as that which is mature, and both the dark and the white,
one should take the cloth, wash it, and cast it into the receptacle of ashes.
One should collect the ashes once the fire has been extinguished,

Alternatively, they should bring cow dung with the *sadyojāta* mantra and,
having mixed it with the ashes of the twice-born in a vessel with the left hand, they should smear [the site] with the *ghora* mantra.

thus is the consecrated ash [prepared] by means of the mantra beginning with "agniriti."

One should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the forehead, shoulders, and belly with the syllables beginning with the five colors,
and on the head with the five-syllabled mantra.
Furthermore, these names should be used by the twice-born and others when wearing the ashes:
Brahmā is to be known on the forehead, and Havyavāhana (Agni) at the heart.
Skanda is at the navel, Puruṣa at the throat, and Rudra in the right arm;
Āditya is in the middle of the upper arm, and Śaśin at the wrist.
Vāmadeva is in the left arm, Prabhajana is in the middle of the arms,
the Vasus are at the wrists, and Hari is remembered to be in the region of the back.
Śambhu is proclaimed as the hump, and the Supreme Self (Paramātman) is remembered as the head.
A devotee of Śakti should wear ashes well-mixed with musk and other fragrant substances,
using either the root mantra or the five-syllabled mantra of Śiva, while remaining non-dvija.
One should apply the *tripuṇḍra* on the forehead, which embodies Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva,

Alternatively, the triple mark (tripuṇḍraka) may be made with the ring finger, the middle finger, and the thumb.
In the Śambhunityātantra:
The measurement for the triple mark (tripuṇḍraka) of Brāhmaṇas is six finger-breadths;
for kings (Kṣatriyas), it is four finger-breadths, and for Vaiśyas, it is three finger-breadths.
For Śūdras and women, the application of ash should be one finger-breadth;
likewise, they may apply a half-tilaka with ash or a horizontal tilaka with earth.
The vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) may be used with the triple horizontal mark (tripuṇḍra), but the vertical mark is not [used] on its own with the triple mark;
this is declared by the sages who have mastered the Vedas to be equal to the sin of killing a Brahmin.

O Great One, that mortal who, having taken up sacred ash, should wash it away on the ground in the Kali age, shall dwell in the Raurava hell as long as the moon and stars exist. For as many atoms of ash as fall upon the earth, for that many thousands of years does that man remain a sinner.

One should make a tilaka with ashes or three puṇḍrakas with clay.

One should perform the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) upon the body, preceded by the placement of the hands (karanyāsa),
after having consecrated the water in front with the cow-mudrā (dhenumudrā).
Then, having consecrated it seven times with the root mantra,
one should further do so with the letters of the Mātṛkā, from 'a' to 'kṣa', accompanied by the bindu.
One should sprinkle water three times upon the head with kusha grass, using the root mantra for each syllable.
In the *Kumārīkalpa* (The Ritual Manual of the Virgin Goddess).
Having first extracted the Praṇava, [the mantra is] Maṇidhariṇī Vajriṇī Rakṣa dvayanta kṣā Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā; immediately after that.
With this very mantra, the wise one should perform the protection;
then, having sipped water again and performed the six-limbed nyāsa, the knower of mantras [should proceed].
Taking water in his left hand,
the drum-sounding Dundubhi sprinkled it seven times over his head while uttering the mantra.

In the Bhīmakrama Tantra.

"By means of *īḍā*, until the end of the body of Kṛṣṇa," and so forth, as in the *Kūmārī-kalpa*.

Then, having meditated upon the God born from the solar disc,

Holding water from the well with the left hand,

In the Yāmala:
Having performed the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa), one should then take water in the left hand and subsequently form a hollowed cavity with the right hand.

O beautiful one of the Kula, it has been taught with reference to a disciple belonging to the Kula.

One should sprinkle water held in the hand seven times upon the head with the root mantra. However, in the left [tradition], it is as follows:
By means of the placement of the hands, one who follows the left-hand path (vāmācārī) should perform service;
the meaning is that having consecrated the water held in the right hand with mantras, one should perform the sprinkling (mārjana) with the left hand.

Not embracing her, however, that [fire] in its remaining form of radiant energy entered within,
purified all the internal impurity, and emerged.

One should offer libations to one's chosen deity seated within the solar disc.

In the Meru Tantra.
With water, at the end of the root mantra, [one says]: "I satisfy [the deity] named so-and-so."
Having said, "It should be offered as libation three times," [it is done] by means of the left hands, according to the Śaiva Āgama.
Then, having recited the Gāyatrī mantra three times, twenty-eight times each.
In the Meru Tantra:
One should recite the Gāyatrī of one's chosen deity twenty-eight times;
in its absence, however, one may recite the Brāhmī Gāyatrī, following the Vedic tradition.
The Tantric practitioner should recite the *Śivagāyatrī*, which is now described:
*Oṃ tanmaheśāya vidmahe vāgviśuddhāya dhīmahi*.
"May that auspicious one impel us"—thus [is the mantra]. As for the meditation on the Gāyatrī, it is [described] in the Tantra:
One should meditate upon Brāhmī, who resembles the rising sun, holding a book and an eye in her hands,
wearing a black antelope skin, and whose voice is like the sound of stars.
At the time of twilight.
The goddess is dark-complexioned, four-armed, with hands resplendent with the conch and discus,
holding a mace and a lotus, and seated upon the orb of the sun.
In the evening, the wise man should meditate upon the boon-granting Goddess Gāyatrī—
white in complexion, clad in white garments, and seated upon a bull.
Three-eyed, bestowing boons, [holding] a noose, a trident, and a human skull.
In the Merutantra: the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
Having recited the mantra and offered it to the deity, and having praised and bowed to the chosen deity,
one should place the Lord from the solar disc into one's own heart.
Then one should bow to the Guru; such is the Tantric twilight ritual (saṃdhyā).
In the Gautamīya [Vinaya].
Alternatively, the practitioner of mantra, due to lack of capacity, may perform a concise twilight ritual;
having meditated upon Kṛṣṇa in the evening, morning, and at midday, he should recite the mantra.
Thus, the three junctions (saṃdhyās) have been described as bestowing success upon those engaged in ritual action (karmis).
The term "Kṛṣṇa" is an illustration; the meaning is "one's own chosen deity."
In the Meru Tantra.
The twilight prayer (saṃdhyā) must be performed in this manner at all three times; indeed, there is no fruit from its omission.
If, however, an omission occurs due to a divine cause, then one should recite the root mantra a hundred times.
Having performed the preliminary expiatory rites, one should perform that which has arrived according to the established rule.
In the Śaiva Āgama.

The omission of the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) must not be committed, for this is the command of Śambhu himself. One who has been initiated but is devoid of the twilight prayers does not enjoy the fruit of initiation.
One who has omitted the twilight prayer should, during the [next] twilight, perform the rite of the preceding twilight first,
and then, free from sloth, perform the rite of the subsequent twilight.
In the Gautamīya [Vinaya].
If the twilight prayer has been omitted or fallen away, one should recite the Gāyatrī ten times.
But in the case of the King of Mantras:
It is stated that for the omission of bathing, the twilight devotions, and worship, one hundred and eight [repetitions] are required.
Thus concludes the twilight ritual (saṃdhyā).
Now, the libation (tarpaṇa). In the Merutantra:
Having performed the Vedic libation, one should then commence the Tantric libation.
In the Kulacūḍāmaṇi:
One should satisfy the gods, the ṛṣis, and the ancestors with the water of the lineage;
then, having meditated upon those whose nature is the lineage, one should satisfy them through the joy of the lineage.

Having invoked the deities who are of the nature of the Kula, who consist of the water of Kula-virya, and who possess divine and human splendor, he performed the worship within the Kula by merging with them through invocation. Likewise:
And for the god Bhairava, who causes the descent of the Bhairava state,
one should first recite the mantra known as Bhairava and bestow it.
The grammatical connection is that [this] is the mantra called Bhairava; and that Ānandabhairava mantra will be stated as before, prior to the libation (tarpaṇa) to the three currents (oghatriya).
In the Yāmala:

One should employ [the mantra] at the beginning of the libation (tarpaṇa) and so forth, [saying]: "May Brahmabhairava be satisfied. However, the mention of the ancestors as being Bhairava in the libation is intended for Vīras; for Paśus, it is otherwise.
In the Mālinītantra.
Facing the southern direction and taking up a handful of *moṭaka* grass, one should perform this libation while reciting: "May the ancestors be satisfied."
In the Śaiva Āgama.
Having meditated upon the deity and properly worshipped him in the water according to the root mantra,
one should then offer libations one hundred and eight times with the root mantra.
One should satisfy [the deities] ten times with half of that [amount], or even half of that again;
thereafter, one should satisfy the deities of the limbs and the surrounding enclosures in their proper order.
Likewise, with each handful [of water], preceded by the root mantra,
one should then worship the Lord of Gods along with his limbs and retinue.
Having drawn [the deity] up into his own heart, he should cause his self to flow forth as being identical with that.
In the Meru-tantra:
Having performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the root mantra;
then, for the triad beginning with the seer (ṛṣi), one should [perform the offering] in front with the cow-mudrā (dhenumudrā).
Chanting "vaṃ," he made the water immortal; then, reciting the root mantra while meditating upon the Lord together with his limbs and retinue, he placed the wheel there.
Having uttered, "I satiate such-and-such a person," one should offer one hundred and eight,
or half of that, or twenty-eight oblations into the lotus of the mouth.
One should satisfy the deity with the waters of that sacred ford (tīrtha) which have the nectar as their foundation;
likewise, one should satisfy the deities of his retinue, one by one, in turn.
Having gratified the deity within one's own heart, one should dismiss the Sun at the sacred bathing place.
In the Yāmala:
Having meditated upon the King of Tantras in the water and having placed the Goddess there,
[one should likewise place] the gods, sages, and ancestors, together with their weapons and retinues.
Whether in water or at home, the wise man should offer libations to the Goddess;
having fully satisfied the lineage of Gurus, he should then offer libations to Vaṭuka and the others.
Having fully gratified the Root Goddess (Mūladevī), one should gratify her retinue;
likewise, one should gratify the deities of the limbs (Aṅgadevatās) as well as Hārapāra and the others.
Then, one should worship Śeṣikā and Sundarī in the west, the Supreme Guru in the northeast,
Parāpara in the southeast, and Parameṣṭhin in the southwest.
One should offer libations to the lineage of gurus starting from the northwest (Vāyavya) and ending at the northeast (Īśa),
as well as to the limbs [of the deity] in their respective locations, and one should offer libations to the Goddess in the center.
In the Mālinītantra:
At the end of the root mantra, saying "I satisfy" (tarpayāmi) followed by "svāhā," this is the intended method of libation. By performing such libations three times, the destruction of sins occurs.
"I satisfy [them]"—this is the specific distinction for Tārā.

Facing the northern direction, one should offer libations to the Goddess alone with water from a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), sesame seeds, ground paste (*kalka*), milk, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*). However, according to the *Mālinītantra*, the libation for the retinue (*parivāra*) is performed with water alone. At the end of the root mantra, having uttered "Tāriṇī," one says "I offer libations to Agnivallabhā" at the end of the root mantra.
The libation (tarpaṇa) is for one's chosen deity; there is a specific rule regarding Viṣṇu in the Gautamīya.
First, having uttered the mantra "Śrī Kṛṣṇa" as well,
a person should perform the libation five times, saying "I satisfy [you]" (tarpayāmi) and ending with "Namaḥ."
But elsewhere, however...

One should join the word "tarpayāmi" (I satiate), then the name of one's own chosen deity, and [the word] "ca" (and) at the ends of the words ending in the accusative case; such is considered the mantra for the rite of libation (tarpaṇa).
Thus [it is said].

Thus, the primary method of satiation (*tarpaṇa*) consists of one hundred and eight repetitions; this is the foremost option. Alternatively, half of that, or twenty, or eight times for each [deity]. If one is unable to perform the satiation for each limb (*aṅga*) and retinue (*parivāra*), one should formulate the mantra as "I satiate the deity [Name] together with limbs and retinue, svāhā," and so forth, and thus satiate the deity alone according to one's capacity.

"One should perform the libation," so say the followers of the Āgamas. "I offer libation to the *Mahākālasaṃhitā* and the venerable *Śrī-Dakṣiṇakālikā*, [saying] *svāhā*. For it is stated in the *Yāmala-vajra*: "Therein, one should worship the form of Bhairava and the goddess Kālikā.
Thereafter, one should offer the *argha* oblation to the Sun. This is also stated in the *Yāmala*.
One should offer the *argha* three times with the mantra "Mārtaṇḍa Bhairavāya";
the mention of "Mārtaṇḍa Bhairavāya" alone is an elliptical reference, for that is indeed the mantra.
Hrīṃ Haṃsaḥ! To Mārtaṇḍa Bhairava, together with the Śakti Prakāśā, this arghya, svāhā!
In the *Tantrarājottara*.
Having recollected the god Bhairava, known as Mārtaṇḍa, the lord of Umā,
[one should worship] that deity with the root mantra or with the mantra of the Sun.
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ), one should then take "sohaṃ" in reverse order;
this is followed by Mārtaṇḍabhairava ending in "ṅe" (Mārtaṇḍabhairavāya), conjoined with the Śakti of Light (Prakāśa).
Thus is declared the mantra of the Sun.
In the Meru Tantra:
Having performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma), the knower of mantras [should recite] the three-syllabled mantra of the Sun,
which is said to be "hrīṃ hraḥ saḥ."
Having thus placed Indra and the others, one should meditate on the Sun with undistracted mind.
82a) Meditation is as follows:

I worship the Sun, the lord of all worlds, who holds a pair of lotuses and the gestures of fearlessness and boon-giving with his lotus-like hands, who wears a crown of rubies, whose splendor is like that of a red ruby, who has three eyes, who sits upon a red lotus, and who is the sole ocean of infinite virtues. (From the *Svatantra*). Standing, one should offer three handfuls of water to the Lord of Day.
In the Nandikeśvara Saṃhitā:
O Goddess of the Suras, as long as the arghya offering is not presented to the Sun,
one should not worship Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, or the Lord of the Devas.
Also in the *Nityāhnika-tilaka*:
And here, in the *Kulamārtaṇḍaka*, the *Saṃkṣepārcanaka* is established as permanent;
thereafter it is taught that the fruit of worship arises from the offering of the *arghya*.
Then, one should offer the *argha* oblation to the Goddess residing within the solar disc.
This has been stated in the Nīlatantra:
Having prepared *arghya* with *kūpīta*, *moḍhra* flowers, *kuśa* flowers, *kuśa* water,
and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) along with mango, one should present it.
At the end of the root mantra, [one adds] "from the word beginning with 'ca' and so forth, to her who dwells in the maṇḍala,
who consists of the consciousness of Śiva, svāhā"— this is remembered as that mantra.
Red sandalwood kept in a vessel, a flower from a noble family, and menstrual blood;
In this regard, the state of being blackened has been established.
Having performed the Tantric bath according to the very procedure just described,
because of the statement "this indeed is the Kaulika Sandhyā."
This is because of the statement in the *Brahmayāmala*: "It was told [to me] with reference to my disciple Kulaga."
The ritual action performed by a Kaulika is not called Kauvaidilika.

Because of the statement in the *Rudrayāmala*: "The ritual act performed by one who follows the Vedic path is not designated as Kaulika. Furthermore, some say that in the *Nirakṣema* [tradition], the term "karma" refers to the *Atharvaveda*, and thus Vedic rites such as bathing, the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*), and libations (*tarpaṇa*) should not be performed by the Kaulikas. That is not so; for it has been stated: "Having first performed the Vedic bath, one should thereafter perform the Tantric rite."

The meaning of those statements must be interpreted otherwise, because they contradict the *Tripurārṇava* statement—"Having performed the Vedic bath, one should then perform the Tantric [bath]"—as well as the *Merutantra*, and because of the contradiction with the *Merutantra*'s own statement: "Having performed the Vedic and Tantric *saṃdhyā*, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*). Therefore...
Let it be so; this is merely a dispute that should be noted by the wise. (From the Merutantra)
Having bowed to the Guru, the lords of the directions, and the birds,
he should proceed silently while holding a water-pot filled with water, remembering his chosen deity within his heart.
One should go to a secluded, uninhabited place that is pleasing to the mind and free from defects;
one should not look back toward other directions until one has reached home.
Thus concludes the libation.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Kulamuktikallolinī composed by Śrī Ādyānanda.
Now follows the ritual procedure for worship.
And that [attainment] is threefold, according to the distinction of superior, middling, and inferior, as was previously stated. Thus it has been said:
In the Phetkāriṇī Tantra.
Accompanied by the Śaktis, the Mūrtis, and the Guardians of the Quarters (Lokapālas),
the sacrifice performed according to the sequence of the Pīṭha and Yantra is the supreme Nityayāga.
The external enclosure is not manifested by the entire *pīṭha* alone;
it is fully endowed with fire-rites, oblations, and ornaments.
The sacrifice previously performed with mantras is the middling daily sacrifice (nityayāga);
likewise, the worship of each [deity] accompanied by the purification of the ritual materials [constitutes it].
Having set aside various kinds of clothing, ornaments, and objects,
and having omitted the fire-ritual according to the requirements of time and place.
Worship performed with material substances is considered the lowest form;
because its practice depends upon one's capacity, it has been omitted here due to its great extent.
Therein, he first states the rule regarding the location.
To Phetkāli.
In a place with a single linga, or in a cremation ground, a deserted house,
or at a crossroads— staying there, the yogi should accomplish the Vidyā, the Mistress of the Three Worlds.
In the Rudrayāmala.
In a solitary linga, in a cremation ground, in an empty house, at a crossroads,
or at the foot of a family tree, he remains focused on the contemplation of a corpse.
Whether in a vehicle, in the womb, or specifically in the vaginal flower,
one should worship the Vidyā with excellent substances such as lac, barley-meal, and vermilion.
A person should recite [the mantra] six thousand times at each junction of the day (sandhyā), accompanied by fish and meat offerings, incense, lamps, and various kinds of food offerings.
This great vidyā bestows accomplishment through its mere recitation;
situated therein, the yogi shall achieve the vidyā that liberates from the three worlds.
The Ekaliṅga has been described in the Phetkārīya [Tantra].
Where one does not perceive any other sign within the space of five *kośas*, that is declared to be the "Single Sign" (*ekaliṅga*); there, supreme accomplishment (*siddhi*) is attained.
The cremation ground and so forth are explained in the *Triśaktiratna*.
There, where it is crowded with corpse-stakes, the lifeless are burned;
it is surrounded by vultures, jackals, crows, and others greedy for flesh.
That place is known as a cremation ground, frequented by hosts of piśācas, filled with crows and other scavengers, and infested with worms, mushrooms, and the like.
That place is called an empty house which has been abandoned by the citizens from afar due to the cause of arising fear, and where heaps of grass have grown upon the mansions.
Where the meeting of four roads occurs simultaneously,
that is called a crossroads (catuṣpatha), which bestows wealth upon the night.
Each preceding one among these is praised, while each succeeding one is inferior.
The Dialogue between Hara and Gaurī.
She should be worshipped with effort in an empty house, at a crossroads,
in a temple of Śiva, at the root of a bilva tree, and always in the kula-maṇḍala.
Also in the Vīratantra:
Every moment is indeed auspicious; no inauspicious time exists anywhere.
There is no distinction between day and night, nor between the twilight and the deep of night.
In the *Phetkāriṇī*.
If all [rites] such as the worship of the goddesses (vali-pūjā) are performed at night,
each of them becomes inexhaustible through the grace of the Goddess Tārā.
In the Kulārṇava:
Having examined the state of the self, the purification of the body is the fifth [stage];
O Goddess, as long as this is not performed, there is indeed no worship of the deity.
The purification of the self and so forth will be explained [later].
It was made like the surface of a mirror by means of sweeping, smearing with cow dung, and other preparations;
it was adorned with canopies, incense, lamps, and the like, and beautified by extended banners.
The painting with powders of five colors is called the purification of the site;
thereafter, the best of practitioners, touching the mantra at his heart, [proceeds].
The yogi whose mind is not directed toward external objects should then enter the stage of yoga.
In the Meru Tantra.
Having performed a circumambulation of the sacrificial hall and having washed his feet and hands,
he sipped water (ācamana) and stood within the entrance of the house for worship.
In the *Kumārīkalpa*.
Then, having brought water with his left hand while reciting the mantra *oṃ vajrodake hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, the knower of mantras should purify the seat.
The meaning is "with the left hand toward the left direction. Likewise:
Having first extracted the Praṇava and likewise the Lakṣmī-bīja,
one should then say "O Viśuddha, pacify all sins."
At the end of "aśeṣa," there should be the syllable *anta*; remove that which follows it.
O Dear One, the mantra for washing the feet consists of the seed-syllable *kūrv*.
Likewise, the beginning of the Vedas, as well as Māyā, Svāhā, Ī, Manu, and Ṛta.
In the Bhairava Tantra.
Having sipped water (ācamana), the wise one should then lie down upon a seat such as a woolen blanket;
facing north, he should then assume the heroic lotus posture (vīrapadmāsana).
Having sat down, the practitioner of mantra should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana), which bestows all accomplishments;
having drunk [the water] with the three mantras beginning with *kalpa*, he should touch his lips with the mantras beginning with *kālya*.
Having wiped the lips twice with two [hands] and once with one, he should wash his hand;
then he should touch his mouth, nose, eyes, ears, nostrils, and arms.
Having performed the *ācamana* (ritual sipping of water) in this manner, the reciter shall behold her after one year.

"The bath as before" is an elliptical expression [for the following]: the morning duties, including bathing, *saṃdhyā*, *arpaṇa*, washing the feet, *ācamana*, binding the topknot (*śikhā*), and so forth, as well as the worship of the door (*dvārapūjā*).
One should also understand the rules for sitting on the seat and so forth; by the phrase "facing north," the possibility of facing other directions is precluded.
Regarding the phrase "with *kāla* and so forth," the author of the *Tantraratna* explains that it means performing three sips of water (*ācamana*) with the three syllables beginning with *hrīṃ*.
However, in reality, "with *kāla* and so forth" means with the seed-syllables of Kālī, Kūrca, and Lajjā.
Regarding the phrase "by Kalpā and the others," the meaning is "by the fifteen Śaktis beginning with Kālī and Kapālinī."

The meaning is that he describes the ritual rinsing (*upasparśana*) with two verses beginning with "Kālīkapālinī. With one [verse], he describes the ritual rinsing in the form of Kullā and others, such as Kurukullā. Regarding the passage beginning with "āsyā" (mouth), there is the placement (*nyāsa*) of two powers (*śakti*) each upon the nose and other organs; "kaṃ" refers to the head, and the placement of two powers is on the two arms. This is the sequence for the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*).
This should also be performed by those who rely on that [deity] during bathing and other such rites; "having sat upon a seat" refers specifically to the place of worship.
In the Uttaratantra:
Having sipped water and attained purity, and having bathed well for the worship of the deity,
one should stand outside the sacrificial altar at a distance of four cubits, with a focused mind.
And standing at the doorway of the house, he should bow his head to the guru.
In the Meru Tantra.
Standing at the doorway of his house, having mentally bowed to his guru,
he should salute his own chosen deity and even the deities of the two doorposts with his mind.
Whatever sin was previously accumulated, whether on that very day or on another,
one should recite these two mantras for the purpose of removing that sin.
O Goddess, this mind of mine has been made at dawn possessed by sin;
therefore, O Consciousness-Sun, expel that sin from me—*phaṭ phaṭ*, and salutations to you!
The sun, the moon, Yama, time, and the five great elements—
these are not witnesses to one's good or evil deeds.
Having uttered "huṃ phaṭ" with a steady, wrathful gaze, one should look toward the sides.
When this is performed first for the purpose of crushing sin, whatever sin is most solid will be driven far away.
By performing worship in the past, one returns once more to one's own station;
furthermore, whatever sin may be even very slight, it goes to destruction.
For one who has abandoned sin through worship, whatever is desired shall be accomplished in an instant.

In this regard, a specific instruction is stated in the *Merutantra* that the offering of water (argha) to the Sun should be presented, as follows: "Having prepared a mandala on ground smeared with cow dung..."
Thereafter, having entered the form [of the deity] with vermilion and seated upon his own throne,
he, intent on devotion, should bow to his chosen deity while facing the east.
Having performed three breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma) with the Sūrya-mantra, the knower of mantras,
having meditated as before and worshipped according to the procedure prescribed in that ritual manual (kalpa), [should proceed].
Having prepared a square mandala with water in front [of oneself],
one should place there a copper vessel containing water together with its base.

The wise one should offer arghya, consisting of perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, darbha grass, and dūrvā grass combined with mustard seeds, up to the head [of the deity] while reciting the Sūrya mantra.
One should utter the words *hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ sa* followed by the terms for the planets, zodiac signs, and lunar mansions;
then likewise, the terms for the yogas, karaṇas, and the revolution of the seats (*parivṛttāsana*).
The mantra for the offering of water (argha) to the venerable Sūrya is recorded as: *saṃsthitaḥ śrīsūryāyārghaṃ gṛhṇa svāhā*.
This consists of thirty-four syllables and is used for the presentation of argha to the Sun.
Then, with one-pointed mind, he should mutter the Sūrya-mantra according to his capacity;
thereafter, that best of preceptors should meditate upon the Sun submerged in half that amount of water.
Having praised and bowed down, he should dismiss the Sun at the end of the mandala;
then, having risen, he should duly commence the worship at the entrance.
In this regard, even the offering of arghya to the Sun is entirely without contradiction, according to the Svatantra.
Having driven away all the hosts of obstacles situated on the ground and in the sky with unhusked rice, white mustard seeds,
and sesame seeds, one should enter the seat.
In the Bhairava Tantra.
Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should prepare the general offering (sāmānyārghya).
Thereafter, one should fashion a mandala consisting of a triangle, a circle, and a square.
Having worshipped the foundational power (ādhāraśakti), one should place the support (ādhāra) there;
having purified the vessel with the weapon-mantra (astra), one should worship it with the heart-mantra (hṛdayamantra).
Having invoked the sacred bathing place (tīrtha), one should cast down the scents and other offerings with the Praṇava;
then, displaying the cow-mudrā (dhenumudrā), this is considered the general procedure for the arghya offering.
O Goddess of the gods, one should worship the deities of the gateway with the general offering (sāmānyārgha),
namely Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapāla, Vaṭuka, and the Yoginī.
Then one should enter the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, Lakṣmī, and Vāṇī.
In the Meru Tantra:
Sprinkle the door and the path with water for the guest-offering (argha), and in their midst, one should worship the Lord of Obstacles (Vighnapa).
The name [of the deity] consists of its first syllable joined with a bindu (anusvāra), followed by the name ending in the dative case (ṅe).
Having recited [the mantra] up to the heart, one should worship those deities.
Also in another tantra:
One should worship Gaṇeśa with *yām* as the first syllable, Vaṭuka likewise with *vām* as the first syllable,
Kṣetrapāla with *kṣām* as the first syllable, and Yoginī likewise with *yām* as the first syllable.
In the upper left and right, and in the lower right, respectively;
and from the top downwards at the threshold, according to the context, they worship Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Śrī Lakṣmī, and Aiṃ Sarasvatī.
A specific detail is stated in the Merutantra.
These eight yoginīs of the goddess Sūrya are the guardians of the gates:
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī; |||
Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Śrī—thus [are they worshipped] from the western door; salutation to the threshold (dehalī) of the worship circle.
The meditation on these will be explained; as for the meditation on Yamunā, it is as follows:
I bow to the excellent Kālindī, who causes fear, whose form is dark,
who is mounted upon a black tortoise, and who wears a garland of blue lotuses around her neck.
Also, the meditation on Lakṣmī.
[He saw] Mahālakṣmī, whose limbs were as fair as purified gold,
most beautiful, with three eyes, and holding a rosary, a water-pot, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons in her hands.
The meditation on the threshold is as follows:
I salute Dehalī, who is mounted upon a lion, dark-complexioned, bearing a sword and a shield, standing below, facing west, and endowed with auspicious marks.
Then, having scattered *dūrvā* grass and other items around the house, one should meditate on the obstacles as being burnt away.
That mantra is found in the Kumārī-kalpa.
Having first extracted the Praṇava, then the words "sarvavighnān," followed by "utsāraya" twice, then "hūṃ phaṭ svāhā."
And with this very mantra, the wise one should dispel all obstacles.
In the Meru Tantra:
Having approached the western door and performed three *tāla*-hand gestures,
one should open the door with the *astra* mantra, [scattering] consecrated mustard seeds and unbroken rice grains.

Having then assumed the form of a Śava, a man shall become a poet and an eloquent speaker;
for the sake of attaining all perfections, the Sūtra spoken by Svayambhū must be performed.
In the absence of a corpse, however, the seat (viṣṭara) is proclaimed to have the form of a corpse;

By this sequential yoga, what is not accomplished on the surface of the earth?

having uttered the *praṇava* and the *Bhuvaneśī*, one should then utter that [mantra].
"O you who have the form of a Śava, O great Preta, grant me the eight siddhis.

Whether it be flowers or other such things seen or personally known to be defiled,

therefore, the practitioner of mantra, uttering the seed-syllable *chroṃ*, should touch [the object] with the *devatīrtha* [of the hand].
Having seen the water situated within the jar, the practitioner of the rite,
holding the jar located at his left side with his left hand, [should proceed].

[the syllable] consisting of the first letter of its own name, joined with a bindu and the half-moon (*ardhacandra*).

Whatever other defilement may arise from ignorance regarding the vessel or the water—
such as contact with a corpse in a reservoir or association with those standing in the water— [it is removed by this].
Such objections as these would vanish when one worships the God who is dear to that [deity].

for those who do so, O Great Goddess, there is suffering at every step.
Without liquor there is no mantra, and without mantra there is no liquor;
since they are mutually contradictory, how can the worship be performed?

therefore, the path of the Vedas must never be abandoned by the twice-born at any time.

such is the clear meaning. Let the virtuous remain free from dispute. In Vijaya and Alpa.

Of this glorious *Samayā* mantra, Ānandabhairava is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the sovereign (*samrāṭ*) is the meter (*chanda*), the goddess Samayā Vāgvādinī is the deity (*devatā*), *hrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *klīṃ* is the bolt (*kīlaka*), and *sauḥ* is the power (*śakti*). for the attainment of mastery over speech (*vāk-siddhi*), and for the purification of the *samayā*.

"I worship the Goddess Vijayā, the Sovereign of the Universe, who dwells in the three worlds, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation through the sequence of the staff that rests upon the staff, and who— like a beautiful woman using the collyrium of passion— conquers hundreds of excellent enemies."
Having meditated thus, one should consecrate it seven times with mantras.
Having consecrated it seven times with mantras, everything will certainly become purified.

Furthermore, she is fourfold— Brahminī, Kṣatriyā, Vaiśyā, and Śūdrā— due to the distinction between white, red, yellow, and black.
