You are the giver of purity to the Bhairavas; may you always be auspicious in nature.
Oṃ, homage to Brāhmī, svāhā! One should thus purify the Brāhmaṇī [lineage].
O Goddess Siddhamaulīkriyā, you who awaken those of inferior understanding!
O Queen who brings subjects under control, O Slayer of Śakra’s throat!
Aiṃ! Homage to the Kṣatriyā, Svāhā! Thereafter, one should purify.
O fire whose flames are kindled by the fuel of ignorance, O fire whose form is knowledge,
I pray for the attainment of bliss, joy, and perfect wisdom.
Hrīṃ, salutation to Vaiśyā, Svāhā; then one should purify the Śūdrā.
I bow, I bow to her who points out the path of Yoga.
O Mother, in the Trailokyavijaya [mudrā], when the samādhi is established,
O Umā, the mantra "klīṃ śūdrāyai namaḥ svāhā" is declared.
Or else, one may purify all [the vessels] with a single mantra alone.
That has been stated in that very same place.
After *amṛte amṛtodbhave amṛtavarṣiṇi*,
then the pair *padam tataḥ amṛtam ākarṣaya*, and after that the word *siddhiṃ dehi*.
Then one should say "sarvam me 'tha tataḥ" and thereafter "vaśam ānaya";
this mantra, ending with two *ṭha*s, is declared for the purification of all four [elements].
In the Uttaratantra, another method common to all is also stated as follows:
One should place the root mantra seven times above the end [of the name].
Then follow the mudrās for invocation and so forth, as well as the dhenu and yoni mudrās thereafter.
One should loosen the bonds of impurity with finger-snaps preceded by the utterance of the *traya-tāra* (the three syllables of the *praṇava*),
and likewise, one should destroy obstacles with divine vision and strikes of the heels.
Reciting the root mantra, one should satisfy the Guru seven times in the Sahasrāra lotus at the Brahma-randhra by means of the Tattva-mudrā.
The practitioner, whose mind is intent on accomplishment, should satisfy [the deities] with devotion in three ways;
he should utter the word "aiṃ vada vada," followed by the word "vāgvādini."

90a) Then, one should offer oblations into the mouth with the mantra: "O you who are firm on the tip of my tongue! O you who bring all under control! Svāhā! (mama jihvāgre sthirīti bhava sarvapadaṃ tataḥ | sarvavaśaṅkari svāhā).
If it is asked: "Since no specific qualification is heard in these statements, how can it be said that they refer to those other than Brahmins?"
One should avoid all intoxicating substances, such as gold and the like;
therefore, the one who commits such a transgression is a sinner—this is the dharma of the foremost among those who know the Vedas.

"O God, by giving liquor to a Brāhmaṇa, one who is devoted to Brahman falls from his state; by giving the blood of one's own body, one incurs the sin of suicide"—accept this according to the statement in the Bhairava Tantra. Thereafter, one should begin the purification of the self through breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and other practices.
Thus it is said in the Kulārṇava:
O Dear One, purification through bathing and the like, as well as through breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and other means, is called external purity;
while purification of the self is said to be achieved through the application of all the six-limbed nyāsas.
Therein, first is breath control (prāṇāyāma).
To Sanatkumāri.
Having sat down in a comfortable posture and performed breath control (prāṇāyāma),
one should then perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and subsequently carry out the ritual placement (nyāsa).
The one born from a jar.
Whatever action is performed without breath-control (prāṇāyāma) is rendered fruitless;
therefore, those who seek auspicious results should practice breath-control with diligent effort.
In the Tantra:
One should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas) with the root mantra or with the syllable Om;
alternatively, purification occurs according to the prescribed rule by means of the seed-syllable of the mantra.
Thus it is.
One should fill the breath with sixteen [counts] and perform the retention (kumbhaka) with four times that; one should exhale with half of the retention, or, if unable, by a quarter.
Also elsewhere.
If one is unable to do that, then the restraint of breath (prāṇasaṃyama) should be performed as the fourth [alternative];
for without prāṇāyāma, there is no fitness for worship and other such rites.
In Viśuddheśvara.
One should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas) with the divine [mantra] in between them.
In the *Samayāṅkamātṛkā*.
One should fill the breath through the *iḍā* once with the root mantra;
then, O fair-faced one, one should perform the retention (*kuṃbhaka*) through the middle [channel] four times with the same mantra.
One should exhale through the Piṅgalā channel in the sequence of the number of eyes (two);
again and again in that same sequence, it should be done three times.
In the Kumārī Tantra:
Then, having diligently brought a sixteen-year-old woman—
a young girl intoxicated with passion, well-attired, and possessing a beautiful smile— [he proceeded].
The wise man should place on his left that woman who is always longing for sexual union, whose forehead is marked with vermilion, and who is devoted to the practitioner.
The term "left" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa); it should be understood to apply also to the worshiped yantra mentioned in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*.
In the conduct of the samaya.
Placing his hand on the left shoulder and then placing his own body upon the child's body with a feeling of identity,
the worship should be performed according to the prescribed rite.
Having been turned back.
Then [he recites] the mantra for sipping water (ācamana), the mantra for the consecration of the flowers,
the mantra for tying the knot, and the mantra for purifying body, speech, and mind.
In this context, the ritual action is described by means of the mantra;
the mantra for sipping water (ācamana) has already been written above, and the mantra for consecrating the flower is found in the Kumārīkalpa.
By means of the empowerment of the flower, one should first utter the *praṇava* (oṃ),
then the word "śatābhiṣeka," and after that, "śatābhī."
The word "ṣaketi" is proclaimed, followed by "hūṃ phaṭ svāhā";
then the Praṇava, Puṣpaketu, and likewise Rājārhata.
Puṣpapuṣpe mahāpuṣpe supuṣpe puṣpasaṃbhave | puṣpa ca yāvakīrṇe hūṃ phaṭ svāhā thereafter.
According to Manu, one should then perform the purification of the flower for the Goddess;

the tradition is that one should tie a knot in the hem of the upper garment using scattering materials with the *śikhā-bandhana* mantra as prescribed for the *saṃdhyā-vandana*. The mantra for the purification of the body and so forth is found in the *Kumārī-tantra*.
Having first extracted the Praṇava, and immediately after that [the syllable] *me*,
the mantra *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā* is declared for the purification of body, speech, and mind.
*Rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ phaṭ svāhā* shall be the mantra for self-protection.
Now follows the purification of the hands.
The specific details of that are found in the Merutantra.
Then, with palms joined in reverence, having bowed to the Guru and Gaṇapati at his left and right sides, and to his chosen deity in front;
The knower of mantras, taking fragrant flowers smeared with sandalwood paste,
should rub them with the *klauṃ* mantra and the *kavaca-astra* mantra.
Taking that flower with the left hand,
one should whirl it around one's head while reciting the *tāra* mantra, and then smell it again.
Oṃ! This verse is likewise recited at the eastern gate:
"May all those who indeed harm me go to total dissolution. O you seven! [Hauṃ].
May the fears arising from the afflictions fall upon the heads of the enemy;
having offered this with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), one should cast it in all directions using the *nārāca* mudrā.
This is called the purification of the hands.
91a) In the *Uttaratantra*:
The practitioner should take a flower with the Viṣṇu-mantra using the tip of his finger for the purpose of rubbing it during the rite of hand-purification.
One should crush the flower with both hands using the *prāsāda* mantra; then, while purifying it with the *kāmavija*, one should smell it again with the *akṣa* mantra.
One should perform renunciation with a gracious mind, especially in the northeastern direction;
having wiped [the vessel] with the left hand, one should then smell it with the left hand.
Then one should cast the flower held in the palm of the hand toward the northeast;
when this is done, there shall be incomparable purification of the two palms.
The wise know that the fingertips become pure by grasping flowers; however, through the crushing of three claps of the hands, complete purification arises.
Free from the sense of "mine," with the back of the hand reaching as far as the tip of the nose— the supreme point—
the sacred fords (tīrthas) come together at the tip of the nose and the hand.
Therefore, O Bhairava, these rites should be performed with effort;
[the mantra] is joined with the void (zero) and colored by the moon (1) on the side of Ka (2).
This mantra, touched by the end of Rudra (the letter *ha*), is considered Vaiṣṇava.
The letter *ha* is at the end; at the beginning [of the word] is the moon on the head—the nasal *anusvāra* as a half-moon (*ardhacandra*)—which is the void (*śūnya*).
The end of Rudra is the long vowel *ū*; thus, [the seed-syllable is] *hūṃ*.
The syllable *pra*, joined with the vowel *au* and the letter *va*,
followed by *śambhu* (the letter *śa*), the crescent moon (*cūḍā*), and the nasal bindu— this is called the *prāsāda*.
The letter *ha* is [the substitute] for the final [consonant] and so forth.
Vāsudeva is the syllable *o*; from that comes the conjunction (*sandhi*), which is *hau*. Śambhu is the crest (*cūḍā*), the topknot (*śikhā*), and the half-moon (*ardhacandra*).
The seed-syllable of desire (kāma-bīja) should be understood as Vāsudeva (the letter A), the moon (the vowel I), and the bindu;
it consists of the first consonant and the last [vowel], preceded by the final consonant and the penultimate letter.
The first and the last of the two [groups], followed by a consonant and the Praṇava (Oṃ) at the end—
this is declared to be the Brahma-bīja, which destroys all sins.
It is to be understood from another tantra; this is the remainder [of the sentence].
He extracts the seed-syllable of Brahmā.
*Vāśudeva* is the syllable *o*; *indu* is the half-moon (*ardhacandra*); *bindu* is the nasal dot (*anusvāra*). Thus, [the mantra] begins with *oṃ*.

The first and last consonants are the final consonant, which is devoid of vowel; that is the letter *sa*. That [letter *sa*] is what precedes it, hence *sat*. Following the *praṇava* (*oṃ*), there are two [instances of] the first and last [consonants], each followed by the *praṇava*, making two pairs of first and last [consonants].
Regarding that, he states the distinction: subsequently, there is a second letter *ta*, a consonant devoid of vowel; by this, "oṃ tatsat" is produced.
Also in the Merutantra: "Then, with the Astra-mantra, one should perform the three Tāras."
With that mantra, one should perform the binding of the directions (*digbandha*) higher and higher; and with that same [mantra],
one should generate the splendor of fire by means of the *vahni-prākāra-mudrā*.
One should protect oneself with the root mantra and perform three breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma).
In the Uttaratantra:
Having completed the purification of the hands, the preceptor should then perform three claps with the root mantra, as well as the binding of the directions, moving progressively upward.
The splendor generated by that shall provide protection on all sides.
In the Bhairava Tantra.
With the mantra "KŪRCAM VIYADVINDUYUTAṂ ŚAKTYASTRĀYA PHAṬ," one should perform the binding of the directions by snapping the fingers and other gestures.
The syllable *kūrca* is *hūṃ*; the letter *ha* with the nasal dot (*anusvāra*) is the *śakti*, namely *hrīṃ*.
Here, the form for the weapon-mantra (*astra*) is *phaṭ*, which includes the elision of the *visarga* when combined with the deity.
Likewise.
Having performed the preliminary ritual resolve as before,
one should then draw the yantra in a vessel made of gold or other precious materials, which has been smeared with red sandalwood paste.

In this regard, some maintain that there is indeed an option regarding the sequence of the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and the drawing of the yantra, because it is observed [in the scriptures] accordingly.
For otherwise, there would arise no contradiction with the statement: "Having thus disposed the body, one should draw the King of Wheels."
That which is written in the Ugra [Tantra].
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Kulamuktikallolinī* composed by Śrī Ādyānanda.
Now follows the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
In the Meru Tantra:
Then one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi); its procedure is as follows, O Dhruva.
In the Bhairava Tantra.
Having placed the two hands upon the limbs, one should perform the *satattva* [mudrā] joined with the *kuṇḍalinī*, using the mantra "Viya-dvi-ndu-yugaṃ Bhṛguḥ Sargavān."

Then, having pierced the seed-syllables and the wheels, and having joined the red Citkalā to the auspicious lotus situated on the head, one should recite slowly while meditating upon her at the navel.
Having purified his body with the wind from the nostrils of Vāmana and having consumed that sin by means of blazing fire, he was thereafter liberated.
One should visualize the seed-syllable of the bride (Vadhū-bīja), yellowish in luster and having the form of air;
while reciting it and meditating on it in the heart, one should fill the right nostril with breaths and not expel the ashes outward through the opening of the left nostril.
Having brought the syllable *hūṃ*, which has the luster of the full moon, onto the lunar disc at the forehead,
one should then cause nectar to descend from its recitation.
Having caused those bones to be washed away,
one should then generate a body by means of the mantra "So'ham," [visualizing] the principles (tattvas), the seed-syllable, and Kuṇḍalinī in their proper sequence.
92a) Just as one brings [the disciple] to the proper place, [one should recite] "Tāriṇī mayam. One should meditate that "Tāriṇī mayam" refers to the deity within one's own hand.
In the Vārāhī Tantra:

The practitioners of Tantra should cause the vital breath (prāṇa), which has risen from the mūlādhāra, to unite with the Supreme Self at the station of Puṣkara by means of the Haṃsa through the path of Brahman.
In the Rudrayāmala.
One should perform the withdrawal of the phonemes; having withdrawn the letters beginning with *kṣa* and those beginning with *a* in reverse order, one should unite them within the Supreme Self.
Then, one should join the five elements and the five [senses], beginning with the first, into the Supreme Self.
In the Meru-tantra:
From the feet up to the knees, it is square and marked with a vajra;
joined with the syllable *laṃ*, it is yellow in color, the ground-abode, and has Brahmā as its presiding deity.
The station presided over by the power called Nivṛtti is said to be one;
one should contemplate it as the single form of the souls for the purpose of their arising.
From the knees up to the navel is the locus of water, white in luster;
it resembles a half-moon, has two peaks, and is marked by a lotus.
One should meditate upon that which has Viṣṇu as its deity— a hexagon joined with six dots and conjoined with the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, and endowed with the *pratiṣṭhā* kalā.
From the navel up to the throat, the region is reddish and has Rudra as its presiding deity;
it is joined with the seed-syllable "Raṃ" and endowed with the digit known as Vidyā.
One should contemplate the element of fire (vahnitattva), which has assumed a triangular shape endowed with blazing svastikas and is the locus of the great dissolution.
The *kaṇṭhā* [mantra] extends to the middle of the eyebrows; it has taken the form of a six-cornered charcoal [triangle], marked with six dots, encircled by a circle, and black in color.

One should contemplate the station of air, presided over by the power of pacification (śāntikalā), having Śiva as its deity, joined with the seed-syllable *yaṃ*, and possessing the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of all beings.
The space from the midpoint of the eyebrows to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) is called the station of Ākāśa;
it is circular in shape, smoke-colored, and marked by a very tall banner.

One should meditate upon the seed-syllable *haṃ*, presided over by the power (*kalā*) called Śāntyatītā and having Śiva as its deity; having thus meditated, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the elements within the body.
Having visualized it as arising from the bulb of the Dharma, beautifully adorned with the stalk of wisdom,
situated within its pericarp, and resembling the flame of a lamp;
Through the Suṣumnā, the practitioner, joined in yoga, should unite the individual soul with the Supreme Self by means of the "So'ham" mantra according to the prescribed method.
One should contemplate all beings dissolved right there;
one should contemplate the person within the excrement in the left side of the body.
The sin stands in the left side of the belly as a man with the luster of collyrium;
he has the murder of a Brahmin for his head and the theft of gold for his two arms.
The drinking of liquor is associated with the heart; violating the Guru’s bed is the two hips;
association with such persons is the pair of feet; and minor sins are the limbs and sub-limbs.
One should contemplate the sinner as having hair like that of a minor offender, with red beard and eyes, holding a sword and a shield, cruel, harsh, and wicked.
In another tantra:
One should visualize the sinful one holding a sword and shield, the size of a thumb, facing downwards, black in color, and situated in the right side of the belly.

"One should visualize, on the right side of the belly, a black being resembling a *tatpuruṣa*, possessing sin accumulated from beginningless existence, and holding a sword and a shield," so it is said in the *Svatantra*.
Also in the Merutantra:
Having become composed of pure consciousness alone, one should contemplate the Person of Sin (pāpapuruṣa) situated in the right side of the abdomen,
black in color and the size of a thumb, and so forth.

In the *Merutantra*, it is revealed that those following the left-hand path (*vāmācāra*) should meditate on the Person of Sin (*pāpapuruṣa*) in the right side of the abdomen, while those following the right-hand path (*dakṣiṇamārgin*) should meditate on him in the left side of the abdomen; and in the center is the syllable *yam*.
In the Yāmala:
Then the practitioner, with a steady mind, should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi),
placing his own two hands face upwards before him.
In the *mūlādhāra*, the root-vidyā is the *kulamuṇḍalī* in its own form,
having the shape of a sleeping serpent and consisting of three and a half coils.
Slender like a wild-rice seedling, she is the embodiment of all sciences;
her appearance is like ten million flashes of lightning, and she encircles the self-manifested linga.
Having meditated upon her with the Haṃsa-mantra, or again with the Praṇava,
or with the Kūrca-bīja, O Goddess, the Guru should firmly cause [the obstacles] to flee.
Having brought about the unification of the individual self and the supreme self,
one should contemplate the supreme void, wherein the earthly element has dissolved into water.
One should contemplate water as being made black by fire, and fire as having the form of light.
One should meditate upon Nirvana as having the nature of wind.
The wind, not drawn from space, dissolves into its respective mind;
but I, who am under the sway of the mind and ego, have been drawn away by the Great One.
Then, by its very nature, the Great Principle (mahattattva) should contemplate Prakṛti;
she is eternal, of the nature of light, and identical with the essence of Brahma-vidyā.
She is absolute, solitary, peaceful, devoid of qualities, and of the nature of the Supreme Self;
she is this supreme light and the ultimate state free from all affliction.
The supreme state, whose nature is emptiness, resides in the center of the thousand-petaled lotus.
In the same way.
One should contemplate a smoky charcoal-colored wind at the region of the navel;
by means of that, for sixteen *mātrās*, one should indeed dry up the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*).

Having performed the ritual of the action-nature (karmātmaka) by means of sixty-four [repetitions] and having retained it in the *kuṃbha* [vessel], one should practice it; or again, with thirty-two measures (*mātrā*) on the right, or by means of that [same method].
One should contemplate the red-colored seed-syllable of fire at the base of the genitals;
one should burn the body with that, which is the *liṅga* consisting of the seat of impurities.
By means of the sequence previously described, following the order of the months of Dakṣa,
one should again perform it on the right side with the appropriate measure, ending with the syllable *ra*.
The seed-syllable of fire (raṃ) is red in color; it is located in the penis, and its number is likewise [six]; one should exhale through the left nostril.
Speech is the daughter of Varuṇa.
And having visualized the seed-syllable at the uvula.
Having produced nectar from the thousand-petaled lotus,
one should cause it to flood [the body] by means of inhalation and other breath-control techniques, down to the soles of the feet.
One should visualize the syllable *laṃ*, the seed-syllable of the earth, at the root of the anus;
by that very same sequential yoga, the wise one should cause it to be completely immersed by means of the intellect.
The supreme body of Śambhu is liberated from both sin and merit;
one should subsequently accomplish it by that very same aforementioned path.
Thus, with the mantra, "May they live," one should bring her into the lotus of the heart;
then, one should again bring that goddess Kuṇḍalinī to the base of the root (mūlādhāra).
In Phetkārīṇī.
The wise man, having extracted with the *praṇava* the *liṅga* situated in the heart— the consciousness that is the witness of all—
should bring it out through the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
Having encapsulated [the object] with that very [mantra], one should hold it above;
thus the body, both external and internal, becomes devoid of consciousness.
Having meditated upon the seed-syllable *yaṃ*, smoke-colored, situated in the middle of the circle of wind located at the center of the navel-mandala, one should purify by means of it.
By means of the seed-syllable *raṃ*, which has the form of fire and is situated within a circle of fire,
one should burn that [body] until it becomes a heap of ashes, the form of the body being thus reduced.
One should meditate upon Varuṇa within the lunar orb, situated either between the eyebrows or in the heart;
he is shaped like a half-moon and marked with two lotuses at his feet.
Then, in that manner, one should flood the form of Mādhavī after having placed the earthly seed-syllable,
while meditating upon the golden earring.
Having divided [the self] into two by means of the *praṇava*, one should then contemplate the Self therein as having the form of consciousness and the form of the deity of the mantra.
Having explained the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) in the form of breath control (prāṇāyāma), [he says:]
In the Vīratantra:
Then one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) through the yoga of the letters of the Svatantra.
93b) In the Gandharva Tantra.
For it is said: "As is Kālī, so is Tārā; as is Tārā, so is Unmukhī."

"One should perform all [rites], beginning with the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), just as in the case of Tāriṇī," according to the statement in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*. Although the purification of the elements is not contradictory here either when performed by means of the three seed-syllables of Nīlasarasvatī in the stated order, nevertheless: "Having fashioned the yantra in this way, he should place a flower before it."

Thereafter, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), uniting oneself with Kuṇḍalinī; having joined the individual soul (jīva) with the Haṃsa via the central channel (madhyanāḍī) into Śiva.
The cruel sin situated within the belly should be dried up and burned internally by means of the syllables of wind and fire; having washed it away, one should cause it to move outward.
Thus, by means of the mantra, I shall restore that very [deity] to its proper place;
thereafter, with his body purified, he should perform the ritual placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa).
Thus, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) exactly as described in the Bhairavī Tantra;
for in the case of Tāriṇī, there is no justification for any ritual procedure other than those consisting of the three seed-syllables.
In the Uḍḍīśa [Tantra].
Alternatively, having united the Goddess Kuṇḍalinī with the five elements and so forth within the Supreme Self, one should contemplate the identity of those two.
Through the yoga of meditation, one should contemplate "I am He, I am He" with the mind;
and this very same sequence is taught even in the *Śāradā* for those who are incapable [of other means].
In the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā:
Thus, having meditated with the mantra upon that primordial [power] at the end of the resonance (nāda), which is cultivated by the perfected ones (siddhas),
one should place the digit of the individual soul (jīvakalā) from the aperture of Brahmā into the heart.
In the Kumārīkalpa.
Having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) for this purpose, one should contemplate oneself in the form of the Goddess;
then, one should perform the placement of the individual soul (jīvanyāsa) within the self contemplated as the Deity.
The meaning is that one should contemplate oneself in the form of the Goddess.
In the Meru Tantra.
O Bhoja, one should duly honor the self within the heart as the Supreme Self,
[visualizing] the body as having the form of light by means of the *haṃsa* mantra according to the prescribed rite.
One should contemplate that what has arisen is fit for the propitiation of the deity.
Likewise.
A worship performed by one who is devoid of the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) is like black magic;
it yields a contrary result, just as worship performed without devotion does.
In the Tantra:
Then the preceptor should install the individual soul (jīva) by means of the Prāṇa-mantra.
In the Meru Tantra:
Having thus performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should carry out the installation of the vital breath (prāṇasthāpana).
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are proclaimed by those learned in the Tantras;
the meters of the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman are spoken of by those proficient in prosody.
The deity of the nature of consciousness, whose essence is the vital breath (prāṇa), is declared to be Śakti;
she is said to reside in the heart, preceded by the elements beginning with the letter *ka* (earth).
And immediately thereafter, that which is expressed by "Śiva" and many other words,
along with the group beginning with the organs of knowledge (jñānendriyas), is proclaimed as the Śikhā.
The armor is proclaimed with the organs of action beginning with the ka-group;
the eye is declared with the organs of speech beginning with the pa-group.
If his weapon-mantra is prescribed as being joined with [the syllables] beginning with *vṛddhi* (vowel lengthening),

First, however, the placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkā-nyāsa), and then that known as Śrīkaṇṭha;
likewise:
One should assign the triad beginning with the Ṛṣi to the head, chest, and heart of the vessel in due order.

Although the placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkānyāsa) is not explicitly mentioned here, nevertheless, one should certainly perform the Mātṛkānyāsa, because of the statement in the Vīracūḍāmaṇi: "O child, one should perform everything, such as the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and so forth, as in the case of Tāriṇī."
There is also another [method] regarding the sequence of time.
One should place Śrīkaṇṭha and the others in the positions of the Mātṛkās in their proper sequence.
Just as Meru is for the autumn clouds.
Now I shall describe the Śaivahitā Mātṛkās beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha;
Dakṣiṇāmūrti is said to be the sage, and Gāyatrī the metre.
The Lord who carries away half of the Mountain-born Goddess is the command for the attainment of all perfections;
the vowels and the powers reside in the secret place, the heart, and the feet.
Having made the short and long vowels the interval, one should place the groups [of consonants] as before, together with the sun (ha), up to the letter ra;
having joined them with the six long vowels, one should assign the six limbs and so forth to the body.
I constantly meditate upon Him who resembles a *bandhūka* flower or gold, holding a beautiful rosary, a noose, a goad, and the gesture of granting boons with His own staff-like arms;
who wears the crescent moon as an ornament, possesses three eyes, and has half of His body merged with the Goddess Ambikā.
We formerly took refuge.
Having joined *hasau* with the Mātṛkā, one should utter *veśa* at the end of the deities;
then, in the place of the Mātṛkā, one should utter the [seed-syllable] ending in *ṅ*, its power (*śakti*) ending in *ṅām*, and finally *namaḥ*.
One should state skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen as the [seven] constituents (dhātus).
Furthermore, among the ten vowels beginning with 'a', one should use the forms ending in 'ṅ'—namely, *śaktim*, *krodham*, and *snānam*—for each of the ten.
Śrīkaṇṭha, Pūrṇodarya, Ananta accompanied by Virajā,
Sūkṣmeśa, Śātmalī who is liberated, and Trimūrtikṛt joined with Lolākṣī.
Amaleṇa is joined with Vartulākṣī, Arghīśa with Dīrghaghoṇā,
Bhārabhūti with Dīrghamukhī, and Atithīśa with Gomukhī.
Sthāśvīṇa is joined with Dīrghajihvā; Yugadhara is joined with Kuṇḍodarī;
and Kaṇṭhīśa, who belongs to the element of earth (Bhautika), is joined with Vikṛtāsyā, whose hair stands erect.
Sadyojāta is joined with Jvālāmukhī and Anugraholkāmukhī;
in Akrūra, Mahāsena is joined with Śrīmukhī and Vidyāmukhī.
Krodheśa with Mahākālī, Caṇḍeśa with Sarasvatī,
and Pañcāntaka joined with Gaurī are proclaimed as the bestowers of all spiritual accomplishments (sarvasiddhi).
Śivottameśa, joined with the Trailokyavidyā mantra, should be placed;
likewise Ekarudra with the power of the mantra, and Kūrmaśa joined with the eight Śaktis.
Ekanetra is joined with Bhūtimātrā, and Caturānana is joined with Lambodarī; Ajeśa is said to be joined with Drāviṇī.
Śāmeśa is joined with Saveśānāgarī; Lāṅgalīśa is joined with Khecarī;
and Rūpiṇī is joined with Dārukeśa by means of Mañjarī.
Vīraṇyā is indeed Ardhanārīśa, while Umākānta is joined with her again;
likewise, Kākodaryā is said to be joined with Āṣāḍhī and Pūtanā.
Daṇḍīśa is joined with Bhadrakālī; Yugatrinetra is joined with Yoginī;
Mīneśa is joined with Śaṅkhinī; and Makheśa is joined with Tarjunī.
Lohita is joined with Kālarātri, Śikhīśa with Kurdinī,
Chagalaṇḍa with Kapardinī, and Dviraṇḍeśa with Vajrā.
Mahākāla is joined with Jayā; Vālīśa is joined with Sumukhī;
Bhujaga is joined with Revatī; and Pinākin is joined with Mādhavī.
Khaḍgīśa is joined with Vāruṇī; Vakeśa is joined with Vāyavī;
Śveta is joined with Rakṣovadhāriṇī; and Bhṛgu is joined with Sahajā.
Nakulīśa conjoined with Lakṣmī, Śiveśa conjoined with Vyāpinī,
and Saṃvartaka conjoined with Mahāmāyā— these indeed are the Mātṛkās.
One should employ Īśa there, beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha and ending with Īśāna;
all are remembered as having beautiful forms, red in color, and holding tridents and skull-bowls.
Those capable ones, established in the seats of Rudra, possess bodies reddened by vermilion;
their lotus-like hands are adorned with a red lotus and a skull-cup.

The ritual application (*prayoga*), however, is as follows: *hasauṃ aṃ śrīkaṇṭheśāya pūrṇodaryai namaḥ*; *hasauṃ āṃ anaṃtāya virajayāyai namaḥ*, and so forth. Regarding the ten [deities] beginning with the letter *ya*, one should know the following: *hrīṃ hūṃ hasauṃ yaṃ tvagātmane vālīśeśāya sumukhyai namaḥ*, and so forth.
In the Śāradā [script], however, the specific variation is: *hrīṃ trīṃ hūṃ aṃ śrīkaṇṭheśa-pūrṇodarībhyāṃ namaḥ*. Thus ends the Śrīkaṇṭha-ādi Nyāsa. Now follows the Ṣaḍaṅga Nyāsa.
In the Meru Tantra.

Having performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma), the practitioner should duly perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Ṛṣi, Chandas, and Devatā of that [mantra] using the root mantra (mūlamantra).
One should perform the other ritual placements (nyāsa) preceded by the placement on the hands and limbs.
In the Kālikalpa.
Bhairava is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), Uṣṇik is cited as its meter (chandas),
Kālikā is declared to be the deity, and the seed-syllable of modesty (lajjābīja) is the seed-mantra (bīja).
The seed-syllable *kūrca* is the Śakti; Aniruddha-Sarasvatī is the presiding deity.
Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of poetic composition (*kavitva*). Thus is the visualization of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and the other [elements].
In the Kālīkrama.
The first seed-syllable shall serve as the ritual stake (kīlaka) for the accomplishment of the fourfold aims of human life.
In another tantra:
One should place the Ṛṣi on the region of the head, the Chandas upon the lotus-face,
the Devatā upon the heart, and the Bīja in the secret region.
One should place the Śakti on the two feet and the Kīlaka on all the limbs;
the placement of the Ṛṣis and so forth, as well as the Mudrās, is according to the Sārasaṃgraha.
In the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the sages, meters, and deities, the fingers are likewise prescribed.
They are devoid of the four thumbs.
Then, one should place [the mantra] ending with Śakti.
The foremost of practitioners should fix the ritual stake (kīlaka) upon all limbs with both hands.
The *Yogitantra* describes the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the sages and so forth as follows:
One should place the Ṛṣis and so forth, ending with the Heart-mantra in the fourth case, O Goddess.
In the Kālītantra: 99b) [it is stated: "In the Kālītantra."
The placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and the placement on the hands (karanyāsa) are now described according to rule;
one should perform them with the seed-syllable preceded by the Praṇava and endowed with the six long vowels.

The seed-mantra is the syllable *hrīṃ*, and the *praṇava* (oṃ) is the initial seed-syllable; these are to be differentiated by the six long vowels. One should perform the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) using the three sections of the root mantra, according to the statement in the *Svatantra-tantra*:
"In that regard, the six-limbed rite is to be understood as being performed in two ways by means of the three sections of the root mantra."
The definition of the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) is stated in the Tāropaniṣad:
"The practitioner of mantra should perform the six-limbed placement; he should say 'Salutation to the Heart'."
Having recited one's own respective mantra, [one should place] the "Beloved of Fire" (svāhā) upon the head;
thereafter, one should also place "Śiva-kha-yava-vaṣat" in the middle of the shoulders.
One should utter the *kūrca* seed-syllable at the base of the arms for the armor (*kavaca*);
one should then assign the eyes (*netra*) with the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes.
The practitioner of mantras should place [the seed-syllables] on the hands with "Astrāya Phaṭ," according to the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) as described in the Tantra-cūḍāmaṇi.
The wise one should place [the mudrās] on the heart with the middle, ring, and index fingers;
one should perform the placement on the head with the middle and index fingers.
One should place the *śikhā* with the thumb, the *kavaca* with ten [fingers],
the eyes with three, and the *astra* upon each successive limb three times.
These are known as the limb-mudrās (aṅgamudrā) performed with the middle and index fingers;
the meaning is that one should perform the three claps (tālatraya) in succession on the head with the middle and index fingers.
Now, the *Yāmala* states the meaning of the six-limbed mantra (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*).
By the word "to the heart" (hṛdayāya), that embodied one is called the joyful Doṭha;
his supreme knowledge has the mind as its object.
The word "head" (śiras) is used because the deity is preeminent;
with the utterance "svāhā," all objects of sense are offered to the deity.
The state of being the very nature [of the deity] is for the *śikhā*, and *vaṣaṭ* is also said for that;
the pervasiveness of the deity is designated as the *kavaca*.
The pervasive splendor of the deity is manifested by the syllable *hūṃ*;
by the word "eye" (*netra*), the state of being manifest is revealed for the God.
At that very moment, the warding off [of obstacles] was declared by the sound of the mantra *vauṣaṭ*;
the burning energy [of destruction] is said to be expressed by the word *phaṭ*.
He who, having understood the meaning of the mantra and its application, performs the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon his limbs,
attains all his goals and is honored even by the gods.
In the Bhairavī Tantra.

The practitioner of mantra should place the six limbs either three times or once, according to the sequence; having thus performed the placement according to the rule, he should carry out the placement of the phonemes (varṇanyāsa).
100a) In the Bhairava Tantra.
Then one should perform the deposition of the phonemes (varṇanyāsa), which bestows the fruit of divine nature,
by placing the letters of the Mātṛkā together with the bindu upon the heart, the two arms, and the pair of feet.
Afterwards, one should arrange [the deities] in rows and perform the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa);
one should perform the pervasive placement with both hands while reciting the root-mantra (mūlavidyā).
Having thus performed the placement once— starting from the feet and ending at the head, and starting from the head and ending at the feet— the practitioner becomes one with that.
Also in the Vīracūḍāmaṇi:
One should place the ten syllables beginning with *a* in the heart,
and likewise the ten beginning with *e* on the right arm.
Having placed the ten syllables beginning with *ḍa* on the left arm,
one should then place the ten syllables beginning with *ṇa* on the right shank.
One should place the letters beginning with 'ma' and ending with 'kṣa' upon the left shank.
The formal application is as follows:

One should place *namaḥ* with *a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, *ḹ* upon the heart. With *e*, *ai*, *o*, *au*, *a*, *aḥ*, *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *namaḥ* upon the right arm. With *ṅa*, *ca*, *cha*, *ja*, *jha*, *ña*, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *ḍa*, *ḍha*, *namaḥ* upon the left arm. [With] *ṇa*, *ta*, *tha*, *da*...
*Dhaṃ naṃ paṃ phaṃ vaṃ bhaṃ maṃ namaḥ* on the right calf; *maṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ kṣaṃ namaḥ* on the left calf. This is the *varṇanyāsa*.
Now, because the placement of the breaths (prāṇa) is necessary here, the *prapañcanyāsa* is written out.
In the Meru Tantra.
In the arrangement of the Mātṛkā-nyāsa, on the left path of the Kaulikas, one should perform the nyāsa known as Prapañcayoga; that is now described.
In Śrīprapañca, there is Dvīpamāyā; likewise, Kamalā is in Jaladhi;
Giriviṣṇuvallabhā is in Pattana; and Padmadhāriṇī is in [Padmapura].
The daughter of the ocean is on the seat; Kṣetra, Yū, Śloka, and Mātṛkā;
likewise Vanā, Kamalavāsinī, Indrī, Rā, Cā, and Śamā.
Māgu, hetu, amāna, dyau, padma, catvaraka,
as well as nārāyaṇa, priya, abhijit, svedaja, siddhi, and lakṣmikā.
Aṃtraja, Mahālakṣmī, Jarāpūjā, and Jalakṣmī;
in the place of the vowels (svarasthāna) there are sixteen pairs, and then those born of the consonants (sparśaja).
Āryā, Alavālūtir, Māyā, Caṇḍikā, and Kalānvitā;
Kāṣṭhā, Durgā, the one called Nimeṣā, Śivā, and Aparṇikā.
Aṃvikā is indeed Ghaṭikā, and Mūhūrta is joined with Sanī;
Īśvarī is Prahara, accompanied by Divasa, O Śāṃbhavī.
Then, having established the state associated with Sarvamaṅgalā, [one should place] Īśānī, Vāpī, Sandhyā, and Pārvatī conjoined with Rātri.
Likewise, one should place ten thousand [recitations] of Dākṣāyaṇī and Vārāhaimavatī;
then, one should place the Nakṣatra together with Mahāmāyā and the Yoga.
Māheśvarī is the instrument (karaṇa), and Mṛḍānī is indeed the lunar fortnight (pakṣa);
Rudrāṇī is conjoined with the month, and Śarvāṇī is conjoined with the zodiacal sign (rāśi).
Then the supreme sovereigns are Kālī conjoined with the seasons,
Kātyāyanī conjoined with the solstices, and Gaurī conjoined with the years and the yugas.
Then, one should place Bhava and Anila in their respective positions;
Brāhmī is joined with the five elements and conjoined with the five subtle essences (tanmātras).
Then Vāgīśvarī is Speech (Vāṇī) endowed with the five organs of action;
Sāvitrī is the organ of perception, and she is both Nīlā and Sarasvatī.
Gāyatrī is endowed with qualities, Vāk is possessed of instruments,
Śāradā is joined with states, and Bhāratī is united with the primary elements.
One should place the pervasive [mantra], "She who is endowed with faults and yet beloved," following the root-vidyā preceded by the three *tāras* and followed by the letters of the *mātṛkā*.
One should say, "Obeisance to Śrī, whose form is the manifold universe (prapañca)," in due order;
thus there shall be the Prapañcanyāsa, and now the Bhuvananyāsa is described.
At the end of the root mantra consisting of three *tāra*s,
having pronounced the syllables individually along with their *anusvāra*s, one should utter the name beginning with "A-tala" and so forth.
One should utter the "place of abandonment" consisting of a hundred times ten million world-abodes;
this is the name of the Mūladevī Yoginī, as well as the Supportive Power (Ādhāraśakti).
Having uttered "Devyai namaḥ," one should assign it by placing it upon the limbs as they are recited;
as for the division of the syllables, there are three groups beginning with the letter 'a'.
In the four places joined with the half-moon, there are two in each pair of locations;
likewise, the seven classes beginning with *ka* are in the fourteenth [place].
Now, the names of the worlds are Tala, Vitala,
that which is called Sutala, Mahātala, Talātala, and Rasātala.
Pātāla, Bhūr, Bhuvas, Svar, as well as Mahar, Jana, Tapas, and Satya— whatever is said to exist in whichever place, beginning with the secret [realms].
Then, in the second [section], there is the Guhyāntala, which is exceedingly secret and inconceivable;
that is the Mahāguhya-tantra, the supreme secret foremost of all.
And the Yoginī, at the proper place, [bestows] desire, secret knowledge foremost, and secret action; thus, liberation is applied in the eighth.
The secret is Ḍākinī, and the great secret is Hākinī;
Kākinī is the great concealment, and Śākinī is the even greater concealment.
Afterwards, Śrī Hākinī is the Guptā (Secret) and Yākinī is the Mahāguptā (Greatly Secret).
Then, in sequence, the limbs are the two feet, the two ankles, the two calves, and the two knees.
The thighs, the secret place, the *mūlādhāra*, the *svādhiṣṭhāna*,
the navel, the heart, the throat, the nose, the forehead, and the *brahmaraṃdhra*— these are the locations in successive order.
At the end of the root mantra, preceded by the three stars (oṃ āḥ hūṃ), one should utter "bhuvaṃ" fourteen times;
then, one should perform the heart-pervading placement (hṛdvyāpaka-nyāsa) with "nādhipāyai," "parāṃ vāyai," and "devyai."
I shall now explain the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the forms; first, one should utter the three *praṇavas* and then recite the root mantra—this is how the placement is performed.
The fourth [syllable], joined with *namaḥ*, should be proclaimed and placed upon the limbs;
beginning with the feet (*prapadādi*) and ending with the heart (*priyānta*), it is placed on the head (*mastaka*) at the imperishable Keśava.
Nārāyaṇa is in the mouth, Mādhava on the excellent right shoulder,
Govinda is on the left together with Īśānī, and [Viṣṇu] is accompanied by Ugrā.
Viṣṇu is on the bridegroom’s right side, Madhusūdana on his left;
Ṛddhi is on the left side [of the bride], and Trivikrama on her right hip.
Rūpiṇī is on the left hip; Vāmana, having cut off his own life-force, is there;
Śrīdhara is on the right thigh, and Doṣā is situated on the left thigh.
Ekanāsā and Hṛṣīkeśa are situated on the right knee; Ekāriṇī and Padmanābha are on the left, and Ādyavatī should be at the beginning.
Then Dāmodara was born from the right shank; Vāsudeva was enjoyed [as the fruit] from the left shank.
For the sake of the Sun’s splendor, there is no luster in the mantra of the left shank.
Accompanied by Saṃkarṣaṇa on the right foot, joined with Pradyumna on the left foot,
and indeed Aniruddha joined with Adharā on the lower part.
These sixteen [syllables], preceded by the anusvāra, are to be deposited;
this is proclaimed as the ritual deposition (nyāsa) for those endowed with the power of Viṣṇu.
In the Śaivanyāsa, Bhadra and Bhava are placed on the right foot and hand;
on the left are Khaga, Vala, Aśava, Ugra, Īrimadri, and Phalaprada.
Rudra is joined on the right side, while Paśupati is remembered on the left;
likewise, Ghaṇṭādhara and Padmadhara are joined on the right arms, as is Ugraka.
On the left arm, he is accompanied by Ānanda and holds the moon;
then on the neck is Mahādeva, joined with the Bhīmachaṃda meter and the syllable *mayī*.
One should place these five in the faces, starting from the east;
Īśāna is the abode of the world, and Tatpuruṣa is the mass of water.
Aghorā and Jñānanādā, then [the one] joined with Ṭaṅkadhārā;
then Vāmadeva and the one called Sadyojāta, along with Ṭaṅkakarī and Ḍāmarī.
Then there may be the nyāsa known as Brahma: Brahmā and Pakṣiṇī on the feet;
Prajāpati and Arañjinī on the shanks; and then [the others] on the knees.
Vedhā and Lakṣmī are said to be in the pair of thighs, Parameṣṭhī and Vakriṇī in the private parts,
and Pitāmaha and Śiśudhāriṇī likewise in the secret region.
One should likewise place Vidhātṛ at the region of the navel, along with the dissolution of the six supports;
similarly, one should place Viriñci, the leader of all, in the heart.
In the same manner, one should place the Creator (Brahmā) on the throat, with a smiling face;
and likewise, one should place Lalitā and the Four-faced One (Brahmā) on the forehead.
One should place Kṣamā and Hiraṇyagarbha in the Brahma-randhra;
at the end of the root mantra preceded by the three Tārās, one should utter "Śrītrīmūti."
One should perform an all-pervading placement with reverence to the Noble Goddess Parā;
having thus performed the placement of the forms (mūrtinyāsa), one should carry out the placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa).

Having thus performed the rite of placement (nyāsa), whoever performs [rites] such as victory and the like shall not be oppressed by spirits, ghosts, people, or others, nor even by their masters. Thus it is said.
Now follows the sixfold deposition (ṣoḍhānyāsa).
This has been stated in the Vīra-tantra:
Having formed the pure alphabet (mātṛkā), one should enclose that alphabet within the *tāra* (the syllable Om).
Encased within the interior of the Mātṛkā.
The best of practitioners should place the *tāḍha* enclosed by the *mātṛkā*;
that [tāḍha] should be enclosed by the *śrī-bīja*, and that [bīja] should be enclosed by the *mātṛkā*.
One should place the Goddess enveloped by Kāma, and then place that [Kāma] enveloped by her;
likewise, one should place Śakti enveloped by Śakti, and place that [Śakti] enveloped by her.
Having again placed the pair of seed-syllables— ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, and ḹ— as before,
one should place the mantra according to the rule, both in direct and reverse order.
One should perform the pervasive [protection] one hundred and eight times with the root mantra;
thus is the sixfold limb-protection of Durgā proclaimed by Gupta.
When this supreme ritual of placement (nyāsa) for Tārā, Kālikā, Unmukhī, and likewise for the other [goddess] has been performed,
all sin is destroyed.
It removes poison and wards off death, destroys the afflictions caused by planets, and all wicked ones perish; enemies turn into friends.
The waves of his poetry are a succession of grape-juice flavors;
the eightfold supernatural powers, beginning with atomization (aṇimā), reside in his hand.
Whatever misdeed there may be— whether physical, verbal, or mental—
all of it is destroyed by reflecting upon the Nyāsa.
Whatever minor offenses there may be, they reach destruction;
whatever form is seen by whomsoever, he indeed assumes that very form.
He whom the Great Goddesses, their forms arranged in six layers, bow down to, shall immediately become short-lived; the deity trembles with fear.
The meaning is that it is encapsulated by the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*).

With "śrīṃ aṃ śrīṃ aṃ śrīṃ aṃ namaḥ," one should place [the mantra] on the forehead. With "śrīṃ āṃ grīṃ āṃ śrīṃ āṃ namaḥ," one should place it on the circumference of the face. In this manner, one should assign [the mantras] to the locations of the Mātṛkās. Likewise, with "hrīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ namaḥ," one should place [the mantra] on the forehead. In this manner, one should assign [the mantras] to the locations of the Mātṛkās. [The root mantra is] "hrāṃ."
*Hrāṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ klaṃ mūlaṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ klaṃ hrāṃ hrāṃ ṛṃ ṝṃ klaṃ mūlaṃ namaḥ*— thus [one should place it] on the forehead.
102a) One should likewise place [the syllables] at the beginning of the mouth, the conduct, and so forth.

The meaning is that, having placed the root mantra alone in the positions of the Mātṛkā both in forward and reverse order, one should perform the pervasion (vyāpaka) with the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
This has been stated in the dialogue between Hara and Gaurī:
I shall describe the sixfold nyāsa, difficult to obtain in the three worlds;
having performed which, practitioners become as desired and resemble Bhairava himself.
One should first arrange the Mātṛkā; this is remembered as the first Nyāsa. [Then one should perform] the syllable encased by Śrī, and Śrī encased by the syllable.
Having thus arranged them in sequence, the second [mantra] is proclaimed:
Lakṣmī encapsulated by Kāma, and Kāma encapsulated by Lakṣmī.
One should place [the mantra] in the locus of the Mātṛkās; this is declared to be the third [method]. One should enclose Lakṣmī with Lajjā and Hri with Śrī.

The practitioner should perform the placement as before; this is declared to be the fourth placement (nyāsa). One should place the pair of *lajjā* (hrīṃ hrīṃ) mounted upon the circle of the mouth (*mukhavṛtta*), followed by the pair of *namaḥ*.
Having placed Kāma upon the crescent moon and established him in the position of Śakra,
one should enclose the mantra within that enclosure using the root syllables.
One should perform this placement according to the stated method; it consists of five types of placement, performed solely in the locations of the letters both in direct and reverse order.
Having placed the root [syllable], [one recites] Medhā.
One hundred and eight times, root-ward.
This sixth placement (nyāsa), performed upon the body after recitation and expansion, is proclaimed;
this is declared to be the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa) of the Kālikāmata-rāja.
Thus, one who possesses the mantras and is equal to Bhairava should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa);
he is Hara, he is Hari, and he is the Goddess herself—of this there is no doubt.
One should perform this ritual placement (nyāsa) for Tārā and likewise for Unmukhī;
such a person shall become a lord of the eight supernatural powers, beginning with atomization (aṇimā).
Now follows the secret sixfold deposition (guhya-ṣoḍhā-nyāsa).
This has been stated in the Rudrayāmala:
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim this secret Sixfold [Rite], O Beloved;
this must not be revealed anywhere, if one desires what is beneficial for oneself.

O Pārvatī, one should place the syllable *kapūra* enclosed by the letters of the Mātṛkā in the location of the Mātṛkā; one should then install each letter here, likewise enclosed by that very [syllable].
O Goddess, the pair of *kūrca* seeds should be carefully placed;
likewise, O Goddess, one should place the *śakti* seed at the beginning, followed by the root mantra.
On the right, one should place the three previous seed-syllables beginning with Kālikā;
O Goddess, [then] two Kūrca seeds and again two Lañjā seeds.
Likewise, O Goddess, the conjoined [seed-syllable] with Vahni (Ra) and Yaya (Sa) should be placed;
then, having placed all that, O Deity, as the pervasive one.
The sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa) has been taught here for this twenty-two-syllable mantra;
it bestows success in this world as well as among the gods and the asuras.
Daily practice must necessarily be performed; neither worship nor recitation [is required otherwise].
Even when these are performed, the excellent practitioner becomes equal to Mahādeva.
Thus, this certain secret has been told to you regarding Ghoradākṣiṇī;
it must never be disclosed, whether among the gods or among men.
Karpūra and the other two seed-syllables are the root of Mātṛkā, beginning from the first letter, the letter 'A'.
Now follows the assignment of the principles (tattvanyāsa).
In the Svatantra Tantra.
One who knows the Self should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the reality of the auspicious principles (tattvas).
The meaning is that one should perform the nyāsa from the heart up to the head with the mantra "Oṃ, salutation to the Ātmatattva," beginning at the base (mūla) and ending at the crown (akhaṇḍa).
Now follows the deposition of the seed-syllables (bīja).
In the Kumārī-tantra:

One should place the seven seed-syllables in the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head), between the eyebrows, on the forehead, at the region of the navel, in the private parts, in the mouth, and on all the limbs.
Now follows the placement of the mantra syllables (mantravarṇanyāsa).
In the Vīrabhadra Tantra:
On the head, the eyes, the forehead, the pair of eyebrows, the ears and cheeks, the face, the teeth, the tongue, the region of the shoulders, and the throat;
One should place the mantra-syllables on the arms, heart, both sides, back, navel, Rudra (the genitals), waist, anus, hands, and feet, and everywhere else.
In Rudra, in the *liṅga*, everywhere, and in the entire body; as stated in the *Triśaktiratna*:
On the crown of the head, on the two cheeks, on the two eyes, likewise on the two ears,
again on the pair of nostrils, and likewise on the pair of lips;
One should place the syllables upon the two teeth, between the eyebrows, at the heart, in the secret region,
on the pair of arms, on the pair of feet, and on all the limbs.
In the ritual of placement (nyāsa), the sequence for the pair [of hands] should be understood as beginning with the left; thus the order has been stated.
In the independent tantra.
O Dear One, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa) nine times with the root mantra.
In the Bhairava Tantra.
One should cause [the mantra] to pervade [the body] fivefold, or ninefold, or likewise sevenfold by means of the root mantra; this is the remainder [of the sense].
In the *Kumārīkalpa*.
Then he should assume the appearance of a woman, with his forehead marked by vermilion,
enriched by the glow of erotic ornaments, and his mouth filled with betel.
In this same manner, one should cause all things, such as the dress and so forth, to be made for Venitā as well.

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the rites beginning with the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) up to the pervasion (vyāpaka), as well as the ritual placements (nyāsa) and so forth mentioned in the fifth sacrifice, are indicated.
103a) After that, the placement of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa) follows: the Foundation (ādhāra) preceded by Śakti,
as well as Prakṛti, Kamaṭha, Śeṣa, and likewise the Earth.
The ocean of nectar, the island of jewels, the wish-fulfilling gem as a house,
the cremation ground, the Pārijāta tree, and at its base, a jeweled altar.
The preeminent practitioner should place a pedestal upon that upper mandala,
and in the four directions, the sages, the gods, corpses, and severed heads.
O Maheśvarī, having placed Dharma and the others, as well as Adharma and the others, upon the four limbs and body parts, one should likewise place the lotus, the sun, and the moon in the heart.
Having likewise placed Vaiśvānara, as well as sattva, rajas, and tamas,
within the self, one should place the Śaktis in the lotus of the heart.

One should place Dharma and the others on the two shoulders and the two thighs; Adharma and the others on the mouth, the left side, the navel, and the right side, in clockwise order. By the word "ātman," the fourfold set consisting of Ātman, Antarātman, Jñānātman, and Paramātman is meant.
The Śaktis, as well as the Pīṭha-Śaktis.
In the Jñānārṇava.
She is Will, Knowledge, and Action; she is the Desirous One who bestows desires;
she is Rati, the beloved of Rati, and Bliss; she is Manonmanī within the pericarp.
Having first uttered the Vāgbhava [syllable],
immediately thereafter [the words] "to Parā," "to Aparā," and "to Parāparā" should be spoken, followed by "Hsauṃ."
Then, "Sadāśiva-mahāpreta-ṅentam" and "Padmāsanam," followed by "Namaḥ"— this is declared to be the mantra for the seat-consecration (pīṭhanyāsa).
In the Bhairava Tantra.
Then one should perform the worship of the seats (pīṭhapūjā) with the nine principal śaktis:
Ugrā, Ugrā, Caṇḍā, Cāmuṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā, Vikaṭā, and Utkaṭā.
Saṃkaṭā, Caṇḍogrā, and likewise Maṅgalacaṇḍikā—
thus it is said that these nine Śaktis are to be worshipped in the eight directions and in the center.
The seat-powers (pīṭha-śaktis) of the seat-mantra are the same here as they are for Tārā.
Thus is the opinion of Vīracūḍāmaṇi.
Herein is the praise of the ritual placement (nyāsa).
In the Kulaprakāśa.
The wise declare that reciting the *virāj* mantra without the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) is demonic and fruitless;
having become one with it through placement, and having become a deity, one should then recite it.
In the Meru Tantra.
He who constantly performs the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the path taught in the scriptures attains the state of the deity, and the perfection of mantra arises.
O Dear One, when one who is protected by the armor of the nyāsa recites the mantra,
the obstacles flee upon seeing him, just as elephants flee upon seeing a lion.
That fool who attempts to achieve victory without first performing the various ritual depositions (nyāsa) will certainly be overcome by obstacles, just as a young deer is by tigers.
103b) Due to the abundance of ritual applications (*nyāsa*), the fruits [thereof] are also manifold.
One should not abandon the previously mentioned application; rather, one may perform further [applications] according to one's desire.
In the *Kumārīkalpa*.
In this way, one should contemplate the chosen deity upon the seat consisting of the body.
In that regard, there is this distinction in the *Svatantra-tantra*:
Then, through meditation on the Kāmakalā, one should invoke the auspicious Kālikā and,
with flowers and the gesture known as kūrma-mudrā, cause her to be established in the center of the wheel.
"Having invoked" means having caused [the deity] to drink the nectar of emission (visargāmṛta) and having brought [him], in the form of Kuṇḍalinī, into the heart.

"In the center of the wheel" means within the eight-petaled lotus situated at the heart, specifically in its pericarp (*karṇikā*). This refers to the meditation on *Kāmakalā* as described in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*.
The face has the form of a crescent moon, and below it is a pair of breasts,
filled with the nectar of all knowledge and bestowing the power of all speech.
Accomplishing all aims and causing the delight of all people,
beneath that is the supreme half (parārdha), with its well-adorned mandala.
He is the essence of all gods and others, saluted by all the gods;
he is completely full of delight for all and the one who brings about the welfare of all.
This meditation on the *kāmakalā* accomplishes all aims, brings all the gods under control, and sets [all things] in motion; it is to be kept strictly secret by the most excellent practitioners.
One should join the index finger of the left hand with the little finger of the right,
and likewise join the thumb of the left hand with the index finger of the right.
One should raise the right thumb and place the middle and other fingers of the left hand upon the back of the right hand.
One should perform [the offering] with the left hand using the *pitṛtīrtha*, with the middle and ring fingers likewise; these should be turned downward from the right hand.
In this manner, the Karakacchapa bestows all accomplishments;
one should close both eyes and bring [the deity] near to the heart.
Holding the body, head, and neck straight, the wise practitioner of mantra, being most steady,
should begin meditation, which destroys all sins.
In the Meru Tantra:
Then the practitioner of mantra should perform meditation according to the path described for that specific auspicious time;
that too is said to be of two kinds: with attributes (saguṇa) and likewise without attributes (nirguṇa).
Within the lotus of one's own heart, the pericarp and filaments blaze;
it is in full bloom, resplendent with the mandalas of the Moon, Sun, and Fire.
There, one should [worship] one's own chosen deity as taught in the scriptures and through recitation.
Meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa-dhyāna) is as described in that very same [text].
The realization that "I am He," which is the oneness of the individual soul and Brahman—
that alone is known by the knowers of Brahman as meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa).
Thus, that which is with mental activity (avadana) is indeed called meditation with qualities (saguṇa-dhyāna).
That meditation is as described in the Svatantra-tantra.
104a) Now I shall describe the meditation on the Goddess, who is adorned by all the deities—
the auspicious Goddess whose face is formidable and who resembles a mountain of collyrium.
She is strewn with a garland of severed heads, has loosened locks and a smiling face;
she stands upon the lotus-heart of Mahākāla, possessing full breasts.
She who delights in the perverse, who is intent [on her purpose], whose fangs are terrible, who indeed has Śiva as her companion,
who wears a snake as a sacred thread, and who has the crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
Adorned with every ornament and embellished with pearls and gems,
she has a thousand dead hands bound as her girdle and is clad in the directions as her garment.
She is resplendent with thousands of millions of Śivās and Yoginīs;
her lotus-like faces are filled with blood, and she promotes the drinking of wine.
She has eyes like fire, the sun, and the moon; her face quivers with redness;
and she has made earrings for her ears from two young fawns whose shoulder-blades have fallen away.
In the Phetkārī-tantra and the Kālī-tantra.
One should meditate upon the divine Kālikā of the South— terrible, with a formidable forest-like appearance, her hair disheveled, four-armed, and adorned with a garland of severed heads.
Her left upper and lower hands hold a freshly severed head and a sword,
while her right upper and lower hands display the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons.
She has the luster of a great cloud, is dark-complexioned, and likewise naked;
she has a garland of severed heads suspended from her neck, smeared with dripping blood.
She who is terrifying with a pair of corpses used as ear-ornaments,
possessing formidable fangs and a gaping mouth, and endowed with full, elevated breasts.
Her girdle fashioned from clusters of corpses, her face grinning with laughter,
and her countenance flashing with streams of blood flowing from her two breasts.
She is of terrible form, exceedingly fierce, dwelling in the cremation ground at the time of dissolution;
she has protruding teeth, extends to the south, and her mass of hair hangs down loose.
O Mahādeva in the form of Śava, she who is seated upon your heart and surrounded on the four sides by Śivās of terrible roar.
And she was seated with Mahākāla, overcome with passion;
her face was serene and her eyes were bright, her lotus-like countenance beaming with a smile.
Thus, one should contemplate Kālī, who dwells in the abode of the cremation ground.
When the hymn to Mahākāla has been performed.

The visualization of the hands is described as follows: in the upper left hand is a sword, and likewise in the lower left hand is a severed head; in the right hands are the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting.
In the Bhairavī Tantra, however, meditation is described in a different manner.
Terrible with her hands, face, and feet, with disheveled hair and four arms.
She is dark-hued, divine, adorned with a garland of severed heads, and receives sacrificial fees.
With her two upper lotus-hands holding a sword and a freshly severed head,
and her two lower lotus-hands granting fearlessness and the boon of boons.
She has the radiance of a great cloud, is slender, and likewise naked; she has a garland of severed heads hanging from her neck, smeared with dripping blood.
She had led the ears of the virtuous to serve as her earrings; she was terrifying with a pair of skulls, possessed formidable fangs and a gaping mouth, and had full, elevated breasts.
Her limbs adorned with every ornament, she who liberates from all that is inauspicious,
she who resides upon the heart of Mahādeva in the form of a corpse.
She was surrounded on all four sides by auspicious jackals of terrifying howls,
and together with Mahākāla, she was intent upon the pleasures of inverted union.

Therefore, in this meditation on the hand (*hastadhyāna*), there is only conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); there is no assumption of syntactic unity through the explanation of the meaning of the words, because there is no decisive evidence (*vinigamaka*) [for such a connection].
"In the Merutantra, the specific distinction is that she is joined with Mahākāla and is intent on embracing a corpse."
In the meditation on the hand.
Holding in her hands a sword, the gestures of fearlessness and generosity, and a severed head.
But in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*, however:
It is said that she was adorned with ears [shaped like] arrows joined with the feathers of spears.
Therein, the arrow-dhyāna is in the upper part of the ear.
But in the place of the father, however.
"One who has removed [the flowers] from two young horses and made them ear-ornaments"—
this very statement of Svatantra is what should be meditated upon, and not a conceptual construction.
In the Bhairava Tantra.
There, one should meditate upon the goddess Kālikā, known as Dakṣiṇā, who is resplendent,
with disheveled hair, most terrifying, with a formidable countenance, and auspicious.
Terrible, four-armed, and divine, she is adorned with a garland of severed heads;
in her two left hands, held one above the other, she holds a sword and a recently severed head.
The wise one should meditate upon her who grants fearlessness and boons with her pair of right hands,
dark as a fresh rain-cloud and resembling a mass of crushed collyrium.
Adorned with skulls as ornaments for her neck and smeared with blood dripping from them,
she was terrifying with a pair of human corpses as her earrings, making a dreadful sound.
Clad in the directions, with a formidable face and full, elevated breasts,
she wears a girdle fashioned from a multitude of recently severed hands, her face breaking into a laugh.
One should worship the Goddess who dwells in the cremation ground, whose face is radiant with streams of blood dripping from her two breasts, and who is terrifying to behold.

In the term *ghoravāṇa*, *vāṇa* means an arrow; it has gone upward (*ūrdhvagata*) from Karna (the ear), situated upon a pair of corpses (*śavadvandva*), serving as the position for the ear-ornament (*tāṭaṅka*).
But in the Vīracūḍāmaṇi:
Then one should perform meditation upon the Supreme Goddess in the heart-cakra—
terrible, with a face like a crow's, her hair disheveled, and possessing four arms.
One should worship the divine Cāmuṇḍā of the south, adorned with a garland of severed heads,
her lotus-like hands holding a sword raised upward in the right and a freshly severed head held downward in the left.
She displays the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons with her right hands;
she possesses the radiance of a great cloud, is dark-complexioned, naked, and adorned with a head-ornament.
She is smeared with blood dripping from the garland of severed heads suspended around her neck;
she has leaf-patterns as ear-ornaments and is terrifying to the pair of Śiva and Śivā.
She had terrible fangs and was formidable, with full and elevated breasts;
she wore a girdle made from a multitude of corpses and had a laughing face.
Her face is made radiant by streams of blood flowing from her two corners of the mouth;
she is of terrible form, exceedingly fierce, and dwells in the cremation ground.
Mahārudra, dwelling in the cremation ground, is Mahākāla, naked as the directions;
he holds a skull and a flaying knife in his left hands, and a trident and a khaṭvāṅga staff in his right hands.
Though his limbs were adorned with serpents, he was decorated with ashes, bones, and jewels;
he stood in the midst of a blazing fire, established within a bed of ashes.
There, having performed the inverted sexual union upon the heart,
one should consume what is to be drunk, chewed, and sucked, while gazing at one another.
Thus one should worship the Goddess with devotion; all perfections are thereby produced.
In the Kumārī Tantra:
In this manner, he should worship according to the prescribed rite with mental enjoyments, with perfumes, flowers, and lamps, as well as with wine accompanied by sacrificial offerings.
Then, O Bhairava, one should perform mental recitation (japa), as well as fire-offerings (homa) and so forth;
having thus paid homage and offered praise, one should then perform the external sacrifice.
Now follows the inner sacrifice.
This has been stated in the Rudrayāmala:
Now I shall describe the internal sacrifice (antaryajana), which bestows both visible and invisible fruits,
by means of which the yogis always become wise and self-controlled men.
The wise one should perform meditation on the Guru as before;
thereafter, he should perform his ablutions for the sake of attaining Being-Consciousness-Bliss.
One should bathe in the pure sacred ford of Puṣkara, which resides within the heart;
if a man bathes in Vindutīrtha, rebirth is no longer found.

Having raised Kuṇḍalinī from the Mūlādhāra and caused the nectar of the moon at the forehead of Sadāśiva to flow, the bathing consists of the flooding of the Binducakra and the flooding of the Anāhatacakra; this is the meaning. Alternatively, in this body where the Iḍā and Suṣumnā—acting as the Śiva-tīrtha—flow, full of the water of knowledge, one bathes with the waters of Brahman within those two.
"What need has he of even the waters of the Gaṅgā or of Puṣkara? Thus concludes the section on bathing.
The time at which the union of Śiva and Śakti occurs is proclaimed as the *saṃdhyā* by those established in the *kula* who abide in meditative absorption.
Thus concludes the twilight ritual (saṃdhyā).

Having raised Kuṇḍalinī, who consists of the forms of the moon, sun, and fire, from the Mūlādhāra, one should pierce the Supreme Bindu and satisfy the deity of the body with the nectar arising therefrom.
This has been stated in the *Navaratneśvara*:
With that divine nectar which has flowed forth from the union of the moon, sun, and fire,
one should satisfy the Supreme Deity.
Having filled with the essence of the digits (kalāsāra) that supreme lunar vessel situated below the aperture of Brahma (brahmaraṃdhra), one should satisfy the Khecarī [with it].
Thus ends the libation.

The one of pure intellect should perform the perfection of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) by placing [the letters] in the support (the *ādhāra*), the *liṅga*, the navel, the heart-lotus, the root of the palate, the forehead, the two petals, the sixteen-spoked [wheel], the twenty-two, the ten-petaled [wheel], the half of twelve, and the four; then at the end of the abode, in the middle of the hair, together with the throat and the base of the throat, the vowels, and *ha* and *kṣa* in the middle of the bow.
For the sake of accomplishment. Thus ends the internal Mātṛkā-nyāsa. Now follows the internal Ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa. However, in the *Gotamīya*, it is stated as follows:
Resembling a thousand-spoked jewel, adorned with all colors,
enriched with three lines beginning with the letter 'A', and beautified by three hundred thousand [deities].
In the center of that, one should meditate with a concentrated mind upon the supreme bindu, which consists of creation, maintenance, and dissolution; this is the internal ritual placement (nyāsa).
One should meditate upon the Bindu, whose nature is consciousness, from the base (mūlādhāra) up to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra);
satisfying the Mātṛkā-syllables with the essence of nectar flowing from that Bindu.
Pronouncing each syllable individually from the *mūlādhāra* to the space between the eyebrows,
ending with "namaḥ"— this is proclaimed as the internal placement (*nyāsa*).
Of Gotamī.
Being meditated upon by the heart, this self, which consists of consciousness and is the essence of the heart,
is thereafter rendered focused upon that [Supreme] by means of the *hṛn-mantra*.

The Guru, through ritual action, removes the objects of the senses from the Supreme Self— which is the nature of pure consciousness and exalted with qualities such as omniscience— by means of the mantra placed upon the head.
The teachers perform a firm visualization of the dissolution of one's own body into the abode of consciousness in the form of the heart and head, using the Śikhā-mantra.

For the body whose essence is mantra, a protective armor is fashioned on all sides by means of the mantra's external splendor; thus, there is protection and concealment from every direction through the mantra.
That which bestows supreme knowledge within the Supreme Self, whose nature is consciousness, is the splendor consisting of the heart and so forth; it is designated as the "eye."
It destroys the internal and other forms of the practitioner;
that mantra is the net of ignorance, proclaimed as the supreme abode.
I am the unconditioned conventional reality, characterized by being inviolable.
Now, meditation.
By Udayākara and Paddhaya.
One should meditate on the reality consisting of light, situated within the cavity of two powers and known as the pair of lotuses, through the application of the *kula* and *akula*.
Furthermore: 106a) [The following:]
Situated between two śṛgāṭas and enclosed by a pair of śaktis,
that which is eternally in a state of equal flavor (samarasa) is the object of meditation for the yogins of that Kula.
In the Meru Tantra:
Abiding in the rays, situated in the fire, and positioned between the moon and the sun,
the king of yogis remains full, having brought about dissolution in the great void.
The great void is the aperture of Brahma.
Likewise.
That radiance which arises in the void state that is without support—that is the supreme, eternal, and non-existent; for this indeed is the meditation of yogins.
One should contemplate that which resides within the heart as "Gaṅgarbha" (the Womb of Gaṅgā);
the realization that "I am He," which is the unity of the individual soul and Brahman, is that [contemplation].
The knowers of the Vedas understand that very state to be meditation devoid of qualities (nirguṇa-dhyāna).
Thus ends the section on meditative absorption.
Now, the worship.
One should worship with various kinds of flowers; at that very moment, one becomes identical with that.
Also elsewhere.
Through the state of identification with that [deity] and the realization "I am He," one should worship with a mind free from deceit,
egoism, passion, and pride.
The wise know the ten flowers to be non-delusion, non-hypocrisy, non-hatred, non-agitation, non-envy, and non-greed.
Non-violence is the supreme flower; the restraint of the senses is a flower;
compassion is a flower; forgiveness is a flower; and knowledge is the fifth flower.
With these aforementioned supreme flowers, one should worship the Supreme Deity.
Thus ends the worship.
In the Mātṛkā-ārṇava.
The fifty-fold garland is proclaimed as the power of the thread, whose essence is Śiva;
the Kuṇḍalinī power is strung together, and at the end of the Kalās, she is established upon Meru.
Thus is the recitation.
Now follows the fire-oblation (homa).

One should offer oblations into the fire of consciousness (cidagni) in its center— blazing with the fuel of latent impressions (vāsanā)— within that square cit-kuṇḍa which consists of the Self, the Inner Self, and the Supreme Self, which has bliss as its girdle, is composed of the half-measure (ardhamātrā), and is adorned by the Yoni.
This has been stated in the Candrikā and other works.
In the triangle situated at the mūlādhāra, which is a blazing cauldron for the fire of the deity and is endowed with dharma and adharma, one should proceed with the root mantra.
The wise person should offer oblations one by one, saying "I offer, svāhā!"—
offering as the sacrificial oblation the ego-sense, untruth, backbiting, lust, anger, and so forth.
The mind alone is said to be the sacrificial ladle (śruva), and the state beyond the mind (unmanī) is declared to be the offering-spoon (sruc).
Furthermore, other matters should be understood from another tantra.
In this case, at the end of the root [verse].
In the fire of consciousness at the navel, kindled by knowledge, I perpetually offer the activities of the senses as oblations with the ladle of the mind.
"svāhā"—this is the first oblation.
At the end of the root.

106b) With the mind as the ladle, I perpetually offer the oblations of merit and demerit into the fire of the self, which is kindled by them, through the channel of the *suṣumṇā* while the senses remain withdrawn from their objects.
"svāhā" is the second offering.
At the end of the root.
Supporting the *unmanī* ladle with my hands of light and space,
I offer into the fire that which is filled with the oil of the digits of merit and demerit.
"svāhā" is the third oblation.
At the end of the root [mantra].
Into the fire of consciousness— which blazes forth without internal fuel or external cause, which completely dispels the darkness of illusion,
and which is the ground for the unfolding of certain wondrous rays— I offer the entire universe, from the earth up to the ether.
The fourth oblation is with "svāhā."
Having performed this internal sacrifice, one becomes directly composed of Brahman;
for such a person, there are neither sins nor merits, and he certainly becomes liberated while living.
In the Kumārīkalpa.
He should indeed worship these according to the prescribed rite with mental enjoyments, with perfumes, flowers, and lamps, and with wine accompanied by the *āvali* offering.
Then indeed, one should perform mental recitation (japa) as well as the fire-oblation (homa) and so forth;
having likewise offered salutations and performed praise, one should then carry out the external sacrifice.
Thus concludes the internal sacrifice.
Now, the Āryā verses as stated in the Merutantra:
