Now I shall describe the internal purification (antaryarjana); comprehend it exactly as it is. Having drawn up the left channel (vāmanāḍī), one should slightly contract the anus.
One should recite by means of the equal path, cause the tongue to reach the palate,
join the *śakti* with the state of *Śiva*, and slightly contract [the anus] below.
Having performed this, the knower of mantras should worship the pedestal by means of the path of ritual placement (nyāsa);
upon that pedestal, he should worship his chosen deity in a formal anthropomorphic form.
Having meditated, one should worship with mental offerings beginning with sandalwood paste and ending with food;
at the time of eating, however, one should perform the internal Vaiśvadeva rite.
Egoism, truthfulness, backbiting, desire, anger, and so forth are the oblation;
the mind alone is said to be the sacrificial ladle, and Suṣumṇā is declared to be the sacrificial spoon.
At the conclusion of that, having become one with it (tanmaya), one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times;
all of that should be offered to the deity for the sake of attaining all prosperity.
Then, having prostrated before the Guru, one should draw forth the circle of worship (pūjācakra).
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Kulamuktikallolinī composed by Śrī Ādyānanda.
Now follows the Hiraṇyagarbha sacrifice.

Since it has been stated that "having thus disposed the body, one should draw the king of yantras," in this [author's] view, the construction of the yantra occurs prior to the ritual placement (nyāsa); thus, there is no contradiction with the statement beginning with "having thus disposed."
In the Bhairava Tantra.
Then, one should draw the yantra in a vessel made of gold or other precious materials and smeared with red sandalwood paste.
The self-arisen one, being pure, should likewise [draw the mark] with a brush of red sandalwood or a golden stylus, using either flowers or red [pigment].
Or, in this context, the word "vā" (or) functions as a restrictive option; thus, with that animal, [the ground] should be smeared with red sandalwood.
The meaning is that the hero, being self-arisen, should himself draw the yantra smeared with flowers.
In the Muṇḍamālā:
In a copper vessel, or in a skull, or in one made from wood from a cremation ground;
or on a Saturday or a Tuesday, or when a corpse has appeared in the body.
Likewise, a disc made of gold, silver, or iron should be worshipped according to the prescribed rite.
Here too, the injunction regarding the skull and so forth is intended for the Vīra; it is the same here as well. But in the *Svatantra*, however:
Having thus arranged [the deities] within the body, one should draw the King of Wheels (cakrarāja) on gold,
silver, copper, stone, or the eight metals.
In the Rudrayāmala.
On wheels made of gold, silver, copper, crystal, or even wood,
the Goddess should be worshipped by the best of men according to the prescribed ritual.
For crystal and other substances of stable form, even a mere line or a yantra is highly recommended.
In the *Sārasaṃgraha*:
In copper it lasts for twelve years, but in crystal and other materials it lasts forever;
among these, crystal shall indeed bestow all accomplishments.
In another tantra:
O beloved, it may last for as long as one lives when made of gold; twenty-two years when made of silver;
twelve years when made of copper; and half of that [six years] when made of birch bark.
In the Rudrayāmala.
Having taken one tola, two tolas, three tolas, four tolas,
or as much as he desires, a man incurs sin.
Likewise.
It is said that [the merit] is a hundred-thousandfold when offered in copper, and it becomes ten-millionfold in silver;
in gold, it yields infinite fruit—so what need is there to speak of [offerings made with] jewels and the like?
O beloved, [one should place it] in a yantra fashioned from coral,
or from ruby, or from sapphire, or from cat's-eye, or even from crystal or emerald.
One certainly obtains wealth, sons, as well as a wife and fame.
In the ocean of jewels.
The golden fish should be one finger-breadth [in size], and likewise the silver one;
those of copper should be of the aforementioned measurements, while for rubies and other gems, it may be according to one's desire.
In the Gaurīyamala:
Indeed, here there are fourfold arrays of the wheel;
the earth-tortoise, the lotus-array, and likewise Mount Meru are of that same nature.
The conjunction of downward lines has been described by me in the *bhū-prastāra*;
in the *kūrma-padmaka-prastāra*, the upward line has been described by me.
In the Sautrāmaṇī Tantra.
Straight lines indicate prosperity, while curved lines indicate poverty.
In the Meru Tantra:
Kings become submissive when [the yantra] is fashioned on a seat made of gold;
a yantra made of silver bestows long life, freedom from disease, and the fulfillment of desires.
A yantra fashioned from copper is considered bestower of all sovereignty;
a yantra made of clear crystal grants the heart's desired objects.
A yantra fashioned from rubies bestows sovereignty as well as worldly enjoyment and liberation;
a yantra made of emeralds destroys all enemies.
The yantra produced from the three metals is considered the seat of all sovereignty;
the crystal yantra, however, is transparent and bestows whatever the mind desires.
A yantra fashioned from rubies bestows sovereignty as well as worldly enjoyment and liberation;
a yantra made of coral destroys all enemies.
A yantra produced from the three metals is considered to bestow all accomplishments;
sandalwood is known to grant peace, while red sandalwood provides nourishment.
The seat made of śrīparṇī wood is prescribed for worship; it bestows wealth and sovereignty.
On a seat of vaidruma wood there is abundant prosperity, and on a seat of birch bark (bhūrjapatra) there are four-footed animals.
On the Bhavapāṣāṇa rock by the Gaṇḍakī river, enjoyment and liberation are not far off;
a mark fashioned on the ground with vermilion powder grants all desires.
If one makes [a footprint] in lead, bell-metal, or similar materials, it destroys one's progeny;
one should never place it on a wooden plank or on a wall.
If it is established by a Mahā [planet], it shall destroy that person's family and wealth.
In the Bhairava Tantra.
Within the triangle of Śakti and Agni, one should draw a hexagon and therein three Śaktis;
then an eight-petalled lotus on the ground, provided with four gates.
Having thus constructed the yantra, he should place a flower in front of it.
The Śakti is a downward-facing triangle and Agni is an upward-facing triangle; by these, a hexagon is formed, in the center of which are three downward-facing triangles—thus it is perfected.
In the Kumārīkalpa.
Having first inscribed a triangle, one should inscribe another triangle outside of it;
having drawn a triangle outside that, one should then draw a hexagon outside.
In the center, however, is the Vaindava-cakra adorned with the seed-syllable and Māyā;
outside of that is a six-cornered [figure], then a lotus, and it is joined with a single enclosure of earth (bhūpura).
Having understood this, one attains liberation; of this there is no doubt.
In the Svatantra Tantra.
With this application of fragrances, one should draw the *yonicakra*;
then one should fashion two *yoni*s, and after that, a hexagon.
Then, [one should visualize] the eight-petaled ground provided with four gates;
this wheel has been described to you, and here one should scatter a handful of flowers.
In the Kālītantra:
Having first inscribed a triangle, one should place another triangle outside of it;
then the practitioner of mantra should indeed draw three excellent triangles.
Then, having drawn a circle, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus;
having drawn another circle according to the rule, one should draw a single square enclosure.
Also in the Nīlatantra:
Having drawn the five powers (pañcaśakti), characterized by downward-facing faces.
In the noble lineage.
Afterwards, one should inscribe a triangle, and again another triangle;
then a nine-cornered figure there, and in its center, one should place Śivā.
In the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*.
Having first inscribed the primordial Śakti, one should then inscribe two further Śaktis;
having inscribed the Fire-Śakti, one should differentiate the External-Śakti.
By the very sequence of piercing the knots, one should cause the fire to expand downward;
by the very sequence of piercing the knots, one should also pierce upward through the power (*śakti*).
By means of the division of the upward fire, one should divide the fire below;
three [divisions] belong to Śakti and two to Vahni—this is called the Southern Yantra.

In this *Bhairavatantra*, according to the *Kumārīkalpa* and the *Svatantramata*, it takes the form of three downward-facing triangles situated within a hexagon. According to the *Kālitantra* and *Nīlatantra*, it consists of five downward-facing triangles. According to the *Kulasadbhāvamata*, it takes the form of the nine-yoni wheel (*navayonicakra*), wherein the worship of Bālā is prescribed in the center of a hexagon.

According to the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*, the central wheel (*madhyacakra*) consists of two downward-facing triangles and three upward-facing triangles; thus, it is described as being "liberated" (*mukta*). Some, however, fearing the occurrence of eight defects—as stated in the passage: "By postulating the abandonment of validity and invalidity, and by the loss and non-abandonment of [the original state], there would likewise be eight defects"—[avoid this].

According to the inherent sense of the Merutantra, Vīracūḍāmaṇi states that for those who have broken their tantric commitments, there is a downward-facing orientation, and its purpose lies solely in the form of the five downward-pointing triangles.
First, five triangles, then an eight-petalled lotus at their front, and a square enclosure with four gates; this is declared to be the worship yantra.
In the *Kumārīkalpa*.
One should engrave this [diagram] upon a copper plate smeared with kuṇḍagola,
adorned with self-arisen flowers, and treated with saffron and aguru.
In the Svatantra [Tantra].
Self-arisen flower, that which arises from the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa*, *rocanā*, *guru*, saffron,
musk, wine, and sandalwood from the Malaya mountains.
This fragrance has been fully described as one that is always dear to Caṇḍikā;
with this combination of fragrances, one should draw the *yonicakra*.
As for the mantra for drawing the yantra, it is stated in the Merutantra:
"Āḥ surekha vajrarekhe hūṃ phaṭ svāhā"—
with this mantra, one should draw a beautiful lotus diagram.
And in this regard, it is said in the Kulārṇava:
The practitioner must never bend the yantra at night;
if it is bent through negligence, he shall incur the curse of the deity.
In the Siddheśvarī Tantra:
O Goddess, O Sovereign of the Gods, having established [the deity] before him upon an auspicious seat,
the practitioner should offer a handful of flowers there with the root mantra.
O Goddess, O lady of excellent complexion, one should install the Cakra on a cloth produced from *śrīkhaṇḍa*, red *śrīkhaṇḍa*, or *śrīparṇī*, and not on any other.
In the Matsya-sūkta.
While the mantra has not yet been released, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus with a six-cornered pericarp,
adorned with circles and the four gates.
In the independent [tantra].
Having thus drawn the yantra, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Regarding the term *bhūtaśuddhi*, since the word *bhūta* signifies the number five, it means the purification of the five *makāras*.
In the Kumārī-tantra: 108b).
One should place [the deity] before oneself upon a pure seat, which is strewn with self-arisen flowers, reddened with saffron, and unseen by ordinary beings.
The Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā.
And because it has been stated: "On the stones of the Gaṇḍakī, enjoyment and liberation are not far off."
And in this regard, regarding yantras, images, and so forth, other [points] have also been stated in the Merutantra for fear of the defects that will be described hereafter.
When [the image] is broken, cracked, burnt, fallen, devoid of its measurements, mutilated,
touched by unworthy persons, or has fallen upon impure grounds;
The gods do not grant their presence in these ten cases: when a mantra has been worshipped by another, or when it has been defiled by the touch of a fallen person.
The worship of Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, and Īśa, as well as Devī, is performed in sequence;
these ten locations have been established for the purpose of worshipping the deities.
The presence of all the deities will certainly reside within the mantra;
for the mantra is said to be like the soul, while the image and other such objects are like the body.
Even when the collection of causal factors is complete, the fruit is indeed not attained without the mantra—
whether it be in a Śiva-linga, a gem, a yantra, a śāligrāma, a water-pot, or the sun.
One should perform worship on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), in the fire, on the head, or in the region of the heart;
worship performed upon the bare ground destroys one's sons, longevity, and wealth.

Regarding the question of why there is worship of the head of the Śālagrāma here, he says that it is because worship on a stone marked with the syllable *Hnām* is also highly praised for Mahākālikā; and in connection with that, the origin of the Śālagrāma is written right there.
Ishvara said:
Listen to the most wonderful account of the origin of the Śāligrāma as told by the Gaṇḍakī; O my deity, you have indeed been propitiated by me.
All those [gods] always desire to grant happiness to their sons through birth;
yet by her ascetic penance, Kṛṣṇa, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara [were moved].
Ready to grant a boon, she chose to become his son;
unable to grant that boon, they were then cursed by her in anger.
"Because you repeatedly committed deception against me, you have entered the wombs of insects; for they cursed you in their anger."
"O you who have fled while practicing penance, we were cursed by you without due reflection;
therefore, as a result of that karma, become a dark river, Jāhnavī."
Hearing this mutual deception, a great tumultuous outcry arose;
the gods were shaken and they reported it to Brahmā.
"Indeed, due to the great curse resulting from the mutual fall [of the weapons] out of anger, [the world would be destroyed].
Having heard these words of the gods, Brahmā spoke to Śaṅkara.
Śiva said to the Creator: "I am the agent of dissolution;
you are the creator of the universe and the protector Viṣṇu, most endowed with intelligence."
"He should be questioned so that happiness may arise for both of us without fear.
Having heard these words of Maheśvara, Viṣṇu spoke.
Listen, O Brahman Mahādeva; listen, O Goddess Gajānana!
Here, my two attendants, the Brāhmaṇas Grāha and Mātaṅga, are the lords of the quarters.
I shall effect the liberation of those two when their bodies have become decayed;
then, those things produced from their fat and marrow will perish.
"Insects dwelling within stones shall become known as 'vajras';
this very day, the meritorious Gaṇḍakī, a great river equal to the Gaṅgā, shall come forth."
May she be the one who pleases all the gods and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
and may those stones which are contained within her be deities.
"May all [of you], except for the portion belonging to the earthly king, become insects within the diamond;
by this very act, you shall also attain the status of sons to the Gaṇḍakī."
At the end of that time, there will be a sign arising from that deity;
having recognized it, they shall worship it, and that deity will be pleased with them.
Neither from the worship of a mechanical image, nor a sculpted idol, nor even a tree,
does satisfaction arise for them as it does from the worship of the Gaṇḍakī stones.
Having heard these words of Viṣṇu, Brahmā spoke this speech:
"O Viṣṇu, what kind of stone is to be worshipped, and which one is dear to whom according to its marks?"
"What is the fruit, who is the qualified seeker, and by what path? Tell me that.
Having heard these words of Brahmā, Viṣṇu spoke these words.
A stone of one's own caste and character should be worshipped by Brahmins and others for the attainment of happiness;
a smooth stone brings success in mantras, while a rough one causes failure.
Green garments bestow fame, while those washed black with charcoal take away reputation;
white garments pacify distress, whereas soiled ones produce a sinful mind.
Yellow [smoke] bestows the fruit of sons; the color of the Arka flower brings daughters; blue bestows fortune; and smoke-colored smoke grants liberation from rebirth.
The red-colored one bestows disease; the vermilion-hued one brings great strife;
the crooked one causes poverty; and she who is even (straight) accomplishes all goals.
The gross [faults] destroy longevity, while the subtle ones bring about a premature death.
The fruit of worship is for one marked by the *yoni*; the fruit is for one marked by the *yoni*; [but] the fruit is without the *lāñchana*.
The Kapilā cow causes mental instability, while the Karvurā causes eye disease;
the Vahucakrā should be known as one that destroys both broken things and those who do not break. The Mānatā cow brings about pride.
One that lacks other characteristic marks brings about separation from one's wife;
one with a large mouth destroys the family; and one with a large wheel takes away one's sons.
A wheel that is stuck brings unhappiness; one with a loose wheel causes great disease;
one with a broken wheel leads to poverty; and one turned upside down results in total destruction.
The Vyālamukhī [vein], being uneven and various in its course, produces many disorders such as skin diseases (kuṣṭha) and the like,
through its distorted windings.
The cutting off of the lineage of householders arises from the Narasiṃhī [lineage];
a curved line brings suffering, while according to its subtlety, there is happiness.
Just as there is Lakṣmī, so too listen to the distinctions of the one possessing Lakṣmī (Kṣmīmat).
(109b) He who possesses Lakṣmī is to be known as Hari; wherever there is a lotus, there is a discus.
Or, he who possesses only a garland of forest flowers and grants the desires of householders— Vāsudeva is to be recognized by him, in whose door there is a pair of discs.
Whether continuous or even uniform, white in color, and destroying sins—that is to be known as Saṃkarṣaṇa; and it should have a pair of discs at the front.
Attached to the front portion, it is large, red, and very beautiful;
Pradyumna has a subtle wheel, and its aperture is long and variegated.
Yellow [sandalwood] grants one's desires, though it has many internal cavities and is hollow within.
Aniruddha, however, is blue-hued, circular, and exceedingly beautiful;
it has two lines on its surface and is marked with a lotus.
That [diagram] should be known as Keśava; it consists of either one or two [circles], with the weapon-wheel (astracakra) facing eastward, and being four-cornered, it brings good fortune.
Nārāyaṇa is dark-complexioned, has a prominent discus at the navel,
is endowed with long lines, and possesses a broad cavity on the right side.
That stone slab which has the form of Hari, whose face is turned upwards,
and whose door appears like that of Hari, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
He who is marked with a lotus and a discus should be known as Parameṣṭhin;
he is shaped like a bilva fruit, white in luster, and possesses a very large, pleasant back.
Viṣṇu, however, should be black in color; on his chest are two very beautiful discs, and likewise, a line is seen above the door in the middle region.
The Narasiṃha [mark] is tawny, with broad wheels and a large mouth;
there should be three or five drops, but not for householders.
Kapila Narasiṃha, however, should resemble molasses and lac;
he has two large wheels in the center and a very beautiful line at the entrance.
The Great Narasiṃha is to be known as endowed with the characteristics previously mentioned;
his lines are shaped like manes, and his face is long and terrifying.
Lakṣmīnṛsiṃha is to be known as having four discs and three dots;
he is endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics and is resplendent with a garland of forest flowers.
This is Vārāha; it is marked with a trident, a linga, and a discus, and likewise possesses uneven [proportions];
it is radiant like a sapphire and should be adorned with three lines.
That earth, named Vārāhī, is a stone in the form of a boar;
it is curved, marked with a single circular line, and bestows sovereignty upon those who attain it.
That stone is to be known as Matsyākhyā when it is adorned with three dots;
resembling bell-metal in appearance yet possessing the luster of gold, and being elongated, it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The stone known as Kūrma, however, should be circular and elevated on its surface;
it possesses a green color and is marked with the Kaustubha gem.
That stone which is shaped like a tortoise should be known as the Kūrma;
likewise, one that is circular and marked with a discus, when worshipped, bestows the supreme state.
110a) Hayagrīva’s [lineage] has lines shaped like kusha grass near the wheel;
the back is marked with many dots and is as dark as a rain cloud.
O gentle one, that Hayagrīva should be known;
the Hayagrīva stone is characterized by a long line, and the line joined with lines would be like this.
He whose face has the form of a horse should be known as Hayaśīrṣa;
alternatively, his head may be in the shape of a lotus, likewise accompanied by a rosary.
Vaikuṇṭha has the luster of a white lotus, possesses a single discus as well as a banner,
and above his necklace there is a beautiful line in the form of a mark of worship.
Śrīdhara, likewise, O God, is marked with a forest garland;
he has the appearance of a kadamba flower and is adorned with five lines.
That which is dwarfish, triangular, circular, resembling the flower of the linseed plant (atasī), and adorned with a central dot (bindu) should be known as Vāmana.
Named Dadhivāmana, it is joined with wheels above and below;
possessing great luster and being very short in stature, it bestows abundance and security.
Likewise, Sudarśana is dark-complexioned and of great splendor;
on its left side are the mace and the discus, while there is but a single line on the right.
That which is named Sahasrārjuna consists of various lines;
it is shaped like a wheel with three spokes, and it bestows lost wealth.
He whose broad Dāmodara line has a wheel established in its center,
who is dark-green like Durvā grass, thick at the base, and marked with yellow lines, is a bestower of wealth.
Āmodara is to be known from the south-east; it possesses upper and lower wheels and is not excessively long-mouthed. With a hanging line in the middle, it bestows enjoyment.
He who is marked with two discs is to be known as Dāmodara;
he should have a subtle opening, and when worshipped, he always bestows happiness.
It should be infinite and of many colors, marked by the coils of a serpent,
intersected by numerous wheels, and the bestower of the fruits of all desires.
He whose faces are seen in all directions, intermediate points, and above, is named Puruṣottama; he is the bestower of the fruits of the goals of human existence.
He whose crest bears the Liṅga should be known as the Lord of Yoga;
he is the destroyer of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and the bestower of the perfections of yoga.
Padmanabha, who is likewise red in complexion and endowed with a lotus-umbrella,
when worshipped daily with Tulasī, shall cause even a poor man to become a lord.
It has rays of flame, a golden mouth, the luster of the moon, and resembles crystal;
or else it is born marked with streaks of gold.
That which is to be known as Garuḍa has two wings in the middle;
a very long line is seen there, and it is the destroyer of snake venom.
He on whose belly there are four distinct and clearly visible discs is to be known as Janārdana; he brings satisfaction to the ancestors.
110b) Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is to be known as having his chest marked by a forest garland (vanamālā),
possessing a subtle door and four wheels, and bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
He should be known as Hṛṣīkeśa, dark-complexioned and of great luster;
he has a pair of discs on his left side, while there is a single line on the right.
Kṛṣṇa is to be known by a black stone, whether it bears a discus or is without a discus,
marked with a clockwise spiral and adorned with a forest garland.
He should be known as four-faced; two wheels are situated in the middle region, and there are four side-lines on each flank; he is the bestower of the Vedas, the Shastras, and the Agamas.

These are declared to be the manifestations (bhedas) of Viṣṇu; one should cause Hari to enter right here [into the image], and at the conclusion of the worship, one should perform the dismissal (visarjana), but one should not perform the formal installation (pratiṣṭhā) here.
Śāligrāmas should be worshipped equally; there is no distinction between them. However, those that are unequal are indeed worshipped differently, for one is considered most worthy of worship.
A person who constantly worships the twelve Śilās with devotion experiences an increase in righteousness and the destruction of sins day by day.
That man who, with devotion, worships a hundred Śālagrāmas for a hundred days achieves his desires and attains perfection.
Listen now to the characteristics of those whose very nature is the Śāligrāma;
by the service of which one’s desired goals are attained both in this world and the next.
He should be known as Śivanābha; having assumed the form of a liṅga, he possesses the shape of a self-manifested (svayaṃbhū) liṅga and is the bestower of the attainment of mantras.
He who is adorned with three drops (bindus) is to be known as Traiyambaka;
likewise, a line in the form of a trident bestows the state of having transcended manhood.
He on whom three lines resembling matted locks (jaṭā) are clearly visible should be known as Dhūrjaṭi; when worshipped, he bestows knowledge.
Śambhu should be known as pale white, while the bindu at the top of the head is black;
the radiant Vilvapumān, when worshipped, brings women under one's control.
Īśvara is to be known as *matu*; the red *vindu* is at the top.
It may have one wheel or two wheels, and the footprint of the cow is below within it.
He should be known as Mṛtyuñjaya (the Conqueror of Death), the destroyer of even the slightest death.
Below is the discus, above it is a white line, and [above that] is the trident.
That which is named Candraśekhara is shaped like a crescent moon;
in its center are two wheels, and from its worship comes the destruction of disease.
He alone should be known as Rudra, with his head anointed by Kapila;
a line should be drawn in the center of the wheel to destroy the lineage of enemies.
Now I shall describe the Śāligrāmas, which originate from the Śaktikīṭa;
by worshipping them, the goddess Bhavānī becomes well-pleased.
In the Śrīvidyā Sātala, a parasol is seen above the wheel;
her head is marked with a water-pot externally, she is glossy and dark-complexioned, and she grants all desires.
She who is endowed with these marks should be known as Mahākālī;
she is rough, thick, and flat-nosed, and one should worship her by way of the left path.
Vārāhī, however, is endowed with the mark of a boar’s face;
she is bathed with the blood of sacrificial offerings and should eat that [victim] for the sake of the evening rite.
All stone slabs that have two holes and so forth, and those marked with a triangle, as well as those whose shape is upward-pointing like a weapon— therein one should designate the Goddess.
One should worship that goddess Śilā, who possesses the discus, by means of the right-hand path;
when worshipped by means of the left-hand path, she brings happiness in both worlds.
One should worship that goddess who is wheel-less on the left side as Śilā;
she must not be touched by Brahmins, nor should she cause agitation in the assembly.
O gods, in the Kali age, the solar stone (saurīśilā) is generally very difficult to find;
it should have the luster of crystal and releases water when heated by the sun.
When fire is placed upon Tulasī, she, having been consecrated, causes it to rain down;
a false oath made while standing upon her brings about leprosy.
He who is marked by his own trunk (śuṇḍā) is to be known as Gaṇeśa;
or even a stone in the shape of a trunk, or one resembling the face of an elephant.
The stone whose middle circle and subtle circle are in a particular direction—that is the direction for that [stone]; it should be worshipped in that direction, as it bestows sovereignty.
Where two fragments are seen in the shape of a half-moon, [that is the sign].
That moonstone which is triangular is considered a Mars stone;
O Goddess, a Mercury stone is to be known by its arrow-shaped mark.
A heavy stone slab that is long and square is considered suitable for Jupiter;
one that is five-cornered is for Venus, and one shaped like a bow is for Mars.
The form of Rohiṇī shall be that of the sun, while that of Kaṭu shall be the shape of a banner;
this occurs when the terrible Kali age has arrived, characterized by the mixture of left-hand practices.
In a land crowded with barbarians who disregard the distinction between what is fit and unfit to be eaten,
pervaded by lust, anger, and other passions, and utterly conquered by women;
Where is the disciple, where is the guru, where is the mantra, where is the recitation, and where are the spiritual accomplishments?
When ten thousand years of the Kali age have passed, Viṣṇu will abandon this earth, which is like a stone.
Half of that is the water of the Ganges, and half of that is the deity-stones;

With perfumes, flowers, fresh incense, lamps, food offerings, and mirrors.

Having performed this for three days, one should thereafter practice the daily Tryakrama.

The application of the yantra is also called *upanaya*.
One who follows the path of the Vedas should not commit great sin like a beast;
Agni is pure and most observant of vows, and the Brahmin is pure as proclaimed in the Śruti.
They are tainted by minor sins born of ignorance that are destroyed by the performance of the twilight prayers; therefore, they are remembered as mere beasts.
The yantra held in the left hand is intended for their field of vision;
that causes agitation in the deity, and the practitioner becomes distracted.
This yantra, worshipped with ritual fees (dakṣiṇā), possesses a splendor equal to the sun and fire;

Just as everyone beholds the rising sun when it is positioned by Dakṣa, so too does the meritorious soul behold that which is established by name.

likewise, for the gods, both the left and right hands are paths.
The preeminence belongs to women in the left limb and to men in the right limb;
likewise, there is a path for both, distinguished by what is to be done and what is not to be done.
A Brahmin should perform the rite of fire-transference (agnyuttāraṇa) using mantras prescribed in the Āyurveda,

In the hymn "Agniḥ saptim vājam," which consists of seven verses, the subject is called Sapti;

Reciting this hymn, which is devoid of the word "agni," one hundred times,

Just as wood is purified by means of fragrant pastes and the like, and gems and such by water alone,

Having worshipped the weapon-mantra in the cardinal directions, one should install the conch-vessel;
for without a vessel there is no preservation, and the Mothers are not satisfied.
Therefore, according to the prescribed rule, the support should be made of metal, consisting of three or four parts,

Having said, "At the end of the root mantra, I establish the vessel that is the support for [the deity] Vāmuka," one should then place the conch and other supporting vessels within the mandala.
Having said "Maṃraṃ dharmaprade," one should speak that which consists of ten kalās;

Then, having uttered "Obeisance to the support of the argha vessel," one should worship it;

And then, with the weapon-mantra (astramantra).
Constructed from gold and other such materials.
Then, having washed the vessel for the *arghya* offering and so forth with water consecrated by the *vāṇamantra*, [one says]:
"I establish the *arghya* vessel for such-and-such deity."
Having spoken thus, one should establish [the mantra] upon that support and speak again as follows:
"O bestower of wealth, twelvefold; O you whose self is the *kalā*s. Then one should say:
One should worship the name of the deity, "Sūryamaṇḍalamucāṅenta," with this mantra, saying "Salutation to the Argha-vessel."
Then, one should visualize that very vessel as the ground mandala;
there, one should worship the six limbs as before.
The twelve digits (kalās) of the sun are said to be for the circumambulation of the vessel;
then, reciting the Mātṛkā at the end of the root mantra, [one should perform the rite] with waters consisting of nectar.
The worshipper should fill it in reverse order with this mantra:
"O you who grant desires, ṅeṃ saṃ, sixteenfold, O self of the Kalās."
"Obeisance to the fifteen [deities] of the ocean"— this mantra is for filling the conch shell with scents,
flowers, unbroken rice, barley, tips of kuśa grass, sesame seeds, and mustard seeds.
O gods, *dūrvā* grass is said to be one of the eight substances for the arghya vessel;
having offered water along with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should worship and honor them.
Then, having performed the installation even for the sixteen parts (kalās) including the moon within all the parts,
and having offered flowers and so forth with the arghapātra vessel,
one should display the Gālinī-mudrā, the Dhenu-mudrā, and the Amṛtīkaraṇa-mudrā.
112b) Having meditated there upon one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), having performed the worship of the six limbs and the binding of the directions,
having displayed the conch mudrā and covered [the vessel] with the fish mudrā, one should recite the root mantra eight times; this is the argha.
Then, at the conclusion of the worship, the practitioner should perform the ritual installation (sthāpana) for the arghya water and the consecration of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā).
As before, having invoked the Tīrtha there with the root mantra,
having joined it [with the deity], and having placed a flower with the Netra-mantra, one should perform the rite with the Śikhā-mantra.
Having displayed the Gālinī mudrā and the mudrā known as Dhenusamjñā,
the practitioner, according to the prescribed rule, renders [the offering] nectarine by means of the seed-syllable of Sudhā.
Having meditated upon one's chosen deity there, if the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa is to be performed;
"By means of the placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and by the weapon-mantra (*astra*), etc."
To the north of the seat, one should place the vessels for the water for the feet, the water for sipping, the honey-mixture, and so forth.
This, however, is useful for the right-hand path; I shall explain the special *argha* offering for the left-hand practitioners (*vāmin*) to you hereafter.

Having consecrated the articles of worship with the root mantra and the weapon-mantra according to the prescribed rule, one should display the dhenu-mudrā; this is proclaimed as the purification of the substances.

Buttermilk, milk, jaggery, honey, curd, ghee, sesame seeds, sugar, oil, and marrow— these are recorded as the ten types of substances.
In the Meru Tantra:

Having installed the deity upon the pedestal and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should sprinkle it with the water of the arghya offering while reciting the root mantra; then, one should display the dīpanī mudrā three times.

Having thus performed the purification of the deity (*devaśuddhi*), one should thereafter perform the purification of the world (*jagatśuddhi*); this concludes the purification of the deity. The *Dīpanī* should be recited first. Now, the specific purification (*viśeṣaśuddhi*): the purification of the Kula-substances and the Śaktis should be recited first. *Oṃ pratadviṣṇustavate vīryeṇa nago na bhīmaḥ kucarogaviṣṭāḥ | yasyoruṣu triṣu...* [etc.]
One should purify the flesh with the mantra: "In their strides, they have pervaded all the worlds."

One should employ the mantra "Prataviṣṇu" for the purification of meat, according to the scriptural injunction. One should purify the fish with the mantra: "Oṃ, we worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of nourishment; may he deliver me from death as a cucumber from its stem—may I not be separated from immortality. This [mantra] belongs to Tryambaka.

According to the statement, "One should perform the purification of the fish with the mantra," [one should do so]. With these two mantras— *oṃ tadviṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padaṃ sadā paśyanti sūrayaḥ divīva cakṣurātataṃ tad viprāso vipanyavo jāgṛvāṃsaḥ samindhate viṣṇoryat paramaṃ padam*— [one should form] the mudrā.
One should purify.

May Tvaṣṭṛ, while fashioning, adorn the forms.

It should be made of rice, circular in shape, resembling the orb of the moon,

One should perform the libation with mantras in the water.

In the Meru Tantra.

Datura seed, vijayā, jasmine leaf and fruit,
as well as akārakara, O child, and nāga equal in measure to khākhasa.
Having crushed liquor and a portion of *bhogavṛddhā*,
this drop, known as *aśvagandhā*, is dear to the deity.

therefore, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with Vijayā, or with liquids, or otherwise, in their absence.

The definition of that [tallakṣaṇa] is stated in another tantra:
Since this was fashioned by Viśvakarman from the gods using portions taken from each of them, it is therefore called a *kalaśa*.
But according to Pādapadmācārya, "kalaśa" means that which is surrounded by *kalās*. He states the measurement of the *kalaśa* as follows; it is stated in the Svatantra itself:
The height of the pitchers shall be twelve finger-breadths when they span fifty finger-breadths in width;
likewise, the mouth of the pitchers shall be eight finger-breadths.

In the mandala and the flask, there is the substance consisting of the orbs of fire, sun, and moon.
The word "should worship" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
The term "square" (caturasraka) is an indicator for the mandala as previously described.
In the Tantra:
With the mantra "yoni dvayaṃ ha," one should place there a jar adorned with red garlands, made of gold or other materials according to one's means.
O practitioner of mantra, one should visualize the solar disc here as endowed with twelve digits (kalās),
and fill it with the pure root mantra as the cause.
One should meditate here upon the lunar disc, perfected with its sixteen digits;
one should protect it with the weapon-mantra and veil it with the armor-mantra.
The practitioner of the rite should gaze [upon it] with that very root mantra and sprinkle it;
having worshipped it thoroughly with perfumes and other offerings, he should contemplate it as being of the nature of the deity.
The practitioner of mantra should worship the triad of images with three *tāra* portions; "with three *tāra* portions" means with the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*.
Now follows the ritual application.

To one's left, having drawn a triangle within a hexagon, along with a bindu, and having constructed an outer circle and square, one should sprinkle it with the water of the general *arghya* and worship it, saying: "Obeisance to the Support-Energy (*ādhāra-śakti*) and the others. Then, having washed the support (*ādhāra*) with "Obeisance," and having placed it upon the mandala, [one worships] the fire-mandala (*vahnimaṇḍala*) with "Oṃ, obeisance to the fire-mandala."

Having worshipped with "Obeisance to the one whose self consists of ten kalās," and having rinsed [the vessel] with "phaṭ," one should establish the *ādhāra* (base) with red cloth, red garlands, and so forth, perceiving it as the Goddess. Then, having worshipped with "Obeisance to the solar orb (*arka-maṇḍala*) whose self consists of twelve kalās," one should recite the reverse *mātṛkā* and the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) while using the *kāraṇa* [vessel].
Having filled the *kalaśa* with the substances, one should worship it with: "Oṃ, obeisance to the lunar disc consisting of sixteen digits.

Then, having protected it with "Phaṭ," veiled it with the *avaguṇṭhana-mudrā* while reciting "Hūṃ," inspected it with the root mantra, sprinkled it profusely with "Namaḥ," and having taken the scented water three times with the root mantra, one should place a flower in the *kalaśa*.
One should perform the drinking of the curse. By virtue of this context, the preparation of liquor is also explained.
In the Meru-tantra:
Having boiled twelve *prasthas* of water with four *prasthas* of rice until it is reduced to half a *prastha* of rice,
one should prepare sprouts of that same quantity.
Having placed it for two days in a place free from cold and other such elements,
one should afterwards set it upon the fire and cook it until it resembles charcoal.
One should place a *prastha* of rice grains and a corresponding amount of sprouts;
having left them for two days, one should arrange it in this same manner again.
Having taken half of that, one should pour it into rice grains;
having done this again three times, that rice is known as *surā*.
This alone would be Soma, the bestower of the fruit of the Soma sacrifice;
the sacrifice of the *dūtī* would be the sacrifice, and that is traditionally known as the drinking of Soma.
That goal which is attained by the Kaulikas through the Soma sacrifice becomes, for the Vāmins,
both worldly enjoyment and heaven without any hardship.
In this way, that which is prepared from barley flour is known as *devasoma*;
when barley is combined with rice, it is called *śaktisoma*.
The fumes of *kuddī* and *aga*, combined with *samakiśva*,
are placed for twelve days and then matured in *vāruṇī*.

That liquor, known as Sūrya, which causes the intoxication of the Yoginīs, should be drunk at the end of the worship of that cakra, or it may be offered during recitation; thus it bestows the fruit [of the practice].
This very leaf, prepared in three ways along with wine, becomes fire;
by drinking it, one obtains the fruit of the Agnihotra sacrifice.
When fire is placed within the apparatus seven times with the Vāruṇī [mantra],
it becomes known as Vaḍavānala, the consumer of great sins.
115a) Ten *prasthas* of jaggery are prescribed, as well as an equal amount of *śūlajātu*;
one part of *jaṃbu* bark, one part of *pātakī*, and half that amount of *puṣpa* and coconut [products].
The flower should be half of that, and half of that again is the harītakī;
indeed, the bhītaka is said to be that much, and the three pungents (kaṭutraya) should be a fourth part.
At that time, one should take twelve parts of jaggery from that *citraka* and thoroughly rotate it with the hand in both forward and reverse directions.

By means of one hundred and eight revolutions at the three junctions of the day every day, the cooking shall be completed with a twelfth part; thus the Vāruṇī [mercury] should be cooked while situated in the yantra.
This is renowned as Gauḍī, which produces great intoxication and is highly esteemed;
it was created by Śiva in the past and drunk by the Bhairavas themselves.
One should add double the amount of water called *makaranda* to the jaggery;
after sixteen days, it becomes ready. The rest is as previously stated.
This is beloved by all the gods and is a wondrous means of subjugation;
even the powers of the gods are brought under control, so what need be said of human women?
[The ingredients are] *harītakī*, *citraka*, black pepper (*marica*), and likewise *dhātakī*.
One part each of madhūka flowers and honey, not increased [in quantity], mixed with eighty parts of jaggery; the remainder is as previously stated.
This captivating substance is the supreme drink for the Yoginīs;
O gods, in the absence of wine, I shall describe a drop that is superior even to wine.
One should take buffalo curd mixed with fourteen parts of liquor,
as well as the juice of ripe, crushed plantain fruit.
One-fourth part of the "ocean of the graspable" (grāhyodadhi) should be ground together and placed in a jar within a mire thick with lotuses for forty-eight days.
Having placed it [in a vessel] and covered it with solar rays, one should thoroughly dry it;
when it reaches the state of being like a piece of wood, then one should prepare the *kṣubhā* pill.
One should place that vessel into a handful of water filled with *guñjā* seeds;
this is declared to be even more excellent than [giving] gold to Brahmins.
Surā is traditionally said to be of three kinds: that distilled from molasses (gauḍī), that from honey (mādhvī), and that from flour (paiṣṭī).
This [last-mentioned kind] is permitted for Śūdras, but forbidden for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.
This divine liquor is drunk by Brahmans, gods, and Kaulika Brahmins;
it does not cause them intoxication, for it increases their wisdom.
If the latent impression of liquor should arise from the mouth of a Brahmin, he should be cast out like a Caṇḍāla; he is not a Kaulika who merely wears the [Kaula] garb.
The deities reside in the mouths of the Vāmins and the Kaulikas;
they carry that fragrance, and he who perceives it is worthy of being known even by Hari himself.
He in whose mouth the deity does not reside is indeed a caṇḍāla.
Liquor made from flour (paiṣṭī) bestows all perfections, while that made from molasses (gauḍī) grants worldly enjoyment.
The honey-wine (*mādhvī*) is known as the bestower of liberation; the wine of grapes (*rājā*) is said to grant sovereignty;
the sugarcane wine (*aikṣavī*) bestows knowledge; the date-palm wine (*khārjurī*) destroys enemies.
The *tālaja* [bead] is praised for immobilization (*staṃbhana*), while the one known as *apanasa* bestows auspiciousness;
that produced from coconut grants prosperity, and the *vaṃjā* destroys diseases.
The honey-derived [milk] bestows knowledge, while that from the *aireya* plant destroys diseases;
it is blissful, appetizing, fragrant, and captivating to the mind.
That supreme liquor is the deity that brings delight to the gods;
Brahmā resides in its liquid, Viṣṇu in its fragrance, and Rudra in its luster.
The Supreme Self resides in that bliss; therefore, O beloved, this [wine] should be consumed, for it is well-refined and removes the diseases of the gods, as well as suffering, calamity, and fear.
It increases longevity, prosperity, fame, enjoyment, and the knowledge of the Dharma;
otherwise, both the giver and the consumer go to hell—of this there is no doubt.
Intoxicating liquor is unwholesome; it brings about quarrels, disease, and suffering.
It destroys longevity, prosperity, fame, good fortune, virtue, and knowledge.
Therefore, having consecrated the family substance according to the rules, one should then worship it;
without the preliminary consecration of the substance, one should neither recite nor perform the victory rite.
For those who remember Mahāmukha, there is suffering at every step;
for there is no liquor without mantra, and no mantra without liquor.
Therefore, one should perform its purification; this is the implied meaning.
In the *Kulāmṛtadīpikā*.
Having seen her, he first bowed down to that form of the Vāruṇī-kalā.
In the Guhyasiddhi Tantra.
The goddess renowned as Vāruṇī was not honored by Varuṇa;
because the gods drink her constantly, she is known by the name "Sura" (the intoxicating one).
She who is eternally worshipped by Madana is proclaimed as Madyadayā;
in the ultimate sense, she is proclaimed as the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) who has arisen.
Having offered a flower with the *tāra* mantra, one should sprinkle it with water from the *astra* mantra;
having offered unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) with the *nārāca* mantra, one should protect the navel at the end of the root mantra.
Having released [the semen] from the *śukranāpa*, one should purify it with the *pavamāna* mantra;
one should dry it with the *vāyu* mantra and subsequently heat it with fire.
Above that, O Goddess of Devas, the practitioner of mantra should visualize the solar orb upon the sun with the solar mantra,
while mentally reciting the Vāruṇī mantra.
One should contemplate a stream of nectar falling from the sun onto the moon,
while reciting the seed-syllable of Soma, ending with *Hāṃ* and the crescent moon, consisting of pure ambrosia.
The practitioner of mantra should fill the vessel with the prescribed *dhenumudrā* and recite the *amṛta* mantra seven times while forming the *kūrmamudrā*.
Then, having led [the disciple] to the state of immortality, one should seat him with camphor and other substances;
having raised him slightly and placed him in another vessel, one should cast fire [into it].
O Goddess of the gods, one should demonstrate the Yonimudrā according to its true nature as Vidyā; thereafter, one should meditate upon the Goddess there, who consists of all beings.
Having brought that [consciousness] into unity with oneself, one should join it with the Great Self;
thereafter, one should contemplate the self as consisting of all beings.
That form is the form of the deity; the solar mantra is "Haṃsa. It is "amāmayī," consisting of nectar (*amṛtamayī*). The lunar seed-syllable is "Sa.
That which ends with *ha* is the letter *ha*; the union with the half-moon occurs within the letter *ha* itself. Thus (116a).

"Thus, 'I am He' (so'ham) is established. Now the Amṛtā Kūrma-mudrā will be described. One should cast the fire [into the vessel]; the Vidyā residing in another vessel is, in its true nature (tatvena), the Vidyā. By the mantra, 'In its true nature, I purify the subtle body, svāhā,' one should, as before, raise Kuṇḍalinī—who consists of all beings—and unite her with Śiva, and [unite] oneself."
The meaning is that one should meditate on [the self] as consisting of all beings. The mantras for liberation from Śukra’s curse have been stated.
In the Kumārī Tantra:
Listen to something else, O Goddess of gods, regarding the rites of the Kula and so forth.
No loss occurs for those who know; indeed, O beloved, listen to the mantras.
The Supreme Brahman alone is eternal, consisting of both the gross and the subtle;
by that [Brahman], I destroy the sin of killing a Brahmin born of my own mental fluctuations.
O Goddess, born from the solar disc, arisen from the abode of Varuṇa,
consisting of the seed-syllable Amā, may she be liberated from the white [stain].
If the *praṇava* is the seed of the Vedas and consists of the bliss of Brahman,
by that truth, O Goddess, may she remove the sin of killing a Brahmin from you.
Having thus consecrated the auspicious food with these three mantras, one should indeed offer it to the body of the deity and take it into one's own stomach as an offering.
The method for release from the curse is at the end of the Tārārṇava.
O fair-faced one, having first extracted the Praṇava, take the seed-syllable of the Moon (Om),
conjoined with the six long vowels and endowed with the Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā.
Then, one should offer salutations to Surādevī, who was liberated from the curse of Śukra;
for the sake of release from Śukra’s curse, one should recite the mantra twelve times.
But in the commentary:
Salutations to you, O Goddess Sudhā, who have been liberated from the curse of Śukra, and who are differentiated by the six long vowels beginning with 'A' and ending with 'U'.
It is said that one should recite the mantra twelve times for the sake of liberation from the curse of Śukra.
Therefore, between these two methods of liberation from Śukra’s curse, which serve the same purpose and are equally effective, there can be no option; rather, their combination is possible.
There is also a specific distinction regarding this in the Merutantra.
The young girl, who had been transformed into three colors by Māyā and Ramā, was awakened;
she was released from Śukra’s curse and once again possessed that same complexion.
The mantra of sixteen syllables, encased by the seed-syllable of that [goddess] whose worship is performed, is known as such; it should be recited one hundred and eight times.
It renders the sādhya free from curses, making it the sole vessel for both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Then, by reciting ten times the mantra: *oṃ vāṃ vīṃ vuṃ vaiṃ vauṃ vaḥ brahmaśāpavimocikāyai surādevyai namaḥ*, there is liberation from the curse of Brahmā. *hrīṃ śrīṃ āṃ krāṃ krīṃ krūṃ kraiṃ krauṃ kraḥ suro kṛṣṇapāpaṃ mocaya | amṛtaṃ srāvaya srāvaya* (O Goddess Surā, release me from the sin of Kṛṣṇa; cause nectar to flow, cause it to flow).
By reciting "svāhā" twelve times, one should effect liberation from black sins. Thus it has been said:
Salutations to the Goddess Sudhā, who liberates one from the curse of Brahmā, and whose seed-mantra is the syllable *va* (the first of the Vedas) modified by the six long vowels.
One should recite the mantra ten times for liberation from the curse of Brahmā;
[the mantra consists of] Māyā (Hrīṃ), Śrī (Śrīṃ), and Aṅkuśa (Kroṃ), differentiated by the six long vowels.
At the end of the form of Kṛṣṇa, [recite] *suro*, *pāpam*, *moca*, *tatparam*,
*amṛtam*, *srāvaya*, *dvam dvam*, and thereafter *vahnimāyaḥ*.
By means of this mantra, the practitioner shall be liberated from black sin;
Pavamāna is supreme bliss, and Pavamāna is the supreme essence.
And having written the Pavamāna mantra: "Pavamāna is supreme knowledge; by that, I purify you."
Afterwards, one should recite these verses and the mantras of Dīpanī and Amṛteśī:
"O Supreme Essence, whose nature is the sword, the partless, single-flavored digit of bliss!"
O you who manifest according to your own will, O treasure-trove whose form is nectar,
abiding in Akula, whose nature is immortality, the supreme one who brings about purity and knowledge!
For immortality is deposited in this reality, which has the nature of the moist;
having performed the touch of the hand upon that which possesses its form, it indeed becomes one with its own essential nature.
Having become deceased in the form of Parā, perform a vibration within me.
Thus it is stated in the Merutantra.
The meditation on Bhairava and Bhairavī is among the substances. This has been stated in the Tārārṇava:
Resembling ten million suns and as cool as ten million moons,
the god has eighteen arms, five faces, and three eyes.
Seated in the midst of the ocean of nectar, established upon the Brahma-lotus,
mounted upon the bull, blue-throated, and adorned with all ornaments.
The god who bears a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff, who sounds a bell and a ḍamaru drum,
who holds a noose and a goad, and who carries a mace and a club.
He holds a sword, a shield, a battle-axe, a mace, a trident, and a tusk;
he carries a variegated shield and a severed head, and utters the sounds of "Varada" (boon-granting) and "Abhaya" (fearlessness).
The best of practitioners should meditate upon Lohita, the Lord of the Gods;
having thus visualized him, he should worship with three handfuls of flowers while reciting his own mantra.
Then, one should meditate upon Ānandabhairavī, as described in that very same place.
In his embrace was the goddess Surā, possessing the splendor of ten million moons,
white as snow, jasmine, and the moon, with five faces and three eyes.
Endowed with eighteen arms, ever intent on bestowing all bliss,
smiling, large-eyed, and facing the God of gods.
Alternatively, one should worship Ardhanārīśvara, the Lord of the gods of gods.
Having meditated thus, one should worship with one's own mantra; and the two mantras are stated in the Tantra:
Śiva, Candra, and the end of Mātṛkā; likewise Akṣa, Mala, and Vahni;
and Vāyu adorned with the left ear (the letter *u*) and followed by the Bindu.
Having uttered this seed-syllable as well as Ānandabhairava ending in the letter *ṅ*,
one should write down the previous seed-syllable conjoined with the crest-mantra (*śikhāmantra*).
Having abandoned this first moon, one should place it in the ear; from the left,
one should join it with *surā* for the Goddess, and then *vauṣaṭ* for Īśānānandabhairavī.
With this pair of mantras, preceded by meditation, one should worship in the heart:

*Śiva* is the letter *ha*, *Candra* is the letter *sa*, the end of the *Mātṛkā* is the letter *kṣa*, *Vahni* is the letter *ra*, *Vāyu* is the letter *ya*, and the left ear is the letter *u*. These two [letters] should be joined with *eka* (the letter *e*), ending in the fourth case with the suffix *ṅe*.

The *śiṣā* mantra is *vauṣaṭ*. Regarding the *bhairavī* mantra, he says "the first seed-syllable" and so forth; an exchange of the first two letters must be performed. Having omitted the letter *u* from the final syllable, the letter *i*—which is the "left eye"—is to be joined.
The meaning is that this becomes the *ānandabhairavī* mantra.
Combined with the first *māyā* and joined with fire (*ra*), *māyā*, and the moon (*i*), it is uttered as "paramasvāmini"; it is the void of the supreme ether (*paramākāśaśūnya*).
"Vāhini candrapadānte sūryāgnibhakṣiṇī,
pātraṃ viśa viśa svāhā"— one should recite this mantra ten times.
Vāṅmāyā, Kamalā, Prānta, Ānandeśvarī, Vighnahā;
"We meditate upon the Goddess Sudhā"—thereafter, Nārīśvarī.
The wise person should recite the Gāyatrī ten times with the mantra "pracodayāt."
In the independent [tantra].
Then, O beloved, meditating on the substance as nectar with a red luster,
one should then recite the three syllables beginning with *kā* (kā-ā-hūṃ), adorned by three hundred thousand repetitions.
In the previously mentioned *yonimudrā*, one should contemplate the union of Śiva and Śakti as the substance of nectar; one should recite the *amṛtā* mantra eight times.
Having written the sixteen vowels in the triangle starting from "A" and so on; the sixteen consonants beginning with "Ka" in the left row;

and the sixteen consonants beginning with "Tha" in the right row; and having written the "Ha-La-Kṣa" in the center, one should raise Kuṇḍalinī according to the previously mentioned procedure, unite her with Śiva, and [receive] the stream of nectar flowing from that union.

The meaning is that, having visualized [the substance] fallen into the middle of the nostrils while inhaling, one should meditate upon the substance as nectar (*amṛta*). This is the *Amṛtā* mantra. [As stated] in the *Merutantra*:
Having uttered "aiṃ klīṃ hrauṃ juṃ saḥ," one should then speak the words: "O Amṛtā, O Source of Nectar, O Mistress of Nectar, O Showerer of Nectar."
"Amṛtaṃ srāvaya yugaṃ svāhā" is the mantra for the purification of substances, ending with "svāhā";
it is declared to consist of thirty-five syllables, beginning with "amṛte".
But in the Kulārṇava:
Having uttered "aiṃ pluṃ srauṃ juṃ saḥ svāhā," [the rest] is the same as "amṛte amṛteśvarī" and so forth.
Having consecrated it three times with the previously mentioned mantra for kindling, [one should do so] three times.
The mantra is like Mount Meru within the Dipinī.
The Vāgbhava [syllable], the pair of words "vāgvādini," the Vāgbhava again,
"klīṃ klinne kledini kledaya mahākṣobhaya"— thus it is said.
Form the pair *kuru* and the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*); form the pair *sau-mokṣa*.
Then *prāsāda* and *parā-prāsāda*: this is the thirty-seven syllabled mantra.
"Manu has declared [this] to be the illuminator."
This recitation was taught in the *Kulāmṛta* prior to the arousal of Kuṇḍalinī; therefore, it should be practiced here according to one's own tradition.
But this is the cause, O Goddess, that it is frequented by the hosts of gods;
for this very reason, its name is "Sure" (the divine) throughout the three worlds. Its fragrance is praised by Keśava, while the fragrance of the Kaulika is [praised] by the scentless.
One should worship the supreme goddess Caṇḍikā, Kālikā, and Śivā.
In the Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi, purification is described by another method as follows:
In the continuation [of the ritual], one should fill the jar with substances;
having first drawn the yantra there, whatever originates from the Kula [should be placed].
Having meditated there upon one's chosen deity, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times;
then, having visualized the *dhenu-yoni*, one should contemplate that which has issued forth from it.
Having seen the nectar nearby, the hosts of Yoginīs dance;
all the Bhairavas dance, and the hosts of Bhairavīs dance.
Whatever originates from a particular family, and whatever kind of yantra belongs to a particular deity—this is the meaning.
Having meditated thus, the supreme practitioner should recite the two vidyās,
followed at the end by "Māyā-lakṣmī-dvayasya ante namaḥ bhagavati."
O Maheśvarī, at the end of the *svarūpa*, [recite] "sarvapaśujaneti" and "namaścakṣustiraskaraṇaṃ kuru," followed by the dual form and two *ṭha* syllables.
Likewise, [one should worship] another, Tiraṣkariṇī; then Lajjādvaitamaheśvarī;
then Vāṇī; then Agni; then Tiraṣkaraṇa; and finally Sakalajaneti.
She is called Vāgvādinī and the progenitor of all those who observe the vows of the bound souls (paśu).

The mantra is: *manaśca śrotrajihvāghrāṇoktiraskaraṇaṃ kuru dvayaṃ ṭhadvayaṃ ca sa-visargaṃ śiraḥ*. (O mind, make the two ears, the tongue, the nose, and speech silent; [the syllables] "ṭha" twice, followed by the Visarga, constitute the head.)
One should recite one's own root mantra and the Varuṇa mantra seven times over that;
by this procedure, one should perform the purification of the ritual substances.
The dhenumudrā and the yonimudrā.
Furthermore, with the little fingers and ring fingers joined facing one another,
as are the index and middle fingers, this is the Dhenu-mudrā, which bestows nectar.
The middle fingers should be curved and positioned above the index fingers;
the ring fingers should be placed in the middle, and the little fingers likewise in that same position.
All [the fingers] should be joined together and pressed by the thumbs;
this is known as the Yoni-mudrā, the mother of the origin of the three worlds.
Thus it is stated in the Tantra.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Kulamuktikallolinī composed by Śrī Ādyānanda.
The ritual placement of the Arghya offering.
In the Bhairava Tantra.

One should perform the rites of offering water for honor (*arghya*) and so forth, as well as the ritual of installation (*sthāpanā*), keeping them to one's left. [These include] the water for the feet (*pādya*), the water for honor (*argha*), the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), the general water for honor (*sāmānyārgha*), and the specific water for honor (*viśeṣārgha*).
O beloved, listen to the specific rules for the *argha* offering: vessels made of iron, gold, copper, silver, or coconut shell, which take the form of the *bhaga*.
Likewise.
The middle section consists of a conch shell serving as a vessel for the heroes' drink.
Hell, the guardians of hell, the moon, and silver.
"In the middle" means: therein.
Between the object to be accomplished (sādhya) and the means of accomplishment (sādhaka), there should be thirty-six finger-breadths (aṅgulas);
twelve finger-breadths above and likewise [twelve] finger-breadths in the lower part.
The wise one should place it there, situated in the middle of twelve finger-breadths.
Likewise, a finger-breadth (aṅgula) is twelve finger-breadths; likewise.
Having abandoned twelve [fingers] for one's own sake, one should abandon twelve for the sake of the deity;
there, one should place the arghya water situated within twelve aṅgulas.
In the *Kumārikalpa*.
Then, O beautiful goddess, the practitioner of mantra should place the water-offering vessel to his left.
In the *Triśaktiratna*.
To the right of the jar, having drawn a triangle joined with a circle,
a hexagon, and a square, one should [proceed] from the center of that.
One should draw the full moon and a gandharva;
one should worship the seat beginning with the syllables *o*, *jā*, *pū*, and *kā* in its four directions.

Having worshipped the Support-Energy (Ādhāra-śakti) within the hexagon using the limb-mantras (aṅga-mantras), and likewise the Yantra-śakti according to the threefold division of the root-mantra as before;
One should place there a vessel made of a large conch, coconut, gold, silver, copper, or even mother-of-pearl.
"Vilasad" refers to the syllable *mī* of the Gandharvas; "ojāpūkādi" refers to Oḍḍiyāna, Jālandhara, Pūrṇagiri, and Kāmarūpa.
Their worship is performed on the lines of the square [maṇḍala], starting from one's own front and proceeding clockwise, according to tradition.

In the worship of the limbs (*aṅgapūjana*), the word "namaskāra" (salutation) alone should be appended at the end of all their respective mantras; however, no other class of words [such as "namaḥ"] should be used. This is because it is observed in the worship of the enclosures (*āvaraṇapūjā*) that the limbs are worshipped with mantras ending in "namaḥ. When capable, one should perform the worship of the Support-Energy (*ādhāraśakti*) within the triangle using the three divisions of the root mantra—that is, with the three sections of the root mantra—at the letter *i*.
The yantrikā is the support; its worship, consisting of ten hands, is indeed the worship of the fire.
In the Bhairava Tantra.
Having placed the beard-grass (*kūrca*) in the vessel and the sacrificial seat (*bhaga*),
he should then perform purification with [substances] produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa*, or with a *svayambhū* flower.
Having filled it with the heroic substance while reciting the root mantra, [one should proceed].
The varieties of vessels are described in the Merutantra.
[The vessels] made of coconut, gold, silver, and mother-of-pearl originating from the head;
those produced from conch, true wood, and tortoise-shell; and those made of skull, gourd, and clay.
It is proclaimed as superior, middling, or inferior according to whether it belongs to a Brahmin or other classes. One should avoid that which is too thick, too thin, cut, or split.
One should not have a vessel made from metals such as copper or bell-metal;
all success is attained through gold, while effort [is rewarded] by means of a silver vessel.

Peace is [attained] on stone; a pillar is [effective] when made of clay or coconut; subjugation and other such powers are [attained] on tortoise-shell; knowledge is [attained] on mother-of-pearl, which bestows liberation.
The rosary-bead vessel made from a sacred tree destroys sins and provides for one's livelihood;
success as a hero is attained in a skull, and the perfections of yoga are achieved in a bottle-gourd.
Whether it be made of bronze or silver, or even of conch or shell, everything—even a coconut—will surely perish.
O Maheśānī, he who gives ten million maidens as well as hundreds of gold pieces when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu;
The fruit of that [offering] is multiplied ten millionfold by means of a vessel for the coconut offering;
in the absence of such a vessel, one should worship using another vessel.
Likewise, O highly fortunate one, the vessel of a king is to be known as the most excellent.
O Goddess of beautiful hips, the vessel known as the coconut is to be understood as superior and middling;
the jewel-vessel, O lady of fair loins, is to be known as the most excellent type.
In the *Triśaktiratna*, following the word "vessel" (*pātra*).
Having worshipped as before, the practitioner should fill the conch with the substance while reciting the syllables of the root mantra in reverse order, which are intensely radiant.
Having worshipped there as before, one should draw a circle and within it a hexagon;
then, from the center of the circle, one should draw a triangle with three lines starting from the letters *a*, *ka*, and *tha*.
One should worship the triangle using three segments of the root-mantra;
then, one should worship the six limbs in the hexagon and thereafter meditate upon that which consists of the holy waters (tīrthamaya).
One should also worship Ānandabhairava, because he is indeed conjoined with his consort.
Perform worship with the five jewels; for the substance in the argha vessel, [recite]: *mlūṃ gaganarakṣāyai namaḥ*.

*mlūṃ*, obeisance to the Jewel of the Sky; *plūṃ*, obeisance to the Jewel of the Netherworld; *mlūṃ*, obeisance to the Jewel of the Earth; *nlūṃ*, obeisance to the Jewel of the Nagas. Thus, one should perform [this worship] in the four directions starting from the front and in the center.
The family substances (kuladravya) are those originating from the jar-born [Agastya] and others; as stated in the Kumārīkalpa.
The wise practitioner, with great care, should place the materials for the *argha* offering into the *argha* vessel,
as well as substances produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa*, and likewise the *svayambhū* flower.
No unrighteousness exists, O Svabhru, in the accomplishment of this great mantra.
In the *Sārasaṃgraha*:
One should apply fragrance with the Matsya-mudrā to the left front of oneself, upon a surface smeared [with unguents] that is triangular, encircled by a circle, and surrounded by a square.
Having worshipped with fragrances, one should finally offer the *argha* to the deity with the mantra ending in "namas.
Likewise, the limbs [of the deity] are placed in the corners and in front of the square [mandala].
Having worshipped the weapon-mantra in the cardinal directions, one should place the conch-stand;
and with the root-mantra, one should install the conch-stand that has been washed.
In the same way, one should extract the letter *kā* with a bindu, followed by the Lord of Serpents (*bhujaṅgeśa*).
Then [one adds] "to the mandala" (*maṇḍalāya*) at the end of the fire-syllable (*vahni*), and likewise "bestower of dharma" (*dharmaprada*).
Having uttered "Salutation to the one whose self consists of ten parts," one should worship with scents and other offerings.
The section beginning with "the triangle" and ending with the method for constructing the wheel describes the sixfold worship within the corners and other parts of that very square.
Therefore, regarding these two options, one should practice according to the instruction of one's own guru.
And the Matsya-mudrā is described in the Tantra.
One should place the palm of the left hand upon the back of the right hand and move the two thumbs;
this is the Matsya-mudrā, the form of the Fish.
The letter *kā* (ka), the letter *la* (la), the *bindu* which is the *anusvāra*, and the *bhujaṅga* which is the *repha* (*ra*)—likewise, it is joined with the *bindu*.
Here, the individual fire-energies (*vahnikalā*) are also to be worshipped, as is seen elsewhere. Thus:
Having placed a conch shell washed with water upon that [altar], one should worship it;
the *arghyapātra* should be one *prādeśa* in length and four *aṅgulas* in height.
"This is called the argha vessel; I establish it with this mantra."

One should say "to the orb of the sun" (amarkamaṇḍalāya), which means twelve; then, having uttered the word "to the self of the kalās," one says "to the vessel of oblation" followed by the heart-mantra (hṛnmanu).
Having worshipped the conch with this, one should worship the digits of the sun.
In another tantra:

Then, O Mantrin, having washed the auspicious great conch— which is free from the seeds of anger and the seeds of weapons— upon its base while reciting the [appropriate] mantra, one should place it there.
Śivā, endowed with the three long vowels; Kālī, joined with Brahmā and Ramā;

To the All-Sustainer, to the All, to the Non-existence of All through sound;

By means of the two seed-syllables of wrath and weapons, namely *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*, and by its own form *krīṃ*.

The long vowel *ā* joined with the letter *ka*, the mark of Śacīpati (*la*), Vāyu (*ya*), and the heart (*namaḥ*)—by this, *hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ kālīkapālāya namaḥ* is the first mantra. At the end of Manmatha (*ma*) is the mantra-syllable *īṃ*; the three long vowels in the form of *ā ī ū*, followed by *kālīka* as the essential form, and again as before.

"Obeisance to the Skull"—with this [mantra], *mtrāṃ mtrīṃ straṃ*, [one recites] "Tāriṇī, obeisance to the Skull"; this is the second mantra. The syllable *ha* (the letter *śiva*) joined with the three long vowels *ā ī ū*, followed by the word "nīla," and after two blue syllables, as before, "obeisance to the Skull"—with this [mantra], *hāṃ hīṃ hūṃ*.

"Obeisance to Nīlākāpālā"—this is the third mantra. [The seed-syllable] consists of *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*), the final *parā* (*saḥ*), the seed-syllable *śambhu* (the letter *ha*) joined with the moon of the left ear (*u*), and the vowel *u* joined with the *anusvāra*. The form of the word is "sarva. *Kāma* is the letter *ka*; *Kālarātri* is the letter *pa*; it is joined with the long vowel *ā*, and thus it is written as *lāpyati*.

Svarūpa, kānti, ākāra, and kṣut constitute the syllable *yakāra*. Thus: *hrīṃ saḥ hūṃ*, "Obeisance to the Skull of the Goddess, which is for all, the support of all, the all, the source of all, consisting of purity, reddened by the blood of the Asuras, beautiful, and the vessel of the gods"—this is the fourth mantra.
There, the practitioner of mantra, knowing the ritual procedure, should worship the mandala of the hot-rayed one (the Sun),
filling it with the root mantra while perceiving it as nectar through his intellect.
Having cast perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains, one should again display the three segments;
there, O practitioner, one should worship the mandala of the Moon of Nectar.
The syllable *Tāra* (Om), the power (*Śakti*) *Ame*, the power adorned with the nasal bindu (*Anusvāra*),
the third root [syllable], and the seed-syllable of Bhairava’s wrath, blazing intensely.
By means of this mantra, the practitioner should meditate upon the eight radiant [deities].
The letter *E* is Śakti; having cast nectar with Śakti, one should display the Śaṅkha-mudrā.
Having meditated upon Kuleśvarī in the manner to be described, within a beautiful central core consisting of a circle, an eight-petaled lotus, and a hexagon;
The knower of mantras should worship her with the ritual services using the root mantra;
by joining the thumb and ring finger, he should satisfy Tāriṇī with that [mantra].
By the union of the index finger and the thumb, by the union of the middle finger and the thumb,

having honored it with perfumes and flowers, one should then worship the sixteen Kalās.
The letter *ka* is Karna; the letter *u* is Candra; the half-moon is the Anusvāra bindu; by these, *oṃ*.
The Kalās have been described in the Merutantra and the Kulārṇava.
Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī,

The ten digits (kalās) arising from the letters beginning with 'a', which bestow the ten qualities, belong to the fire element:
Tapinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, and Ruci.
Suṣumnā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Vodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā— these twelve, beginning with Ka and ending with Sa and Ra, are said to be the bestowers of wealth.
Amṛtā, Mānadā, Bhūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati,
Dhṛti, Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, and Aṅgadā.
O Mistress of the Kula, these sixteen digits born of the vowels— Pūrṇā, Pūrṇāmṛtā, and so forth— are said to be gentle and bestowers of coughs.

The meaning is that one should worship the lunar digits (candrakalā) by first placing the ten letters beginning with *ya* joined with the bindu, which correspond to the fire-digits (agnikalā); then the letters from *ka* to *ṭha* and from *bha* to *ḍa* in reverse order joined with the bindu, which correspond to the sun-digits (sūryakalā); and finally the sixteen vowels from *a* onwards joined with the bindu, which correspond to the moon-digits (candrakalā).
Likewise.

One should cause the bathing substance, which is pure and fragrant, to be removed from the water with scented water.
Regarding "bathing," this is according to the statement in the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā* and the *Triśaktiratna*.

having offered a single libation, one should recite the root mantra and the *pādukā* mantra.

for Caṇḍikā, the ring finger is used with the thumb.
