The *tatvamudrā* is proclaimed to be formed by the joining of the index finger and the thumb; it is said that this [mudrā] is used for purposes other than libation (*tarpaṇa*), such as in meditation and so forth. Having uttered the worldly name of the gurus preceded by "Śrī," and having appended the titles "Guru," "Paramaguru," and so on at the end, one should perform the libation in this manner: "I offer libation to the sandals (*pādukā*) of [Name]. Thus one should offer the libation.

The Tradition (*saṃpradāya*). By this sequence following the three currents (*oghatriya*), the meaning of the three is established. "The vessel of the Goddess" refers specifically to the vessel of special offering (*viśeṣārgha*); with its contents, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) in this manner: "I satisfy the venerable [Name] Goddess, together with her limbs, her retinue, her weapons, and her vehicle. This is the meaning. Prior to the invocation (*āvāhana*), it is performed with the measure of the "procession of enjoyment" (*bhogayātrā*).
They satisfy.
In the conduct of the samaya.
Taking up the substance for purification, perform the libation with the appropriate mudrā;
holding the thumb, index finger, and middle finger on the left side, grasp the purity.
The wise practitioner should satisfy the Goddess with neither the left nor the right [hand].
Some maintain that because it is stated "with the left and also with the right," there is an optional choice between the two hands for the goddess during the libation (tarpaṇa).
Alternatively, one should satisfy the goddesses with the left hand holding the vessel of purification and the right hand in the *tattva-mudrā*.

They say that the mention of the thumb, index finger, and middle finger refers merely to the purification (*śuddhi*), because the method for the *tarpaṇa* (libation) by means of the *tattvamudrā* has already been stated in another way.
Then one should perform the purification of reality (*tattvaśuddhi*). Regarding this, there is a scriptural authority (*śruti*):

Oṃ, may my prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna breaths be purified; may I become light, stainless, and free from bonds—svāhā! Oṃ, may my earth, water, fire, air, and ether elements be purified; may I become light, etc.—svāhā! Oṃ, may my nature (prakṛti), ego (ahaṃkāra), intellect (buddhi), mind (manas), and ears (śrotra) be purified... [and so forth].

"May they be purified," and so forth; "Oṃ, may my skin, eyes, ears, tongue, nose, and speech be purified," and so forth; "Oṃ, may my hands, feet, anus, genitals, and sounds be purified," and so forth.

122a) *Oṃ, may my touch, form, taste, smell, and space be purified,* and so forth; *Oṃ, may my wind, fire, water, earth, and self be purified,* and so forth— reciting these seven mantras while reflecting upon them.

One should touch all the limbs seven times with both hands; this is the purification of the elements (*tattvaśuddhi*). Now follows the offering of the *bali* to Vaṭuka and the others. As it is stated in the *Merutantra*:
One must certainly perform the worship of Vaṭuka at the beginning, in the left [quarter], and so forth;
in this path, Vaṭuka is the principal deity, established by the beginning and end of the gods.
Without him, the gods do not accept [offerings]; therefore, his worship [is essential].
He who, out of delusion, should worship a deity while leaving Vaṭuka unworshipped, [commits an offense].
There is no fruit from worshipping him alone, and Vaṭuka becomes enraged;
therefore, one should worship the Gaṇa with perfumes, flowers, and various kinds of meat.
By means of those respective mantras and according to the prescribed ritual, one shall obtain the favor of the deity.
"Vaṭuka" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa), meaning Vaṭuka and the others. Likewise, one should then offer the bali-oblation to the Kṣetrapālas. As stated in the Jñānārṇava:
O Dear One, having prepared mandalas in the northeast, southeast, southwest, and northwest corners as before, worship them there as previously described.
O Maheśānī, O beloved, one should offer the bali-oblation as before for the sake of all prosperity, to Vaṭuka and to the Yoginīs.

But in the conduct of the observance (samayācāra):

"May he who is served by spirits and vetālas be eternally the bringer of peace for me.

May Khecarī, Bhūcarī, and Vyomacārī always be pleased with me.

Whether above the cosmic egg, or in heaven, in the expanse of the sky, or in the partless realm, on earth, in the netherworld, in fire, in water, or in wind— wherever they may abide; whether established in sacred fields (*kṣetra*), seats (*pīṭha*), or other such sites,
may those goddesses, equal to the lords of the gods, who are pleased by offerings of flowers, incense, and the like, always come to us with the rite of auspicious oblations (*bali*).
At the end of this, O Maheśānī, one should write the seed-syllable *yāṃ*, followed by *yoginī*, then *bhyaḥ svāhā*; at the end of all these syllables, one should write the word *yoginī*.
Having written the armor (*kavaca*) and the garment (*vastra*), one should again write the consort of fire (*vahnijāyā*).
With this mantra, the goddess Yoginī should receive the offering (*bali*).
In the Meru Tantra.
One should utter the three *tāra*s, followed by "tathā ehi ehi devi putra vaṭukanātha ucchiṣṭahāriṇe haṃ hūṃ haḥ hūṃ," reciting this twice.
"O Kṣetrapāla, destroy all obstacles"— reciting this couplet,

Gṛhṇa gṛhṇa hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the six-syllable mantra.

May he, pleased by this offering of bali, grant me protection from all [harm].

O Goddess praised by heroes, having consulted with [the attendants] regarding the purpose, one should offer the bali-oblation to all beings three times with the sixteen-syllable mantra.
Then [one should utter] Tāra (Oṃ), Bhuvaneśānī, then the word "sarvavighnebhyaḥ" (to all obstacles),
then "kṛtya", "sarvabhūtebhyaḥ", the syllable Hūṃ, and Vahnivallabhā (Svāhā).
While reciting [the mantra], one should offer the *vali* with the mudrā known as *tattva*.
In the Meru Tantra:
One should utter "tāra" three times, followed by "sarva bhūtebhyaḥ sarva eva ca," and then "bhūtapatibhyaḥ"; this is said to be the seventeen-syllable mantra of the heart.
Beings of various forms— celestial, terrestrial, and those dwelling in the intermediate space,
as well as those situated in the depths of the netherworld— have been purified through the yoga of Śiva.
The Dhruvas and others who are free from malice, as well as Indra and the other deities established [in their stations],
being satisfied and pleased in mind, accept this bali offering.
And in this context, the offering of the *bali* to Vaṭuka and the others is mandatory for the Vāmas;
for those following the Dakṣiṇa [path], it is optional, since it is stated that even in the Tārā and Haṃsī [systems], it occurs at the end.
Now follows the worship of the seats (pīṭhapūjā).
In the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*.
The wise one should worship the seat according to the prescribed ritual for the worship of the seat;
having worshipped the support (ādhāra) and the others, he should worship the nine powers.

Regarding "the support and so forth": having worshipped the support (ādhāra), the power (śakti), primordial nature (prakṛti), the tortoise (kūrma), bliss (ānanda), the earth (pṛthvī), the ocean of nectar (sudhā-samudra), the island of the nine jewels (navaratna-dvīpa), the jeweled pavilion (maṇi-maṇḍapa), the cremation ground (śmaśāna), the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), the jeweled altar (ratna-vedikā), the jeweled throne (ratna-pīṭha), the sages (muni), the gods (deva), the corpse (śava), the corpse-bearer (śavamūṇḍa), the one with abundant flesh (vahumāṃsa), and so forth, together with the joyful Śivā, in the pericarp (karṇikā).

In the corners starting from the southeast (āgneya) of the earth-fortress (bhūpūra), there are Dharma, Aiśvarya, and so forth; at the gates starting from the east, there are Adharma, Ajñāna, Avairāgya, and Anaiśvarya.
In the center is the bulb of bliss (*ānandakanda*), with consciousness as its stalk; it consists of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) as its petals and transformation (*vikāra*) as its filaments.

Its pericarp is enriched with the seed-syllables of the fifty letters, and it contains the solar, lunar, and fiery mandalas, as well as the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and the Self (*ātman*), the Inner Self (*antarātman*).

The meaning is that one should worship those whose nature is the knowledge of the Supreme Self. Regarding the "nine powers": as stated in the Kumārītantra, they are located on the eight filaments and in the center—namely, Icchā (Will), Jñānā (Knowledge), Kriyā (Action), followed by Kāminī (Desirous One), Kāmadāyinī (Bestower of Desires), Ratī (Delight), Ratipriyā (Beloved of Delight), Ānandā (Bliss), and the ninth is Manonmanī (Beyond Mind).
Ugrogrā, Caṇḍā, Cāmuṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā, Vikaṭotkaṭā,
Saṃkaṭā, Caṇḍogrā, and likewise Maṅgalacaṇḍikā.
Or as stated in the Bhairavītantra.
The meaning is that it is stated according to the tradition of Vīracūḍāmaṇi.
This is an illustration.

One should also worship the central seat with the *pīṭha-mantra* as stated in the *Kumārītantra*: "Aiṃ parāyai aparāyai parāparāyai hyauḥ, salutations to Sadāśiva Mahāpreta seated upon the lotus-throne. Likewise:
Therein, one should worship the external Sāraṅgī with ritual offerings;
having raised Kuṇḍalinī, one should pierce the Brahma-granthi.
Having brought [the breath] into the path of sound and established it on the twelfth petal,
one should then pierce the Brahma-tīrtha and satisfy [the deity] with that stream.
Having worshipped the Goddess within the heart, one should perform the external worship;
having led her through the central path of the *suṣumnā* into the interior of the *vilā*.
One should perform japa while established in meditation, contemplating the state of essential identity (sāmarasya).
Having invoked the Goddess residing therein, one should visualize the wheel of command (ājñācakra).
Placing [the breath] upon the nose by means of the middle path through the nostrils,
one should recite the root mantra and awaken the word "Kālikā."
"Come, come, O Great Goddess, O Treasure of Compassion! [I offer] the sandals, the mental resolve, the seat, and so forth; now display the *yonimudrā*."
In the Kālītantra:
Then, having invoked the supreme digit (kalā) vibrating within the heart-lotus into the center of the yantra, one should duly perform the entire network of ritual placements (nyāsa).
In the *Kumārīkalpa*:
Then, with the mantra beginning with "Deveśī," the wise practitioner should invoke [the deity] from the image and so forth— she who flashes within the heart-lotus and has the form of lightning.
O Queen of the Gods, may devotion be obtained by me together with my retinue;
as long as I worship you, O Goddess, may you remain steadfast.

Now, one might ask: how can there be the manifestation of a deity in a yantra and the like, given that [the deity] is partless (*niṣkala*)? Although this was stated previously, it is nevertheless addressed here.
In the Meru Tantra.

Having made the formless appear as if possessing form, people devoted to the ritualistic section [of the Veda] are like the milk produced from all the limbs of cows that flows from the openings of their udders.
Likewise, O Lord, [the Tathāgata], though omnipresent, manifests in images and the like,
both because of the beauty of the physical form and especially because of the merit of worship.
Through the practitioner's faith, the deity attains presence;
just as the scent residing within the entire body does not nourish itself.
That which is fashioned by one's own karma and bestowed [upon others] nourishes those very people in turn;
thus the Supreme Lord resides within every body, like clarified butter.
Without worship, the gods do not bestow fruit upon men;
having performed the ritual identification (sakalīkaraṇa), one should [offer] their vital breaths and their sense organs.
One should install and worship the deities; otherwise, it is considered fruitless for those who do not understand the pervasion of the yantra of the deity in the form of mantra.
O Śāmbhavī, all that has been performed, such as worship and other rites, becomes fruitless.
Therefore, worship with a yantra and so forth is recommended.
By means of the mantra beginning with "Deveśī" and so forth, [one should extract her] from the lotus situated at the head of the cakra.
In the Svatantra-tantra.
Then, having invoked Kālikā at the end of the meditation on the Kāmakalā,
one should place a flower in the center of the cakra using the mudrā known as Kūrma.
The kūrma-mudrā is described in the tantra.
The index finger of the left hand and the little finger of the right,
as well as the thumb of the left hand upon the right index finger— one should thus conquer one's own [senses].
The right thumb is raised, while the middle and other fingers of the left hand [are placed upon it].
One should join the fingers on the back of the right hand.
With the *pitṛtīrtha* of the left hand, using the middle and ring fingers likewise,
one should then perform [the offering] with the right hand facing downwards.
One should make the right palm level like the back of a tortoise;
such is the "tortoise-hand" (karakacchapa) which bestows all accomplishments.

Having displayed the mudrās beginning with the invocation (āvāhana), and having performed the ritual integration of the parts (sakalīkaraṇa) by means of the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa), one should perform the consecration of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) using the lolling tongue mudrā (lelihānamudrā). As for the mudrās, it is said in the Tantra:
Invocation, installation, and making [the deity] present,
as well as confinement and likewise bringing [the deity] face-to-face— these are what have been described.
Having performed the stabilization of the vital breath (prāṇasthāpana) with their respective mudrās, one should proceed.
Their characteristics have been explained in the *Lakṣasaṃgraha*.
Having joined the palms with both hands, one should place the thumb upon the root joint of the ring finger;
this is considered the *āvāhanī* (invoking) mudrā.
Indeed, this [image] should be facing downwards; one should perform the rite of installation.
Their characteristics have been stated in the *Lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*.
Having formed a *añjali* with both hands, one should place the thumbs at the root joint of the ring fingers;
this is considered the *āvāhanī* mudrā.
This [line] should indeed be facing downwards; one should perform the ritual of installation (sthāpana). The characteristics of these have been described in the *Lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*.
Having formed a *añjali* with both hands, one should place the thumbs at the root joint of the ring fingers;
this is considered the *āvāhanī* mudrā.
Indeed, when this [mudrā] is with the face turned downwards, it is called "sthāpanī" (the installation mudrā).
From the joining of two fists with the thumbs raised is the *sannidhāpanī*;
that same mudrā, when the thumbs are inserted within, is considered the *saṃbodhinī*.
The *karaṇī* mudrā consists of two hands with palms facing upward and fists joined,
while the index finger of the left hand is extended downward.

When this *avaguṇṭhana* mudrā is rotated all around the limbs of the deity, it constitutes the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), which is the act of making [the deity] complete (*sakalīkṛti*).
The *amṛtīkaraṇa* (nectar-ification) and the *dhenu-mudrā* have been described;
[the former] consists of the thumbs interlocked and the other fingers extended outward.
O beloved one, this supreme Mahāmudrā is joyful in its performance;
one should employ these mudrās in the rite of summoning the deity.
In this regard, regarding the five mudrās, they recite in sequence: "Come here! Stay here! Be present here! Be face-to-face here!"
In the Uḍīśa [Tantra].
Therefore, in the worship of the deity with a full [offering],
that which brings about the presence of the deity before one with reverence is here called *āvāhana* (invocation).
For this very reason, it is because of the display of the *āvāha* mudrā.
Likewise.
The wise have declared that the installation of the pervasive Lord within the yantra consists of performing worship,
receiving honor, and accepting his grace and other benefits.
May she have the power to perform this;
may her presence be sought, as well as the presence of the All-pervading Lord, which extends even unto the completion of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa).
The non-contradiction of the teachings has been indicated with devotion by men who know the mantras;
for the sake of bliss, the true nature of reality is characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Therefore, in this context, that which pervades the *sakala* [state] should be meditated upon as the *avaguṇṭhana* (veiling).
Having performed the *sakalīkaraṇa* (the rite of making one possessed of parts) with these mantras, one should then achieve oneness.
The act of immortalizing [the body] should be performed for half the duration required for the destruction of the limbs along with the possessor of those limbs;
forgiveness of its transgressions should be understood as the supreme act of restoration.
The offenses consisting of the conceptualization of the unlimited Brahman as limited through the invocation and other ritual acts do not constitute offenses regarding its form.
Other mudrās are found in the Bhairavatantra.
Having stated, "Adorned with the five mudrās,"...
Yoni, Bhūtinī, Bījākhya, Daityadhūminī,
and Lelihānā— these are proclaimed as the five secret mudrās.
One should discern these very [elements] right there.
The wise know that the womb (yoni), the illusion (māyā), the breast (dhara), the cow (dhenū), the vulva (vadhū), and the beard (kūrca) are, respectively, their seed-syllables (bīja).
I shall now describe their characteristics in due order.

Yāṇiḥ, Aiṃ, Māyā, Hrīṃ, Adharāṃ—immediately following these is Bhūtādhenuṃ; Vaṃ, Vadhuḥ, Strī, Kvacca(?), and Hūṃ are the seed-syllables (bījas). Likewise, [these are placed] on the index finger, ring finger, middle finger, and little finger, as well as upon the wheel.
One should perform the recitation with the hands joined by separating the roots of the little fingers;
having placed the tips of the thumbs [therein], it is proclaimed as the "Great Yoni" (mahāyoni). Also, in another Tantra:
Having formed the *vadhū* [mudrā], one should indeed place it in the middle of the *kuṭilā*; with the thumb at its tip, this is considered the *bhūtinī* mudrā.
In the Bhairava Tantra.
With both hands turned outward, the thumbs and index fingers joined,
one should simultaneously and evenly form the ritual gesture (mudrā) in the shape of a half-moon.
Drawing the little finger downward, one should apply it to the middle fingers;
this mudrā, O Goddess, is called Vījā, whose nature is knowledge.
Having turned the two hands over, one should place the little fingers and the dark (middle) fingers [on top],
while the pair of ring fingers is below and the pair of index fingers is separate.
Interlocking the thumbs and the ring fingers at their tips—
this mudrā, O beloved, is called the Cometary Fire (Dhumaketu) of the Daityas.
Having made the mouth curved and wide open, one should move the tongue downward;
with a pair of fists placed at the sides, this is celebrated as the *lelihānā* [mudrā].
Then, one should perform the preliminary rite of *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (the installation of the vital breath) in the heart of the Goddess with the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra, using the *lālī* mudrā.
The *lalihā* mudrā is as follows:
One should make the index, middle, and ring fingers equal and face them downward;
one should place the extended little finger straight upon the ring finger.
This is the lelihānā mudrā, proclaimed for the placement of life-force (jīvanyāsa).
In the Svatantra Tantra.
Having meditated upon the Goddess and invoked her, one should display the yoni-mudrā;
then, with the supreme [mudrā], one should indeed display the sword, the severed head, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness.
Having joined the little finger and the ring finger with the right thumb,
while the remaining fingers are extended and clearly touched together, this is the sword mudrā (khaḍgamudrikā).
As for the Varada and Abhaya mudrās, perform them as [the gestures of] granting boons and fearlessness.
Having joined the two hands in the *saṃpuṭa* (cavity) gesture, one should join the tip of the thumb with the base of the little finger; this is declared to be the *parayoni*.
Having formed a fist with the left hand with the fingers tucked inside,
one should likewise carefully grasp it with the two middle fingers of the right hand.
O Lord, the practitioner should then join the right hand into the left fist, with the tips of the middle finger and thumb meeting at their very ends.
One should display it on the right side; by this "mudrā of the shaven head," one is liberated.
In the Bhairava Tantra.

Then, having drawn forth the Goddess from the heart-lotus in the form of radiant light into the lotus of his hand by means of the nostrils, he should place her within the yantra while uttering the seed-syllable.
Having conceived the form [of the deity] by means of the root mantra, one should then establish the vital breaths;
thereafter, one should invoke the Goddess with the previously mentioned *prāṇa-mantra*.
One should display the mudrās with the seed-syllables (bījas) beginning with the invocation (āvāhana);
these are the Yoni, the Bhūtinī, the one called Bījā, and the Asuranāśinī.
The commentary on the *Dānavadhvaṃsinī* is the *Lelihānā*, following the sequential order; the characteristics and seed-syllables (*bīja*) of these [mudrās] are proclaimed in the *Tārākalpa*.
But this is indeed its instigator.
Or rather, O beloved, listen as I describe the characteristic of Suranāśinī:
having positioned the left thumb and released the index finger.
Extending the right fist upward with the index finger stretched out from it— this mudrā, formed thus,
destroys enemies and annihilates asuras.
The seed-syllable of this [goddess] is proclaimed to be enriched by the fire of desire (KĀM) and the drop (bindu).
Holding the board with the seal (mudrā), one should sprinkle it while reciting [the mantra].
In the Uttaratantra:
O Bhairava, the binding with the mudrā should be performed using the second [syllable] of Vāgbhava and the Kāmarāja [mantra], and the display [of the mudrā] with the root mantra.
But the renunciation [of obstacles] should be performed with the mudrā and released by means of the *kūrma* seed-syllable.
In the heart of Kālī.
Having meditated upon the Goddess and invoked her, one should display the *yoni-mudrā*;
then, displaying the sword, the severed head, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhīti*), and the lotus-womb (*padmayoni*).
Also in the Merutantra and the Kulārṇava:
Having established the Goddess upon the pedestal, while meditating, one should sprinkle her three times with the water of honor (arghya) using the root mantra;
likewise, the Dīpinī mantra should be recited three times over it.
Furthermore, from the letter 'a' to the letter 'kṣa', they are again threefold by means of the Mātṛkās.
The illuminating mantra is said to be for the accomplishment of the liquor.
The *Dīpinī* is declared to be the mantra that increases the splendor of the deity.
Thus, having invoked the Goddess there, having displayed the *āvāhana*, *dīpanī*, and *mudrās*, having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*,
and having rendered her complete (*sakalīkṛtya*) by means of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), [one performs] the *avaguṇṭhana*, *dhenu*, *yoni*, *khaḍga*, and *muṇḍa* [mudrās].
Having displayed the Bhayavarā mudrās, one should perform worship.
In the Meru Tantra:
Just as mothers rejoice upon seeing the performance of their child,
so do the deities rejoice upon seeing a mudrā performed with devotion.
Likewise.
One should never display the mudrā in a gathering of many people;
the deities become agitated with him—what fruit, then, could there be from such an act?
In the Kulārṇava:
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should install its vital breaths and its sense organs, and then worship the deity; otherwise, it will be fruitless.
In the *Triśaktiratna*:
As before, one should satisfy the goddess with the nectar of the goddess’s journey.
In the Vīracūḍāmaṇi.
Having performed the sixteen services beginning with water for the feet and including the honey-mixture (madhuparka),
one should worship Kālī and sacrifice to her along with her limbs and her retinue.
And the ritual applications (upacāra) have been described in the Merutantra.
Then one should worship the God with whatever offerings can be obtained according to one's capacity;
therein, the wealthy should perform the worship with the sixteen types of offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra).
A seat, a welcome, the arghya offering, water for the feet,
water for sipping, the madhuparka, again water for sipping, a bath, clothing, and ornaments.
One should employ perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and sandalwood paste in the worship; these are the sixteen services (upacāras).
The intermediate [form of worship] consists of ten services; it is prescribed for householders.
These are: water for the guest (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and again water for sipping (ācamana).

The ten services (upacāras) are traditionally known as beginning with fragrance (gandha) and ending with the offering (nivedya). The fivefold worship (pañcopacārikā pūjā) consists of those same services beginning with fragrance and ending with the offering.
In the Maṇtraratnāvalī.
Water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, bathing, clothing, ornaments, fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and further water for sipping.
Then, one should employ betel, a hymn of praise, libations, and prostrations;
these are the sixteen services to be utilized in the worship.
Then, having offered water for the feet (pādya), the respectful oblation (arghya), food (anna), and likewise water for sipping (ācamanīyaka),
as well as the honey-mixture (madhuparka), incense, and flowers.
Incense, a lamp, and food offerings—these are considered the ten modes of service (daśopacāra).
In the Meru Tantra.
Whether they be non-householders or householders, those intent on their duty should perform it;
first, however, the Vedic practitioner should perform the worship with Vedic mantras.
And thereafter, according to the tantras, both the woman and the Śūdra [should be initiated] with the mantras of the Tantric tradition.
In the *Prapañcasāra*:
Worship is said to be threefold; one should resort to it for one month at a time, according to the distinctions of the sixteen, ten, or five modes of service.
In the Kuloḍḍīśa [Tantra].
Whatever may be difficult to obtain among all the ritual services,
one should mentally visualize all of that and provide it by means of scattering flowers.
In each of those instances, one should offer water for the feet and so forth at regular intervals between the ritual procedures.
In the Meru Tantra.
"Ahaṃ haṃ ham idaṃ idaṃ idaṃ gṛhāṇa ṭha dvayam | yāhi eḥ"— this fifteen-syllable mantra is used in all ritual services (upacāras).
A Vaidika person, however, may recite Tantric mantras at the end of a Vedic [recitation];
in all cases, a Śūdra should recite "namaḥ" in place of the "vahni-jāyā" (svāhā) and other such endings.
Now, by way of ritual service.
Also in the Sārasaṃgraha and the Merutantra:
On the left side of the deity, one should offer a seat with the root mantra;
it may be made of flowers, wood, cloth, leather, a basket, or metal.
Six kinds of seats have been declared which cause delight to the deity:
the floral seat, fashioned from flowers and the like, and that joined with *kuśa* grass, threads, and so forth.
[One should offer] flowers that are multicolored, fragrant, soft, and grant all desires;
however, whatever flowers are prohibited for a particular [deity], if [an offering] is made with those, [it is ineffective].
A rosary made solely of these destroys the practitioner's desires;
it should be produced from sacrificial wood, or from *tāla* wood, or from sandalwood.
One should desire to offer as a seat either a *gaṃbhārī* or a *śrīparṇī* leaf;
it should be thorny, contain milky sap, and be devoid of the sound of the *tāra*.

One should avoid wood produced from a shrine or a cremation ground, as well as the *vibhītaka* tree; likewise, one should avoid that which is grown from hair, from bark, from a sheath, or produced from excrement.
The four types of excellent skins are declared to be, in order of precedence:
those of the lion, the tiger, the hyena, the goat, and the buffalo.
The most excellent seat is fashioned from the skins of elephants, horses, and the black antelope; those made from donkey or dog skin are forbidden.
The horns of a jackal, a wolf, a cow, a hare, and likewise a monkey;
as well as *kūśa*, *kāśa*, *śara*, *granthi*, *yava*, *dūrvā*, and *valvaja* grasses.
The bull, the elephant, the serpent, the peacock, and the jasmine—each subsequent one is used in the absence of the preceding;
their respective seats are prescribed as being similar to the seat of the Yoga-pīṭha.

The ten types of silk (kauśa) are traditionally held to be of progressively superior quality, each subsequent one being better than the preceding; among gold, silver, pearls, gems, coral, and iron, each succeeding one is more excellent than the one before.
Base metals such as iron, brass, lead, tin, and bronze are prohibited;
a *viṣṭara* (seat) consists of twenty-seven blades of *kuśa* grass.
In this way, by means of the poison.
Having displayed the *svāgata* (welcome) mudrā and uttered, "Welcome, O Śrī Amukadevī," it should be performed.
In the Kālī-kalpa.
The knower of mantras should offer water for the feet at the feet with the mantra "namas."
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
This [mantra] is declared to be recited over water together with *yāmāka*, *dūrvā*, and *viṣṇukrāntā*.
In the Meru Tantra:
At the time of arrival, at the time of bathing, and upon the conclusion of the food offering—these are the three occasions for the *pādya*; *pādya* consists of the washing of the feet.
In the Bhairava Tantra:

Then, having meditated upon the Goddess once more, the wise and awakened one should worship her with all ritual offerings while reciting the root mantra, presenting the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and the flower bud (kalikā).
In the Kali age.
One should first worship Mahākāla, and afterwards one should worship the Goddess.
One should worship Mahākāla, who is smoke-colored, to the right of the Goddess.
Carrying a staff and a khaṭvāṅga, with a face terrifying due to its fangs, the child has his waist wrapped in a tiger skin; he is pot-bellied and resembles blood-red [in hue].
Three-eyed, with hair standing erect on his head, adorned with a garland of severed heads,
and fierce as if blazing, he bears a crescent moon resting upon his mass of matted locks.
Having meditated thus, one should worship with the Mahākāla mantra itself;
then, having extracted the armor (kavaca), [one recites] *yāṃ rāṃ lāṃ vāṃ cakauṃ*.
Having uttered "Mahākālabhairava" and "Destroy all obstacles," and having again said "Destroy," one should extract Māyā and Lakṣmī.
A mantra joined with "phaṭ" and "svāhā" accomplishes all aims.
The meditation and so forth described in the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi* are optional.
In the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
Having recited the root mantra, one should then say "this is the water for the feet" (pādya),
followed by the words "and obeisance to Dakṣiṇakālikā," O Śivā.
O Goddess, please accept this most beautiful water, fragrant and prepared with ritual substances,
which I have offered with devotion as *pādya*.
With this mantra, one should offer water for the feet (pādya) to the Goddess at the place of her feet.
In the Kali age.
O Goddess of the gods, one should offer the arghya above the head with the mantra "svāhā."
In the Meru Tantra.
Then one should offer the *arghya* on the head; his time is considered to be threefold:
for one who has arrived, for the act of worship, and for one who has bathed during the month.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should offer the *arghya* to the deity who desires to depart;
having recited the root mantra, O Goddess of Devas, one should remember: "This is the *arghya*."
One should offer [the oblation] to Śrī Dakṣiṇakālikā with the *svāhā* mantra at the head;
it should consist of water from a conch vessel combined with the eight substances.
"O Maheśvarī, please accept this arghya offered by me";
with this mantra, one should offer it at the head of the Goddess.
Thus it is because [the term] has been declared as a *saṃhitā*.

In that interval.
Sauvīra, yāvana, nakhyam, māyūra, śrīkara,
and likewise darvikā-meghanīla— these are the six types of collyrium (añjana).
One who is endowed with devotion should offer bells, incense, and oils to all the gods and goddesses upon a stone slab or a metallic vessel.
When copper and other metals are melted in a fire combined with ghee and oil,
the collyrium that is produced is designated as *darvikā*.
One should prepare the supreme collyrium for the Great Goddess from the eyes of a widow;
the practitioner should not apply the eye-salve in an earthen vessel.
Now follows the offering to the Nairṛtas.
This has been stated in the Matsyamukta:
One should offer milk-rice, rice-and-pulse porridge, sesame, and rice; and one should give rice-and-pulse porridge mixed with sugar and jaggery.
Therefore, one should cause clarified butter mixed with curd and honey to be offered;
likewise, the flesh of the śāla fish, the pāpīna, and the guodhika are excellent.
One who knows the mantras should carefully offer food mixed with honey;
the *śālamatsya* is well known as the *mahāśāla*.
In the *Svatantra* [Tantra].
One should repeatedly offer to the Goddess as an oblation food that is roasted in a pan, cooked in oil, or mixed with ghee, and which is pleasing to the mind.
"Kandu-pakvam" refers to roasted rice, flattened rice (*pṛthuka*), and the like; "sneha-pakvam" refers to sweets such as *laḍḍūkas* cooked in oil or ghee.
In the Muṇḍamālā [Tantra]:
One should offer the śāla fish, the pāṭhīna, the śakula, and likewise the gaṇḍa; as well as the madgula, the cellisa, and the meat of the buffalo.
Bird meat originating from various sources.
The great meat of the black goat, the lizard, and likewise the deer;
the meat of aquatic fish and also the meat of the gaṇḍakī.
Various milks with diverse condiments and many kinds of side dishes.
In the Śaktiyāmala:
Having thus propitiated [the deity], one should offer the *nirvaidya* (medicine) separately for each;
one should present bone, flesh, and hair along with blood and clarified butter.
One should offer ghee, well-prepared soups, milk, and various meats— whether from creatures of the sky, the earth, or the water— fried and seasoned with the six flavors.
Chewable, suckable, lickable, and likewise drinkable—alcohol is said to be of ten kinds; one should offer it according to its various colors.
In the Kumārī Tantra:
Listen now to other offerings suitable for practitioners:
betel leaf with camphor, and coconut with sugar.
He [offered] milk-rice with ghee, ginger with jaggery,
as well as rice with sesame seeds, and curd with sugar.
The rose-apple, the jackfruit, and likewise the hog-plum;
the plantain, the *titilī*, and the *śrīphala*—the most excellent of fruits.
The Karañja, the Bakula, the Tāra, and the Khajūra,
as well as other fragrant substances and sweet fruits.
In the Rudrayāmala.
