A wise person should prepare the sacrificial offering (naivedya) even with wood from a sacrificial tree;
however, in the absence of all these, it may be made of clay, provided it is fashioned by one's own hand.
Having placed that which is appropriate in the arghya vessel, one should present it.
In the *Sārasaṃgraha*:
Having placed it in a vessel made of gold,
one should place that within the mandala and perform the fourfold consecration according to the path of the scriptures.
Having sprinkled [the site] with the weapon-mantra (astramantra) and protected it with the discus-mudrās (cakramudrā),
one should dry it with the wind-seed-syllable (vāyubīja) and burn it with the fire-seed-syllable (vahni-bīja).
The knower of mantras, touching [the offering] with the tip of his right hand using the *sudhā* seed-syllable (*vīja*),
transforms it all into nectar once again with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
Touching it with both hands, one should consecrate it eight times according to the prescribed rite;
then, displaying the dhenu-mudrā, one should worship it with perfumes and flowers.
In the Tantra:
O Goddess, one should present the food offerings with the mudrā called Tatva;
having offered betel-leaf with the root mantra, the practitioner [should do so] with that same mudrā.
With that root mantra and mudrā.
In the Yāmala:
One should offer all the ritual implements and so forth, ending with the root mantra;
if one is unable, one should give them mentally, for this rite must not be omitted.
One should offer a handful of water according to the rules and display the five mudrās;
then, having offered another handful of water, one should present excellent betel.
Combined with cardamom, cloves, camphor, nutmeg, and other ingredients,
it is colored with portions of tamāla leaves and camphor.
In the independent [tradition].
The Great Goddess does not accept that which has been offered by others, even if it be placed in an arghya vessel and presented with hundreds of ritual procedures.
And the sequence of the food offering is according to the Svatantra Tantra.
One should draw a mandala on the right, the left, or both sides;
it consists of a triangle, a circle, and the square of the earth, worshipped as the Support Power (Ādhāraśakti).
In the Yāmala:
One should present perfumes, flowers, and ornaments in front;
one should offer lamps to the right or in front, but not to the left.
The incense should likewise be on the left, or in front, but not on the right;
the food offering (naivedya) should be on the right, or on the left, or in front, but never behind.
In the Yoginītantra.
Fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, as well as food offerings,
whatever clothing, ornaments, or gold is given to whomsoever;
Having uttered the name of their respective deity and performed the sprinkling and worship,
one should offer the oblation (naivedya) with the root mantra after releasing [the deity].
In the Meru Tantra:
Having offered water for the feet and water for sipping, one should present the food offering (naivedya),
placing it upon a golden vessel together with its stand within the mandala.
Having established it within a square, one should consecrate it according to the path of the scriptures;
it should be sprinkled with the Astra-mantra and protected by the Cakra-mudrās.
And with the seed-syllable of Vāyu, one dries up defects such as touch, vision, and so forth.
Touching with the tip of his right hand.
One should burn it away with the seed-syllable of fire.
Having rendered it nectar with the *vaṃ-vīja*, he should then touch it again with both hands according to the rule and consecrate it eight times with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
Having displayed the *dhyanumudrā*, one should worship with perfumes and flowers;
having worshipped the deity, one of concentrated mind should perform a handful of flower offerings (*puṣpāñjali*).
Accept this divine, well-prepared, supreme rice-milk (paramānna), placed in a golden vessel and endowed with the five colors and six flavors, for the sake of my accomplishment.
Having recited the root mantra ending with "svāhā," one should offer water;
while touching the vessel with both hands at the conclusion of the food offering, one should utter "namaḥ."
Having poured water into the right hand of the deity, one should recite this:
"Thou art the spreading of nectar, svāhā," followed by the syllable *bhava*.
One should display with the left hand [the gesture] resembling a full-blown lotus;
having displayed it, one should perform the five breath-offerings (prāṇāhuti) while showing the morsel-gesture (grāsamudrā).
The joining of the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb is the *mudrā* of *prāṇa*.
Having taken a morsel with it, one should say: "Svāhā to *prāṇa*."

One should utter the word for apāna by joining the index finger, middle finger, and thumb; it ends with the letter *ṅ* and concludes with *svāhā*. Then, one should likewise utter [the mantra] for vyāna.
Saying "svāhā," one should then offer [the oblation] by joining the middle, ring, and thumb fingers;
excluding the little finger, the housewife should offer it to the fire with all [fingers] together.
Having uttered "svāhā" with all [the mantras] combined, one should finish the first morsel;
then, in a vessel made of gold or other materials, [one should place] pure water with the *dhenumudrā*.
Having consecrated [the offering] as nectar (amṛtīkṛtya), one should offer it to the deity while reciting this mantra:
"Salutations to you, O Goddess of the lords of gods, the excellent bestower of all satisfaction."
Accept this supreme water— unoffered to others, pure, in its natural state, most cooling, and filled with supreme bliss.
Having spoken thus to the deity, one should place the water vessel on the left.
Likewise.
Food cooked for the sake of the gods should be offered by members of the three castes;
it should be fried in ghee or prepared with milk, cooked solely over fire.
It is proper that a horse made of sugarcane be offered; this is praised for a Śūdra.
Then, one should offer a handful of flowers and perform the binding with the Astra-mantra.
Having made the directions a curtain, one should place [the offerings] all around the Lord;
then one should utter "namas" again over the nectar-like food offering (naivedya).
Then, having displayed the dhenumudrā, one should meditate upon the deity as partaking of the food.
In the Gautamīya [Vinaya].
Having reflected for a moment, the wise one should offer the food offering (naivedya) with the water of honor (arghya).

At the end of the meal, one should offer water for rinsing the mouth (gaṇḍūṣa) and then water for sipping (ācamana). Having given betel-leaf and water, and having bowed down, one should display the yoni-mudrā.
The ritual gesture (mudrā) of service is as follows:
In the Compendium of Characteristics.

On the seat, for the lotus gesture (padmamudrā), both hands are turned downward; O virtuous one, this is the mudrā. For the question regarding well-being, the deity [uses] it again with the hands turned upward.
The *mudrā* for welcoming is the *argha-mudrā*, while the *añjali* is said to be the [general] gesture. By extending the ring finger and the thumb, it is called the noble *pādya-mudrikā*.
The wise practitioner, having placed the hands with the palms facing upward and the undersides turned down,
should join the four fingers, excluding the little finger, and hold them raised.
This mudrā for rinsing the mouth has been taught by me as being turned downwards;
when the thumbs are touched [together], it is proclaimed as the mudrā of the garment.
This same ring finger, when touched, is known by the name of the *mudrā* ornament;
indeed, the little finger, when touched, is the seal (*mudrikā*) of the sacred thread (*upavīta*).
The *mudrā* of fragrance is formed by touching the tip of the little finger with the tip of the thumb;
having turned the hand downward, one should join the tips of the index fingers.
O Supreme Goddess, this mudrā with the tips of the thumbs joined is called Puṣpā;
O Great Goddess, one should touch the tip of the forefinger with the tip of the thumb.
This is declared to be the mudrā for incense, which is pleasing to all the gods.
One should touch the tip with the tips of the index fingers, or with the middle fingers in the presence of the deities.
Dīpamudrā, Muditā, Sarvadevapriyā, and Śubhā;
O Goddess, the preceptor should touch the tip of the Amā finger with the tip of the Jyeṣṭhā finger.
The Naivedya mudrā is said to bring satisfaction to the deity.
Kāli is in the heart.
One should worship the Goddess with a sword and a severed head in her upper left and lower left hands;
one should worship the [deity] with the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting in the upper right and lower right hands of the Goddess.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Kulamuktikallolinī composed by Śrī Ādyānanda.
Now follows the offering to the protective deities (āvaraṇapūjā).
In the Meru-tantra.

Then, at the conclusion of the flower offerings, one should perform the worship of the surrounding deities (āvaraṇārcana) using the letters of the Mātṛkā, each encased by the mantra and accompanied by the bindu.

One should worship the limbs of the deity in sequence with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; thereafter, one should worship the Mothers by merging them into their respective positions on the limbs.
Having worshipped the first enclosure, one should then worship the deity;
likewise, one should again worship the eight deities of the second enclosure.
In the Somabhujagāvalī:
Then, the wise practitioner should offer libations three times with the root mantra;
having taken up the water of the Great Goddess, he should worship her attendants.
The first ritual procedure is with the six limbs; the second is with the gurus;
the third should be with the retinue; the fourth with the world-protectors;
and the fifth is said to be with their weapons—such is the general sequence.
In the Śaktiyāmala:
Having informed the Goddess, one should then worship her attendants;
thereafter, having performed the worship of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), one should worship the lineage of gurus.
Thus it is said: "The Vāyavyā [Nityā] shall be eternal and her power indeed imperishable;
she is proclaimed by name as the one who possesses the six ancillary deities (ṣaḍaṅgadevatā)."
134a) In the Meru-tantra:
One should worship the heart-mantra and the others in the filaments, beginning from the southeast corner.
The eye-mantra at the front, and the weapon-mantra in the directions.
In another tantra:
One should worship the six limbs upon the bodies and the filaments of the goddess.
Regarding the phrase "in the filaments":
The sequence of worship is also [found] in the Jñānārṇava.
The worship of the limbs [of the deity] is performed in the intermediate directions—namely, southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast—and in the center.
In the Somabhujagāvalī:
Having performed the sacrifice, one should worship the heart in the southeast and the head in the northeast;
the crest-lock (śikhā) is to be worshipped in the southwest, and one should worship the armor (kavaca) in the northwest.
Having worshipped the Eye (Netra) in front, one should then worship the Weapon (Astra) in the cardinal directions.
Meditation on the deity with six limbs.
In the Merutantra and in the Śāradā[tantra].
And the deities of the limbs are to be meditated upon.
The principal female forms have rays that are white as frost, crystal-like, dark, blue, black, and reddish; they hold the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Therefore, O limb, the deities should be meditated upon by the wise in that very sequence.
In the Mānasollāsa.
Between the one to be worshipped and the worshipper, the direction facing east is proclaimed by the wise;
that which is to the right of it is the south, and that which is to the left is the north.
Also in the *Sārasaṃgraha*:
The deities facing the sacrificer and the ten directions facing the deities—
these are to be known as the quarters beginning with the East in rites such as worship and fire-offerings.
In the Meru Tantra.
In the worship of the enclosure (āvaraṇa-pūjana), the eastern direction should be understood as being in front of the deity;
from that point, the worship of the retinue is performed in a clockwise direction.
And thus.
As for the worship of the Brahmī and other goddesses, it should begin from the foremost petal of the Goddess and proceed clockwise, since no specific rule to the contrary has been stated.
Then there should be the worship for the selection; one should first designate the east.
Furthermore, it should be understood from the statement in the *Nṛsiṃhakalpa* that the worship of the retinue begins with that [deity] and proceeds clockwise.

This same principle should be understood for the worship of the wheel (*cakra*) and so forth. Prior to the invocation of the deity, the worship of Dharma and the others is performed in the corners starting from the southeast (āgneya), and the worship of the pedestal-shaktis (*pīṭhaśakti*) is performed on the eight filaments starting from the east; this has been stated previously.
In that very same way, one should worship those worthy of worship in their true nature, because at that time there is no distinction between the object of worship and the worshipper.
In the Tantra.
One should worship the lineage of gurus starting from the northwest and ending at the northeast.
The lineage of gurus—the assembly of the divine stream, the accomplished stream, and the human stream—has been explained previously.
In the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*, Bhairava said:
O Mother Goddess, O Mahāmāyā, who brings about both bondage and liberation!
Now I desire to hear about the unsurpassed form of the Guru.
The goddess said:
The lineage of gurus is indeed manifold due to the weight of the extensive mantras;
since time itself is beginningless, how can I describe it to you?
Without knowing the category of the family (kula), one will have lost the way;
for one who has lost the way, the knowledge of mantras does not come within the range of its proper fruit.
If there is no lineage succession among the gurus and their disciples, then the mantras, tantras, and vidyās are fruitless; of this there is no doubt.
If a disciple does not know twenty, or even nine, seven, or three generations of his gurus' lineage, he is one whose spiritual succession is lost.
One should know that the lineage of the Guru is more wondrous and greater than one's own lineage;
O Maheśvara, the giver of mantras should be known as superior even to one's father.
Therefore, O Lord of Gods, listen briefly to these gurus in all cases:
first, O Lord of Gods, everywhere the giver of the mantra is the primary guru.
You are indeed the supreme-non-supreme Guru, and from you I am the Parameṣṭhī;
in all mantras and vidyās, I am myself the embodiment of Prakṛti.
Then there is the form of the Puruṣa, and then the lineage of one's own gurus;
for they indeed are portions of myself, and especially my devotees.
O Lord, the gurus of the divine lineage (divyaugha) and likewise the gurus of the accomplished lineage (siddhaugha) bestow success everywhere and in all mantras.
I shall briefly describe the multitudes of human beings before you;
therein is the goddess Kālikā—listen now to her lineage of gurus.
Mahādevī, Mahādeva, Tripurā, and Bhairava—these are declared to be the Gurus of the Divine Current (divyaugha). Now I shall describe the Siddhas of the Siddha Current (siddhaugha).
Brahmānanda, Pūrṇa, Calacitta,
Calācala, Kumāra, Krodhana, Varada, and Smaradīpana.
O beloved, hear now of Māyā and Māyāvatī, along with the multitudes of their descendants:
Vimala, Kuśala, Bhīmasena, and Sudhākara.
Mīna, Gorakṣaka, Bhojadeva, Prajāpati, Mūladeva, Araṃtadeva, Vighnaśa, and Hutāśana.
Samaya, Ānanda, and Saṃtoṣa are remembered as the gurus of Kālikā.
Likewise, the words of Śiva to the Goddess are divine and eternal in the presence of the gods; they are perfected both on earth and here as well.
Among the multitudes of human beings, they always assume my form;
ending with the word Ānandanātha, these gurus bestow all spiritual accomplishments.
Even women and those in the form of gurus are proclaimed as being both the beginning and the end;
O Goddess, one should worship one's own guru at the conclusion of the stream of human beings.
In the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*.
Alternatively, the gurus have been previously mentioned in all the scriptures.
135a) "Previously" refers to what was stated regarding the morning duties.
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*.
Whichever heavy syllable-groups (gaṇas) are prescribed for whichever mantras, those very ones are to be worshipped at the beginning of the ritual service; this has been stated by me in brief.
One who does not know the names of the gurus should worship three gurus, or four; beyond that, no restriction should be made.
The Guru, the Supreme Guru, the Guru of both the Supreme and the Non-supreme,
and the Parameṣṭhi Guru— these are declared to be your Gurus.
O child, if one should perform worship without first worshipping the Guru, it will be defective in every respect; however, through the worship of the Kula, it becomes endowed with all virtues.
O Vaṭukeśvara, whether it be initiation, the master, the noble lineage, or the family itself— having brought the Guru into that body, one should meditate upon the Guru in the form of the Kula.
In that regard, the lineage is as [important] as the Guru, but not so the family practitioner;
and the lineage of the Gurus, once explained, must be guarded with great effort.
O Kuleśvara, this [initiation] should not be given anywhere to a practitioner who has fallen from yoga, nor to one who is a mere beast; indeed, their names should not even be uttered.
Whether in the Vaiṣṇava, Śākta, or Gāṇapatya Tantra,
one should first meditate upon one's own Guru, and thereafter upon the fourfold lineage of Gurus.
Having performed the worship, one should sacrifice to the deity and not practice any contraction [of the ritual];
thereafter, at all times, one should invoke and worship the goddesses.

As for the ritual application (*prayoga*): "I worship the Śrī Mahādevī, obeisance to the Śrī Pādukā. Having worshipped thus, one should satisfy [the deities] three times or once with the nectar from the Guru-vessel as before. In this sequence, one should then worship and satisfy the deities of the host of rays (*raśmivṛnda*).
In the Meru Tantra.
Then, one should worship in the corners starting from the east and proceeding counter-clockwise;
first, in the triangular section, one should worship Kālī, Kapālinī, and Kulyā.
In the second triangle, one should place Nīlāṅganā and Calākā;
in the third, Kuru-kullā and Virodhinī; and in the fourth, Vipracittā.
One should worship Ugrā, who possesses fierce radiance and is blazing, in the fourth triangle;
and one should worship Mātrā and Mitā in the fifth triangle.
In the Kali age.
O Supreme Goddess, Kālī and the others are to be worshipped in sequence;
practitioners must perform the worship of all of them three times each.
Now, their meditation [is described] in the Kālitantra and the Merutantra.
All are dark-complexioned, holding swords in their hands, adorned with garlands of severed heads,
displaying the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) with their left hands, and smiling.
Now, regarding the eight-petaled [lotus] in the Kumārī-kalpa.

One should worship the [deities] beginning with Brāhmī on the petals; one should worship the Bhairavas at the tips of the petals; then the world-protectors (lokapālas) on the outside, and their weapons further outside than that.
135b) Regarding the true nature of the family.
And outside the mandala are Brāhmī, Nārāyaṇī,
Māheśvarī, Cāmuṇḍā, Kaumārī, and Aparājitā.
Vārāhī is likewise to be worshipped, and Nārasiṃhī in the same way.
In the Meru Tantra:
Brāhmī, Nārāyaṇī, Māheśvarī, Cāmuṇḍā, Kumārikā,
Aparājitā, Vārāhī, and Nārasiṃhī are on the eight petals.
Likewise.
The limb-mantras (aṅgamantra) for worship should end with "Oṃ namaḥ," and likewise for the oblation (homa).
And ending with "svāhā."
The meditation and worship of the Brāhmī and other goddesses are as described in the Mahākālasaṃhitā.
Then [I worship] Tāra, Pāśā, and her consort; thereafter, I worship Brāhmī and the Śrī-pādukā.
Then, indeed, one should meditate upon her, the beloved of Brahmā.
Brahmāṇī is mounted upon a swan, golden-hued, four-armed, four-faced,
and three-eyed, holding a beard and likewise a lotus.
The supreme practitioner should meditate upon the Goddess, who wears a mass of matted hair, possesses a beautiful smile, and holds a staff, a lotus-seed rosary, and a sacred thread.
Having meditated thus upon the consort of Brahmā, O beloved, one should worship her according to one's capacity;
then, having remembered the sandals of Nārāyaṇī, thereafter—
Having uttered "I worship," O Dear One, one should meditate upon that Vaiṣṇavī,
the daughter of Nārāyaṇa, who is greatly radiant, dark-complexioned, and mounted upon Garuḍa.
Adorned with various ornaments, possessing beautiful hair and four arms,
she is the supreme goddess holding a bell, a conch, a skull-cup, and a discus.
O Maheśānī, having meditated thus upon her who is beautiful in every limb and whose showers of nectar flow most intensely, one should then contemplate her with great effort.
Having worshipped Mahādevī, one should worship Māheśvarī again; O Dear One, having uttered "Sa-vindu-sa," one should then invoke Māheśvarī.
Then, having uttered "the auspicious sandals" (śrīpādukām), one says "I worship" (pūjayāmi);
thereafter, O lady of excellent hips, I shall tell you the meditation upon this [deity] during the night.
Māheśvarī is mounted upon a bull, white in color, endowed with three eyes,
and holding a skull, a *ḍamaru* drum, a boon-granting gesture, an abhaya gesture, and a trident.
Having performed meditation upon the Great Goddess, one should worship the Divine Lady— who holds a chisel and is adorned with various ornaments— according to one's ability.
Having uttered the seed-syllable *ṛm* and *Cāmuṇḍā*, [one says] "I worship the Śrīpādukā.
Having worshipped the Great Goddess, one should then perform meditation.
[I bow to] Cāmuṇḍā, who has a fierce laugh, whose face is revealed, whose countenance is terrifying, and who possesses three eyes;

she has the luster of a blue lotus, a joyful body, and a garland of human heads and skulls; she holds a sword, a trident, a skull-cup, a vessel of human heads, and a shield, and she is mounted upon a corpse.
And I visualize her as being intoxicated by wine, joyful, and possessing a fierce form.
Having meditated thus, one should worship the goddess Cāmuṇḍā, the sovereign of the world;
and with the syllable *ṛ*, one should perform the meditation after worshipping Kaumārī.
Kaumārī has the luster of saffron, is three-eyed, and is seated upon a peacock;
she has four arms and bestows the spear, the noose, the goad, and the gesture of fearlessness.
One should contemplate the goddess Kaumārī as adorned with various ornaments and in a state of playful intoxication; having performed meditation, one should worship her according to one's capacity.
One should worship the Great Goddess Aparājitā with the Vāgbhava [syllable] according to all the previously mentioned rites; thereafter, one should perform the meditation.
And one should meditate upon Aparājitā, who is yellow in luster, holding an eye, a mudrā, and the granting of boons,
as well as a lotus and a citron.
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite, the practitioner should worship with devotion;
then, with the syllable *auṃ*, he should worship Vārāhī in her beautiful attire.
O Supreme Goddess, understand that the meditation on Vārāhī consists in her state of being free from fear;
one should meditate upon the auspicious Vārāhī, who has the luster of smoke-colored hue and the face of a boar.
One should worship this supreme goddess Vārāhī according to the prescribed rite, holding a shield, a sword, a mace, and a plough in her four arms.
By means of the emission, the foremost of practitioners attains the Nārasiṃhī;
she who possesses a body identical to that of Nṛsiṃha becomes Nārasiṃhī.
I shall explain her meditative absorption (dhyāna); O Goddess, listen to that.
Her tongue trembling with rage, her own mouth wide open, with eyes of the moon, sun, and fire, stained from foot to navel with blood, and having torn apart the body of the lord of the Daityas; |||

I praise the Man-Lion (Nṛsiṃhī), who bears the discus, conch, noose, goad, thunderbolt, mace, and ploughshare; she is terrifying with her sharp, prominent fangs and adorned with various ornaments made of jewels.
Having meditated thus, one should worship Maheśvarī according to one's ability.
In the Jñānārṇava:
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Śukra, Krodha, Unmatta, Bhairava, Kapālī, and Bhīṣaṇa; Saṃhāra is remembered as the eighth.
Now follows this meditation.
In the Tripuroṣārasamuccaya.

They bear staffs, skulls, and tridents as dark as collyrium and blue lotuses; they possess lightness endowed with power, have three eyes, and wield fierce staff-like arms like those of poets. They wear elephant skins draped over their shoulders, their foreheads are furrowed by knitted brows, and the tips of their hair are adorned by swarms of playful bees.
Having meditated upon them as being joyful within their hearts and possessed of their own youth, their mantra is as follows:
The short vowels, joined with the bindu and preceded by Vāk and Māyā.

One should perform worship starting from the east in a clockwise sequence. With that [mantra]: *aiṃ hrīṃ aṃ asitāṅgabhairava śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi namaḥ*. *Aiṃ hrīṃ iṃ rurubhairava śrī...* and so forth should be understood accordingly.
However, according to the Mahākālasaṃhitā, it is stated that in the place of the Bhairavas, there are indeed Bhairavīs.
Then Bhairavī is to be worshipped at the tips of the petals,
followed by Mahābhairavī, and after that, Siṃhabhairavī.
Having likewise worshipped Dhūmrabhairavī, then Bhīmabhairavī,
thereafter Unmattabhairavī, and Vaśīkaraṇabhairavī.
Mohanī Bhairavī is to be worshipped, and thereafter one should sacrifice in the underground chamber (bhūgṛha).
In another tantra:
And Bhairavī, Mahāsiṃhī, Dhūmrā, Bhīmā, and the others;
then Unmattabhairavī and Vaśīkaraṇabhairavī.
At the tip of the leaf is Bhairavī, whose nature is the perfection of all beings; their visualization is just like that of Bhairavī herself.

In that regard, the *Śāradātilaka* states: "I worship the Goddess, who possesses the splendor of a thousand rising suns, who wears a crimson silken garment and a garland upon her head; whose breasts are smeared with red pigment; who holds in her lotus-like hands a rosary, a book, the gesture of knowledge (*vidyā*), the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and the gesture of boon (*vara*); whose beauty is like a lotus face shining with three eyes; and who wears a crown of jewels and the cool-rayed moon."
[She who possesses] a gentle smile; [as stated] in the Mahākālasaṃhitā.
The wise practitioner should worship the guardians of the directions (dikpālas), beginning from the east and ending with the northeast;
having first uttered the seed-syllable of Indra, he should then [offer] to Indra.
Having offered [the oblation] to the Lord of Suras (Śiva) together with his limbs (aṅgas),
immediately thereafter to him along with his retinue (parivāra), and after that to him equipped with his weapons (sāyudha).

Then, one should worship him along with his vehicle, ending with the word "namaḥ. One should likewise worship the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) using their respective seed-syllables (bījas) beginning with *laṃ*, *raṃ*, *yaṃ*, *kṣaṃ*, *vaṃ*, *yaṃ*, *śaṃ*, *haṃ*, *aṃ*, and *kaṃ*. As for the visualization (dhyāna), it is found in the Merutantra and the Tūrṇayāga.
I worship Indra, the lord of the gods, who is yellow, mounted upon Airāvata,
all-pervading, thousand-eyed, two-armed, yellow, and the wielder of the thunderbolt.
I bow to the Lord who has fire as his splendor, who is red in hue, whose hand holds a white spear, who is well-adorned, whose vehicle is a ram, and whose eyes are red at the corners.
Yama, the lord of the departed, is black, seated upon a buffalo,
holding the staff of Time, cruel, and surrounded by terrifying messengers.
[One should visualize] Nirṛti, the lord of the Rākṣasas, mounted upon a corpse-eater;
smoke-colored, with a sword in hand, and possessing tawny eyebrows, beard, and mustache.
I bow to Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures, who is seated upon a crocodile, whose lotus-like hands resemble lightning, whose body is white, and who is pot-bellied.
One should worship Vāyu, the lord of the vital breaths, who is smoke-colored, holds a supreme red goad in his hand,
is mounted upon a vātapramī deer, and is running with great speed.
And Kuvera, the lord of the Yakṣas, white in color, holding a trident and a mace,
seated upon a lion-throne, together with Medalā and Citriṇī.
The Lord of Knowledge (Vidyādhipa), holding a blue trident, riding upon a bull,
possessing three eyes and the moon upon his forehead, wearing a mass of matted hair, and white in complexion.
I worship Ananta, the lord of serpents, who is white in color, adorned with a circle of hoods upon his head, stout and tall, holding a discus, and emitting poison.
I worship him, the Lord of the World and the Creator, who is red in color, holds a beautiful lotus in his hand,
is mounted upon a swan, and performs the recitation of the Vedas.
In the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
One should worship everything according to the procedure taught by Indra; one should worship Śeṣanāga between Rakṣas and Varuṇa, O Supreme Goddess.
Then, one should worship Brahmā between Īśāna and Śakra.
Outside of that, O Goddess, one should worship the thunderbolt (vajra), the spear (śakti), the staff (daṇḍa),
the sword (khaḍga), the noose (pāśa), the goad (aṅkuśa), the mace (gadā), and the trident (triśūla).
Likewise, the discus (cakra) should be worshipped between Rakṣas and Varuṇa;
thereafter, one should worship the lotus (padma) between Īśāna and Śakra.
In the Kālītantra:
An offering (bali), as well as worship, should be given to all of them;
likewise, unguents, fragrance, incense, lamps, and a beverage.
The practitioners must perform the worship three times for each of all [the goddesses].
In that very same [text].
One should worship Mahākāla on the right side of the Goddess’s vulva.
The ritual for the worship of the retinue is found in the Bhairavatantra.
The seed-syllables of the letters of the names today are those ending in the suffix -ṅ, followed by "namaḥ."
In the Kālī-kalpa.
Having first extracted the word *śrīpada*, one should then extract the word *pādukā*;
thereafter, one should say "I worship" (*pūjayāmi*), and subsequently worship the deities of the limbs (*aṅgadevatāḥ*).
In the Kumārī Tantra:
Then, having worshipped the root goddess with water for the feet and other offerings, one should satisfy her.
In the Bhairavī Tantra:
Then one should offer incense and lamps to the Goddess, as well as an offering of food (naivedya),
and with devotion present three handfuls of flowers along with the special arghya water mixed with unhusked rice.
Kālī is in the heart.
One should worship the Goddess with a sword and a severed head in her upper left and lower left hands;
one should worship the gesture of granting boons (varada) and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) in her upper right and lower right hands.
In the Meru-tantra:
Again, having recited the root mantra,
one should utter "sāṅgāyai saparivārāyai" and then pronounce the name of the Goddess ending in the dative case.
Now, the offering (bali).
In the *Yāmala*:
O Maheśvarī, one should offer the bali-oblation at the conclusion of worship and at the beginning of meals.
The mantra for the offering of the *bali* to Mahākāla is as follows:
In the Kālīkulārṇava.
And from Mahākāla, one should say "Lord of the Cremation Ground" (Śmaśānādhipa);
then, ending with "Īmam," one should offer a double oblation of meat and food.
Then, cause me to grasp the pair of feet that ward off obstacles;
perform [this] for me and grant me success, joined with the *svāhā* exclamation.
One should cause [the offering] to be given to the god Mahākāla with [the mantra] beginning with the Praṇava (Om).
The mantra for the offering of the *vīradāna* to Kālī is also in that very same place.
137b) Come, come, O Mother of the worlds, likewise the progenitress of the worlds! Accept,
accept this constant offering of bali from now on.
Grant success! [Then] the pair of feet; then "destroy the enemies";
having uttered the word "yuga," then again the pair of *kūrca*s.
Having first extracted two *hṛllekhās*, and then again two at the end, one should then extract the mantra; with *phaṭ* at the end, it is Vahnisundarī.
This wonderful rite of offering is concealed in all tantras;
according to the names [of the deities] among all the Kālī vidyās, one should cast the offering.
In this context, the offering of a goat and so forth will be described hereafter.
In the Kālītantra:
Having thus first performed the worship at the root according to the prescribed rule,
one should repeatedly offer food offerings and other gifts to the Goddess according to one's ability.
In the Kumārīkalpa.
Then one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) ten times with lamps.
In the Kālitantra:
Then, being composed, the practitioner, having bowed his head to the Guru situated [above] and having meditated upon the Goddess,
should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times.
With a rosary made of ivory beads, using the upper canine tooth as the central Meru bead,
one should place the hand— imbued with the fruit of the recitation consisting of radiant energy— into [the disciple's] hand.
The knower of mantras [should perform this] with the mantra: "O you who guard the most secret of secrets."
In this context, before the recitation of the root mantra, the recitation of the Mahākāla mantra is also mandatory.
This has been stated in the Vīracūḍāmaṇi:
One should recite the great mantra of Mahākāla one hundred and eight times;
one should likewise extract the Praṇava, the Hṛllekhā, and the Kaulinī seed-syllable.
One should utter the seed-syllable *kartṛkā* for Mahākāla;
then, having uttered the seed-syllable *prasāda*, one should utter that which follows for Mahādeva.
One should extract Krodhīśa mounted on Vahni, with the left eye and the bindu;
then the word "Kālikāyai," and finally, one should extract the seed-syllable of Prāsāda.

Mahādeva is Mahākāla, the bestower of all accomplishments (*siddhi*). *Kaulinī* is the seed-syllable *kṣmrīṃ*; *kartṛkā* is the seed-syllable *hūṃ*. *Krodhīśa* is the letter *ka*; *vahni* is the letter *ra*; the remainder is easily understood. After the recitation of Mahākāla and prior to the recitation of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), there is also the *kullukā* of Kālī.
"Japyā" means they are to be deposited (nyastavyā). This has been stated in the Rudrayāmala:
The Lord said:
Having visualized the *kullukā* upon the head, one should contemplate the bridge (*setu*) in the heart;
then, one should extract the great bridge (*mahāsetu*) in the *viśuddhi* [cakra] and the thousand-spoked [cakra].
In Maṇipurī, however, is Nirvāṇa; Mahākuṇḍalinī is below;
Kāmarāja is in Svādhiṣṭhāna; and Kākinī is situated in the head.
Having reflected according to the rule, O Goddess, one should meditate on [the energy] extending from the vicinity of the mūlādhāra to the end of the viśuddha, as slender as a fiber of a lotus stalk.
For the all-pervading Lord has enveloped the root-mantras from the location of the Vedas down to the tip of the tongue.
In the Meru-tantra:
Then, with the root mantra, one should perform all the preceding nyāsas;
[the recitation should be] one thousand and eight times, or half of that, or three hundred times.
Or, one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times without sloth.
In the *Maṇtratantraprakāśa*.
Having performed the internal sacrifice with devotion one thousand and eight times, one should recite that which is done daily; this is known as the obligatory recitation (*nitya-japa*).
In the Uttaratantra:
The practitioner should never recite fewer than three hundred [mantras];
rather, he should recite one thousand and eight, or half of that, or three hundred.
Or one should recite it one hundred and eight times daily, remaining free from sloth.
And the recitation (japa) should be performed preceded by meditation (dhyāna).
Regarding the recitation that kindles [the fire], it is said in another tantra:
The seed-syllable of Jīvanī, adorned with three feet,
accompanied by the vowel *anusvāra* and the digit (*kalā*), is declared to be the triad of seed-syllables.
Then one should offer the *tumburu* oblation, and after that, the *saṃhāra*;
O Goddess, at the beginning of the Vidyā, one should perform the sacrifice endowed with the three *bindus* and the *kalās*.
This illuminating Vidyā is saluted by all the Āgamas;
he who recites the supreme Kālikā without knowing this illuminating Vidyā [is ignorant].
Before long he meets with death, and having died, he goes to hell.
That has been stated in the Nīla Tantra:
I shall now proclaim the meditation on the mantra, which bestows omniscience through recitation;
O Great Goddess, even a slayer of a Brahmin attains perfection through meditation on the mantra.
One should contemplate the syllable Hṛllekhā in the mūlādhāra-cakra, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns, and the second syllable, yellow in color, in the svādhiṣṭhāna-cakra.
At the navel, the practitioner should visualize the seed-syllable of the beard (KŪRC), possessing great luster and the hue of a dark cloud,
resembling the moon, as it was previously perceived by the yogis.
One should meditate on the *kūrca* seed-syllable in the heart, resembling the fire of cosmic destruction;
or else, one should meditate on the *kūrca* at the crown of the head, shining like the full moon and radiant as nectar.
One should then visualize the tongue as being set ablaze by the spreading masses of its light.
One should contemplate all ignorance as extending from the base to the aperture of Brahmā.
Resembling ten million suns, she was previously beheld by yogins.
The seed-syllable of Māyā is HṚLLEṢĀ.
Or else, meditating on the Kuṇḍalinī composed of light, extending from the base (mūlādhāra) to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
The characteristics of japa are described in the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*.
Japa is the repetition of syllables; I shall now describe its varieties.
Japa is said to be of two kinds: vocal (vācika) and mental (mānasa).
The first type, the *aupāṃśu*, is proclaimed to be twofold and performed loudly;
the *jihvājapa* is to be understood as that which is performed by the tongue alone.
When one recites a mantra with the mind alone, that is called mental recitation (*mānasa-japa*).
Whispered recitation (*upāṃśu*) is ten times superior to loud recitation (*uccair-japa*).
Muttering with the tongue is a hundredfold [more effective], while mental muttering is a thousandfold;
this is achieved by placing the deity within one's heart and making one's own heart steady.
Having bowed to Śiva and the other gurus, one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind—
very slowly, indistinctly, neither too fast nor too slow.
In the Meru Tantra:
Japa is the repetition of syllables; it is proclaimed to be of three kinds:
the inferior is vocal japa, the middling is physical, and the best is mental.
If a mantra is recited with words that are high, low, or circumflex in pitch, yet with clear syllables and distinct words,
one who lacks the proper vocalization is known as a *vācaka*.
One should recite the mantra slowly, moving the lips slightly;
that which is audible to some extent is the physical medium, and it is called "middling."
One should utter the sequence of words and syllables with awareness according to their proper places;
preceded by the recollection of the meaning, this mental recitation (mānasajapa) is the most excellent.
The recollection of the meaning of the mantra is described in the Yāmala.
Perceiving through his intellect the identity of the deity, the guru, and the mantra,
he should recite the mantra with its latent impressions (vāsanā), being contented and of steady mind.
The *Uttaratantra* speaks of the objective impregnation (*arthavāsanā*) along with its latent tendencies (*savāsanā*):
"Now I shall declare, O Great Goddess, the determination of the reality of the impregnations."
From the three seed-syllables, she is Śāmbhavī, consisting solely of the power of consciousness;
by means of the two [syllables] of Hṛllekhā alone, she brings about creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
In the two seed-syllables of sound, she is indeed the awakener of the science of grammar;
by the very word of invocation, she is eternally the embodiment of perfect consciousness.
This Great Vidyā remains ever awake, manifesting pure consciousness alone;
it is neither asleep nor cursed, and therefore it bestows the fruit of the scriptures.
Prior to extraction, there is a cognition of the sequence of sounds according to the sequence of meanings from the two types of seed-syllables.
I shall explain the meaning of the single syllable, which directly bestows the fruit of liberation;
because it possesses the nature of Śiva through the letter *ka*, it alone grants liberation.
O Goddess of gods, by means of the three seed-syllables, she brings about creation, maintenance, and destruction;
through union with the blazing sun, she is auspicious and composed entirely of splendor.
O Goddess of the gods, she bestows the fruit of absolute liberation through the *bindu* and her partless nature; through the three seed-syllables, she is devoted to the Supreme Lord of Consciousness.

Through the individual soul (*jīvātman*) and the three seed-syllables (*bīja*), she is of the nature of Śiva and Śakti; through two seed-syllables, she is the source of both meaning and sound, yet devoid of conceptualization (*bhāva*).
In the Meru Tantra:
The vocal [mantra] performs the six rites; the physical accomplishes all siddhis;
the mental achieves liberation; and any other than these performs minor rites.
Through constant recitation, the deity, being praised, becomes pleased;
from recitation comes accomplishment, from recitation comes accomplishment, from recitation comes accomplishment—it is not far off.
Just as a minor lord becomes satisfied with wealth,
so too do the minor deities become satisfied by offerings and worship.
Just as a lord becomes submissive through great virtues because he possesses such qualities,
so too do Viṣṇu and the Sun grant fruits solely through the power of recitation (japa).
The descriptions such as "wearing a turban" and "wearing a tunic" and so forth should be understood according to the section on the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*).
The mantra for grasping the rosary.
Having sprinkled it with the *arghyā* water, one should then pray to it as follows:
"Oṃ Māṃ! O Rosary, O Great Illusion, you whose nature is all-pervasive power!"
"The fourfold aims have been entrusted to you; therefore, grant me success. Having thus worshipped it, one should then take the rosary in the right hand.
Having first uttered the seed-syllable (bīja) of Gaṇapati, immediately thereafter—
Placing a garland in his right hand while mentally meditating upon the Goddess, he says: "O Mālatī, grant that there be no obstacle."

One should contemplate the Guru upon the crown of the head according to his color and other attributes; one should meditate on the mantra in the middle of the throat as being yellow in color and golden.
One should place Mahāmāyā in the heart, oneself at the feet of the Guru.

Having meditated thus, one should hold the rosary near one's own heart and perform the recitation while moving each bead with the tip of the thumb. At the conclusion of the recitation, having prayed: *Hrīṃ, salutations to Siddhi;
O Rosary, you who grant pleasure to all the gods, bestow auspiciousness upon me.*
"O auspicious lady, bring me welfare and increase my fame and heroism. Having spoken thus, the victory garland should then be placed in secret upon the sacrificial victim while it is being wrapped.
In the Kālītantra:
The knower of mantras should offer the fruit of the recitation, consisting of radiant light, into the hand of the Goddess with the mantra: "O you who are the protector of the most secret of secrets."
Having poured water into the right hand of the deity, one should offer it.
Thus it is said regarding the left hand of the Goddess in the Bhairava Tantra.
Praising [the deity] and circumambulating [them], one should prostrate on the ground like a staff;
thereafter, one should recite the armor known as the *Śrījaganmaṅgala*.
Then, preceded by the ringing of bells, he praised him with hymns of praise.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the Kulamuktikallolinī composed by Śrī Ādyānanda.

Those who have performed the *dhūti* [purification] of the seed-syllable "Karpūra"— which consists of the middle and final vowels, is devoid of the nasal bindu, joined with the left eye (the letter 'i'), and followed by the syllables "mātṛ" and "taṃ tripuraphara"— are victorious.
For those who have attained all perfections, prose and verse issues forth spontaneously from the cavity of their mouths like beautiful rain-clouds pouring down streams of nectar. || 1 ||
O Great Goddess, if a person ever recites even once another seed-syllable— surrounded by Īśāna, the Moon, and Vāma-śramaṇa, and ending with the couple (Śiva and Śakti) whose luster has faded—
he shall conquer the Lord of Speech, long delude even the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), and captivate the multitude of lotus-eyed women.
When he who has the crescent moon as his crest-jewel and the most terrible young lion as his ear-ornament prevails. || 2 ||
Those who recite the mantra "ĪŚO VAISVĀNARASTHAḤ ŚAŚADHARAVILASADVĀMANETREṆA YUKTO BĪJANE DVANDVAMANYADVIGALITACIKURE KĀLIKE" [attain their goal].
They slay the hater and bring even the three worlds under their control when [the mantra] is on the two corners of the mouth,
on the face bearing the two streams of weapons, and on the right [side] of the three-syllabled [mantra]. (3)
Above, in the left palm, is a sword; below that, in the right, are the gestures of fearlessness and boon. O Hara, O Kālikā, who are enriched by the three worlds!
Having recited this mantra of yours, they meditate upon its power for that purpose.
Eight of these reside in the hands of the three-eyed Lord, manifesting as accomplishments upon his face.

O Mother, Consort of the Destroyer of Smara, those who recite this mantra— beginning with the first letter of the class [Ka] joined with fire [Ra], followed by the three very charming crescent-moons [I], the pair of *kūrca* [Ū], the pair of *lajjā* [Śrīṃ Śrīṃ], and then, O smiling-faced one, having joined the pair of *ṭha* [Ṭha Ṭha] below that— and who meditate upon Your own form, they become the very play of the dance of Lakṣmī.
Those with eyes like lotus petals become capable of assuming any form at will. || 5 ||

Whether individually, in pairs, or even all three together— having joined these supreme seeds, which are the ultimate secret, with your name, those who always meditate upon and recite them find that Kamalā dwells within their lotus-eyes and Vāgdevī resides in their bright, pure faces.
[O Goddess] who possesses a garland of divine skulls, whose breasts are abundant, full, and adorned with a necklace of trembling gems.

Meditating upon you— the creator of the three worlds, the three-eyed one, clad in the directions as her garment, standing in the cremation ground upon a bed of corpses, with hips resplendent with a girdle formed by a multitude of lifeless arms,
and intensely engaged in amorous play with Mahākāla— [I seek refuge].
O Mother, even a monkey is dull-witted. ||7||

They meditate upon you, the youthful consort of Hara, who have entered and are ever contented within a cremation ground that is intensely crowded with auspicious yet terrible heaps of corpses, heads, and bones,
and where you manifest your passion through amorous dalliance above it; they never turn their thoughts elsewhere.
Their contempt. || 8 ||
O Mother, what can we of dull intellect say to you? Neither the Creator, nor Īśvara, nor even Hari knows your supreme nature.
Nevertheless, devotion to you makes us speak out even though we are bowed down;
therefore, this must be forgiven, for anger toward those who look upon you as cattle is surely not appropriate. 9.
If a devotee, attached to young women whose breasts and hips are full on all sides, recites your mantra at night— even if naked,
meditating on you with disheveled hair— all the hosts of Siddhas shall come under his control.
The poet lives for a very long time on earth. || 10 ||
If one always meditates upon you, O Great Kālī of supreme erotic bliss, while reciting the mantra in reverse once it has become even and composed,
then for that wise man wandering upon the surface of the earth, the consort of Hara shall become submissive at his lotus-hand.
The multitudes of great siddhis.
O Mother, you give birth to saṃsāra; you sustain the entire world, beginning with the earth, and at the time of dissolution, you withdraw it all.
Therefore, does even Dhātṛ, the lord of the three worlds, Śrīpati, and indeed Maheśa as well— nay, does almost everyone praise you?
Many deluded ones serve the multitudes of gods who are superior to you; O Mother, they do not know anything at all of the Supreme.
I have freely taken refuge in the primordial one, who is worshipped by the wise such as Hari, Hara, and Viriñci, for the sake of the essence of spontaneous delight.
Delighting in great bliss.
The earth, the water, the pure fire, the wind, and the sky—you alone, O auspicious Kālī, consort of the Mountain, are everything.
What praise can there be for you, O Mother? Be gracious toward me, who have no other refuge, and deliver me from the cycle of existence.
My birth has become more abundant.

O Mahākālī, one who dwells in a cremation ground with hair loosened and flowing, wearing a garment of directions (the sky), reciting your mantra a thousand times with flowers whose essence has been shed by the sun,
and intent on meditation upon you— one such as this may freely attain [your state].
Surrounded by the earth.
On a Tuesday at midday, one who has recited even a single name of Kālī with love should offer flowers whose potency has not faded from being swept up in the house, along with their roots,
upon a funeral pyre; mounted upon an elephant and surrounded by his retinue, he shall constantly travel across the earth.
The opening of the attachment.
If a devotee, meditating again and again upon the great palace of the flower-bowed God (Kāmadeva), strewn with exquisite blossoms, recites your hymn and mantra,
he becomes like the lord of the hosts of Gandharvas in his poetic eloquence; never again miserable or wretched, he finally merges into the supreme state.
It prevails.

O Mother, he indeed meditates upon you at night on the five-and-three-spoked seat, within the heart of the corpse-Śiva— your face smiling, intensely united with Mahākāla, and delighting in the beauty of the essence of passion; while he himself is likewise absorbed in the bliss of love for the sake of all people.
He may be the destroyer of Smara.
Whether it be hair, fur, bone, meat, a cat, or even a goat, a sheep, a man, a buffalo, or a ram—
by offering such as these as a sacrifice in your worship to me, O Virala-vaktra, will you not attain every supernatural power?
On every step, something unprecedented comes forth.
One who eats sacrificial food (haviṣya), is devoted to the day, and is intent on meditating upon your lotus feet, should mutter the mantra one hundred thousand times;
furthermore, O Destroyer of Smara, at night, while naked and engaged in the sport of love, a person should properly recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
Equal upon the surface of the earth.
O Mother, recite this hymn of praise known as the *Svarūpa*, which follows the *Mātastava* and includes the ritual for worshipping the pair of your lotus feet, for the sake of complete liberation.
Whether one performs worship at midnight or even during the time of the observance, for him who recites this, the nectar-like essence of poetic eloquence flows forth, even from mere idle chatter.
A multitude of fawn-eyed women imitates him with love-trembling devotion; even the lord of the earth, a veritable representative of Kuvera, is under his sway;
and his enemy, by a mere fragment of his playful power, is cast into prison. Thus, the true devotee, liberated while yet living, prevails.
The representative.
Thus ends the *Karpūra-stotra* composed by the venerable Mahākāla.
Now follows the Trailokyamohana-kavaca (the armor that deludes the three worlds).
The Goddess said:
O Great God, God of gods, who brings joy to the cycle of existence, you are the sovereign of all knowledge; tell me truly whether that knowledge exists within me.
Śrī Mahākāla said:
Listen, O Goddess, to the Great Vidyā, the most excellent among all vidyās,
the Sovereign of All, the Great Vidyā worshipped by all the gods.
By whose mere sidelong glance Hara became the conqueror of the three worlds, and the Lord Brahmā, the progenitor of creatures, became the lord of a single digit of the moon.
Indra, the lord of Śacī and king of the gods; Yama, the leader of Dharma;
Gaṅgā, the purifier of the three worlds; and Kamalā Śrī, the beloved of Hari.
The Sun is the lord of the day, the Moon is the lord of the night,
Varuṇa is the lord of the waters, and Kuvera and others are the lords of wealth.
Vāyu of unimpeded movement, Gajāsya the leader of obstacles,
Vāgīśvara, the preceptor of the gods, the preceptor of the Daityas, and Grahaṃkapi.
For in this way, O Dear One, even all the gods and all the lords of siddhis should guard her secret armor (kavaca) like a mother guards her own child.
Śrī Mahākāla said:

Of this armor (*kavaca*) of Śrī Dakṣiṇakālikā, Mahākālabhairava is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Śmaśānakālikā is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of attaining all desires and liberation during recitation.
May Krīṃ, who is eternally worshipped by Maheśa, protect my forehead;
and may Kriṃ Kriṃ, who was worshipped by Viṣṇu in ancient times, protect my eyes.
*Krīṃ hūṃ hrīṃ*, having been worshipped by Brahmā, certainly protects the nose;
*krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ* protects the face, she who grants all desires when propitiated by Śakra.
*Hrīṃ svāhā*, worshipped by Yama himself, protects the ears;
*krīṃ hūṃ hrīṃ svāhā*, served by Gaṅgā, protects the tongue.
May Oṃ Krīṃ Hūṃ Hrīṃ Svāhā always protect my row of teeth;
may Kālī, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, grant me prosperity when she is constantly well-served.
May the mantra *krīṃ krīṃ hūṃ hūṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ* always protect my upper and lower lips;
this lore, propitiated by the Sun, bestows all accomplishments.
May Mahākālī protect my throat; Oṃ Hrīṃ Krīṃ Svāhā—this mantra is indeed always [efficacious].
Knowledge that has not been propitiated under the Moon does not bestow the fruits of the four aims of life.
May she protect both my hands at all times: *krīṃ krīṃ hūṃ hūṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ svāhā*.
Kālī, the bestower of happiness and liberation, is served by Varuṇa.
Oṃ krīṃ hūṃ hrīṃ phaṭ svāhā—may this heart-mantra protect [me] at all times.
Kālī, the bestower of all prosperity, is served by Kuvera.
May the pair of breasts, [invoked with] *aiṃ hrīṃ oṃ aiṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, always protect [us].
Kālī, worshipped by Vāyu, bestows fame, strength, and happiness.
*Krīṃ krīṃ hūṃ hūṃ hrīṃ phaṭ svāhā!* May Kālī, the bestower of all accomplishments, who is served by Gaṇanātha, always protect my back.
*Krīṃ*, O Dakṣiṇakālikā, *hrīṃ svāhā*—may she always protect the navel;
Kālī, the bestower of pure awakening, is ever served by the Guru.
May the Liṅga protect [me] always, hūṃ hūṃ; O Kālikā in the south, hrīṃ hrīṃ!
Worshipped with white [offerings], Kālī is the bestower of victory over the three worlds.
Pātvaṇḍakoṣe krīṃ krīṃ, O Kālikā of the south, krīṃ svāhā!
This Vidyā, when practiced by Dharā, bestows all jewels.
May Krīṃ Krīṃ protect the anus; Hrīṃ Hrīṃ Svāhā, O Kālikā in the south!
This twelfth Great Vidyā is always worshipped by Rāghava.
May she protect my knees: Oṃ Hrīṃ Dakṣiṇe Kālike Hrīṃ Svāhā.
This Ekādaśī Mahāvidyā was practiced by Meghanāda.
*Krīṃ krīṃ*, O Kālikā of the south! *Hrīṃ hrīṃ svāhā*, may she protect the shanks.
And the twelfth great vidyā was practiced by Prahlāda.
*Krīṃ hūṃ hrīṃ dakṣiṇe kālike krīṃ hūṃ hrīṃ svāhā*.
O Śukadeva, the pair of feet of the Fourteenth [Kālikā] has not been served by you.
KṚĪṂ HRŪṂ HRĪṂ, O Kālikā of the right; KṚĪṂ HŪṂ HRĪṂ, O Kālikā of the right; KṚĪṂ HŪṂ HRĪṂ, likewise upon the fingers.
May Kālī Dvādaśī, who is served by Kṣetrapāla, protect me!
Oṃ krīṃ hūṃ hrīṃ, O Kālikā of the South, krīṃ hūṃ hrīṃ svāhā!
May the Mistress of the Fifteen Śrīs always protect my nails entirely.
Krīṃ Krīṃ Krīṃ Hūṃ Hūṃ Hrīṃ Hrīṃ Krīṃ Krīṃ Krīṃ Hūṃ Hūṃ Hrīṃ Svāhā!
May Ṣoḍaśī Bhairavī, served by Bhairava, protect [me];
may *krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ* protect the body hairs, and may *hūṃ hūṃ* guard the skin.
Hrīṃ hrīṃ, may it always protect my flesh;
O Dakṣiṇakālikā, krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ, may it protect my blood; hūṃ hūṃ, may it always protect my bones and marrow.
Hrīṃ Hrīṃ! May the white [syllable] always protect the joints and apertures; may Svāhā protect [them].
This twenty-two-syllable Vidyā is worshipped by all the worlds.
This Vidyā, the sovereign of all vidyās, is concealed in all tantras;
it was [revealed] by Jamadagni, born of the solar lineage and the son of Śaumyanarāma.
By Jayanta, Sanda, Vali, Narada,
Vibhishana, Cyavana, and Triguṇa Kāśyapa.
By the Lord of Monkeys, by Vasiṣṭha, by Bhauma, by Tripura,
by Mārkaṇḍeya, by Nara, by Droṇa, and by Satyabhāmā.
By Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Kaśyapa, Bhāradvāja, and Jahnu—
all together— the knowledge that destroys old age and death was mastered.
Pūrṇavidyā is proclaimed as Mahākālī, the Queen of Vidyās;
she is Kālī, Kapālinī, Kullā, Kurukullā, and Virodhinī.
Vipracittā, as well as Ugrā, Ugrajvālā, and Prabhā;
Nīlādyanāvalākā, Mātrā, and also Mudrāmitā.
All these [goddesses] hold swords, are adorned with garlands of severed heads, and,
with loud laughter accompanied by the sounds "Hūṃ Hūṃ," are constantly drinking me everywhere.
May Brahmāṇī protect me in the east, and Vaiṣṇavī always in the southeast;
may Māheśvarī protect me in the south, and Cāmuṇḍā always in the southwest.
May Kaumārī protect in the northwest, Aparājitā in the north,
Vārāhī in the north, and Nārasiṃhikā in the northeast.
May Kālī protect [me] below and above; may Kālikā protect my sides and back;
[may she protect me] in water, on land, in the netherworld, and in bed, in the vessel, and in the house.
In Rajasthana, in disputes, in death, in battle,
in the wilderness, on the mountain, or in a desolate place— Kālikā is always my refuge.
On a corpse-seat, in a cremation ground, in an empty house, at a crossroads—
wherever fear may arise, may Kālikā protect me everywhere.
In the constellations, lunar days, and weekdays; likewise in the yogas and karaṇas;
in the month, fortnight, and year; and in the watch, the daṇḍa, and the nimeṣa.
May Śivā protect [me] by day and night; may Kālikā protect during the two twilights;
may Kālikā protect everywhere; may Kālikā protect always.
Whoever should read or hear this divine armor created by Śiva,
having abandoned all sins, shall go to the abode of Śiva.
The best of practitioners who recites this divine armor, which deludes the three worlds and is difficult even for the gods to obtain, shall be endowed with victory in all undertakings.
The Dharma is the source of all dharmas, the Lord of the lords of all vidyās;
he is the overseer of the treasury of Kuvera and possesses a voice like that of the cuckoo.
In poetry he is like Vyāsa; in retaining what he has heard, he is like Gaṇeśa;
in beauty, he is equal to Kāmadeva; and in prowess, he is like Vāyu.
Like Maheśa, he was a lord of yogins; like the leader of the gods, he possessed sovereign power; like Bṛhaspati, he was endowed with equal wisdom; and he was entirely free from old age and death.
He is all-seeing, free from sin, and dear to all.
With unimpeded movement and at peace, accompanied by wife, sons, and daughters,
he who constantly makes his body a suit of armor, the very embodiment of the mantra, [is liberated].
There is no sorrow, no fear, no affliction, no disease, and no defeat;
even amidst great poison and despair, there is indeed no fear of censure.
And conquer your enemies in battle, just as fire consumes straw;
for the Brahmāstra and other weapons and missiles, as well as the Kaṇṭhaka arrows, are indeed at your command.
They cannot pierce his body; his form becomes like a diamond.
[This applies even to] the planets, spirits, piśācas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kinnaras.
Indeed, all flee from afar; the perpetrator of violence surely perishes.
Fire does not burn his body, nor does the sun scorch it.
The wind does not dry her up, nor does the sun cause her distress;
she is protected by Kālī like a son, and the moon makes her bloom like the Himalayas.
The sun and moon reflected in water shall protect him; of this there is no doubt.
What more need I say? He shall obtain every accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Having obtained the bliss of various enjoyments, one may become Śiva even by one's own will;
or, having written it down or worshipped it, one should wear it attached to the body.
There shall be delusion, paralysis, attraction, killing, and eradication;
and for a woman who is a "crow-barren" one, or one who is barren, or one whose children have died.
If one writes this and wears it on the neck or on the left hand,
then a son shall truly be born who is long-lived, wise, and pure.
He too shall be beloved by his master and endowed with wealth, grain, and progeny;
yet, if one should employ the mantra of Kālikā without knowing this armor, [the result will be otherwise].
Through meditation and ten million recitations, his vidyā will not be accomplished;
at every step he will experience suffering, and he will certainly be reviled by the world.
He who, knowing the guru to be equal to food itself, disregards him, shall experience great suffering in this world and go to hell in the next; [therefore, one should protect] the supreme armor.
O fair-faced one, his sciences will truly, truly be perfected;
he who reveals this divine armor shall become a destroyer of Śiva.
One should teach it to a devoted disciple who has performed the required penance and is a practitioner.
Thus ends the armor known as Trailokyamohana, from the Śrī Rudrayāmala, in the dialogue between the Goddess and Śaṅkara.
Now follows the hymn of one hundred names.

Oṃ. Of this hymn of one hundred names of the illustrious Kālikā, Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), the illustrious Dakṣiṇakālikā is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is by means of these one hundred names.
Karālinī, Mahātejā, Lokadhātrī, Arundhatī, Sarasvatī, Viśālākṣī, Prajñā, and likewise Vidyāśvarī.
The enchanting Māyā of Śambhu, the destroyer of wicked Daityas,
is intoxicated with the pride of the Great Makara, her eyes red as wine.
She who is fond of human flesh, the dark-complexioned one, whose limbs are dark,
the bestower of happiness, the bliss of consciousness, the play of the non-conscious, the very nature of consciousness, and the creative power of consciousness.
Kāmeśvarī, Karālāsyā, Kālī who bears a skeleton, she who is skilled in inverted sexual union, the end of desire, and the sweet voice of the passionate woman.
Śavarī, Ḍākinī, Cāṇḍālī, and Aparājitā; Kaulinī, who resides in the wheel of the Kula, Kumārī, and Kālapañcamī.
She who is dear to Bhaga, whose form is Bhaga, the Bhārūṇḍā, the one garlanded with Bhagas;
she who is the counter-anger, the one who protects at dawn, the giver of joy, and she who dwells in the midst of the Pratas.
The Yoginī, the weaver of the tantra, the great pestilence, seated upon a corpse;
the terrible one with a loud laugh, the formidable Jayantī, who dwells in the Vindhya mountains.
Victorious Durgā, Bhadrakālī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Caṇḍanāśinī;
she who possesses the three qualities, pure consciousness, the beloved, and the dweller in the forest.
The Great Goddess is the Mistress of Yoga, attainable through yoga, and stainless;
she is Mahācaṇḍeśvarī, the terrifying one, abiding in the fire of the night of time.
Padmāvatī, Śivāṅkasthā, Lalajjihvā, Bhayānakā, Gāndhārī, Kinnarī, Pūṣā, and Hināñcanā are the residents of the mountain.
Vaśinī, Njobhinī, and Jemā, who dwells in the center of the maṇḍala of the womb;
she is Jemaṅkarī, in the form of a jackal, Vārāhī, Vāruṇī, and Śivā.
She is the dancer who delights in dancing upon the stage of the great dissolution;
she is deformed and yet possesses the form of the universe; she is born from the essence of valor and passion.
Mahāpracaṇḍā, Pramadā, Candrikā, Caṇḍaśītala,
Nāda, Bindu, and Rūpā— all these are of the nature of seed-syllables.
Partless, beyond action, peaceful, utterly tranquil, and of peaceful form—
these one hundred and eight names have been proclaimed out of a desire for your welfare.
Though suffering, one becomes eternally happy; though poor, one obtains wealth;
and even the dull-witted gains speech that unfolds with unrestrained eloquence.
Success as a sky-walker (khecarī) is attained shortly thereafter;
on the eighth lunar day at midnight, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
Then the perfection of the sixfold action arises, beautiful in the world;
likewise, it brings fear regarding calamities in the assembly as well as in battle.
When great fear has arisen and there are many obstacles and calamities,
the best of practitioners, having meditated on Kālikā in his heart, should recite this ear-whispered teaching.
They all go to utter destruction, according to the word of Mahādeva.
Thus ends the hymn of one hundred and eight names of Dakṣiṇakālikā, the essence of the entire Śrī Kālīkula.
Now, the hymn of a thousand names entitled "The Essence of Mantras" from the Dialogue with Harakumāra is written here.
Delightful as the peak of Kailāsa, adorned with various flowers,
situated amidst wish-fulfilling trees, and graced by diverse forests.
Once, while the Blessed One, the Teacher of the World, was seated comfortably in the midst of a jeweled pavilion frequented by sages and gandharvas;
He holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament,
carries a trident and a ḍamaru drum in his hands, and has a great bull as his vehicle.
The god who wears a mass of matted hair, adorned with Vāsuki around his neck,
the god decorated with sacred ash, blue-throated, and three-eyed.
Clad in a leopard skin, resembling pure crystal,
radiant as a thousand suns, and adorned with half the body of the Daughter of the Mountain.
Having bowed his head to the Lord, the cause of all and the one whose form is the universe,
the one whose vehicle is the peacock joined his palms in reverence and made this prayer.
The illustrious Kartikeya said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O author of creation, preservation, and destruction!
You are the refuge of all the gods; you are the refuge of all embodied beings.
You alone are the refuge of all the worlds, and you indeed are the protector of the distressed;
you alone are the support of the universe, and you alone are the cause of all that exists.
"You alone are worthy of worship by all; apart from you, I have no other refuge. What is the supreme secret in the world, and what indeed is the one ultimate goal?"
What is the one supreme excellence? What is the yoga that grants liberation from everything—without pilgrimage sites, without austerity, without gifts, and without sacrifices?
By what meditation without a substratum could one attain perfection?
In what does creation arise, and in what does dissolution occur?
O Lord, who is it that crosses over this vast banyan tree of saṃsāra?
Therefore, O Maheśvara, I wish to hear that; please tell it to me.
The illustrious Mahādeva said:
Excellent, excellent! You have asked me well, O son of Pārvatī.
There is something most secret, my son; I shall tell it to you without doubt.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas; Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others;
and whatever other numerous beings there are, all of whom arise from primordial nature (prakṛti).
She herself is the goddess Mahāśatī, the dark-complexioned Dakṣiṇakālikālikā.
She alone gives birth to the universe; she alone protects the universe;
she alone withdraws this entire world of moving and unmoving beings.
She is the support of all beings and thus the remover of the affliction of disease;
she consists of will, action, and knowledge, and has the nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
She is the triple power by her very nature, the cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction;
she creates in the form of Brahmā and protects in the form of Viṣṇu.
In the form of the Guru, she withdraws this entire world of moving and unmoving beings;
in her womb, the whole universe proceeds in its midst.
In her the universe dissolves, and from her it is born again;
by propitiating her, the three worlds attained the supreme state.
I shall now declare her thousand names; listen to them.
Oṃ. Of this mantra of the *Śrīśyāmā Bhagavatī Sahasranāma Stotra*, the venerable Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti Vāmadeva is [the seer]. (143b)

The Seer is Jagatī; the metre is Jagatī; the deity is the venerable, divine, dark-complexioned Śyāmā Bhagavatī, who possesses inconceivable power, is the most secret of all secret traditions, and has transcended the Kula and Kaula systems;
Krīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Haṃ is the power (śakti), Hrīṃ is the pin (kīlaka); Jīva is the seed-syllable, Buddhi is the power, and Udāna is the pin.
The Suṣumnā channel is Sarasvatī, the Śakti; its application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of recitation (japa) and study for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.

I worship her who possesses the splendor of the orb of the rising sun, marked by three lines of time (the trident), resembling an autumnal cloud, adorned with a crescent moon crown, and seated between two tufts of hair.

Vāṃ vīṃ is the water that removes ignorance; nīraṃ nīraṃ vāṃ śrīṃ vīṃ is the wind and water.
Oṃ vīṃ śrīṃ vāgurā svāhā; śrīṃ vīṃ śrīṃ rāṃ, you who are exalted by slaying; vīṃ śrīṃ truṃ, you whose form is slaughter; vāṃ vīṃ, may she who torments be praised!
Śrīṃ vāṃ hūṃ hrīṃ hsauḥ svāhā, she who is served by the son of the Wind;
vāṃ vīṃ śrīṃ vānarī svāhā, vīṃ śrīṃ vānīravāsinī.
Śrīṃ Klīṃ Hrīṃ is she whose form is Viṣṇu; Śrīṃ Klīṃ is she who is served by Viṣṇu.
Vāi is she who resides in Vaikuṇṭha; Vāṃ Vī is the Mistress of the Universe (Viśveśvarī) and the Waters (Payaḥ).
Vāṃ truṃ sauḥ klīṃ Vitastā, vīṃ he Vetravatī, payaḥ; vāṃ vīṃ śrīṃ Varadā Svāhā, vīṃ Vipāś, iha raṃ vanam.
Aiṃ Śrīṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ—Tu Indrāṇī; I Śrīṃ Iṅgudivallabhā;
Oṃ Śrīṃ I Vāṃ Śrīṃ Hlīṃ Svāhā—she who is seated upon the seat of reeds (īṣīkā).
IṂ VĀṂ ŚRĪṂ CĪṂ ILĀṂ SVĀHĀ | IṂ VĀṂ ŚRĪṂ KLĪṂ ĪḌĀVANAM | OṂ IṂ INDRA SAMĀNĀBHĀ IṂ IṂ YUTARŪPIṆĪ ||
*i* *śrīṃ* *vīṃ* *strīṃ* *lphuṃ* *svāhā*—this has a radiance equal to ten million suns;
*dhaṃ* *vāṃ* *śrīṃ* *kuṃ* is the wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmadhenu*), who grants the water of the boon of desire (*kīṃ*).
KṚĪṂ DHŪṂ, praised by Dhātṛ, svāhā! OṂ ŚRĪṂ, served by Vāta, svāhā!
VĀṂ ŚRĪṂ AIṂ, the Sovereign Lady (Īśvarī), svāhā! She who bears the digit of the crescent moon (Aiṇāṅkakalādharā).
VĀṂ VĪṂ VASUMATĪ SVĀHĀ; VĀṂ VĪṂ VĀSAVE VĀṂ THEN.
Vīṃ, indeed, is Śravaṇā; Caṃ is service that bestows fruit; Krīṃ, Śrīṃ, Kamalinī, Svāhā; Krīṃ, Krīṃ, Kumudinī, [the essence of] water.
*Krīṃ līṃ*, O Kālī, take this water, *svāhā*! O bearer of the skull, *hnīṃ*!
*Śrīṃ*, O you who dwell in the cremation ground, *svāhā*! *Śrīṃ śrīṃ*, O Śmaśānakālikā!
Oṃ śrīṃ bhaiṃ bhairavī svāhā truṃ trāṃ Tripurabhairavī.
Uṃ Ūṃ Usrarakālī, and Gesauḥ Paścimakālikā.
Oṃ śrīṃ sauḥ klīṃ hlīṃ aiṃ sauḥ, she who is worshipped by Bhairava and Īśvara;
Oṃ krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ Karālī, krīṃ krīṃ, she whose form is like a shower of sparks.
Oṃ Śrī Kāruṇyarūpā and Oṃ Śrī Kāruṇyarūpiṇī!
Vāṃ Śrīṃ Mīṃ Śārikā Svāhā! Śaṃ Śāṃ Śāṃ Rī! Hara the forest!
Oṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ juṃ hsauḥ svāhā! O you who dwell upon the left limb of the left limb of Śiva!
Oṃ drīṃ aiṃ śāṅkarī svāhā! Krīṃ huṃ hrīṃ! O Hariṇī, grant me a moment!
Krīṃ Krīṃ Krīṃ Hūṃ Dvaṃ Hrīṃ Hrīṃ Svāhā—this is Dakṣiṇakālikā. Krīṃ Krīṃ Krīṃ Huṃ Huṃ Hrīṃ Hrīṃ—this is Śyāmā Dakṣiṇakālikā. Oṃ.
Thus, no one is capable of fully describing the greatness of this *Māyā*, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, contains a thousand names, and is the very essence of mantras.
This *Śyāmāsahasranāma*, which is the means for conquering the three worlds,
was spoken in the *Rudrayāmala* and revealed by Kumāra.
O son, that man who, endowed with purity, recites this meritorious [text] issued from the mouth of Purāri, the granter of boons, at the time of death;
Listen, my child, to the fruit of that practitioner’s great success:
in the beginning, just as he was dark-complexioned, so too shall he become.
There is no one else superior to him; as for us, we are nothing more than mere talk. All the Brāhmaṇas beginning with Brahmā, as well as the Vaiṣṇavas beginning with Kṛṣṇa, [are his followers].
All the Bhairavas beginning with Nada, as well as the Śivas beginning with Prabhṛti;
the gods beginning with Indra, and likewise the Kṣatriyas beginning with Rāma.
The rivers and other [deities], the Pramadās, the Gaṇas headed by Gaṇeśa,
the Rākṣasas beginning with Rāvaṇa, and the Ṛṣis and Īśvaras beginning with Puraṃdara.
Yama and the others, the messengers of Yama, the scribes such as Citragupta,
the radiant ones, the suns, and likewise the stars beginning with Śūdra.
147a) O Mahāsena, all men, the nine planets beginning with Āditya, the secondary planets (*upagraha*), as well as Svarbhānu and the rest, [are under the power] of Vālya.
The asterisms beginning with Aśvinī, the fields, the movements and dispositions of the planets,
as well as the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā and the lakes beginning with Mānasa.
All the serpents beginning with Śeṣa, the birds beginning with Garuḍa,
the elephants beginning with Airāvata, and the horses beginning with Uccaiḥśravas;
O son, there are likewise the four ages beginning with Satya,
the three gods, the three fires, and the lords of sages such as Vasiṣṭha.
O son, likewise, by the recollection and worship of that dark-complexioned goddess, and by the direct recitation of her [mantra], all four oceans as well as the three worlds [are subdued].
Or likewise, O Śikhidhvaja, through these [mantras], there is peace;
the diseases of the sick are released, and one who is bound shall be freed from bondage.
O son, one shall be liberated from terrible fear; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
It is equal to the gift of ten million [gold pieces] and possesses the splendor of ten million wish-fulfilling trees.
Reciting this ten thousand times is equal to the gift of a mountain;
moreover, one who suffers from leprosy and one with eye disease are both liberated from their ailments.
A man afflicted with fistula who consumes a *lakṣa* of this decoction shall be liberated from fistula; O son, this is the truth, there is no doubt.
Whether it be a king, a woman, or even one whose son has become an enemy,
that mortal who recites the Śatāvarta will suddenly bring them under his control.
O son, my king is equal to Śakra and is devoted to me;
by either reciting or hearing [this], his enemy does not survive.
O son of Pārvatī, by means of those sons, the earth shall become completely filled;
even in his house, O Śikhidhvaja, there shall be unshakable prosperity, like a woman who has cast off her clothes.
Neither from weapons nor from floods of water does fear arise for him;
nor from the terrible rākṣasīs, yakṣiṇīs, piśācīs, or khecarīs.
"By remembering this, these [demons] shall be deluded at that very moment;
thus, this hymn known as the 'Thousand' has been taken up by me."
The secret of all awakening and tranquility for all embodied beings belongs to that mortal who always maintains this supreme hymn known as the Thousand Names.
By the grace of the Goddess, no fear arises for him anywhere,
even if his life-span is exhausted, death has arrived, or he is seized by a great passion.
By the granting of a boon by Śyāmā, one immediately attains a beautiful countenance;
it pacifies all poverty and increases all auspiciousness. 147b)
Whoever recites this on the day of Nivāsa shall go to heaven through yoga;
and so too shall a man who seeks sons, wealth, or even a wife.
Having recited it for one month, day and night, facing the east, the rider of the peacock (Skanda) [attains his goal]; what is the use of saying more here regarding its greatness?
In this world, a man will certainly be liberated hereafter.
Moreover, O son, I shall speak further concerning the specific details that grant success.
The mortal practitioner, having sat upon a dead hide,
[should recite] this thousand-name hymn of the Goddess consisting of mantras.
The direct vision of the Goddess Śyāmā is always attained;
this should be given to a son, a disciple, or one who is devoted to the guru.
It should be given to anyone who desires it, even to a practitioner;
yet by giving it even to one's own sons if they are not devotees, one would fall into hell.
There is no fruit for a root medicine; how could there be one for that which is difficult to obtain?
O Great Being, [this is] through action, mind, and speech, in truth.
By giving it to one who is unworthy but of noble lineage, a man becomes a Kṛṣṭī.

Thus ends the *Trailokye-vijaya-nāma-mantragarbha-śyāmāsahasranāmastotra*, a hymn of a thousand names of Śyāmā containing mantras, from the dialogue between Kārttikeya and Mahādeva within the great tantra, the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*.
Now follows another dialogue between Paraśurāma and the hymn of a thousand names.
148a) The illustrious Saṃkara said:
This great mantra has been declared, the most excellent among all mantras;
having attained which, I have reached this supreme state of sovereignty.
Endowed with supreme devotion, you should perform the worship of the Goddess according to the prescribed rite,
desiring victory over the three worlds.
Paraśurāma said:
O Supreme Lord, as if pleased with this ancient [prayer], O Ancient One!
O Lord, by the grace of the Supreme Goddess, please tell me the secret:
[the practice] without worship, without fire-offering, without ritual placement (nyāsa), and without the sacrificial offering (bali).
The fragrance of discipline and the activity arising from the absence of afflictions.
Without breath control, without meditation, without the purification of the elements,
without recitation, and without charity— just as Kālī is pleased [in this way].
The illustrious Śaṅkara said:
O wise one born of the lineage of Bhṛgu, you have asked an excellent question;
though you are devoted even to those who are not devoted, you shall thus achieve your goal.
O Dānava, you have seized the Goddess, the slayer of millions of demons, who is fond of blood,
who delights in hymns of praise, who is fierce, and who is devoted to passion and curiosity.
One whose heart is always joyful, or whose mind is attached to meat; one who is fond of honey-wine, fish, and meat, and who is devoted to blood and wine—such a woman is called *rogiṇī*.
Dwelling in the cremation ground, surrounded by hosts of pretas, she is the great festival;
she is the radiance of yoga, the mistress of yoginīs, residing in the hearts of the lords of yogis.
