O Ugrakālikā, you ought to please my hair-pores;
her hymn of great merit was revealed by Kālī herself.
I shall tell that to you; having heard it, my child, retain it in your mind.
This supreme secret, which must be concealed from those who have not attained [realization], must not be recited to others.
By reciting this at any time, all obstacles, becoming utterly agitated,
flee in every direction like moths falling into a blazing fire.
His speech, consisting of both prose and verse, flows like the current of the Gaṅgā;
by the mere sight of him, disputants are rendered lusterless.
Even kings fall into servitude; what need be said of other people?
For him, indeed, there is success in all things through destiny; of this there is no doubt.
At night, in a secluded place, one who is naked and endowed with power should meditate in the mind upon Kālī, who is being embraced by Mahākāla.
He who recites this hymn called the *Sahasranāma*, which is the treasure-trove of liberation,
will find Kālikā pleased with him and favor him as her own son.
Just as the Supreme Goddess is pleased when worshipped with Brahma-nectar and Brahma-flowers,
so too does Kālī become pleased when praised with this hymn.

Of this hymn of a thousand names of the illustrious Kālikā, Mahākālabhairava is the seer, Anuṣṭubh is the meter, Śmaśānakālikā is the deity, and it is applied for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Oṃ! Śmaśānakālikā, Kālī, Bhadrakālinī!
Guhyakālī, Mahākālī, Kurukullā, Virodhinī, Kālikā, Kālarātri, and Mahākālanitambinī.
And the wife of Kālabhairava, who reveals the Kulamārga,
is Māmadā, a passionate woman whose nature is most desirable.
She whose body is blue with the essence of musk, who moves like an elephant.
She whose every limb is the color of the letter *ka*, she who is full of longing,
the goddess of desire, afflicted by passion, possessing a form of desire, the wish-fulfilling cow, and the possessor of all arts.
She whose form is beautiful, whose nature is desire, who possesses the eye of desire, and who protects the lineage;
she who is of noble birth, the forest-dweller of the Kula, and the destroyer of the suffering of distress.
Kaumārī, born of the Kula, dark-complexioned, with a dark body and a slender waist;
she of delicate limbs and vajra-like form, uttering the sound "Krīm," a digit of the lotus-born Lakṣmī.
Karālāsyā, Karālī, Kulakāntā, Aparājitā, Ugrā, Ugraprabhā, Dīptā, Vipracintā, and Mahānanā.
She is like a dark cloud, the measure, the white and black seal;
she is the grain, the consort of Nārāyaṇa, the auspicious one, the most auspicious, and she who is affectionate toward her devotees.
Māheśvarī, Cāmuṇḍā, Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhikā, Vajrāṅgī, Vajrakaṅkālī, Nṛmuṇḍasṛgvinī, and Śivā.
Molinī is adorned with a garland of human heads from which blood drips;
her limbs are anointed with red sandalwood paste, and her head is crimson with vermilion.
She is of terrible form, with terrible fangs, most formidable yet auspicious;
she has great fangs and a massive body, with beautiful teeth that are jagged like the end of an eon.
She is beautiful-eyed, yet has deformed eyes; she is large-eyed and three-eyed.
Her face is as serene as the autumnal moon, her lotus-like mouth is quivering with a smile, and her countenance is ever-pleased. She speaks with gentle smiles and is sweet of speech.
With a face like a clear lotus, smiling countenance, and pleasant speech; with deep-set eyes, of noble lineage, great, and talkative.
Sumati, Kumati, Caṇḍā, Caṇḍamuṇḍā,
Veginī, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍikā, Caṇḍī, Carcikā, and Caṇḍaveginī.
She has beautiful hair, loose hair, long hair, and abundant locks;
she wears a corpse as an ear-ornament, and has a corpse for a hand and an excellent girdle.
O Dear One, she has the seat of a preta; the pretas have made their abode in the land of pretas.
She dwells in the cremation ground, is meritorious, the bestower of merit, and the wise lady of the lineage.
Pārvatī is the foremost abode of grace, possessed of a meritorious body and a virtuous reputation;
she is the most excellent, purified by her father, and adorned with ancient merit.
She whose name is auspicious, the remover of fear, the bestower of boons, holding a sword in her hand;
she who holds a human skull in her hand, the praised one, and she whose nose is severed from her head.
Dakṣiṇā is dark-complexioned, youthful, peaceful, with full and elevated breasts;
she is naked, of terrible form, with blood dripping from the corners of her mouth, and a taker of blood.
She is the howling jackal, the one who is both united and disunited, afflicted by passion, intoxicated, and utterly heedless; she is the woman dwelling in the ocean of nectar.
Excessively intoxicated, she is the great minister who performs all types of attractions;
she is fond of song, delights in instrumental music, and is devoted to the dancing of the pretas.
Four-armed, ten-armed, and likewise eighteen-armed;
Kātyāyanī, the Mother of the World, the Supreme Sovereign of the universe.
She is the kinswoman of the world, the sustainer of the world, the bringer of joy to the world,
the one whose essence is the life-force of the world, the daughter of Himavat, Māyā, and she of great speed.
Her body is adorned with a serpent-sacrificial thread; she is the female serpent, she who moves among serpents;
she is the daughter of the Nāgas, the daughter of the gods, the Gandharva woman, and the sovereign of the Kinnarīs.
She is the great night, the great darkness, possessing a terrible radiance.
She is the Vidyādharī, Vasumatī, Yakṣiṇī, Yoginī, and Jarā;
she is the Rākṣasī, Ḍākinī, composed of the Vedas, and adorned by the Vedas.
The Veda, the Smṛti, and the Great Science (Mahāvidyā) are ancient.
She is the conceivable and the inconceivable, Svadhā and Svāhā, Nidrā (Sleep) and Tandrā (Lassitude), Pārvatī, Aparṇā, Niścalā (the Immovable), Lolā (the Fickle), and the mistress of all sciences.
Gaṅgā, Kāśī, Śacī, Sītā, Sattī, Satyaparāyaṇā,
Nīti, Sunīti, Suruci, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Dhṛti, and Kṣamā.
Vāṇī, Buddhi, Mahālakṣmī, Lakṣmī, Nīlasarasvatī,
Srotaḥsvatī, Sarasvatī, Mātaṅgī, Vijayā, and Jayā.
She is the river Sindhu, composed of all things, Tārā who dwells in the void;
she is the pure wave, Medhā, Lākinī, and she of manifold forms.
She is gross, subtle, and subtler still, conforming to the Lord;
she is the very nature of the Supreme Self and the embodiment of consciousness and bliss.

May Sunandā, whose nature is worthy of praise, who consists of eternal bliss through her supreme intellect, who is the very embodiment of all joy, and who is the daughter of Nandin, be propitious to you.
Raṅkiṇī, Ṭaṅkiṇī, Citrā, Vicitrā, Citrarūpiṇī;
Padmā, Padmālayā, Padmasukhī, and Padmavibhūṣaṇā.
Hākinī, Śākinī, Śāntā, Rākiṇī, she who is fond of blood,
Bhrānti, Bhavānī, Rudrāṇī, Mṛḍānī, and the crusher of enemies.
She is Upendrāṇī and Mahendrāṇī; she is Jyotsnā, whose nature is like the moon;
she is of the essence of the sun, the consort of Rudra, Raudrī, the female, the primordial nature, and the male.
Śakti, Sūkti, Mati, Mātā, Bhukti, Mukti,
Pativratā, Sarveśvarī, Sarvamātā, Sarvāṇī, and Haravallabhā.
She is omniscient, both accomplished and unaccomplished, capable and incapable, the remover of fear;
she is the creator, the destroyer, and the protector; she is the night, the darkness, and compassion.
She is a dark night, steadfast, firm, and ascetic;
she has beautiful limbs, is restless, with a flickering tongue, yet possesses lovely conduct.
She was modest as Pārvatī, free from shame like Arjunī, radiant as Rohiṇī, devoted to truth, steadfast in righteousness, and a speaker of words that endure.
Gavaṣṭhā, Duṣṭā, Saṃhartrī, Viśiṣṭā, Śreyasī, Ghṛṇā, Bhīmā,
Bhayānakā, Bhīmanādinī, and Bhīḥprabhāvatī.
She is Vāgīśvarī, Śrī, Yamunā, the performer of sacrifice, the beloved of the Yajus;
she is the abode of the Ṛk, Sāman, and Atharva Vedas, the passionate one, and possesses a beautiful voice.
She who has a sweet voice, she whose neck is like a conch, she who is devoted to the flute and the lute;
she who possesses the bamboo flute, she who belongs to Viṣṇu, she who is pure, the nurse of the world, Śrī, the sovereign of the universe.
Madhumatī, Kuṇḍalinī, Ṛddhi, Siddhi, Śucismitā, Rambhā,
Ūrdhvaśīrā, Rāmā, Rohiṇī, Revatī, and Maghā.
Śaṅkhinī, Cakrinī, Kṛṣṇā, Gadinī, and likewise Padminī;
Śūlinī, Parighāstrā, Pāśinī, and Śārgapāśinī.
Pinākadhāriṇī, Dhūmrā, Śarabhī,
Vanamālinī, Rathinī, Samaraprītā, Veginī, and Raṇapaṇḍitā.
Jaṭinī, Vajrinī, Nīlā, Lāvaṇyāmbudhicandrikā,
Valipriyā, and likewise Daityendramathinī are always worthy of worship.
The slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura, the passionate one with red teeth,
the drinker of blood whose limbs are smeared with gore, and the bearer of a blood-stained skull-bowl.
She is fond of blood, delights in flesh, and has her mouth filled with entrails;
she is adorned with a garland of heads from which blood drips, serving as her neck-ornament.
Seated upon a corpse, dwelling within the funeral pyre, she is Māheśī, whose vehicle is the bull;
she wears a tiger skin as her garment and is clothed in fine silk, riding upon a lion.
She is Vāmadevī, the Great Goddess, Gaurī, the one who brings about omniscience;
she is the girl, the young woman, the old woman, the mother of the aged, and the one afflicted by decrepitude.
Subhrū, Vilolinī, Brahmavādinī, Brāhmaṇī, Satī, Svapnāvatī, Citrarekhā, Lopāmudrā, and Sureśvarī.
Amoghā, Arundhatī, Tīkṣṇā, Bhogavatī, Anurāgiṇī, Mandākinī, Mandahāsā, Jvālāmukhī, and Svarāntakā.
She bestows honor, she is proud, she is honored, and she is worthy of respect;
she is intoxicated with passion, she is wine, she is the madness of abundance, she is pure, she is to be accomplished, and she is the perfecting one.
Possessing infinite virtues and a beautiful waist, she is the supreme excellence at the end of all worlds;
she is the giver of victory, the unconquered, the victorious, the glory of victory, and she who shines with triumph.

She is the giver of happiness, the giver of auspiciousness, the truthful assembly, and the cause of universal agitation; she is the messenger of Śiva, possessed of prosperity, the manifestation of power, and the one with a terrifying countenance.
Kaumārī, Kulajā, Kuntī, Kulastrī, Kulapālikā,
Kīrti, Yaśasvinī, Bhūṣā, Bhūṣyā, and the beloved of the Lord of Beings (Bhūtapati).
She who abides in the ultimate limit of the foundation of qualities, who is established in primordial light;
she who is the most excellent Dhaniṣṭhā, the giver of wealth, the auspicious one, the earth, and the self-luminous.

The command of kings is vast, weighty, heavy, supreme, endowed with the six qualities, and consisting of the three gunas; O highly wise one, it is both possessed of the six attributes and yet devoid of qualities.
Born of a noble lineage, she is free from desire, yet she lives as both desire and the absence of desire;
she is the delight of the arts of Kāmadeva and the dancer of Śiva.
The wish-fulfilling gem, the desire-granting creeper, ever-awake, kind to the day,
the full moon of Kārttika, the star Kṛttikā, the magical power, Ayodhyā, and the peerless one.
The minister Sumantā, the whirling one, the gladdening one, the destroyer of afflictions,
the mother of the three worlds, she who is honored by all, the fleshless one, and she whose form is stainless.
With a belly as deep as a lake, possessing withered flesh and bones,
the charming city of Mathurā in Avantī is capable of purifying the three worlds.
She whose form consists of the manifest, the unmanifest, and the beyond; she who roars with a terrifying sound;
she who bestows forgiveness; she who brings about auspiciousness; and she who causes universal delusion.
Ūrdhvā, Tejasvinī, Klinnā, Mahātejasvinī,
as well as Advaitā, Bhoginī, Pūjyā, Sūbhīrā, and Sarvamaṅgalā.
She who makes all dear, she who is to be enjoyed, the wealthy one, the flesh-eater;
she who causes fear, the remover of sin, the stainless one, and the subduer of all.
Hope is thirst; the digit of the moon is sleep; she is swift as the wind, radiant like a thousand suns, and possesses a splendor equal to ten million moons.
She is the destroyer of Niśumbha and Śumbha, the annihilator of Raktavīja,
the slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, and the killer of the demon Mahiṣāsura.
Abiding in the center of the fire-maṇḍala, she is established within all sentient beings;
she possesses all modes of conduct, and she is the goddess who is the daughter of all the gods.
She is the daughter of Dakṣa, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, the savior from misfortune;
she is the object of worship, worthy of adoration, fearless, prosperity, fame, and the embodiment of Brahman.
Rambhoru, Caturārākā, Jayantī, Karuṇā, Kuhu, Manasvinī, Devamātā, Yaśasyā, and Brahmacāriṇī.
She is the bestower of success, the giver of prosperity, the primordial prosperity herself, and the granter of all things;
she possesses unfathomable form, is worthy of being meditated upon, and dwells in the *mūlādhāra*.
She is command, wisdom, and a mind full of fulfillment; she has a moon-like face and is well-disposed;
she is the one who utters "vaṭu," possesses a deep navel, is truth itself, the twilight, and firm in her vows.
She is Ānvīkṣikī, Daṇḍanīti, and Trayī; she is the beauty of the third heaven, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, the Daughter of the Mountain, and Vindhyavāsinī.
Pratyayā, Khecarī, Dhairyā, Turīyā, Vimalāturā, Pragalbhā, Vāruṇī, Chāyā, Śaśinī, and Visphuliṅginī.
Enjoyment, accomplishment, constant attainment, irresistible will, greatness, minuteness,
success according to desire, mastery, lordship, and the power of dwelling above.
Laghimā, Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Bhuvaneśvarī,
Manoharā, Citā, Divyā, Devyudārā, and Manoramā.
Piṅgalā, Kapilā, Jihvā, Rasajñā, Rasikā, Arasā,
Suṣumnā, Īḍā, Bhogavatī, Gāndhārī, and Narakāntakā.
Pāñcālī, Rukmiṇī, Rādhā, Rādhyā, Bhāmā, Adhikādhikā, Amṛtā, Tulasī, Vṛndā, Kaiṭabhī, and Kapaṭeśvarī.
Ugracaṇḍeśvarī, mother of heroes, beautiful among heroes,
Ugratārā, known by the name Yaśodā, the goddess honored by the gods.
The stainless goddess of consciousness, the wrathful one who illuminates the Kula,
the sovereign of the Kula-speech, the flame, the Mother, the one who liquefies, and the melting one.
Yogīśvarī, Mahāmārī, Bhrāmarī, she whose form is the Bindu; the Secret Messenger, Mistress of Life, Guptā, Vahulā, Bhrāmarī, and Prabhā.
Kubjikā, Jñāninī, Jyeṣṭhā, Bhuśuṇḍī, Prakaṭākṛti, Drāviṇī, Gopinī, Rāmā, Kāmavījeśvarī, and Priyā.
Śākaṃbharī, Kokanadā, Asumanā, Tilottamā, Ameyavikramā, Krūrā, Samyachīlā, and Trivikramā.
Svasti, Havyavahā, Prīti, Uṣmā, Dhūmrārcis, Aṅgadā, Tapinī,
Tāpinī, Viśvā, Bhogadā, Dhāriṇī, and Dharā.
She who has three parts, the awakener, the subduer, the all-encompassing one whose form is sound;
she whose form is the seed-syllable, the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā), the mistress, and she whose form is yoga.
Anaṅgā, Anaṅgākusumā, Anaṅgānaṅgā, Mekhalānaṅgarūpiṇī,
Anaṅgāmadanānaṅgā, Rekhānaṅgāṅkuśeśvarī.
Anaṅgamālinī, Kāmeśvarī, the accomplisher of all aims, consisting of all mantras, the gladdening one, ruddy-hued, and the embodiment of the bodiless god of love.
And Vajreśvarī is victorious, the destroyer of all suffering;
she possesses the six limbs, is youthful, joined in yoga, and garlanded with flaming rays.
She who possesses evil intentions, who is difficult to support, who is hard to conquer, and who has an inaccessible form.
She whose end is difficult to reach, who removes misdeeds, who is hard to fathom and difficult to transcend;
she is Haṃseśvarī, residing in the triangle, and is devoted to Śākambharī.
The eternal one residing in the triangle, anointed with supreme nectar;
she is Mahāvidyeśvarī, Śvetā, Bheruṇḍā, and Kulasundarī.
She is swift, endowed with devotion, and eternally subject to devotion;
she consists of the bliss of devotees, is cherished by devotees, and is the benefactress of devotees.
She is the abode of all beauty, endowed with all auspiciousness,
the source of all enjoyment, and the embodiment of all happiness.
A maiden observing her vow.
The maiden is happy with devotion; the maiden is the bearer of form;
the maiden is dear to her worshiper; the maiden is the beloved who bestows affection.
Kumārī, Sevakāsaṅgā, Kumārī, Sevakālayā,
Ānandabhairavī, Vālabhairavī, and Vaṭukabhairavī.
Śmaśānabhairavī, Kālabhairavīpurabhairavī,
Mahābhairavapatnī, and Paramānandabhairavī.
Surānandabhairavī, Unmadānandabhairavī,
Yajñānandabhairavī, and likewise Taruṇabhairavī.
Jñānānandabhairavī and Amṛtānandabhairavī,
the greatly terrifying one, who possesses a fierce and most intense penetrating vigor.
Tripurā, Parameśānī, Sundarī, Surasundarī,
Tripureśī, Pañcadaśī, and Pañcamīpuravāsinī.
Mahāsaptadaśī, Ṣoḍaśī, Tripureśvarī,
Mahāṅkuśā by nature, and likewise Mahācakreśvarī.
Navacakreśvarī, Cakreśvarī, Cakreśvarī, Tripuramālinī,
Rājacakreśvarī, Rājñī, Mahātripurasundarī.
The illustrious Tripurasundarī is radiant with a stream of vermilion;
she is beautiful in every limb, red-hued, and wears a red garment upon her face.
She who wears hibiscus, lac-dye, vermilion, and red sandalwood;
she who assumes the form of hibiscus, lac-dye, vermilion, and red sandalwood.
She has hair as dark as the curling locks of a yak-tail, pure and lustrous;
she blazes with a crown and earrings set with diamonds, pearls, and precious gems.
Adorned with jeweled earrings, her cheeks were beautiful and radiant;
her nose was graced by pearls emerging from the frontal globes of elephants.
Her breast-regions were adorned with necklaces of pearls, coral, rubies, and other gems;
her ornaments consisted of the touch of sun-crystals, moonstones, and other such jewels.
Her supreme row of teeth shone like the seeds of a citron fruit,
while her curved eyebrows, like the bow of the God of Love, rained down sidelong glances.
With breasts like the frontal globes of an elephant, with hands as skillful as a webbed palm,
with beautiful armlets, and with a gait that rivals the movement of a female swan;
It illuminates the four arms with the luster of ruby armlets and is adorned with pure gold ornaments shimmering with various gems.
Her hands were marked by bracelets fashioned from the tusks of the lord of serpents;
her limbs were variegated with wonderful rings, and she wore diverse tiny bells.
Clad in garments of fine silk, wearing golden ornaments, she was anointed with camphor, agallochum, musk, and saffron.
She dwells upon a ground of variegated jewels, where wish-fulfilling trees stand;
she resides upon a lion throne of shimmering gems on an island of jewels.
She who pierces the six chakras, whose form is supreme bliss,
abiding within the lunar mandala at the end of the thousand-petaled lotus.
She who sports in manifold pleasures in the lap of Śiva, whose form is Brahman;
she who is served by Hara, Viṣṇu, Viriñci, Indra, and the lords of the planets.
She whose source is the Self, whose source is Brahman, whose source is the universe, and who is born of no womb;
she whose form is fortune, who dwells in fortune, who sustains all, who possesses fortune, and who is garlanded with fortune.
She whose essence is the *bhaga*, who takes the form of the support of the *bhaga*, who is adorned with the *bhaga*;
she who expresses the *liṅga*, who is fond of the *liṅga*, and who dwells in the embrace [of the *liṅga*].
She who abides in the *liṅga*, she whose form is the *liṅga*, she who is beautiful as the *liṅga*;
she who has great delight in the song of the *liṅga*, and who possesses great bliss in the song of the *bhaga*.
The name of the *liṅga* is eternal bliss; the name of the *bhaga* is eternal delight. The name of the *bhaga* is eternal bliss; the name of the *liṅga* is eternal delight.
She whose garland is the *liṅga*, whose neck-ornament is the garland of *bhagas*,
who is adorned with the *bhaga* and *liṅga*, who delights in the dead, [she who is] the *bhaga* and *liṅga*.
She is the very nature of the bhaga and liṅga, and she brings about the bliss of the bhaga and liṅga.
Delighted by the flowers of the Self-Existent One, she is worshipped by the Self-Existent One;
her life-breath is the flower of the Self-Existent One, she is the [essence] of the Self-Existent One...
the Self-Existent One... the Self-Existent One.
Self-arisen, fashioned from flowers, she who bears the self-arisen flower.
The self-arisen one has a floral tilaka; the self-arisen one is adorned with flowers;
there is no creeper for the self-arisen flowers... [text missing].
The Self-Existent One is composed of flowers;
having offered a flower to the Self-Existent One, she is dear to the Self-Existent One as a flower.
Her mind was intoxicated with the longing to gather flowers for the Self-Existent One;
she was [immersed] in the waves of bliss from the flowers of the Self-Existent One.
The self-existent one whose abode is flowers, the self-existent one who dwells in flowers.
Glistening with self-arisen flowers, longing for self-arisen flowers,
creating flowers from the self-arisen, [she is] the one whose flowers are the self-arisen...
She is the self-arisen one whose knowledge is flowers, the self-arisen one who enjoys flowers.
She who causes the blossoming of self-manifested flowers, she who showers down self-manifested flowers,
she who rejoices in self-manifested flowers, she who is the essence of self-manifested flowers.
Svayambhū Kusumakā and Svayambhū Puṣpasundarī.
She who is worshipped by the self-arisen flower, she who arises from the self-arisen flower,
she who is intent upon the self-arisen flower, she who is filled with the flowers of the self-arisen.
She whose life-breath is the Self-Existent One; she who is dear to the worshipers of the Self-Existent One;
she who is the support for those who revere the Self-Existent One; she who is the ender of those who revile the Self-Existent One.
The Self-Existent One [honors] the ten bodiless ones; the Self-Existent One [honors] the ten bodiless ones. The Self-Existent One [honors] the ten bodiless ones.
Delighted by that which arises at all times, having as her essence that which arises at all times,
manifesting that which arises at all times, she is born from that which arises at all times.
Born from the *kuṇḍa* and the *golaka*, she whose very nature is that of one born from the *kuṇḍa* and the *golaka*.
She whose support is semen, whose form is semen, who dwells in the ocean of semen;
she whose abode is semen, whose enjoyment is semen, whose worship is semen, and whose constant delight is semen.
She who is to be worshipped by Śukra, she for whom the fire-oblation of Śukra is auspicious,
she who is affectionate toward Śukra; she whose form is Śukra, whose body is Śukra, and who is the mother of the worshipper of Śukra.
She who abides in semen, she who possesses semen, she who longs for semen, she who is beautiful with semen;
she who has bathed in semen, she who produces semen, she who is exceedingly served by semen, she who is full of semen.
She is the great Śukrā, born of Śukra, the bestower of showers of Śukra;
she is designated as Śukrā, worthy of Śukra, and praised by those who worship Śukra.
She who brings bliss to Śukra, she who eternally bestows bliss upon Śukra;
she whose festival is Śukra, she who is ever Śukra, she who is the fullness of Śukra, and she who is delightful to Śukra.
She who honors semen as her all-in-all, she who destroys those who revile semen;
she whose essence is semen, the perfection of semen, and the one who effects the attraction of semen.
She whose abode is red, whose portion is red,
who is worshipped with red offerings, who always delights in passion, who is to be worshipped with red [substances], who performs fire-offerings with red [substances], and who is fond of the red.
Red in color, she is the mother of those who worship with blood.
She is the fire of passion, the goddess who longs for the red, and the beautiful one who is crimson;
she is designated as "the Red One," worthy of the red, and the one who is praised by the caves of red.
She is intensely red, the bestower of red [splendor],
she who bathes in blood, she who delights in blood, she who is to be served by blood, and she who removes passion.
She who causes delight to those who are devoted, she who eternally bestows bliss upon the devoted;
she who is attached to the devoted, filled with the devoted, served by the devoted, and enchanting.
O worshiper of blood, [you who are] the very essence of all...;
you whose form is blood...; you who effect the summoning of blood.
She whose passion is for blood, who is intent on the consumption of blood,
who generates delight through blood, and whose form is as smooth as a wave.
She who dwells within the practitioner brings happiness to practitioners and destroys the enemies of practitioners.
She dwells in the hearts of practitioners,
she brings delight to practitioners, she is the mother of practitioners, and she acts for the benefit of practitioners.
Śāradā, who bestows abundant bliss and supreme happiness upon the practitioner,
is the very life-breath of the practitioner, her mind being entirely devoted to him.
She is the all-in-all of the supreme practitioner, the drinker of blood for those practitioners who are not devoted;
she is the joy and satisfaction of practitioners, and the destroyer of the enemies of practitioners.
She is the knowledge of the Self, the knowledge of Brahman, and the Supreme Brahman as the consort;
she resides on the three peaks, yet is beyond the peaks, and her body consists of all peaks.
The rosary consists of beads made of all colors, serving as the means for performing the recitation.
The illustrious Śaṅkara said:
Thus ends the Thousand Names of Śrī Kālikā, spoken by Śiva;
it is a secret [teaching] that directly destroys even the greatest of sins.
Whether at the time of worship, at midnight, or during both twilights,
the best of practitioners who recites this immediately attains the status of a leader of the Gaṇas.
Whoever recites it, causes it to be recited, or even hears a single word,
being completely liberated from all sins, goes to the state of Kālikā.
Whosoever among men should recite this, whether with faith or even without faith,
having crossed over from difficulty to greater difficulty, shall attain the supreme goal.
Whether she be barren, or one who has borne only stillborn children, or a woman whose offspring die young,
by hearing this hymn, she obtains sons who live long lives.
Whatever desire one may long for, by reciting this hymn while offering white flowers endowed with fragrance— flowers combined with hibiscus,
fire-ash, vermilion, and red sandalwood— [that desire shall be fulfilled].
With fish, meat, and so forth,
along with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) offered by the devotees and consecrated with mantras, together with the *śaktis*.
Having worshipped the Great Goddess with the five types of offerings, with meatless foods, with many bloods, and with captivating incenses and lamps;
Having bathed, one should recite the hymn of praise with devotion,
being single-minded, firm in intellect, with hair disheveled, and clad only by the directions (naked).
Mounted upon a corpse, or situated on a funeral pyre, or having come to a cremation ground;
or likewise gone to an empty dwelling, or lying in a womb—such is the one whose nature is Śiva.
He became known as Kālikāputra;
he was the foremost among all possessors of knowledge and, in wealth, was like the Lord of Riches.
Equal to the wind in his power over the world, difficult to conquer, the crusher of enemies,
he has been delivered from all perils and is endowed with all supernatural accomplishments.
Being praised by the Goddess herself as one like a celestial being, he was like Maheśvara;
the lord of yogins was honored by all sentient beings.
He is a woman of desire, possessing a form at will, the one who effects the attraction of all;
he is the paralyzer of sages within the sun reflected in water, and the favorite of kings.
He will be illustrious, a true poet, wise, possessing the voice of a cuckoo in spring;
he will have many sons, be a lord of elephants and horses,
righteous, accomplished, long-lived like Mārkaṇḍeya, and free from old age and grey hair.
He shall possess fresh youth even if he has reached a thousand years;
what more need be said of him who recites this supreme hymn?
Nothing that is imagined in the mind is difficult to obtain in this world—
not even the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, or violating the teacher’s bed.
By the grace of this hymn, everything is indeed attained very quickly; even a menstruating woman, upon seeing her vulva and reciting the great mantra of Kālī, [attains her desire].
Having praised with this hymn, what could the practitioner not accomplish—
even one devoted to another's wife— by reciting the mantra and chanting the hymn?
By means of wealth and other offerings to the god Kuvera, one becomes like Madana;
having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times and having consecrated the vulva, the knower of reality [attains this].
By uniting with her and reciting this, one becomes a lord of all vidyās. Even one who is naked, has disheveled hair, lies on a bed, and engages in sexual intercourse—
if they chant and praise Mahākālī, they will after some time become a *khecara* (sky-walker).
And at the time of emission, he was devoted to recitation and worship.
By praising Śmaśānakālikā, one becomes a poet among the Vatsas;
or by contemplating the naked wife of another while reciting the *Ārokalana* [mantra].
Having recited and praised Mahākālī, one is liberated from all sins;
likewise, even during sexual union, having recited the mantra and praised the auspicious Goddess Bhagavatī.
By [this], a person shall become like Śuka, freed from all sins, on the new moon,
the full moon, the Saṃkrānti, and on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days.
On the ninth lunar day, which falls on a Tuesday, the diligent practitioner should recite this hymn;
and at midnight on a Tuesday coinciding with the new moon, a man should go to a crossroads.
Having offered an oblation of black gram and boiled rice, along with milk, fish, and blood,
and having recited the mantra one hundred and eight times, one should recite the Thousand Names.
By whatever means one becomes devoted to the praise of Kālī, one shall quickly become Sadāśiva, served by gods and gandharvas.
One may paralyze all the worlds, delude even a king,
fashion a celestial maiden, and bring even Keśava under one's control.
One should slay all haters and exterminate enemies with the blood of a man,
a cat, a buffalo, a goat, and a mouse.
With bone and flesh, with honey and nectar, with milk-rice (pāyasa),
with water that has washed the womb, and with the nectar of the vulva and the phallus.
The practitioner who, at the conclusion of the recitation, has gratified Kālī with white offerings and,
being devoted to her with supreme faith, praises the Goddess with the Thousand Names;
Like a mother, Kālikā acts for his benefit in every situation toward those intent on censuring others, harming others, and slandering others.
She is auspicious to the wicked, to those dependent on others, to the eldest, to the practitioner, and to the devotee; she is malevolent toward the corrupt, the defiler, and the evil-minded.
To one devoid of devotion to Hari, to one intent on the wives of others,
to one lacking in worship and recitation, and to one who reviles women and wine;

One should not display the *stava* [hymn] to heaven; having displayed it, one would become a destroyer of Śiva. [However, it may be given] to one of noble lineage, of great aspiration, and who is devoted to Durgā.
To the pure Vaiṣṇava, to the devotee of devotees, to the practitioner of mantra,
to the one whose nature is non-dual bliss, and to the supreme recipient of offerings.
Then, by the command of the Guru, one should offer a hymn to Mahākālī for the sake of the practitioner;
[one should worship] Maheśvarī under the different names of Guru, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa.

The practitioner of mantra should meditate [on this] everywhere; he becomes Maheśvara, of this there is no doubt. He is a devotee of Śakti, a devotee of Śiva, and indeed the most excellent of Vaiṣṇavas.
He who, having offered worship, praises Kālī while maintaining a non-dual state of being—
rejoicing in the bliss of the Goddess and possessing devotion toward the Goddess— is truly devoted.
He is the most fortunate of the six, for whose sake Maheśa is agitated in mind;
having desired him there, he should utter praise with devotion according to his wishes.
He becomes free from all diseases and arises like the god of love;
one should wear this wheel or the Vāstava-sena on the body.
Having properly and correctly drawn that very form of Kālikā,
a virtuous man should eat whatever food has been offered to the Goddess.
Having assumed a divine body, one shall become a companion by the side of the Goddess;
upon seeing one who reviles the food offering, the hosts of Yoginīs will take his form.
All were intent on drinking blood and intent on satiating themselves with flesh and bone;
therefore, having seen what was offered to the Goddess, a human being should eat it.
Turning his back on all diseases, the person does not revile [them] with mind or speech;
meditating upon himself as the very self of Kālikā, he offers praise.
Having meditated upon the Guru as being like Śiva, he is indeed Sadāśiva himself.

In whosever house this ear, inscribed by those skilled in the ritual, surely resides— prepared with gorocanā, lac, saffron, camphor, and liquid vermilion mixed with beeswax— there Bhavānī herself shall dwell.
Therein, there is no fear of thieves, no mental anguish from enemies, and no dread of destructive fire;
nor is there any apprehension even of calamitous winds, for Fortune herself is present there.
A person who is intent on serving the feet of Kālī gains infinite merit from reciting hymns;
he fully attains the fruit of ritual worship according to the injunctions, and his every desire is completely fulfilled.
Liberated and devoted to the glorious lotus-feet of the Lord,
they attained [the highest state] even in this world.
For the illustrious Śaṅkara, who meditates upon the feet of Mahākālī with devotion, liberation is his very form; for him, the fruit of his own praise is already held in the palm of his hand.
In the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
Thus, having completed the recitation of the armor (*kavaca*) and the recitation of the hymn (*stotra*), one should indeed offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*);
the fire is the support for the offering, and the ritual of the other [deities] should be performed.
In the absence of that [fire], water is for the former, and earth for the latter;
indeed, the substance is one's own...
[the householders] are gladdened by the cooked offerings, and their souls are satiated by the sesame-based *modaka* sweets.
For the Kaulikas, however, each *pala* is well-spoken as the first established doctrine.
The "Honey-Smeared Burnt Fish" is declared as the second;
in the absence of both, [one should proceed]...
Now, I shall first explain the mantra of the former with a very clear extraction.
Having proclaimed each of those [deities] individually and having separated each respective substance,
one should offer them into the fire in sequence, or, in the absence of such [substances], with [other materials].
Piśācanī, Bhūtinī, Siddhā, Apsarā,
Bhādaṇḍā, Kuṣmāṇḍī, Ghoṇakī, and Śakti as well.
O Beloved, these twenty-two have always been declared to be the attendants of the Goddess;
they are born from that [source], and at its end, they resemble those [attendants].
The Śiromantra and the Valermantra have also been declared by me;
[these should be recited] before the Vaiśvadeva offering, using either a metallic vessel or one made of clay.
In the absence of two [pots], it is prescribed that the Vaiśvadeva rite be performed using either vessels or a leaf-cup; O Goddess, listen now with a concentrated mind to the sequence of this rite.
That designation which has become established as "Vaiśvadeva" is proclaimed to be the presiding deity over the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice and other such rites.
The "Viśva" (All) is designated here as the totality, and these deities are worshipped in this manner;
for that reason, it is indeed called Vaiśvadeva.
155b) Now, O Goddess, let the mandala of this [deity] as it appears on the ground be understood, and then likewise the sequence of mantras.
The general *argha* that has been set out for worship before Kālikā—
having first awakened the deities, one should perform the *vaiśvadeva* rite.
The womb from which one is born measures thirty-two finger-breadths;
such is the maṇḍala, circular in shape and perfectly round.
O you who are worshipped by the gods, one should perform that maṇḍala with two revolutions using the ring finger of the right hand, taking [the substance] from the vessel of honor (argha).
Likewise, two lines each should be drawn in the cardinal and intermediate directions according to the sequence of the ritual;
they should extend slightly upward, piercing through the mandala.
The moon-line (candrarekhā) is formed by the [curved] stroke, and those two are covered;
in this way, sixteen houses and lines are indeed produced.
One should perform the touching with water held at the tips of all the fingers;
one should touch each of the two lower joints of the fingers eight times.
Thus, in all eight [directions], the commencement of the rivers is below those two;
in the house situated at the beginning of all [the directions], it is from the very center of the middle of the pair.
Having arrived at the central mandala, she is the final one for all;
she likewise resides below those two who are situated in the center of the wheel.
O Goddess, one should touch each pair [of lines]; one [line] stands between those two. One should touch the single central [line], the place situated within the eight petals of the goddess.
In this manner, one hundred and twenty-one oblations are produced;
having recited each respective mantra and having taken hold of the substance therein.
Having meditated upon each respective deity, one should place the offering (bali) in its corresponding location;
then, having offered the bali, one should [sprinkle] with the water from the arghya vessel using the ring finger.
One should perform the consecration everywhere without abandoning the proper sequence:
first the Tāra (Oṃ), then the name of the deity in the middle, and finally the Hṛt (Namaḥ).
O Pārvatī, in all cases, that [name] must be treated as ending in the fourth case-ending;
therein, I shall explain both the singular and the plural forms following the mention of the planets.
The ten directions,
starting from the east, are to be known as facing the sacrificer and facing the gods, in rites such as the worship of the lotus petals and the lotus pericarp.
Knowing this, the offering (bali) should be given in those respective directions and intermediate points:
Indra, Varuṇa, Kubera, and following Yama.
Agni, Nirṛti, Vāyu, Śeṣa, and the one named Īśāna—
one should worship these, who possess a single form, in their respective places.
First is Kṣetrapāla, then Vighnanāyaka; beyond this, the third is said to be Bhairava, followed by Vaṭukanātha.
A *bhūta*, a *piśāca*, a *rakṣas*, and a *yakṣa*— these, in that order,
are associated with the descendants of Pulastya, Vālakhilya, Adhara, and Bhaga, respectively, as indicated by the use of plural forms.
Mahāmāyā, Kālarātri, Agnijihvā, Prabhañjanā,
Saṃhāriṇī, then Jāraṃdharī, and likewise Laṃbodarī.
Then, after everything has been completed,
Pherurāvinī is to be worshipped by me in the eastern direction with the offering of water and bali.
Then Aparājitā, Lakṣmī, Śāktā, Gaurī, as well as Śraddhā, Vijayā, and Sarvamaṅgalā, accompanied by Meṣā.
O Pārvatī, these are the eight mudrās for the offering of oblations:
Kuṃbhodarī, Ḍamarukā, Virūpā, and likewise Ulkāmukhī.
Pūtanā, Kharakarṇī, Vikarālī, and Kapālinī—
these are to be worshipped in the southern direction with water offerings and oblations.
Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, Sarasvatī, and the auspicious Aruṇā; Jayā, Padmāvalā, and Bhadrā—these are said to be in the north.
Raudrā, Kātyāyanī, Durgā, Caṇḍikā, Ugrā, Śūlinī,
Bhīmā, and Kālikā— these are declared by me to be located in the south-eastern intermediate direction.
Pradīptā, Meghanādā, Kṣobhaṇā, and likewise Tāmasī;
Jayantī, Visvarūpā, and Karālā immediately after that.
Vikarālī and Rambhā are said to be in the intermediate direction of Vāyu; following these are Brahmāṇī, Vaiṣṇavī, Māheśvarī, and Kaumāryā.
Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī, Aindrī,
and likewise Śivadūtī are proclaimed for the offering of the bali-oblation in the south-western direction.
Caṇḍeśvarī, Mātaṅgī, and then Bhuvaneśvarī;
Kubjikā, Siddhilakṣmī, and likewise Tripurasundarī.
Harasiddhā and Phetkārī are said to be in the intermediate direction of the northeast;
these sixty-four goddesses are each accompanied by a single attendant.
The directions starting from the east, as well as the southeast and the intermediate directions, and indeed the center—two by two, they are to be worshipped; grasp that method.
First the eastern direction, then the eastern again, after that the western, and the northern; these four forms of Hari are thus declared in sequence.
O Dear One, the four intermediate directions— namely Āgneyī, Nairṛtī, Vāyavyā, and Śānī— are proclaimed by their respective names. 156b) These are the four intermediate quarters (vidiśaḥ).
The Sun, Venus, Mars, and Rāhu are most intent on devouring; after that, the Moon, then Mercury, and finally Jupiter at the very end.
These are considered, in order, the presiding deities of those respective cardinal and intermediate directions;
the word for "direction" and "intermediate direction" is *diś*, and that very thing is the cardinal or intermediate direction itself.
O Pārvatī, one should also worship the station of their presiding deity, joined with the fourth case ending and the word "kavaca," at those respective locations by means of the offering of a *bali*.
O Goddess, a separate sentence must be formed for each of the lords of the directions;
the two words [of the mantra] remain as they were in the previous sentence, situated between the heart and the *tāra*.
In the remaining mantra, there is one word and a previously unenjoined *sthala* syllable;
thereafter, one should worship two deities at a time between each pair of *rakāra*s.

O Goddess, Brahmā and Viṣṇu are indeed not to be worshipped in this sequence in the eastern direction; rather, they are to be worshipped in the cardinal and intermediate directions. Now, learn their names.
Time, space, Rudra, death, and the six—these, when joined with the singular number, are ten; they are further established as many through the multiplicity of the vessels to be described.
The Yugas, the seasons, Parjanya, the treasures, as well as the trees, the herbs, and the constellations— beyond that [is he].
The sacrifices and the ancestors—these two pairs have been well-proclaimed as eight.
Below these two, one should again place a single wheel in the center.
The oceans, the mountains, the nāgas, and the sages;
likewise the meters, the years, the islands, and thereafter the sacred fords.
Having spoken thus, they did not even mention the fourth [vowel] in their speech. Now listen, O Goddess; the letter *ta* is situated in the middle of all.
Taking the excellent substance with his right hand and moving it,
the practitioner should slowly recite these mantras that are about to be described.
The gods, asuras, humans, nāgas, the ancestors, and hosts of apsarases;
likewise the bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and the hosts of yakṣas and rākṣasas.
The Viśvedevas, as well as the Sādhyas, the Siddhas, and the Vasus;
the Ādityas, the Rudras, the Maruts, and the Grahas.
Trees, animals, herbs, birds, aquatic creatures, and land-dwellers;
the lame, the blind, the hunchbacked, the deaf, and those tormented by hunger.
Those who are mute, those afflicted by great diseases, those born from the wombs of animals, as well as horned creatures, fanged beasts, stinging insects, moths, and ants;
Those beings who arise from various wombs through the experience of their own karma,
as well as those born in forests and those who go to hell; ||| 157a) ||| [all these are included].
Those who have been born, those currently being born, and those undergoing torments—
for whom there is truly no means whatsoever for the cessation of hunger and thirst.
Those living beings who have entered the womb and are tormented by sensations—
whether they be mobile or immobile, and even those who are merely breaths of life.
To all those who have been celebrated as the moving and the unmoving within the three worlds, and to those who have not been celebrated—
to all of them I offer this oblation for the sake of the cessation of misfortune.
Having recited these mantras, one should place the offering (bali) in the very center;
then, with water situated in the middle of the arghya vessel, [one should sprinkle] upon one's own head.
O Goddess, one should perform the consecration and utter these mantras:
"Oṃ! May prosperity be mine eternally; may misfortune go to its destruction."
May I become one whose nature is clear like space; may all diseases and obstructions perish, and may my sins be destroyed along with the hosts of my enemies.
May all obstacles perish; may friends and kinsmen rejoice;
and may the lineage of sons, grandsons, and descendants attain perpetual prosperity.
May death quickly dissolve; may my desires be fulfilled;
may I have victory in battle, as well as in dispute and quarrel.
"May devotion always be mine to the two feet of Guhyakālī.
With these four verses, one should perform the consecration upon the head.
"O Goddess, it has thus been told to you how the Vaiśvadeva bali is offered, whether with kuśa grass, flowers, or even with the fingers of the hand."
This task must be performed daily with devotion by one who desires the satisfaction of Kālikā;
from its performance comes an abundance of fruit, but from its non-performance comes fear.
Having thus understood its permanence, practitioners should always perform the purification of vessels, as well as that of liquor, fish, and meat, by means of this.

He who partakes of the Śrīpātra without first performing this Vaiśvadeva offering for the body, for the power of the Goddess, and for the sake of all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis), [incurs a fault].
Having consumed only foul-smelling pus and blood today,
the base man eats meat like wine for the sake of filling his belly.
Likewise, O fair-faced one, the practitioner excels even without the Vaiśvadeva offering when using liquor and meat;
I shall tell you another illustration here.
For just as a king, having chosen all [his subjects] and then himself bestowed [the earth], subsequently causes them to eat the same food from his own seat; so too [does the teacher].
Likewise, how could the Sovereign Guhyakālī, who sustains the three worlds,
fail to grant [boons] to all beings, both moving and unmoving?
For he himself will accept the worship; therefore, he is remembered as Vaiśvadeva.
Then one should perform the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma). This has been stated in the Jñānārṇava:
Having made this resolve, O Supreme Goddess, one should perform the ritual for the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma).
But it is volition.
It is of such a form as: "I shall offer these oblations for the pleasure of such-and-such deity."
In the Nīlatantra:
I shall now describe the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma) by which one attains all goals;
having brought the fire according to the rules, one should discard the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (kravyād).
Then, having uttered the mantra, one should spread the fire upon the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), or likewise upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
or upon the ground, by means of the three Vyāhṛtis.
Having offered three oblations, one should then perform the six-limbed fire-sacrifice (ṣaḍaṅga-havana).
Thereafter, having invoked the Goddess with the root mantra, one should offer six oblations.
Having performed [the ritual], having praised, and having paid homage, one should dismiss [the deities] into the circle of the drop (bindu-maṇḍala).
According to tradition, one should cast a single ember—the portion of Agni that is carnivorous—toward the southwest, uttering the mantra: "Obeisance to the carnivorous beings" (*kravyādebhyo namaḥ*).
In the *Sārasaṃgraha*:
But having invoked the deity into the fire of the *saṃskṛta* rite, the knower of mantras,
having worshipped with the root mantra, should offer twenty-five oblations.
In the Merutantra:
One should perform the rite of fire-offering (homa).
As before, having invoked the deity into the consecrated fire, the knower of mantras,
having worshipped with the root mantra, should offer twenty-five oblations.
With honey and clarified butter as the oblation, with sesame seeds, auspicious milk-rice,
with rice grains mixed with sesame or even plain *agha-puṣpaka* flowers.
One should offer one oblation for each of the deities of the limbs and the armor;
then, having dismissed the deity and the fire, one should proceed to the place of worship.
Having sat upon his seat, the practitioner of mantra should then offer the bali-oblation to the spirits.
Likewise.
At the conclusion of the ritual service for the Vāminas, they should perform the satiation (tarpaṇa) immediately;
however, for them, the fire-oblation (homa) is occasional, while the satiation and sprinkling (secana) are obligatory.

Thus, there is an option between twenty-five and sixteen oblations. However, the consecration of the fire (agnisaṃskāra) must be performed exactly as stated in the Nīlatantra, with nothing added. This is because of the specific statement: "The rites beginning with the installation of the fire (agnyādhāna) are accomplished through the daily homa. As for the offering (bali), it is as described in the Merutantra:
Having drawn a mandala in the northeast, one should place a support there—
a vessel rich with food, side-dishes, and water, and filled with flowers and other offerings.
Having worshipped the spirits there, one should then offer them an oblation (bali):
"Those who are fierce, whose deeds are fierce, and who dwell in fierce abodes."
The yoginīs of fierce and terrible form, the lords of the hosts,
those who move on earth, those who move in the sky, and those who dwell in the intermediate space;
"May you all, with joyful minds, accept this bali offering!"— with these words, he should offer a stream of water from that vessel using his left hand.
Having taken up a handful of flowers, one should pray to the spirits.

May all the beings who dwell here upon the earth, having received this offering presented according to the rite, attain satisfaction and depart; may they grant forgiveness for this, and salutations be unto them!
In the Merutantra:
Having offered a handful of flowers and bowed down, one should then dismiss [the deities] with the "Bhūtāni" mantra and the *nārāca* mudrā, dwelling thereafter as one pleases.
Having meditated that the deity is satisfied, and having considered the food offering to be devoid of essence,
one should then place that vessel in the direction of the Rakshasas (the southwest).
The purification of the place for the food offering (naivedya) is performed with cow-dung water while reciting the Astra-mantra;
then, taking the remains of the deity's meal, one says: "Salutation to the consumer of the floral remains (nirmālya)."
Having cast [the water] toward the northeast, one should then wash one's hands;
thereafter, one should offer water for sipping (ācamana) once more, as well as for rubbing the hands.
Having offered pure water for sipping (ācamana), he should scent his hands with fragrant substances;
then he should offer twelve-leafed betel (tāmbūla) to Viṣṇu.
A garland made of powdered khadira, ilālavaṅga, and moon-like (camphor) leaves, combined with the petals,
inner calyx, and bark of the jasmine, along with musk and filaments.
Now, the betel nut is said to belong to the Sun when it is accompanied by musk;
however, that of Vighneśvara is devoid of both musk and tamāla.
The five-fold powder consists of khadira, parṇa, pūgīphala, induka, and oil;
that belongs to the Goddess, while the pair of jātī and keśara belongs to Maheśvara.
Then one should present the crown and other ornaments;
likewise, one should show the mirror and provide the parasol and fly-whisks.
Having placed the dūrvā grass, unbroken grains, and the purifying thread upon the head of the deity.
Now follows the offering of the *ārātrika*.
In the Jñānārṇava.
Then, for the sake of accomplishing all desires and aims,
one should perform the *ārātrika* ceremony in a vessel made of gold, silver, or bronze, which is as beautiful as the eyes of the world.
O lady of beautiful countenance, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with saffron;
place a single lamp upon the pericarp and lamps upon many of the petals.
[He offered] cakes made of barley, wheat, and sesame, combined with sugar and milk,
adorned with the beauty of circular rims, and filled with ghee.
Then the mantra-practitioner, having consecrated [the vessel] with the Ratnaiśvaryā mantra,
and having worshipped it further with the root mantra and the Astra-mantra, should then perform the ārātrika ceremony.
Having gathered that vessel, one should perform the *nīrājana* rite for the Great Goddess nine times by repeatedly waving food over her head.
During the Nīrājana rite, one should display the Cakra mudrā for the Great Goddess.
In the Merutantra:

Then, for the sake of attaining dharma, desire, and wealth, one should perform the *ārātrika* ceremony with a lamp made of gold, silver, or bell-metal, which is beautiful to behold like the eyes of the world.
One should draw a very beautiful eight-petaled lotus with saffron;
a great lamp should be placed in the pericarp, and eight small lamps on the petals.
[He offered] those made of barley and wheat, combined with sugar and milk,
adorned with the beauty of circular ornaments, and filled with ghee.
Then, having consecrated [them] with the nine-syllable mantra of Ratneśvarī, the practitioner of mantras [should recite]: *Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Glūṃ Mlūṃ* as before, and then *Śrīṃ Hrīṃ* in sequence.
Then, having indicated [the vessel] with the syllable for the Mistress of the Petals (daleśvarī), one should worship her with the root mantra (mūla).
Then, lifting that vessel again and again up to the top of the head.
One should rotate it nine times and display the *cakramudrā*.
The Ratneśvarī-vidyā is also stated in the Jñānārṇava.
The best of mantra-knowers should inscribe the seed-syllable of Śrī and the seed-syllable of Parā;
thereafter, he should inscribe the letters ga, sa, ya, ma, and na, followed by those situated in the position of Indra (la), in their proper sequence.
Joined with the left ear [the letter *va*], endowed with the bindu and nāda, and placed in reverse order within the first seed-syllable—this is the nine-syllabled Ratneśī mantra: *yaṃ*.
The supreme *māyā* is the seed-syllable; *indra* is the letter *la*; the left ear is the letter *ū*. In the first seed-syllable, there is the *śrī*-seed and the *parā*-seed, thus:
*śrīṃ hrīṃ glūṃ mlūṃ plūṃ mlūṃ mlūṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*. In this way, Ratneśvarī is accomplished.
The wheel mudrā has been explained in the *Lakṣaṇasaṃgraha*.
Having inverted the palms of the left and right hands,
one should interlace the two thumbs between the little fingers and the ring fingers.
159a) This is taught as the Wheel Mudrā, auspicious and the bringer of all accomplishments.
The circumambulation of the food.
In the Uttaratantra:
One who desires dharma and artha should perform circumambulation and prostration with the Purāṇic and Vedic mantras, as well as the root mantra (mūlamantra).
In the Yāmala:
It is everywhere described as being triangular in shape, never otherwise than Śakti.
Bowing is circumambulation from left to right.
Likewise.
The half-moon is said to be behind Maheśa;
indeed, during the circumambulation of Śiva, it is performed with mantras according to the sequence of the half-moon.
One should not cross the *somasūtra* line while moving to the left;
rather, one should properly circumambulate the deity three times in a clockwise direction.
A single prostration with one hand, even a single circumambulation,
or seeing Viṣṇu at an improper time destroys one's ancient merit.
One circumambulation should be performed for Caṇḍī, seven for the Sun, three for Vināyaka,
four for Keśava, and half for Śiva.
Now, the bowing.
And that [discipline] is twofold, by way of the division into eight-limbed and five-limbed.
And so it has been said in the Merutantra:
Then, being well-restrained in the acts of worship, one performs either the eight-limbed or the five-limbed prostration with both hands, both feet, the two knees, and likewise the chest.
Through the head, the gaze, as well as speech and mind, one is freed from the eightfold misfortunes.
And in this regard, another type of *nati* is also mentioned in the *Tantra*: "Facing forward (*saṃmukha*), square (*caturasra*), circular (*vṛtta*), and cow-faced (*gomukha*)."
The *yoni-mudrā* is thus described; these are the five mudrās in the act of salutation.
In that case, the *saṃmukha-mudrā* consists of joining the palms together at the ground with the head also joined [to it].

The square mudrā (*caturasra-mudrā*) is formed by placing the back of the right hand, with its fingers pointing downward and the palm facing upward, across the upturned palm of the left hand which is resting on the ground; this is placed upon the head. The circular mudrā (*vṛtta-mudrā*) is formed by joining the two fists with their thumbs upturned, resting on the ground, and placing them upon the head; however, some [teachers] maintain [a different view].
Having interlaced the fingers of both hands, when the two thumbs are placed crosswise, they call this the *vṛtta-mudrā*.
In the Mahākālasaṃhitā, the fruit of prostration is stated.
O Great Goddess, hear the collection of fruits resulting from prostration:
performed with the two feet, the two hands, the two knees, the chest, the head, and the eyes.
With speech and mind, this is declared to be the eight-limbed prostration (aṣṭāṅga-vaṃdana);
likewise, with the two feet, the two knees, the head, and speech.
This five-limbed prostration (*pañcāṅga-praṇāma*) is used in acts of worship; it consists of two [limbs] being extended.
The wise person who, having fallen upon the ground, performs this salutation (*praṇati*) to the Goddess—
Having performed [this] a thousand times, one shall attain Vaikuṇṭha;
the prostration everywhere in the shape of a triangle is declared to belong to the Śākta tradition.
Prostration before Maheśa while holding the half-moon is said to yield the same fruit that a man obtains by giving land to those learned in the Vedas.
Having performed the circumambulation with devotion, he obtains that fruit.
In the Merutantra:
Then, having offered the *arghya* vessel while reciting the root mantra, [he says]:
"Whatever action has been performed by me, whether good or bad."
"O Blessed One, O God, accept all this as my supreme worship.
Having thus offered the water for the arghya, [he says: "Accept my supreme worship."
Having thus offered the water for the arghya, the wise one should place a small portion to the right of the deity’s hand;
thereafter, he should offer the completed worship.
Having bowed with devotion to the Lord of Gods, one should ask for forgiveness with these verses:
"Whatever food, leaf, flower, fruit, or water has been offered through mere devotion..."
Please accept with compassion this offered oblation;
I do not know how to perform the invocation, nor do I know how to perform the dismissal.
I do not even know how to perform worship; you alone are my refuge, O Supreme Goddess.
In deed, thought, and speech, I have no other resort but you.
O Supreme Goddess, you are the beloved of all beings through your internal movement;
you are the source within the thousands of wombs into which I go.
May there always be eternal devotion toward You in each and every one of those [states].
The God is the giver and the enjoyer; the God is this entire world.
"O God, you are victorious everywhere; for that very God who exists is indeed I myself. Then, with the water from the arghya vessel, one should perform the offering of worship.
In the Kulārṇava:
Having performed all the rites of worship and so forth preceded by the appropriate mantras,
one should offer them to the deity from this point forward, beginning with the east, while reciting the mantra.
The extraction of mantras is found in the Sārasaṃgraha.

One should first utter this word "pada" (the state), and then one should utter "prāṇabuddhi" (vital breath and intellect) according to the jurisdiction of the attributes of the body throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
In all circumstances, one should utter the word "speech" (vāc);
and likewise through action—with both hands, with the feet, with the genitals, and with the stomach.
One should speak with a joyful mind, recollecting the sacred word that one utters; and whatever has been spoken or done, may all of that become an offering to Brahman.
The offering to Brahman is declared by Brahmā to end with "svāhā";
indeed, the unsurpassed offering to Brahman is said to conclude with "svāhā."
In the Merutantra:
Then, with the mantra "brahmārpaṇam," one should perform the offering to Brahman;
preceded by the syllable Om (Tārā), it is recited as "prāṇabuddhi... and so forth.
Regarding the domain of the body and its functions, having described the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep,
one should then satisfy that [Self] through mind, speech, and the two types of action (body and intellect).
Whatever is uttered with the stomach, whatever with the penis, whatever is remembered, and whatever is spoken or done— let all that be an offering unto Brahman.
And this mantra, "svāhā," is declared to consist of six syllables each.
The manner of dedication, however, is found in the Śaiva Āgama.
Having thus offered the water for the arghya, the wise one should offer a small portion from the right side of the deity into the hand, O beloved, once the worship has been completed.
In this context, regarding the offering to the goddesses, one should offer it into their left hands; thus, "one should offer it into the left hand."
According to the words of Vīracūḍāmaṇi.
In the Merutantra:
Then one should dismiss the deity along with the host of attendants;
having thus offered a handful of flowers and prostrated, one should meditate upon [the deity].
Having meditated upon that auspicious form of light as having completely dissolved into the body of the God, [the preceptor] should say again and again, "Proceed."
One should dismiss [the deities] with the saṃhāramudrā.
Having placed the hands back-to-back, with the fingers interlaced in the middle.
As it is being turned over.
One should make the two index fingers straight; this is declared in the Tantra as the *visarjana* (dismissal) mudrā, known by the name *saṃhāra* (withdrawal).
In the Merutantra:
Having asked for forgiveness, one should cause the deity to ascend into the lotus of one's own heart, saying:
"Go, go to the supreme abode, your own station, O Supreme Lord!"
These gods, beginning with Brahmā, do not know the supreme state;
[one should realize it] by means of this mantra, followed by the filling breath (pūraka).
Meditating with this mantra and having visualized her, one should establish her in the heart:
"Stay, stay in the supreme place, O Supreme Lord, in your own abode!"
"Wherein all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, reside within my heart"—
having thus established [the deity] and worshipped it, one should indeed meditate upon the Self as being identical with That.
This has been stated in the Kulamūlāvatāra:
Having prepared a mandala in the northeast, devoid of doors and lotuses,
for the purpose of dismissal and for the worship of Nirmālyadhāriṇī.
Having discarded the floral remains (nirmālya) therein, one should worship with the mantra.
In the Merutantra:
In the northeast, one should construct a mandala, excluding the gate and the lotus.
"For one who consumes the remains of an offering for the sake of worship."
O Rudra, [this is] the mantra.
O Caṇḍeśvarī, Great Goddess! [I offer] the remains of offerings (nirmālya), such as camphor and the like;
as well as food to be licked, sucked, eaten, and drunk, along with garlands and ointments that are remains of offerings.
"By the command of Śrī Śiva, I give this food, which is equal to the remains of the offering (nirmālya).
Having thus given the remnants of the food offering (naivedya), one should bow and bid farewell.
The practitioner should place the remains of the offering upon his head while reciting the root mantra.
In the case of the five sense bases.
Indeed, five [deities] are to be worshipped; one should worship Īśa in the center.
Laṃbodara is the splendor of Gaṇeśa, and Caṇḍa is that of Vivasvat.
O Great Goddess, the mantra of Caṇḍeśvara has been declared for Viṣvaksena, while that of Bhavānī is for Caṇḍeśvarī; one should perform the removal of obstacles with these mantras.
Thus, according to the words of Meru.
Now, also [the ritual for] the offering to the Sun.
Then, with this mantra accompanied by the seed-syllables *hrīṃ hrīṃ*, one should again offer worship to the Sun for the sake of ensuring the rite remains flawless.
Salutation to Vivasvat, who is equal to the radiant sun, the splendor of Viṣṇu,
the pure creator of the world, the progenitor, and the bestower of the fruits of action.
Then, with palms joined in reverence and having steadied the mind, one should recite:
"Whatever flaw there may be in my sacrifice, whatever flaw in my austerity, and whatever flaw in my worship,"
May all that be flawless through the grace of the Sun.

Having thus offered the *arghya* to the Sun, one should pour that remaining water over one's head, consecrate it eight times with the root mantra, and sprinkle oneself with it. Then, having consumed the water, one should subsequently distribute the food offering (*naivedya*) among the devotees; having eaten oneself, one should conduct one's activities while absorbed in Him (*tanmaya*).
Happiness.
Now, regarding the consumption of the remains of offerings (nirmālya) by the Śaivas:
A Śaiva, however, is entitled to the grace of the *nirmālya* of Śiva;
another [who partakes of it] goes to hell, yet there is no fault in the union of the five.
Whether they are non-Śaivas or Śaivas, those who with devotion visit the Svayaṃbhū Liṅga Tīrtha or even its sacred precincts (prasāda) are liberated from the mass of their sins.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the *Kulamuktikallolinī*, composed by the venerable Ādyānanda.
But in the left-hand path (vāmamārga), however:
"One should consume that *ucchiṣṭa* together with the Kaulikas and their Śaktis," according to the statement of Meru.

Here, after the dismissal (*visarjana*) and before the offering to Brahman (*brahmārpaṇa*), the *guru-pātra* (the vessel for the Guru) should first be given to the Guru by the heroes (*vīras*) after they have worshipped it with devotion. For it is said in the Tantra: "Then [it is offered] to the one who is the manifest form of the venerable Guru..."
To the Self who is Paraśiva, having lifted up the vessel with both hands, one should offer it together with its companion vessel.
Also in the *Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi*, regarding the position of three vessels:
"Having divided the vessel for the *argha* offering into three parts, one part is for the Guru."
Having thus given [the portion] to the family, one should indeed satisfy the deities with a single [portion].
To the power of the nest; likewise also in the Merutantra:
But he who, though capable, partakes of the family substance (kuladravya) without having first offered it,
his worship is fruitless and the deity does not become pleased.
The libation for the deities (*devatarpaṇa*) consists of the drink itself. For it is said thus in the *Merutantra* and the *Kulārṇava*:

One should offer the substance accompanied by the mantra into that which has the form of Kuṇḍalī, whose nature is consciousness, which arises from the triangle that is the root of one's own self, and which possesses a splendor equal to ten million suns.
In the Merutantra:
This infinite vessel is filled with that supreme nectar;
it is characterized by the acceptance of the oblation into the fire consisting of supreme I-consciousness.
Also in the *Samayācāra*:
And for the purpose of satiating Kuṇḍalinī, one should employ the vessel of enjoyment;
having recollected the internal Śakti, one should satisfy the deity of the body.
From the Kaulikas, from the vessel of the hero, the Yoginī is the other Śakti.

Having given the nectar along with its purification from the vessel, one should partake of it oneself; this is the additional requirement in the case of the view that emphasizes the purity of the vessel.
In the Kulārṇava and the Merutantra.
One should drink the substance without mantras; this is prescribed as the expiation. One should never drink liquor, nor likewise should one drink it without mantras.
He who drinks liquor without a mantra is called a *surā-pa* (drinker of spirituous liquor).
Manu has been mentioned in that very same place.
I drink this purifying nectar; may it be my medicine, the cause proclaimed by Bhairava for the total severing of the bonds that bind the individual soul.
Because the continuum of consciousness is the essence, because it consists of bliss,
and because all phenomena are composed of that [consciousness], the state of being dissolves into the flavor [of bliss].
Wine is drunk by those established as gods for the sake of expanding their own autonomy;
therefore, I offer this wine—the gods—to the fullness of pure I-consciousness.
O Goddess of the gods, the knower of mantras, with an undisturbed mind, should slowly drink the honeyed liquor while reciting this root mantra.
One should drink the honey until the very limit of one's exhilaration.

He who acts without understanding the distinctions of drinks, the fruits [of actions], the longing for results, the means of purification, and the nature of stability, will become the foremost among those in calamity.
The classification of drinks is in that very same place.
Drinking is said to be of three kinds: divine, animal, and human, in sequence. Divine drinking is [drinking] in front of the Goddess once the dismissal of the heroes has been performed.
That which is drunk according to one's own will like an animal is called *paśupāna* (animal-drinking).
O Pārvatī, through the purification by mantra-saṃskāra and the drinking of nectar,
the state of divinity arises, which brings liberation from the bonds of worldly existence.
And so forth; this has been stated in that very same place.
The authoritative means of knowledge (pramāṇa) is also found in that very same place.
Bliss is the form of Brahman, and it is established in liberation;
because it is manifested by knowledge, that which is attained is not consumed.
The divisions therein are as follows:
the infantile, the tender, the youthful, and the mature.
Beyond that is Unmanā, and Anavasthā is indeed the seventh.
This is their definition, beginning with the first.
In that regard, O Ambikā, the threefold commencement has been described;
likewise, the youthful state and youthfulness itself have been described as bliss.
O beloved, youth is said to be the perfect blossoming of the mind;
the stumbling [of the senses] is designated as *ḍha*.
The obstruction of one's own desired activity is proclaimed [as the state];
the Unmanā [state] arises repeatedly from falling, rising, and fainting.
The lack of control over the body and the senses is called instability;
this is the connection with reality.

This is because, preceded by the mantra, the three handfuls of non-dual nectar (*culuka*) constitute the beginning, and furthermore, another method for the purification of the principles (*tattva-śuddhi*) has been stated [elsewhere] regarding the head and so forth.
And thus, in another [tradition], it appears in the Meru Tantra that there is a grasping three times within the interval.
Meat, beans, liquor, and intoxicants, equal in measure to a *ka*—these should be accepted by the disciples; otherwise, there would be a fault.
Stability is the boundary, as for example:

Free from fear, pure, wise, shameless, and devoid of deceit,
one who has ascertained the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras may drink the Ambāruṇī that bestows boons.
Having worshipped the gods and the ancestors according to the path prescribed in the scriptures,
a woman who drinks liquor and eats meat while remembering her Guru incurs no fault.
Contemplate with the thought that the Guru, the deity, and the mantra are one.
In this context, the "fathers" (pitaras) are indeed the Guru, the Paraguru, and so forth.
Likewise.
Having lifted the vessel with the left hand and formed the mudrā with the right,
one should take it with the second hand according to the ritual rule while reciting the mantra.
"Mudrā is purity by means of the second"—here the instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment.
At the end of a meal, liquor is poison; at the end of intoxication, food is poison.
One should know that food together with wine is nectar;
liquor accompanied by the act of chewing is always declared to be nectar.
Drinking without chewing is merely consuming poison.
He who gives to the uninitiated (paśus) the "chewing"— that is, roasted chickpeas and the like— which is the Kula substance of the Śrīcakra.
Whether out of affection, greed, or even fear, he becomes a *paśu* (bound soul) for the *yoginī*;
nevertheless, the union of vessels (*pātramelana*) must be performed there according to one's authority.

One should not associate with substances with those who are uninitiated, who lack proper conduct, who do not know the Tantras, who are godless, who are defiled, or who have fallen from their commitments (samaya).

One should not form associations with those who consider themselves possessed of supernatural powers, those who observe elaborate vows, those who are like cattle, or those established in petty rituals.
And one should not give the substance intended for Bhairava if it is placed in an unsuitable vessel;
if one should so give it, O Maheśānī, one would incur the curse of the deities.
To Bhairava, the practitioner.
Likewise.
Or, by means of the division of the currents, the Kaulika should perform the union of the vessels.
The meaning is that, at times of extreme confidence and when there is unity with the Veda (Āmnāya), one should perform the *śaṃkara* [rite].
Likewise.
The unification of the east and south, as well as of the north and west,
should be performed by heroes who are equal to others in their sequential worship.
And one should perform that [rite] with amorous women and the fourfold stream of currents.

By this, it is implied that there is no unity whatsoever between the Upper Tradition (Urdhvāmnāya) and this [Lower Tradition], and thus [the latter] is merely a figurative designation for the former. Likewise:
One should drink the substance that is the Śakti’s leavings and chew that which is the Hero’s leavings;
one should not give away one's own leavings, nor should one consume what belongs to another.
162b) That which belongs to another, the leavings of another man— even therein there is a distinction;
likewise among the sons of the Guru’s Śakti, and between the elder and younger brothers of the Guru.
O Pārvatī, one may eat the leavings even of one's own elder brother, but not those of anyone else;
one may consume the leavings of women, but one must never give them to them.
O Ambikā, one should give one's own remnants to one's younger disciples;
however, if one gives them out of affection to others, he shall become a vessel for calamities.
But that person of deluded intellect who takes up a vessel that has not been wiped clean—
whether out of affection, greed, or even fear— shall incur the curse of the deities.
In this regard, the seniority and juniority of these sacred sites (tīrthas) is determined solely by the order of their instruction.
For it is so stated in the Rudrayāmala and the Merutantra.
Even a child who was initiated first is senior according to the family tradition;
likewise, even a twice-born who was initiated later is junior to one initiated earlier, even if the latter is of low birth.
The twice-born who is younger is indeed the elder; such is the settled conclusion of the scriptures.
As long as the gaze does not waver, and as long as the mind does not waver—
One should perform the drinking [of wine] for that long; after that, one may drink like a beast (paśu).
