However, for those who have been consecrated but are devoid of the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), all seven exultations (ullāsa) are prescribed.

"Having caused one's own power (svaśakti), the hero-power (vīraśakti), and the initiated woman who is the embodiment of the Guru to drink [the wine], one should drink it oneself; such is the definitive conclusion of the scripture."
Therefore, having worshipped the auspicious power (śakti) with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and so forth, one should offer the vessel of enjoyment to the deity with a focused mind.
It is as follows:
Together with practitioners, either in the form of a circle or in the form of a row;
again, correctly either in the form of a row or in the form of a circle.
One should have one woman and one man sit down together in order,
or else, having formed a pair, have them sit down in succession.
If one is endowed with power, having sat upon the seat according to the sequence of pairs and pairs;
Having applied sandalwood paste and unbroken rice grains (akṣata) to the forehead as a temporary mark (sāmayika), one should prostrate with the thought that it is Śiva and Śakti,
provided that the Guru is present there.
Then, first having adorned the Guru with perfumes, flowers, sandalwood, and so forth,
and having offered him a vessel accompanied by purification, one should prostrate before him.
In the absence of the Guru, one should cast his vessel into the water.

163a) Then, having given that vessel endowed with purity to her— the recipient of the descent of power (śaktipāta)— he should also give the vessel endowed with purity and so forth to the initiates (sāmayika), according to the order of seniority. Thereafter, the initiate [should receive] the vessel with both hands.
Having taken up the root mantra and recited it eight times, and having gratified Ānandabhairava and Bhairavī as before,
one should gratify the gurus and the deities as before.

Then one should perform the purification of the reality (*tattvaśuddhi*). Thereafter, the Lord of the Mandala (*cakreśvara*) himself, together with the initiates (*sāmayika*), should perform the salutation of the vessel (*pātravandana*). Having performed mutual salutations, he should drink it with their permission, as follows:

I salute this first vessel, joined with the lotus-hand, which is the arrival of bliss, consisting of nine parts, the manifest nectar of the three sections; it shines with the remaining nectar of the glorious Bhairava, is drenched in nectar, and is worshipped by the hosts of Yoginīs, Siddhas, and the Lord of the Field.

"Bestowing purity. Having thus paid homage, lifting the vessel with the left hand and performing a mutual salutation, one says, "I receive," and having received the command of the Guru and the Śakti, the procedure is: "May you be pleased with these eyes. Then, one should visualize the Kuṇḍalinī, in the form of the chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), rising from the Mūlādhāra up to the tip of the tongue.

Having recollected the sandals of the Guru (gurupādukā) and contemplated "I am Śiva," one should grasp [the vessel] with both hands, recite the root mantra, and satisfy the Goddess at the mouth of Kuṇḍalinī. This has been stated in the Udayākara-paddhati:

Having assumed the form of the mantra, one should meditate upon the state of the Guru, the Goddess, and the digit consisting of pure consciousness. Afterwards, one should prepare an excellent vessel held in the leaves [of a tree], joined with brightly blazing lamps, consecrated with flowers and other offerings, and fashioned to destroy delusion; those who indeed practice this even through mere contemplation shall surely attain worldly enjoyment.
Supreme liberation.
Also in another tantra:
Having applied a vermilion tilaka on the forehead and wine-liquor to the hand,
one should meditate upon the Guru who has transcended the Vedas, as well as the Goddess who is composed of pure consciousness.

Then, having placed the vessel upon its support and again taking the supreme nectar (parāmṛta) in that same sequence, one should perform the salutation of the vessel as follows: "O left [hand], you have offered a golden fish that brings forth flavor;
what more need be said of the drinks and so forth? O you with eyes like a trembling red lotus, tell her this!"
Placing in my hand that which effects purity and complete purification, I now worship this second vessel, which increases sole bliss.
Then, as before, having accepted the bowl.
One should perform the veneration with another vessel.
For example:
Upon the foundation were the foremost of the serpent-lords, along with hosts of gods and asuras, who acted as obedient servants and attendants.
Having thus paid homage—here, according to the tradition, the *śāntistotra* follows the salutation to the vessel (*pātravandanā*)—it is as follows:
Victorious is the lotus-foot of the Goddess Hara, which bestows grace, the nectar of liberation, and the left-hand path.
I bow to the host of Yoginīs, numbering sixty-four, who awaken the mind toward the infinite Siddhānta.
I bow my head to the Lord Bhairava, beloved of Bhairavī, who stands in the center of the circle of Yoginīs and is surrounded by the mandala of Mothers.
Salutations to the venerable Lord-Physician, the one who dispels the terrible darkness of beginningless saṃsāra and who provides the medicine for the Kula.
Calamities, misfortunes, and diseases all arise from transgressing the conduct of the tradition;
yet all of these are dispelled by union with the divine wheel.

May there be long life, health, sovereignty, the attainment of fame, auspiciousness, and the successful recitation of mantras; may all my heart's desires be fulfilled, and may all the deities protect me.

May the Blessed One, the Lord of the Family (Kuleśa), grant peace to those who worship and protect these [teachings], as well as to the lords of ascetics (yatīndra), the lords of yoga (yogindra), and likewise to the Dharma, to the entire world, the kingdom, the city, and the king. May he cause joy even for the practitioners and for those who behold him, having created the great ocean of the fourfold teachings known as the Aghora-mantra; yet may he be gentle...

Those devoted to all the Kulas and Kaulas, others for the Supreme (Parā), and those who distinguish the specific stages for Śambhu; may the Siddhas, Gurus, and their lineages, the elders and juniors, the initiates (samayins), the Vaṭukas, and the Kumāris rejoice!
O King Nanda, may the world of the earth-lords, cattle, and the virtuous twice-born be produced by the six noble families of the best of heroic yoginīs.
But Nanda’s teachers were skilled in ethics, established in faultless conduct, free from envy, and devoid of affliction;
they were constantly devoted to the stainless [Brahman], dedicated to their gurus, possessed of minds both fierce and profoundly peaceful, and had removed all sorrow and fear.
But those devoted to yoga, liberated through the Kula-yoga—the masters, the initiates bound by the rules, the practitioners, and the spiritual sons—[honored] Nanda.
Cows, young brahmins, ascetics, and maidens; may Dharma and Bhava be intent upon them, joined with teachers and disciples.
O Nanda, may the curses of the Yoginīs, which have reached their ultimate limit upon the Maṇi mountain, fall upon me this very day if I am not a master of the Kula practice.
May that indescribable state of Śambhu manifest, in which the lotus feet of the Guru alone are attainable— that state in which the stages of the Cakras and Krama reside within the channels (nāḍīs).
Those which abide in the tree of the body, dwelling within the pores of the skin, and those which are established within the elements.

May those goddesses worshipped by the Kaulas—who move with the rising and falling waves of the breath, who dwell within the inhalations and exhalations, and who are intent on devouring the faction of enemies—be satisfied. May those divine goddesses born of the Kula who reside in the earth, those who dwell in the waters, and those Mothers of renowned splendor who eternally abide in fire, each in their own abode; may they [be satisfied].

May those who are the nectar of the sky, the nectar of water, who are all-pervading, bestowers of everything at all times, and devoted to protecting the path of the Kula— may they all grant me peace. Whether they reside above in the cosmic egg or in heaven,
in the expanse of the sky, on the surface of the earth, in the partless realm, in the subterranean world (Pātāla), in fire, or in water and wind— wherever they may be situated.

The goddesses who have taken their places in the sacred fields (*kṣetra*), seats (*pīṭha*), and secondary seats (*upapīṭha*), and who delight in incense, lamps, and the like, as well as in meat— those who are worshipped with the ritual of offerings (*bali*) and gifts, O Lord of Heroes (*vīrendra*), are worthy of homage. [They include] Brahmā,
Śrī, Śeṣa, Durgā, Guha, the Gaṇas, the Bhairavas, the Kṣetrapālas, Vetālas, Ādityas, Rudras, the Planets (*agraha*), and the Vasus.

May all protect us: the sages, the Siddhas, the Guhyakas and others; the Bhūtas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Ṛṣis, Pitṛs, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, Nāgas, Yogīśvaras, Cāraṇas, Kiṃpuruṣas, Munis, and Suras who dwell within the wheels; as well as all the deities residing in the body, the elephant-faced [Gaṇeśa], the lords of the sacred fields (Kṣetrapālas), the Bhairavas, and the Yoginīs.

May the Vaṭukas, Yakṣas, Pitṛs, Bhūtas, Piśācas, Grahas, other terrestrial and directional deities, sky-dwellers, Vetālas, and Ceṭakas be satisfied by this excellent drink, my own, as I drink it, O noble son! If the Guru, Dakṣa, the gods, and the Pitṛs are true; if the Vedas, Āgamas, and Yoginīs exist; and if Śiva and the other deities are real—then [let them be satisfied].
If the Vedas are indeed authoritative; if the Śākta philosophy exists; if the Vedas are to be known and are not to be discarded;

and if the Kaulikas are also true—then may I always be victorious! May all the practitioners, the oceans along with the lords of the Gaṇas, the Yoginīs, and the Kṣetrapālas be satisfied within my body.
Established from Śiva down to the earth, including Brahmā and all beings up to a blade of grass— from the beginning of time until the end of Śiva— may the universe be satisfied by this sacrifice.
In the Rudrayāmala:

having lifted the vessel with both hands while recollecting the root mantra and the *pādukā*.

Having drunk again and again, and drinking once more, until he falls upon the ground.
Having risen and drunk again, rebirth no longer exists;
through bliss the Goddess is satisfied, and Bhairava himself is intoxicated by the swoon.
Since all the gods [arise] from vomiting, one should therefore perform this triad.
In the Kulāmṛta.
If the dust of the earth should cling to the limbs of a knower of Brahman who, while following the family tradition, repeatedly stumbles after drinking wine; [then he is purified].
For that long, numbering as many particles of dust as there are, he rejoices in the world of Brahmā.
Likewise.
Having drunk again and again and having recited [the mantra], O Goddess, one shall dwell in the world of Brahmā along with ten million kinsmen; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
Right there he attains pervasion (vyāpti) and shall not fall back into this world again;
having drunk [the nectar] and worshipped the Lord, he certainly attains lordship.
In that very state one attains dissolution and does not return again; this, however, is essential for the Kaulikas.

Then, having praised and paid homage, one should perform the union of enjoyment;

Likewise, an actress, a tavern-keeper, a prostitute, a washerwoman, a barber’s wife,

having brought some of these [maidens] there to the circle of fire, [one should proceed].
Having worshipped the Great Goddess, one should then engage in sexual union.
In the Devīyāmala:
Now I shall describe the fruit of worship, which becomes increasingly superior;
by worshipping with one's own capacity, the merit is ten thousandfold, while in the worship of another's capacity, it is even greater.
Beyond that, the prostitute is to be known as more [degraded], and the washerwoman is even more so;
the weaver-woman is superior to the washerwoman, and the leather-worker woman is superior to the weaver-woman.
O fair-faced one, it is said that a woman who is the cause [of such sin] is more blameworthy than that;
even more so is she who is born from within [the womb], and the Cāṇḍālī is even worse than her.
165a) From her was born Mātaṅginī, the most excellent; from Mātaṅgī, Puṣkaśī;
from Puṣkaśī, Akṣatā, the most excellent; and from her was born Sudatī, who is remembered for having very beautiful teeth.
Sundarī is said to be beyond that; she is full of love, compliant, and devoted. O Supreme Goddess, she is intent on Him, intoxicated, and possesses auspicious marks.
Endowed with the conduct of the samaya, knowing the mantras, and free from fear;
she is clever, experienced, and possessed of fortitude and independence.
One should worship all women endowed with such qualities—
whether they be one's own or another's— for, O Maheśvarī, they are nothing but Śakti.
The presiding deity of the mantra should be worshipped with the intellect using all ritual offerings,
including various fruits, betel leaves, garments, ornaments, and gold.
Having worshipped according to the rules with devotion, one should cause many offerings to be presented;
he who performs the worship of Śakti while maintaining the latent desire for sensual enjoyment [is so described].
He incurs poverty and will certainly become a denizen of hell.
Even for the crest-jewel of heroes.
Having brought a beautiful young woman, distinguished by her noble lineage and conduct— a maiden of sixteen years with full and elevated breasts—
Unmattā, Mattamātaṅgī with eyes rolling from intoxication,
Mṛgaśāvakanetrā, Śāraṅgī, and Mṛduhāsinī.
One who is free from anger, greed, compassion, hypocrisy, delusion, and deceit;
who is devoted to the dharma of her husband, truthful, and always pure.

A courtesan, an actress, a woman of the Caṇḍāla caste, a female servant, one born of adultery, or one who wears yogic hand-gestures (mudrās), or one who carries a hide, or even a painted woman— [these are not to be approached].
Endowed with the four castes and excellent, originating from the mountain;
having drawn a triangle, a lotus, and a circle on the left side.
The practitioner, facing east, should worship the goddess who faces west— she who is joined with white and red, blue, and smeared with vermilion.
According to the ritual procedure for the *pīṭha-śaktis*, one should worship the nine powers:
Rati, Prīti, Priyā, Kānti, Kāminī, and Kāmamālinī.
The nine Śaktis— Kandarpī, Dalinī, Durgā, and Bhāvinī—
[are formed] by pronouncing the syllable *viyat* (the letter *ha*) followed by *bhṛgu* (the letter *sa*), conjoined with the nasal drop (*bindu*) and the digit (*kalā*).
After reciting this mantra, beginning with the word "mahāpreta" and ending with "hṛdayānta," one should utter the root mantra followed by the word "saṃbuddhyātāriṇī."
"Come, come! he says, and then, repeatedly taking the footprints with his left hand, he should place them upon the seat using the two sandals.
O Dear One, one should worship her whose limbs are smeared with red sandalwood, who is adorned with red flowers,
endowed with all ornaments, and naked.
One should cause her, who is intoxicated by liquor and enveloped by gestures of amorous allure,
to drink as much as reaches up to her throat.
O Maheśānī, one should perform meditation in the cavernous mouth of the crocodile,
[visualizing] the form of a cock's crest and possessing a luster equal to that of the elephant-faced one.
One should contemplate the Goddess, the Vidyā who deludes the worlds, situated therein; first the Tāra (Om), then [the mantra] ending with the heart, and afterwards the abode of Madana.
O Goddess, one should worship at the end of the dative case-ending and cast a flower upon the *bhaga*;
having cleansed the *kula* with the ritual substance, one should honor it with perfumes and flowers.
Having offered incense, lamps, and so forth, one should thereafter worship the enclosure:
Icchā, Jñānā, Kriyā, followed by Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrikā.
Thereafter, one should worship Rati, Prīti, and Kāma, who holds a bow and arrows of flowers, together with Vasanta, accompanied by leaves and sprouts.
O Goddess, one should worship Cikura, endowed with the vibration of the vital breath (ali-spanda);
one should worship Viriñci at the navel, and Hara-Hari at the heart.
Then, O Maheśānī, one should worship the Trimūrti in the stone face;
[the goddesses] Kāmeśī, Vajrīśī, and Bhagamālinī should be worshipped as well.
O Maheśānī, one should worship the five arrows at the root of the eyebrows:
Drāviṇī, beginning with *drām*, on the head; and Kṣobhiṇī, beginning with *drīm*, on the feet.
One should place *klīṃ* before *vaśīkariṇīṃ* on the face; *vlūṃ*, preceded by the seed-syllable, before *guhya*;
and again *ākarṣiṇīṃ* on the heart, joined with *bhṛgu* (s) at the end of emission (*visarga*).
This worship with arrows, which causes complete delusion, has thus been described in sequence;
one should worship the Sun and the Moon in order upon the mouth of the two *karma*s.
Having worshipped Vahni with the mantra Nakṣatramālinī in the tongue,
one should worship Prāṇa in the nose and Tripathagāminī in the Ājñā-cakra.
One should worship Akṣobhya on the crown with offerings of perfumes and flowers;
one should place a garland of flowers around his neck and then, according to one's ability, the wise person should perform recitation.
This sequence of worship is not for the lunar mansion (nakṣatra).
In the Jñānārṇava.
One should also contemplate within one's own body the ritual placements (nyāsa) performed upon the body of the messenger (dūtī).
In the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*.
Now I shall explain another [method]: one should meditate upon the self as Śiva.
"Śivātmānam" means "having Śiva as one's self. Likewise.
One should install Mahādeva with five faces, endowed with the Kalās, in due order:
"Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām" is the first Kalā, Śaśinī.
166a) "The Lord of all beings," then immediately after that,
"the Overlord of Brahmā," and at the end of the word [for] "Overlord," again "the Overlord of Brahmā."
May Śivomā, the bestower of the desires of Brahmā, be present; one should place the Marīci-sampuṭa, having uttered "Sadāśiva," and then the supreme Aṃśumālinī.
We know that Tatpuruṣa; thus is Kalā-śānti proclaimed. We meditate upon Mahādeva; likewise, [we know] Kalā-vidyā.
"Then 'tanno rudraḥ', the 'pada' (word), then 'paścāt' (afterwards), the 'pratiṣṭhā' (foundation) is said to be the 'kalā' (digit);
having uttered 'pracodayāt', there shall be 'nivṛtti' (cessation) after that."
O Goddess, one should sequentially assign the *aghorebhyaḥ* mantra and the *tamaḥ* digit (*kalā*) to the east, west, south, and north, as well as to the heart.
Then, one should place *mohāṃ* from the *ghorāḥ* upon the neck;
thereafter, following the end of the *ghorāḥ*, one should place *kriyā* on the right side.
"Salutations to you"—after this, one should place *kṣudhām* (hunger) and *kalām* (a digit) on the back in sequence;
at the end of "to those who have the form of Rudras," there are the words ending in *nṛṣāntāra* and *namaḥ*.
Having placed [the mantra] "Salutation to Vāmadeva" at the end on the secret region of the right testicle,
one should protect it with "Salutation indeed to Jyeṣṭha."
"Salutation to Rudra; [place] Rati behind [him]; [place] this digit (kalā) on the left scrotum;
at the end, 'Salutation to Kalā'; [place] Pālinī on the right thigh."
O Goddess of the gods, having uttered the word "namaḥ," one should worship Kalakāmā on the left knee for the sake of Vikaraṇā, and Saṃyamanī on the right knee.
Commanded by the ritual action of *vala*, for the sake of dispersal (*vikaraṇa*) on the left,
one should utter the word "vṛddhi" at the end of the *namaḥ* mantra and place it upon the right hip.

O bestower of the bliss of liberation, who relishes the taste of the Supreme Brahman;
though beyond the qualities (guṇas), You possess qualities; O dancer at the end of the great aeon!
Assuming the form of a maiden, you who are the very nature of both consciousness and ignorance have come to this house of mine for the attainment of the worship of Śarada.
For the announcement of this auspicious annual festival,
I am indeed blessed, I have fulfilled my purpose, and my life has become fruitful.
Since you, O Guhyakālī, having assumed such a supreme youthful form, have arrived here with the desire to receive the annual worship.
In that very form, you were formerly entreated by the gods;
you granted them sovereignty as well as their desired boons.
O Goddess of gods, being well-worshipped today, grant a boon to me as well;
for in the past, you bestowed upon Brahmā the power of creation.
And you alone gave to Viṣṇu the power of protection;
likewise, O Śivā, you bestowed upon Mahārudra the agency of destruction.
O Sovereign, you are the inner controller even of the Daityas' skill in destroying the gods,
and you are the dwelling place for the inhabitants of the three worlds.
I declare to you, O sole witness of all ears:
may there be the destruction of my enemies, the attainment of a kingdom, and indeed the health of my body.
I desire devotion to Your lotus feet; grant me these four boons.
Salutations to You, O Blessed Mother; salutations to You, O Compassionate One toward devotees.
Salutations to you, O support of the universe; protect me always.
O Mother, I do not know your form, nor your body, nor even your qualities.
With single-minded devotion, I know your worship through that devotion residing in my heart;
you are the mother, you are the father, and you alone are the venerable one, O Sovereign of the Universe.
You are my goal and refuge; you are heaven itself, and you are liberation as well. O Mother of the World, having abandoned you, I know no other deity.
"Salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations again and again!
With these verses, O fair-faced one, one should perform the praise of the maidens."
One should indeed offer water for sipping (ācamanīya) with haste at the conclusion of the meal;
thereafter, one should present betel-leaf scented with musk and camphor.
Having first followed [the ritual] with the sounding of musical instruments and so forth, one should dismiss them;
O Pārvatī, I shall now declare to you the auspicious and inauspicious results.
In that regard, I shall first describe the auspicious [rites], and then its opposite;
thereafter, one should give what remains of that to the jackals on the ground.
Or else, O Goddess, one should bury it, or having thoroughly stirred it, one should cast it away.
If one first offers it to the devotees, there will be abundance of food in the realm.
Through milk-rice (pāyasa), the sacrificer’s increase of cattle is produced;
through ghee, there shall be an abundance of longevity; and through worship, sovereignty and prosperity flourish.
Likewise, there will be an abundance of descendants from sweetmeats and meat-balls; from fish there is gain of wealth, and from rice-and-pulse porridge, prosperity.
From meat, however, there shall be the gain of a son; O mind, you shall become a woman of desire.
Indeed, I shall describe the various distinct fruits of each specific type of meat.
Through the meat of a boar there is gain of wealth; through that of a rhinoceros, victory in battle;
and through the flesh of a buffalo, the attainment of a kingdom will certainly occur.
Health is swiftly attained through *hāriṇa*; eloquence through the essence of *kārṣṇya*; wisdom is commanded by *medhāvitā*; and one may even attain freedom from old age in kingship.
O Goddess, by eating meat from the belly, one shall obtain all auspiciousness;
by eating the head, there is the gain of land; and by eating the limbs, one attains great power.
From the *vārdhnīna* one gains the destruction of enemies; from the *haṃsa*, the subjugation of men;
from the *taittira*, the attainment of desired objects; and from the *vartaka*, the total destruction of sins.
Delight of the mind results from *rasālā*; mastery over one's own radiance comes from *phaṇita*; great fame from *dadhi*; and unsurpassed prosperity from milk.
In flour-based foods there is the attainment of a son; in leafy vegetables, the destruction of enemies;
in wine, an increase in merit; and in dry foods, prosperity and eloquence of speech.
There is the arrival of wealth from molasses and the rising of prosperity from inspissated milk;
there is gain from the bottle-gourd, the round gourd, the pumpkin, the snake-gourd, and the patola.

O Goddess, when a mantra is prepared with ghoṣa, sūraṇa, dīrghāṅghri, and mūlaka, there shall be the acquisition of knowledge, O Goddess, as well as proficiency in speech through the consumption of buttermilk.
If a reflection appears in an object made of wheat flour, liberation will occur upon seeing the Goddess; if it appears in a pavilion, there will be advancement.
The bestowal of the sight [of] the chowrie, the parasol, the palm-leaf fan, the couch,
as well as the bell and the mirror, brings supreme prosperity.
O beloved, when the hands are not afflicted and there is pleasant touch, movement, and sight, various kinds of happiness arise for the husband.
Many such activities and omens of this kind arise as auspicious portents; now hear from me about those that are the opposite.
If the chief maiden becomes insane for two or three times,
famine will certainly arise, and the subjects will also be afflicted.
If a maiden weeps, the king comes to ruin;
if she voids excrement, there is a great plague; if she voids feces, the city is consumed by fire.
By not eating, there is fear of enemies; by eating too much, there are calamities. By not speaking, however, there may be insults; by speaking too much, there are misfortunes.
Various afflictions arise from the movements of the hands and feet;
excessive modesty leads to ruin, while lack of modesty leads to impurity.
Various portents occurring during silence or sleep indicate the destruction of one's speech;
however, if they occur while she is frightened, there is total ruin, and if she is angry, it is indeed death.
At that very moment, the king shall be possessed and die; of this there is no doubt.
If she is suspicious, there is fear of an enemy; if she is exhausted, there is fear of death.
If she is merely thought of, the downfall of that very kingdom is to be known;
in delusion there shall be loss of wealth, and in dullness worship is fruitless.
If there is fickleness, the fortune of the worshipper herself becomes fickle;
if the maiden there is as if possessed by dejection, she will likewise become so.
O Pārvatī, at that time the kingdom was afflicted with disease and its subjects were likewise stricken;
the king himself died of illness, and the people were born as if diseased.
If it sheds tears today, there will be famine, pestilence, and terror;
if it shakes its head, then total destruction shall occur.
When the enemy is terrified, protection is granted to that king;
yet if the cosmic age (kalpa) is at an end, the Supreme Goddess Kālikā turns her face away.
If the Goddess keeps her head low due to dissatisfaction, then the lord of the earth shall have a short lifespan; if her voice is faltering, he shall likewise be short-lived.
If the worshipper becomes distressed or agitated,
and if she becomes agitated through delusion, then the entire city will fall into disorder.
If she suffers from pain due to the force of destiny, disease will arise, along with sweating and the loss of husband and wealth;
if the maiden passes downward wind by the power of fate, [the same results follow].
Then that city will be oppressed by a foreign army;
if a young girl there sings a song while devoid of ritual action, [the same result follows].
If, at some time after the death of that king— who was beloved by his subjects and kingdom—
a dispute should arise between two principal [ministers] who had accompanied him to the funeral rites;
Then, why would he, through his power of illusion, encounter a most terrible foreign army—
whether together with anyone at all, or by means of anything whatsoever?
The maiden spoke with fear dispelled and her timidity slightly diminished:
"Then, in his realm, the six enemies were born."
O beloved, by moving their hands during the enjoyment of food, they bring about the reversal of fortune; for them, whatever is desired by the mind becomes both dispersed and fully realized.
If the king touches with both hands that lotus-essence which has been offered as a gift to the Goddess upon the sacrificial altar, he shall become terrified and flee in all directions.
If a young maiden should extinguish a lamp with the breath from her mouth,
then there will be a derangement of the intellect, and the lamp of knowledge will perish.
For if, by the power of fate, young maidens dance with confused cries,
then the king along with his kingdom becomes like a cremation ground.
If the young girls there should cast off their garments and become naked,
then the king will be slain by his enemies at the forefront of the battle.
If they leap about after spitting and whirl around while clutching their hands, a possession by a spirit (bhūta) occurs for the lord of the earth; of this there is no doubt.
If a young girl speaks thus at the time of a meal, saying "I shall vomit" or "I shall urinate," then there will be the danger of a great pestilence.
Whether on the left or the right, with her pupils flickering,
the young girl moves her head about with blood-red, fierce eyes.
If men standing there let out a loud, piercing laugh (*vāṭṭahāsa*),
then possession by spirits (*bhūtāveśa*) will occur, and the *preta*s will dance in the city.
If, clenching his teeth against each other, he makes a grinding sound like that of a cat,
he goes to death accompanied by his wife, children, and kinsmen.
Having fixed her unblinking gaze and bitting her lip with her teeth,
the young maiden indeed threatens him, as if intending to sever his head.
That very fruit which is indicated by the sound of crunching teeth is attained;
one should observe absolute silence and not touch food with the hand.
One should bend the head very low and draw upon the ground with the thumb;
one should draw lines on the earth with the fingernails even when there is no purpose.
If one scratches the head with both hands joined together,
or cuts nails without a valid reason, or cracks the fingers, [these are inauspicious].
One should cover the eyes with both hands, or place them over the two ears;
or one may perform the *vāhurikā* gesture, or rub the heels together.
He takes large morsels of food; he stands with his mouth wide open;
and he repeatedly yawns or lets out a deep sigh.
If one takes food with the hand and throws it in the four directions,
or if one stands up or moves away after having abandoned the end of the worship;
Either vomiting occurs in her, or horripilation and perspiration arise;
or else, while the pus is being discharged from her limbs, there is a discharge of oily matter from within.
If she suddenly utters a plaintive cry without cause,
speaks indecorously or frivolously, and weeps for the sake of her own kinsmen;
Standing in that place, she might cast off her ornaments, or say, "I am going home," or she might even utter insults toward anyone at all.
Or she might reproach someone, or even strike him with her hand; or she might tear off her bracelets from her own wrist without apparent cause.
When some relative has died there, she grieves for him; or that young maiden laments something or other without any apparent cause.
O you who are worshipped by the thirty gods, all of this should be known as inauspicious:
famine, loss of wealth, disease, pestilence, and likewise fear.
At every step there are calamities, grief, diseases, enemies, and arrogance;
why has there been a fire in the city and in the house upon the arrival of a foreign army?
Fear of death, poverty, separation from kinsmen,
and even the presence of ghosts, spirits, and demons are found in every house.
By the eight great diseases, the destruction of living beings occurs;
oppressed by fear, people run hither and thither.
O Queen of the Gods, what is the use of much speaking? In this case, the craft shall be instantaneous; for others there may be little fear, but for kings, the danger shall be great.
Indeed, through the movements of a maiden, the auspicious and inauspicious,

Death, the bond of suffering, happiness, fear of enemies, the increase of strength,
the expansion of the kingdom, oppression of the subjects, physical deformity, and the destruction of the army.
Through the worship of a maiden, and even through her meal, everything is known;

O Goddess of the gods, when an auspicious occasion has arisen, it is especially appropriate to perform worship with food, whether it be at the temple or elsewhere.

Also because of the mention of instruction.

And furthermore, O Hero, this refers specifically to the domain of those whose names end in *-kṛṣṭa*; and thus one should recite the "Slaying of the Divine Heroes" (*divyavīravadha*) thirteen thousand times. The Tantrikas maintain that "eleventh" refers to the *amukhāra*. Likewise:

Having thus worshipped the Mistress of the Pīṭha and honored one's chosen deity,

Leaving aside all other seats (pīṭhas), I dwell within his body;

Having visualized the letters from *a* to *kṣa* situated within the *brahman-āḍī*,
and having joined them with the vowel *a* and the nasal bindu, the wise one should mutter the excellent mantra.

O Goddess of the Universe, having joined [the vowels] beginning with *a* and likewise those beginning with *ka* in their proper sequence, one should then conceive of the Meru of the letters (*ārṇameru*) therein.
Then the writing should be done with a rosary of fifty beads;
by means of this, the recitation of all mantras accomplishes every purpose.
