Through the division of the eight groups (vargas), there are one hundred and eight [mantras];
one should recite the mantra with each one separated by an interval, for it thus bestows the fruit.
When recited with each individual syllable of the mantra joined by a sequence of letters arranged in both direct (anuloma) and reverse (viloma) order, they grant swift accomplishment.
If even other mantras, such as those of enemies, [are ineffective] for men, how much more so the others?
Therefore, O lotus-eyed one, the application of the rosary of beads is merely secondary.
Likewise.
Liberation is attained by twenty-five [verses], the accomplishment of wealth by thirty;
all objectives by twenty-seven, and malevolent rites by fifteen.

Success in the five types of activities shall be achieved with fifty [recitations]; likewise, with four more (fifty-four), and with one hundred and eight [recitations], all success is attained by one who has fashioned a garland of protective charms.
Likewise.
A rosary made of one hundred and eight, fifty-four,
or twenty-seven beads is suitable for all types of recitation (japa).
In the Merutantra (191b):
Alternatively, it is said regarding the practice of the rosary:
for the sake of liberation, one should always recite [the mantra] twenty-five times with [beads] numbering according to the lunar days (tithi).

With thirty [letters], there is an increase of Dharma; with fifty-four, one's desires are fulfilled; with one hundred, there is equanimity; and with one hundred and eight, all perfections (siddhis) are attained.
Now, the rosary of the hands (karamālā).
In that very same [text].
Alternatively, one may perform the recitation (japa) using the fingers as a rosary; that is described as follows:
beginning with the ring finger and the middle finger, proceeding in sequence down to the little finger.
The finger-garland (karamālā) is proclaimed to extend from the middle finger to the base;
one should form it by joining the pair of middle joints of the middle and ring fingers.
Or alternatively, starting from the base of the little finger and proceeding in order through the fingers up to the tip of the index finger,
and then from the middle of the middle finger to its base, there are ten [points].
In the *Mantratantraprakāśa*.
Recitation counted on the fingers is said to have a single-fold merit;
one should know that it is eight-fold when using lines, and a hundred-fold when using [rosary] beads.
In that regard, while performing finger-counting (aṅgulijapa), one should count with the fingers including the thumb;
an action performed without the thumb shall be fruitless.
One should always perform the recitation of the mantra by means of the joints of the fingers.
Likewise, in another tantra:
Starting from the little finger and proceeding in order up to the base of the index finger,
two joints of the ring finger constitute what is proclaimed as the "hand rosary" (karamālā).
Likewise.
Beginning from the base of the ring finger and proceeding in a clockwise direction,
one should recite over the eight joints up to the base of the middle finger.
Making the middle joint of the ring finger the Mount Meru, one should not cross over it;
this [rule] pertains to the recitation of the mantra one hundred and eight times.
In another tantra:
Beginning from the base of the ring finger and proceeding in a clockwise direction up to the base of the index finger,
one should recite [the mantra] over the nine joints.
The middle finger and the three [fingers] to be grasped, as well as the root of the ring finger—
making the ring finger and the middle finger one, one should not cross over the *meru*.
If a person joins the tips of the index finger and the middle finger there,
his four qualities— longevity, knowledge, fame, and strength— will perish.
And this [mantra], recited twelve times, is for the purpose of performing one hundred and eight recitations at most.
But regarding Sundarī, it is stated in the Yāmala:
O Maheśvarī, the two joints at the base and the tip of both the ring finger and the middle finger, as well as the three joints of the little finger and the index finger, [are to be touched].
O Goddess, the ring finger and the middle finger form the auspicious Mount Meru;
performing circumambulation in the proper order, one should mutter the mantra of Tripurasundarī.
192a) Regarding the Vaiṣṇava and other [traditions], it is stated in the Sanatkumāra-saṃhitā:
Beginning from the ring finger and the middle finger,
and starting from the little finger up to the base of the index finger, one should perform the recitation across these ten joints.
Likewise.
One should not separate the fingers; one should slightly contract the palm.
In the Merutantra.
One should never separate the fingers while reciting;
by the separation of the fingers, the recitation leaks away through the gaps.
One should not skip any count, nor should one contract the thumb;
one should not show the hand, otherwise the Rākṣasas seize the fruit.
In the Muṇḍamālā [Tantra]:
One should always perform the daily recitation (*japa*) with the hand, but never the optional (*kāmya*) recitation.
However, if no rosary is available, one may perform even the optional recitation with the hand.
"It does not exist" means that it has not been established as existing.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Kulāmṛta*:
When the Goddess is in the form of Vṛddhi, then worship is performed on the seat of the mind;
this was previously declared by me specifically regarding the Great Mantra.
O Goddess of the gods, recitation performed with the mind, using the mental rosary and the path of the mental boundary of phonemes, bestows liberation and the fulfillment of desires.

When the supreme Goddess Kulakuṇḍalinī is in the form of consciousness (citirūpā), then worship is to be known as occurring in the yantra; the fire-oblation (homa) is prescribed in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
O Great Goddess, recitation performed with a rosary made of beads such as gems, or even with a string of seeds, should be done in a whisper;
this bestows swift accomplishment.
O Goddess, when one worships her in the form of the *yoni* within the *yoni-maṇḍala*,
O Mistress of the Gods, the fire-oblation (*homa*) is performed right there according to the rule through sexual union.
O Maheśānī, the recitation (japa) should be performed in that same manner using the hand as a rosary for one who is liberated.
In the deep abyss of the family root.
Jewels originating from conch shells are said to bestow prosperity;
those made of crystal grant enjoyment, while lotus seeds increase nourishment.
The meritorious Rudrākṣas bestow enjoyment and liberation, and grant all spiritual perfections (siddhis).
Those originating from the Putrajīva tree, O son, bestow sons, cattle, grain, and wealth.
Gems originating from coral bestow wealth, good fortune, and the power of subjugation;
pearls are said to grant liberation as well as all forms of prosperity.
Those made of kuśa grass remove evil, while those made of gold and silver grant all desires.
In the Merutantra:
Rudrākṣa is considered to grant all perfections; coral bestows wealth; crystal is held to bring about the attainment of one's desires and provide worldly enjoyments in battle.
The *putrajīva* beads grant sons, the *padmākṣa* beads increase nourishment,
the coral (*vidruma*) beads bring about subjugation, and the pearl (*mauktika*) beads are considered to bestow pearls.
Those made of kuśa grass remove sin; those made of gold grant all desires;
those made of pearls increase one's wishes; and with indrākṣa beads, the supreme state is attained.
The resin of *haridrā* brings women under control; that of *āryā* subdues men;
that of *lākṣā* removes fever; and that of the sword-plant (*khaḍga*) effects the satisfaction of the ancestors.
A [needle] made of copper is recommended for the eradication of the sun, for the attainment of knowledge with bilva fruits,
for all purposes with ivory, and for the purpose of deluding.
For killing, the bow-born [arrow] is prescribed; for the sake of wealth, the white lotus-born;
for neutralizing poison, that arising from sandalwood; and for pacification, that born of wood.
For the purification of Yakṣiṇīs and others, one should use incense produced from red sandalwood seeds;
for the sake of satisfaction, that produced from Padmaka wood; and for the removal of affliction, that produced from Devadāru.
Ritual action performed with wood from a black tree succeeds in tamasic rites;
for the immobilization of spirits, [wood] born from a neem tree is used, while for the immobilization of people, [wood] from a sami tree is appropriate.
With *mahānimba* and *ḍākinī*, and with *bhūnimba*, there is the immobilization of diseases;
from the *indravṛkṣa* tree comes the immobilization of battle, or the warding off of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), when the monkey is stationed [there].
With the bones of bears, one attains success in the forest; with those of tigers, the deity [is pleased];
by means of human bones, rākṣasas are brought under control; and by means of the bones of heroes, horses are subdued.
Success in minor feats is attained through the bones of a donkey, while honor is gained through the bones of an elephant;
a garland made of gems roasted in clay bestows the siddhis of Śabara.
A Brāhmaṇa should recite with knots of Kuśa grass; a Kṣatriya with gold and gems;
a Vaiśya with beads made of Putrañjīva seeds; indeed, all may recite with lotus seeds.
Likewise.
One should not place anything between the rudrākṣa and the sphaṭika-indrākṣa;
by placing something in between while performing the recitation, one destroys both desire and liberation.
Likewise.
It is said that due to the specific excellence of its fruit, it is superior to rudrākṣas;
Śiva is the single wheel, and his rosary removes [the sins] of one who recites [mantras].
This two-faced [mantra] named Umāśaṅkara removes sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, as well as bestows desired things such as sovereignty.

He who bestows the happiness of the householder’s stage of life shall be three-faced and of the nature of fire; he shall be the destroyer of sins such as the killing of a cow and the destruction of sins such as the killing of a woman.
Dharma, artha, and kāma are accomplished through its retention and even by its recitation;
one becomes the four-faced Brahmā, and [it] destroys the killing of a guru and other such sins.
All sciences flash forth and the perfection of speech is also born;
Śiva himself, the five-faced one, is remembered as the remover of all sins.

For those of the Śaiva, Gāṇeśa, and Śākta traditions, success is swiftly attained through the recitation of that [mantra]. Furthermore, that which has issued from the mouths of Kārttikeya destroys the sins of one's vows.
By wearing [the mantra] on the right arm according to the prescribed rite, one gains victory in battle;
furthermore, by reciting it, one becomes a great seven-faced serpent named Ananta.
Infinite accomplishments arise, and fear of snake venom does not occur;
one becomes the eight-faced Gaṇeśa, the dispeller of all obstacles.
Through the recitation of that [mantra], all enemies such as desire, anger, and the like perish;
Bhairava becomes nine-faced, and the deities abide on the left-hand path.
By recitation alone, those who stand on the left arm and destroy obstacles become propitious;
Janārdana becomes ten-faced, and through the power of recitation and concentration, they are destroyed.
By wearing this, Piśācas, Grahas, Vetālas, Brahmarākṣasas, and serpents [are subdued];
indeed, Ekādaśamukha Rudra himself is present through its wearing.
Through recitation, one becomes a partaker of the fruits of sacrifices such as the horse-sacrifice;
likewise, by that recitation and by its retention, one becomes the twelve-faced Sun.
Radiant and majestic, he shall partake of the fruit of the Gomedha sacrifice;
he is remembered as being manifest with thirteen faces and having the Viśvedevas as his very essence.
If recited at the time of a Śrāddha ceremony, it bestows an inexhaustible state upon the ancestors;
when chanted with fourteen mouths, it becomes infinite.
O Lord, he is honored by gods and men, and through protection, he attains a favorable rebirth.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
If one should perform recitation with *indrākṣa* beads, rudrākṣas, or crystal beads, nothing else should be used in between; one should obtain a son and so forth.
If other beads are employed in a rosary for the practice of recitation,
that which bestows what is dear does not grant him either his desires or liberation.
In another birth, O Goddess, he is born as one who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāngas;
thereafter, he enters into a state of friendship with Cāṇḍālas of sinful deeds.
It should be understood that the statement from the *Rityuttara-tantra* refers to the addition of something distinct from the entire [set].
Nārada said:
A Brahmin should recite with knots of *kuśa* grass; a king, with gold and gems;
a Vaiśya, with *jīva* seeds; and all [castes] may likewise use lotus seeds.
In the Tantra.
Likewise, a wise person should fashion a garland for a Vaiṣṇava jewel from beads produced from the *amalaka* tree or made from *tulasī* wood.
For Gopāla, the white lotus-seed rosary is recommended; "with a concentrated mind, [one should recite] with a rosary of white lotus seeds," according to the words of Gautama.
In the *Nārada-pañcarātra*: 193b) [it is stated].
They say that the counting of the recitation should be done with lotus seeds, which increase devotion.

Based on the statement beginning with "But he who, having become a Bhāgavata... and concluding with Varāha’s words, "And [the rosary] made of Rudrākṣas is excellent," a rosary of Rudrākṣas is recommended even for Vaiṣṇavas. However, the recitation of Śakti-mantras with a Rudrākṣa rosary and so forth is prohibited. This is stated in the Yoginītantra:
O Dear One, if one recites the Śakti-mantra with Rudrākṣa beads during the day intended for Brahmā (Brahmayoga), he incurs misfortune;
his recitation becomes fruitless.
In the Bhairavī-vidyā and the Vārāhī-tantra.
One may fashion a garland from gold, jewels, crystal, or conch-shell, or even from coral; however, one should avoid using putranjiva wood.
Specifically, the lotus-seed (padmākṣa), the rudrākṣa, the indrākṣa, and the cākṣa.
Now, that which is prohibited:
In the Merutantra:
A rudrākṣa that is excessively thick, too fine, cracked, fragile, light, split, previously worn, or decayed is not considered auspicious.
From mutual friction alone, the loss of the recitation (japa) will certainly occur;
one should therefore place knots in the middle, but not insert pearls or similar materials therein.
Now follows the time for the consecration.
On the fourth lunar day, one should string the rosary with the mantras of Gaṇanātha;
on the seventh lunar day at midday, or on a Sunday, with the mantras of the Sun.
On the twelfth day, the Vaiṣṇava rosary should be strung with the Viṣṇu mantra;
on the thirteenth day, at twilight, the Śiva rosary [should be strung] with its own mantras.
On the eighth, the fourteenth, or the ninth lunar day, the Śaktis should also be worshipped at night in the Bhūminandana garden, having first eaten according to the prescribed rule.
In the Merutantra and in the Yoginīhṛdaya.
A garland for the pleasure of the Goddess should be strung with silk thread;
indeed, a Vaiṣṇava garland should be made from lotus fibers or otherwise.
Is it made from wool, or from bark, or from threads of hemp or cotton?
A specific distinction regarding cotton thread has been stated.
In the Merutantra:
O best of the twice-born, listen to the procedure for the production of the thread for almost all the deities: the thread should be spun by a virtuous woman and must be free of knots.
Having tripled it three times and washed it with great care, it should be taken up.
In the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara.
A garland woven with thread spun by a beautiful woman who has living children and is beloved by her husband brings auspiciousness.
Constructed with a cord, a ribbon, and a triple-strand tassel,
it is fashioned from gold and silver; even when made of gold, it brings auspiciousness.
Tied with a thread spun by a maiden and personally knotted by the Guru,
this auspicious *dhṛṣṭyālikā* is formed into a circle like the tail of a cow.
One should by all means avoid yellow thread, as well as thread produced from village cotton or from *caitra* cotton, during the act of stringing [the rosary].
In the Merutantra:
Having first observed a single meal, the practitioner, having performed his daily rites, being pure and unwearied, should himself string [the rosary] during the aforementioned lunar days.
Those with white, red, golden, and black complexions correspond respectively to the twice-born classes starting from the Brāhmaṇa;
among these, the Brāhmaṇa is the most excellent for the purpose of making a rosary for recitation.
In the absence of twice-born men, however, those of one's own respective caste may be accepted;
for in the Kali age, Brahmins who abide by their own dharma are as difficult to find as [true] Brahmins are.
Likewise.
Now I shall describe the method for making a rosary; one should wash it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
In the Gautamīya, he states the measurement for the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One *pala* of the milk portion and an equal amount of cow urine are prescribed;
there should be one *pala* of ghee and two *tolakas* of cow dung.
The curd should be the measure of one handful; this is known as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). Alternatively, it is said that the portions of the five products of the cow should be equal.
Having first observed a single meal, the practitioner,
having performed his daily rites and being purified, should himself string [the rosary] in the prescribed sacred sites, knowing the mantra.
Having diligently gathered the nuts according to one's desire and as they were obtained.
Regarding the collection of the five products of the cow according to the distinction of their colors, the Āmerutantra states:
"The milk is from a golden-colored cow, and the cow dung is from a white one."
The cow's urine should be from a copper-colored cow, the curd from a blue-colored cow, and the ghee from a black-colored cow; this same procedure applies to the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) as well.
In those regions, cows of various colors are easily found;
there, one should collect the five products of the cow according to their respective colors.
There is a fault in the loss of color; one should avoid that which is deficient in measure.
One should give twice as much cow-urine and four times as much clarified butter.
Milk is said to have eight qualities, and likewise curd in the *pañcagavya*.
Having taken cow urine with the *gāyatrī* mantra, one takes cow dung with the mantra "gandhadvārām."
One should offer milk with the mantra "āpyāyasva," curd with "dadhikrāvṇo akāriṣam," clarified butter with "tejo 'si śukram," and water from *kuśa* grass with "devasya tvā."
One should wash [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the mantra beginning with "sadyojāta";
then, one should rub it with sandalwood, agallochum, perfumes, and so forth, while reciting the vāmadeva mantra.
One should also fumigate with *aghoram*, black aloe-wood (*kṛṣṇāguru*), and *suguggulu*;
and one should smear [the image] with sandalwood and other substances using the mantra known as *tatpuruṣa*.
One should recite the mantra "Īśānaḥ sarvam" a hundred times for each [deity],
and with that same mantra one should consecrate Meru, and one should also consecrate it with the Aghora mantra.
In the Heart of the Yoginī.
They should be uniform in shape, neither too thick nor too thin,
free from defects such as insects, and indeed neither worn out nor brand new.
Having washed each of those separately with the five products of the cow,
it should be understood that this is to be done first on the previous day, except when one has the capacity for more.
Cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with Kuśa grass—
this is declared to be the "five products of the cow" (pañcagavya), which destroys even the most heinous sins.
One should arrange nine *aśvattha* leaves in the shape of a lotus;
then, one should place the thread and the jewels therein after they have been washed with scented water.
Then, having placed the Tāra, the Śakti, and the Mātṛkā upon the beads with the thread itself,
one should worship them with external offerings and perform oblations according to one's capacity.
However, a specific rule regarding the rudrākṣa is stated in the Kālottara:
Skanda said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, Lord of creation, maintenance, and dissolution!
O Maheśvara, how should one fashion a rosary for recitation with rudrākṣas?
And how, O Lord, should the consecration be performed, and what kind of fruit does it yield?
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Khaṇmukha, I shall explain how a rosary is made with rudrākṣa beads according to the ritual procedure,
by which it bestows success in recitation.
In the Merutantra and the Kālottara.
Some should be made with one face, two faces, four faces, five faces, or even six faces; however, one should avoid mixing these types together.
The mouth should be joined to the mouth, but one should avoid joining the mouth to the root;
having joined the mouth with the mouth, one should join the back with the back.
The elevated part of the rudrākṣa is said to be its mouth, while the depressed part is its tail;
the best is like the fruit of the dhātrī tree, and the middling is similar to the jujube (badara) fruit.
The jujube fruit and the jujube seed.
The lowest desire would not exist; for one inferior to that, it brings about ruin.
In the Merutantra:
A single Mount Meru should be given there to all, endowed with bulk and free from decay.
In the Kālottara [Tantra].
Its upward-facing aspect, called Meru, should be made; one should leap over that.
In the Merutantra.
The first [knot] should be thick; then one smaller than that, and then one even smaller still;
one should fashion it in the shape of a serpent, with a *brahmagranthi* at each jewel.
In the Śaiva Āgama.
It should be made resembling a cow's tail, with its tip as focused and firm as Mount Meru.
195a) In the *Uttaratantra*:
A single Meru, produced from the gross [element], should be given there to all;
therefore, one should place it in sequence, since it is shaped like a serpent.
One should fashion a Brahma-granthi for each seed-syllable according to the prescribed rule.
In the Merutantra and the Uttaratantra.
Alternatively, it may be provided with a firm cord that is free from knots.
The Brahma-knot is as described in that very same place.
Having turned three times through the middle and then half a turn at the end,
the knot that winds to the right is called the Brahma-knot.
In the Merutantra:
Now I shall describe another consecration of the rosary using leaves of the *aśvattha* tree;
having arranged nine [leaves] in the shape of a lotus, one should place [the beads] therein.
Having washed the gem-string with scented water,
one should then consecrate each individual gem in sequence with the syllables of the Mātṛkā, preceded by "Oṃ Hrīṃ."
Having placed the sūtra there and performed worship, one should then offer the oblation.
With sesame and clarified butter, or with clarified butter alone, using the five mantras beginning with *sadyojāta* individually, one should offer one hundred, eight, or twenty-eight oblations.
In the absence of fire-offerings (homa), recitation (japa) is prescribed;
one should then string the rosary, making it like a cow’s tail, with a single-pointed seat as its central axis.
Then, one should display the eight mudrās beginning with the invocation (āvāhana);
thereafter, the washing and other rites should be performed as before with the mantras beginning with Sadyojāta.
Immediately thereafter, the worship is performed according to the procedure prescribed in its own ritual manual.
There is a distinction in the left [hand].
In that very same [text].
In the Kaulika and other traditions, this specific rite is the satiation with wine and jewels.
Thus ends the procedure for the consecration of rosaries made of Rudrākṣa and other materials.
Now, the fruit of wearing rudrākṣas is also being written down here as a related topic.
Likewise.
Even one devoid of devotion who wears a rosary of rudrākṣas around his neck,
though he be a constant evildoer, is honored in the world of Rudra.
And whatever Vedic rite a Brahmin may constantly perform while wearing Rudrākṣa beads, that rite shall become fruitful.
During bathing, giving gifts, recitation of mantras, burnt offerings, the Vaiśvadeva rite, worship of the gods, penance, as well as at a Śrāddha ceremony, and especially at the time of initiation;
By wearing Rudrākṣas on the neck, the head, the hands, the ears, and as a sacred thread, O Lord, a human being becomes Rudra himself.
Even while eating meat, drinking liquor, or consorting with those of the lowest castes,
one whose soul is instantly purified by wearing a rudrākṣa on the head.
Those gods who devour other gods are, according to the Vedas, merely beasts;
those who torment them in the world of Yama— Yama himself is their punisher.
For the sake of protecting them, there is nothing else on earth superior to the rudrākṣa;
rudrākṣas bestow the accomplishment of mantras for all the gods.
Whether one is impure from remnants of food, engaged in forbidden acts, or burdened by all manner of sins,
a man is liberated from all evils by wearing rudrākṣa beads.
If even a dog dies with a rudrākṣa resting upon its neck, it too attains the state of Rudra; how much more so, then, for humans and others?
If a Brahmin, out of delusion, performs any Vedic rite while not wearing rudrākṣa beads,
he obtains only a sixteenth part of its fruit.
Now follows the consecration of the rosary for the sake of women and Śūdras.
That has been stated in the Merutantra:
For the sake of a Śūdra or for the sake of a woman, the consecration of a garland (mālā-saṃskāra) is prescribed;
having worshipped Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Durgā with devotion.

Then, having consecrated that garland with the seed-syllable *mālā ha sauḥ*, one should place it in the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for three days, reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
But in the fourth [case], having extracted it, one should wash it with the weapon-mantra (astramantra).
In the Yoginītantra.

Having fashioned a rosary from the beads mentioned, strung with mantras according to the prescribed method, the best of practitioners should place it in a vessel smeared with perfumes and other substances.
Having completed the worship beginning with the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and so forth, one should perform worship there;
having invoked Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Durgā, one should worship them.
In that regard, concerning the garland:
Having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and consecrated it with the mantra "Hauṃ," one should lift the garland from there and place it in a golden vessel.
Then, having performed the rite of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) in due order with milk, curd, ghee, honey, sugar, and so forth, as well as with various other incenses, the wise one [proceeds].
Having placed it there in due order, one should bathe it with cool water;
thereafter, with sandalwood, fragrant substances, musk, saffron, and so forth.
Having smeared it with that [ointment], one should mutter the mantra "Hraum" one hundred and eight times;
then, having worshipped the Guru, one should take up the auspicious rosary.
In the Bhairavī Tantra.
At the outset, the wise man, being well-composed, should worship the deity Gaṇapati, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Umāpati, and Durgā with the rosary.
One should place the rosary in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and consecrate it with the Plāsāda mantra;
then, having lifted the rosary, one should place it in a golden vessel.
Having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and with cool water,
[one should anoint it] with fragrant sandalwood, musk, saffron, and so forth.

196a) Then, having performed the consecration with this mantra, the knower of mantras [should perform it] upon the vital breath (prāṇa) mounted on the life-force (jīva), which is the syllable *oṃ* adorned with the vowel [sound].
One should duly install the king of mantras joined with the bindu and nāda;
then, having worshipped the nine planets, one should perform the worship of the guardians of the directions.
Then, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with sesame seeds mixed with ghee according to one's capacity.
Having performed one hundred and eight [repetitions], one should place them; *prāṇa* is the letter *ha*, and *jīva* is the letter *sa*.
But in the Meru Tantra, however:
Having tied it together with the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra), one should place it upon the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila).
Then, that garland should be weighed and placed in a golden vessel.
Having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and with cool water,
[one should anoint it] with fragrant sandalwood, musk, saffron, and so forth.
Then the practitioner should perform the consecration with the mantra *ha sauṃ*;
having worshipped the nine planets, he should also worship the guardians of the directions.
Then, one should perform oblations according to one's ability with sesame seeds mixed with ghee;
thereafter, one should give gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor, equal in number to the gems.
While reciting that mantra, one should feed Brahmins learned in the Vedas;
or, in the absence of a golden vessel, one may use a leaf of the Aśvattha tree for the clarified butter.
What is called the consecration of the rosary (mālā-saṃskāra) is the recitation (japa) that bestows accomplishment (siddhi).
And furthermore:
In the Kubjikātantra.

One should place [the materials] along with the color-pigment into the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for three days; or alternatively, on the fourth day, one should wash the thread with mantras of the weapon (astra).

The most excellent practitioner should string [the beads] with a thread of the same color while reciting the *hṛdayāṇu* (heart-mantra), or he may string them using threads of gold and other precious materials.
Then one should place the *brahmagranthi* or even the *nāgapāśa*;
with the *kavaca*, being intent on meditation, one should grasp the rosary.
Then, at the end of everything, the best of practitioners should string together Mount Meru, provided with two threads, and bind it by means of the *tāra* [mantra].
Having thus completed [the preliminary rites], O Goddess of the Gods, one should perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
Having drawn a maṇḍala upon the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) according to the sequence of the rules for the respective divisions.
Having worshipped the chosen deity in due order according to the rules,
one should first perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) and then recite the mantra one thousand and eight times.
And one should perform oblations with a tenth part [of the total] of whatever is dear to whichever deity;
thereafter, the wise person should place that rosary in the center of the mandala.
Then, having performed the placement of the weapon-mantra (astramantra), one should contemplate [the rosary] as being like a deity;
having attained a state of non-difference, one should fashion the rosary as being of that same nature.
Then, together with those most excellent practitioners, one should offer the oblation according to the prescribed rule;
having thus established the desired deity within the rosary.
The mantra-practitioner should worship the preceptor and the artisan according to the prescribed rule;
he should not recite another mantra there, if he desires his own success.
The mantra beginning with the weapon-syllable (astra) should be recited; by means of those oblation substances, the offering for the rosary should be taken.
Now follows the consecration of the rosary, beginning with the arts required by the Kaulikas.
This has been stated in the Merutantra:
For the sake of the accomplishment of those who wear garlands of bones and so forth, the Kaulikas, and the Vāmins,
I shall explain the consecration that is hidden in all the Tantras.
One should first honor the artisan with garments, perfumes, and ointments;
then, being well-pleased and drinking honey, one should have him fashion the garland purified by mantras.
In the Kubjikātantra.
At the outset, one should honor the artisan with garments, perfumes, and ointments;
being well-pleased, one should have him fashion a pure garland of excellent form.
The wise practitioner should fashion a pierced garland according to what is appropriate,
consisting of fifty seed-syllables in the form of letters.
In the Merutantra:
One should prepare [a mixture] with fifty gems and insert it into the vagina of a woman in her menses;
after leaving it there for one night, one should then wash it out with cleansing agents.
One should consecrate [the image] with pure water using the root mantra and with the juices of *vijayā*.
After washing it, one should fumigate it and subsequently thread it with desired strings.

One should visualize the Sūtra as blue for one's own desired recitation, black for the rite of killing, green for deluding, smoke-colored for paralyzing, and the color of a venomous serpent for subjugating enemies.
For pacification and nourishment, it should be white; for hatred, red; for eradication, it should be yellow;
for subjugation, yellow; and for causing distraction, it is considered to be brown.
Then, having performed the worship of the wheel one thousand and eight times,
the practitioner should offer oblations of liquor and meat with the root mantra.
Then, one should cause the offering (bali) of buffaloes and other animals to be presented according to the rule,
while also feeding the Śaktis and the practitioners (sādhakas), numbering as many as the gems.
Having thus consecrated the rosary, one should show it to the animal (paśu);
with whichever mantra the rosary was made, one should recite [the mantra] using that [rosary].
From the recitation of another mantra, a curse from the deity arises.
Now follows the procedure for the consecration of the secret rosary, as established by tradition.

Having consecrated [the offering] seven times with the mantra *oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ hraḥ phaṭ svāhā*, and having worshipped Ka along with his retinue with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), one should recite the root mantra while contemplating the seed-syllable, transform it into nectar by means of the *dhenumudrā*, veil it with the *kavaca* (armor) mudrā, and then cover it with the *mahāmudrā*.
Meditating on the goddess as the end of the form of the garland, one should perform the casting of the drop (bindu).

In that regard, the mantra is: *oṃ hrīṃ svāhā*, *oṃ huṃ svāhā*, *oṃ phaṭ svāhā*, *oṃ strīṃ svāhā*, *oṃ hrīṃ hūṃ svāhā*, *oṃ hrīṃ phaṭ svāhā*. With this, one should perform the sprinkling of the drop (*bindu*) one hundred times.
Having offered incense and other substances with hands as fragrant as musk, camphor, and nectar, and having removed [the vessel] from the fire, one should consecrate it with these mantras.
Therein is the mantra: *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ mahāvajriṇi mahāghorarūpe karkaśe mahāsthimaṇḍale praviśa sarvasiddhiṃ prayaccha oṃ hūṃ krīṃ hrīṃ svāhā mahākapālini*.

*Mahāghorarūpe svāhā*. Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Having worshipped with *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice (*akṣata*), having performed the kindling (*uddīpana*) with the seed-syllable of Kandarpa, having worshipped with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), having inflamed [the fire] with the *mātṛkā* mantra, and having encircled it with the syllable *hūṃ*, one should offer the oblation (*bali*). It is as follows: Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ oṃ hūṃ.

HŪṂ OṂ PHAṬ HŪṂ OṂ OṂ HŪṂ SVĀHĀ OṂ HŪṂ MAHĀYOGINI TRIBHUVANATĀRIṆI MAHĀŚAṄKHĀSTHIMĀLĀMADHYE NIVĀSAṂ KURU KURU SARVASIDDHIṂ DEHI DEHI SURĀMĀṂSOPAHĀRĀN GṚHṆA 2 GṚHNĀPAYA 2 HRĪṂ TRĪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. By this [mantra]:
Having offered the *bali* with the substances as previously described and having dismissed the Goddess, one should wear the garland in a secluded place.
In the Merutantra and in the Ratatantra.
One should fasten a strong thread as the practitioner of recitation would;
when the thread has worn out, one should join a new thread and recite [the mantra] one hundred times.
In the Merutantra:
At the time of turning [the manuscript], one must not cause any clashing;
for when it creaks with the sound *khaṭakhaṭ* while swinging, the mind becomes agitated.
In the Śaiva Āgama.
When that garland has been strung and consecrated as before,
one should recite the mantra with undivided attention while it remains installed.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for consecrating the rosary.
Now, O Lord, what is the nature of the *kullukā*, and what is the nature of the bridge (*setu*)?
What is the Great Bridge like, and what is Nirvana like?
Or whatever else has been spoken to me, tell me, O Lord, what that is like.
The illustrious Lord said:
O Goddess, out of affection for you, this most secret of secrets is told;
O Great Sovereign, without this [knowledge], recitation and other practices are fruitless.
O Goddess, the *kulluka* of Tārā is Mahānīla-Sarasvatī;
the five-syllabled mantra of Kālikā is declared to be her *kulluka*.
O Parameśvarī, the mantra *kālikūrca-vadhū-māyā-phaṭ* at its end,
when combined with *chinvāyā*, O Maheśānī, becomes the eight-syllabled *Kullukā*.
One should recite "Vajra Vairocanīye" and at the end proclaim "Varma.
This is considered the *kullukā* of Bhairavī, the first [deity] who bestows prosperity.
The twelve-syllable Kullukā of the illustrious Tripurasundarī consists of the first seed-syllable, Vāgbhava, followed by Kāmarāja.
Then one should extract the seed-syllable of modesty (LĀM), followed by Tripureśī, and after that the word "Bhagavatī"; finally, at the end, one should extract the two letters ṬHA.
Thus, O Goddess, this Kullukā has been described by me in brief.
That dull-witted, base person who recites this Kullukā without knowing it [is lost].
One quickly meets death, success is lost,
the mantras turn away, and the failure of the mantra occurs.
Likewise, all [practices] such as recitation will be fruitless; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, with every effort, one should join Kullukā to the crown of the head.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain that which is dear; listen, O beloved one, by the knowledge of which recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites become fruitless.
The Praṇava is the bridge for Brahmins, and likewise for Kṣatriyas;
the syllable Phaṭ belongs to Vaiśyas, while Māyā is said to be for Śūdras.
O Goddess of the gods, he who recites a mantra without having first performed japa in his heart indeed has no authority over any mantras whatsoever.
And the Mahāsetu, O Queen of the Gods, is for Sundarī; Bhuvaneśvarī is for Kālikā; one's own seed-syllable is for Tārā; and the *kūcca* syllable is her seed-mantra.
O fair-faced one, for other [mantras], however, having first recited the Great Bridge (mahāsetu) which is the seed of the bride, one should then recite the mantra with undistracted mind.
In wealth he was equal to the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), in speech he was like the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati),
when angry he resembled the God of Death (Yama), and among women he was like the God of Love (Madana).
For him, every moment may be a time for recitation; of this there is no doubt.
Just as water without a dam flows downward in an instant, so it is with him.
In the same way, the mantra of sacrificers becomes bridgeless and flows away in an instant;
therefore, in all mantras, the twice-born are of four classes.
Taking the *setu* (bridge) as one's support on both sides, one should begin the practice of recitation (*japa*).
The *praṇava* is proclaimed to be the bridge for mantras, just as it is for the twice-born.
The fourteenth vowel, joined with the moon and the anusvāra, belongs to the others.
Now I shall speak of Nirvāṇa; listen to it, O sinless one, for it is free from [duality].
Having first uttered the Praṇava, one should then recite the beginning of the Mātṛkā.
Then, O Maheśānī, one should utter the Mūla-mantra, followed by the Vāgbhava-mantra;
then the entire Mātṛkā, and once again, one should utter the Praṇava.
Thus one should recite the root mantra in the "jewel-filling" (maṇipūraka) breath-retention;
O Īśānī, that base person who does not know this [method] of Nirvāṇa is indeed a fool.
Even in a hundred million years, accomplishment does not arise for him.
Therefore, O Maheśvarī, one should practice with every effort that which has been taught.
Then, according to the procedure of the master, one should recite that unsurpassed mantra,
[considering] the seer, the meter, the deity, the seed-syllable, the power, and the wedge.
O Goddess, one should meditate upon that, and thereafter recite the mantra for one's own desired goal and so forth;
if the practitioner of mantra recites the unsurpassed king of mantras in this manner, [the result is attained].
Within six months one attains perfection; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
He himself is directly the Lord of the worlds; of this there is no doubt.
He alone is worthy of refuge, he alone is possessed of true knowledge, and he alone is a knower of the reality of mantras;
he alone, being liberated, may wander upon the earth as if in his own home.
By the mere sight of him, enemies flee.
Having acted thus, whoever recites the King of Mantras encapsulated by the *praṇava* (Oṃ),
and having likewise recited the *kullukā* ending with it together with the worlds (*bhuvana*), for them all the worlds and the eight supernatural powers (*siddhis*) will be in their hands.
Out of affection, this secret word has been spoken for [them] throughout many successive births.
Now follows the extraction of the *śrā* vowel.
This has been stated in the Rudrayāmala:
Distressed by the slaughter of his father’s preceptor, Bhārgava, that bull among sages,
visited lakes, sacred rivers, and holy hermitages.
Greatly agitated, he wandered about excessively and could not find release from his state of being born; then, with a focused mind, the wise one went for refuge to Hara.
Having reached Siddhāśrama, free from all attachments,
he practiced difficult austerities there for a long time with unwearied diligence.
By the power of his asceticism, Śiva appeared before him;
seeing the sage absorbed in meditation, he smiled and spoke these words.
"O Rāma, Rāma, O you of mighty arms, I am pleased; I am a granter of boons, O smiling one!
Choose a boon, O highly wise one, whatever dwells in your mind."
The sage Bhārgava, beholding the Blessed One standing before him, praised Him with hymns, bowed down, and, being humble, spoke these words.
O Mahādeva, O All-pervading Lord, if you are pleased with me, then instruct me so that I may be liberated from the slaughter of my mother before long.
Thus entreated by Paraśurāma, the Supreme Lord spoke these sweet words: "Listen, O son, O descendant of Bhṛgu."
As you recite the Gāyatrī mantra of Mahākālī, the southern direction,
the sin born from the slaughter of your mother shall come to destruction.
Thus consoled, Rāma spoke again to Maheśvara:
"O Śaṅkara, tell me about that goddess named Dakṣiṇā."
"What is her form, what is her conduct, how is she to be served, and what is her nature?"—
having been thus entreated, the God spoke again to the Lord of Sages.
"Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom! You have asked rightly. Come now, my son, I shall explain this to you; be attentive."
O Sage, that which is sung of as the power of consciousness (cicchakti), whose form is truth, existence, and bliss, and which, having pervaded everything, remains as the presiding southern direction.
In her, creation is led forth and in her it is dissolved;
having attained her grace, Brahmā becomes the creator of the world.
Viṣṇu protected her, and Sadāśiva withdrew her;
assuming various forms, she sports upon the surface of the earth.
This city is considered the bestower of all accomplishments through mere recollection;
when worshipped and meditated upon, this city grants the desired success of the practitioner.
Having heard these words, the sage spoke again to Sadāśiva: "O Maheśvara, I have a doubt regarding the past; please dispel it."
Thus addressed by the descendant of Bhṛgu, the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain then spoke:
"Once upon a time, a certain practitioner of firm mind..."
He recalled the goddess Dakṣiṇā, whose mind was always devoted to him alone,
and how the game of dice with me had commenced in the sky.
O Sage, having gone there where the practitioner was and having spoken to him, she turned away;
then, with an angry mind, I cursed her.
Since she has come into the presence of the practitioner having abandoned her own flesh,
therefore you shall become a bestower of swift results in the South.
Then the queen, her mind dejected, was satisfied with those nine new hymns;
and being pleased by her, I spoke to her once again.
O slender-waisted one, when you are recited encased within the Mahāvidyā,
you shall then be liberated from the curse and become a bestower of fruits.
From that time forward, this vidyā shall swiftly bestow its fruits;
O fortunate one, practice it for the sake of liberation from the slaughter of your mother.
Having spoken thus, the Lord vanished while Bhārgava was looking on;
and Bhārgava, the best of sages, fixed his mind once more upon ascetic penance.
This curse lasts for exactly twenty-two fortnights;
for the twenty-two-syllable vidyā bestows swift accomplishment.
Pierced by that Great Lord during the dialogue between Hara and Maya,
the Great Vidyā, acting as a catalyst for awakening, should be fashioned into a casket.
"In this way, O Bhairavī, success is attained through the grace of the Guru;
thus they say, according to the words of the *Tisiddhavidyāpradīpa*."

For the removal of the curse of Aurdva, the reversal of the seed-syllables (*bījas*) at the beginning and end of the twenty-two syllable mantra must be performed. Alternatively, it is stated in the *Mahākālasaṃhitā* that the *Kālī* seed-syllable should be uttered four times at the very beginning.
In the Viśvasāra: 199a) [it is said].
I shall proclaim the withdrawal of the curse performed by the sage Vasiṣṭha;
having recited twenty-four hundred thousand [mantras], he cursed him out of anger.
From this day forward, O Goddess Kālikā, you whose form is Time,
there shall be no difficulty whatsoever in attaining perfection through your mantras.
Having heard this, the Great Goddess appeared and said, "Be appeased, my son; why have you bestowed this curse in vain?"
O Lord of Sages, act in such a way that this fruit may not come to pass,
for you have granted a knowledge that is difficult to attain and hard to acquire even by the gods.
Then, having joyfully obtained a boon consisting of knowledge conjoined with realized wisdom,
he spoke with a delighted mind to the one afflicted by the curse during the crisis of the mantra.
O Mother, having spoken thus out of anger, I shall now declare the remedy for that:
first extract the *praṇava* (OM), and then [the words] "Ghorarūpe" and "Dakṣiṇe."
Having uttered "Siddhiṃ kuru dvayam," one should then say the word "Kālike," followed by:
"O Draviṇa, quickly grant me my desired fruit and prosperity."
Having uttered the mantra at the beginning of the recitation and reciting it again at the end,
success will then arise without delay, O Supreme Goddess.
Now follows the offering of food.
That has been stated in the Merutantra:

I shall now fully explain its procedure; one should arrange it according to the four kalpas. Furthermore, the *vali* (offering) is to be known as threefold: the Tantric, the Smārta, and likewise the [ordinary].
And it is Vaidika; among these, first, the Tantrika is remembered as being of eight kinds:
the human, the buffalo, the boar, the goat, and likewise the crane.
The pigeon and the cock are common [species], each being superior to the one preceding it.
Vārāhī is the bearer of patience.
Now, therefore, the procedure for the offering of meat (validāna) is here proclaimed:
the yak, the black antelope, the fish, the sheep, and the boar.
The buffalo, monkey, rhinoceros, monkey, goat, and so forth may be [the sacrificial animals].
In the Merutantra:

O Goddess, in that great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha) during the Kali age, a man who is diseased and deformed should be offered as a sacrifice by the preeminent practitioner; he shall then become healthy and handsome.

One produced by the increase of the elements, one with black hair, one made at the beginning of a cycle, one born in natural order, one purchased for a price, one ground [by hand], one belonging to a deity, or one that has come of its own accord.
Whether for a year or six months, one who maintains conduct according to his desire becomes fit for the bali offering;
no other, such as one whose wealth has been seized by thieves, is so.
The buffalo, originating from the forest, is five cubits in height and ten cubits in length; even the village buffalo is extremely fierce, having a uniform dark color throughout its body.
One with reddish eyes, upward-pointing horns, a long tail, and a fleshy body; one who does not carry burdens, is fearful, and has skin suitable for wrinkles—such a bull is not excellent. (199b)
He who is white in color and dwells in the forest, protected within the forest itself.
A boar that has a large tusk, is fleshy,
and is between three and seven years of age, and which is fleshy though lacking a frontal gem (maṇi), is said to be fit [for sacrifice].
He who possesses a uniform color and appearance, yet is free from the defects of color and form,
who is dense-bodied, possesses horns, is the leader of the herd, and is fragrant with medicinal herbs and the like— he is [the bull].
Having removed the odor, it should be joined to the bracelet; this is indeed the most excellent of all.
In the Vārāhī-saṃhitā:
One should offer two black goats, and afterwards, one should present the great oblation.
To the one who possesses the wish-fulfilling cow.
O Goddess, I shall describe specifically the characteristics of the unborn (aja):
it has upward-pointing horns, upward-pointing hair, long ears, and is stout.

Possessing a sense of self, with a well-nourished body free from wrinkles and grey hair, with long ears and a pure black complexion— he possesses the auspicious characteristics of a sacrificial animal.
White, black, red, tawny, variegated, and pale—
these six types of goats are declared to be the supreme sacrificial offering for householders.
Dhātṛ, Mausita, Kṛṣṇa, Madhyama, Citra, and Pāṇḍura are the [first] six;
Lohita and Kapila are proclaimed as the youngest.
From three months onwards, up until two years, this is declared the superior *bali*; after that, it is considered inferior.
When a goat is black in color, has six humps, and possesses a white tail,
the wise man should avoid such a beast from afar.
Thus, a wise man should always avoid one that is white with a black tail;
likewise, if a black-colored goat has a white backbone, it should be avoided.
One should recognize that as praiseworthy and avoid the opposite;
a white buffalo five years old is proclaimed to be praiseworthy.
Likewise, a buffalo that is black is excellent, while one that is white is the lowest;
as for birds, all those of beautiful appearance are highly praised.
And after three fortnights have passed, one should also avoid [the practice] on that day.
In the Merutantra:
For all castes as well as for the deities alike,
this sacrifice is distinguished by its entitlement and its capacity to bestow delight.
Even one who is inferior, if he possesses the horns of a ram and the speed of a goat,
shall remain in his home for two and a half years as a powerful man.
The excellent crane was not capable of giving away the burden of his own flesh;
the pigeon, though bearing a body as beautiful as a peacock's throat, carried only his own nourishment.
One that has been raised in a house for more than a year is said to be suitable for the purpose of strength;
it caws in many tones at dawn, preceding all others.
But one that is fleshy, of a single color, or with copper-colored crests is especially distinguished.
As for those that are prohibited, it is stated in the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
"I shall describe certain things that are prohibited even among the offerings prescribed for the bali."
Furthermore, in the rite of offering oblations (bali-karman), the practitioner should never employ a woman, whether she be domestic or other animals or birds.
Having offered a libation preceded by knowledge, one falls into hell;
through ignorance one escapes, yet one still incurs some degree of sin.
One should not employ an animal born within the last three months;
nor should one ever offer to the Goddess one that is less than half that age.
One whose horns are broken, whose tusks are broken, whose tail is severed, one who is black, one afflicted by bodily disease, and likewise one struck by a thorn;

One should not offer an animal that is diseased, whose hair has fallen out, which has lost its milk, or whose eyes have dropped; likewise, one should not offer such an animal as one that has been abandoned.
With its beak and wings severed, broken and deprived of food,
it could not fly away and remained instead nestled upon its mother's lap in the *kāśa* grass.
Even if they have been prescribed, one should not give animals or birds if they are not properly identified.
In the Merutantra:
One who is diseased, lacking a tail, castrated, young, or old is not commended.
In the Vārāhī-saṃhitā:
A wise man should avoid one who is lame, as well as one who is humpbacked, one with a physical defect, one afflicted by disease, or one who is toothless.
Likewise.
One should not give the meat of a female animal or a beast, especially in offerings to the gods (havya) or the ancestors (kavya).
Thus [it is said].
Now follows the sprinkling.
To the one who possesses the wish-fulfilling cow.
The illustrious Pārvatī said:
O God, how are the sprinkling of animals and the various types [of offerings] performed for the All-pervading Lord?
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Whether for the sake of sacrifice, worship, or constant sprinkling, an animal [is required];
killing it without sprinkling is either useless or results in even greater sin.
In the Mahākālasaṃhitā:
The consideration of what should and should not be given has been described to this extent,
as well as the location, the recipient, the authority, the desired object, the time, and the sequence of giving.
Now listen to the sprinkling of all [the items] with a single form.
In the Vārāhī-saṃhitā:
Oṃ Vārāhī, Yamunā, Gaṅgā, Karatoyā, Sarasvatī, Kāverī, Candrabhāgā, Sindhu, Bhairavī, and Sāgarā.
O Maheśānī, one should effect the presence [of the deity] here during the bath;
O Night, one should sprinkle [the external area] with pure water from the arghya vessel while reciting the root mantra.
Salutation to the one who destroys the bonds of the bound, who dwells on Hemakūṭa,
who is both transcendent and immanent, the supreme abider, and whose form is the syllable *Hūṃ*.
Then, one should cause the sprinkling to be performed with these bilva leaves and water,
wherever there is an abundance of cattle, according to one's means.
In that very place, O Goddess, one should first release a sacrificial animal that is endowed with all auspicious marks, vigorous, beautiful, and strong.
Immediately thereafter, it proceeds in due order, and there is no deliberation therein;
one should proclaim that consciousness is the vessel for the fetters.
One should again utter the mantra: "Lead [him] away from the fear of animality, svāhā! Having recited this mantra, one should bathe the sacrificial animal with water.
Then, taking a garland or a flower in his hand,
he should place it upon the head of the sacrificial animal with the mantra that is about to be recited.
After that, having uttered *praṇaka*, *yoginī*, *kūrca*, and *garuḍau*, followed by *gandhanyante*, may they grant the state of a Gandharva, *phaṭ*!
