In the Merutantra:
Having wrapped a pumpkin, a coconut, a bilva fruit, or even sugarcane in cloth, one should cut it with a knife or similar instrument.
This is declared to be the *smārta* bali for those who follow the *dharmaśāstras*;
even here, each preceding one is said to be superior as a means of pleasing the deity.
The deity is pleased by whichever person has greater devotion toward them.
Likewise.
One should offer a Vedic bali consisting of cooked rice and boiled mung beans,
along with yellow pigment and vaṭakas, to the exceedingly cruel deities.
Likewise.

The forest-dweller, the celibate student, the householder, and the mendicant who is beyond [worldly ties], as well as one who is sattvic, established in Brahman, and free from violence— [these are the foremost].
Therefore, O fair-faced one, they may offer animal oblations even while practicing according to the human ritual manual,
for the sake of attaining the fruits of those various animal sacrifices.
By making various sacrificial animals from ghee, wheat, barley, molasses, and other such substances, and offering them, one shall obtain the respective fruit thereof.
Otherwise, it is stated in the Śaktisaṃgama-tantra:
O Lord of Gods, tell me the procedure for the secondary rite (anukalpa);
as one established in sattva, one should never manifest the taking of life.
O Goddess, listen attentively as this *sāttvika* offering is described:
one should offer the *kuṣmāṇḍa* pumpkin as a buffalo and the *karkatī* melon as a goat.

An eggplant becomes a cock, and a fourth [variety] a ram; the *raṃbhā* flower is the form of the seed, and in the Age of Strife (*kaliyuga*), the physical body (*piṇḍa*) becomes the individual soul (*jīva*).
One should obtain a panasa fruit by being human, a stalk of sugarcane by being a fish,
a śūraṇa root by being a śabara, and likewise a kośātaka fruit by being a deer.
Milk-rice [is the fruit] of being an elephant; horse-gram of being a cat; a bitter gourd of being a pig; and likewise, sugar of being a sand-worm.
O Great Goddess, when I was a rhinoceros, there was a plantain fruit in my being;
when a rat, a radish; and when a deer, a *kaliñjaka* seed.
Having prepared coconut, fish, and likewise plantains,
all these should be offered as the "all-encompassing power" (sarvabalitva), followed at the end by *kṛśara* for everyone.
With milk-rice, flour-cakes, sweets, and rice-and-pulse mixtures ending with *kṛśara*;
likewise with vegetables, leafy greens, soups, oil-cakes, fresh ginger, and *polikā* cakes.
The *vaṭaka*, *alasuṇa*, *gṛñja*, *kaliñja*, *vīja*, and *sahodara*—
these are proclaimed as the *valirekhā* through various methods and six flavors.
O Goddess, in the rite of cruel magic, one should fashion a sacrificial animal made of flour,
or even one made of barley meal, or else one produced from grain.
O Goddess, one should perform all rites with an image made of ground black gram (māṣa);
likewise, half-jaggery, curd-and-jaggery, salt, and jaggery alone [are used].
O Maheśvarī, if it is to be applied by means of a secondary method (anukalpa),
one shall obtain the aforementioned fruit by following the prescribed rule exactly as stated.
Thus ends the offering of the sattvic oblation to Śakti.
In the future.
If the offering of oblations (bali) is lacking, there will be famine; if the fragrance is lacking, illness;
likewise, if the incense is lacking, there will be distress; and if the clothing is lacking, there will be loss of wealth.
If the lamp is lacking, there will be the destruction of the city and the town;
everything devoid of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) becomes useless—of this there is no doubt.
Thus concludes the procedure for the offering of the sacrificial fee (validāna).
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Kulamuktikallolinī composed by Śrī Ādyānanda.
In the Merutantra.
The Goddess said:
Therefore, since no accomplishment is seen anywhere even among those established in the paths of Tantra within this very life, what will there be in the next?
If karma were the primary factor, what would be the use of propitiating the deities? If propitiating the deities were truly effective, why are practitioners so full of suffering?
Cut through this doubt of mine: what is the purpose of the *cakras* and the *mātrikās*, and how are the ritual refinements (*saṃskāras*) of the *mātrikās* to be performed? Tell me that.
The Lord said:
One should perform three rites while in the womb, ten as soon as born, and then three more;
thus, the sacraments (saṃskāras) are traditionally recorded as sixteen.
The Guru should perform the three rites with the mantra for the twice-born;
then the disciple should perform them ten times, and once again three times when the mantra has been mastered.
Six birth-sacraments are prescribed even for women and Śūdras;
likewise, six mantra-sacraments alone are proclaimed for them.
For those such as the Cāṇḍālas, there are four [births] in their mantras; indeed, they are exactly that many.
And for the Yavanas and others, there are three; likewise, these three also apply to their mantras.
Listen to how they should be employed according to the distinction between the left and the right:
one should arrange liquor in the place of clarified butter on the left for the purpose of the fire-oblation and other rites.

In the rites of cooking and so forth, meat is used; in the rites of piercing and so forth, it is traditionally held that they consist of women. Sexual union and celibacy likewise involve the mudrās and those who perform their respective actions.
First, the rite of conception (garbhādhāna) should be performed according to the procedure prescribed in one's own ritual manual;
then, one should perform the sacrifice to the messenger (dūtīyāga) on the right or on the left.
One should satisfy the limbs of the deity with mantras and the yoni from the sacred sites (tīrtha);
one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) upon the limbs of that goddess.
Having performed the complete installation within one's own body, one should contemplate that Bhairavī;
and having oneself become Bhairava, one should engage in the act of sexual union.
Seated on a comfortable seat, having formed the *bhaga* and the *dhvaja*, one should recite this mantra five thousand times; thus one obtains a son according to one's desire.
If Lakṣmī is indeed the mistress of my life, protect me with the nine-syllable mantra;
her seed-syllable is in the Moon, his is in the Sun, and the embryo resides in the space between them.
Now, the second sacrament called Puṃsavana should be performed;
the wise man should perform the Puṃsavana rite in the third month.
On the day prescribed by the Vedas and declared [by the authorities], according to the procedure stated in one's own ritual manual (kalpa),
there, in the place of the Vedic primary fire-sacrifice (homa), one's own deity [is to be worshipped].
One should offer oblations according to the specific purpose, by way of four offerings;
at that time, for the deities of the enclosure, there are two for each of the persons.
For those who follow the path of the left (vāmamārga), there is one [offering] for the women; the remainder has been declared as before.
For every purpose, the offering (*bali*) to Bhairava consists of a portion of meat (*māṃsa*) and liquor (*rasu*).
In the fourth, sixth, eighth, and tenth months, it is middling; in other months, it is inferior.
On a day prescribed by the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra), according to the method taught in her own ritual manual (kalpa),
she [the officiant] should recite the mantra of the deity Vāmī during the *sīmanta* ceremony with a beautiful hymn.
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon one's limbs, which removes the affliction of childbirth;
thereafter, one should not approach that wife out of fear of the deity’s curse.

Whether performed out of desire, or through delusion, or at an improper time, or according to [an incorrect] rite, or by another person— if such is the connection [of the rite], it is a *sīmantonnayana* [performed improperly].
The Brahmin should perform the rite called *jātakarman* according to the procedure prescribed in his own ritual manual.
Upon the birth of a daughter for Brahmins, or the birth of a son for a Śūdra,
one should perform the rite silently, preceded by the remembrance of Viṣṇu.
One who follows the left-hand path (vāmācārī) should not perform the rite for generating intelligence;
rather, he should write it with a golden stylus at the tip of a kāravya reed.
One should place the root-mantra in the region of the palate and likewise the mantra on the tongue;
thereafter, one should satisfy the deities, while the other ritual acts are performed as prescribed for the right hand.
Now, I shall describe this rite called the fifth consecration, which is eternal.
For all of these, once the period of birth-impurity has ended, one should commence the naming ceremony on an auspicious day according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Kalpa.
Having investigated those sixteen wheels of the measures (mātrā-cakras) which are taught in the tantras, one should perform [the practice]; if done thus, it will be fruitful.
If such a name has not been given here, then the Guru should perform the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka); that [consecration] is described as being accompanied by a seed-syllable (sabīja).
For it is through skillful qualities that the success of brahmins is fully realized.

"I shall explain the Tārā-cakra," and so forth; the intention is that one should perform the naming of the lineage (kūla-nāma-karaṇa) with one's own mantras at the beginning of the Tārā-cakra and other such [mandalas]. The *cakra* here is also to be understood as belonging to Avalokiteśvara. As for the *caura-mātrā* and other *cakras*, however—
It is written here by virtue of the context; in that very same [work].
The sixth sacrament, the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana), is common to all people;
for Śūdras and others, it is performed according to the procedure prescribed in their own scriptures, but without the recitation of mantras.
In that regard, on the path of the Left (vāmamārga), the Bhairavas and one's own chosen deities (iṣṭadeva) are to be worshipped by the father;
indeed, they remain to be worshipped at the conclusion of the worship of the cakra.
He should offer a tīrtha with water and recite the root mantra;
for one who has performed the rite in this manner, no obstacle shall arise.
Now listen, O Pārvatī, to the seventh sacrament called *caula*,
which is prescribed for all and destroys the sins committed during childhood.
A lock of hair from both Buddhists and Yavanas should be placed here;
by means of that, it should also be performed for women for the increase of good fortune and health.
On the left, the hair, equal in number to the seed-syllables of the mantra, should be gathered from the crest;
having thrown it into sacred water, one should bury it in the ground—this is the specific rule for women.
Now, the wheel of Tārā.

I shall now explain the Tārā-cakra for the attainment of mantra-siddhi by children: A, Ā, Ha, Ya, Ra, E, and Ca are considered to be in the asterism of Dūrvā; likewise, I, U, Ū, Va, and Hni are in the asterism of Bharaṇī.
Ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, and Lṛ belong to Rohiṇī; E belongs to Mṛgaśiras and Śiva-bha (Ārdrā); Ai belongs to Punarvasu; O and Au belong to Puṣya; and Kha and Ga belong to Āśleṣā.
In Maghā (the Pitṛ-bha), *gha* and *ṅa* are prescribed; in Bhāgya (Pūrvaphalgunī) and Ārdrā, *cha* and *ja*;
in Hastā, *ṛ* and *ṭa*; in Mṛgaśirā, *ṭha* and *ṭa*; in Ārdrā, *kha* and *ti*; and in Svātī, Viśākhā, and Anurādhā, *ḍa* and *ṇa*.
Likewise, when the letter *ta* occurs under Anurādhā, *tha* under Jyeṣṭhā, *na* under Mūla, *pa* under Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and *va* under Abhijit; and when *bha* occurs under Śatabhiṣaj;
O Maḥ, may you grant success at Dhaniṣṭhā and at the Śata-tārakā;
O Vaśau, may you be under my control at Pūrvabhādrapadā and at Sahā. May they be near to me.

One should count one hundred thousand [repetitions] for each syllable of the mantra, starting from the first letter of the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) and proceeding through the asterisms; the results are obtained by repeating this three times.

Loss of position, association with the wicked, excessive friendship, and suffering from mental anguish or physical disease—these may befall the practitioner; yet, through him, the success of his undertakings is achieved.

Having understood that this water [of fate] results in the destruction of many enemies, misfortune, or prosperity, one should act accordingly according to the fruit of the circle of stars (tārācakra).
Now, the wheel of the Gaṇamātṛkās.
Having understood the division according to the *mātṛkās* as spoken by Tāra for both the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the object of practice (*sādhya*),
whether they be female or male, one should examine the wheel of those two.
The *nara* group is known to consist of the *sthira*, *vimaghāgra*, and *raudra* [nakṣatras];
the *harṣaṇya*, *mitra*, *ādina*, *indu*, *vā*, *tejya*, *kara*, and *ghoṭaka* [nakṣatras] are likewise [reckoned].
If the gods are in the *śeṣa* [houses] and the Rākṣasas are in the *sādhya* [houses], the result belongs to the practitioner (*sādhaka*).
If the human and divine [groups] are in the *sādhya* and *śeṣa* respectively, the result is swift; if they are reversed, the result is obtained with difficulty.
If the human and the Daitya are separated by the favor of Manu, death shall occur;
if the gods and the Dānavas are separated, their battle shall be fruitless.
The *nāgamātṛkā* wheel:
Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśirā, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣya, and Aśleṣā.
A Ā, I Ī, U Ū, Ṛ Ṝ, E AI, O AU, Ka Kha Ga.

Maghā, Pūrvāphalgunī, Uttarāphalgunī, Hasta, Citrā, Svāti, Viśākhā, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, Pūrvābhādrapadā, Uttarābhādrapadā, and Revatī constitute the Gaṇamātṛkācakra.
Ga, Gha, Ṅa; Ca, Cha, Ja, Jha, Ña; Ṭa, Ṭha; Ḍa, Ḍha, Ṇa; Ta, Tha; Dha.
This is the Gaṇamātṛkācakra.

Ārdrā, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Āśleṣā, Maghā, Pūrvaphalgunī, Uttaraphalgunī, Hastā, Citrā, Svātī, Viśākhā, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūlā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, Pūrvabhadrapadā, Uttarabhadrapadā, Revatī, Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī,

Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Āśleṣā, Maghā, Pūrvaphalgunī, Uttaraphalgunī, Hastā, Citrā, Svātī, Viśākhā, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūlā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, Pūrvabhadrapadā, Uttarabhadrapadā, Revatī, Aśvinī, Bharaṇī.
In Rākṣasa, Kṛttikā, Aśleṣā, Maghā, Citrā, Viśākhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Śatabhiṣaj—
now I shall describe the Siddhimātṛkā for the accomplishment of Mahāvidyā;
therein, sixteen squares should be known according to the sequence of the roots.
One should duly arrange the letters of the Mātṛkā alphabet in these squares in sequence:
[beginning with] Ku, Trī, Śāṃ, Ka, ṅka, Ābhi, Su, rpadi, ṣa, du, ṣṭendu, pā, vṛṣā.
In that [grid], squares are proclaimed to be five, nine, and thirteen;
first, one should know that in the four groups of four squares, the Siddhas reside in the intermediate directions.
In that case, however, one should count again according to the teacher’s instruction so that the syllables are equal in their respective compartments:
a *siddha* mantra becomes effective through recitation; a *siddha-sādhya* becomes effective by doubling [the number].
The *siddha* [planet] brings success; the *susiddha* brings attainment; the *siddhāri* destroys those born in one's lineage;
the *sādhya* succeeds through great effort; and the *sādhyasādhya* causes extreme suffering.
Through worship, the *sādhya* becomes well-accomplished (*susiddha*); the *sādhya-ari* (enemy of the *sādhya*) takes away one's own wife.
Through half as many recitations as the *susiddha*, the *siddha* is attained; and by much more recitation, one becomes devoted to that [state].
If the yoga is excessively swift (atidruta), it is twice as effective; a well-accomplished (susiddha) yoga destroys one's lineage,
while an enemy-accomplished (arisiddha) yoga kills one's son, and an enemy-to-be-accomplished (arisādhya) yoga kills one's daughter.
An enemy planet that is well-aspected brings about the death of one's wife; an enemy planet that is inimically aspected destroys the practitioner.
In the Piṅgalāmata:

Whatever name may be well-known, or whatever birth-name he may have, or whatever name has been bestowed by the preceptor through the rite of the falling of flowers for the ascetics; [that is his name].
One should also cause the letters of that very name to be divided [into their constituent parts].
Also elsewhere.
Then, a name well-known in the world was likewise bestowed upon him by his mother and father.
Also elsewhere.
Whether asleep or awake, that which speaks even from afar,
and which one utters even when the mind is elsewhere— that is the name-mantra to be grasped.
Also elsewhere.
One must strive diligently to purify the debt incurred toward one's mother and father.
And that [first syllable] is to be observed from the letter of one's birth-star; it is stated there that the first syllable of the mantra is [derived] from that.
Where it is well-known, however, it is by means of the birth-name itself.
In the Merutantra:
In this context, "name" (nāma) would be that by which one who is asleep becomes awakened.
In this very context, the calculation of the Siddha and other [categories] for each syllable has been stated.
Having separated the syllables of the name given by the mother and father, as well as that which was assigned by the kinsmen,
according to the distinction between vowels and consonants;
In that very manner, according to the syllables of the mantra, one should then begin the purification;
[the sequence] arises from the bindu, the two bindus, the upadhmānīya, and the tongue and feet.
Having abandoned the four sections consisting of syllables that result from combined pronunciation, those with extra syllables,
and corrupt (apabhraṃśa) syllables, one should [recite] according to the definition.
One should purify each letter of the name together with the syllables of the mantra:
the consonants with the consonants alone, and likewise the vowels with the vowels.
The first [syllable] should be purified by the first [seed-syllable], and the second by the second;
whether in the mantra or in the name, the syllables may likewise be uneven.
Then, O fair-faced one, having commenced the mantra, one should fill it evenly until [the end],
provided that the perfected syllables are at the beginning of the mantra.
In a very short time, that [mantra] which is joined with the beginning and end of the sādhya grants all accomplishments; however, that which is otherwise succeeds only with great difficulty.
That which is well-perfected at the beginning and the end bestows all desires and prosperity;
however, that which has enemies at the beginning and the end should be abandoned along with its mantra.
That which is established at the beginning but requires proof at the end is accomplished by doubling [the effort];
that which is established at the beginning and has a well-established conclusion is accomplished through recitation as prescribed.

One who is "siddha" at the beginning and an "enemy" (ari) at the end must be abandoned by the best of mantra-practitioners; however, one who is "sādhya" at the beginning and so forth becomes "siddha" through threefold recitation.

First, one who is "to be accomplished" (sādhya) succeeds through the well-established doctrine according to the prescribed path; however, one who begins as "well-accomplished" (susiddha) and ends as "to be accomplished" (sādhya) requires fourfold effort.
One that begins with *susiddha* and ends with *ari* is proclaimed as mediocre;
likewise, one that begins with *ari* and ends with *siddha-ari* must also be avoided in this ritual practice.
Established at the beginning, middle, and likewise at the end, it bestows auspicious results;
it is declared by the Self-Existent One in the Tantra to be "all-accomplishing" (sarvasādhya) and "indifferent" (udāsīna).
One who has successfully mastered the three positions shall accomplish all goals;
however, a mantra whose enemy occupies the three positions is death, without a doubt.
The one beginning with *siddha* and ending with a pair of *sādhya*s is called "useless" by the wise;
however, that which begins with *siddha* and ends with *susiddha* is effective for accomplishing all purposes.
The Siddha and others ending with the pair of enemies are proclaimed to be destroyers.
If [the planet] is an enemy at the beginning, a Siddha in the middle, and a Sādhya at the end,
there is accomplishment of the task with great difficulty, and its fruit becomes very small indeed.
If there is an enemy in the first [house], and a pair of neutral planets in the middle;
An undertaking may be delayed, yet it is praised when completed quickly at the end;
when the beginning and end are noble, the task accomplished in the middle becomes truly successful.
When the beginning and the end are accomplished, that which is to be accomplished arises in the middle;
for both that which is to be accomplished and the accomplishment itself are achieved through an abundance of recitation.
Combined with Arisa, it becomes Siddha; likewise, it becomes Susiddha.
It should be known as the destroyer of everything for the practitioner; of this there is no doubt.
Whether the mantra to be accomplished (sādhya) is separated by a Siddha or separated by a Susiddha, this mantra is quickly perfected; so the Lord Himself has declared.
Even if one were to become well-accomplished, an enemy who is obstructed would not truly be overcome;
rather than being a foe to the mantra, he merely causes it to be accomplished with great difficulty.
If the goal is obscured by another, even if it is established or well-established,
one should avoid such a definition from afar upon seeing it.
A mantra corrupted by an enemy must never be given away; it leads to ruin.
Also in the Nārāyaṇīya [section].
A mantra that abounds in harsh syllables is considered censurable.

And thus, the meaning in the Piṅgalā [Tantra] is that one should accomplish one's own desired aim by means of a favorable mantra, and the undesirable aim of others by means of a mantra unfavorable to them.
In all these faults, having first cast upon them either deceit or desire, one should bestow prosperity for the sake of liberation from those very faults.
Regarding the planets within the planetary mantras, one should examine the zodiacal wheel: three, four, and three; two pairs; and the sixth and the last [twelve]. The sixth and the sixteenth.
Furthermore, there are six groups [of letters]; wherever the first letter among those belonging to the two—namely, the scales (tulā) and the self (ātman)—occurs, there this result shall come to pass.
The Sun is a beloved servant, a nourisher, one who creates passion, a giver of sons, and brings auspiciousness.
It brings happiness from women, produces wind, bestows good fortune, and accomplishes one's undertakings.
This *rāśimātṛkā* (matrix of signs), described as both the producer of gain and the cause of expenditure,
is the means of worship through the names and mantras of women, Śūdras, kings, and Rāmas.
The previously mentioned dispositions (āśayas) are to be understood.
And from a twice-born man and so forth, one should accept [food] from the Mīmāṃsaka and others; however, among these, the Vedic Manu is to be accepted here especially.

Oṃ. To the Blessed One, the Lord of Speech, the God of Gods, this is the mantra:
E Ā Ā Jaya Jaya Vāja Vāja Je Ja Va Ta Svāmi. [Mantra Number: 11002000] iṣṭam.
O Kaulika, you shall explain the accomplishment of the path (*mārgasiddhi*), the ritual action (*kṛtyā*), and the elemental [deities].
One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the five principles (*pañcatattva*): wind, fire, earth, water, and space.
Two vowels each should be written on the base; then again, starting with the letter *e*, the six groups beginning with *ka* (*kavarga*, etc.), as well as the two syllables *yakṣara* and *asa*.
The name should be written again and again.
The mantra is equal to its syllables; therefore, it should be written again as a whole, with the completion occurring simultaneously.
Having written it down to that extent.
Now, one should investigate the reality of the phonemes.
One should establish one part for the neutral form; its strength is likewise [applied] to the friendly state, and one quarter to the indifferent state; their sum is divided by five.
If the form with its half-portion (samedala) at night should be auspicious, yet difficult;
and likewise, if a quarter is in a friend's [sign], that too would be difficult, consisting of a sixteenth part (kalā).
One should perform the mantra practice when the desired [planets] are in their exaltation;
otherwise, bhūtas, vetālas, and piśācas will harm the person.
There is friendliness between earth and water, and likewise between fire and wind;
there is a commonality between fire and earth, and similarly between water and wind.
The wheel of the enemy is the reverse of this, O Bhautika.

One would say, "It is Kaulika. This is the explanation of the *nyāsa* of the *cakra*. Now, for the sake of awakening the ignorant, there is the example of the calculation *cakra*. Therein, the lines indicate the quarters by means of lines. The desired sum is 5|15. Now, [this is] a *paṅkti* of twelve syllables. Divided by twelve, the quotient is zero; the remainder is 5. The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet;
having pervaded the earth on every side, he transcends it by ten fingers' breadth.
The Person alone is all this— whatever has been and whatever is to be;
he is indeed the lord of immortality, since even beyond that he does not transcend.
Such is his greatness, and yet the Puruṣa is greater than this; all beings constitute one quarter of him, while his three quarters are the immortal in heaven.
The Puruṣa rose up, three-quarters of him being above; one-quarter of him remained here again.
From there he strode out in all directions toward that which eats and that which does not eat.
From that, Virāj was produced; from Virāj, the Puruṣa was born. Once born, he extended beyond the earth both behind and before.
When the gods performed the sacrifice with the Puruṣa as the oblation,
the spring was its clarified butter, the summer its fuel, and the autumn its offering.
Seven were its enclosing sticks, and thrice seven were the fuel-sticks prepared;
when the gods performed the sacrifice, they bound Puruṣa as the victim.
Sprinkling that sacrifice upon the sacrificial grass— Puruṣa, who was born in the beginning—
the gods, the Sādhyas, and the Ṛṣis sacrificed with him.
From that sacrifice in which everything was offered, the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) was collected;

from that cows were produced, and from that goats and sheep were born.
When they divided Puruṣa, into how many parts did they apportion him?
What was his mouth, what were his arms, and what are said to have been his thighs and feet?
The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth; the Rājanya was made from his arms;
that which was his thighs became the Vaiśya; and from his feet the Śūdra was born.
The moon was born from the mind; from the eye the sun was born;
from the mouth Indra and Agni were born; and from the breath the waters were born.
From his navel the intermediate space arose; from his head the sky evolved;
from his feet the earth, and from his ears the quarters—thus he fashioned the worlds.

I meditate upon Agni, the first, the wise one; many kindle him, the benefactor of the five peoples.

We pray for wide space and for one who bestows wide space; may the mind release you, O laughing one! I praise Agni, whose alone is this breath, that which blinks and that which moves, and all that is born and being born;
unasked, I call upon him repeatedly—may he release you, O laughing one! I honor Indra, the foremost, the wise.

The hymns of praise have approached for comparison. May he who comes swiftly to the call of the generous donor release us from laughter. When he leads the battle, may he, the one who is to be honored, bestow the threefold nourishments. Unasked, I loudly invoke Indra; may he release us from laughter.

I consider this, O Mitra and Varuṇa; take note of it, you who possess true power, as you drive away the mountain. Protect the one born of wealth on the same chariot from the fierce one; release us from sin. That chariot-rein of yours, the ray of light whose law is truth, which moves among men, approaches him who corrupts it. I praise Mitra and Varuṇa.

When we have not invoked you, O Aśvins, release us from sin. We meditate upon the ordinances of Vāyu and Savitṛ, who are the two who increase and protect the three worlds. You two, who have spoken as the encompassers of the universe, release us from sin. The most excellent offerings have been established for us by the gods; I praise Vāyu.

O Savitar and Nāsatyas, do not deliver us over to the enemy; release us from our transgression. O most excellent charioteers, renowned as such, you who are most swift to aid the pious man with your well-governed horses—O Gods among gods, whose vigor is most sharpened, release us from our transgression.

When the two who desire to sit together in assembly with the three-faced one came to the sacrifice of Sūryā, I praise the two gods, the Aśvins; though unasked, I have invoked you—release us from this sin! We are subject to the command of the Maruts.

Speaking these words of love, may all protect us all. O you who are being pressed for swift aid and for our protection, may they release him through that power. The sharp weapon, the tormenting, the victorious divine host in battles—those Maruts, the givers, I praise; even though unasked, I cry out to them. May they release him through that power. Of the gods...
In the midst, may the Adityas grant us this loving speech; may all the Viśvedevas protect us on every side.

I invoke the swift ones for well-being and prosperity; may they release us from that [evil]. Whatever distress assails me, whether caused by men or by the gods, I praise the All-Gods; even though unasked, I call upon them—may they release us from that.

May Anumati favor this sacrifice among the gods; and may Agni, the bearer of oblations, be a source of joy to the donor. O Anumati, approve of this; grant us prosperity and fulfill our purpose. May the ten fingers [of the priest] impel us forward; may you extend our lifespan and protect us from harm. May Vaiśvānara guard us as we observe our sacred vows.

From afar, Agni comes through the power of Truth. Asked about in heaven, asked about on earth, Agni, having been asked about, has entered all plants. May Vaiśvānara Agni, asked about with might, protect us from harm by day and by night. Those two who have spread themselves out with immeasurable powers, those two who have become the two foundations.
I praise the Vasus; I invoke them with my mind from the earth for the sake of wealth; deliver us from distress.
O wide Heaven and Earth, you who are most excellent, make room for us; as the two wives of the field, may you speak in our favor. I praise Heaven and Earth; I call upon them with a prayer.
Deliver us from this distress. Whatever we have done against you, O most powerful one—whether knowingly or unknowingly, whether as sin or as no sin—make it right through your purifying bath.

From Aditi, sinless, may another [sin] rest upon Agni, who supports all. Just as at your sacrifice, O worshipful ones, even the Gaurī cow was released from that enclosure, so do you release this great sin from us;
O Agni, prolong our life further.
Then, with the four *yājyā* verses beginning with "O Indra and Varuṇa," and using the formulas "To Indra and Varuṇa" for the relinquishment (*tyāga*) in every instance as prescribed.
O Indra and Varuṇa, whatever bodies you have for our protection, release my distress from them. O Indra and Varuṇa, whatever powerful bodies you have, release my distress from them.
O Indra and Varuṇa, as far as your powerful bodies extend, with that [power] release me from this sin.
O Indra and Varuṇa, as far as your radiant bodies extend, with that [radiance] release me from this sin.
One should offer oblations with the eight verses beginning with "yāvāmindrā varuṇā," and the dedication (*tyāga*) should be made everywhere as follows: "to Indra and Varuṇa."

O Indra and Varuṇa, whoever has offered you an oblation in the fire, him I appease for you with that. O Indra and Varuṇa, whoever has well offered you an oblation from two-footed beings, him I appease for you with that. O Indra and Varuṇa, whoever has well offered you an oblation from four-footed beings, him I appease for you with that. O Indra and Varuṇa, whoever [has offered] in your houses...

Whatever wasting disease is in you two, O Indra and Varuṇa, in the waters, with that I appease you. Whatever wasting disease is in you two, O Indra and Varuṇa, in the plants, with that I appease you. Whatever wasting disease is in you two, O Indra and Varuṇa, in the herbs, with that I appease you.
O Indra and Varuṇa, whatever injury there is in the trees, that I expiate for you with this.
The *Pāvamānānu* is renowned as a collection of seventeen verses;
therein, from the first [verse], there are sixty-three statements consisting of mere words of power (*śakti*) and those pertaining to Śakti.
Just as one who is devoted to barley (*yavamāninī*) cannot be told by the Śāktas to abandon it,
nor can one who is devoted to Vṛṣa be told by the Śaivas to abandon it, so too is it for the one devoted to Yava.
Measuring out the barley, well-born and moving through the filter with wide-ranging motion.
May he who is the purifier purify me.
The second [offering] is for the words of my father, for the divine folk, for the Maruts, and likewise for the Viśvedevas; thus it is declared that there is no abandonment of me.
O divine people, do not [speak] against us; purify our minds with wisdom.
May all the waters purify us.
The third [verse], however, consists of four sentences; beginning with "to Agni Jātavedas," the renunciation is expressed as "this, not mine"—that *ṛc* is now revealed.
O Jātavedas, with the purifier, purify me; O Agni, shining like a god with your white brilliance, purify me according to the sacred law (*ṛta*).

The fourth [verse] consists of three sentences, namely the *ṛc* "agne ye na... and so forth; the fifth is also three-sentenced, with the renunciation (*tyāga*) being made to both Savitṛ and Tvaṣṭṛ as prescribed.
That filter of yours which, O Agni, is spread out within your flame—
By that [means], O Brahmán, let us purify ourselves. O divine Savitṛ, by both the means of purification and the impulse, let us purify this prayer.
The sixth [chapter] consists of four statements in verse, and its renunciation is described therein.
And as she [the goddess] went with the Vaiśvadeva hymns, saying "O gods, do not neglect me," so the purifying Vaiśvadeva goddess has come.
She whose two bodies are the fires and whose backs are the wide-expansive [verses]—rejoicing with her, may he prosper among the sacrificial offerings.

216b) May we be [worthy] of the two who are joined, of the [gods] who bestow nourishment. For Vaiśvānara Vāta, for the one who impels, for wealth that brings joy—for Dyāvāpṛthivī; thus is the renunciation (tyāga) prescribed in the seventh [verse]. Vaiśvānara...
May [the waters] purify me with their rays; may Vāta lead me through the breath; may the two worlds, heaven and earth, become full of milk;
may those who abide in Truth purify me with their waters and milk.
The seventh [offering] consists of four sentences, while the eighth is considered to consist of three sentences;
"Savitre agnaye na mama" is the formula for the renunciation on the eighth day, and it is likewise performed there.
O Agni, purify me with great, triple-layered, most exalted, and divine hymns; with skillful means, purify me from this point forward.
Beyond this, for the sake of the divine Brahman, I relinquish [the self].
As for the ninth [verse], it belongs to the *yavamānī* verses; as for the tenth and those following, they are as follows.
By that with which the gods purified themselves, by which [they attained] the divine garment—
by that divine Brahman, we here purify this Brahman.
He who studies the *yavamānīs*, the essence gathered by the *ṛṣis*— he eats everything pure that is impelled by Mātariśvan. He who studies the *yavamānīs*,
the essence gathered by the *ṛṣis*— for him Sarasvatī, against the malicious one, pours forth milk, ghee, honey, and water from the *yavamānīs*.

Bringing prosperity, yielding milk abundantly, this essence is honored by the seers; immortality is deposited among the Brahmins. May you, who bring barley, protect our quarters—both this world and the one beyond—and may you fulfill our desires.
O Goddesses, accompanied by the gods, bringing barley and bestowing well-being, flow forth with abundance.
Dropping ghee, the essence gathered by the seers, immortality is placed within the Brahmins.
The barley-measures reaching to the quarters, may they delight us;

may they bring prosperity to our two-footed and four-footed creatures. O Goddesses, together with the gods and the Mothers, you who are barley-measures, who lead us across, and who are well-heard by the learned—this essence has been gathered by the seers; it is sought after as nectar for the Brahman.
With that purifier by which the gods always purify themselves, may it purify us with its rays; may the venerable one purify me.
As before, there is the ritual renunciation (*tyāga*); however, there is a specific distinction for the *ṣoḍaśī* [offering] of the learned Brahmin (*śrotriya*).
Listen to the *ṣoḍaśī*: "To Prājāpatya, to Pavitra... [and so on]. The *prājāpatya-pavitra* consists of a hundred threads (*śatodyāma*).

"Golden is it; by that we, the knowers of Brahman, purify ourselves with the pure Brahman. One should then say: "Accompanied by good guidance for Indra, accompanied by prosperity for Soma, and accompanied by harmony for Varuṇa."
One should recite [the hymn] for Pūṣan together with the *praghṛṇās*;
likewise, one should recite "sa īm" for Jātavedas together with the *mūrjayaṃbhis*.
Those men by whom the seven types of possessions have been abandoned should say, "This is not mine."
By these [verses] the cleansing is performed; by them one has bathed in the waters of the Ganges.

May Indra purify me with good guidance; may Soma with well-being, and Varuṇa with concord. May King Yama purify me with his cleansing powers; may Jātavedas purify me with the strength-bestowing [oblation].
One should offer oblations with the twenty-verse hymn beginning "yad devā devaheḍanam.
In that rite, the renunciation [of the merit] belongs first to the Ādityas, as follows:
O gods, whatever offense against the gods we have committed, O Ādityas, release us from that; by means of the Truth, deliver me from it.
To Agni Gārhapatya on the second day, and on the third likewise;
and to Dyāvāpṛthivī and Sarasvatī—thus according to the Ṛgveda verses.
O gods, for the sake of one desiring life, we have extracted the two nectars from speech.
May Agni Gārhapatya release me from that sin; may he make me free from evil and bring me into a state of blamelessness.
By Truth, O Heaven and Earth; by Truth, O Sarasvatī.
May the two who do not release me from the truth laugh at the harm I have committed.
Then, on the fourth [day] with the *jātavedasa* mantra, and on the fifth, the renunciation (*tyāga*) is made for Agni Gārhapatya; the two verses for that are as follows.
Born from the womb, he is like a brother; he is a crow upon the ridge, or perhaps a crow of speech.

Whatever sin has been committed by us through ignorance, O Jātavedas, born from the foot or wrought by the gods— release us from that! Whatever falsehood we have uttered with speech or mind, with arms or thighs, with knees or with the penis— may Agni Gārhapatya release me from that sin and from whatever misfortunes there are.
May he make me free from sin.
The offering to the Rāṣṭrabhṛt deities is on the sixth day, and the offering to the Apsarases is on the seventh.
One should not say "I have measured" to Agni Gārhapatya; one should simply say "to Agni."

Whatever sins of the hands he has committed, smelling the skin of dice; whatever [sins] behind and from afar, O Rāṣṭrabhṛt, may the Apsarases wipe away those misdeeds. Whatever unrighteous act this king has caused to be done, or whatever he has commanded, may Agni purify that sin of his from these [people].

May Gārhapatya Agni release me from whatever evil I have done, whether intentionally or unintentionally; may he release me from that sin which my mother committed while I was in the womb, or which she caused to be done. May Gārhapatya Agni release me from that sin and from whatever evil I have done, whether intentionally or unintentionally; and also whatever [evil] my mother [committed].
One should meditate with a joyful son.
O Agni, I have not harmed these two men; therefore, may I become free from cruelty.
One should recite for Agni Gārhapatya in the tenth and eleventh [verses];
but in the twelfth, for both Agni Āhavanīya and Agni Gārhapatya.
If he should ever abandon the atmosphere, the earth, the heaven, or even his father, who is more closely joined to him—himself.

May Agni Gārhapatya release me from this sin; may he also release me from whatever misdeeds I have committed, and let him not hold me in remembrance as one who has sinned. Whatever evil I have done through foot-fettering, through verbal abuse, or through hostility, and whatever sin I have committed—may Agni Gārhapatya release me from that sin and from all misfortunes. May he also release me from whatever misdeeds I have committed.

May he make me free from sin. May I cross over my transgressions and evil deeds by means of this boat of yours, O Mitra, in our common dwelling—there where both the doers of good and the doers of evil reside—I ascend to that world of the righteous.

Trita Deva purified it; with that, the god Trita purified this [soma] among men. Therefore, if anything has reached me [from that], may Agni Gārhapatya release me from that sin and from whatever evil deeds I have committed; may he make me free from guilt. (In the fourteenth [chapter], one offers) to Agni, then to the Waters, then to Varuṇa; thereafter, two *doṃ* offerings for two [deities].
In the eighteenth and the nineteenth [verses], however, it says "to Agni and Varuṇa";
those born of heaven and born of water were produced from the plants.

May those waters born of Agni, which are themselves purifying, cleanse us as they flow. Whatever sin we have committed by day or by night, whether new or old, O golden-hued ones, drive that away from us. O Varuṇa, hear this my invocation; be gracious to the one who calls upon you for help, and protect the one who seeks your shelter. I approach you with prayer.
Worshipping with oblations, the sacrificer then prays for this: "May Varuṇa, being unprovoked, hear our call;
do not steal away our common life-span. O Agni, you who know the ways of the god, appease his wrath and leave us remaining.
As the best bearer of the sacrifice, shining brightly, quickly release us from all hatred. That, indeed, is ours...

O Agni, be most gracious with your protection; you have been appointed by Varuṇa at the dawning of this morning. O Varuṇa, being pleased, release us from our sin; grant us mercy, O you who are easily invoked. This hymn dedicated to Vaiśvānara Agni consists of twenty verses.
Then follows the offering to Agni Vaiśvānara consisting of eight verses, which has been proclaimed. O Agni...
He is endowed with the wisdom that is free from effort and is beneficial.

218a) You have carried away the oblation that was not offered, O guardian of the remedy. May Vaiśvānara come forth from afar like one observing his vow, Agni with his ruddy vehicle. [I praise] Vaiśvānara, the observer of Truth, the light of Truth; O Unborn One...

We pray for righteousness. From the wondrous deeds of Vaiśvānara, one great singer has emerged through his own power, a wise seer. Both parents, born from the great progenitor, are Agni—heaven and earth—endowed with abundant splendor. Sought in heaven, sought on earth, Agni, sought by all, has entered into every dwelling as our protector.

May Vaiśvānara Agni, touched by power, protect us from harm by day and by night. When you were born, O Agni, you pervaded all beings like a beast upon the mountain; you are the protector, the one who moves around. May we find the path through prayer to Vaiśvānara; do you all protect us always with blessings. O Agni, you who are radiant with your flame...
Filling both heaven and earth as he was being born, O Vaiśvānara Jātavedas, you released the gods from the curse by your greatness.

May you firmly establish for us a kingdom that is full of food, undecaying, and rich in heroic strength. Through your protections, O Agni Vaiśvānara, may we conquer the mortal enemy and win the prize with our might. [This is] of Vaiśvānara.
The beloved one, the stainless, the bringer of day, the glory of the worlds; born from here, he beholds this entire universe for Vaiśvānara, the Sun who descends.
Then, having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and having taken up the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*),
he should take a full water-pot and go to a crossroads in the southwest direction.
Having washed his feet and sipped water, he then, facing the east together with his wives, should observe the auspicious and inauspicious shadows therein.
One should meditate on "siṃho me manyuḥ" and recite the *pāka* [mantra];
then, one should pour it out with the mantra, "sumitrā na āpa oṣadhayaḥ santu."
If some water should subsequently rise from the ground accompanied by a jar,
ill-wishers shall cast that jar behind him.
In whichever direction his enemy may reside, he should cast [the offering] right there;
afterwards, having sipped water, the twice-born man should enter his own home.
One should perform this for seven days during the three junctions of the day;
when one perceives a clear reflection within the water, then [the rite] will be successful.
The sacrificer, having been well-purified, should then perform the rite again;
thereafter, having received the words of benediction, he should feed the Brāhmaṇas.
As long as one performs ritual action, one should maintain silence;
one who partakes in the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) should offer the oblation only once.
One who has conquered the senses and dwells upon the earth shall bestow [the fruit] earned in previous births;
one becomes liberated from the creator of obstacles to mantra-siddhi, and not otherwise.
For the sake of destroying whatever sin has been committed in this birth, whether through ignorance or through negligence, one should perform oblations with the Kūṣmāṇḍī mantras.
He whose ancestors were experts in the Vedic tradition, yet fell from the Kaulika path due to defects in knowledge and were afflicted by poverty and other such misfortunes;
If one is afflicted by mental distress, for the sake of removing that sin and for the sake of establishing oneself in both worlds, he too should perform [the penance] in secret.
For stealing gold, drinking liquor, killing a cow, murdering a Brahmin,
or violating the teacher’s bed, one should perform this vow for one year.
For theft, for killing an embryo, for discharging semen in a non-vaginal opening,
for betraying trust, and for misappropriating a deposit, one shall perform the Ayana penance.
In the event of accepting an improper gift, or during an eclipse of the moon or sun,
or after receiving a gift while standing in water or in a temple of Śiva, one must perform a Kṛcchra penance for each season.
Whether it be false testimony, usury, acting in dance, taking the hand [in marriage],
or exercising authority over gods or Brahmins— whatever one should practice at the end of a fortnight [is purified by the Kṛcchra].
For eating prepared food [at improper times], for visiting a prostitute, for slaughtering animals,
for participating in a *gaṇa* feast for the sake of the gods and others, and for the omission of the three daily prayers (*trisaṃdhyā*), the penance lasts one day.
Having heard [the mantra] regarding the hair and beard, and having bathed while surrounded by it in a sacred reservoir of water,
one should perform the fire-oblation with the Kuṣmāṇḍī verses immediately after the portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga).
One should daily recite the Sāvitrī and other purificatory mantras according to one's ability;
a Brāhmaṇa should subsist on milk, while a Kṣatriya should subsist on barley gruel.
A Vaiśya should consume curd-mixture (āmikṣā) when he is capable;
at that time, he may also rely upon boiled rice, roasted grain, parched grain, or even clarified butter.
One must not consume anything other than this; the rules regarding celibacy and so forth remain as before.
The fire-oblation, however, should be performed with cow's ghee alone; in its absence, one may use sesame oil.
In the first section (kaṇḍikā), the abandonment of whatever offense against the gods there may be, specifically toward the Āditya gods, is prescribed therein.
"Viśvebhyo devebhyaḥ" is declared as the second;
the third is said to be the same as the previous [verse] regarding the offering, yet it is described as being distinct from the *ṛc*.
Whether out of a desire for life or because we have committed falsehood,
O All-Gods who delight in the light, do not abandon us here.
O Sarasvatī, protect us with truth as the river or the earth protects; O Goddess of Truth, guard us from the sin of whatever untruth we have uttered.
May the Ordainer (Kṛtānta) protect us from that which we have spoken falsely.
"O Indra, Agni, Mitra, Varuṇa, Soma, Dhātṛ, Bṛhaspati!
May there be safety for you"—this is now declared as the *asāri* for the fourth [day].
Indra, Agni, Mitra, Varuṇa, Soma, Dhātṛ, and Bṛhaspati—
by them may he be released from whatever harm has been wrought by another.
The fifth [alternative] is considered to be "sa jātasaṃsādi," as previously stated;
or else, it is that which begins with "yanmanasā" preceded by "ṣaṣṭi."
My renunciation through Jyotiṣa is called the seventh,
and my renunciation through Agni is likewise declared to be the eighth.
By which Trita rose up from the well three times, by which Sūrya was released from darkness, and by which Indra drove away all hostilities—
with that light, attaining light through light, I have reached the eye. Whatever debt is not yet acknowledged by me,
for which I move about as the debtor of another— by this, O Agni, I become free from that debt even while living, according to your ordinance.
I bestow.
The first oblation was that which was previously declared as "Thou art my mother";
the tenth oblation was that which was previously declared as the "Mother of Pishas."
When "antarikṣam," "pṛthivī," and "prāk" are recited, it is called the eleventh oblation; when "yad āśāsani" and "āśaseti" are recited, it is called the twelfth oblation here.
Then he should offer three oblations into the fire; thus there are fifteen oblations, and the sixteenth should be the previously mentioned one with the mantra "yad apo naktam."

The renunciation [of the offering] is prescribed for these golden-colored ones with the mantra beginning "guṃ syāstyāgaḥ. Furthermore, the five verses beginning with "idam eva ruṇe" have been previously mentioned.
Those twenty-one offerings are declared to be the renunciations;
the twenty-second renunciation is for Indra and Agni, and that verse is now being stated.
In that state, I was intensely desirous of giving dwellings to the people.
"May Agni and Indra, acting in concert, release me from this—[the curse] of the fierce Pasyā and Rāṣṭrabhṛt Apsarases. Thus he should speak.
O Ugra, look upon the sins of the kingdom; for this is the conduct of dice-play.
Having paid his debts with his eyes, leveling them as he were free from debt, the honest man has gone to the world of Yama.
O Varuṇa, we appease your wrath with prostrations; we seek your favor through sacrifices and oblations.

O King, O Asura-like lord, forgive the sins we have committed against you. Loosen from us the highest bond, Varuṇa, loosen the lowest, and loosen the middle one. Then, O Āditya, may we abide in your sacred law.
May we be sinless before Aditi through you.
In the thirty-first [chapter], Saṃkusuka and Vikūsuka are the deities of the Nairṛta quarter;
renunciation is taught through the sounds [of these names]. That verse is now being recited.
Saṃkusuka and Vikusuka, you who are Nirṛti and the Resounding One—
drive the consumption that afflicts us away from us, far, far away, so that we remain sinless.
Then, for the two [offerings], there is the offering to Agni and Tvaṣṭṛ; that is considered the first.
The offering to Āyuṣmān Agni is held to be the thirty-fifth.
And may you drive away consumption and witchcraft, as well as destruction.

Therefore, whoever seeks to encounter us, him we drive away for him. Whether he be one who is difficult to overcome, or one who follows closely behind, or one who pursues us with a wager—no other shall encounter us;
him we drive away for him.
May he be united with splendor, with milk, with bodies, and with a great, auspicious mind. May Tvaṣṭṛ here provide us with nourishment; may he smooth over whatever is injured in our bodies.
May this most excellent Agni bestow nourishment upon you from every side. Your breath returns to you; O you who are well-disposed, drive away consumption.

The renunciation of the lifespan-oblation (*āyurdāya*) is for Agni in the thirty-sixth [year], and then in the one following that: to Agni, to Varuṇa, to Āditya, and to the Viśvedevas. O Agni, giver of life, enjoying the oblation, with ghee as your face and ghee as your source, come; having drunk the sweet and pleasant cow’s ghee, protect this man as a father protects his son.
O Agni, make this man worthy of long life; O Varuṇa of sharp power, sharpen him well.
O Aditi, grant him protection, so that all the gods may be pleased with him as he acts.
"To Agni, for him who is being cooked, [is] yours; thirty-three [times] in three [vessels].
Therefore, the renunciation is said to be "to Agni Jātavedas, yours."
O Agni, extend our life; grant us pasture and strength; bestow upon us nourishing food. And drive far away all misfortune.
May the fires of Agni bestow upon him rain, heroic vigor, and even nourishment.
Agni is the seer, the purifying one, the benefactor of the five peoples, the domestic priest.
O Jātavedas, driving away those born later and overcoming those born before us, subdue that great host of darkness.
Shine for us with a gracious mind; may we abide in your protection, O Atri, within your victorious shelter, through your power.
Driving away those who have been born as rivals, O Jātavedas, drive back those yet unborn;
speak for us, be well-disposed toward us, and may we be prosperous—driving away those who have been born as rivals.
Then, for the forty-third [verse], "To Agni, the slayer of Vṛtra";
from that, however, "To Agni" should be followed by "uṣaseniḥ suce."
O Agni, when people surround us from all sides, whether as one or many, seeking to strike us down— O slayer of Vṛtra, do you destroy them and bring wealth to us.
O Agni, when there is no distinction between us and you, and our goals are the same,
may we make him into fuel for you, O Agni, so that you may consume him.
May Dawn and Night destroy all the evil of that person who curses his own feet, and whoever curses one who is cursing him.
In the forty-sixth [verse], there is an offering (tyāga) to the gods;
in the one following that, an offering to Jātavedas and Agni; thereafter, there should be an offering to Agni.
O gods, he who is a companion, he who is a delight when intoxicated with soma—
nothing at all remains of him, just as nothing remains of a log that has been consumed by fire.
O Jātavedas, whoever hates me and those five whom I hate, burn them all up together with their kin;

and those whom I hate and those who hate me—burn them all. Whoever acts with enmity toward us, whoever is hostile, hateful, or injurious, whoever reviles us or seeks to harm us—reduce them all to ashes.
To Śitriya, to Brahmaṇaspati, and to Agni the forty-ninth;
likewise to Agni Antaka and to Vaiśvānara. May he sharpen my sacred knowledge (*brahman*); may he sharpen my vigor and strength.
May he sharpen the victorious ruling power (*kṣatra*) of him whose domestic priest (*purohita*) I am. May his arms rise up...
Exceedingly radiant and powerful, I destroy my enemies with sacred prayer; I raise up my friends here on this earth.

May my mind come back to me again and again; may my life-span come back to me; may my sight come back to me, and may my hearing come back to me again. May my breath come back to me, and may my intention come back to me; may my consciousness come back to me, and may my reflection come back to me. May Vaiśvānara, the protector of our bodies, bestow these upon us and drive away all misfortunes.
Having performed the oblation in this manner, he should then remain standing facing north, silently praising the fire with twelve verses on the south side of the fire.
We announce this to Vaiśvānara; high above men is the assembly of the gods.

May he, releasing these regions, grant us knowledge; may he release us from reproach and from sin. May Vaiśvānara, purifying with his filters, drive away that which we have pursued in our assembly through ignorance of mind or through what has been done here against us.

He has descended to the pure realm. Among the desirable fortunes in heaven, where the two stars of the *Nāsatyas* are revealed, he has entered this hundred-fold canopy of nectar-smile that liberates the bound.
Desiring to conquer the worlds and supporting the foundations of thought, you release the bound one, just as the unshakable embryo is released from the womb; thus, indeed, [he releases] all.
He has been honored. May he, the wise Prajāpati, the first-born of Cosmic Order (*ṛta*), accept it with full knowledge.
May we follow that which you have bestowed beyond old age;
may we move along that path of Manu. Some follow the heated cord of those for whom the ancestral gift has come to them. Others give without attachment.

If you wish to give, O Śakra, grant them that heaven; O Manu, begin it, for you two together traverse the common path with clarified butter. Whatever has been offered as a gift, whatever remains, and whatever is in the fire—for that sake, O husband and wife, begin this work for your kin here. With your feet, you have traversed the atmosphere and the earth.

Whatever offense I have committed against my mother, my father, or my kin, may Agni Gārhapatya deliver me from that sin and from whatever misdeeds we have done. Mother Earth, Aditi, is our source; the mid-air is our brother who removes the curse of sin. Our father is the ocean; may he grant us well-being through his paternal care. May there be no kinship with evil.

Having entered [the world], may I not desire [to dwell in] those worlds where the virtuous with kind hearts rejoice, having abandoned disease and the frailty of their own bodies; there in heaven, with unimpaired limbs and undiminished, one beholds both father and son.

Whatever debt I have incurred toward the gods through intoxication, or what I shall incur through the *ṛta*, or whatever I am about to do; whatever offense I have committed against the gods in their sight, O God, and whatever I have accepted as a gift—may Agni make me free from that debt.

Whatever food I eat in various forms, clothing, gold, and cattle—cows, goats, and sheep; whatever I have accepted from the gods, whether it be a cow or a horse, O God, may Agni make me free from debt for all that.
Having thus worshipped the fire, one should offer a fuel-stick held in the hand with the mantra to be recited hereafter,
making the renunciation (tyāga) to Vaiśvānara.
Whatever sin has ever been committed by me through mind or speech.
Therefore, having merged everything from that, one should know the state of innocence as *guṃ*; thus, *guṃ svāhā*.
Thereafter, one should perform recitation (*japa*) and fire-offerings (*homa*);
this has been described as the expiation that wards off the effects of actions committed in this life and previous births.

This has been stated regarding the twice-born. Now follows the method for the destruction of the sins of Śūdras. That is stated in that very same work: "Now, moreover, it is being told regarding the Śūdras."
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, having performed his daily obligatory rites and being pure,
he should eat a single meal of sacrificial food (haviṣya), and on the ninth day, he should observe a fast at night.
On the eighth and tenth days, one should observe a fast; on the eleventh day, one should fast as well;
and on the twelfth day, having performed the shaving of the head, one should worship the Brahmins and the deities.
Having received from the mouth of the Guru the eight-syllable mantra, beginning with one's own preferred seed-syllable and ending with "Namo Nārāyaṇāya," one should perform the recitation.
Eating the remnants of twice-born men, devoted to that service, one should perform the recitation eight hundred thousand times,
sleeping on the ground and observing celibacy, except at midday.
When the [period of] recitation is complete, one becomes free from sin; otherwise, one should perform it again.
The signs of being free from sin will be described here, as well as those for the previously mentioned fire-offerings (homa).
On the day of commencing the *homa* and other rites, one should procure a pure, firm earthen jar free from cracks and place it in a secure location.
In that [vessel], one should pour water from sacred bathing places (tīrtha) measured by a jar;
one should place a thread originating from Śṛṅgala Island into a glass vessel.
There, one should perform the worship of Hari and Hara using only a *pala* of each;
having performed the worship on the day of examination, one should pray for that water.
The waters are Nārāyaṇa himself; truth is established in the waters.
By that truth, may that true knowledge of the Truth be mine.
Having thus prayed to the water, one should then offer a handful of water;
then one should look at the reflection of one's own body in the water as well as in the liquid.
Just as it is with taste, so it is with water: if one sees that sin has departed, yet when the reflection in the water appears faded, then indeed the sin has not gone.
One should perform the expiation again until the shadow becomes stainless;
when one's faults are destroyed, O Lord, one partakes in the success of the *puraścaraṇa*.
Whosoever recites even a single syllable of a Vedic mantra or the Name-mantra,
it destroys the sins committed during one lifetime.
For Viṣṇu, for me, for Gaṇeśa, and for the Sun, [the recitation] destroys sin; for a follower of Tantra it is half that; for an ordinary person (*prākṛta*) it is a quarter;
and for one who uses corrupt speech (*apabhraṃśa*) it is half of that—this is declared everywhere.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the *Kulamuktikallolinī*, composed by the venerable Ādyānanda.
Having thus rendered the body free from sin, one should commence the *puraścaraṇa*.
For example, as stated in the Kālitantra:
First, one should perform the preliminary service according to the rules and the prescribed method;
thereafter, once the mantra is mastered, the practitioner is fit for its application, and not otherwise.
In the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā.
Just as a living being deprived of life is incapable of performing any actions,
so too is a mantra proclaimed to be when it is devoid of *puraścaraṇa*.
In the Vīracūḍāmaṇi.
For one who is devoid of *puraścaraṇa*, the accomplishment of the mantra does not arise;
therefore, at the outset, one should perform the preparatory rite (*puraskriyā*) according to rule and in accordance with the prescribed method.
In the Surendrasaṃhitā:

One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice with red lotuses numbering one-tenth of that amount in a consecrated fire; thereafter, the mantra becomes perfected.
In the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi*.

The wise practitioner of mantras should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice with one-tenth that number; by offering lotuses smeared with honey, a person becomes a lord of speech.
In the Ekavīrākalpa.
For those devoid of meditation, who are base and small-minded, recitation is said to require fourfold effort for success; otherwise, it will not come to pass.
In the ocean of stars.
Having meditated thus, one who subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya) should recite [the mantra] four hundred thousand times;
or, taking the secret rosary, one should recite it exactly one hundred thousand times.
In the Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā.
The number prescribed for the Kṛta age remains as stated; in the Tretā it becomes double;
in the Dvāpara it is said to be triple; and in the Kali age, the number is fourfold.

Thus, according to the *Vaiśampāyanīya-saṃhitā*, the meaning of the statement is that the attainment of mantra-perfection (*mantra-siddhi*) occurs through an increase in the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), such as doubling them for each successive age; this is the explicit sense. However, it appears here that it is only the obstacles produced by conditions such as past misdeeds (*duṣkṛta*) that obstruct the attainment of mantra-perfection, and not the differences between the ages themselves.

Regarding the fourfold recitation for the *ekavīrā* (the solitary heroine) as stated in the ritual manual (*kalpa*): for those who lack clear meditative visualization, for Śūdras, and for those of limited intellect, the term "fourfold" refers to the destruction of whatever sin exists; furthermore, according to the statement in the *Merutantra*, "Having performed the preliminary rite (*puraskṛti*), one should perform [the practice] once the removal of evil deeds has been accomplished," when the elimination of misdeeds is achieved, there is service according to the [specific] age (*yuga*).
Exertion should not be disregarded.
And likewise, in the Muṇḍamālā:
Kālī, Tārā, Mahāvidyā, Ṣoḍaśī, Bhuvaneśvarī,
Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, and likewise the Vidyā Dhumāvatī.
Vagalā, Siddhividya, Mātaṅgī, and Kamalāmbikā—
these ten Mahāvidyās are proclaimed as the Siddhividyās.
O Maheśānī, there is nothing whatsoever that can ever be accomplished with difficulty through the practice of Siddhividya, Mahāvidyā, and service during the [proper] yuga.

The accomplishment of the mantra occurs precisely through the number of recitations prescribed for each respective Kalpa; thus, the ritual procedure for the destruction of sins has been fully explained.
In the Vīracūḍāmaṇi.
Having bathed well and being purified by his vows, the wise man should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times;
eating only at night and subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya), he should avoid women, meat, and the like.
Having bathed, wearing white garments, and being pure during the day, one should diligently perform the daily rites and the fire sacrifice (homa) with milk-rice or sesame seeds.
One should perform worship at night according to the ritual of the five mudrās;
by this very procedure, the wise practitioner should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.
Having placed one's own respective karma before oneself, one should perform the recitation (japa) during the day while pure;
likewise, one should do so at night according to that same number, through the application of the left and right [nostrils].

At night, established in that full moon and on the day of the Śarvarī constellation, one should perform one hundred thousand recitations; one shall become a master of all supernatural powers (siddhis).
One should perform gestures such as *hāva* and *bhāva*, and one should gather the great *cīna-latā*.
With those very [substances], one should always perform libations (*tarpaṇa*), bathing, drinking, and so forth.

Purascarana is prescribed for Brahmins by day according to their respective duties, and for Shudras at night; however, for all twice-born classes (dvijas), the ritual procedure here is said to be performed during the day.

And for Śūdras, it is likewise declared that [initiation] performed at night yields great fruit, according to the statement in the Merutantra: "For Śūdras, it is thus proclaimed that [initiation] performed at night brings great fruit."
In the Kālīkrama.
Constantly devoted to his own proper conduct and purified, he should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times during the day;
or else, whether he be a divine practitioner or a hero, he should perform the recitation of one hundred thousand times at night.
In the *Phetkāriṇī*.
Having restricted his food to alms and the like, he is ordained to eat only once at night;
during the day, the twice-born man performing the *puraścaraṇa* should engage in silent recitation (*japa*).
Every day he should take his meal consisting of vegetables, barley-gruel, or sacrificial porridge mixed with ghee, or curd, or even fruits.
Likewise, celibacy has been prescribed, as well as bathing at the three junctions of the day;
and having performed the worship of the deity especially during the forenoon.
All mantras, beginning generally with the *praṇava*,
should be recited by one who is seated on a prescribed seat, restrained in speech, and single-mindedly focused.
In the Merutantra:
One who is pure should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times during the day while consuming sacrificial food (haviṣya);
likewise, one who is impure should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times at night.
One should perform the fire-oblation with clarified butter ten times [the number of recitations], and one should satisfy and consecrate [the deity].
Also in the accumulation of lineage.
Then, wearing white garments, pure and with a restrained mind,
one should perform this during the day for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals.
In the Svatantra Tantra.
During the day, having become pure and eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), the wise man should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times;
thereafter, O Dear One, he should perform a fire-oblation with sacrificial food consisting of one-tenth of that number.
One should satisfy [the deities] with water from a sacred ford, or with milk, or even with clarified butter,
or with honey, or with water mixed with sugar, O Supreme Goddess.
O Dear One, one should consecrate the Goddess with waters equal to one-tenth of the libation (tarpaṇa),
and with food offerings equal to one-tenth of that, one should feed [the Brahmins] with devotion.
O beloved, one should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins who know the Kālī-mantra and to the preceptor;
now hear the ritual manual (kalpa) concerning the animal sacrifice (pāśava), as it has been described.
Having worshipped the Goddess according to the prescribed rite with meat and liquor at night, he should then,
naked and even if covered in secretions, take pleasure with a naked woman.

Then, O Goddess, having recited [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in a blazing fire situated within a vulva-shaped sacrificial pit (yoni-kuṇḍa), using clarified butter,
meat, and fat.
The excellent practitioner should satisfy [the deity] with ten parts of wine mixed with meat;
having performed the consecration with a tenth part of that satisfaction, one should [worship] her who consists of the entire world.
The practitioner, dear to Kālikā, should properly feed one-tenth of that number;
he should provide liquor, meat, fish, and the ritual libation.
Then, O beloved, one should satisfy the Guru with devotion through gold and other offerings;
O Goddess, by these two methods, the mantra will certainly be mastered.

In this regard, it is stated that for a human [practitioner], the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and the libation (*tarpaṇa*) are performed with the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) as the womb and with the ritual substance itself.
In the Kālītantra.
One should recite the vidyā one hundred thousand times while eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) during the day with purity;
at night, lying on a bed with betel leaf in the mouth, one should recite it for the measure of one hundred thousand.
In the Bhairavatantra.
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times while consuming sacrificial food (haviṣya), with the senses subdued during the day,
remaining devoted to celibacy (brahmacarya) during the rite of preliminary purification (puraścaraṇa).
Likewise, at night one should recite the mantra a hundred thousand times, intent on the lute and sexual union;
in this very manner of the Kula practice, one should accomplish one's own mantra.
O Lord, when performed according to the ritual injunctions, the mantra itself will surely be accomplished; of this there is no doubt.
Having thus recited two hundred thousand [times], the knower of mantras [should perform] a tenth part of that.
"O Goddess, one should perform ten thousand oblations, distinguished by day and night," so it is said in the Kumārī-kalpa.

Having received the ritual of initiation from the presence of a Guru and having obtained the mantra, he who recites this one hundred thousand times by day— eating sacrificial food at night, free from envy, devoid of lust and anger, and with a mind not wavering— is indeed a sovereign among practitioners. At night, after the conclusion of sexual union with his consort, he remains naked, liberated from all defects, and absorbed in you.
"Thus ends the *Dantacintā* in the *Bhairavayāmala*."
Reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times, devoted to eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), intent on meditating upon the pair of your feet during the day,

and furthermore, at night, naked and delighting in the sport of embracing [the consort], that person shall become equal to the Destroyer of Smara (Śiva) upon the surface of the earth. Thus it is stated in the *Mahākālastuti* regarding the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the hearing [of the mantra].

In the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*), the recitation (*japa*) consists of exactly two hundred thousand [times]. Herein lies the distinction: for a twice-born (*dvija*) endowed with three characteristics, it may be performed day or night; for a twice-born endowed with two characteristics, by way of the "beast-state" (*paśubhāva*) during the day and the "hero-state" (*vīrabhāva*) at night; and for one endowed with five or four characteristics [the same applies].

According to the natural sense of the scriptural statement, for a *paśu* (an uninitiated person), there is only the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) twice; for a twice-born (*dvija*) endowed with only the [external] marks, it is like that of a *śūdra*, consisting of a single course through the lineage of the Guru. However, the investigation into the characteristics [of these] should be seen in the twenty-second chapter. [As stated] in another Tantra:
Having indeed fashioned the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the shape of a womb, measuring one cubit in height and likewise one cubit in width, and also making it that deep below;
In that regard, the ritual for establishing the fire should indeed be performed with the mantra;
and one should offer the first oblation to the deity Mahākāla.
Thus, with fresh meat, cooked food, and blood, O Kṛṣṇa,
[one worships] with black flowers, musical instruments, and especially with red [garments].
The wise practitioner should likewise offer oblations in the cremation ground with the *āsiṣa* and other mantras,
and should also perform libations with milk as well as streams of blood.
Likewise, by means of marrow and similarly by her own excrement,
and by the purification of the lineage of the girl who has been drawn forth.
One should indeed satisfy the Supreme Deity with the blood of sheep and buffaloes, as well as with human blood,
and the blood of mice and cats.
One should wipe [the vessel] with that very same valid substance ten times its weight;
and for whatever limb [of the ritual] may be deficient, one should perform twice as many recitations as the number of those deficiencies.
In the Matsyasūkta:
Seated comfortably on a soft cushion, with eyes like a great conch shell,
one should recite the mantra with a focused mind for three months or three fortnights while holding a rosary.
"Eating only at night and consuming sacrificial food (haviṣya), one should recite the Vidyā two hundred thousand times"— this statement is the truth regarding the fallen hero.
In the Tantra.
At whatever time the initiation occurs, at that very time this [rite] should take place.
In the Merutantra:
Having bathed according to the prescribed rules at an auspicious moment, under a favorable constellation, and on a propitious lunar day,
he should gratify the Brahmins with food, clothing, and other gifts.
Having satisfied his own guru with garments, ornaments, and other gifts,
he should thereafter commence the recitation (japa), preceded by the guru’s permission.
In the Dakṣiṇāmūrtikalpa.

The eminent and learned man, having bathed according to the rules at an auspicious moment, under a favorable lunar mansion, and on a propitious lunar day, should commence the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa).
Having bowed to the Guru, the Lord of Ganas, and having bowed to Durga, the Mother;
The first fortnight is the bright fortnight.
In the Merutantra:
One should commence the *puraścaryā* on an auspicious day as prescribed for initiation;
first, having prostrated before the Guru and having fully worshipped the Brahmins and Gaṇeśa.
In the Vaiśampāyana-saṃhitā.

One should begin [the practice] during the bright fortnight on an auspicious day when the moon and stars are favorable, starting from Capricorn; however, one should not recite [the mantra] while Viṣṇu is asleep.
In the mantra of the Yoginī.
Having received the command of the Guru, the person whose internal faculties are purified should then perform the preliminary rite with the desire for the complete accomplishment of the mantra.
Likewise.

Therefore, at the outset, the wise man should perform [the rite] himself or have the preceptor perform it; in the absence of a preceptor, he should have a brahmin who is devoted to the welfare of all living beings perform it.
A friend who is affectionate, learned in the scriptures, and endowed with various virtues;
or a woman who is perfected in character, of good conduct, and devoted to her husband.
Now, the locations for the *puraścaraṇa* rite, according to the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*:
Sacred fields, pilgrimage sites, forests, groves, temples, rivers, lakes, huts, and secluded places— these locations grant success in mantra practice.
In the Yāmala:
In a secluded and pure place, free from the fear and anxiety caused by barbarians, wicked beasts, and serpents, and devoid of censure, one should remain endowed with devotion.
One should dwell in one's own country, in a righteous kingdom that is well-supplied with food and free from calamity,
in a delightful place where a community of devotees resides, and not under the patronage of another.
On whatever path kings, ministers, royal officials, and powerful men travel, the knower of reality should not dwell there.
