One should not dwell in ruined temples, gardens, or at the foot of trees near houses; nor on riverbanks, mountain slopes, or in cavities in the earth.
In the Merutantra:
I shall describe the places for recitation, both natural and artificial,
which are kept secret in all the tantras for each respective deity.
The sacred field of Mahāgaṇapati is Māyūda on the bank of the Narmadā;
it is the great cremation ground of Māyūra, where the mantra of Gaṇeśa grants spiritual perfection.
Prabhāsa, Kurukṣetra, Puṣkara, Bhṛguparvata,
the banks of the Yamunā, and Kāśī— O Lord of Day, these grant the perfection of the Manus.
Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Māyā, Kāśī,
Badarikāśrama, Gayā, the banks of the Gaṇḍakī, and Dvārakā— these bestow the perfection of Viṣṇu.
Kedāra, Tryambaka, Kāśī, Kāñcī, Avantī, Ujjayinī,
the banks of the Gaṅgā, Vaidyanātha, and Rāmeśa, which bestows success upon Śiva.
Jvālāmukhī at Prayāga, Kāminī at Mālikāpada,
and the bank of the Sarasvatī bring about the accomplishment of the Śakti-mantra.
On the shore of Kamaleśvarī is the solitary Yakṣaparvata;
Aṅga, Vaṅga, and Kaliṅga grant the siddhi of minor deities.
Kāmarūpa, Nepāla, Hiṅgulā, Vindhyavāsinī,
Jālandhara, and Pūrṇagiri grant success through the left-hand path (vāmamārga).
The banks of lotus ponds, groves of plantains, sugarcane, and Arka trees,
and a village surrounded by coral— these are exceedingly dear to Gaṇeśa.
Lotus ponds, riverbanks, forests, oleander trees,
groves, wheat fields, and patches of dūrvā grass are dear to the sun.
In the vicinity of tulasī, aśvattha, dhātrī, sugarcane, and śāligrāma stones;
in a cow-pen, in a village of learned Vedic scholars, in a pair of villages, or in the presence of those devoted to the Vedas who are dear to Hari.
In a temple of Śiva where the Liṅga faces west, excluding Nandīśvara;
near a banyan tree, at a confluence, in a forest, or by a lake—therein lies the propitiation of Śiva.
The plantain, mango, *caṃvelī*, *sevantī*, and *varvarī* grow in the forest;
on the banks of rivers known as *granthi*, there is delight for Śakti in solitude.
In marshes, at night, in *vakola*, *śākoṭa*, and *madhuka* groves,
on anthills, and by dried-up rivers, the minor deities rejoice.
In the father’s house, in the cremation ground, at the triple-pathway and the crossroads,
in an empty dwelling, and on ground strewn with corpses, the Vāmakas find satisfaction.
In the house, in the cow-pen, likewise in a garden, in a forest, on a mountain peak,
by a river, at its confluence, or in a temple— the Vedic [rite] shall be superior.
In that region where, having become like cattle, they do not even speak the words of Brahman,
and where they do not cause the Śūdras to hear them, there is no Vedic accomplishment.
In the Kumārītantra:
The cremation ground of Kālikā is indeed praised; no other place is recommended.
Therefore, one who desires prosperity should perform worship in the cremation ground.
In the Mahāmanthāna Bhairava Tantra.
In all the *pīṭhas* and *upapīṭhas*, and in all the *kṣetras* and *upakṣetras*,
the mantras residing there— belonging to the path of ritual action (*kriyāmārga*) and the *valañjakas*— are worshipped.
The sacred seats (pīṭhas) are as described in the Merutantra.
Now I shall declare the most secret mystery concerning the origin of the sacred seats (pīṭha),
knowing which all practitioners attain accomplishment, and not otherwise.
There are fifty-one pīṭhas and the deities residing in the five Āmnāyas;
O gods, thirty-three [deities] also reside there.
Those deities who are proclaimed as the *upapīṭhas* in the sixth tradition (*āmnāya*),
their location is indicated there, above the heart.
The followers of the Vedas remain wherever his footfall has occurred.
Likewise, the southern path is accomplished where the leftward one is.
The letter *A* is said to be the first sacred seat (*pīṭha*) called Kāmarūpa;
it is that seat, O Goddess, wherein the path of the Kula was set in motion by me. There you fell into the womb; having seen that, I did what was pleasing to you.
The Kula scripture, however, bestows liberation upon the knowers who belong to the Kaula tradition.

Success comes quickly for those who recite five times, but it does not arise at all for those who do not measure [the time]; therefore, let the time for success regarding the *pādya* and other offerings be understood accordingly.
The root of Śrīvidyā is indeed that menstrual flow which occurs monthly;
however, if there is a transgression regarding the Kula-siddha, the obstruction of the flow (rajas-tambha) arises.
Its two secondary seats (upapīṭhas) are Āsāmaṃtava and Mūtraṇa;
Vangākhya is born from the hair, and the Siddhi is Śāvaracetakī.
The form is Kāśikā, and the seat has become a division of your heart;
that which is called Mahokhara is that which does not perish even at the time of universal dissolution.
Where there is neither sin nor merit, and where the renunciation of the body is the supreme state—
therein the two-fold fruit consists of enjoyment arising from righteous action.
The tortures resulting from sin there are terrifying; at every step lies a seat of suffering.
It is impossible for me to describe them all, even with the jars of your breasts.
A pair of streams issued forth, and Varuṇā became possessed of a sword;
the area extending one yojana outside Kāśī is known as the land of the gods.
And there, the mantras propitiated bestow their fruits immediately;
likewise, the deities residing in the tradition are situated in the four directions at that place.
The deities abide there; their accomplishment comes from mere preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa).
That place on the opposite bank of the Gaṅgā is sanctified by a portion of Kāśī.
Due to the curse of Vyāsa, that place became the wondrous Gardabha-kṣetra;
at that time, the realization of the six Āmnāyas arises there.
Upapīṭha is on the bank of the Asī, while Sāranātha is to the south;
there, the mantras of the Southern Path bestow accomplishment (siddhi).
To the north-east of Varuṇā is Sāranātha, and likewise to the north;
there is an upapīṭha of Vāma, and these [sites] bring about spiritual accomplishment on the path of the Left.
Nepāla, however, is the letter *i*, and Bhudam is located there, O Pārvatī;
therefore, that is said to be the root-place of the Vāmamārga.
There are fifty-six lakhs of Bhairavas and likewise Bhairavis;
two thousand Śaktis and three hundred Pīṭhas.
Fourteen cremation grounds are situated there,
and eight sacred seats (pīṭhas) that bestow spiritual accomplishments (siddhi) are located there on the path of Dakṣa.
The efficacy of Vedic mantras resides in those four sacred seats (pīṭhas);
wherever their impurity fell, there arose the secondary seats (upapīṭhakas).
To the east of Nepal, that region is inhabited by Kirātas;
indeed, thirty thousand beings of divine origin dwell there.
The origin and location of the vowel *ī* is Prauṇḍravardhana;
because your left eye has fallen there, it is called that great sacred seat (*mahāpīṭha*).
Through the recitation of any mantra whatsoever, accomplishment (siddhi) arises;
therein, the deities follow the left-hand path (vāmācāra), and the vision of the deity occurs.
The origin and location of the syllable *ukāra* is said to be Kāśmīra; because the ear fell there, it is therefore known as that supreme *pīṭha*.
Whichever deity’s mantra a person recites there,
they shall become one who has reached the further shore of all sciences and likewise become a knower of reality.
O Goddess of the Gods, for those who have fallen away from the Vedic, Kaula, Smārta, or Dvādaśamārga paths, there are penances to be performed therein.
The sacred sites established by me grant immediate proof of their power;
yet in the Kali age, they will become extremely hidden, shrouded by barbarians.
The place of origin for the letter *ū* is Kānyakubja;
there, your right ear fell, which is exceedingly auspicious.
Between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, that region known as Antarvedī was prepared as a dwelling place for the gods who drink the Soma juice.
There, the gods beginning with Brahmā established their respective sacred fords (tīrthas);
there, the gods attained the perfection of Vedic mantras at every step.
From that deity was born [the city] known in the world by the name Indraprastha, situated on the bank of the Yamunā, which is a celebrated secondary sacred seat (upapīṭha).
Because the Vedas were forgotten by Brahmā through the power of this seat (pīṭha), they were recovered once again;
therefore, this sacred ford (tīrtha) became known as Nigamabodhaka.
There Kālī performed penance with the desire for a boon, thinking: "May those who satisfy me with the five [offerings] obtain such a result as that."
Having reached that supreme Mahākāla there at the beginning of the world-cycle, she then dispatched [the disciple] into the fifth state and bestowed manifest perfection upon him.
The letter *ṛ* is Bhūḥpūrṇagiri; there the nose has fallen.
Therefore, through the perfection of yoga, the powder (*cūrṇa*) is produced there.
The place of origin for the letter *ṛ* is Mount Arbuda;
it descends from the left, and by that, this [letter] becomes beloved.
There, the Śakti named Āṃvikā is always fond of the left-hand path (vāmācāra);
even when a single rite of preliminary service (puraścaryā) occurs during a time of enjoyment, it bears fruit.
There, the deity presiding over the mantra becomes directly perceptible;
in that sacred seat (pīṭha), liberation occurs through union with a thousand vulvae (bhaga).
That place belongs to celestial women; however, Pārvatī made a great vow with me regarding her descent.
That man who shall practice celibacy in my field for twelve years shall alone become my husband.
Even the Buddhist has erred there [regarding] the solar year minus three days.
For in that case, the applications of the left [hand] indeed become the knowledges on the right.
The place where the letter *U* originated and where Asātakeśvara resides, where Dakṣagaṇḍa fell— that is a great and most wonderful sacred seat (*pīṭha*).
The Yakṣas such as Dhanada and the Yakṣiṇīs such as Dhanadā dwell there;
for one who recites [the mantra] there, success is produced.
In ancient times, the origin of the letter *ukāra* occurred at Ekāmra;
there, many nails were shed by the Vidyādharas as they performed intense penance.
For students, however, that seat (pīṭha) bestows their desired knowledge;
by reciting the Sarasvatī mantra there, they understand even a text they have not heard before.
The three folds on your belly have fallen into the triple stream of your single birth;
your garment has become threefold, falling first in front, then behind, and then to the right.
There are three secondary seats (upapīṭhas); a householder succeeds there, and only a twice-born (dvija), not any other caste, [attains success]. The Manuscripts are situated in the Manus (manavas).
The letter Ai became Kāmakoṭi; there indeed your navel fell.
There, all mantra-rites for desire are accomplished, without a doubt.
Having propitiated you, O Kāminī, while you were dwelling on the banks of the Chāchikā river,
he attained the capacity for the enjoyment of sixteen thousand women.
O Pārvatī, upapīṭhas have arisen there in the four directions;
that is the abode of the apsarases, where the mantras are associated with women.
All those deities of that particular tradition attain accomplishment there;
indeed, by merely beholding them, one obtains the desired and delightful [attainment].
The syllable *Oṃ* became Kailāsa within the interior of the Himālaya mountains;
there, the fingers fell and, by their joints, attained the state of being lingas.
Whatever mantra a twice-born man recites there with a rosary of beads,
the deity becomes pleased by that alone through the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
In ancient times, the origin of the vowel *au* occurred at Bhṛgupīṭha;
there your teeth fell, and that sacred site is most wonderful.
All Vedic mantras and those prescribed in the Kalpas remain there in their original form; by virtue of service there, they become perfected for you.
Let that which was produced from Kedāra fall upon your right palm;
for when it has fallen upon that seat (pīṭha), the supernatural powers (siddhis) will reside in your hand.
To its south is the secondary sacred seat (upapīṭha) known as Agastyāśrama;
there a bracelet fell, which bestows all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis).
After that, the falling of the ring occurred, and you became that wonderful seat named Indrākṣī, where in former times you were worshipped by Indra.
O Ambikā, it is said that after that, your bracelets fell into the water;
therefore, she is called Rājarājeśvarī.
Even there, accomplishment arises quickly through the left-hand practice (vāmācāra). O God, moreover, the Yakṣiṇīs become visible within the range of one's sight during the recitation.
The syllable *Aḥ* is situated in the city of the lunar orb on the left cheek;
there all mantras are perfected, of this there is no doubt.
The letter *ka* is indeed in the Śrīpīṭha; it has fallen upon the head of the earth.
Generally, in the Kali age, the arrival there of sinners is difficult to find.
Where all powers abide by His unswerving will,
they do not afflict Him who is vigilant, yet they consume that which is contrary to the Law.
The *upapīṭha* arises from the ornamentation of the ears, as before;
there resides the Brāhmī Śakti, the illuminator of the knowledge of Brahman.
In the southeast corner, from the ear upwards, is the Bhūdrapapīṭha;
the power (śakti) there is Māheśvarī, who is considered to be the purifier of the mouth.
Where the folds fall to its right, there you shall become;
at that place is the Upapīṭha, where the Śakti Kaumārī brings victory.
The Kaṇṭhamālā, however, fell upon the Upapīṭhaka in the southwest;
presided over by Vaiṣṇavī, it became a bestower of the perfect accomplishment of the Indrajāla.
After that, the pearl from her nose fell and became the Upapīṭhaka,
presided over by Vārāhī, which effects the crushing of enemies.
The head-ornament, having fallen from the wind onto the pedestal of the sun, became presided over by Indrāṇī; that [ornament] bestows the status of sovereignty.
The Śṛṅkhaṇikā is situated above the Upapīṭhaka;
it is presided over by Cāmuṇḍā and bestows success upon even minor deities.
To the northeast of the Veśyābharaṇa, there is an upapīṭha presided over by Mahālakṣmī; therein lie the accomplishments (siddhis) of the Sūktas.
The letter *kha* became the syllable *oṃ* at the sacred field of Amarakaṇṭaka;
from the falling of its neck, the seat (pīṭha) presided over by Narmadā came into being.
There, all the best of sages performed great penance by means of the worship of the Praṇava;
consequently, those great ṛṣis became liberated while living.
North of that is the secondary seat (upapīṭha), which became Kañcukī due to his falling;
it is the abode of Jyotiṣmatī and the illuminator of the Jyotis-mantra.
227a) That ancient portion, the *tīreṅgavilepana* of Bhadra,
has fallen as the *upapīṭha*; it bestows masculinity upon women.
Jālandhara is the abode of Kāla; situated there is your breast. Dakṣa fell there, and thus a great and wondrous sacred seat (pīṭha) was produced.
Jālapā is renowned there, and austerity was performed by Vahni;
he attained the state of being the mouth of the God and remains upon his secondary seat (upapīṭhaka).
That fire, renowned as Jvālāmukhī, is the deity of the mouth;
the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for the substance consists of a specific number of recitations.
There, a fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed, and the perfection of mantra arises;
it was there indeed that Gorakṣa formerly attained the eight siddhis.
Mālava, however, is situated here on the left shoulder of the letter Gha;
it is worshipped by the Gandharvas and bestows knowledge of melody without hesitation.
At the end of the lineage, a *phukāra* sound arose and fell upon your armpits;
therein, the ritual applications for hatred, eradication, and death grant success.
In the *dṛk* [position], however, there was the letter *ca*; the left armpit was established there. The *siddhi* called *daivajaya* was obtained by the Rākṣasas in that place.
The origin of the letter *cha* is proclaimed by Gokarṇa;
it fell there into the belly, and that became a most wonderful sacred seat (*pīṭha*).
The letter *ja* is born from Māruteśvara;
there your offering (*bali*) falls first upon the seat that reveals the mantra of Śiva.
The place of the letter *jhakāra* is Aṭṭahāsa; there the supreme series has fallen. It is considered to be that which effects the accomplishment of the mantra of Gaṇeśa.
The letter *ña* is indeed the dustless (*viraja*) locus; therein lies the final row, where the accomplishment of all Viṣṇu-mantras is not difficult to attain.
Its origin was in Rājagṛha;
there, your bladder burst, and below that, a small bell fell onto a small stool.
That which is called *vyaṃtika* is declared to be a successful form of sorcery (*indrajāla*);
the accomplishment of the purpose of the *Upaveda* shall become a marvel within the royal palace.
On the great highway, you became a pillar, and your hips fell down;
there, by the twice-born who were corrupted by their lineage, your own body was offered up.
Having attained another birth, O God, those who destroy the path of the Vedas—
such as the Aghoras and others following the Krama path— bestow divine happiness upon them.
The syllable *U* became Kaulagiri; there, the power of all the Valadevas fell upon you, and thus accomplishment (*siddhi*) was not far off.
The letter *ḍha* was in Elāpuṭa; Dakṣa fell upon you.
That seat (*pīṭha*) of Vālā is declared to consist of few syllables, and this brings about the attainment of the goal.
O lady of beautiful thighs, Kāleśvara has become the cause of your downfall;
yet, there indeed the mantras that grant longevity and victory over death are perfected.
Jayantī, however, is the location for the letter *ta*; one who prostrates there with his knees and performs recitation (*japa*) will master the science of archery (*dhanurveda*), without a doubt.
In Ujjayinī, the letter *tha* is on the left knee; there your fall occurs.
It is said that the Siddhas protect those who possess the armor-mantras (*kavaca-mantra*).
The origin of the Dasyu [occurs] in the Yoginī; there the Jaṅghā was struck down.
The Kaulika and Vāmaka mantras are perfected there, and no others.
The letter *Dha* is in the *kṣurikā*; there, O Śāvarī, is your left calf.
There, the *vaitālīka* mantras attain accomplishment.
The origin of Hastināpura is proclaimed as the origin of the syllable *na*.
There, his ankle and anklet fell at Dakṣa’s side;
that became the secondary sacred seat (upapīṭha) known as Nūpurārṇava.
There, at the sacred seats (pīṭha) and secondary seats (upapīṭha), the solar mantras are accomplished.
The seat (pīṭha) of the letter Pa is called Uḍḍīśa;
there, the left ankle has descended, and it bestows success upon the practitioner.
May the great tantra known as Uḍḍīśa be accomplished there,
where the anklet fell, as well as the Ḍāmara and the Upapīṭhaka.
Let there be a journey to the place of the letter *pha*; here, however, the essence of the body is such that wherever it falls, white clay is seen there.
Between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, as well as at Vārāṇasī—
in such places as these, O best of the twice-born, those [seeds] were sown by you.
Those sacred seats (pīṭhas) were sacrificed up to the edge of the earth;
and to the east of the Gaṅgā is Vagalā, a truly great secondary seat (upapīṭha).
To the north shall be Cāmuṇḍā, indeed a most wonderful secondary sacred seat (upapīṭha);
in the middle of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, she herself is Rājarājeśvarī.
Bhuvaneśī is established on the southern bank of the Yamunā;
therefore, Prayāga is called the king of holy places (tīrtharāja) and the king of sacred seats (pīṭharāja).
The sixth lord is the locus of the letter *va*; there, O Goddess, your two heels have fallen to the south; here indeed is the accomplishment of the sandals (*pādukā-siddhi*).
At Māyāpura, his left heel fell upon that ground;
there, the illusory powers of the gods, dānavas, and gandharvas are perfected.
The letter *ma* is in the sacred seat (pīṭha) called Malaya, where your arrow fell;
that place, adorned with red garments and the like, is the site for the accomplishment of the mantras of the Buddhists.
On Śrīśaila, however, there was the letter *ya*; there, O Ambikā, is your bile.
All mantras are perfected there, especially those of Viṣṇu.
The abode of Himāga, however, is the peak named Meru;
from its falling fat, Svarṇākarṣaṇa Bhairava arose as a drop.
Wherever the letter *la* arises for you upon the seat of speech (*girapīṭha*), there the tip of the tongue has fallen; through recitation (*jāpa*) there, speech is certainly perfected.
The station of the letter *va* is Māheṃdra;
there, O Majjāpati, the accomplishment of all power-mantras (*śakti-mantra*) occurs, without a doubt.
The *vāmana* [mudrā] of the letter *śa* arises from the position of the thumb;
indeed, by reciting there, one attains preeminence among counselors.
The letter Śa, born from Hiraṇyapura, is on the left;
O God, that is the seat of the thumb, which is superior in the left-hand path.
And upon the seat of Mahālakṣmī, the letter *sa* became your desire;
having fallen there from your body, all accomplishment (*sarvasiddhi*) is produced.
The letter *ha* is in Oḍḍiyāna; there the *bhū-dhamanī* (earth-vein) falls.
The accomplishments (*siddhis*) that you desire are present there, established within the range of your vision.
The letter *la* is the seat of shadow; I have seen your shadow as the Earth.
Since this [Earth] has been obtained as a virtuous wife, therefore that is the seat of the Shadow-Earth (*bhū-chāyā-pīṭha*).
The letter *kṣa*, which constitutes the mass of hair, has arisen upon the seat of the parasol;
O Goddess, wherever it has fallen, there accomplishment (*siddhi*) is not far off.
O Goddess, this secret concerning the origin of the sacred seats (pīṭhas) has been proclaimed by me.
Likewise.
Barbarians, heretics, rogues, kings, and their quarreling subjects,
as well as young women— when these do not prevail there, success is not far off.
One should not dwell in dilapidated temples, gardens, or houses, nor at the foot of trees,
nor on riverbanks, mountain peaks, or in cavities in the earth.

Decaying reaches even to the trees; the prohibition against riverbanks refers specifically to those eroded by the waves of the ocean. Having reflected thus, a wise man should perform the ritual acceptance of the ground after worshipping the Earth-Bristle-boar (Pṛthvī-varāha) and with the strength of the son of the Earth (Mars).
One should say: "For the sake of accomplishing the *puraścaraṇa* of such-and-such a mantra, I accept this ground; may this mantra be perfected."
In the Yāmala:
Having demarcated the land on all sides according to its extent,
it is traditionally held that the area within a *krośa* in a village and twice that in a city constitutes the site.
At rivers, mountains, sacred fords, and other such places, one should take stakes made from milk-exuding trees that are free from defects in size and consecrated with mantras.
In the Merutantra:
One should take ten pegs made from any of the following trees— Nyagrodha, Dumbara, Aśvattha, or Plakṣa— each measuring one span in circumference.
One should drive eight [stakes] into the eight directions starting from the northeast;
one should drive the ninth into the center, with the understanding that it extends both upwards and downwards.
One should then fix a ritual stake (kīla) with the mantra between the southwest and the west;
likewise, one should perform worship with the Astra-mantra and worship the fire within them.
Likewise.
And when the field is thus pinned down, the practitioner of mantra is not overcome by obstacles.

Regarding the phrase "the weapon": some say that one should worship the weapons of the respective guardians of the directions (dikpāla) corresponding to whichever direction the [deity] is proceeding toward.
Others maintain that the weapon-mantra (astra) is the sixth limb of the root-mantra, and one should worship it with that specific weapon-mantra.
In the Yāmala:
There, the best of those who know the ritual should worship the guardians of the field and others according to the rules;
having offered the sacrificial oblation (bali) to the lords of the directions, he should then take refuge in the sacred field.
In the Merutantra:
One should offer cooked mung beans (*māṣa-bhakta*) mixed with clarified butter to the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*) in the various quarters;
and in the center of the field, one should worship Kṣetrapāla and Gaṇeśvara.
One should give the third person, Vāstu-puruṣa, three folds [of cloth] from among those.
The mantra for the offering to the Kṣetrapāla is as follows; it is stated in the Prathamatantra and the Merutantra.
Having fully worshipped the guardian of the field (kṣetrapāla), one should offer the bali-oblation according to the prescribed rule.
Having said, "Come, come, O wise one," he should perform the pair of *amurubhañja* steps;
then, after performing the pair of dances, he should say, "O destroyer of obstacles, destroy the obstacle!"
"Bhairava Kṣetrapāla, accept the offering, svāhā!
This forty-three-syllable mantra is for the offering to Kṣetrapāla.
One should offer an oblation to him along with his retinue, but one should not consume it.
As for the sequence of worship:
Then, in the proper place, one should draw a triangle and a circle outside it; outside that, a square—and there, in that field, one should perform worship.
With such words as "Come here," he should again place the offering vessel, filled with water and other substances, in front of the triangle.
A buffalo should be offered there by the Vāmis, likewise a ram by the Kaulikas,
and a sheep by the Siddhāntins, with this mantra.
With the mantra "Ehyehi" [one should invoke]; however, in the Vīracūḍāmaṇi, it is as follows:
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the sages, meters, and so forth, one should offer oblations (*bali*) to the deities of the directions.
One should write the word "Bhairava" followed by "Asitāṅga," ending with the feminine suffix *ṅī* (i.e., *Asitāṅgī*). Then one should write the word "Brāhmī."
"Accept the offering" (*valiṃ gṛhṇa*), followed by "divide into two" (*dvidhā kuryāt*), ending with *svāhā* (*dviṭha*); this is the mantra for the offerings to the directions.
[The lords of the directions are] Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, and Unmattabhairava.
Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra are the eight Bhairavas;
then Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī.
Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, and Cāṇḍā follow immediately after;
Mahālakṣmī is likewise proclaimed, according to the sequence beginning with their respective seed-syllables (bīja).
Having worshipped with incense and lamps, afterwards...
Having first uttered the Praṇava, [one should utter] Māyā, Lakṣmī, and Manmatha;
then, having uttered the word "Indrāṇyai," [one should utter] the word "Cāmuṇḍe" thereafter.
The word "vicce" is for Pañcānna; then the mantra again for Nairṛtī, Vāruṇī, Vāyavī, Kauverī, Īśānī, and Bhairavī.
Having first uttered the mantra, one should again address the Goddess, O Dear One;
one should offer the bali-oblation in due order, presenting the bali in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Having first extracted the Praṇava, one should extract the seed-syllable Hṛllekhā;
thereafter, the word "Vaṭukāya" and "Āpaduddharaṇāya."
Having recited the two *kuru*s, one should extract the word ending in *māṃ* [i.e., *māṃsāntara*].
The mantra, joined with the wife of fire (*svāhā*), should offer the oblation (*bali*) to Vaṭuka.
Having offered the bali-oblation in the southeast, [one should worship] Māyā, Lakṣmī, and Manmatha;
having extracted the seed-syllable Vāhāhī, one should again [place] the seed-syllable Pañcāntaka.
The word *gaṇapataye* comes first, followed by *varada-varada*;
then one should say *sarvajanaṃ*, and likewise say *vaśamānaya me*.
One should first offer the wives of the fire-gods, and then the great mantra of the Gaṇas.
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Vārāhī, *glauṃ*, which is the fierce one consisting of three qualities (*triguṇa*), one should likewise extract Nārāyaṇa.

Having extracted the Lord of the Seed and the Subtle (vījasūkṣmeśa), one should extract the seed-syllable of Amareśa; then [one should extract] Kṣetrapāla ending in the dative case, followed by "gṛhṇa" twice.
The mantra of Kṣetrapāla is proclaimed as being joined with the wife of Vahni (the fire-seed).
Having written the seed-syllable of Vāyu three times, [one should place] Ananta and likewise Mādhava.
Then, having taken [the offering] from Vattulākṣī and likewise from the Yoginīs,
the mantra joined with the wife of Fire (svāhā) is the bali-offering for the Yoginī in the northwest.

The letter *kṣa* is Raudra; *āṃ* is Nārāyaṇa repeated three times (triguṇaṃ trivāraṃ); *iṃ* is Sūkṣmeśa; *uṃ* is Amareśa; the letter *ya* is Vāyu-bīja; *ā* is Ananta; *i* is Mādhava; and *u* is Vartulākṣī.
One should extract the syllable *kṣa* mounted upon the letter *ka*, and at its end the fiery syllable (*ra*),
for the removal of all obstacles from all beings.
Having extracted "bhyo varma phaṭ," one should then cause the offering to be accepted;
ending with "svāhā" (dviṭha), this is declared to be the bestower of success, and with it one should offer the bali-oblation to all beings.
A maker of garlands, a maker of mādrī-fruit—by him [is offered] what? Rice, milk-rice, milk, as well as fish and meat.
Modaka, pūlikā, pūpa, and vaṭaka; three kinds of liquor;
savory boiled rice; cooked foods; clarified butter; and honey with sugar.
One should perform everything everywhere according to the prescribed rules; one should not engage in quarrels during the Durgā festival.
In the Merutantra and the Yamala.
Having taken recourse to the center of the field, one should examine the tortoise-diagram (kūrmacakra);
for one who understands the tortoise-diagram, great obstacles arise.
In the *Sārasaṃgraha*:
That [karma] exists in the world in four ways, and its varieties are described accordingly:
first is the supreme (para), then that which we perform, and likewise that which pertains to a specific region (deśagata).
It is established as fourfold: in a village, in a cow-pen, in a house, and on the road.
In the Merutantra:
The tortoise is of four types, distinguished by its foreign lands, villages, and houses.
In the King of Tantras:
In the Deśakūrma, there are the consonants; likewise, in the Guhakūrma, there are the vowels.
In the Grāmakūrma, there is that pair [of both]; in the Parakūrma, there is that same pair.
In the Merutantra:
One should not contemplate the abode of Kūrma at Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, Mahākāla, or Kāśī.
It is stated thus even in the Devīyāmala.
In the Gautamīya [Vinaya].
If one performs the *puraścaryā* on a mountain, by the bank of a river, in a sacred forest, or on the shore of a stream,
one need not worry about the tortoise there.
A person should divide a country, a village, or even a house into nine parts.
In the Merutantra:
One should construct two squares divided into nine compartments;
the seven consonant groups beginning with *ka* are to be written in the directions starting from the east, and the two *lakṣakas* (vowels) are placed in the remaining spaces.
In the northeast, one should draw two by two [syllables] within the central circular square;
the vowels are to be written starting from the east, and the seed-syllable of Śrī (Śrīṃ) is to be placed in the central square.
The tortoise facing the east is always produced as the outermost shell;
it is situated in that direction which corresponds to the name of the region and so forth.
230a) In that direction, there should be the face of the village-tortoise; however,
it should be understood that there are two faces, namely, from the vowels and likewise from the consonants.
If the face of the house-tortoise were the door,
then its two forelimbs would be on either side of the face, and its belly and feet would be here and there [in the interior].
It has one tail, one middle, and six backs; it possesses six limbs.
Success in all matters occurs when it is in the mouth, while minor successes occur when it is in the two hands.
If it is on the hips, there is no servitude; if it is on the feet or the tail, death occurs.
In the Gautamīya [Vinaya].
In the belly there is constant fruitlessness; in the feet, no accomplishments at all; in the tail, death is certain; and on the back, the accomplishment of all goals.
Therefore, having understood that thoroughly, one should perform all [rites], such as recitation and the like.
In the Siddheśvarī Tantra.
Therefore, one should undertake every task by relying on the *mukha* (mouth-position);
if that is unavailable, one may also rely on the *kūrma-sthāna* (tortoise-position) using the *kara* (hand-position).
O you who arise in the dark [fortnight]!
Wherever the solar nature of the names of both the site and the practitioner is found,
one should identify those respective sites through the teachings of Dakṣa and abandon them.
In the Gautamiya [Vinaya].
If even friendliness arises through a single syllable of the mantra or by means of the name of the illuminator,
why then would the practitioner not achieve success by means of his own name?
The lords of the field (kṣetrapālas), whose forms are universal, exist in the form of fifty phonemes;
therefore, that field is endowed with qualities for the sake of spiritual accomplishment, and not otherwise.
If it is defective, even for one facing eastward, you will not attain success;
therefore, having thus examined the wheel, [one should know that] a friend indeed bestows all accomplishments.
In whatever region the Lord of Lamps named Saguṇa resides through the two mantras, one should go there with effort; that is considered a rare sacred seat (pīṭha).
In the Merutantra:
If even a single initial syllable among the field-accomplishing mantras is present,
that mantra will certainly bestow the fruit of all accomplishments.
Likewise.
In great enmity there is loss of life; in enmity there is loss of wealth;
even in minor enmity there is a diminution of happiness—this is now being declared.
Agau, ṛṭhau, paujaṣau, paṣaujaṭhau, ivau, ūtau,
phadhau, bharau, and yasau are proclaimed as the Mahārīs.
Likewise, ṛcchau, odayaṣau, taṭaurikhau, budhauḍhalau, and so forth.
In this context, both the short and long vowels are to be understood.
In the fifth group, O dear one, there may be some degree of enmity between *ca* and *ṭa*,
as well as between *ya* and *cha*, *ta* and *ṭa*, and also *ḍha* and *śa*.
When there is affection for one's own group within a single class, double that [value] for one's own group;
add the square of the position and divide by eight— these are called the *cāpas*.
The square of the place is doubled; the square of itself is divided by eight and the remainder taken.
Whichever of the two has a remainder when their positions are subtracted from one another, that planet remains as the giver of wealth;
the other is the seeker of wealth and shall not bestow it.
In another tantra:
Having thus understood this sequence, O Śivā, the wise one should abandon the position of the enemy;
for it is the very first syllable of the mantras used for the accomplishment of the field.
If that [mantra] should exist, it will certainly bestow the fruit of all accomplishments;
if its enmity is ascertained, one should purify it starting from the second syllable.
Having thus occupied the place, the mantra-practitioner should offer the bali-oblation there.
In the Gautamīya [Vinaya].
One should draw the Lord of Lamps in the center, worship him, and meditate upon him.
In the Merutantra:
One should worship Amṛta, Vṛṣabha, Śailarajas, and Vāsuki, as well as Artha, Kṛt, and Śaktikṛt, with offerings at the eastern direction and so forth, by means of one's strength.

The middle [type of practitioner] should perform his recitation as a householder, having constructed a dwelling upon the back of a tortoise, using a lotus-origined [stone], a great conch, and also one called "Shadow."
In the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*.
Or, having taken recourse to its front, one should construct a hut for the performance of penance,
four cubits in length and square, with a well-made altar raised one cubit high.
Adorned with moon-shaped ornaments, banners of penance,
and arches, it was secluded, beautifully plastered, and surrounded by a wall.
Having performed the rite of emanation, one should then observe a single meal on an auspicious day;
having bathed in the morning, one who is self-restrained should then recite the Gāyatrī ten thousand times.
First, for the sake of destroying both known and unknown sin, [one should perform the following] thereafter.
Many maintain that the Gāyatrī is Vedic.
One's own deity is Gāyatrī; may she know this truth of ours.
In the *Tārāpradīpa*:
Having constructed a pavilion according to the rules that is pleasing to the eye,
the learned man should place a water-pot upon it and worship it with the waters of sacred fords.
Having cast the nine gems and again the eight fragrances there,
he should invoke and worship the Goddess together with [the deities] therein.
One should recite the mantra over the mouth of the jar until the prescribed number is completed;
then, having arrived when it is complete, the Guru and the deity [should be worshipped] according to the ritual injunctions.
One should consecrate the disciple on the head with the water from the vessel and its petals;
thereafter, the disciple should diligently gratify the guru with the best of his wealth.
231a) Sanatkumāra.
Now I shall describe the supreme preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) of the mantra:
having performed the ritual ablution according to the rules and having received the mantra from the mouth of a guru.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rule at an auspicious moment, on a favorable lunar day, and in a sacred field,
he should diligently gratify the Brahmins with food, clothing, and other offerings.
Having gratified his own guru with land, wealth, clothing, ornaments, and other gifts,
he should thereafter commence the recitation (japa) following the guru’s permission.
In the Agastyasaṃhitā:
Whether eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), vegetables, or even barley-gruel; or milk, roots, or fruit—whatever is available at whatever place.
During a vow, one should avoid tamarind, nālikā greens, peas, as well as nikuntaka,
kadamba, coconut, and pumpkin.
If one recites [the mantra] while possessing soiled garments, disheveled hair, and foul breath,
the deity abiding in the secret [mantra] quickly consumes that person.
One should avoid laziness, yawning, sleep, drowsiness, spitting, fear,
contact with low persons, and anger during the time of recitation.
In another tantra:
Sleeping on the ground, observing celibacy, and eating only at night, one should recite the mantra.
In the Kulārṇava:
Whatever action one performs apart from the prescribed rules (niyama),
not even the slightest fruit thereof is accomplished due to the fault of violating the proper sequence.
Deficient rites never bear fruit;
indeed, virtuous deeds performed here according to the prescribed rules do bear fruit.
The ritual action performed according to that injunction— such as recitation, fire-offerings, and worship—
shall be pleasing to the deity and bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In this regard, sexual intercourse with one's own wife during her fertile period is not prohibited.
"A practitioner of mantras should not touch even his own wife except during her fertile period," according to the statement of Gautama.
In the Merutantra:
If one's own wife has been embraced through negligence, then as a penance for that fault,
having bathed while still wearing wet clothes and remaining silent, one should [offer] water measured by ten jars.
One should give a thousand supreme noble women in the house of a learned Vedic scholar.
And the recitation (japa) must be performed after having formed a formal resolve (saṃkalpa).
This has been stated by the Pot-born Sage (Agastya):
Then, having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for ten thousand [repetitions].
But it is volition.
In the Merutantra:
Having performed the *puṇyāhavācana* rite, one with *kuśa* grass in hand should say:
"May Sūrya, Soma, Yama, Kāla, the two twilights, and all beings protect me."
May the wind, water, fire, earth, space, the sky-dwellers, and the immortals,
having established the command of Brahmā, remain present here for the fulfillment of this rite.
Having recited this and placed *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, and unbroken rice grains into a copper vessel,
one should perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the year and other periods, beginning with "May it rise" (*udastu*) and "May it be well" (*svastu*).
There, one should utter twenty repetitions for each of the following:
a year, a month, a fortnight, and the five limbs [of the mantra].

One should state the positions of the nine planets according to the day, the asterism, and the muhūrta; these should be declared as equal [to the standard] yet modified by the specific requirements of one's own locality.
In such-and-such an island, in such-and-such a region, in such-and-such a district, and in such-and-such a settlement; in such-and-such a field, one should utter the lineage and the *pravara*.

One who desires the accomplishment of a mantra should [use] one's own name, the name of one's caste, and at the end of the name, the suffixes *śarman* for a twice-born (*dvija*), *varman*, *gupta*, or *dāsa*, followed by "of so-and-so" (*amukasya*).
"Starting from today, provided there is no obstacle, I shall perform this *puraścaryā* consisting of recitations of this specific number within these many days."
One should form the resolution "I shall do" by means of the mind alone;
one should express the desire with speech, and one should accomplish it through action.
One should perform the worship of the Guru, Gaṇapati, Durgā, the Mothers, and the Tattvas.
In the Sanatkumārasaṃhitā, however, the *saṃkalpa* (ritual resolve) is stated differently.
And the *puraścaraṇa* rite for Caṇḍikā.
Having performed worship in this manner, one should perform the recitation; one should not recite the mantra alone.
In the Nārada Pañcarātra.
Having performed worship, one should then perform the recitation for two praharas.
In the Tantra.
One should worship the deity at the three junctions of the day, or twice, or once, according to the prescribed rule.
In another tantra:
Either worship may take place once, but one should not perform recitation without worship;
there should be worship at the end of the recitation, or one should recite the mantra at the end of the worship.
In the Muṇḍamālā [Tantra]:
O beautiful one, if one is unable to perform worship due to a lack of materials,
the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) is prescribed to be accomplished by means of recitation alone.
But in the Yāmala:
The specific rule regarding women has been stated.
The observance should be known to apply to the man, never to the woman.
Also in the Vīra-tantra:
In this case, there is no ritual depositing (nyāsa) for women, nor meditation, nor worship;
the mantras of women are perfected through mere recitation alone.
Now follows the procedure for recitation (japa).
In the Gautamīya Tantra.
Mantras existing in the state of the individual soul (paśu), consisting solely of the form of phonemes,
attain their sovereign power when uttered in their respective sounds.
One should contemplate the syllables of the mantra as strung upon the thread of consciousness within that very [space],
in the restraint (*yama*) known as supreme nectar in the sky.
One should manifest one's own true being even without worship, fire-offerings, and the like.
In the Kulārṇava:
If a birth-impurity (sūtaka) is known at the beginning, it should be treated as death-impurity (mṛta-sūtaka) within the mantra;
a mantra joined with both types of impurity does not succeed.
O Supreme Goddess, having bestowed the seed-syllable of Brahmā upon the mind at the beginning and end [of the rite],
one should recite the mantra seven times for liberation from the two types of birth-impurity.
Having thus performed the recitation previously, one should offer the form of light into the right hand of the deity with perfumes, flowers, and water for the arghya offering.
Having realized that it is fruitful, one should perform *prāṇāyāma*;
one should perform three [cycles] at the end of the recitation (*japa*) and three at the beginning of the recitation.
In the Rudrayāmala.
However, the recitation of a mantra during the time of sleep does not bestow fruit;
the time of sleep is the flow of the left (nādī), while wakefulness is the flow of the right.
In another tantra:
One may recite a hymn with the mind or mutter a mantra with the voice;
both become fruitless, like water poured into a broken vessel.
In the Rudrayāmala.
That mantra which another hears while one is reciting it is said to be void;
it is like a serpent deprived of its seer, meter, and deity.

One should not speak with women or Śūdras at night, nor should one devoted to *japa* do so. One should not perform *japa* during the time of the two twilights (*saṃdhyā*), nor when it is dark, nor when one is ill.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Whatever recitation, fire-offering, or gift is performed with a dry cloth when in water, or with a wet cloth when on land,
all of that becomes fruitless.
In the Merutantra.
One should abandon twenty actions that cause obstacles to success,
and one should perform twenty actions that bring about the perfection of recitation.
Greed, anger, stinginess, lust, hatred, and physical assault;
hypocrisy, sorcery, anointing [for magic], and likewise false speech that is pleasing.
Singing and instrumental music, the sweet shade of the *vibhītaka* and *karañja* trees, meat, accepting gifts, garlands, betel, and sinful speech.
A wise person should avoid these; now hear from me what must be performed:
the restraint of the mind, reflection on the meaning of the mantras, and the daily obligatory rites.
Purification based on specific causes, silence, sweeping the dwelling, self-restraint, sleeping on the ground, bathing three times a day, and constant devotion to the worship of the Lord.
Constant giving of alms, worship of the Guru’s feet, restraint in food,
bathing with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and wearing the sacred thread.
Performing obeisance at the three junctions of the day, the five sacrifices, the fourfold libations,
and wearing clothing as prescribed— this is now declared to be the expiation.
When a sound is uttered once, one should recite the *praṇava*;
even when the word "go" (*sara*) is reached, one should perform a single breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*).
In the event of much idle chatter, one must certainly place the limbs [of the mantra] and then perform the recitation;
likewise in the case of hunger, after touching [the body], and also upon touching various locations.
Upon breaking the vow of silence, one should mutter a mantra or meditate upon Hari;
one should avoid looking at those who have fallen from their status, but should gaze upon a radiant person.
The sun, fire, the moon, Venus, the sages, the lunar mansions,
the stars, the learned, cows, and Brahmins— [if one insults these], one is deprived of splendor at every step.

In the event of sneezing, while walking, upon falling down or similar occurrences, or when speaking, one should cease the recitation; likewise, having sipped water (ācamana), one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) along with the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga).
Having performed [the ritual], one should subsequently recite the mantra; in the event of yawning, one should utter the name of Viṣṇu.
[One should likewise avoid seeing] a cat, a cock, a curlew, a dog, a vulture, a donkey, and a monkey.
Having seen [an impurity] at Campā, one should perform the ritual action; having touched it, bathing is prescribed.
If one has spoken untruths due to fate, one should recite the *pauruṣa* hymn along with the *saraha*.
Whether wearing many garments or only one, with hair loose or covering the neck,
wearing a turban or a bodice, naked or even with the head wrapped;
One who is agitated by anxiety, or is angry, deluded, or overcome by hunger;
or one whose feet are covered by sandals, or likewise one who has gone on a journey after drinking wine.
One who is angry, or has unwashed feet, or faces the west;
likewise one wearing soiled garments, or with the upper garment tucked up, or whose garment is doubled over.
One with disarrayed garments, one with red garments, one with glossy garments,
one with the upper garment tucked up, one with the outer garment tucked out, one without an upper garment, one with the lower garment untucked, and one with only a single tuck.
If one who wears a loincloth, has swollen feet,
or wears sewn-together garments becomes intent on recitation due to negligence, he is seized by Rākṣasas and receives [only] the fruit [of that state].
In the Rudrayāmala:
O Dear One, one should perform the recitation endowed with faith, conviction, compassion, devotion, self-restraint, resolve, contentment, and other such virtues of pure dharma.
Excessive eating, travel abroad, idle chatter, lack of restraint in observances, attachment to people, and fickleness— by these six, the mantra is not accomplished.
In the Kulārṇava:

For those desiring spiritual accomplishments (siddhi), mental recitation is prescribed; for those desiring nourishment (puṣṭi), whispered recitation; and for killing (māraṇa) as well as for praise, vocal recitation is declared to be recommended.
Whether one is impure or pure, whether walking or sleeping,
there is no fault in mental recitation (japa) at all times and in all places.
In the Uttaratantra and the Merutantra.
At the beginning of the recitation (japa) and other rites, one should carefully worship the rosary by sprinkling it with water;
having placed it within the mandala, it should be held in the left hand.
The sprinkling of the rosary with the chosen mantra is thus proclaimed.
Oṃ māle māle; having worshipped it as before, one should then take the rosary in the right hand.
Thereafter, one should perform the recitation (japa), remaining established in meditation as before;
having meditated upon the Guru at the crown of the head according to his color and other attributes.
One should meditate on the mantra in the middle of the throat as yellow-colored and golden;
one should meditate on Mahāmāyā in the heart and on one’s own self at the feet of the Guru.
Thereafter, having brought about the oneness of the guru, the mantra, oneself, and the goddess within the *ājñācakra*, one then proceeds by way of the *suṣumnā*.
That single reality is its own essential nature; one should traverse the six cakras, having meditated with effort for a moment upon Mahāmāyā within those six cakras.
One should worship the first sixteen wheels with the root mantra;
she who resides in the first sixteen wheels bestows [attainments] upon practitioners.
The practitioner, alone, should meditate on the Goddess and begin the rite of recitation;
it is said that at dawn, one should [visualize] the three maṇḍalas above the eyebrows.
The region at its edge is a triangular place, six-cornered and four finger-breadths in size;
it is red and is called the Ājñā-cakra by those who know the yoga of the Vakula tree.
In the throats of men, there is an encircling of three channels—
Suṣumnā, Iḍā, and Piṅgalā— that forms a hexagon measuring six finger-breadths.
That is declared to be the six-chakra [system], white in color, situated in the middle of the throat.
The sixteen-chakra system is liberated right there; and at the heart, the unity of all three channels occurs.
That locus should be sixteen-spoked and measure seven finger-breadths;
it is said to be yellow, belonging to the first of the yogas, and situated within the sixteen wheels.
In the Merutantra:
Having reflected thus, one should place the garland in the middle portion of the center.
In the Uttaratantra and also in the Merutantra:
Holding the garland together with his own heart by means of his right hand.
The word "should recite" (japet) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
In the Merutantra, a Shaiva Agama.
One should touch the garland with the index finger and move it with the tip of the thumb;
while reciting the previous mantra, one should then touch the other jewel.
If he uses his thumb [to count], that recitation is always fruitless for him.
Thus has been stated the characteristic of the number [of recitations] for the perpetual japa.
The goddess should contemplate the mantra to be recited and touch [the object] with her left hand.
In the Merutantra and the Mahākapila-pañcarātra.
With a single-minded focus and a serene soul, the performer of the rite should be pure;
holding the dice-stick upright with his neck raised, he should remain calm, free from itching or blinking.
The wise one should recite the mantra in sequence: clearly with the visarga, with the long vowel (mātrā), with the bindu, and with the syllable; neither as mere sound nor without rest.
In the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā.
Contemplating with his intellect the identity of the deity, the guru, and the mantra,
he should recite it with a one-pointed mind from the morning until midday.
Whatever has been undertaken according to a specific number must be performed day and night;
if one performs it less or more than that, one becomes fallen from the vow.
In the Muṇḍamālā [Tantra]:
The time for recitation is proclaimed to extend from morning until midday;
one should perform the recitation day after day neither deficient nor excessive.
The rule of uninterrupted practice has been declared; one must not cross over [the day]. If a day is passed, an obstruction to the accomplishment of men arises.
Having recited the mantra, one should consume food and drink; likewise, bathing and mental sustenance [are performed].
The phrase "at dawn" and so forth refers to the period during the day until its completion.
The Moonlight of Puraścaraṇa.
Having meditated upon the form of one's chosen deity, one should recite the mantra while identifying oneself with it;
when the count is complete, one should again perform the visualization and other practices, as well as breath control (prāṇāyāma).

Regarding "completion of the count" (*saṃkhyāpūtau*), it refers to the completion of the daily count; "ṛṣyādi" indicates the intention of performing the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seers and so forth.
In the Merutantra:
Having recited one hundred and eight times at the end of the *japa*, one should place it upon the head.
"Garland," it is said.
The mantra of the rosary is prescribed for the acts of grasping, fixing, and worship;
thereafter, one should pray to one's chosen deity using the five-syllabled mantra.
"Guhyātīti" means "from the secret."
Having recited the root mantra, one should offer it into the hand of the deity;
at the time of midday, one should likewise offer that recitation with the water of the arghya.
Thereafter, having bathed as before, the one who knows the ritual procedure should perform the entire rite previously mentioned, including the specific placement of mantras (nyāsa).
In the Siddhāntasāra:

Having performed the recitation (japa) in this manner, the mantra-practitioner should offer oblations (homa) with blue lotuses smeared with clarified butter (ājya) amounting to one-tenth of the recitation, and should satisfy [the deity] with one-tenth of that amount.
With pure perfumed waters mixed with liquid *kālāguru*.
In the Meru Tantra.
Then, from the worship up to the fire-oblation (homa), he should begin the recitation (japa) until the end of the day; thereafter, the twice-born man, having bathed again, [should proceed].
Having performed the twilight worship as before, one should again worship the deity.
As stated in another tantra:
Upon completing the count, one should perform [the rite] with one's own substances according to a tenth part of the number of recitations.
As it has been taught, one should offer oblations into the fire-pit while remaining concentrated upon the calves.
Alternatively, having recited [the mantra] every day, one should perform oblations amounting to one-tenth of that number;
then, with one-tenth of the oblations, one should worship the deity in the water.
One should perform the libations and other rites.
In the Merutantra:
Having finished his meal, he should constantly perform [the twilight worship] at the rising of the stars.

The meaning is that after performing the daily duties at the end of the *puraścaraṇa* and following the salutation during the twilight (*saṃdhyā*) worship, one should dismiss [the deity] with the word "visṛja" (be dismissed).
Likewise.

One who eats the fruits and roots of the six medicinal plants, one who subsists on pure alms, one who eats sacrificial oblations (haviṣya), or one who observes the milk-vow—these are the best; their characteristics are now described.
Āruṣkara, ratnamūla, piṇḍāru, kaseruka,
raktahastī, śaṅkha, and madhusāruka are said to be the most excellent.
Grapes, mango, rose-apple, jackfruit, wood-apple, date-palm, pomegranate, and coconut;
Parūṣaka, kṣīriṇī, aratnī, uduṃbara, dhātrī, and āru are purifying.
Śatrumūla, Tvacāmūla, Vimala, Pañcamījaṭā,
Akavāku, and Kuvāku— these six roots bring about purification.
For those who are endowed with Vedic conduct, pure, prosperous, and virtuous;
born in a noble family and station; and for the twice-born who subsist on alms—
Barley-gruel, roots, fruits, milk, curd, alms-food,
and roasted flour— these seven kinds of food obtained through begging are to be consumed by those established in their vows.

The sacrificial offerings (haviṣya) consist of fifty varieties: white rice, unhusked rice, and rice grown from snow; also sixty-day ripening rice (ṣaṣṭika), and three types of each of the three kinds of grains.
Black sesame, *kalāya*, and *tripuṭa* beans, as well as *kaṅgu*,
*makuṣṭha*, *pāvamāna*, and *kanaṃśikā*— these are for the head.
Kāraka, śocavāstūka, kara, vūrhila,
mocikā, cakravartin, cakramarda, palaṅka, and śatapuṣpikā.
The root of *hemantaja*, white *rājakalmāṣaka*, sesame, lotus stalk,
*muśalī*, *dyoṭā*, *śatamūlī*, and *vidārī*.
Sarvapiṇḍālu destroys worms and diseases; vārāhī, kaseruka, āruṣkara, kañcuka, kelūṭa, and māṇavāruka [are likewise beneficial].
Sea salt, rock salt, cow's curd and ghee, the milk of cows, goats, and buffaloes,
sugarcane juice, sweet fruit, and grains with few seeds [are pure].
Having abandoned the jackfruit, mango, myrobalan, tamarind, and the unripe fruit, as well as molasses, sugarcane products, and all future or leftover food, one should avoid fish, liquor, and meat.
Cow’s milk is said to be the best; that produced by the Surabhi cow is middling;
buffalo milk is the lowest; and all other types are prohibited for those observing a vow.
That which abandons forbidden food and follows the scriptures in all respects is considered middling; that which avoids forbidden places and families but accepts what is praised is known as inferior.
Now, the fifty prohibited items are being described:
white mung beans, liquor, kodrava grain, and three kinds of chickpeas.
Black gram, soil-salt, leaf-vegetables, various juices, honey, alkali, capala, garlic, and eating from a bronze vessel;
Meat that has been boiled, salt, māḍhakī-cāra,
mālaka, stale food, oil, betel-leaf, and minor grains.
Also the patola, the vṛntāka, the radish, and the kaliñjaka;
burnt food, and cooked food, and sprouted grains from the heap.
Upodikā, garlic, onions, molasses, jaggery, tuṇḍī, eggplant, pumpkin, gojihvā, and gaḍuvida;
Mushrooms, small dates, madhuka, the fruit of the palmyra palm,
tūṇḍa, kukkuṭapādā, bamboo shoots, and the cirbhiṭa;
One should listen to the specific deities according to the distinctions of caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama), namely: Rājakośāta, Āmrāta, Vaṃdhyā, and Karkoṭakī.
Sesame oil purified by mantras is sanctifying and difficult even for the gods to obtain;
having rubbed it on his body, a householder should indeed always perform his bath.
The twice-born should perform the meal by first spreading the base layer (upastīrya) and then pouring the clarified butter (abhiṣārya);
they should cook with Vedic mantras and through rites such as sprinkling (prokṣaṇa).
Having consecrated it again with the root mantra, one should eat while reciting the heart-mantra;
when thirsty during the meal, one should drink water consecrated with the root mantra.
One should eat from a palāśa leaf, avoiding the middle leaf;
in its absence, one may use a leaf from the kadalī, madhūka, or sarjaka tree.
Having eaten, he should lie down on a very clean bed upon the surface of the earth,
or on a pure bed of darbha grass spread over an unwashed covering.
Having consecrated [the bed] with the root mantra, with anger conquered and the senses subdued,
and meditating upon his chosen deity, he should sleep at night with his head toward the east.
Having risen at midnight and performed the purification of the feet,
and having sipped water (ācamana) and recollected the Lord, one should quickly perform worship as before.
One should perform the recitation according to one's capacity and likewise offer it to the Lord;
thereafter, one should sleep and report whatever dream was seen to the guru.
This recitation is prescribed for those dwelling in the forest and for those practicing celibacy.
Thus ends the daily practice up to the conclusion of the recitation.
235a) Thereafter, the fire oblation and so forth.
In the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*.
Then, one should perform the fire offering (homa) every day with a tenth part of the number of recitations;
or alternatively, one should perform the fire offering when the count reaches one hundred thousand.
The separate mention of "two full lakṣas" refers to that which is intended for the *Siddhasārasvata*, where the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of many lakṣas.

Having performed the recitation in this manner, the mantra-practitioner should offer oblations with blue lotuses and *akoḍa* flowers amounting to one-tenth of that number, and should satisfy [the deity] with one-tenth of that portion.
In the *Sārasaṃgraha*:
Then, having worshipped the deity in water with a tenth part of the oblations (homa),
one should offer libations upon the head with water, reciting "I satisfy" at the end of the mantra.
Then follows the sprinkling.
For thus says Vaiśampāyana:
Reciting the mantra ending with "namaḥ" and using one-tenth of the quantity used for the libation (tarpaṇa),
one should sprinkle one's own head with water by means of the mudrā known as the "water-pot" (kumbha).
In this context, they join [the mantra] with "I consecrate so-and-so upon the head"; the *kumbha-mudrā* has been explained specifically in the section on the daily bath (*nityasnāna*).
In the Vīracūḍāmaṇi.
At the conclusion of the libation, the great mantra-practitioner should perform the consecration;
he should draw a lotus petal on ground smeared with cow dung.
One should place a water-pot there and worship the Kalā (the digit) with fragrant substances, durvā grass sprouts, or with aśoka flowers and mango shoots.
Having honored [the deity] with offerings such as perfumes and flowers, one should worship thoroughly;
having uttered the Mātṛkā-mantra, one should recite each individual mantra.
One should sprinkle water upon the head while reciting the words, "I consecrate you."
Then, with a tenth part of the materials used for the purification, one should feed the devotees of one's chosen deity and the Kaulikas using the aforementioned substances.
In the Tantra.
For Brahmins who are unable to perform the fire sacrifice and other rites, the recitation (japa) shall be double;
for the other castes, however, it shall be three, four, or five times that number.
The doubling [of the number of oblations] and so forth occurs solely through the observation of the [required] reduction in the fire-oblations and other rites.
To Sanatkumāri.
If any limb [of the body] should become broken, the recitation (japa) shall be double that number;
in the absence of fire-offerings (homa), the recitation should be performed at four times the number of the homas.
The number of qualities for Brahmins and Kṣatriyas is traditionally held to be equal;
for Vaiśyas it is eightfold, and this is the rule for these women.
Whatever caste a Śūdra has taken refuge in, he should follow the prescribed rules for that [caste].
In the Agastya-saṃhitā:
If one is capable of performing the fire-oblation (homa), or the worship, or the libation (tarpaṇa),
then [the same result is achieved] by reciting the mantra that many times and by propitiating Brahmins.
O dear one, in this case, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is indeed accomplished by means of these two alone.
Elsewhere as well.
In every way, the wise man should feed [the brahmins] for the sake of accomplishing the ritual with all its constituent parts;
by the mere propitiation of the brahmins, the rite shall always be complete in its components.
In the Merutantra:
Now I shall explain how the accomplishment of mantras may come about for a poor person;
for a Brahmin who is unable to perform the rite of fire-offerings (homa), the recitation (japa) must be twofold.
For the other castes, however, a threefold [increase] and so forth is prescribed;
through twice as many recitations as the number of oblations, the libation becomes complete.
It is said that if the ritual cleansing (mārjana) has not been performed, the recitation (japa) must be doubled for the libation (tarpaṇa).
I have heard from someone that in some cases, the substitution (pratyāmnāya) is the feeding of Brahmins.
In every way, one should feed the Brahmins for the sake of accomplishing the integrity of the rite;
by the mere propitiation of the Brahmins, that which was incomplete becomes complete.
Whatever deeds [are intended] are also lost through the feeding of unworthy twice-born;
they become as useless as seeds sown in barren soil.

In this context, for women and Śūdras, there is only the recitation (japa) as prescribed in place of the fire-oblation (homa); even if they possess the capacity [to perform it], no oblation is to be offered.
For there is a scriptural injunction stating that offerings should not be made preceded by the recitation of mantras by women or Śūdras.
But in the Vārāhītantra, however:
The right to perform the tantric fire-sacrifice (homakarma) belongs to the twice-born;
however, if one is desirous of attaining specific results, even a Śūdra may perform the fire-sacrifice.
Having omitted the wife of Vahni (Svāhā) at the end of "svāhā," it is stated that one should say "namo namaḥ."
In the Tantra.
The recitation (japa) which has been prescribed by the wise for the twice-born in the absence of fire-oblations (homa),
that indeed applies to women with beautiful brows, to their devotees, and to Śūdras as well.
In general, however, the fivefold nature of Śūdras has already been stated.
In the *Puraścaraṇacandrikā*.
Having thus duly performed the preliminary rite (puraścaryā), the most excellent of practitioners should,
at its conclusion, perform a great worship and feed the Brahmins.
One should honor one's own guru with many garments and ornaments;
by satisfying the poor and the helpless, the mantras of practitioners attain success.
In the Merutantra:
Thereafter, one should satisfy the guru with cows, gold, boons, and other gifts;
for when the guru is pleased, the mantra becomes satisfied and is mastered by the practitioner.
In the determination of the ancillaries of the fire-oblation (homa).
Through recitation, fire-offerings, and worship, the mantras grant him success;
it is taught that even by a threefold recitation, the mantras bestow accomplishment.
In the Rudrayāmala and in the Kulamūlāvatāra.
O Goddess, without food, without libations,
and even without fire-offerings, one should recite the mantra three times over for the sake of success.
Regarding obstacles such as those arising from place and so forth during the commencement of *puraścaraṇa*, it is stated otherwise in the *Merutantra*:

If completion must be performed with haste due to fear of calamities such as those arising from one's country, this [method] is declared to be suitable; it is also prescribed for the purpose of subjugation (*vaśyaka*).
Recitation until midday is excellent; for three watches it is middling;
and for three and a half watches it is inferior—these are the characteristics declared for one who has unavoidable duties.
The fivefold method has been proclaimed as that which brings the recitation (japa) to completion;
one should perform the recitation daily according to the Ādya-kalpa until midday.
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with substances prescribed for the Kalpa using one-tenth of that amount;
likewise, having performed the libation (tarpaṇa), the ritual sprinkling (mārjana), and the feeding of Brahmins.
The first ritual procedure (kalpa) is said to require one-tenth of that [number] for its completion;
this second ritual procedure, however, requires one hundred thousand recitations (japa).
Having performed the fire-oblation and other rites for him, one should commence this hundred-thousand-fold recitation;
this is the third method, wherein one should perform the recitation in its entirety.
When the homa is complete, one should first perform the libation (tarpaṇa) as before; such is the fourth ritual method. For those who are poor, the recitation (japa) should be double.
In the absence of fire-offerings and the like, one should perform [the rite] multiplied by three and so forth, divided by eight and so forth;
the fifth method is likewise that which is dear to whichever deity it may be.
That very [number] should be doubled quickly for the satisfaction of the deity;
recitation is dear to all goddesses, while offerings (bali) are dear on the Vāmamārga.

Mahādeva is fond of drink through the Siddhāntas, while Bhāskara is fond of sexual pleasure through the Kaulika doctrines; Mahādeva is fond of fire-oblations, O beloved, and Bhāskara is fond of libations.
The cleansing of Gaṇeśa and the feeding of Brāhmaṇas for Viṣṇu constitute the expiation;
when this has been performed, the twice-born becomes pure.
The Kṣatriyas and other castes [attain success] by means of four, three, or more rounds of preliminary practice (puraścaryā).
Thus ends the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa).
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the Kulamuktikallolinī composed by Śrī Ādyānanda.
Now follows the heroic preparatory rite (vīrapuraścaraṇa).
In that regard, for recitation and other such practices, the time is the deity of night. This has been stated in the Kālāgnitantro:
When the first watch has passed and up until the third watch, one should perform the recitation during the night;
however, one should not recite during the remainder of the night.
And it was previously stated: "Taking up the garland of secrets (*rahasyamālā*), one should recite [the mantra]."
A specific distinction has been stated in both the *Vīracūḍāmaṇi* and the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*.

During the period of *puraścaraṇa*, one who has been initiated should worship the Supreme Power (*paraśakti*) with garments, flowers, and other offerings, as well as with foods consisting of milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Having brought [the offerings] into an empty house and purified them with water for the guest-offering (arghodaka),
and having performed the rite of making them nectar (amṛtīkaraṇa), one should lead the Śaktis forward.
Having brought together the substances and other items required for the worship of Śakti, one should perform the rite of *amṛtīkaraṇa* upon them alone.
Likewise.
Having sprinkled all of them with *arghya* water according to the prescribed ritual,
one should perform the rite of *amṛtīkaraṇa* (the transformation into nectar), and thereafter the rite of *sakalīkaraṇa* (the infusion of the limbs).
Here, after the rite of immortalization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) and so forth, he states the powers (*śakti*) to be worshipped.
In the Kumārītantra:
Now I shall describe the eight maidens who assume the forms of goddesses:
the Brāhmaṇī, the Kṣatriyā, the Vaiśyā, and the Śūdrā, who are the ornaments of their families.
The courtesan, the barber’s daughter, the washerwoman, and likewise the female ascetic—
all these women of auspicious limbs possess extraordinary proficiency.
In the Kārottaratantra:
Beholding the eight maidens' transformation of form and their display of indignation,
they were given names corresponding to the eight Śaktis beginning with Brāhmaṇī.
The forms such as white and black, the quality of gentleness and so forth,
and the names of the Śaktis shall be stated in the hymn that is about to be recited.
He states the manner of worship:
Having first offered a seat, one should again say "Welcome," and then offer water for honoring (arghya),
water for the feet (pādya), drinking water, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and water once more.
One should bathe [the image] with water scented with perfumes and flowers, perform the grooming of the hair,
and having fumigated the hair with incense, one should then offer a silken garment.
Then, after the bath, having spread out a seat and [placed] a pair of sandals;
Having given [these] and seated her there, having adorned her with various ornaments and applied unguents, one should present perfumes and garlands.
Having invoked that respective power, one should bring it down upon their heads;
then, in the middle of the dining pavilion, [one should place it] in a beautiful golden vessel.
Indeed, there are foods to be chewed, sucked, licked, drunk, eaten, and even those to be crunched.
"In the *Kulasarvasva* it is also stated: 'When they may be uninitiated, then one should offer [the victim] to Māyā.
The meaning is that one should invoke that Śakti upon the head of whichever woman is designated by the name 'Tāntām' and worship her."
Or rather, this [rule] regarding the vehicle is stated even in the middle; it ought to apply from the very beginning, since it is seen to be so everywhere.
237a) There, one should then perform the hymn of praise at their left ears:
"O Mother Goddess, salutations to you, who bear the form of Brahman, O Infinite One!"
Out of compassion, remove my obstacles and grant me the perfection of mantra;
O Great Goddess, granter of boons, whose form is supreme bliss!
"Out of compassion," and so forth.
Kaumāri, sovereign over all obstacles, you who are supreme in the playful sports of Kumāra.
"Out of compassion," and so forth.
O Goddess who bears the form of Viṣṇu, you who carry the son of Vinatā!
"Out of compassion," and so forth.
O Vārāhī, O boon-granting goddess, O you who lifted up the earth with your tusk!
"Out of compassion," and so forth.
O Goddess who assumes the form of Śakra, you who are worshipped by the gods beginning with Śakra!
"Out of compassion," and so forth.
O Cāmuṇḍā, adorned with a garland of severed heads and smeared with blood, O destroyer of obstacles!
"Out of compassion," and so forth.
O Mahālakṣmī, who bestows great liberation and destroys agitation and torment!
"Out of compassion," and so forth.
O Goddess, who consists of measure and the measurer, who stands beyond all measures; O Goddess, who are manifold, most extensive, and whose form is the universe—salutations to you!
Whoever, being self-restrained, recites this hymn at the commencement of mantras,
or upon seeing a learned woman, for him no obstacle shall arise.
If they are overcome by shame regarding the meal, they should depart from that house;
meanwhile, one should recite hymns of praise until satisfaction is produced.
Having sipped water for ritual purification, one should offer betel leaf and areca nut.
Likewise.
Then one should offer a garland again, along with auspicious, well-prepared sandalwood paste;
having bid farewell, performed circumambulation, and requested a boon, one shall become happy.
If others do not go, then his own daughter, his younger sister, his elder sister,
his maternal aunt, or his mother— along with her husband— [should go].
A female friend, a female relative, a married woman, or even a widow—
each subsequent one being honored in the absence of the preceding— since women are entitled to a share.
O Kulabhairava, if even a single young woman there is honored or merely looked upon,
then all the goddesses are thereby honored.
And this preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) should be performed at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end; for it is said in that very same [text]:
If one does not especially worship with a full hundred thousand [recitations] at the beginning, the end, and the middle, then one is destroyed by obstacles.
In the Vīracūḍāmaṇi.
Having first purified the site, which should be pleasing to the mind and marked by equal lines,
one should have an altar constructed there and place a *muṇḍa* (skull) in its center.
One should perform the smearing with beeswax and draw an eight-petaled lotus in the center;
one should know that the pairs of vowels are to be written in sequence, starting from the east.
One should write the eight groups [of letters] there, and in the center, one should draw a palace;
likewise, one should place the Sky (ga) joined with a bindu, as well as Lāṅgulīśa.
O beautiful lady, he should then write the Visarga upon the filaments;
having worshipped the support and so forth there, the wise one should establish the seat.
Having sat upon a seat anywhere— even on a mere tuft of grass— the hero should strike with his heel three times and then perform three *śocikā* movements.

The wise one, using the mantra for the weapon that binds the directions, should [place] Pinākīśa— adorned with the *nāda* and *bindu*— in the east and so forth in due order, when the *vakra* is pacified.
Having uttered the word *paśu*, followed by the supreme weapon-mantra ending with *ramā*,
this is the Vidyā known as Pāśupata, which destroys all obstacles.
The letter Śa is the Lord with matted hair (Śiva), and the letter La is the Lord who wields the Pināka bow (Śiva).
Having first performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) according to the prescribed rule, preceded by the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Likewise.
On ground smeared with cow dung, one should draw a mandala;
one should perform the smearing with honey or with yakṣakardama paste.
The lotus indicated by the thread is symmetrical and captivating;
it is red, white, or green in color, with black petals and beautiful filaments.
A square, richly adorned with beauty, and in its center a pair of *yoni*s;
and in the middle of that, a triangle—one should contemplate the void within the void.
One should unite with the woman who has been thus illuminated and there worship the mantra;
having established her right there, O Goddess, she who is beautifully eyed and slightly smiling.
A sixteen-year-old young woman, who has recently given birth,
is an ascetic under her own control, wearing clean garments, and laughing with a loud, fearless laugh.
She possessed intense wisdom and firm conduct; her hair was disheveled and she was naked, yet she bore the yogic gesture (yogamudrā) and was entirely devoted to the practice of yoga.
At the time of sacrifice, one should worship her who is thus endowed with mantras;
she is Mātaṅgī, the weaver of threads, who destroys the fear of rebirth.
The staff-bearer, the leather-worker, the female attendant,
the barber’s wife, the market-woman, and especially the one who is soft and strewn with beautiful flowers.
