One should pour into one's own vessel— the general offering (sāmānyārgha), the special offering (viśeṣārgha), and the power-vessel (śaktipātraka)—
the substance arising from the nectar of equanimity (sāmarasya).
The wise practitioner should purify each one with the mantra of the five tattvas;
the heart-mantra consists of the digits of fire, the sun, and ends with the digits of the moon.

One should draw a triangle in the center, and within that triangle, the letters beginning with A and ending with Kha, then those ending with Ṣa, then those ending with Na, then those ending with Ya, and finally those ending with Dha, together with Śakra (the letter Sa).
Joined with the left ear [the letter *v*], adorned with the *bindu* and *nāda*,
this mantra known as Ratneśvarī consists of the essence of the five jewels.
Having worshipped with the six limbs, one should consecrate [the object] with the root mantra.
238a) Here, the uninterrupted sacrifice is as before.
But the libation (tarpaṇa) is as follows:
Having gratified the power Kuṇḍalinī according to the ritual of the five mudrās— namely,
wine, meat, fish, [grain], and sexual union—
Wherever the five *makāras* are present, there the Goddess resides; of this there is no doubt.
Wine is not the liquor made from *mādhavī* flowers; wine is that which arises from the essence of the *śakti*.
Suṣumnā, Śaṅkhinī, Matsya, Mudrā, and Unmanā are the supreme [states]. That which is the bliss of immortality through the state of equanimity (sāmarasya) is that union (maithuna) which is Sadāśiva.
The divine, the heroic, and likewise the animal, as well as the threefold drink—
the hero who delights in the animal and the drink is to be consumed by the hosts of yoginīs.
The hero who delights in divine drink shall attain union with the Goddess;
indeed, by means of the hero’s drink, the teacher goes to the world of the Goddess.
The practitioner who drinks the liquor of the animal (paśu) shall go to the Raurava hell;
[therefore, one should practice] the equalizing of prāṇa and apāna, withdrawal of the senses, and the steadying of the mind.
Because it pierces the solar orb and resides in the center of the lunar orb,
it constantly pours down streams of nectar through the path of the Suṣumṇā.
This is declared to be the supreme divine drink that brings about all accomplishments;
it is the complete abandonment of all latent desires and the entire accumulation of root-impressions.
One should satisfy [the deities] through the yoga of Kālikācāra by means of the five principles;
one should offer the substance accompanied by mantras, piercing through the center of the six cakras.

The supreme state is found in the worship of meditation; the unsurpassed drinking of the hero’s wine belongs to one who is attached and greedy, yet free from hypocrisy regarding the purpose of the mantra.
One who is lustful regarding the assignment of tasks is called a *paśupāla*.
In the Siddheśvara Tantra.
The power that exists within the root tubers, which takes the form of a serpent, is understood by the wise to arise from the rotation of the earth; therefore, it is so described.
Moving, clearly sweet, and warbling, she likewise arises;
going through the aperture of Brahma, she enters her own abode.
One should effect the dissolution of the mind there through the very process of coming and going;
by that, the crest-jewel of mantra is born, which is the illuminator of all accomplishments.
Therefore, just as nothing appears in a house when it is properly joined,
yet nothing appears when the crest is missing, so too there is no purity in a mantra even after ten million eons.
O Svacchanda Maheśvara!
Even if there is a schism in the Saṅgha, if one is unattached, one should simply practice meditative cultivation.
This internal sacrifice, consisting of the offering of arghya before its placement for daily worship, must be performed even by an animal.
In the Svatantra Tantra.
At night, one should perform [the rite] according to the previously mentioned procedure beginning with "The goddess with meat and blood" (rātrau māṃsāsava-devīm).
Also in the Vīracūḍāmaṇi.
One should perform the libation according to the rules, with the number of drops equal to the number of syllables in the *Raktadhāraṇī*,
using either honey, clarified butter, wine, milk-rice, or water.
In this context, the distinction is as follows: [the agent is] a hero, a deity, and so forth; [the object is] an animal, water, and so forth.
In the Agastyasaṃhitā:
O Maheśvarī, by the perfect accomplishment of a single mantra through the worship of its five limbs,
all mantras become effective through your grace.
In the *Tantraśeṣara*.
While he practices in this manner, during the first three years, many obstacles arise: lack of faith, absence of devotion, and unwholesome compassion.
In this matter, if the practitioner should have a mind free from anxiety and possess the conviction that "I shall succeed," then he will become a partaker of accomplishment.

Moreover, even though one is shaven-headed (muṇḍa), because the secret preliminary rite (rahasya-puraścaraṇa) is mandatory, one should meditate upon the Guru on the head and the Goddess in the heart while reciting with a secret rosary; having performed the preliminary rites, the rest is the same.
On the day of beginning the initiation and the preliminary rite, as well as on the day of completion, one should pray for a dream at dawn.
The tradition; its specific manner, however, has already been explained.
Now, the signs of accomplishment.
In the Vakratuṇḍakalpa.

Clarity of mind, contentment of the intellect, moderation in eating, aversion to sleep, and the perception of vehicles and other such things in dreams— these are the immediate signs of one who has attained perfection.
In the Bhairavītantra.
One perceives light everywhere, or the body endowed with radiance;
indeed, one's own body becomes composed of the deity itself.
In the Nārada-pañcarātra and the Meru-tantra.
O Nārada, for one capable of propitiating the mantra, many obstacles arise during the first three years; such is his discipline.
If the practitioner does not experience agitation through either action or mind,
then after the third year, kings and sovereigns [will come under his influence].
Even those who are proud and self-important seek [your favor] through ancient offerings;
O Lord, let grace be bestowed, for it is the cause of uplifting the mind.
And they behold him blazing with splendor and majesty;
therefore, O tiger among sages, they are unable to speak harshly.
After the ninth year, the king of mantras becomes self-perfected;
indeed, various forms such as the Sun and others, consisting of the perfection of mantra, reside within the heart.

O Brahmin, these [powers] quickly bestow extreme bliss both externally and through direct perception; yet one of dull intellect remains exhilarated for only a moment, and then for another moment [returns to his former state].
He heard from the sky the sound of cymbals and drums,
and for a moment, a sweet melody accompanied by various songs.
For a moment he smells the fragrance arising from camphor and musk;
for a moment, moreover, he sees himself by means of his own self as if leaping up.
For a moment, the twice-born man should gaze upon the sky filled with the rays of the moon and sun; for an instant, he should listen to the sounds of elephants, cows, and bulls.
Even for a moment, the yogin hears the agitation of intense light and perceives the various stars situated in the sky.
The practitioner of the mantra-vow always sees [the deity] at one moment causing [him] to rise up,
and at another moment making a joyful "kili-kila" sound as well as the cry of a swan or a peacock.
In one moment he perceives the rising of the sun when night and day exist,
and in another moment he beholds the world at night with the sun shining by day.
He was filled with strength and resembled the sun in brilliance;
he was like the full moon in beauty and like a bird in his gait.
It is endowed with evenness, maturity, and a profound countenance;
it is not found even when practiced repeatedly for a long time, if one’s seat is too small.
Indeed, there will be a reduction in urine and feces, as well as victory over sleep;
the practitioner of mantra engaged in recitation and meditation does not experience exhaustion.
"O Sage, for a fortnight, a month, and so forth, even without food or drink"—
by such signs as these, which cause great astonishment.
When activity has commenced, one should be fully awakened; the lineage of mantras is pure.
In the Merutantra:
The sign and characteristic of the Great One’s gateway to accomplishment is said to be a marvel,
occurring either in a dream or before one's eyes, which bestows supreme joy.
If it arises spontaneously,
it must not be revealed anywhere by one who desires worldly accomplishment, except to a guru.
If one reveals the bliss born of mantra through delusion or impatience,
the accomplishments that were near at hand depart far away from him.
Sufferings and various sorrows manifest;
there is little food, very little sleep, and the mind is always dejected.
And when joined with light, the body and speech become true.
Salutation to Vaudha.
There are three signs of success: being a giver, being an enjoyer, and not being a beggar.
In the *Prapañcasāra*.
For from that recitation of the mantra, such signs indeed arise:
a lamp placed at night becomes established so that the house is free from darkness.

He becomes like the sun in his splendor; what will he not accomplish? He constantly destroys diseases with his very glance, and quickly bestows wealth, grain, and noble lineage upon those who approach him.
The gods constantly offer salutations to him; serpents do not bite him; his sons, grandsons, and friends remain steadfast;
thereafter, in times of calamity, he attains the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
In the Phetkāriṇī Tantra.
If success is not obtained through an excellent rite because of an obstructing or adverse factor,
one should perform it again two or three times.
In the Merutantra:
When the mantra is thus accomplished, many supernatural powers arise, which obstruct the path to liberation and cause the depletion of one's ascetic merit.
If one does not descend from even minor accomplishments, powers such as *aṇimā* will not arise;
and if one is submerged in *aṇimā* and the other powers, news of liberation becomes exceedingly difficult to attain.
Austerity that perishes in an instant is inferior, and that which arises from pride is mediocre.
It has also been stated that for one capable of performing the primary *puraścaraṇa*, [the practice] is to be performed even after each individual *puraścaraṇa*.
In the Muṇḍamālā [Tantra]:

on a Tuesday or a Saturday, one should procure the head of a human being that has been shaven.

Because of the statement, "A Śūdra should always do so," they desire to perform the *puraścaraṇa* after giving some gold with the ancestors as the intended recipients.

The meaning is that during the autumn season, starting from the fourth day of the lunar fortnight up to the ninth, one should recite six thousand [mantras] every night; furthermore, one should observe a fast on the eighth and ninth days.

should perform the worship and other rituals after following the previously mentioned procedure.
Kāmadeva alone should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times;
having planted [the seed] at the base of their leaf and gathered it, he should place it upon his head.
Great accomplishment shall arise immediately from the sight and worship of the creeper.
On the eighth day, at the time of twilight.

The four letters beginning with *ka*, the *jihvāmūlīya*, and the *upadhmānīya*—thus the *ka*-group is tenfold;

The letter *pa* joined with the *upadhmānīya*— therefore,

One should encase the mantra of one's family deity with the *bhūtalipi* (earth-script);
by performing this repetition a hundred times in forward and reverse order, accomplishment (*siddhi*) will be attained within a month.
One should recite the letters of the consonant groups (vargas) in sequence, beginning with the last letter of each group and then the second, fourth, and third letters respectively.
Then, with forty-two syllables,
one should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times for the deity Atyugra, who consists of the three "hot" stages.
If she is worshipped three times a day with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and again at midnight with the five [offerings],
as well as with the Kaulika and other [substances] for six months, she becomes pleased.
Likewise.
Whether due to a curse or because it is pinned down, there should be eight means for that purpose:
inflaming, nourishing, liquefying, awakening, and subjugation.
Oppression, nourishment, and emaciation, as well as burning—that is said to be its ritual action.
Having procured birch bark, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus.
With the eight fragrant substances, or with yellow pigment (rocanā) and sandalwood paste,
one should write the mantra interwoven with the letters of the practitioner's name for the sake of the deity.

One should write the name of the practitioner, beginning with the syllable *tāra* (oṃ), starting from the first [petal] and continuing until the completion of the two [names], across the eight petals.
Two by two, the vowels should be written, and one should meditate properly upon that which consists of nectar;
having encircled it with clay, the Brāhmaṇa and the others should thoroughly wrap it around.
Afterward, one should wrap it with white cloth and other materials,
and then place it in a small earthen vessel filled with the three sweets.
One should place that [substance] in a small vessel within a new jar filled with milk;
having established the fire, one should keep that jar in its vicinity.
One should establish [the deity] with the three sweets and perform the fire oblation (homa) with the root mantra;
one should pour the residue of the oblation (saṃpāta) into the pitcher, numbering one thousand and eight times.
Having completed the fire sacrifice (homa), one should cast the water-pot (kumbha) into a body of water;
one should satisfy one's own guru and the Brahmins with food, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and other offerings.
This is said to be the nourishment through the union [of the breaths]; if success (siddhi) does not occur, one should then perform the liquefaction (drāvaṇa), the method for which is described here.
Having tied it with the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, one should write the mantra on birch bark using uśīra,
gorocanā, realgar, camphor, and saffron.
One should place that written [diagram] in the midst of milk, clarified butter, honey, and water;
through worship, recitation, and fire-offerings, it becomes liquefied and yields its fruit.
If he is not perfected even after being melted, one should cause him to undergo awakening;
having encapsulated him with the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable, one should recite it.

When this mantra is written by these [scribes] upon beautiful birch-bark leaves and worn around the neck, it brings one under control; otherwise, it will cause affliction.
One should recite the first [syllable] with an udātta accent when the tone is anudātta; the second with an udātta when it is udātta;

while pronouncing the words with the anudātta accent, he should meditate on the deity situated below.

Standing upright with joy, one should recite the mantra a thousand times over the tip of the thumb; thereafter, one should write it on birch bark with the milk of a cow that has calved for the first time.
One should step upon the end of the mantra with the left foot and perform the fire oblation (homa);
when the mantra is thus afflicted one hundred and eight times, it becomes truly propitious.
If it is not yet perfected, then it is called "to be nourished" (poṣya); its ritual procedure is now described.
One should write the mantra encased within the *sauḥ* seed-syllable on a birch-bark leaf (*bhūrjapatra*).
One should apply *rocanā* and *kuṅkuma* with curd and milk;
this is called nourishment (*poṣaṇa*), and it is said to dry up the humors (*doṣa*).
One should write one's desired mantra on birch bark with the ashes of a sacrifice, interspersed with the seed-syllable of Vāyu; then, one should wear it around one's neck.
This is called the "Shokhaṇa" [mantra]; now the "Dahana" [mantra] is described, which encircles each individual syllable of the mantra in the four directions.
One should inscribe [the mantra] with the seed-syllable *raṃ* using seed-oil of the *palāśa* tree upon a birch-bark leaf; that should then be worn around the neck, for this is the rite of burning.
Thus are the purificatory rites performed with the mantra.
Now follows the Kavaca for the accomplishment of mantras.
Salutation to Śrī Kālikā.
Oṃ. Having prostrated before the Teacher of the World, who was seated upon the peak of Kailāsa, Pārvatī, bowing with humility, questioned the Lord of the Earth. (1)
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, Supreme Brahman, Savior from the ocean of worldly existence, by what means may success be swiftly attained through the supreme mantra of Kālikā? || 2 ||
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme Kālikā-vaṃcana,
by the recitation of which the accomplishment of mantras is swiftly attained.
The childless obtains a son, and the poor obtain wealth; furthermore, no fear of planetary influences, thieves, or kings exists here. (4)
By wearing [this] on the head, or on the neck, or on the left or right hand— whether on birch bark, gold, or the three metals— all perfections (siddhi) shall be attained.
The Veda situated upon yellow cloth effects the immobilization of all;
if it is employed upon black cloth, the death of enemies is certain.
Abiding in the blood, it brings about great bliss and brings the world under one's control. || 6 ||
Having bowed with my head, O Pārvatī, listen to the armor (kavaca) of Kālī:
[it is to be recited] in the east, the southeast, the southern quarter, the southwest, and likewise the west.
May the goddess Dakṣiṇakālikā— who bears a sword and a severed head— protect [us] in the northwestern direction, in the northeastern direction, below, and above.
May the goddess Kālikā, whose hands grant boons and fearlessness, protect [me] always—in front, on both sides, in the pores of the hair on the back, and everywhere. 9.
O Kālikā, protect [me] in the region of the crown, on the forehead, the eyes, the ears and nostrils, the mouth, the throat, the heart, and the belly. 10.
May Kālī, the bestower of all accomplishments, grant protection at all times in the secret parts, in the hands, in the feet, in the fingers, and in the nails. 11.
O Goddess, bestower of all perfections, protect me everywhere—in my inferior, superior, and middling limbs—whatever parts I possess. 12.
May the eastern triangle protect [me], as well as the southern triangle; may the western power-triangle and the northern triangle grant protection. (13)
And that power which is in the very center shall always protect with worship;
may the Mothers of the wheel protect, and may the Yoginīs protect at all times. (14)
May Sadāśiva, the Great Lord in the form of Śava, protect forever;
may all the Mothers, beginning with Brahmāṇī, grant protection at all times. 15.
May Kālī’s wrath always protect [me] in water, on land, in the great forest, in great delusion, and in great fear; may Kapālinī protect my knowledge.
May Kullā grant happiness, may Dāpā and Kurukullā remove suffering;
O Brahmin, may she who wards off desire and is ever the wish-fulfilling jewel protect your mind. 17.
May Ugrā always protect my wife; may Ugraprabhā protect my son;
may Dīptā protect my brother, and likewise may Nīlā protect my inner self.
May the King protect the kingdom; may the Crow protect from the enemy; may the Mother always protect Dharma; and likewise, may the Mudrā protect against Adharma.
Bearing a sword and a severed head, she protects the families of friends and enemies;
the Goddess stands in the center of the wheel, the dweller within the Great Wheel. 244a) 20.
May she who is the primordial nature (prakṛti) always protect me;
may she likewise protect the fivefold lower region and that which stands to the south.
May that which stands on the left, the five-cornered [triangle], protect all at all times;
may the triad of Kālīs protect the head, and likewise the pair of Māyās protect the face.
The two *kūrca*s, the heart, the belly, and likewise the right [side];
O Kālikā, protect my secret parts; and likewise the three *kālī*s for the feet. (23)
May Lajjā protect my two [eyes], all my limbs, my sides, my back, and my buttocks; may Svāhā always protect me at the tips of my hair, in my pores, and in my joints. (24)
Protect me from the wicked, O Kālī, who causes fear to all the wicked;
protect me always on the right side from bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas.
O Kālī, you are the warder-off of all seizing spirits, including kings, thieves, and planets;
this is due to my constant remembrance of you and my meditation upon your feet.
"May all obstacles perish and may peace be unshakable.
Thus, O Goddess, I have told you the auspicious armor (kavaca) of Kālikā. (27)
This should not be given to a human being who is lacking in devotion or who is envious;
through recitation the perfection of the mantra will be attained, and likewise through its retention—of this there is no doubt. (28)
O Pārvatī, in whose house this remains situated and is anointed with sandalwood paste, Lakṣmī dwells there forever, remaining steadfast.
Whoever listens while fasting, pure, and with the mind fixed upon that [deity],
on the eighth or the fourteenth day, for such a person success rests in the palm of the hand.
Thus ends the Kālī-kavaca in the Śrī Kālī-kulāmṛta.
Now, the lamp that brings about the accomplishment of mantras is presented, along with other lamps that are dependent upon it.
As it is stated in the Merutantra:
The illustrious Goddess said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, the vessel for splendor is born of the Sun;
therefore, out of compassion, please tell me the mantra and the fruit of this lamp.
The venerable Lord said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the wonderful ritual of the lamp;
first, the lamp for Gaṇeśa determines what is to be done and what is not to be done.
I shall explain that which is to be performed; it is traditionally remembered as an eightfold action:
pacifying (śāntika), nourishing (pauṣṭika), killing (māraṇa), paralyzing (stambhana), and subjugating (vaśa).
For those [rites], one should perform the lamp-offering in sequence for delusion, eradication, and inciting hatred;
[the wicks] should be made from wheat, barley, and black gram, and the oil from earth, gold, and hemp.
One should gradually fashion the bowl from copper using threads of white,
yellow, black, blue, crimson, red, green, and pigeon-grey.
One should perform [the ritual] facing each of the eight directions in sequence, beginning with the east:
north, east, south, west, fire (southeast), rakṣas (southwest), water (northwest), and the lord of the gods (northeast).
The practitioner should face forward toward his own ritual action;
[he should use] cow's ghee, sesame oil, mustard oil, and oil from sarṣapa seeds.
One should draw a sun-lotus (sūryadalapadma) upon a mandala smeared with cow dung, using buffalo ghee, umā-oil, or oil derived from sesame or safflower.
Beginning from the direction of the lamp, one should worship the Gaṇeśas there:
Sumukha, Ekadanta, Kapila, and Gajakarṇaka.
Laṃbodara, Vikaṭa, Vighnanāśa, Gaṇādhipa,
Dhūmraketu, Gaṇādhyakṣa, Bhālacandra, and Gajānana.
Whoever recites or even hears these twelve names at the commencement of learning, at a wedding, at entering [a new home], or likewise at departing;
In battle and in times of distress, no obstacle shall arise for him.
One should worship these deities there, and afterwards, one should wave the lamp.
When the lamp is placed in its vessel, if the flame flickers up and down with a clean wick, then the task to be performed will be successfully accomplished.
If the light is perfectly clear, the task shall be accomplished through a horizontal tremor;
however, if the light is dim, it is said that there will be a delay and an obstacle here.
One should bring forth a maiden or a youth born among the hosts of gods;
or, having properly brought a woman dressed in pure attire, one should worship her.
One should place a wide, purified bronze vessel filled with water below; then, while looking at it, she should remain with a steady gaze.
Having reflected upon her own task, she should cast her gaze upon it with undiminished clarity; according to the requirements of the work, she should observe the marvelous display of the dolls.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme Vagalādīpa,
by the performance of which the multitudes of obstacles of the mantra-practitioner are dissolved.
Indeed, O friends, having threshed the pure seeds with a pestle and having gathered them together, you must prepare a beautiful and well-pleasing lamp.
A firm wick, well-colored, should be made with thirty-six threads;
and for the rite of lighting the lamp, one should use either cow’s clarified butter or Kusumbha oil.
Having first brought these [articles], one should then cause a lamp to be offered;
being pure and patient, one should put on a garment dyed with turmeric.
Seated upon a yellow cloth, wearing yellow garlands and ointments,
and facing the northern direction, one should sprinkle turmeric upon the ground.
Having fashioned a triangle and carefully established a lamp therein,
the wise one should fill it with ghee, insert a wick, and light the lamp.
Having recited the root mantra, one should then say "this lamp";
thereafter, one should say "cause to accept" at the end of the Yuga, and then utter the wife of Fire (svāhā).
Having first performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) with due resolve, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
practicing thus at night for only a month, the practitioner—
One may accomplish what is unattainable, achieve one's desired goal, bring one's enemies under control,
cause agitation, incite hatred, paralyze, or even cast [them] down.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the lamp offering to Vaṭukanātha, which is concealed in all tantras and bestows the fruit of all desires.
One should utter Tāra, Māyā, Ramā, Kāma, Māyā, Lakṣmī, and Vāgbhava;
then say "to the Omniscient" and "to the Fierce One," and "to Prowess."
One should utter the words, "O Vaṭuka, take this lamp," and then say the words,
"accomplish all tasks."
"Destroy the wicked ones, yugma; terrify the two, vadet;
grant me protection from all sides, yugma; [and] varma phaṭ."
" Svāhā! This lamp-mantra consisting of sixty-six syllables has been proclaimed;
it belongs to the practitioner who is a devotee of the Bhairava mantra."
And that wick should be prepared with threads measured by the number of syllables of the mantra;
first, however, one should ascertain the feasibility of the task by means of a small lamp.
Thereafter, one should perform the *dīpaka* rite when the task is easily accomplished, as it has been taught;
however, for a difficult task, it is considered to be performed twice as much, and for a very arduous one, three times as much.
One should never perform the rite for an incurable case, as it would cause terror;
whatever vessel and other materials were prescribed for a minor rite [should be used].
All that should be known as follows: two palas is said to be the measure of the vessel;
the wick should consist of eight threads, and the oil is traditionally held to be one pala in measure.

Action is said to be of two kinds: auspicious or inauspicious. When [the action] is auspicious, there shall be no suffering for another; it is auspicious, consisting of rites for peace (śāntika) and prosperity (pauṣṭika).
In that regard, the meditation on Bhairava is described: he is white and four-armed.
With white teeth, holding a silver *bhṛgu* in his right hand and a rosary in his left,
wearing a crown upon his head and clad in a white loincloth.
Three-eyed and blue-throated, adorned with ornaments of pearls,
he causes suffering to others and performs acts such as killing.
Blue in color, with disheveled hair, adorned with a garland of skulls,
equipped with a string of tinkling bells, three-eyed, and terrifying.
Furthermore, one should meditate upon him who holds a serpent-noose and a bell in his left hands, and a club and a skull-bowl in his right hands, possessing a body as sharp as a razor.
In every auspicious rite, the oil should be scented with flowers;
the vessel should be made of wheat flour or else of rice.
O beautiful one, white wicks should be prepared that absorb a *kuḍava* measure;
having soaked that grain in water during the *soma* [lunar] period, one should dry it thoroughly.
On a Tuesday, the practitioner should not perform the grinding of substances with the hand of a maiden;
rather, he should recite the *Bhairavakavaca* while holding the lamp-vessel.

Those syllables of the *śvetamantra* which are conjoined with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) should be employed in the ritual application for desired ends; this, indeed, is the procedure for the wick.
Three, five, or seven lamps should be lit according to the gravity of the task; a lamp in the abode of the gods is commended for auspicious rites.

For rites of pacification (śānti), one should face north; for rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika), one is considered to face east. Now I shall describe the lamp-yantra: one should construct three auspicious circles.
Above that, one should draw a great triangle;
within its triangles, one should draw a hexagon, and outside of that, one joined with sixteen petals.
One should draw an eight-petalled lotus; this is declared to be the mantra of the lamp.
It is prescribed for the purpose of testing the perpetual lamp as well as for rites performed for specific desires.
And oil scented with flowers bestows the fruits of all desires;
likewise, black gram, wheat, mung beans, sesame seeds, and rice in equal proportions [yield the same].
The lamp-vessel fashioned by them bestows the fruits of all desires;
with twenty-one white threads, it shall grant all wishes.
It is near Bhairava, in the presence of Śāligrāma, and likewise near a crystal Liṅga; it grants all desires.
And at the root of an Aśvattha tree, for the fulfillment of all desires,
there should be eight hundred and eight palas of [substances] for a rite for the Guru.
In the middle [wick], one made from a thousand threads weighing eighty palas is used; for a great rite of middling scale, it should be measured at twenty-eight [palas].

In the case of a minor task, it should be performed with three hundred [recitations], but with one hundred for [ordinary purposes]. One desiring prosperity should use sesame oil; the vessel should be made of castor-oil seeds.
Alternatively, one should offer a lamp made from cloves, camphor, saffron, and cardamom at the king's gate; within a year, there will be great prosperity.
A poor person [should offer] speech in a copper vessel adorned with musical instruments such as lutes,
and for the sake of the arrival of travelers, a lamp with sesame oil.
A vessel with powder as fine as wheat or rice flour is highly praised;
at the royal gate, twenty-one thread-lamps should be offered.

One should perform five white rites; for the purpose of subjugation (*vaśya*), one should proceed for twice the number of days of the [specified] path, using a vessel of linseed oil (*atasī-taila*) filled with rice-flour paste.
One should carry a lamp at the king’s gate with a wick dyed with saffron;
for the destruction of disease, the oil should be mustard oil and the vessel should be made of muṅga.
In the presence of Hanumān, the lamp should have a wick dyed with safflower;
for the purpose of killing, the oil should be made from black mustard or from the marking nut (bhallātaka).
One should offer a lamp for the purpose of killing at the king's gate or in the father's house;
one should prepare the lamp facing the southern direction in a vessel of iron.
In the *mṛtyu-svara* of an enemy, the ritual action should be performed with a wick made of black threads;
for the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), the oil should be derived from human nails and the vessel should be made of black sesame.
And for the purpose of creating enmity, one should employ a wick made of blue thread at the royal gate; the oil should be madhūka oil, and the vessel here should be made of kulattha beans.
The offering of a lamp at a crossroads should have a variegated wick;
for the purpose of deluding, the vessel is made of *āḍhakī* wood and the thread is said to be madder-colored.
There should be sesame oil for the lamp; one should carry this [lamp] at the king's gate.
For the purpose of victory in battle, however, there should be a vessel made from the flour of black gram.
In the presence of Durgā, one should offer a wick made with red threads.
At the junction [of the day], one should offer a vessel made of *tripiṣṭaja* (rice-flour) or clay from a riverbank,
and at the confluence, one should offer a lamp with a wick of tripled form.
Twenty-one threads of this sound are prescribed;
one should also prepare an earthen vessel for the offering of lamps at a crossroads.
One should offer a lamp at the hair-tuft of an image, before spirits and the like, at crossroads, on uneven ground, at mountain peaks, or in the presence of a deity.
Or, for the accomplishment of the six rites beginning with killing, at a crossroads,
one should use a vessel made from a human skull and [an offering] of buffalo ghee.
One desiring knowledge should begin on the fourth lunar day, placing a white wick soaked in cow’s ghee into a vessel made of ivory in the presence of Gaṇeśa.
One should perform this at the king’s gate for the sake of release from bondage, or in a prison;
the lamp should be in a copper vessel, and the wick should be smoke-colored.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the auspicious and inauspicious signs of small lamps and those for desired objects, by which the determination of what should and should not be done is made.
Upon seeing a Brahmin and the others, success in the sequence of the lamps is attained:
full, three-quarters, half, and equal to a quarter, and then the binding.
The vision of barbarians and the like is said to be the lowest; the vision of cats and the like is middling; and that of the blue-necked peacock and the like bestows glorious fame and victory.
If the flame of the lamp arises smooth and circumambulates [the object], his success will be achieved within eight days; of this there is no doubt.
If there is a harsh-throated flame of light, death occurs along with one's kinsmen;
if the flame is black, then the enemy's purpose is achieved and one's own task does not come to pass.
If the lamp is extinguished quickly, there will be success, but with delay;
however, if the lamp goes out while it is being lit, one should declare that the task has failed.
The vomiting of a lamp, its theft, the destruction of cattle, the breaking of a vessel,
the extinguishing of a lamp during a festival, and its removal from the ornamentation there [are inauspicious].
Having performed all the ritual assignments (nyāsa) and so forth, one should offer the lamp facing east;
this is proclaimed as the procedure for the lamp of Vaṭuka.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain that which brings satisfaction to the Śaktis:
one should arrange the offering of a lamp within a triangular vessel for the sake of the Śakti.
For the Śaktis of the Dakṣiṇāmnāya, [the vessel] should be made from any one of the three metals;
for the Ūrdhvāmnāya, it should be a vessel of flour, glass, or stone.

The *ārtika* for the deities of the Western Tradition is to be offered with meat; for those of the Eastern Tradition, it is with a human skull; and for those of the Leftward Tradition, it is, in sequence, cow’s milk, clarified butter, and clarified butter.
Sesame oil is prescribed for the white [wick], and muscle fat for the red; likewise, the wicks are made of white, red, green, yellow, and black threads, respectively.
Lamps should be offered according to the oral tradition of the gods for the propitiation of the deities at a temple of the gods,
on a riverbank, in a royal palace, or at a crossroads.
Lamps offered in the cremation ground bring satisfaction to their respective deities;
here, like Gaṇeśa, the examination determines what is to be done and what is not to be done.
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare that which bestows auspiciousness, which is the illuminator of Śiva,
which pacifies all sins, and which destroys all calamities.
One should prepare a lamp-wick from threads of five, six, and three [units];
one should offer a lamp in the temple of Śiva using a vessel made from bilva leaves.
Thus, for twelve days and nights, it blazes with twelve colors;
by his lineage, there shall be no poverty nor untimely death.
A lamp for Śrī at the eastern gate; for heaven and liberation at the southern;
this one for good rain at the western; and for all remaining purposes at the northern.
A lamp made with cow's ghee is extremely dear to Śiva;
in the case of malevolent rites (abhicāra), one should consider the relative gradation [of other oils] such as sesame oil.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the "Sun-Illuminator" (Bhānudīpaka), which destroys diseases;
one should prepare it in a vessel made of gold, or in its absence, one of copper.
With twelve threads made from safflower, that [wick] for the Hero (Rāva) is twelve finger-breadths long; one kuḍava of ghee is prescribed.
Having caused that lamp to be offered, if it does not touch the entire [wick] when the ghee has been ignited and it is extinguished,
then the destruction of disease is certain.
Having observed the strength or weakness of the disease,
one should determine the measure of the lamp and the oblation, starting from a *pala* up to a *khārī*, in accordance with local custom.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the most wonderful lamp offering to Viṣṇu:
all desires are fulfilled with cow’s ghee, while killing [of enemies] is achieved with buffalo ghee.
However, for acts such as causing enmity, the vessels for the three [goddesses] should respectively be made of copper,
iron, and glass, according to the sequence of the three rites.
One should perform this *āmali* rite for the pleasure of Viṣṇu during the appearance of dust;
by means of the lamp of Viṣṇu, evil dreams, calamities, spirits, and so forth are destroyed.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain this lamp that brings about the accomplishment of mantras, which is concealed in all tantras and must not be told to just anyone.
When the sum of the days of the fortnight is divided by the powers and so forth, the number of syllables is produced;
one should then arrange the lamp for each syllable of the mantra in successive order on those days.
In the evening, O King, one should prepare a wick with a *kuḍava* measure of clarified butter and threads;
as long as that lamp burns, one should gaze upon it and recite the mantra.
Then, on that day, when the lamps equal in number to the syllables of the mantra have been lit,
if a lamp is lit once more, she is clearly perceived within that lamp.
One should declare one's own desired object and mentally petition for what is wished for;
the deity, being pleased, grants it—this secret has now been revealed.
A deity who is fond of lamps may become equal to Kārtavīrya;
that treasury of lamps is proclaimed in various ways within the Tantras.
Thus has the procedure for the Sun, accompanied by the lamp-offering, been declared to you.
Hereafter, regarding whatever you desire, ask me about that.
Thus concludes the auspicious procedure for the lamp, beginning with the accomplishment of the mantra.
Now, the practice for attaining heroism (*vīrasādhana*), from the *Yoginīhṛdaya*.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, knower of all tantras and expert in all treatises,
you previously indicated the preliminary practice to be performed in the cremation ground.
Tell me now, if you have any affection for me at this time.
The Lord said:
In that place where success has not been attained by men even through great exertion, practitioners of spiritual discipline must perform the *vīrasādhana*.
In former times, when the duty for kings was at hand for the sake of attaining perfection,
there was nothing else that brought swift success except for the *vīrasādhana*.
Therefore, with every effort, the heroic practice (vīrasādhana) should be performed by one who is free from fear, pure, and desiring all accomplishments.
O Girijā, there is nothing desired by the practitioner that is difficult to attain through this [practice];
therefore, I shall now request it with effort and reveal it.
On the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights—
and especially during the dark fortnight— one should accomplish one's welfare by means of this [practice].
In the Vīra-tantra:
The Goddess said:
O Great Hero, O God, that which was indicated by your stride has not yet been revealed;
O Mahādeva, please explain that great [teaching] which bestows all accomplishments.
Bhairava said:
O Goddess, it directly bestows all accomplishments, is saluted by all the gods,
removes all sins, and destroys all diseases.
O future one, [this shall be the glory] of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others,
as well as of all the world-protectors, the Bhairavas, the Gandharvas, and the Yogins.
O Goddess, it eternally bestows accomplishment and is the great abode of all;
O Goddess, there is nothing else that grants accomplishment apart from the practice of the heroes (vīrasādhana).
Possessing great strength, a great hero, and great courage, he is pure;
endowed with a most clear and exalted mind, he is devoted to the welfare of all beings.
O Great Goddess, for their sake, the Vīrasādhana has been taught.
Likewise.
One should tie a cloth around the waist with the root mantra and wrap it around the body;
then, having sprinkled that same cloth with clarified butter, one should apply it as an ointment to the limbs with the root mantra.
Having bound the turban with the root mantra and applied the vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍraka) with vermilion,
one should bow to the chosen deity and the gurus, and set out on the journey at midday.
And she should be served together with the practitioners, while contemplating the mantra in one's heart;
provided that the practitioner is a hero (vīra), he may eat while remaining unperturbed.
Having partaken of divine food there,
one should perform the spiritual practice on the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights.
On a Tuesday mixed with [the asterism] Tamiśrā, one should accomplish the supreme siddhi,
having taken up the ritual services (upacāra) as well as the nectar of the kula and the mercury.
The food offering (naivedya) shall consist of meat with fat, jaggery, goat meat, liquor,
flour-cakes, and various fruits, prepared according to the specific prescriptions of their respective ritual manuals.

Having brought [the corpse] to the cremation ground, the practitioner himself— free from fear and accompanied by friends who are endowed with similar virtues and holding weapons in their hands— [should proceed].
One should not look in the four directions; one who is intent on that [practice] is called a deity. If the practitioner is afraid there, then there are practitioners in the four directions.
If not, he is proclaimed as Bhairava alone,
adorned with garments, ornaments, and decorations, facing the east.
Having gone to the cremation ground that has not been washed,
the best of practitioners should generally have the heap of bones washed if it has not already been washed.
One should sprinkle the sacrificial grounds with the weapon-mantra (astramantra) and the root-mantra (mūlamantra),
while meditating upon the dust from the feet of the Guru, as well as Gaṇeśa and Vaṭuka.
The Yoginīs and the Mātṛkās, preceded by the Vā [mantra],
as well as the gods and terrifying Rākṣasas who are stationed here.
Piśācas, Siddhas, Yakṣas, and the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases;
Yoginīs, Mātṛs, Bhūtas, and all the women who roam the sky.
"May they grant success there and likewise be my protectors.
Having prostrated with this mantra, one should cast three handfuls of flowers.
One should diligently worship the Lord of the Cremation Ground, Bhairava, Kālabhairava, and Mahākāla, in the four directions starting from the east.
The knower of mantras should then present the bali offering with water for the feet and other requisites;
thereafter, he should utter the seed-syllable of sound (Śabdarāja), followed by the Lord of the Cremation Ground (Śmaśānādhipa).
O Lord, accept this offering of meat and food at the end;
accept it, cause it to be accepted, and thereafter remove the obstacles for the duration of the age.
"O Goddess, having uttered 'Grant me success' (kuru siddhiṃ me), offer [the oblation] accompanied by 'svāhā' and the mantra beginning with Tārā; this is declared to be the first offering."
After Māyānta and Bhairava, and finally after Bhayānaka,
one should offer the bali as before and then offer the bali on the south.
One should extract [the mantra] from Mahākāla immediately after him, as before;
one should assign it to Kāladeva in the west, preceded by the Praṇava.
At the end of the word, at the end of the word *kāla*, and at the end of the word *bhairava*,
one should likewise remove the phrase "Lord of the Cremation Ground" (*śmaśānādhipa*) from the north as before.
Then, in the middle of the funeral pyre, one should offer the three supreme circumambulations, [reciting]:
"O Kālarātri! O Mahākāla! O Kālikā of terrible sound!"
"O Mother Ambālī, grant me the supreme accomplishment!
*Huṃ*! Svāhā to Kālikā! Having thus offered [the oblation], one should present it to Bhūtanātha.
At the end of the word *śabda* and at the end of *bhūtanātha*, [one should say] "O Lord of the Moon" (*śaśānādhipa*).
With this mantra, beginning with the *praṇava* (OM), one should cause the supreme *bali* offering to be given.
"Hūṃ, O Lord of all Gaṇas, O Lord of the cremation grounds!"—
with this mantra beginning with the syllable *praṇava*, one should cause the supreme *bali* offering to be given.
Then, having gathered the heap of bones from the western side of the funeral pyre, [he should worship] again with this mantra: "Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti."
Having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should write the mantra "ha sauḥ" upon a birch leaf or any other leaf, and then place that [leaf] there once again.
Having placed a seat such as a woolen blanket there for the Power of Support (Dhāra-śakti),
one should worship her there with the mantra "Oṃ, homage to [the Power of Support]," and likewise worship Hīmā and the others.
Then, O Goddess of the gods, having sat upon the seat with Vīrārdana,
[one should utter] the two Kūrca-bījas, O Goddess, and thereafter the pair of Māyās.
Having joined Kālike, Ghoradaṃṣṭre, Pracaṇḍe,
and Caṇḍanāyike, one should then utter "dāraya dānavān" twice.

Then, "Paravīraṃ mahāvighnaṃ chedaya" (O destroyer of the great obstacle, the hero of others), followed by the end of the armor-mantra (*varma*) and the weapon-mantra (*astra*), ending with *svāhā* (*dviṭha*). This is considered the mantra for the subduer of heroes (*vīrārdana*).
One should cast a clod of earth consecrated with this mantra in the ten directions;
in their midst, the god Bhairava is not overcome by obstacles.
O Goddess of gods, if through negligence the practitioner becomes overwhelmed by fear,
he shall not be overcome provided he is protected by various friends.
Having placed a lamp there with a wick made from the roots of *arka*, *indusita*, *vādya*, and *āla*, one should worship the Astra-mantra therein.
When that great lamp is overcome by obstacles,
one should bury the family-lamp beneath it with the Astra-mantra.
One should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and other rites according to the specific ritual procedure for each respective kalpa;
then, having performed the placement (vinyāsa) of either the sixteen or the six-syllable [mantras], one should worship.
In this very [context], there is Vāmalā and so forth.
Then, one should worship the deity before oneself with the fivefold offerings;
subsequently, closing the eyes and meditating upon the Lord, one should recite the mantra.
If it be a single-syllable mantra, one should recite it a thousand times;
for a two-syllable mantra, eight thousand; and for a three-syllable mantra, fifty thousand.
Thereafter, however, the knower of mantras [should recite] one thousand Gajāntakas;
that is, one thousand and eight Gajāntakas.
One should perform [the ritual] starting from midnight until sunrise;
if the ear or eye is injured, one should bind it with a cloth.
If nothing at all is perceived until the end of the night,
one should not scatter mustard seeds with the Jayadurgā mantra for the purpose of the *arghya* offering.
Oṃ, you are the blue-colored goddess, the source of the Gosava sacrifice,
the bringer of satisfaction to the ancestors, the bestower of heaven upon them, and the protector of mortals.
"Bringing peace amidst the obstacles caused by *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas*.
Having thus cast sesame seeds there, [he should worship] with four portions, beginning with Śiva.
Then, having gone seven steps, one should again sit down in that very place;
having thus worshipped there as well, one should recite the supreme mantra.
One should recite the mantra fearlessly until success is attained;
however, fear should be understood as occurring in dreams, while the remainder is to be known from the following day.
In the Vāmakeśvaratantra: 249a).
At the conclusion of the recitation, one should offer an oblation to the deity according to the prescribed rite,
having taken either a buffalo, a goat, or even a boar.
With a joyful heart, he should go home together with his circle of friends.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the funeral pyre.
Now follows the procedure for accomplishing power.
In the Vīra-tantra:
Having taken up the previously mentioned offerings and other requisites,
the practitioner should resort to a place for practice and accomplish the success desired by himself.
The wise person should rely upon everything previously mentioned, beginning with meditation on the Guru;
in a ground marked by the Vīrārdana [mudrā], neither illusion nor delusion exists.
With the mantra beginning "ye cātra... and so forth, one should offer three handfuls of flowers upon the ground;
then, as before, one should present the bali offering to the lords of the cremation grounds.
One should perform the rite of offering (bali) with the mantra known as Aghora;
or one should effect protection with the Sudarśana mantra, or with both.
Māyā manifests a pair; then again, a pair manifests, arising as both terrible and most terrible, followed by the corresponding state.
At the end of the pair of *ca* syllables, there is then a pair of *pracaṭa*;
after that, a pair of *kaha*, a pair of *vama*, and then a pair of *vandha*.
"Destroy the two armors!"— ending with *phaṭ*,
this mantra consisting of fifty-one syllables is composed of the Aghora-weapon.
Having extracted the syllable *hālāhala*, which has the nature of a thousand spokes,
this great mantra of Sudarśana is proclaimed, ending with the armor (*varma*) and weapon (*astra*) syllables.
Then, having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should duly apply the network of ritual placements (nyāsa).
With the mantra known as Jayadurgā, one should scatter mustard seeds in all directions.
"Oṃ durge durge rakṣiṇi svāhā"—this is the mantra known as Jayadurgā. One should also scatter sesame seeds with the mantra beginning "tilosi."
One pierced by a staff, pierced by a spear, pierced by a sword, or one who has died in water;
one pierced by a rope, bitten by a snake, or possessed by a caṇḍāla or a malevolent spirit.
A youth, a handsome hero, who has perished in battle while shining brightly,
having fled without retreat and remaining steadfast in the face of combat.
One who died by his own will, one who has been dead for two years, an elderly woman, and likewise a twice-born man;
one who died from lack of food, one with leprosy, and likewise one who has been dead for more than seven nights.
Thus, having taken one of the previously mentioned corpses that has been abandoned in these eight ways,
one should bring it to the place of worship with the root mantra.
One should quickly perform the sprinkling of the corpse with the Astra-mantra preceded by the Praṇava, which bestows the fruit of accomplishment even when one is overcome by outcasts and the like.
Having offered three handfuls of flowers with the mantra: "Oṃ, kūrca-bīja, obeisance to the dead body, phaṭ," one should prostrate while preceded by physical contact.
O Hero, supreme bliss, Śivānanda, Lord of the Kula!
O Śaṅkara, who has the form of Ānandabhairava and rests upon the couch of the Goddess!
"I take refuge in you, O Vīroha; arise for the worship of Caṇḍikā!
Having prostrated with this mantra, he should thereafter wash [the image].
The mantra is said to consist of the syllable *tāraṃ*, followed by the word *mṛtakārya* ending with *namaḥ*.
This is the mantra for bathing the corpse, taught in all tantras.
Having fumigated it with incense and anointed it with perfumes and the like,
O Lord of Gods, if one smeared with red [pigment] should eat the Kula-practitioner;
Having gone into the presence of the corpse, one should hold [the substance] at the region of the waist;
if it should cause distress to him, one should place spittle into his mouth.
Having washed it again, one should bring it to the place of recitation;
having spread out a bed of *kuśa* grass, one should establish the corpse there.
Having placed betel leaf with cardamom, cloves, camphor, nutmeg,
and the heartwood of khadira in his mouth, one should turn the corpse face downwards.
Having placed it on his back, one should smear it with sandalwood paste;
one should visualize it as a square extending from the base of the arms to the knees.
In the center, one should place a lotus with four doors and endowed with eight petals;
then, one should lay down the skin of a black antelope, covered with a woolen blanket.
Having placed sacrificial wood measuring twelve finger-breadths in the cardinal directions,
one should worship the ten deities there, beginning with Indra.
Then, having inscribed the poison for Indra, the lord of the gods, [the practitioners] should say:
"Accept this offering! Accept it! twice.
Having warded off obstacles, grant success; [this is] the double *ṭha*.
With this mantra, one should first offer a bali-oblation consisting of meat.

One who maintains the corpse as his seat should offer a sacrifice to the gods with liquor.
One should offer the bali-oblation to the sixty-four Yoginīs.

Having placed the materials for worship nearby and the assistant practitioner at a distance, and having worshipped the seat with the excellent mantra at its conclusion, [one should perform the rite] ending with the syllable *trapā*.
One should mount the horse there with the mantra ending in *phaṭ*;
having placed *kuśa* grass under the soles of the feet and having wiped away the hair from the corpse.
Having firmly tied his upper garment and accomplished his resolve,
he ascended upon the corpse and performed breath control (prāṇāyāma).
One should cast clods of earth in the directions with the *vīrārdana* mantra; then,
one should worship the deity with a thousandfold ritual services (*upacāra*).
O Goddess, one should perform the nourishment (āpyāyana) of the Deity according to the rules while [the image] is in the state of a corpse;

Oṃ, O Lord of Gods, be subject to my will;

While reciting the root mantra, the practitioner should then bind the two feet of the corpse with a silk thread; thus, it will not be able to rise.
Oṃ! O terrifying one, O dispeller of fear, O you with auspicious eyes, O source of all existence!
Protect me, O Lord of the gods of gods, O sovereign over the lords of the dead!
Thus, one should draw a triangular wheel on the sole of his foot;

Having seated him again and drawn out his arms from the sides,

Having brought the lips together in a seal, with a steady mind and steady senses,
one should always meditate on the Goddess in the heart and perform the recitation while observing silence.
O Kuleśvara, one should perform the recitation in the cremation ground according to the stated number,
or until the sun sets at the time of twilight.
If nothing is obtained even after reciting until midnight,
then as before, one should perform the offering of water and so forth, and likewise walk seven steps.

Having performed [the preliminary rites] and entered right there, one should perform the recitation with undistracted mind. There is no fear from a shifting seat; however, if fear should arise, one should then speak as follows.
"O Queen of the Gods, whatever you desire—be it an elephant or anything else—that must be given;
I shall bestow it upon you on another day. Tell me your own name."
Having spoken thus in Sanskrit, one should recite again without fear;
if he speaks sweetly once more, then one should likewise speak sweetly in response.
Then one should make a truthful resolve and thereafter request a boon;
for if one does not make a truthful resolve, he will not grant the boon.
Then the wise one, reciting with a one-pointed mind, should again recite:
"The deity who moves here in human form, or whoever else approaches as a man."
Whether it be a human, or those born of divine origin, or his mother, or his daughter, or even his maternal aunt— it must be understood by him with great effort.
Having arrived, he creates an obstacle through his illusory power, concealing his true form.
"Arise, dear child! Your task will be accomplished; of this there is no doubt."

Generally, all kings who wield the rod of punishment [behave] thus.
If at any time one is provoked by someone else,

The deceased ancestors who reside in distant lands come there,

Taking his wife, sons, servants, and others, he is led away by his enemies;
meanwhile, all his sons, younger brothers, disciples, and followers cry out.
O wife, one is led away by the *pālakas* after they have seized the touch of one's own beloved’s body, as well as one's garments, ornaments, and so forth; therefore, one should abandon fear of them.
Whatever suspicion arises on a particular day, that very thing is produced there;
if one is not agitated by it, then what indeed cannot be attained?

The goddess, assuming the form of a woman, and the man, assuming the form of a brahmin, shall indeed say the words "Accept the boon" three times; at the end of those three times, one shall obtain the boon.
If a woman who grants boons is pleased by either a virtuous man or even a non-virtuous one,
then what on this earth cannot be accomplished for that heroic master?
The man is indeed free from sin and well-refined within his family, while the queen, though of noble birth, is unrefined and joined with sin; of this there is no doubt.
Whether speaking face-to-face or otherwise, whoever speaks another [person] in the refined language (saṃskṛta), that person is undoubtedly the Goddess herself; he is Bhairava himself.
And it should not be so, for illusion (māyā) is subdued by being encapsulated;
while choosing the lower therein, one should never proclaim the higher.
If he speaks a discourse on the conditioned, it should be spoken in this manner;
otherwise, one should rather grasp the unconfused worldly speech itself.
Alternatively, one may obtain even a preeminent benefit for oneself;
or a true reputation arises, or even the nectar of immortality is attained.
Having deliberated on all this, one must grasp it; thus has the direction been proclaimed.
The creations of the gods are manifold, while the creations of humans and others are found in various places.
One must certainly fear that place; there is no certainty whatsoever there.
For the Bhairavas and Vaṭukas are devoted solely to the Kula scriptures.
By means of this treatise, those of crooked form shall act;
having become a son, they shall choose [a bride], and having become a woman, they shall delude [the husband].
Therefore, a wise person intent on reality should exert effort in inquiry;
once truth has been attained, one should abandon recitation and other such practices.
Knowing that the fruit has been produced, one should then release the pill;
having washed it thoroughly and set it aside, one should release the binding at the foot.
Having cleansed the footprint-circle, one should cast the ritual substances into the water;
then, having cast the corpse into the water or into a pit, one should perform the ritual bath.
Then, having gone to his own home and offered a bali-oblation on another day,
he said: "I am the sacrificer for those gods who [receive offerings] by fire and at night."
May they accept this bali-offering given by me.
Then, having offered horses, goats, elephants, men,

Also in another tantra:
Alternatively, one should strike an effigy made of barley flour or rice flour with a sword, according to the prescribed ritual and with its specific mantra.
On the following day, he should always drink the *pañcagavya* under the guidance of his preceptor;

Or, decreasing by five each time in sequence up to ten days;
then, having bathed and eaten, one should reside in an excellent place.
If there were no food to be offered to the Brahmins, then one would fall into poverty;
and if poverty should arise because of that, then the God becomes enraged.
One should guard the practice of the *kula* for either three nights or six nights;
if one should indeed go to a woman during her menses, then disease arises.
Having heard song, the deaf man becomes one with sight; by seeing the dance, he who was blind gains speech; yet if he speaks during the day, he then falls into silence.
Indeed, the residence of the Lord within the body lasts for fifteen days;
one should never, under any circumstances, utter disparagement against cows, Brahmins, or the gods.
O King, one who is pure should touch cows, Brahmins, and others every day;
furthermore, at the conclusion of the daily morning rites, one should drink water from a bilva leaf.
Then, when the sixteenth day has arrived, one should bathe at a sacred ford or similar site;
reciting the root mantra ending with "svāhā," one should offer libations with the words "I satiate you, obeisance."
Thus, after three hundred [verses], there is the satiation of the gods with water; the satiation of the sages consists of the number zero, and there is no satiation of the gods.
The meaning is "satisfaction."
By this method, one certainly attains accomplishment;
having enjoyed divine pleasures here, one goes at the end to the abode of Hari.
Having performed this sādhana— whether with omissions or complete, fruitless or fruitful— he shall indeed become most dear to Śakti.
The practice of *vīrasādhana* should be performed either in the presence of a corpse or in a cremation ground;
if one does not worship with those specific dispositions that have been prescribed for each individual.

one should not teach the state of being there, nor should one prescribe worship there.
Having taken it as far as the cremation ground, purification is produced until [the body] is completely cleansed.
Thus ends the Vīrasādhana.
Now follows the sādhana of Vīra by another method.
This has been stated in the Kālītantra:
Listen, O Goddess of excellent limbs, to the supreme *vīrasādhana*;
another method is now being described for the sake of men’s swift attainment of results.
One should dig a pit for a person at the heart [of the site] at the crossroads in the four directions;
then, one should light a single lamp at the *brahmarandhra* and subsequently light lamps [in the other directions].
Likewise, one should dig a single pit in the center;
there, having offered oblations (bali) according to the prescribed rite to the deities beginning with Mahākāla, one should enter upon a seat of earth.

Having completed the worship as prescribed in the ritual manual, one should perform recitation with a restrained mind, using a rosary made of right-hand jasmine seeds, or a *rājadanta* (tooth of a king), or a *meru* (rudrākṣa) bead.
Clad in the directions as his garment, one should recite the mantra dedicated to all the deities ten thousand times;
at the conclusion of the recitation, one should offer an oblation and provide a sacrificial fee according to one's means.
The wise one is the lord of all accomplishments and is saluted by all the gods;
or else, a man [should sit] on a seat of bones in a solitary forest.
Having recited the mantra until sunrise, one becomes a master of all supernatural powers (siddhis);
having diligently placed a corpse upon one's own lap at the foot of a bilva tree.
Having gazed with the Nṛsiṃha-mudrā, a person should recite the Mātṛkā;
having recited it there a thousand times, he shall become a master of all supernatural powers (siddhis).
Taking up water-pots and adorned with garlands of skulls,
they applied a forehead mark with that very [substance] and were embellished by its ashes.
And by reciting it once in a cremation ground, one becomes a master of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhīśvara*).
[One should prepare] sandalwood with saffron, agallochum, musk, yellow orpiment, and so forth.
Having prepared camphor, saffron, and yellow sandalwood in equal proportions together, one should then prepare each of them individually.
The hero should collect blood from the tip of his tongue and from the sky;
having made a pill with that very substance, he should mutter the mantra of Bhadrakālī.
Having applied a tilaka on his forehead, the practitioner himself, free from fear, [should worship] Nīlā, Anīlapatākā, Lalajjihvā, and Karālikā.
At the conjunction of the Mahāṣṭamī and Navamī, standing before [the deity],
one should cast the corpses of goats, buffaloes, and rams in the four directions.
Having spread out a headless trunk with a shaven tail, adorned with lamps and other ornaments,
and having bound it in the middle, he there assumed the form of a Gandharva.
Having filled his mouth with betel-leaf and anointed his eyes with collyrium,
and having meditated upon himself as the mantra, he shall become the lord of all supernatural powers (siddhis).

O Goddess, O Pārvatī, the seed-syllable for each individual substance, as well as for those combined together, consists of the sky (viyat), conjoined with fire (vahni), followed by the end of the eye (netrānta), and adorned by the moon (candrabhūṣita).
The knower of mantras should recite the root mantra three hundred times and more, saying:
"O Cāmuṇḍā of terrible sound, seize the blood upon the tip of [his] tongue!"
"Having accepted the offering, grant a boon in the stainless sky!
O Kālikā, fierce and terrible one! Then [recite] the weapon-mantra (astra) and then the armor-mantra (kavaca)."
This Kālikā has been fully described out of a desire for the welfare of heroes;
O Great Goddess, the pair of kūrca-mantras belonging to Nīlā has been told to you.
O Goddess, [one should utter] *viyadbhṛguvalaṃ*, *valāmitra*, and *valīrati*;
then, joined with *candrakhaṇḍa*, one should speak the word *nīra*.
The mantra is considered to be the eastern peak-syllable ending with *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*.
This great vidyā has been kept secret, but it has been spoken here out of affection for you.
O Dear One, the great vidyā Ugracaṇḍā was previously described;
she is called Lalajjihvikā and should be employed in the practice of Nīla.
That very Vidyā who is Mahātārā is celebrated as Karālī;
when conjoined with the son of the Earth (Mars) on the new moon day, she bestows auspiciousness.
O auspicious lady, by means of the Puṣkara conjunction, that most excellent of heroes should bring Viṣṇukrāntā and cast it upon lands where death has occurred.
Having prepared that [offering] there on the day of the deceased's anniversary,
one should cause a single fish prepared there to be offered with a trident.
And with that water, perform an aspersion over the corpse as before;
then, having prepared the *vijayā* plant, insert it into his belly through the passage of the mouth.
Having cast [the seed] there, one with eyes anointed with collyrium should dig up the fish;
then, having risen, one should recite the mantra with *tilakī* and the previously mentioned substance.
There, the Blessed Lord Bhairava himself is indeed marked with a *la*;
seeing him as he wanders here and there, the hero should mutter the mantra.
O Goddess, if by the power of fortune a staff is obtained there,
then he himself becomes Bhairava and he himself becomes Vīreśvara.
O Goddess of gods, having brought a fish, one should cast it into a dead lake;
by reciting [the mantra] there even once, the union with the deity occurs.
There, O noble lady, having bowed to Mahādeva and Mahādevī and having applied that ash as a tilaka, you yourself shall become Vīreśvarī.
At night, at the marketplace of the dead, the madman Nandabhairava appeared—
naked, stainless, adorned with ashes, and with disheveled hair.
O Great Goddess, if one who bears a skull and holds a sword in hand should recite [the mantra] with the Mātṛkā, then all accomplishments will rest in his hand.
Having brought there a ḍākinī, a yoginī, or even another woman of noble family, and having worshipped her, one shall become a master of all siddhis.
For the accomplishment of the Blue One, one may perform the Heroic Accomplishment (vīrasādhana) using all lifeless beings, with the exception of a Brahmin, a cow, or a woman.
In some places, there is a reading: "he abandoned the *brāhmaṇa-gomaya*.
In that case, the suffix *maṣaṭ* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*), and thus the word *gomaya* here has the meaning of *gā* (cow).
O Goddess, if one worships Pārvatī Śivā without the corpse-seat (mṛtāsana),
one shall dwell in that terrible state until the dissolution of all things (pralaya).
The great *sādhana*s are praised when the primary means and the desired object are at hand;
for practitioners, even the minor ones are recommended, as all grant excellent accomplishments.
Thus, O Goddess, O sinless one, the sequence of the Blue One has been told to you;
out of love for me, O Maheśvarī, it must not be spoken of to anyone.
Now follows the procedure for the unadorned heroic accomplishment (*vīrasādhana*) of Vīracūḍāmaṇi.
Alternatively, O Brahmin, I shall describe the means of accomplishment in another way: having carefully purified the place of recitation by digging it out with effort.
In the center of that, one should offer the bali-oblation and draw a triangular yantra;
having placed a great conch and the five skulls in its center.
There, one should perform the extraction and other rites for a great preta with an unbroken body and beautiful form, and bathe it according to the prescribed ritual.
Having caused her to put on red garments, eye-salve is prescribed; one should place betel and other items in her mouth and apply red sandalwood paste to her forehead.
One should draw the yantra upon the heart, a triangle in the center of a lotus;
then, one should draw the worship-yantra on the forehead with a weapon.
On the head, the shoulder, as well as the hand, the foot, and likewise the waist,
the wise man should place pieces of wood such as khadira and others as playthings.
One should fasten a rope there, binding it with a firm knot;
one should offer an oblation (bali) into six vessels, separately at each and every stake.
One should perform the ritual offering with black gram, meat, fish, milk-rice, the three kinds of liquor,
sweetmeats, and cakes, along with milk.
Having uttered the seed-syllable of armor (huṃ), which consists of the Lord of Wrath (krodhīśa) mounted upon fire (ra), with the fourth vowel (au) and the bindu, one should then say "Śmaśānakālikā."
Having inscribed the primordial seed-syllable (*pūrvabīja*), the supreme mantra ends with the weapon-syllable (*astra*).
Having uttered the illusion-seed-syllable (*māyābīja*), [one enters] the cremation ground...

Another [account] has been compiled and set forth in the Merutantra.
I shall speak regarding rites performed for specific desires; therein, first, pacification (śānti) is described.
Pacification is that which destroys the diseases, malevolent spells, and other afflictions of human beings.

One should divide the day and night into six parts; the fifth part is the bridge for the rite of pacification (śāntika), which should be performed during the winter when the moon does not waver from the asterism Āsādha.
Then,
having emanated a square mandala of white color upon that water element, one should perform the rite of pacification therein.
One should first worship the water with the seed-syllable *vaṃ*; in this rite of pacification (*śāntika*), one should perform the pacifying ritual while facing the north.
One who delights in rites for pacification and the like is worthy of worship; one should display the lotus mudrā.
Seated in the lotus posture and ending with "namaḥ," this is the mantra for pacification.
For pacification, one should offer oblations of ghee upon a seat of *kuśa* grass while employing the deer-mudrā;
when the oblation is offered there while releasing the little finger, it becomes nectar-like.
In the three previous intermediate births, there would be pacification (śāntika).
Alternatively, I shall certainly explain that which brings about self-control over gods,
Rākṣasas, kings, people, serpents, women, horses, and elephants.
In the first watch, the rite of subjugation succeeds during the spring season;
at that time, the wind does not flow through the left nostril, but rather the fire element flows.
For the rite of subjugation (vaśya), one should perform the worship of the fire with the seed-syllable *raṃ* within a triangular copper vessel;
having fashioned it red in color, one should perform the subjugation facing the east.
One should worship Vāṇī and display the Pāśa-mudrā;
having ascended the Svastika-āsana, one should recite the mantra ending with "svāhā."
For subjugation by means of a goat-skin, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the deer-seal (*mṛgamudrā*);
in this case, the oblation is to be performed with red substances, and the visualization (*dhyāna*) is considered to be of a reddish hue.
In the asterism Mṛgaśīrṣa, Puṣya, and Anurādhā, Viśākhā and Kṛttikā are present here.
Now I shall describe the ritual pillar (staṃbha), which wards off such exertion and subdues the fury of elephant-kings, serpents, tigers, and the like.
In the winter season, immobilization is prescribed during the sixth portion of the day;
this applies to fire, water, serpents, enraged beings, and venomous fanged creatures.
Having gone to the ground on one's knees, one should perform the rite of immobilization (stambhana);
it effects the immobilization of paramours, thieves, diseases, and of dharmas, ghosts, and other malevolent spirits.
If the wind, joined with the nose-staff (the breath), should arise,
then one should perform the act of stabilization by means of the syllable *laṃ*, which is the seed-syllable of the Earth.
One should worship her in the mandala endowed with eight vajras.
Facing east, one should perform the rite of subduing (staṃbhaṇa) and worship Ramā there;
for the goddess Vikaṭāsanā, one should display the mace-mudrā (gadā-mudrā).
For the rite of immobilization (staṃbhana), the homa-mantra is proclaimed to end with "vaṣaṭ.
For immobilization, an elephant skin is the seat; likewise, for seizing, it is the deer-seal (mṛgīmudrā).
In this rite, the oblation is performed with yellow substances, and one should wear yellow garments and so forth oneself;
for the purpose of immobilization (staṃbhanam), the asterisms are Bharaṇī, Citrā, Rohiṇī, and the three Uttaras.
Now I shall describe the rite of causing enmity; it results in the destruction of affection between two parties.
In the summer season, the rite of enmity should be performed during the second sixth-part of the day.
When the wind is situated in the middle of the nose, the piercing of the void (kha) and the other elements is prescribed;
one should worship the void (kha) within a circular mandala of smoky color.
O Lord, one should perform the rite of hatred with the seed-syllable *haṃ*, facing the southwest;
Dhūmāvatī is to be worshipped in hatred, and the mudrā should be the mace (*muśala*).
The *home-mantra* (the root mantra) ending with *phaṭ* should be used here while seated on a rough seat;
for the rite of inciting hatred (*vidveṣa*), one should use the skin of a jackal or even a seat made of iron.
The practitioner should offer oblations of smoke-colored substances and wear similar clothing and so forth.
The four stars beginning with Ārdrā, as well as Mūla and Jyeṣṭhā, are considered suitable for the rite of inciting enmity (vidveṣaṇa).
Now I shall describe the rite of eradication (uccāṭana), which is the expulsion of enemies;
it is recommended for eradication during the rainy season at the third and sixth parts of the day.
When the wind falls obliquely, the wind blows there.
One should perform the eradication of the enemy; one should worship him with the seed-syllable *yaṃ*.
O Vāyu, the maṇḍala is hexagonal, black, and marked with six dots;
there, for the rite, one should sit upon a deer-skin facing the northwest.
One should worship Durgā and display the mudrā named Aśani;
mounted upon the Vajrāsana, the mantra for the fire-oblation ends with "phaṭ."
For the purpose of satiation (tarpaṇa), one should bring water mixed with the blood of a ram;
for the rite of eradication (uccāṭana), the visualization (dhyāna) should be smoky-colored, and likewise, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with black substances.
Uccāṭana (the rite of eradication) is recommended during the signs of the zodiac that are swift and mobile.
The act of killing is said to be the taking of life from one's enemies;
however, in the rite of killing, one should avoid Brahmins as well as others who are very righteous.
One should employ women against those enemies of the king who are other than children;
one may do so either because of one's own faults or for the sake of protecting the people.
But a practitioner of mantra should not perform a rite of killing out of greed or fear;
O Goddess, an expiation must be performed for the pacification of that fault.
One should recite the mantra ten thousand times and likewise perform as many oblations with milk-rice mixed with ghee,
or with black sesame seeds drenched in ghee.
The wise should always perform self-protection at the time of ritual action;
specifically, during the fourth and sixth parts of the day for the rites of subduing and killing in the autumn season.
In the rites of subjugation and killing, the worship and other rituals should be performed within a fire-maṇḍala;
facing south, one should perform the rite and worship Bhadrakālī.
One should display the sword-mudrā, enter the auspicious seat (bhadrāsana),
and perform the fire offering with that mantra consisting of the syllable *huṃ*, using either buffalo-horn or iron [as the fuel].
The posture is the Sūkarī-mudrā, which arises from the contraction of the hands;
one should perform meditation on the black-colored [deity] and worship with black substances.
When one's own [planetary] strength, such as that of the Moon, is in the houses of Ugra, Tīkṣṇa, or Iṣudhi,
and the enemy's strength is absent from these, one stands upon a single foot.
For the purpose of satiation, one should use warm water with black pepper;
