however, for killing, one should remain standing, or else place one's foot upon the ground while performing the rite of killing.
Having entered the unbaked vessel, one should perform the libation there.
Now, the miscellaneous rites and those involving extreme sorcery will be described;
in those cases, one should perform them facing south, seated upon the skin of a ewe.
Or, having gone to a seat of iron, one should perform the oblation with the *sūkaryā* mudrā;
one who practices facing west performs the rite that brings about the attainment of wealth.
Mṛgaśīrṣa, Antyā (Revatī), and Citrā are among the Mitra-nakṣatras; meditation upon the gods therein is of the rājasa nature.
For the purpose of delusion (moha), one should recite the mantra ending with "svāhā" while using a seat made of cowhide (gocarma).
One should employ water mixed with turmeric for the purpose of libation;
moreover, the asterisms Svātī and Rohiṇī are excellent for that, as is a comfortable seat.
Now, one should accomplish all fierce rites under the asterism Raudra;
for various kinds of tasks, a tiger skin is prescribed.
With a steady mind, one should meditate on everything as having the appearance of jewels,
endowed with a shower of nectar, and possessing a radiance equal to the full moon.
One should meditate on such a form for the accomplishment of all tasks;
however, for the sake of longevity and for listening [to the scriptures], one should meditate on the deity in his rājasa aspect.
The three [nakṣatras] beginning with Pūrvā and ending with Uttarā are declared to conquer untimely death;
the *homa* mantra ends with *vaṣaṭ*, and one should meditate upon the Rājasa deity.
One should perform the rite of attraction facing the southeast (the fire corner);
everything stated for subjugation is to be understood as applicable here for the successful accomplishment of the task of attraction.
For the sake of accomplishing all-knowledge, one should face Īśāna;
for all activities involving specialized knowledge, a white woolen rug serves as the seat.
In rites for flowers and other offerings, the mantra is joined with the syllable *vauṣaṭ* and the *pallava*;
the *haṃsī* and *tarjanī* gestures are released as the *mudrā* during nourishing (*pauṣṭika*) homas.
As it has been said: "In rites for nourishment (pauṣṭika), one should perform meditation on the deity;
for the destruction of fear in all circumstances, the mantra is offered with 'vaṣaṭ' at its end."
Meditation accompanied by the great *śoṣa* (drying) rite should be performed when there is fear of enemies;
for rites involving the breaking of mantras, the mantra used in the fire-oblation (*homa*) should end with *vaṣaṭ*.
In the Khaḍana [rite], there should be the utterance of "phaṭ"; the homa and meditation, however, are of a tamasic nature.
For the sake of happiness, one should perform the japa facing north during the Ruruvārma [rite].
In battle, one should meditate upon the Tāmasa deity as being like the fire at the end of an aeon.
Now I shall describe which feet and which deities are to be worshipped.
One should always worship Vighna on the day of his lunar mansion (Vāra), Śauca, and Tithīśvara;
thereafter, Kṣetreśa and the presiding deities of those respective rites are to be worshipped.
Then one should worship the chosen deity (iṣṭadeva) and thereafter perform the fire sacrifice (homa);
in due order, [one worships] the two Lords of the Gate, Sūrya, Śiva, Soma, and Ambikā.
One should worship Guha, Aṅgāraka, Agni, Viṣṇu, Caturvaktra, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Indu, Īśa, Kāla, and Sūrya at the beginning of the [planetary] sequence.
Brahmā, the Creator, Viṣṇu, Yama, the Moon, Guha, Indra,
the Vasus, the Nāgas, Dharma, Śiva, and the Sun.
Kandarpa, Kali, the Viśvedevas, and the Pitṛs;
the Guru, the serpents, the Pitṛs, Bhaga, Yama, and Divākara; Tvaṣṭṛ, Vāyu, then Indra and Agni—the two—and Mitra, the lord of the gods.
Nirṛti, Jala, the Viśvedevas, Vidhi, Hari,
the Vasus, Varuṇa, Ojaikapāt, Ahi, Budhnya, and Ūṣaka.
These twenty-eight lords of the constellations, beginning with Aśvinī,
are accompanied by the syllable Om at the beginning, the dative case ending, and the word "namaḥ."
The name-mantras of these [deities] should be taken up for the practice of worship and other rites;
one who has mastered the mantra should perform the rites for specific desires, and not otherwise.
If these rites are performed erroneously, one shall fall into hell;
therefore, one who is devoted to the guru, pure and bathed, and knowledgeable in the procedure for rites performed for specific desires [should perform them].
One may perform rites for the fulfillment of desires for oneself or for others;
if one is the most excellent among those who know the mantras, one may perform the six duties for the sake of another.
One should perform these [rites] for these very persons alone, and never for others—
whether they be a king, a prince, a wealthy man, or anyone else.
It shall belong to one who is a believer, devoted, who has acquired wealth through righteous means,
who is grateful, generous, and a worshiper of the guru and the gods.
The preceptor should perform the ritual for one who is well-behaved and deeply devoted;
whether it be a king, another person, or a practitioner, having first prostrated before him.
Then, according to the procedure prescribed for initiation, the practitioner should choose an officiant;
he should remain restrained, perfectly satisfied with him, and pure.
Having conquered the senses, subdued anger, and being free from the agitation of pride,
one who is devoted to the daily and occasional rites may perform various types of optional (kāmya) rituals.
Having performed the cruel rite as prescribed, one should perform an oil massage;
then, having bathed, one should worship the chosen deity together with the retinue and the limbs.
One should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times for the sake of protection;
having said, "Protect me, protect me," and having bowed to the deity, one should dismiss it.
One should, however, have one's own protection ensured by other very affectionate friends,
through mantras such as the Mṛtyuñjaya and others, and by means of service to the Sun and the offering of arghya.
And through recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and the like, as well as by propitiating Brahmins and so forth,
the ritual application should be performed correctly according to the guru and likewise according to the scriptures.
Having understood this through practice, one should act accordingly; otherwise, one will encounter suffering.
Therefore, the king who causes the rite to be performed should gratify the practitioner with wealth.
Having prostrated repeatedly, one should act in such a way as to bring her satisfaction;
for one whose mantra is perfected, the six supernatural powers (ṣaṭkarmāṇi) are accomplished without a doubt.
If one who has not attained perfection performs it, he will certainly fail and incur the curse of the deity.
Likewise.
For those who perform rites for the fulfillment of desires, there is no world beyond;
the fruit they consider to exist is merely the success of the ritual performance itself.
For a single injunction, O Goddess of Gods, no two fruits are ever seen anywhere; therefore, one should worship the deity without desire for rewards.
Likewise.
One should perform the six rites for oneself and for others by means of oblations, libations, mantras, and various specific meditations.
The practitioner of mantras should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times through the yoga of meditation and ritual placement,
for the sake of pacifying defects in the ritual application and for the sake of self-protection.
If he does not obtain the fruit, he shall incur the curse of the deity.
The signs [of success] are a flame with the brilliance of fire, a smoky color, a fragrant scent, and well-formed crests.
Having understood the messenger, his gestures, and so forth, one should declare the auspicious or inauspicious results;
as well as the contemplation of the essence of mantras and the characteristics such as the possession of the body.
Devotion to the guru should always be practiced, especially at the time of performing ritual actions;
for both worldly and transcendental goals, the guru is the supreme deity.
Killing, expulsion, and other such rites are practiced by those on the left-hand path who pursue trivial ends;
these low deities accomplish such things, for they are not capable of bestowing true happiness.
But for those who are intent on the welfare of others, through the destruction of their enemies,
whatever is desired— such as wealth and so forth— is not established merely by that much.
They offer libations from the right side, yet they sometimes commit evil deeds; for the sake of obtaining authority and other gains, they act exactly as those who are harmful.
Therefore, for them there is an increase of lineage and an eternal world beyond.
Thus is the method stated in the Merutantra.
The knowledge of the seasons is as follows in another tantra:
Starting from sunrise, the seasons beginning with spring occur in succession every ten ghaṭikās throughout each day and night, day after day.
Spring, summer, the rainy season, autumn, winter, and the dewy season—
winter is declared for rites of pacification, and spring for the rite of subjugation.

The cold season (śiśira) is known for paralyzing; the summer (grīṣma) is said to be for creating enmity; the rainy season (prāvṛṣ) is known for driving away; and autumn (śarat) is for the rite of killing.
In the Phetkāriṇī Tantra.
One should draw the rite of immobilization (staṃbhanam) in a jar during the rising of Leo or Scorpio;
rites such as inciting hatred (dveṣa) and expulsion (uccāṭana) during the rising of Capricorn, Cancer, or Libra.
In Gemini, Sagittarius, and Pisces, one performs rites of subjugation, pacification, and nourishment;
in the eighth sign from the enemy's [ascendant], one performs killing, cutting, and other forms of suppression.
Harvyakṣa is a lion; Kromakara is a crab; Kulīra is a crab; Aja is a ram; Meṣa is a ram; Yama is Gemini.
Likewise.

For rites such as subjugation (*vaśya*), the pen should be made of *dūrvā* grass; for attracting (*karṣaṇa*), it should be made from a peacock feather; and for inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*), expulsion (*uccāṭana*), and even killing (*māraṇa*), it should be made from a crow’s wing.
One should visualize the color red for subjugation, attraction, and immobilization;
and white for neutralizing poison, pacification, nourishment, and restoration.
One should visualize [the deity] as yellow for acts of immobilization, smoke-colored for eradication,
resembling a sapphire for insanity, and black for the rite of killing.
The *sāttvika* [form] is for those desiring liberation; the *rājasa* is for those wishing for sovereignty;
and the *tāmasa* is for the destruction of enemies and the warding off of all diseases.
For the sake of pacifying all calamities, one should meditate upon Tāma.
In the Kulaprakāśatantra.
One should worship with white substances for pacification (śānti); with reddish ones for the rite of subjugation (vaśya);
with yellow-colored substances for paralyzing (stambhana); and one should worship with smoky-colored substances for causing enmity (vidveṣaṇa).
In rites of eradication and killing, one should worship with black substances;
at that time, one should likewise adorn oneself with garments and other items of a similar nature.
Rati, Vāṇī, Ramā, Jyeṣṭhā, Durgā, and Kālī are declared to be the deities of the six rites respectively; one should worship them at the beginning of each rite.
In the Kātyāyana-abhicāra [rite], the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is a village of monkeys;
a red garment is prescribed, and a red turban is traditionally taught.
In the north, a sacrificial thread made of gold or of a foul color is prescribed;
for the rites of paralysis and inciting enmity, it is said to be made from the entrails of a cat.
The wise have declared that a sacrificial thread produced from the entrails of a cock is the sacred thread (upavīta) for the purpose of exorcising vāka-demons.
The sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra) produced from an owl's entrails is for the rite of killing;
for subjugation and attracting, it should consist of sacrificial food (haviṣya); and for paralyzing, milk-rice (pāyasa) is prescribed.
In rites for causing enmity, there should be mung beans; in rites dedicated to Vāyu, wheat;
at the end of the Śyāmaka rite, lentil food; and in rites for Śālī rice, goat's milk porridge.
"It shall be food for the act of killing"—thus is the restraint regarding food declared.
Likewise, there are the lotus posture (padmāsana), the auspicious posture (svastika), the wide-stride posture (vikaṭa), and the cock posture (kukkuṭa).
The wise declare that the *vajra*, the *bhadraka*, and so forth are the seats (*āsana*).
The definition has been stated in another tantra:
Having placed the left foot upon the right thigh and likewise the right foot upon the left thigh,
holding them firmly with both hands according to the prescribed method,
one should place the two thumbs at the heart and, looking at the tip of the nose, gaze with the chin [held steady]; this is Vyādhi-bandha.
For those who have mastered the arts and sciences, the lotus posture (padmāsana) is prescribed.
Placing both soles of the feet properly between the knees and the thighs,
sitting with the body straight— this is declared to be the Svastika posture.
Placing one foot upon one thigh while the other thigh is likewise positioned [upon the other foot],
this is declared to be the vikaṭāsana posture.
Having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana) by placing the hands on the ground with one hand over the knee and the other over the thigh,
and having established [the body] in the sky, this is the cock posture (kukkuṭāsana).
Having placed the left ankle above the penis,
and likewise having placed the other ankle upon that, this is declared to be the vajrāsana.
One should place [the feet] at the ankle-joints below the testicles, on both sides of the perineal seam;
then, holding the sides and feet firmly with the hands, one should remain perfectly motionless.
This Bhadrasana destroys all diseases;
I shall now describe its foundation and the application of honey according to the Tantras.
For the attainment of all perfections, a leopard skin [is used]; for the attainment of knowledge, a deer skin;
a cloth seat removes disease, while one made of cane increases prosperity.
Silk is said to be nourishing, while woolen cloth brings liberation from suffering;
for malevolent rites (abhicāra) black color is used, and red for rites such as subjugation (vaśya).
In rites for pacification, white is prescribed; variegated for all rites;
for paralyzing, elephant hide; and likewise for killing, buffalo hide.
Likewise, the skin of a ewe is for exorcism (uccāṭana), that of a rhinoceros for the rite of subjugation (vaśya);
the skin of a jackal is prescribed for causing enmity (vidveṣa), and the skin of a goat is used for the rite of pacification (śāntika).
The rite of subjugation (vaśīkaraṇa) should be performed in an auspicious temple;
the rite of pacification (śāntika) should be performed in one's home; and the cruel rite (krūra-karma) should be performed in a cremation ground.
Alternatively, all the ritual actions may take place in the deity’s abode;
the six mudrās should be known in sequence as those of the lotus, the noose, and the mace-marked [weapon].
One should display the mudrās known as the pestle (muśala), the thunderbolt (śani), and the sword (khaḍga) in rites such as those for peace;
having brought the two hands together facing each other, they should be slightly bent with the fingers raised.
With the thumbs joined within the palms, this is the mudrā known as Padma;
[it is formed] by the index finger of the left fist touching the index finger of the right fist.
Having joined the tips of the two thumbs, one should place them upon the tips of the two index fingers;
this is proclaimed by the learned as the *pāśāhvayā* (noose-named) mudrā.
Having placed the two hands facing each other with the fingers interlaced,
one should further join the two middle fingers and extend them well.
This is declared to be the mudrā of the mace, which increases the satisfaction of Viṣṇu:
having formed a fist with both hands, place the right hand over the left.
This is the Muśala-mudrā, which destroys all obstacles;
by joining the little finger and the thumb, it becomes triangular and is designated as that of Śani.
Having joined the little finger and the ring finger with one's own right thumb,
while the remaining fingers are extended and pressed together, this is the sword mudrā (khaḍgamudrikā).
The square, the half-moon, the triangle, the hexagon,
and the circle are, in sequence, the forms of the mandalas of Earth and the other elements.
One should visualize the mandala of wind at the navel, yellow, white, red, black, and smoke-colored in sequence,
conjoined with its seed-syllable.
One should contemplate the triangular, reddish-pink mandala of fire in the heart;
one should remember the square, yellow mandala of earth at the throat.
Upon the forehead is a half-moon marked with a white lotus;
on the crown of the head is a circular sphere of space (vyomamaṇḍala) with the appearance of a smoky color.
One should contemplate consciousness within these [elements], conjoined with their respective seed-syllables.
For rites of pacification (śānti), water is prescribed; for rites of immobilization (staṃbha) and subjugation (vaśya), fire is declared.
For the rite of immobilization (staṃbhanam), the Earth element is praised; for causing enmity (vidveṣaḥ), the Ether is proclaimed;
for expulsion (uccāṭanam), the Wind is used; and for killing (māraṇam), Fire is considered best.
When each respective fear arises, the practitioner of mantra, with a sharpened mind, should properly perform that specific rite conjoined with its corresponding maṇḍala.
The movement of the earth is rod-like, beneath both its hemispheres;
that of water is upward; and that of fire is upward as well; while the movement of the wind is horizontal.
Movement occurs in the middle of space; the arising of beings is said to be in earth.
One should perform paralyzing (staṃbhanam) in earth and subjugation (vaśyam) in air.
The rites of pacification (śāntika) and enrichment (pauṣṭika) belong to the element of water;
those of killing (māraṇa) and so forth belong to the wind element; and the rites of expulsion (uccāṭana) against adversaries and the like belong to fire.
The destruction of obstacles and the like is prescribed at the rising of the sky;
the five elements, beginning with earth, are known as the kalās starting with Nivṛtti.

Cessation (nivṛtti) shall be self-established; immediately following it is the twofold Peace (śānti), and beyond that is known as Beyond-Peace (śāntyatītā). These [states] are to be worshipped in their respective places.
The addition of the name at the end of the mantra is called the "sprout" (pallava);
it is used for killing, neutralizing poison, and subduing planetary and demonic influences.
In rites of eradication and causing enmity, a sprout is highly recommended;
the placement of the mantra at the end of the name is designated as "yoga."
In rites for pacification, nourishment, subjugation, expiation, and purification,
as well as in rites for deluding and inflaming, the wise employ the yoga.
He is said to be employed for the rites of paralyzing (staṃbhana), expelling (uccāṭana), destroying (uccheda), and causing enmity (vidveṣa).
The mantra is intended to be a "blockage" (rodha) when placed at the beginning, end, and middle of the name.
It is taught as a means for bringing mantras face-to-face, for warding off all diseases,
and for pacifying the afflictions caused by fevers, seizing spirits, poisons, and pains.

Furthermore, in the case of deluding, one should employ those same [syllables] as well as the syllables of the mantra's name; that which consists of each syllable separated by one [intervening syllable] is proclaimed to be the "stringing together" (grathana).
In rites for pacification, that mantra which begins with the name should be placed at the beginning and end;
when it is thus enclosed on both sides, it is defined as being for the rite of pinning (kīlana).
In the divine *mṛtyuñjaya* pillar, there is a divine enclosure (*saṃpuṭa*) consisting of the two mantra syllables,
with each syllable of the name of the person to be accomplished [placed] between them in sequence.
That [mantra] is said to be used for subjugation, attraction, and nourishment when recited over the Vidarbhita [syllables];
however, in cases of subjugation, attraction, torment, and fever, one should employ *svāhā*.
The wise should employ "Namaḥ" for the pacification of anger, for tranquility, and for generating affection;
and "Vauṣaṭ" for enchantment, stimulation, nourishment, and the conquest of death.
The syllable *huṃ* is used for the destruction of joy, as well as for cutting, killing, expulsion, and causing enmity; *vauṣaṭ* is for blinding, and *vaṣaṭ* is likewise.
In the rite of kindling the staff, *vaṣaṭ* is prescribed for both gain and loss;
the classes of mantras are of two kinds, distinguished by mantra and vidyā.
Mantras should be known as having male deities, while Vidyās have female deities;
furthermore, all mantras are declared to possess the nature of female, male, or neuter.
Mantras for males should end in *huṃ* and *phaṭ*; those for females are considered to end in *svāhā*; and those for neuters should end in *namaḥ*. Thus, mantras are divided into three types.
These three types of mantras are taught for the purposes of subjugation, empowerment, and malevolent rites;
one should understand that these mantras possess the nature of both Agni and Soma, corresponding to the cruel and the gentle respectively.
At the end of the *karma* [mantras] and *vahni* [mantras], the *tārā* [mantras] are said to consist mostly of ether (*viyat*);
the *āgneya* *manavas* consist mostly of moon (*indu*), while the *saumya* ones consist of the syllables of death (*mṛta*).
When the vital breath moves in the right [nostril], the fiery [planets] become awakened;
and when the vital breath remains in the other [left] portion, the lunar [planets] attain awakening.
When the vital breath has entered both channels, all awakenings arise;
those who are awakened always proclaim the fruit for the practitioners of mantra.
The colors of the moon, water, earth, ether, air,
and fire are the seed-syllables (bījas) of the mantras for the six rites, respectively.
In the *Mantradevatāprakāśikā*, however:
One should employ "svāhā" in rites of subjugation, attraction, burning, and fire-offerings;
one should utter "namaḥ" for the pacification of anger, for propitiation, and during worship.
Vauṣaṭ is used for enchantment, for crossing over [difficulties], for nourishment, and for victory over death;
likewise, the syllable Huṃ is used for the destruction of affection, as well as for cutting and killing.
In rites of eradication and incantation, as well as in the act of causing enmity, one should use "phaṭ.
For the destruction of obstacles and malevolent planets, one should employ the utterance "huṃ phaṭ."
In the rite of illuminating the mantra, gain and loss are considered to be *vaṣaṭ*;
thus, one should employ the mantra according to the specific ritual action.
In the Śambhunityātantra:
The various classifications of mantras, beginning with the "strung" (grathita), shall now be explained:
the strung (grathita), the encapsulated (saṃpuṭa), the swallowed (grasta), the combined (samasta), and the interlaced (vidarbhita).
Likewise, there is the *ākrānta*, which occupies the beginning and end; the *garbhastha*, which is surrounded on all sides; likewise the *yukti*; the *vidarbha*; and the *vidarbhagrathita*.
Thus, these eleven types of mantras, when employed, grant the accomplishment of one's purpose;
each single syllable of the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) is joined with a syllable of the mantra.
That is declared to be "grathita" (strung together), which is supreme for subjugation and summoning.
One should utter the entire mantra at the beginning, followed immediately by the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
Furthermore, when the mantra is reversed at the end, it is known as "encased" (saṃpuṭa);
it should be understood as effecting pacification and nourishment, and bestowing sovereignty over the three worlds.
The wise practitioner should place half of the mantra at the beginning and half at the end;
that which is placed in the middle and at the end is the object to be accomplished (sādhya), and this is called "the swallowed" (grasta).
In all rites of sorcery and in acts of killing, one should employ [the name];
first one should utter the designation, and afterwards the mantra should likewise follow.
This entire [mantra] is said to cause the eradication of enemies;
therein, two mantra-syllables correspond to each single syllable of the name of the target (sādhya).
That which is interspersed with mantras is said to destroy evil, bring subjugation, and provide protection;
it remains effective provided the object of the rite (sādhya) stands in equal measure.
One should recognize that [the breath] as it has entered [the central channel] bestows the immediate accomplishment of all aims;
however, when situated within the womb [of the central channel], it is used with the *samāna* wind for rites of subjugation and eradication.
One should utter the mantra once at the beginning, and likewise the mantra again at the end;
that which is to be accomplished (sādhya) should be placed in the middle—this they know as the "beginning and end" [structure].
For those who are joined in mutual affection,
one should employ the supreme mantra that causes estrangement twice— both at the beginning and at the end.
The name of the person to be accomplished written once in the middle is called the "womb-thread" (garbhastantu);
when employed, it effects the killing, expulsion, or subjugation of men.

One should recite the entire mantra three times for the purpose of the army, the intellect, the womb, and the pillar, as well as for movement; likewise, one should recite it three times again at the end.
If it is accomplished once, it becomes middling; one should know that to be surrounded on all sides, which pacifies all calamities and wards off great death.
It generates all auspiciousness and is the supreme nectar for the deceased;
one should first write the mantra, then the name, and again the mantra.
In the same way, by dividing it threefold and interweaving it with the *yukti*,
it is declared to be the remover of all diseases and the crusher of *bhūtas* and epilepsy.
Having made each individual syllable of the object to be accomplished interwoven with the mantra as previously described, one should arrange another [syllable] at its beginning and end.
This supreme characteristic of mantra, known as the Vidarbha-grathita,
is declared to accomplish all rites and bestow the fruit of all sovereign powers.
In this very way, the ritual applications of one who has mastered the mantra grant success,
provided they are well-mastered through the oral tradition or perfected under a guru.
And those that are self-established; thus all mantras are considered to be of three kinds.
Likewise.
Japa is the repetition of syllables; its divisions and sub-divisions consist of reciting with high, low, and circumflex tones, using words and syllables that are clearly articulated.
One should utter [the mantra] with speech; that is called vocal recitation (vācika-japa).
One should utter the mantra slowly and move the lips slightly.
That which is barely audible to the ear is known as whispered recitation (upāṃśu-japa);
that which is performed solely with the tongue by the wise is to be understood as vocal recitation (jihvā-japa).
If one should utter the mantra mentally with focused meditation, that is called mental recitation (mānasa-japa). Whispered recitation (upāṃśu) is ten times superior to loud recitation (uccair-japa).

Recitation with the tongue is a hundredfold [more effective], while mental recitation is a thousandfold. Mental recitation is for those desiring spiritual accomplishments (siddhi), whereas whispered recitation is for those desiring nourishment (puṣṭi).
In the case of killing, verbal recitation is indeed declared to be the recommended form of japa.
Likewise.
When preceded by the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ), it grants liberation; when preceded by the *śrī* seed-syllable (*śrīṃ*), it brings the arrival of wealth;
and when preceded by *hṛllekhā* (*hrīṃ*), it bestows great siddhis and brings all under one's control.
O best of men, this Vidyā begins with the syllable Vāgbhava; beginning with Kāma, it is the undeceivable one.
In the Rudrayāmala.
One should recite with the gaze directed upward for pacification; for subjugation, with the gaze directed downward;
for immobilization, with a steady, level gaze; and for the subsequent [rites], by looking toward the side.
In cases of conflict, eradication, and killing, one should gaze at the sun;
for the sake of acquiring knowledge, while standing in the midst of water, one should gaze at the solar disc.
O Goddess, by gazing at the space between the eyebrows, there is liberation, peace, and all that is auspicious; O Goddess, by gazing at the tip of the nose, there is success in every auspicious rite.
In the Merutantra:
One should always perform the recitation with the hands, never with a rosary during the ritual application;
for the rosary prescribed for the ritual application is according to the specific nature of each rite.
In the Tantraśekhara:
For subjugation (*vaśya*), there should be a rosary of lotus seeds; for pacification (*śānti*), it should be made of conch shell.
For immobilization (*stambha*), it should consist of *nimba* or *ariṣṭa* wood; for inciting enmity (*dveṣaṇa*), it should be made from the teeth of a corpse.
A tooth from a horse is for causing expulsion (uccāṭana), while one from a donkey is for killing (māraṇa).
In the Tantra.
A rosary fashioned from rudrākṣas fulfills all desires;
one made of conch shells bestows wealth and fame.
The rosary of lotus seeds always bestows nourishment, fortune, and the destruction of enemies;
it grants sons, long life, and the abundance of cattle and grain.
A garland adorned with pearls bestows abundant good fortune and prosperity;
when consecrated with mantras, it grants the power of flight, as well as the accomplishments of pacification and enrichment.
Likewise, even a crystal rosary bestows liberation;
a ruby rosary [bestows] eloquence, and similarly, one of emerald [bestows] abundant wealth.
A golden or silver garland bestows all desires; one made of coral, when used during the Sārasvata [rite], brings about subjugation and the arrival of abundant wealth.
A rosary fashioned from all these materials— beginning with *kauśī* and *rudrākṣa*, and ending with *kuśa*— which brings about the destruction of evil, shall lead men to liberation.
For the rite of eradication (uccāṭana), a rosary made of dog teeth is prescribed, along with horsehair,
donkey teeth, lower teeth, and human sinew-threads.
A garland strung and fashioned from the teeth of a *preta* or from lower [human] bones is considered a destroyer of enemies; such a rosary for recitation (*japamālikā*) should be made.
In rites of hatred, one should sew [the effigy] with hair from the body of the person to be acted upon;
for a general recitation, one hundred or fifty [hair-strands] should be used.
The accomplishment of desired rites occurs with fifty [recitations];
with one hundred and four, the attainment of all goals is declared for one who has fashioned the garland.
One seeking liberation should recite with twenty-five [fingers] on the fifteenth day during the practice of sorcery;
however, for daily attraction, one should recite using the middle finger and the thumb.
For the rites of inciting hatred and expulsion, one should perform the recitation using the thumb and index finger;
for the rite of slaying an enemy, one should perform the recitation using the middle and little fingers.
For other rites, the wise man should perform the recitation with the thumb and the ring finger; he should prepare the thread for the purpose of taking up the rosary.
White, red, yellow, mixed, black, and smoke-colored are proclaimed;
by way of color and mantra, these deities are prescribed for the six types of ritual actions.
In some cases, meditation is prescribed according to specific ritual procedures;
having thoroughly examined all of that, one should perform the ritual application.
Attraction is like the rite of subjugation; that which is auspicious is said to be like the rite of pacification;
the fierce rite of killing should be understood as such by practitioners in all ritual actions.
The sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) appropriate for each respective rite have been correctly shown by the wise; now they are being described by me according to the rules.
The quadrangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is declared to bring about all accomplishments;
the yoni-shaped pit bestows sons, and the one resembling a half-moon bestows auspiciousness.
A triangular pit brings about the destruction of enemies; a circular one is for rites of pacification (śāntika);
for acts of cutting (chedana) and killing (māraṇa), the pit should be hexagonal or shaped like a lotus.
An eight-cubit sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is declared to bestow rain and pacify diseases; however,
other sages state that the fruits of the various types of pits are otherwise.
In the northeast, for the purpose of paralyzing, it is square; in the southeast, for enjoyment, it is shaped like a vulva;
in the south, for killing, it is a half-moon; and in the southwest, for inciting hatred, it is a triangle.
In the west, for pacification, the practice lasts six months;
in the northwest, for eradication, it lasts seven; in the north, for nourishment, it lasts a fortnight; and in the northeast, for the granting of liberation, it lasts eight months.

One should install the five-crested (pañcāmṛ) vessel in the northeast for the subjugation of spirits and planets, and for the purpose of pacification even in cases of malevolent magic; one should install the seven-crested vessel in the north.
The ground that is white clay is proclaimed as Brāhmī;
the red clay is Kṣatriyā, and the yellow is likewise proclaimed as Vaiśyā.
The wise have declared that black soil is for Śūdras;
Brāhmī soil brings success in all undertakings, while Kṣatriyā soil is considered to bestow sovereignty.
The Vaiśya woman brings wealth and grain, while the Śūdra woman is censured by the wise;
the wise man should draw [this] within the triangle at the end of the pericarp in the center of the Kuṇḍa.
Having caused the seed-syllable of power (śaktivīja) to fall, one should write that series of elemental letters (tadbhūtārṇa),
either strung together with the syllables of the root mantra or interlaced (vidarbhitam) with them.

Or likewise, the mantra-practitioner, with a concentrated mind, should write the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished in a *saṃpuṭa* (enclosed) form, according to the requirements of each specific rite.
Likewise, the tongues are said to be at the tips according to the distinction of their qualities in ritual acts:
Hiraṇyā, Gaganā, Aruṇā, Kṛṣṇā, and the other is considered to be Svaprabhā.
The *vahurūpā* is red and is *sāttvika* for auspicious rites;
another is *padmarāgā*, golden-colored, and the third is *bhadralohitā*.
Furthermore, Rohitā, Śvetā, Dhūminī, Karālikā,
Rājasyā, and Rasanā are the tongues of Fire ordained for rites of subjugation.
Viśvamūrti, Sphuliṅginī, Dhūmravarṇā, Manojavā, Lohitā,
Karālā, Kālī, and Tāmasī are thus described.
These seven are employed for cruel rites by wise counselors,
each with eight oblations of clarified butter accompanied by the syllable Om (praṇava) individually.

The rites of conception (garbhādhāna), the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), and likewise the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana); immediately following these should be the birth-rite (jātakarman) and the naming ceremony (nāmakaraṇa).
Afterwards, the going-forth [from the house] is prescribed, followed by the first feeding of solid food;
then the tonsure and the initiation ceremony, further the Mahānāmnī and the Mahāvrata rites.
Following that are the Upaniṣads, then the five ancillaries (aṅgas), the Dāna, the two doors, and death;
these rites, ending with the Viha, are auspicious, while those [others] pertain to cruel acts.
Those who are ignorant of the fire have declared that [the rites] end with the final oblation;
furthermore, the vessels such as the *prokṣaṇī* and others should be made of gold or silver.
Copper [is used] for rites such as pacification (*śāntika*), while for rites such as inciting hatred (*dveṣa*) and expulsion (*uccāṭana*),
one should use *bahuvāraka*, *kārakṣa*, or any one of the *śobhāñjana* seeds.
The visualization of the ears and other limbs of the fire is described by those learned in the Tantras:
the mouth is in the center, the head in the south, and the two feet are in the northern direction.
For pacification, the face [of the mandala] should be toward Indra (East) and Īśa (North); for rites of desire, toward Agni (South-East);
for killing by means of the Rākṣasas, toward Vāyu (North-West); and for attraction and other [rites], in the center.
In the Rudrayāmala.
The three *mudrās* of the household are said to be Mṛgī, Haṃsī, and Śūkarī. Śūkarī consists of the hands joined together; Mṛgī has the little fingers released.

The Haṃsī mudrā consists of the index finger extended; this mudrā is proclaimed to be threefold, for use in rites of pacification (śāntika), enrichment (pauṣṭika), as well as in killing (māraṇa) and expulsion (uccāṭana).
O Supreme Goddess, Mṛgī is to be known for inciting enmity, immobilization, and subjugation; Haṃsī is to be known for rites of pacification and nourishment.
In rites of sorcery, she is Śūkarī; in rites of inciting hatred, expulsion, and the like, she is likewise.
In the determination of the ancillaries of the fire-oblation (homa).
The gods do not accept an oblation that is devoid of mudrās;
indeed, the dull-witted person who, out of delusion, desires to offer an oblation lacking mudrās [is rejected].
One must certainly cause the sacrificer as well as oneself to fall [into the fire];
and the oblation should be performed only after ascertaining the stability of the fire.
Now I shall explain, O Great Goddess, the rite of fire-oblation (*homakarma*) which bestows perfect accomplishment;
the wheel of fire (*agnicakra*), O lady of excellent hips, which is hidden among all wheels.
The fire consists of the nine planets, and those planets consist of fire;
therefore, having understood their abiding nature within the fire, one should perform the oblation (homa) in the fire.
I shall now describe, according to the prescribed rule, the sequence of their positions within the lunar mansions for rites of pacification, enrichment, prosperity, and even for those that are cruel.
O Goddess, these nine are the celestial wanderers: Sūrya, Budha, Bhṛgu, Śani, Candra, Mahīsuta, Jīva, Rāhu, and Ketu.

O Maheśvarī, one should cause three and then three constellations, beginning with the asterism of the Sun, to be assigned; one should count them starting from the asterism of the Sun until reaching the asterism of the Moon.
O Goddess, listen as I shall describe the results of the sun and the other planets in their proper order:
under the Sun there will be sorrow, and under Mercury, the arrival of wealth.
One should know there is gain during Venus; during Saturn, there is suffering, without a doubt.
During the Moon, O Great Goddess, there is gain; and during Mars, there is indeed imprisonment.
O Maheśvarī, through Guru there is the acquisition of wealth; likewise, through Rāhu there is loss;
and through Ketu, death occurs—such is the fruit.
Having understood this, O Great Goddess, one should perform the rite of homa;
on whichever day an oblation enters the mouth of a benign planet, [that day is auspicious].
O gentle one, the commencement of the *saumya-homa* is prescribed on that day;
likewise, O Goddess, the *krūra-homa* should take place at the mouth of a malefic planet.
O Great Goddess, having understood this, one should perform the optional fire-oblation (*kāmya-homa*);
otherwise, if it is performed incorrectly, there will be fruitlessness and self-destruction.
In the Merutantra:
The mind accumulates that which is beneficial, just as [the body] does not [retain] the essence produced at the beginning or end;
yet, just as a faultless channel carries the internal essence with ease.
Likewise, for a deity, a planet situated in the *devayogya* [division] brings about auspiciousness;
and for a deity, when the Sun is in the *triṣu* or *bheṣu* divisions, prosperity increases during the solar hour (*nāḍī*).
The Vedic mantras nourish [the native], while the Nitaras and Hanti [mantras] cause misfortune;
thereafter, for three [periods], the nāḍī of Saumya brings about the play of the intellect.
Therefore, even for that [mantra], recitation three times bestows abundant nourishment;
however, thereafter, recitation three times would destroy the entire collection of mantras.
For the Moon, it brings nourishment for all mantras during the three [periods] following that;
thereafter, during the six [periods] following those, it causes destruction in the other [period], namely the *pala* of the *ārā*-nāḍī.
Therefore, among the three [periods], the Guru-nāḍī quickly bestows success in mantras;
the Rāhu-nāḍī is superior to that, while the others are not true for the sake of one's welfare.
Therefore, the channel known as Ketu among these three is the heart of the true mantra of the deity.
In the *Gaṇeśavimarṣiṇī*, however, a specific distinction is stated:
"Having drawn nine squares, one should [place] the vowels and the consonants gradually in their respective order."
One should worship Vāyu and place him between the western (Vāruṇī) and eastern (Aindrī) [lines];
one should place the Sun and the others in the central square, and having placed Ketu there, one should assign the fruit.
If the Sun is there, there will be grief; with Mercury, there is the acquisition of wealth;
with Venus, there will be gain of position and wealth; and Saturn would cause loss.
One should know that there is gain when the Moon is [the ruler], and death or imprisonment when Mars is;
for Jupiter it leads to the acquisition of wealth, while Rāhu is considered to cause loss.
Indeed, by means of the Ketu [wheel], one attains death; for that deity is the Fire-wheel.
One should count three and then three [units] starting from the Sun's asterism and so forth, up to the Bhāva.
The offerings should be made by the most excellent preceptors in either a fire-pit or on a sacrificial mound;
in the case of daily, occasional, or Durgā-related oblations and the like, one need not deliberate over the matter.
In the Brahmayāmala:
Now I shall describe the method for maintaining the fire for the successful accomplishment of the rite of oblation;
for the bearer of oblations (Agni) resides in the heavenly world, in the netherworld, and upon the earth.
I shall describe that method for the benefit of practitioners:
the *dhṛti*, the lunar days (*tithi*), the weekdays (*vāra*), and the seven continents multiplied by four.
Having combined [the two], one should divide by three; by the remainder, Pāvaka [is determined]:
with one, he dwells in heaven, and with two, indeed in the netherworld (pātāla).
If the world of mortals is empty, the Fire-god shall dwell there;
if he is situated in the heavenly world, it is an omen of calamity, and if he is in the netherworld, there will be loss of wealth.
When situated in the fire within the mortal world, [the deity] bestows the desired fruit during the *homa* offering.
Having understood this, the knower of mantras should perform the rite of *homa*.
In the Merutantra:
From the conjunction of the lunar day (tithi) and the day of the week (vāsara), the sacrificial fire (hutāsana) arises from the remainder of the calculation;
it is present in the sky, in the earth, in the two eyes, and its true form is manifest in the fire.
If healthy, he may kill the practitioner; on this earth, he takes away wealth. When manifest as fire, he bestows fruit; when abiding in his own form, he grants only what is auspicious.
In another tantra:
The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be made of gold for all rites dedicated to Soma;
these two should be made of iron for rites such as *staṃbhana* (paralysis) and the like.
In the supreme worldly fire, the rite should be for pacification; in the worldly fire, it is for subjugation;
and the rite known as immobilization occurs in the fire born from the *vaṭa* tree.
In the case of creating enmity, it should be known as being in the Ox (Vṛṣabha) sign; for pacifying, it is remembered as being in the Cemetery (Śmaśāna) and the Barren Land (Ūṣara).
These six fires are declared for the six rites of Uccāṭana and Māraṇa.
For subjugation (*vaśya*), one should use the first flowers; for pacification (*śānti*), they should be used together with *dūrvā* grass;
for paralyzing (*staṃbhana*), the sacrificial fuel sticks (*samidh*) should be made from the *rājavṛkṣa* tree and bathed in cow’s ghee.
A ewe's [flesh] combined with ghee is for the destruction of diseases born from hatred;
for the purpose of eradication (uccāṭana), those originating from the *rasālā* tree are used in conjunction with mustard oil.
For the rite of killing, fuel sticks of acacia wood combined with pungent oil are prescribed;
this is declared by wise mantra-experts to be the sacrificial substance for the six types of ritual action.
Likewise.
Through an oblation of ghee, there is the acquisition of wealth; with white mustard seeds (siddhārtha), supreme fame;
with kiṃśuka flowers, the attainment of all desires; and through an oblation of fruits, happiness shall arise.
Through oblations of molasses, *priyaka* flowers, *campaka*, *pāṭala*, and *amāputra*, one attains praise; through *karavīra* flowers, women are brought under control.
Dūrvā grass brings longevity, Guḍūcī bestows the pacification of disease, and sesame seeds are likewise said to grant long life; through the homa of fragrant substances, good fortune is attained.
Through offerings of *śrīpala* fruits, bilva leaves, and likewise water-born lotuses, one who has fallen from his kingdom shall regain his realm; the *mallikā* flower is considered to bestow fame.
Those under the influence of the gods would be [indicated] by *karṇikāra* and *kiṃśuka* flowers;
those under the influence of kings by *kāśamarda*; and those under the influence of the common people (*viś*) by *kṛtamāla*.

With *pāṭala* flowers, one becomes a mother of a Śūdra; with blue lotuses, there will be disease; with *jātī* flowers, one becomes a widow; and with sweet-smelling flowers, there is the attainment of desired wealth.
For the attainment of one's desires, oblations may be made with fuel-sticks of the aśvattha, udumbara, or plakṣa trees;
likewise, the desired result is achieved through sacrificial materials such as barley and rice.
By offering māṣa beans, one's enemies become mute; by offering kodrava grains, the occurrence of disease arises;
and from the oblation of kalāya peas, great fear will certainly come upon one's enemies.
With fuel-sticks of *vibhītaka*, the family of enemies shall become insane;
with fuel-sticks of *śālmali*, the destruction of the enemy's faction will certainly occur.
In the *Phetkāriṇītantra*: [262a]
Now I shall describe the substances according to their respective rites:
for the rite of pacification (śāntika), however, there are milk, clarified butter, sesame seeds, milky trees, and sugarcane.
The creeper called Amṛtā and milk-rice (pāyasa) are prescribed therein for nourishing rites;
by using bilva leaves and jasmine flowers, one shall become a king.

One desiring a daughter should offer oblations with parched grains; likewise, one desiring prosperity should do so with lotuses. By offering curd, one attains fortune; by offering food soaked in ghee, one obtains food.
For the sake of prosperity, the practitioner of mantra should offer oblations with milk, or ghee, or lotuses soaked in honey; for the pacification of great poverty, he should likewise offer them.
Through a hundred-thousand oblations (lakṣahoma) with ghee, bilva, and sesame seeds, one obtains peace;
for the purpose of attraction, however, one uses salt, priyaṅgu, and bilva fruit.

With flowers of *jātī*, *palāśa*, or all of them together, or even with each one individually, along with *rājī* and salt, there is subjugation (*vaśya*); or, when the *pauṣṭika* rite is prescribed, there is likewise subjugation.
One seeking subjugation [should use] *jāti* flowers; for attraction, *karavīra* flowers, or likewise cotton seeds smeared with semen, or even human hair.
Desiring the destruction of an enemy, the mantra-practitioner should offer oblations by combining [the substances];
or, for the purpose of slaying an enemy, he should perform the homa with mustard seeds and oils.
A person should offer oblations with seeds of the *rohī* plant mixed with sesame seeds,
or even with seeds of the cotton plant (*kārpāsika*) combined with thorns.
For all malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), one should offer oblations of mustard seeds mixed with sesame;
likewise, [one may use] the harsh feathers of crows and owls, or *kāraskara* and *vibhītaka* fruits.
For the rite of killing (māraṇa), one should employ black pepper, pure mustard seeds, red milk, the three pungents (kaṭutraya), pungent oils, and the milky sap of the stuhī plant.
The oblation performed in the Agniṣkarṇa fire and others brings about the destruction of enemies; through such oblations, there is the destruction of the ears and other [limbs] of the foe.
Thus it has been said:
If one should offer oblations upon the head of the fire, or into the nose, the ears, or likewise the eyes,
then that [oblation] would quickly destroy those very limbs.
The characteristics of the fire-pit, beginning with its ear, have already been described previously.
Likewise.
One who desires long life should [offer] ghee, sesame seeds, dūrvā grass, mango sprouts, milk, and mango leaves; thus one shall instantly destroy fever.
Guḍūcī is for conquering death as well as for pacifying those whose horses have perished;
by offering oblations with white mustard seeds, one afflicted by fever shall instantly remove the disease.

One who desires rain, having offered oblations with *cetasi* wood, *samidh* fuel, and *pyatraka* wood, attains nourishment; and with *jīva* wood, one obtains a son. O son, [one obtains] a long-lived son.
Through an oblation of ghee and guggulu, one becomes eloquent;
likewise with jasmine, *jāti*, and flowers produced from the *nāga* and *punnāga* trees.
With flowers, one attains the perfection of Sarasvatī; likewise, with milk or salt, one should perform oblations for the accomplishment of all aims and for the warding off of rain.
With red flowers, apāmārga, kola, and subhadraka—
these combined with sweet substances— the practitioner of mantras should perform the rite of subjugation.
By means of dry leaves blown by the wind, wood struck down by lightning,
camel bones, and charcoal from a funeral pyre, the eradication of an enemy shall occur.
A wise person should perform a rite for peace using dūrvā grass, guḍūcī, cow’s ghee, sesame seeds, rice, food offerings, and palāśa wood fuel.
In another tantra:
For auspicious rites, it is prescribed combined with turmeric water;
for killing and paralyzing, it should be with hot water and black pepper.
For the rites of hatred and eradication, water mixed with the urine of a ram is prescribed;
this is declared as the substance for the libation by those who have reached the further shore of the scriptures.
One who knows the tantra should perform the libation while seated comfortably for auspicious rites;
for the rite of immobilization (stambhana), the libation should be performed while kneeling upon the ground.
In rites of hatred and the like, the foremost of practitioners should satisfy [the deity] with a single vessel;
for subjugation and pacification, a golden vessel is prescribed, while an earthen vessel is intended for paralyzing.
For subduing hatred, a vessel made of khadira wood is used; for expulsion, one made of iron;
for killing, it should be a hen's egg; these are the vessels for the libation.
Thus are the applications.
Now, otherwise, there is the injunction for optional rites.
Therein, first is the armor (*kavaca*) which is the means for accomplishing the six rites (*ṣaṭkarmasādhana*).
Salutation to Śrī Kālikā.
O Supreme Lord, O Mahādeva, O Lord of the Universe!
By your grace, I have heard everything regarding the great worship of Kālikā.
O Lord of Life, why have you not revealed to me the web of nyāsa, the collection of mantras, the ritual application, the practice with a corpse, and the armor?
Why then are even these things concealed from me? O Supreme Lord, there is indeed nothing of such a nature to be found within the sphere of the universe.
O wise one, since even that which is spoken of is dearer than life itself, why do you conceal this great armor, which is your supreme deity?
If I am an object of your compassion, if I am worthy of honor, a vessel of your affection, one to be favored, or beloved— then speak accordingly now.
The illustrious Sadāśiva said:
O beloved of my life, I shall tell you this most closely guarded armor, which has never been disclosed to anyone; out of affection, I will speak it to you—listen.
In the battle with the demon Tripura, having bound on his supreme armor,
he pierced the three cities of the Daityas with a single arrow.
O Goddess of the gods, it is by her grace that even the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself attained worshipfulness throughout the three worlds and became the husband of Lakṣmī.
O Goddess, this twenty-two-fold armor was previously taught for Dakṣiṇā;
knowing it to be superior even to life itself, I have concealed it from you as well.
O Goddess, may my head be cursed if I speak anything otherwise concerning you;
there shall be no one at all on the surface of the earth who is equal to him.
One attains every accomplishment, even those difficult for the gods to obtain;
O Great Goddess, this must never be disclosed before anyone whatsoever.
From disclosure, there would be a loss of accomplishment and one would incur the curse of the deity;
O Śivā, for this most secret [teaching] of the venerable [Trika], Tripurāri is the seer (ṛṣi).
The meter is known as Bṛhatī, and the goddess is Dakṣiṇakālikā;
she is employed for the attainment of mastery through the means of the six rites.
May Kālikā of the cremation ground, who goes among the spirits, protect my head;
may Mahākālī, whose form is Time, with the sounds *krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ*, protect my forehead.
Huṃ huṃ! May Krodhakālī always protect the pair of my eyes.
Hrīṃ hrīṃ! May Nādakālī Karālinī protect the pair of my ears.
May Mahotkaṭā protect the pair of cheeks on the right, O Kālikā;
may Kāmakalī, [uttering] "krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ," always protect the region of my throat.
HŪM HŪM! May Kālī of the time of universal dissolution always protect my pair of breasts. HRĪM HRĪM! May the most terrible Kālī protect my pair of staff-like arms.
Svāhā! May Raudrakālī in her own form protect my belly;
may Śrī Caṇḍakālikā always protect my back with the syllables *khphreṃ* and *phreṃ*.
Hasakhaphreṃ: may Tārakālikā always protect the waist.
Aiṃ Krīṃ Klīṃ: may Unmattakālikā always protect the secret place.
May Krīṃ Huṃ Kaṅkālakālikā always protect my two thighs;
may the terrifying Tīvrakālī protect my feet with Krīṃ Klīṃ.
May Navakālī, the deceiver of Time, always protect my entire body.
Oṃ krīṃ drīṃ, O destroyer of demons, paralyze, paralyze the enemies!
Having uttered the two words "māraya" (slay), [say] "pin the tongue, pin it!
Huṃ huṃ! O flame of the fire of wrath, you who blaze, beloved of Agni!"
May Kālī, whose nature consists of these syllables, always protect me amidst my enemies:
Oṃ Krīṃ Huṃ Huṃ, O Enchantress of all people, Beloved of Śaṅkara!
Clad in human skin, dwelling in the terrifying Aṭṭahāsa,
you who attract all and delude the faces of all— delude this couple!
The king, the subjects, as well as the queen, the servants, and the attendants.
"Vaśaṃ kuru kuru svāhā! Thus the King of Mantras is extracted.
May Kālī, whose essence is this mantra, always protect [me] at the king’s gate:
*Huṃ Aiṃ Huṃ*, O conqueror of death, O destroyer of untimely death!
Destroy the supreme mantra, as well as the yantra, the kṛtyā, the powder, the pratyaṅgira, and the mahārāva;
shatter them, shatter them!
"Destroy the pair! Thus it is said: *krīṃ hūṃ hrīṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*.
The Manthānakālikā empowered by mantra is always fourfold:
in the cremation ground, in the midst of water, on the royal road, and in a place of danger.
In the forest, in the desolate wilderness, in a terrible place, on a mountain range,
in an assembly hall, in calamity, or in battle, when afflicted by fear of kings or thieves.
"May the Goddess Kulakālī, the Mistress of the Kula, protect me everywhere.
Thus, O Goddess, this most wonderful armor has been recounted to you.
O Goddess, by the mere remembrance of whom all accomplishments arise through devotion, having sat before the mouth of a Kaulika according to the prescribed rite.
Having worshipped Kālī with the five "ma" syllables at the dead of night,
and having duly gratified the Guru, a person should recite the armor-mantra (kavaca).
Within six months one attains accomplishment; it is not otherwise, as spoken by Śiva.
One’s speech, consisting of both prose and verse, shall become like the flow of the Gaṅgā.
Lakṣmī remains steadfast in his house, and he is beloved by his own kinsmen;
even Indra becomes his servant—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
The accomplishment of the six rites occurs through the grace of the armor-mantra (kavaca).
Having diligently ground sandalwood with the eight fragrances upon a lotus leaf, [one should apply it].
Having written this armor-mantra on birch bark, one should wear it on the right arm;
becoming endowed with all sovereign powers, he shall become a lord of the world.
O Goddess, whatever desire one meditates upon in the heart while wearing this armor,
that very desire one attains, according to the word of the Lord.
O Goddess, during the autumn season at the dead of night, the *kavaca* should be recited with diligence ten thousand times for the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life.
"O Goddess, whoever shall perform the worship of Kālī without knowing the armor-mantra (kavaca), he shall be as good as dead; this has been vowed by me."
Thus ends the *Śrīdakṣiṇakālikavaca* in the *Śrīhāhārāvatantra*.
In the Merutantra.
Thereafter, one should perform the preliminary practices for the sake of attaining the desired results of one's wishes.
In another tantra:
Thus, performing the ritual with its specific signs, one should carry out the rites for desired ends.
Therefore, I shall now describe the worship for desired ends, which grants the fulfillment of the practitioner's wishes.
By means of an oblation of *vandhūka* flowers, one shall bring the lords of the earth under one's control;
by an oblation of ghee and salt, one attracts a beloved woman.
One should offer oblations into the fire with *vakula* flowers; one obtains imperishable good fortune.
Through *mallikā*, *jāti*, *punnāga*, and *kadamba* flowers, one attains nourishment.
By performing a fire-oblation with the flowers of the rājavṛkṣa tree, one enjoys prosperity;
by an oblation of dūrvā grass, sesame seeds, and clarified butter, one attains a long life.
Having performed worship with bilva leaves and clarified butter while reciting the root mantra,
one who offers oblations a thousand times every day attains the supreme goal.
By performing oblations with *mālatī* flowers smeared with ghee, one becomes a poet among spirits;
by oblations of clarified butter, milk, and ghee, great poetic skill shall arise.
A wise person should offer one hundred and eight oblations with red flowers;
he will swiftly bring everyone under his control—of this there is no doubt.
One should offer oblations of milk-rice, minced meat, fish, along with cooked rice, unbroken grains, and sesame seeds; before a year has passed, one shall obtain the desired success.
By performing the moon-oblation with sandalwood, agallochum, saffron,
and musk for one year, the wise man attains incomparable good fortune.
One should satisfy the goddess with honey; thus one shall attain all desires.
In the Kali age.
By means of an oblation of red flowers on the day of Śravaṇa, success is indeed attained within a fortnight;
by means of an oblation of bilva leaves, sovereignty is certainly achieved.
By the oblation of red flowers, one may bring the entire world under control;
furthermore, by the oblation of yellow flowers, one may paralyze even the whole universe.
Through an oblation of *mālatī* flowers, one becomes Vācaspati himself;
through an oblation of black flowers, one slays enemies without delay.
In this matter, the number for every oblation should extend up to ten thousand;
and a *śivāvali* offering must be presented by those desiring all perfections.
In the Merutantra and the Phetkāriṇītantra.
With a serpent as her sacred thread, her crest adorned with the crescent moon,
and her matted locks gathered together, she was situated near Mahākāla.
Having thus meditated upon the goddess— the *kūrca*, the marrow (*majjā*), the pair of seeds, and likewise the pair at the end— one should worship her with red flowers.
Pierced by the arrows of desire, shameless and agitated, the women abandoned each of their own husbands and embraced him as if he were a deity.
In this manner, one should employ *huṃ* at the beginning and *krīṃ* at the end during the act of attraction;
through the performance of recitation and worship, attraction will occur swiftly.
In front, to the south, [one should worship] Kālikā; this is understood from the ellipsis.
One [should be] red with a trident in her hand, and another [should be] holding a trident.

Having meditated upon her as being situated at the forefront of Mahākāla, one should worship her with yellow flowers; one should apply this method individually for each [deity], both at the beginning and likewise at the end.
In this manner, there shall indeed be attraction at all times for both the stationary and the moving,
whether it be that which dwells in the depths of Pātāla or whatever else is situated upon the surface of the earth.
All that is drawn forth according to the words of Mahākāla:
[one should visualize] Kapilā with two arms, holding a ritual knife in her left hand and a skull-cup in her right.
Having meditated thus upon everything, O best of the remaining ones, there are indeed only two [remaining].
Having worshipped in this manner with a flower, one should here worship with a black [flower].
By this, the rite performed with a specific intent results in the killing of that person;
the Piṅgākṣī [mudrā] causes expulsion, while the Kekarā [mudrā] causes terror.
With mouth open, she causes flight; reeling like one intoxicated, she becomes agitated;
when thoroughly shaken, she looks about; and when bent low, she causes [the enemy] to fall.
She contracts when restrained and is awakened when obstructed;
whatever state a person may be in, one should likewise meditate upon her as abiding in that very state.
In all these cases, the intended state of being should be contemplated;
elsewhere, expulsion is prescribed, while in all [other] instances, sexual union is considered appropriate.
Having bathed, wearing white garments, and having performed his daily rites during the day;
at night, he is naked while lying down and when engaged in sexual intercourse.
Speechless and with disheveled hair, by that [mantra] all objectives are accomplished:
namely, paralyzing, bewildering, and subjugating.
Having seen another man’s wife naked, a person should mutter [the mantra] ten thousand times;
he shall indeed always become one who has reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge.
By the mere sight of him, the disputants are considered to be deprived of their luster;
his speech shall be of every kind, consisting of both prose and verse.
Alternatively, a man with disheveled hair who eats sacrificial food (haviṣya) should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times;
this is considered an equivalent substitute.

Alternatively, and so forth; this ritual procedure (*kalpa*) refers to the lay follower (*upāsaka*) who maintains the state of a bound soul (*paśubhāva*), whereas the previous procedure referred only to the hero (*vīra*). This should be understood similarly for what follows. Likewise: "Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should diligently address the *bhaga*."
He who performs sexual union [at this time] shall be endowed with wealth, grain, and sons;
he will become the best among those possessed of all knowledge—of this there is no doubt.
In the Bhairavatantra.
Having likewise seen [the deity] as beginningless and endless, the king should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
and having likewise seen [her] as stainless, he should recite it ten thousand times for the purpose of subjugation.
At night it is without the sun; likewise, O fair-limbed one, when it is in full bloom, it is stainless; and when it has blossomed and opened, it is like fire.
In the Merutantra and the Gandharvatantra.
But that wise man who desires wealth, who longs for great sovereignty,
and who wishes to become equal to Bṛhaspati—

Having recited the mantra one hundred and eight times and having consecrated the female organ, the knower of mantras should engage in sexual union with effort; he should perform a mental recitation of a thousand times.
Through practice for six months, the status of Vācaspati (the Lord of Speech) is attained. Likewise:
having seen [the deity] thus unobstructed, the king recites the mantra one hundred thousand times.
The meaning is that he who recites becomes the earth itself.
And during sexual union, it should be recited for the constant purification of evil.
In the Merutantra and the Phetkarinitantra.
One who worships the Goddess in cremation grounds with thousands of bilva leaves smeared with the blood of one's own body shall attain equality with Vāgīśa.
Even with a leaf smeared with one's own semen, he who worships the Goddess at the cremation grounds a thousand times for the sake of the Sun attains all supernatural powers (siddhis).
One shall become wealthy, powerful, eloquent, and beloved by all women;
one shall be happy—of this there is no doubt—just as Mahākāla has spoken.
Having led a woman to a cremation ground and worshipped her with the mantra a thousand times—
she whose limbs are smeared with red sandalwood paste and adorned with red flowers—
Having first addressed the mantra with flowers, one should then meditate upon Caṇḍikā;
thereafter, having gone [to battle], one shall obtain the kingdom, provided she does not flee.
Furthermore, while lying in a cremation ground or even upon a corpse-eater, one should recite the mantra repeatedly; it will become the bestower of all accomplishments.
And one should satisfy [the deity] within the mouth of the corpse with blood, flesh, and so forth, while filled with wrath;
by uttering these mantras, one shall become a master of all siddhis.
And one should satisfy [the deities] three times with milks mixed with the blood-constituent (raktadhātu)— namely,
with the blood of sheep, buffalo, and indeed human blood.
By means of the blood of a rat and a cat, eloquence arises for him;
likewise, by means of semen and his own hair, the same result occurs.
By washing the vulva of a man or a woman during sexual intercourse,
one becomes wealthy and all accomplishments arise for him.
In speech he is the living soul, and in wealth he is the lord of riches;
by his command he is the king of the gods, yet in beauty he is truly not even the god of love.
For this offering by means of *vali* accomplishes the purpose of all principles;
one should always offer *vali* consisting of meat together with bones, well-prepared.
The flesh of a rat, the flesh of a goat, and likewise the flesh of a sheep or a buffalo—
all these should be offered together with their bones and all their hair.
The wise one should then recite the mantra for each [deity] individually; by that, ten million ages are deluded, and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) becomes fully honored.
One shall become happy; there is no doubt here, according to the words of Mahākāla.
Having led a woman to the cremation ground and having worshipped her with the mantra a thousand times, [one attains success].
All accomplishments shall belong to him; he becomes an eloquent hero.
Nothing whatsoever that exists within the three worlds is difficult for him to obtain.
Having fashioned the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the form of a womb,
measuring one span in height and likewise one cubit in width, and having done so even below that;
In this regard, one should indeed perform the rite of establishing the fire with diligence;
one should offer the first oblation to the deity Mahākāla.
With the flesh of a Ruru deer, clarified butter, cooked rice, and blood—
especially with black flowers mixed with blood and clarified butter.
In this manner, one should also offer oblations into the cremation fire with material offerings and the like.
In the Merutantra:
Having prepared one hundred excellent leaves smeared with the menstrual blood of a woman, the wise man,
reciting the mantra over each one individually, should then offer them as a burnt oblation (homa).
By that, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) equal to ten thousand ages would have been offered;
he shall attain all perfections, and he becomes eloquent and steadfast.
For him who has reached the abode of the cremation ground, with hair disheveled and clad only by the directions, nothing whatsoever on earth ever remains difficult to attain.
One who is most skilled in mantras should recite the mantra ten thousand times for the accomplishment of all desired aims; having mounted a corpse, he should perform the recitation right there.
Having restrained his speech, being fearless and devoted to truth,
he attains the supreme perfection that is very difficult even for the gods to obtain.
In the Vīracūḍāmaṇi.
Next, I shall explain the fire sacrifice (homa) in a triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) shaped like a womb;
or else, one should diligently perform the sacrifice in a pit made of cow dung.
Having gathered a flower from a creeper, one should likewise place it in a vessel of noble lineage;
one should offer as oblation a pure leaf of *nāgavallī* smeared with the creeper-juice.
One should diligently perform the fire-oblation ten thousand times, or one thousand, or one hundred and eight; by doing so, one shall bring the three worlds under one's control.
The female deer carrying the corpse becomes manifest to him;
he attains every siddhi, which is difficult to find even in the three worlds.
The master of speech is born as a mantra-practitioner, while Śravaṇa indeed becomes one possessed of wealth;
he is a yogi equal to Dattātreya and a Purandara-like enjoyer of pleasures.
In wrath he was equal to Vaivasvata, but in truth he was the son of Pāṇḍu;
in liberality he was like Hariścandra, and in counsel he was the delight of the Bhṛgus.
The son of Añjanā is dear to him in valor, and Vāruṇī is dear to him in strength;
by the mere knowledge of this, the eight siddhis will certainly be attained.
Having divided the mantra into three parts, one should diligently perform the fire-oblation (homa) with meat,
sesame, blood, hair, curd, cooked rice, and milk-rice (pāyasa).
One should offer oblations anointed with the three sweets (trimadhu) and bring the three worlds under one's control;
however, one should perform a libation (tarpaṇa) with milk, clarified butter, honey, and incense.
The wise practitioner should likewise satisfy [the deities] with streams of blood and marrow;
at the conclusion of the libation, the great mantra-master should perform the worship of the maiden (kumārī).
One should perform the rites beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and worship [the guest] with the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
Having purified the maiden's lineage, one should worship her with ritual service (upacāra).
The great mantra-practitioner should indeed offer a stream of blood upon the Kula,
consisting of the blood of a rat, a cat, a human, a ram, and a buffalo.
One who satisfies [the deity] with effort goes to the world of the Goddess;
poetic talent arises in him, like another Bṛhaspati.
Having become like a god among men, he attains both worldly enjoyment and eternal liberation;
freed from both sinful and meritorious karma, the man becomes liberated while living.
Devotedly [offer] clarified butter, as well as meat, bone, blood, sugar,
black flowers, and honey, especially with blood.
One should offer the first oblation to the god Mahākāla;
having beheld the flowering abode of the Kula, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
By reciting [the mantra] with the thought that the guru and [one's own self] are non-different, one shall attain union (*sāyujya*).
Seeing another woman naked, the wise man should recite it one hundred thousand times.
His speech shall become priceless poetry, consisting of both prose and verse;
and [this occurs] in a cremation ground, a forest, on a mountain, or at a crossroads.
Having worshipped according to the rules the beautiful and excellent woman, the practitioner,
being a skilled adept, should touch his *liṅga* against her *bhaga* one hundred thousand times.
Having recited this great wisdom, one shall become the foremost among poets;
or else, in a solitary place, according to the sequence of the family tradition.
A person should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times with their own tongue placed in the center of the *bhaga*;
such a practitioner of mantras becomes a speaker of those who have not heard the Vedas and Shastras, and it is not otherwise.

Touching the generative organ while reciting the mantra ten thousand times (ayuta) as the count for the recitation is prescribed as the atonement for both great sins (mahāpāpa) and minor sins (upapāpa).
A man who performs an oil massage with *latā* and recites the mantra ten thousand times brings kings,
cities, and city women under his control.
The practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra while applying [the substance] to the vine for the sake of liberation from great sins;
likewise, in the absence of the vine, the practitioner should carefully remove the semen.
Holding it in one's own hand and having consecrated it with mantras, one shall become a master of all accomplishments.
The practitioner, having risen in the morning, should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with a concentrated mind.
Having joined [the mantra] to go to the limbs of Śakti, the wise one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa);
the entire universe becomes identical with that [mantra], as do recitation, fire-offerings, and libations.
One should not speak ill of them, nor strike them even with a flower; one should avoid crookedness, unpleasant speech, and deception regarding food, whether hard or soft.
Under no circumstances should [this] be done, for it causes an obstruction to spiritual accomplishment (siddhi). Women are creation, women are preservation, and women are the bringers of destruction.
By means of the Mahācīna-krama, primarily through the creeper and flowers,
the practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra over water infused with the creeper; that very water shall become a wish-fulfilling vine (kalpalatā).
The Mahācīnakramalatā has three petals with three lines;
having worshipped it in the cremation ground, the best of practitioners [should recite] a thousand times.
Then one attains a kingdom and is not born afraid;
having worshipped [the deity] thousands of times with *bilva* leaves smeared with one's own blood.
And likewise in a cremation ground or at night, one attains equality with Vāgīśvara.
In the Merutantra:
Having bathed, wearing white garments, pure and with a restrained mind,
one should perform everything during the day for the sake of attaining all desires and goals.
At night, one should not engage in sexual intercourse while naked or with disheveled hair;
this should be done with great care for the sake of attaining all desires and goals.
Herein, the rule for all the twice-born has been shown, and that for the Śūdras has also been fully declared; O highly intelligent one, this great doctrine was seen at night.
The best of practitioners should worship Mahākāla with diligence, and thereafter worship the Goddess;
having divided [the ritual] threefold with the mantras and other elements, he should proceed with care.
For the sake of attaining all perfections, one should diligently offer as oblations meat, blood, sesame seeds, hair, nails, cooked rice, milk-rice, and clarified butter.
Acting thus according to the prescribed rite, one attains the highest accomplishment;
whatever a living being desires, that he obtains constantly.
By constantly offering oblations, one who is ever-vigilant attains the state of a god, the state of a dānava, and likewise the status of a siddha or a cāraṇa.
The mantra practitioner, with a single-pointed mind, should recite the mantra forty thousand times;
as for the fire offering, one should perform it with red flowers in a sacrificial pit according to the prescribed ritual.
By the recitation of this mantra, the practitioner is liberated from the murder of a Brahmin,
as well as from the killing of one's father or mother, and what need is there to mention other minor sins?
Whatever fruit is obtained from the gift of the earth filled with the jewels of tawny cows,
that same fruit is attained by thousands of millions of fire-offerings or by the meditation upon the Goddess.

Touching each [object] repeatedly, one should recite the mantra; whomever one touches, that person will be brought under control. Having recited it one hundred and eight times, one should perform a fire offering (homa) with red flowers.
The practitioner shall bring even the king under his control; there is nothing that cannot be accomplished within the three worlds.
This should be done in an empty house, a temple, or at a self-manifested sacred site.
Eating only sacrificial food (haviṣya) and observing celibacy, one becomes equal to Indra through recitation (japa).
In a triangular-shaped pit (kuṇḍa), this applies likewise for rites of pacification (śānti) and nourishment (puṣṭi).
The mantra-practitioner should offer ten thousand oblations, and again three thousand;
for a rite of desire, having offered a thousand oblations with reddish flowers, one should perform the tenth-part offering.
And likewise, having again meditated upon the Goddess within the fire and worshipped her with the root mantra using bilva leaves mixed with ghee, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa).
By offering a thousand oblations every day, one attains the supreme goal;
by performing homa with *mālatī* flowers soaked in ghee, one becomes a poet instantly.
For one who knows this mantra, there is always nothing that cannot be accomplished—provided he is devoted to the worship of the Goddess and devoted to his guru; it is not otherwise.
In the Kālītantra.
In this regard, I shall describe the procedure for the fire-oblation (homa), which bestows all accomplishments.
