Having prepared one hundred leaves provided with creepers and flowers, the wise practitioner [should proceed].

Having recited those [mantras] over them repeatedly according to the rule, the most excellent practitioner should then indeed offer them as oblations into the consecrated fire in accordance with the ritual procedure.
O Śivā, by this [act], the worship of ten thousand ages is produced;
through this sequential yoga, one obtains that which is difficult to find on earth.
For him, nothing whatsoever in the three worlds is difficult to obtain;
he becomes a hero and eloquent, and shall attain all accomplishments.
With honey, clarified butter, cooked rice, meat, and blood—
especially with black flowers mixed with ghee and blood.
With offerings of meat and other substances, the wise practitioner should likewise perform oblations in the cremation ground;
he should diligently offer to Mahākāla first, and thereafter to the Goddess with great care.
Having divided the vidyā into three parts, the practitioner of purified mind [should offer] flesh,
blood, sesame, hair, nails, cooked rice, and milk-rice.
One should especially offer clarified butter (ājya) for the sake of all accomplishments;
when this is done, one obtains the highest success in every respect.
Whatever desire one may wish for, that one certainly attains;
having become like a god among humans, one enjoys abundant happiness.
I shall describe the procedure for libation (tarpaṇa) by which one may accomplish all tasks;
one should perform the libation with milk and likewise with streams of blood.
Likewise, with marrow and similarly with the mind belonging to one's own body,
and by means of the washing away of the lineage of the maiden who has been summoned.
One should indeed satisfy the Supreme Deity with the blood of a ram, a goat, and a human,
as well as with the blood of a cat.
Thus, the practitioner who performs the libation becomes a master of supernatural powers in person;
poetic talent arises in him like a continuous stream of grape juice.
Having become equal to Bṛhaspati, he rejoices on earth like a god;
for him there are neither sins nor merits, and he certainly becomes liberated while living.
Likewise.
The practitioner with a steady mind, having beheld the flowering *kulāgāra*, should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times.
Only by keeping it secret shall he become a treasury of knowledge;
[this applies to] refined and vernacular words, as well as Vedic and worldly ones.
They all come under the control of the practitioner; it is not otherwise.
Alternatively, the man should eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) while his hair is disheveled.
By reciting this ten thousand times, the wise one shall obtain this very fruit.
Likewise.
One should recite [the mantra] in places covered with creepers for the sake of liberation from great sins;
if no creeper is available, then one should diligently [use] marrow.
Having driven them away, the practitioner of mantra should recite for the sake of attaining the accomplishments of dharma, desire, and wealth;
likewise, he should avoid censuring them, striking them, or doing anything unpleasant to them.
Under no circumstances should one act otherwise, for it creates an obstacle to success:
women are gods, women are life-breaths, and women alone are ornaments.
One should always associate with women; even in the absence of one's own wife, she [the woman] will become situated upon the heart through the practice of inverted union.
One should offer to the deities flowers fashioned by his hand, water fashioned by his hand, and food fashioned by his hand.
If one who is embraced by the great Chinese tree and creeper recites the mantra at night, she herself becomes a wish-fulfilling vine for the supreme practitioner.
Even by a sixteenth part of the fruit obtained from being entwined by the vines of the great Chinese tree, the corpses are not worth even a fraction of that.
Even from a corpse-seat, there is the fruit of entering the house of a creeper;
having come to the abode of the cremation ground, with hair loose and naked as the directions.
One should recite the mantra ten thousand times for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals,
using the marrow of the Mahācīna tree and creeper along with bilva leaves.
Having worshipped the Goddess a thousand times in the cremation ground,
the best of practitioners then obtains a kingdom, provided that she does not flee.
Having worshipped Kālī in cremation grounds with thousands of bilva leaves smeared with the blood from one's own limbs, one shall attain equality with Vāgīśa.
One should recite ten thousand times the mantra "anāvṛta kula dṛśyārtha."
By the mere meditation upon Śukla, poetic skill comes under one's control;
by means of this vidyā, the practitioner may touch even a sinner.
By the mere touch of that [power], he utters speech that is unconfused;
through the yoga of meditation, once it has been drunk, he may pervade the entire world.

One should perform the worship of a virgin girl with a dark-complexioned girl for the subduing of enemies, and with a smoke-colored girl for the suppression of foes, for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals.
Now I shall explain another application for the subjugation of enemies:
at the end of all [mantras], having joined the fire-goddess, one should recite it ten thousand times.
One should meditate upon Kapilā as having two arms, holding a knife and a skull-cup in her right and left hands respectively;
thus one should perform the rite for the slaying of enemies.
Thus, Kālī-manu is proclaimed as the bestower of all accomplishments.
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*.
When only one watch of the night has passed, the man, devoted to the Kula, should then go to the house of the Kula woman and remain upon a bed of flowers.
Having marked the root-cakra with the name of the person to be accomplished within the family-cakra,
and having inscribed one's own name at the beginning, one should perform the family practice (kulācāra).
The practitioner brings his own power and the supreme power into union;
listen with a concentrated mind, my son, to the attraction of the supreme power.
Having brought together women of excellent character and great renown who possess their own splendor,
and having requested the Guru out of devotion to the lineage, he should initiate them with the Kula-initiation.
The Guru, his mouth filled with betel, unshaken and happy, [beheld] the noble-born Satī, whose eyes were full of the nectar of supreme bliss.
The teacher should say to his own daughter: "One should write [the mantra] upon her forehead-plate;
having divided the Śakti-cakra into two parts, one should then write the Kāmakalā."
In the center of that, one should place [the syllable] adorned with the name, consecrated by the mantra;
having invoked the Goddess there and meditated upon her, one should worship the Goddess.
Then, having repeated the root mantra three times accompanied by the Ṛṣi and the metre, he should whisper it into the ear of that daughter with his left hand.
From this day forward, devoted to the worship of the family mantra, you shall act as my daughter,
accepting the command of your own lineage and casting aside shame and indolence.
"Bring about the state of equilibrium according to the prescribed method.
Having received this permission, one should prostrate like a staff upon the ground.
Save me, O Lord, whose conduct is beyond reproach; O Lotus-Lord of the lotus-like women, bestow the shade of Your lotus-feet upon my head, O You who possess glory as Your wealth!
Having elevated one's own family [of deities] to the status of the supreme, one should act according to what has been seen [in the scriptures];
however, if she is unable to endure the worship of the limbs, the enclosures, and so forth, [one should proceed otherwise].

Then, having meditated on the Guru at the crown of the head and having gratified the Kula with the essence of the nectar of the Kula, one should meditate upon the Kula and recite the mantra that is free from agitation.
Then, at that time of attainment, one's own family [resides] upon the surface of the earth;
seated on the left side, it is adorned with red garments.
Adorned with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, it was exceedingly beautiful; richly arrayed in all manner of elegant attire, its eyes were wide and trembling with wonder.

Having drawn a diagram on the forehead resembling the pair of her expansive breasts and the frontal globes of a large elephant, with the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) interspersed [with mantric syllables].
Placing his arm upon her shoulder, with her mountain-like breasts held fast by her devotion,
he approached her family, whose mouths were filled with betel and who were intent upon him.
Having performed the recitation without distraction, one brings [the object] under control at that very moment;
by means of the name of whomever the yantra is written, one attracts that person through its power.
[He saw her] situated within a distance of a hundred yojanas, located between rivers and mountains,
and confined by fetters and other restraints across thousands of other islands.
Her waist was slender, burdened by the weight of her breasts; her tremulous eyes were restless;
and her silken garment, slipping from the curve of her hips, had been carried away by the wind.
The practitioner, with a heart full of longing, enters the interior of the cave,
moving through the space between the enclosures secured by iron door-panels.
If the practitioner is a Kaulika, he becomes like a deity moving about, seated within the body of the practitioner, having thus attained the accomplishment of Kṛṣṇa.
Likewise.
On a Tuesday, one should bring *kula-sindūra* to the site of the funeral pyre;
having fashioned a yantra from that very substance upon a *kula-kāṣṭha* wood, [one should place it] within it.
Then one should write the pair "spheṃ spheṃ kiṭi kiṭi," followed by the mantra of Caṇḍa;
thereafter, one should write nine syllables on the leaf of Mahiṣamardinī.
Outside of that, having written the names of Jayadurgā and then Śmaśānabhairavī,
one should worship Kālī there at night with a concentrated mind.
Having established himself at Kāmākhyā and other such sites, and having meditated upon the body as the digit of desire (kāmakalā),
the Kaulika likewise remains naked, with his hair disheveled and falling loose.
One should meditate upon the Goddess, whose face is formidable with fangs, whose eyes are blue,
who has made a garland of severed hands from her quivering corpse, and who is naked.
Seated in the vīrāsana posture, standing upon Mahākāla,
her corners of the mouth smeared with sandalwood paste and other unguents, she is adorned with the roots of the Vedas.
Her thick breasts were smeared with blood dripping from a garland of severed heads,
and the entire earth trembled as she struck it with the joy of intoxication.
Holding a sword and a severed head in her left hands, and endowed with the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness in her right hands, she possesses a terrible roar and a flickering tongue.
Adorned with arrows whose feathers are joined with bird-wings and decorated with ears of grain,
she was attended by jackals of terrible form who spoke with affection.
O Kāla, the hell was seized by those who were intent on making a dual sound with their terrifying, fierce laughter, fierce roars, and fierce slapping of arms.
The leader of the Kula should meditate upon that supreme Kālikā, who is served by those who serve the entire multitude of perfected beings (siddhas), and then worship her.
Without which, the entry into another's body, the crawling into the interior of a hole,
and whatever minor supernatural power (*kulasiddhi*) there may be— none of these arises even in the slightest degree.
The Goddess bestows all accomplishments even through mere thought or casual reflection;
therefore, she is celebrated in the three worlds by the name Dakṣiṇā.
Therefore, O Bhairava, having addressed Siddhārtha, who is born from Śveta, one should perform the rite with the Kālī mantra as previously described for the sādhya and other purposes.
Having bid farewell to the Goddess and established her in his heart at the crossroads,
he should then enter the supreme city, divested of excellent ornaments.
The goddess, having meditated at the entrance and paid homage to the Kula and the Guru,
took white mustard seeds with her left hand while reciting the mantra.
Where there is a fourfold chain encircled by iron spikes,
the hero, fearless and free from agitation, should break through it and enter.
Having transcended the hundredfold cycle, one may then wander at will in a stable for horses,
a chariot-house, or in the vicinity of a weaver’s workshop.
Even in a temple of the gods, one whose eyes are adorned with collyrium,
having meditated upon the Svapnavatī vidyā, may enter the pavilion of desire.
If anyone cries out in distress, one should not feel fear therein; for when it is asked, "Who are you?", one should say, "We are heroic men."
And Purañjaya was unable either to comprehend or to remember it.
Such is the detailed exposition in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*.
Now follows the sādhana of the staff-sandals.
In that very same [text].
Bhairava said:
O Caṇḍikā, how do the great siddhis such as those of the vetālas come to be? Tell me that, O Goddess of gods, if you have affection for me.
The Goddess said:
The best of practitioners, at midnight on a Tuesday marked by the conjunction of the Śavāśana yoga, should take wood produced from a Nimba tree in a cremation ground.
Having dug [the ground], one should indeed recite the mantra of Mahiṣamardinī eight hundred thousand times;
then, O child, one should perform a thousand oblations right there in that cemetery.
Having extracted a piece of wood and marked it with his own staff-sandalwood emblem,
he should then cast it into a cremation ground on the night of the eighth day of the dark fortnight dedicated to Durgā.
O illustrious one, this staff is dear to the heart of the Yoginīs;
it rests in my hand, O Lord—fulfill my command!
Having thus addressed the Vetāla, wherever he was released,
he reduced each of those places to powder and returned to the weaver in an instant.
Go, go, O illustrious one, O sandals of excellent complexion!
By the mere touch of my feet—*ghrāṃ ghrīṃ ghrūṃ*—travel a hundred *yojanas*.
Now follows the sādhana of the sword.
That has been stated in that very same place.
Having obtained eightfold metal (aṣṭaloha) and fashioned a sword measuring fifty finger-breadths, one should draw the yantra upon it and recite the mantra.
Having offered that thousand [oblations] into the body of a great corpse,
one should dig [a pit], place a living creature at the forefront, and visualize it as being bound and dried up.
On the eighth day of the lunar fortnight at midnight, being composed in the midst of the funeral pyre,
one should first perform a salutation and address [the deity], and then offer oblations in the cremation ground.
Combined with the three sweets and accompanied by bilva leaves,
one should offer the bali from the feet up to the head at the conclusion of the fire sacrifice.
The supreme goddess Mahiṣamardinī, the great illusion, dances;
she approaches with her face full of offerings, her hand extended in a boon, and her gaze directed toward her attendants.
Saying "O child, be firm," one should raise and hold aloft the sword, [addressing it as]:
"O Ghoradaṃṣṭrā Mahākālī, you who have the form of a sword!"
"Kāṃ kīṃ kūṃ, O Kūrma, perform the extensive severing of the adversaries!
Having thus addressed the sword, the man should hurl it at his intended target.
Having cut [them] again and again, and having cut them yet again, it goes and comes, and is carried away once more.
In the section on the ritual offering (validāna), the characteristics of the sword (khaḍga) have been described.
Now follows the method for preparing the collyrium.
Alternatively, one should kill a black cat with a single blow and then bury it at night at a crossroads on a Tuesday, having first consecrated it with mantras.
Having placed a plantain fruit there, the wise practitioner should eat only sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) and recite the mantra every night until a leaf emerges.
Alone and without a lamp, one should perform one thousand and eight [recitations];
having cut the leaf that has arisen as the oneness of the self, one should take it up free from any flaw.
Having eaten sacrificial food (haviṣya) there on that day by the riverbank,
he should bring him [the disciple] along with his circle of friends, washing him while reciting the mantra.
O child, when the bone moves against the current,
one should then worship Kālikā there, who possesses a terrible roar.
Having consecrated it a thousand times with the Kālī mantra on all sides, the practitioner becomes possessed of *siddhāñjana*; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
Having mixed sandalwood, agallochum, and musk, and having ground them upon a bone,
the practitioner attains victory over all by applying the resulting mark.
O Lord of the Kula, having diligently brought the Kulāmīna, the Kulānta,
and the Kulamadya to the place of the Kula, [one should worship] with the substances of the Kula.
Having recited [the mantra] one thousand and eight times while standing upon the surface of the earth,
a cavity is produced there in the ground by a mere hissing sound.
Whether the object to be accomplished is situated a hundred yojanas away, his movement goes right there, as he glides along the surface of the earth.
In this way, even within a narrow opening or a window-lattice,
a man passes through without distortion, having contracted his body.
O Lord of the Kula, my child, without the Durgā mantra as well as the Kālī mantra, spiritual accomplishments (siddhis) never arise in any way whatsoever.
The ritual applications of the Tārā mantra should be performed by the noble one.
And these applications of mantras are to be employed in the case of the Tārā mantra.
This is because of the statement in the previously cited *Gandharva-tantra*.
As is Kālī, so is Durgā; as is Durgā, so is Unmukhī. As is Tārā, so is Nīlā; as is Nīlā, so is Unmukhī.
Furthermore, this is stated in the *Kālītantra* and the *Bhairavatantra*: "The meditation on Durgā and Kālikā is declared here to be identical," and so forth.
In the Rudrayāmala.
If the third lunar day of the month of Caitra is conjoined with the asterism Revatī,
by worshipping Kālī on that day, one attains whatever is desired on this earth.
If one performs a fire sacrifice at night in that fire,
well-consecrated according to the ritual procedure of the Kālītantra, the Goddess becomes pleased with him.
If a practitioner performs the *prapañca-vāgaṃ* on that day during the daytime,
Mahāmāyā will be pleased with him, and that Goddess shall become his daughter.
The *prapañcayāga* is a *homa*, because it is prescribed hereafter specifically as the *prapañcayāga*.
Likewise.
One should apply the mantra in a cremation ground to ward off all that is inauspicious;
he shall achieve all his goals, just as my word declares.
Having worshipped the Śakti according to the rules, the wise man who, having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), causes one hundred and eight sips of consecrated water from a sacred site to be drunk;
Accompanied by the taking of purification, he shall become free from all darkness;
here, in the context of "darkness," suffering produced by planetary afflictions, diseases, and so forth is what is meant.
Likewise.
O Dear One, throughout the day during the solar festival, a person who beholds the sun while reciting the eight seed-syllables— *hrīṃ hrīṃ saḥ haṃsaḥ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ*— [attains success].
The defects caused by the planets are destroyed for him as well; there is no doubt about this.

Although this is a mantra of the Sun, nevertheless, because there is no scriptural injunction for its specific ritual procedure and because it is recited within the context of the Kālī-practice, the deity perfected through the Kālī-mantra has authority over these various applications.
Likewise.
O beloved, he who, having made a formal resolve, offers raw meat along with blood and ghee, divided into six portions, into the fire of the Kula at midnight;
O Goddess, he becomes subject to whomever he offers oblations while aiming in that direction,
[using] milk-rice mixed with honey, clarified butter, and sugar.
The preceptor, with disheveled hair and naked, should offer oblations in the wilderness at night, reciting "huṃ huṃ svāhā" one hundred and eight times.
O Goddess, with a one-pointed mind, one may bring the three worlds under control;
furthermore, the great mantra-practitioner [should worship] Śakti, who possesses youth and is naked.
A man should place her, whose limbs are anointed with sandalwood paste, upon his left side,
and make her drink consecrated honey with the mantra *Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Mati*.
And he himself should respectfully drink the remainder of that [liquid] with this mantra.
O Goddess, when the drinking has been performed, he should [anoint] her vulva with sandalwood pastes.
Having smeared [the site] with unguents, the practitioner should worship the Goddess there with the root mantra;
he should offer nine handfuls of water there while reciting the root mantra.
O Goddess, O Sovereign of the Universe, the preceptor should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra,
while drinking and causing [the disciple] to drink from the Śiva-liṅga.
O Viśveśī, one should feed him excellent rice with ghee at intervals,
even while he is eating, until the seed-syllable is mastered without stumbling.
At that most subtle moment, O beloved, having performed the deposition of the seed-syllable,
one shall bring the entire world under control merely by being seen or spoken to.
"Even by touching or through association—so it was spoken by the Omniscient One.
Having written his name upon the ground with red sandalwood,"
It should be encircled by the syllable *hrīṃ* on both sides, above, and below;
having placed the vessel there, [one recites]: "O beloved *hrīṃ*, you who bring others under control!"
Having fixed his mind on that with the mantra ending in "svāhā," the ascetic, possessing the wealth of austerity, should place ghee and parched grain there,
reciting "hrīṃ svāhā" by means of the *kūrca* seed-syllable.
Having made a firm resolve, one should eat; this will certainly bring others under one's control. Then, O Goddess, having fashioned an auspicious doll out of flour—
One with disheveled hair and naked should cook [the substance] with milk and water;
having eaten it, one whose life-force is established should offer oblations with the name of the target, using *svadhā* and *svāhā*.
O Goddess, a human being shall certainly bring even Mahendra under his control by [reciting]:
*hrīṃ vaśīkariṇi svāhā amukaṃ vaśamānaye*.
O beloved, one should feed the protector of the Kula with the mantra *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*,
[offering] rice leaves, ghee, milk, and water from a sacred bathing place, all cooked together.
Even Indra would become his personal servant;
he should offer meat with sugar into the fire of the cremation ground at night, using this mantra.
O Goddess, even if Śiva himself were present in person, he would bring these ten under his control;
for sandalwood consecrated seven times with this mantra [achieves the same].
To whomever one gives it, O beloved, even Yama himself would become subject to his will.
Likewise.
He who, being well-prepared, offers one hundred and eight oblations of consecrated water from a sacred ford into the mouth of a coughing woman with this mantra, [attains success].
O beloved, he would do everything at my word like a slave;
he [saw] the youthful Kṛṣṇā, long-limbed, with broad breasts and hips.
Having taken a man who is of noble family, skilled in the Kāma-mantras, and free from lust for women,
one should establish him on an auspicious seat in the forest on that day.
Either on a wide grass mat, or on a couch, or on an auspicious seat,
one should offer ten oblations with that water which has been consecrated by mantras.
On her face, let there be an equal amount [of paste], or half a *pala*,
and let the region of the vulva of Sānandā be adorned with red sandalwood.
Having worshipped ten times with *javā* flowers,
the knower of the mantra should offer oblations with this *liṅga-mantra* until the offering of the seed-syllable.
The teacher, having caused her to drink that great [quantity] and having drunk it himself as well,
then gave her a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and bowed to her again and again.
She would enchant the entire world; of this there is no doubt, O beloved—she who was fair-limbed, in the prime of youth, of noble birth, yet now with drooping breasts.
O Goddess, the knower of mantras should sprinkle [the vessel] three times with this mantra;
having placed it on his own left side, he should sprinkle it again three times.

One should perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga-vinyāsa) upon her with the Māyā-mantra joined with the [appropriate] caste-syllable. One should place this [mantra] threefold at the navel and ninefold in the circle of the womb.
The sacred substance (tīrtha), consecrated according to rule and placed in a single vessel, should be drunk by Śiva and Śakti; likewise, one should consume meat of that same kind.
Then, having offered oblations ending with the three vessels, he should delight her with undivided mind—
she who is joined with drinking and chewing, who possesses the Great Mantra, and who is naked.
O Goddess, one should recite this mantra— whether by day or by night— even if it is accompanied by improper speech, devoid of shame, forgotten, or fragmented.
Having brought this world under control, one shall attain the state of Śiva in the hereafter.
Likewise.
Then, having recited the Kāmakalā-bīja seven times over seven repetitions,
to whomever one gives a bilva fruit, that person shall immediately come under one's control.

one should sprinkle each syllable a hundred times with the waters of sacred pilgrimage sites.
And one should recite it ten times for every syllable, O Goddess born of the snowy mountain;
thus for seven days, and on the eighth day as well, O Pārvatī.
One shall be brought under control along with one's sons and others, even if they are like the Destroyer at the end of time.
Likewise.
O Goddess, the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable] is proclaimed for the immobilization of speech;
the Daurga [seed-syllable] for the immobilization of cutting; and the Śiva [seed-syllable] for the immobilization of death.
The seed-syllable of Kāmakalā is supreme for the immobilization of the body;
O Goddess of the Universe, the Śrī-bīja should be employed for the immobilization of all things.
Likewise.
O Pārvatī, for those two with whom one recites this mantra sixty times while aiming at enmity,
their mutual hostility shall become life-destroying through cutting and piercing.

O Pārvatī, when one offers water from a sacred ford one hundred and eight times with this mantra for the sake of Śiva,

when the fear of a great enemy has arisen, and when life itself is in peril.

Having placed a lamp upon it, accompanied by a resolve and desire,

Now, there is also another method.
In the Brahmayāmala:
The great vidyā of Kālikā was propitiated by Kaulapeśvara;
having offered a lamp and understood its fruit, he brought forth the seed-syllable for the first time.
Then, having fashioned a yantra with vermilion and encircled it with the root mantra,
one should place a ghee lamp upon it and recite the Dīpinī at the tip of the flame.
The first [syllable] of the Vedas, Kamalā, Kāma, and Vāgbhava, along with Bhuvaneśvarī—
this is the Dīpinī-vidyā, the Kālikā who brings others under her control.
One should perform [the offering] in vessels made of gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, iron, or clay, according to what is available; at dawn, one should be free from pearls and seeds.
One should prepare a wick that is white, yellow, red, pale-pink, or infused with camphor, making it even for a gentle rite; for a fierce rite, the wicks should be uneven.
For gentle planets, one should recite the armor mantra seven times over cow's ghee or fresh butter; for Mars, it should be recited over the milk of goats and sheep.
Then one should make a formal resolve regarding the task, whether it be major or minor.
In this regard, according to the method taught in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*, one should personally assume the form of a Gandharva and,

having caused the Śaktis to become possessed of such forms, light the lamp. Although it is stated in the *Kālītantra* that "Kālikā alone bestows accomplishment through the *Mahānīla* sequence," nevertheless, in the Kali age, by the Vīra—

Only the path described in the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi* is to be followed. It is that very path which succeeds in the offering of the lamp, and not the path of the beast; for the wick [of the lamp] is mixed with the menstrual blood of a woman for the purpose of subjugation.
And the sūtra must be understood from the mouth of the teacher alone.
Now, the distinction of desires resulting from the distinction of mantras is stated specifically in the Merutantra:
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the supreme eight-syllable mantra:
"O Kālikā, svāhā" is declared to be the eight-syllable mantra.

The ritual placement (nyāsa) is as before; here, the meditation is on Śivā, who dwells upon the corpse-form of Śiva, intent on and devoted to Mahākāla, and surrounded by other Śivās in all directions.
In the sacred seat (pīṭha) endowed with the nine powers, Tājā, Vijayā, Ajitā,
as well as Parājitā, Nityā, and Vilāsinī are also proclaimed.
The seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra) consists of the syllables *dogdhri*, *aghora*, and *amaṅgala*, followed by the letter of fire (*ra*).
*Hrīṃ* *Kālikā* *yogapīṭhātmane namaḥ* is declared [as the mantra].
Having first propitiated the limbs, one should worship them upon the six petals:
Kālī, Kapālinī, Kullā, Kurukullā, and Virodhinī.
O Brahmin, having worshipped Cintā, one should worship [the goddesses] in the nine corners:
Ugrā, Ugraprabhā, Dīptā, Nīlā, Dyutimatī, and Valākikā.
Mātrāmudrā, as well as Mitrā—the Mothers are to be worshipped upon the petals;
those previously mentioned are to be worshipped in the Bhūpura, along with the eight Bhairavas and Bhairavī.
Then there is Mahābhairavī, and the third is Siṃhabhairavī;
Dhūmrā is called Bhairavī, and Mī is Bhīmabhairava, who destroys evil.
Unmattabhairavī is the sixth, Vaśīkaraṇabhairava is the seventh,
and the eighth is said to be Mohanabhairavī.
One should likewise worship the guardians of the directions and their weapons; this is how the worship is proclaimed.
One should perform the preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*) and so forth as before, and carry out the ritual applications (*prayoga*) in the same manner.
Desiring his own welfare, one who is devoted to his wife should avoid striking her, reviling her, being deceitful toward her, or even speaking harsh words to her.
If one should satisfy Kālikā with the blood of buffaloes and other such animals,
all supernatural powers (siddhis) will soon come into his very hand.
Now I shall proclaim another [mantra] consisting of twenty-one syllables:
OṂ HRĪṂ HRĪṂ HRŪṂ YUGA TRIR KRĪṂ; one should utter "KĀLIKE" on the right.
*Triḥ krīṃ hūṃ hūṃ śaktiyugmam*, its placement (*nyāsa*) and other rites are as before.
[One should worship] at the root of a *vilva* tree while mounted upon a corpse, and likewise at the root of a *vaṭa* tree.
Having recited this mantra one hundred thousand times, one shall become a master of all accomplishments;
this fifth representative [mantra] bestows success according to the Dakṣiṇāmnāya.
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the unsurpassed mantra of Śakravarṇa:
KRĪM HRŪM HRĪM, O Kālikā of the South; KRĪM HRŪM HRĪM, O Beloved of the Consumer (Fire).
The sacrifice, as previously described, along with the ritual placements (nyāsa), meditation, recitation (japa), and so forth,
is especially capable of attracting the gods and others.
"Hūṃ hūṃ" three times, "krīṃ" twice, with flickering flames on the right, O Kālikā;
again, "Hūṃ hūṃ" three times, "krīṃ" twice, with flickering flames, ending with the syllables of the word "svāhā."

The ritual placement (*nyāsa*), worship, and so forth are as before; specifically, subjugation (*vaśīkṛti*) occurs through the recitation (*japa*) of this [mantra]. Everything else, however, is as previously described.
Having uttered *krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ hūṃ*, one should then utter *hūṃ* twice for the two *lajjās*.
To the right, "Kālike svāhā" is proclaimed as being of a dark color.
This king of mantras is proclaimed; its worship should be performed as previously described.
Specifically, among the various royal rites, this one shall be the bestower of sovereignty.
The single-syllable mantra *krīṃ* is proclaimed as that of Kālikā;
its recitation, worship, and so forth, as previously described, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation through its specific power.
The six-syllable mantra is proclaimed as *krīṃ muktyā kālike svāhā*.
The ritual placement (*nyāsa*), worship, and so forth are as before; however, there is a distinction regarding the fire sacrifice (*homa*) for the sake of enjoyment.
*Krīṃ hūṃ*—this three-syllabled mantra is proclaimed as belonging to Kālī.
Its recitation and other rites are as previously described; specifically, it bestows progeny.
The seed-syllable of Kālī is *hūṃ*, and the mantra is *hūṃ māyāṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, consisting of five syllables.
The ritual placement (*nyāsa*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and other rites are as before; this [mantra] specifically destroys malevolent spirits (*bhūta*).
Having uttered "krīṃ hūṃ hrīṃ phaṭ," this seven-syllabled mantra ending in "svāhā" performs all rites such as nyāsa as previously described; it is especially a bringer of peace.
Now, for the sake of bestowing grace upon devotees and for deliverance from calamity, the armor-yantra (kavaca) is being written.
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, bestower of grace upon devotees:
how does a person obtain protection from all calamities?
The illustrious Lord said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme armor, more secret than the secret, known as the "Deliverance from Calamity," which is most wonderful.
O Goddess, having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times and meditated upon Kālikā,
the Lord of Śacī was formerly liberated from his bonds by Indrajit.
Oṃ! Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi) of this; the meter (chandaḥ) is Gāyatrī; the deity (devatā) is the Lord;
Kālikā is the application (viniyoga) of this for the warding off of all calamities.
May Kālikā, accompanied by the syllables beginning with *krīṃ*, protect my head;
may Caṇḍikā protect my forehead, and may Parāmbikā protect my throat.
May Cāmuṇḍā protect the heart; may Maṅgalacaṇḍikā protect the navel;
may Ugracaṇḍā protect the hands; and may Pracaṇḍā protect the pair of feet.
Bhairavī, Tvaritā, Durgā, Caṇḍogrā, Caṇḍanāyikā,
Jayadurgā, Viśālākṣī, Bhadrakālī, and Kapālinī.
May Śivadūtī, the giver of flesh, protect me from death in the ten directions.
Tārākālī, Śivā, Svāhā; Jayantī, Maṅgalā, Svadhā.
Yoginī, Yoganidrā, Chinnamastā, and Ḍākinī—
[these are to be invoked] at the royal gate, in water, in an empty place, in battle, in distress, or during planetary affliction.
And when the royal sword falls, or in the terrors of the prison house and the like.
"Thus, may they always protect me everywhere with their supreme weapons.
(273a) Thus, O Goddess, I have narrated to you this armor (*kavaca*) which has the nature of Brahman.
It is called the "Extrication from Calamity," for it wards off all misfortunes.
O Goddess, by the mere retention of this, one destroys all calamities in an instant;
having offered a handful of flowers to the Goddess, one should recite the armor-mantra (kavaca) once.
Truth destroys all misfortunes at that very moment; there is no doubt about this.
By reciting it three times, having destroyed all calamities, truth [remains].
Having become most beloved by all, one shall attain universal sovereignty,
even while situated within an iron cage and firmly bound by neck-chains.
Having worshipped the Goddess in one's heart and recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times,
one shall become invulnerable to swords and other weapons, and will certainly be released from bondage.
Having received [this] from the mouth of the Guru, whoever, being pure, recites it a hundred thousand times,
Kālī will be thoroughly pleased and shall manifest herself before him.
Thus ends the armor known as "The Deliverance from Calamity" from the Śrī Rudrayāmala, in the Kālikalpa.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of the Gods, by your grace, I have heard the entire ritual procedure for the worship of Kālikā,
which accomplishes all desired aims.
Now I wish to hear the armor (kavaca) that grants all desires,
bestows enjoyment and liberation, is righteous, pleasing, and destroys sins.
The illustrious Mahādeva said:
O Queen of the Gods, I shall tell you of the armor of the form of Kālikā, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain; if it were not told, where else could it be found?
O Goddess, it is most highly guarded and difficult to find even amidst the tantras;
O Sovereign of the Gods, hear the essence of worship enveloped by mantra.
Whether by reciting it or by retaining it in memory, it bestows the fulfillment of all desires and aims.

Of this Śrī Kālikā-kavaca, Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), Śrī Kālikā is the deity (devatā), Hrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Hūṃ is the power (śakti), Krīṃ is the pin (kīlaka), and its application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of the four aims of human life.
May Māyā protect [me] at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), and Kāmapāyā at the lotus of the heart.
In the place of the three supports is Kālikā, consisting of four syllables;
she who begins with Speech resides in all limbs, possessing five colors and a beautiful countenance.
May the Ekākṣarī protect the head; may she who is renowned as Kṛīṃkārī-Kokā protect the throat;
may the armor protect the neck; and may the threefold one protect the heart-lotus.
May Kāmākhyā, born from the feet of Śiva, always protect the middle [of the body].
May she who is considered Dakṣiṇakālī, with the mantra *krīṃ hūṃ hrīṃ*, protect all the limbs.
May the eight-syllabled Mahākālī protect [me] eternally in her lotus-hand;
may the ten-syllabled Raktakālī always protect me in the pair of her feet.
Composed of thirty-two syllables, may that Dakṣiṇakālikā,
the goddess of the gods, protect my mind from her southern side.
May that dark goddess Kālikā, consisting of twenty-four syllables, protect me from the left;
may the goddess consisting of thirty-six syllables always protect me from behind.
The goddess Kālikā, who bestows all desires, consists of thirty syllables in her belly;
may she, the goddess of thirty syllables, protect all my limbs.
May Rudracaṇḍā protect in the north; may Vārāhī protect in the south;
may she protect in the west, and may Nandī protect in the east.
May the Āgneya-hṛdaya protect the shoulder and always guard the head;
may the Śikhā protect the chest region and well-guard the middle of the eyes.
May Kālikā, the sovereign of the gods, protect the weapon in the four directions;
may Ādyā protect during the time of creation, and may Nityā always protect during its maintenance.
May Subhadrā protect me in my home; may Maṅgalā, the abode of auspiciousness, protect me;
and may the goddess Anaṅgacāriṇī always protect me in the abode of desire.
May Kāmākhyā protect during times of desire, and may she grant all wishes when there is longing; may Mahākālī protect in terrible fear, and Bhadrā protect in auspicious circumstances.
May Jayā protect me from terrifying and fearsome death in the forest of human disease;
may Māyā always protect me in the great world, and may Bhuvaneśvarī protect my sovereignty.
May Bhairavī protect in terrifying tasks, Tripura in the conquest of the city of Tripura, Durgā in times of difficult distress, and Kālī during the arrival of wealth.
May Kālarātri protect me during the night, Kāmeśī during the day,
Kāmeśvarī at twilight, and Kamalā for my prosperity.
May Kālī protect against the destruction of enemies; may Kāntā protect as one seeks refuge;
may Kurukullā protect in the assembly; and may Virodhinī protect on dry land.
May Vipracintā protect in the forest, and likewise Ghorārājñī in times of fear;
may Ugraprabhā protect against the danger of mantras, and Dīptā among those dear to kings.
May Nīlā protect me from Brahmins; may Udyantī protect me from Kṣatriyas;
may Valākā protect me from Vaiśyas; and may Mātṛ protect me from Śūdras.
May Mudrā protect us from friends and enemies, and may she protect us from foes;
may Brahmāṇī protect us, and may Nārāyaṇī protect us from Yakṣas.
May Māheśvarī protect [me] among the hosts of spirits (bhūtagaṇa), and Cāmuṇḍā protect me from the state of a ghost (preta);
may Kaumārī protect me against the Kuṣmāṇḍas, and Parājitā protect me during meditation (dhyāna).
May Vārāhī protect against insanity, and may Nārasiṃhī protect from all sides; O Dear One, may the lords of the directions, together with their weapons, protect [me] in every direction.
O lady of excellent vows, she is present everywhere, at all times, in all diseases, in all sorrows, in all sūtras, for all people, and throughout all worlds.
May Kālikā, the supreme sovereign who grants the accomplishment of all aims, protect you.
Thus, O Goddess, I have told you this armor (kavaca), which bestows all desires.
One should protect everything together with mantras and even with beautiful syllables;
he who recites this while meditating upon Kālikā is protected by the Goddess of the Gods.
Listen now to this supreme merit of his, which brings about various accomplishments:
he has bathed in all sacred fords and has been saluted by all the gods.
Whoever recites this armor-mantra (*kavaca*) proclaimed by Bhairava with supreme devotion shall destroy the sins accumulated over ten million lifetimes, whether committed knowingly or unknowingly.
By reciting the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) even once, [the sin] is reduced to ashes by its mere mention:
the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, and violating the teacher’s bed.
Having reduced all that to ashes, the reciter attains liberation,
he who constantly recites this armor with self-restraint and concentration according to the rule.
O beautiful one, even for that man, there shall be mastery over speech;
his word shall be a paralyzer, and it shall bring the pleasant coolness of fire.
O Sovereign Goddess of Stambhana, that man who is able to perform this [rite] becomes a bestower of boons even to the lowest of beings; such a person is rare to find on earth.
What more need be said? By reciting this constantly, a man obtains all those desired objects that he has studied.
Having inscribed [the name] upon birch bark with substances derived from lac and saffron,
or else with gorocana and sandalwood, one should likewise place it upon a flower auspicious to Śiva.
On an auspicious day and an auspicious lunar date, avoiding the *gaṇḍabhadrā* yoga,
one should worship the Supreme Goddess right there according to the prescribed ritual.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations for a month with sweet substances and honeyed sequences,
one should take the armor from that fire and wrap it with bitten iron.
Alternatively, one may wear [the image] containing gold within it on the right arm,
or on the left, or in the region of the neck, or likewise on the crest-lock or at the heart.
One may obtain the fruit of worship even without following the formal sequence of worship; what need is there for much speaking? There is nothing else superior to this.
O auspicious lady, it must be kept secret like the pregnancy resulting from a mother's paramour;
this armor proclaimed by Bhairava must not be spoken of anywhere.
If it is spoken [to others], there will be a loss of accomplishment; I tell you this as the truth, the absolute truth.
It should be given to one who is peaceful, to a disciple, to a son, or to one who has given his life [for the teacher].
Or even one who is devoted to the guru and intent upon the performance of worship.
Thus ends the *Kālikā-kavaca*, composed by Mahākāla, within the *Mahāmāyā-tantra*.
Now, the armor (kavaca) for the purpose of the retention-mantra (dhāraṇa-yantra) is written [here], according to the Uttaratantra.
Seated upon the peak of Kailāsa, Bhairava, who bears the moon upon his crest,
was addressed by Bhairavī as she sat upon his chest.
Bhairavī said:
O Lord of Gods, Supreme Ruler, Maker of the worlds and planets!
Why was the armor previously indicated not revealed?
O Kulabhairava, if you have great affection for me,
please out of compassion tell me the armor-mantra (kavaca) of the goddess Kālikā.
Bhairava said:
O Goddess, this is not to be disclosed in the world of men, especially so;
for although you have been forbidden a hundred thousand times, you ask out of the very nature of women.
Bhairavī said:
O Lord, there are many servants devoted to the family dharma,
for they have renounced all hope for their own lives upon the funeral pyre over the corpse.
O Lord, O ocean of compassion, for the sake of accomplishing their practice and especially for the sake of my own protection, I ask you repeatedly; please speak.
Bhairava said:
Listen, O wise one, I shall tell you the supreme armor (kavaca) of Kālikā;
it must be kept secret before the uninitiated, just as one would keep one's own private parts hidden from another.
This Great Queen of all Vidyās has been declared, which is difficult to obtain on earth.
Of this Śrī Kālikā-kavaca, Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi), Uṣṇik is the meter (chandaḥ), Kālikā in her non-dual form is the deity (devatā),

Hrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Huṃ is the power (śakti), Krīṃ is the pin (kīlaka); the application (viniyoga) is for the sake of attaining the perfection of the mantra that precedes the accomplishment of all aims.
Oṃ! May the Guru, white as camphor, seated upon the great thousand-petaled lotus, together with the Śakti residing upon his left thigh, protect me everywhere and at all times.
May the Guru known as Parā protect me, and likewise the Guru Parāparā;
may the Guru Parameṣṭhin protect me, as well as the divine, the perfected, and the human Gurus.
May Mahādevī always protect, and may Mahādeva likewise protect;
may Tripurā Bhairava, who eternally assumes a divine form, protect.
May Brahmānanda protect me always; may Pūrṇadeva likewise protect me; may Calacitta protect me always, and may Calācala protect me.
May Kumāra, Krodhana, Varada, and Smaradīpana,
along with Māyā, Māyāvatī, and the hosts of Siddhas, protect [us] at all times.
Vimala, Kuśala, Bhīmasena,
Sudhākara, Mīna, Gorakṣaka, Bhojadeva, and Prajāpati.
May Mūladeva, Rattideva, Vighneśvara, and Hutāśana,
along with Santoṣa and Samayānanda, always protect us humans.
O Ānanda, all [the deities] ending with the Lords (nātha) and the Mothers (mātṛ) ending with the Ambās follow in sequence;
may Gaṇanātha always protect me, and may Bhairava always protect me.
May Vaṭuko protect me always; may Durgā guard me;
and may Ghoradakṣiṇā protect me from the top of my head down to my feet.
Likewise, may Kālī protect me in the head, and the Root [Mantra] protect my heart;
may the Goddess, through the complete Vidyā, always protect me everywhere.
May *krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ* protect my face; may *hūṃ hūṃ* always protect my heart.
May *hrīṃ hrīṃ* protect me in the east, *hraṃ hraṃ* in the south, and *krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ* protect me from the left.
May Svāhā always protect [me] on the back; may the Mūla-mantra protect me everywhere.
May the youthful Ṣaḍaṅga protect the six limbs along with their presiding deities.
May the King of Yantras, situated above, below, and in the cardinal and intermediate directions, always protect me;
and may the deities residing within the King of Wheels also protect me.
Ugrā, fierce and blazing with intense radiance, protects the eastern triangle;
and Nīlāghanāvalākā likewise protects the other triangle.
Mātrā, Mudrāmitā, as well as Madhyatrikoṇā;
Kālī, Kapālinī, Kullā, Kurukullā, and Vibodhinī.
O Dear One, may Vipracintā protect [the deity] situated outside the hexagon;
all are dark-complexioned, holding swords in their left hands and displaying the threatening gesture (tarjanī).
May Brāhmī protect the eastern petal, and likewise Nārāyaṇī the southeast;
may Māheśvarī protect the southern petal, and Cāmuṇḍā the west indeed.
May Kaumārī protect [me] in the west; may Aparājitā protect [me] in the northwest;
may Vārāhī protect [me] in the north; and may Nārasiṃhī grant auspiciousness.
Aiṃ Hrīṃ: May the Bhairava Asitāṅga protect me in the east;
Aiṃ Hrīṃ: May Ruru protect me in the southeast corner; Aiṃ Hrīṃ: And may Caṇḍa protect me in the south.
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Kroṃ Śauṃ, may Nairṛtya protect me in the southwest; likewise, Aiṃ Hrīṃ Unmattaka protects me in the west; and Aiṃ Hrīṃ Kapālī protects me in the left corner.
Aiṃ Hrīṃ: Bhairava named Bhīṣaṇa is indeed in the north;
Aiṃ Hrīṃ: Saṃhāra is in the northeast, along with the Śivas who reside in the limbs of the Mothers.
Aiṃ Hetuka, the child-ascetic (vaṭu), may he always protect me on the eastern petal;
Aiṃ Tripurāntaka, the child-ascetic, may he always protect me in the southeast.
Aiṃ! May Vahni-Vetāla also always protect me in the south;
Aiṃ! May Agni-jihva-vaṭuka likewise [protect me] in the southwest and in the west.
Aiṃ! May Kālavaṭuka protect; likewise, Aiṃ! May Karālavaṭuka protect. In the northwest, may Ekapāda protect; in the north, may Vaṭuka protect.
Aiṃ! May Bhīma Vatuka protect [me] forever in the northeastern direction.
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Krīṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā! [May] the sixty-four Mothers [protect me].
May she protect me in the upper, lower, right, left, front, and back regions; O Aiṃ Hūṃ Siṃhavyāghramukhī, may you guard me in the east!

Aiṃ Kāṃ Kāṃ: May she with the face of a serpent and the face of a camel protect me always in the southeast corner. Aiṃ Māṃ: May she with the face of a deer and the face of a ram protect me always in the south.
Aiṃ cauṃ cauṃ: May she who has the face of an elephant and a horse protect me always in the southwest.
Aiṃ meṃ meṃ: May she who has the face of a cat protect me always in the west.
Aiṃ Ṣauṃ Ṣoṃ: May Kroṣṭvākhumukhī protect [me] eternally in the northwest corner.
Aiṃ Hāṃ Hāṃ: [May] Hrasvadīrghamukhī, Laṃbodarī, and Mahodarī [protect me].
May she protect me in the northern corner; may she who is at the corner of Śiva—Aiṃ Hrīṃ Hrīṃ—whose shanks are short and whose shanks are like palm trees, and whose lips are long, always protect me.
May these goddesses, who dwell in the cremation grounds, who are terrifying with their distorted faces,
and who grant the desires of practitioners, protect me at all times.
May Indra protect me from the east, and Agni from the south-east;
may Yama always protect me from the south, and likewise Nirṛti from the south-west.
May Varuṇa protect me from the west, and Vāyu from the northwest;
may Kuvera protect me in the north, and Sadāśiva in the northeast.
May Brahmā always protect me from above, and the deity Ananta from below;
may those stationed in the directions beginning with the east, along with the hosts of weapons such as the vajra, protect me.
May Kālikā protect my head; may Kālikā protect my heart.
May Kālikā protect my foundation; may Kālikā protect my feet.
May Kālikā protect me in the cardinal directions; may Kālikā protect me in the intermediate directions.
May Kālikā protect me above; may Kālikā protect me below.
Skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen indeed;
as well as the sense organs, the mind, and the joints of the body.
May Kālikā always protect me from the hair to the feet;
may Kālikā protect me as I enter [the house], and may Kālikā protect me on this path.
May Kālikā protect me on my bed; may Kālikā protect me in all undertakings.
May Kālikā protect my life-breaths; may Kālikā protect my wife.
May Kālikā protect my sons; may Kālikā protect me. Wherever there are obstacles born of my doubt, may they perish by the command of Śiva.
Thus, O Goddess, this armor is difficult to obtain even in the world of Brahmā;
out of affection for you, I have declared it, yet it must be guarded like one's own life-source.
O Goddess, when Your name is remembered, the fruit of all sacrifices is obtained;
all sins go to destruction, and one finds fulfillment in every desire.
The hymn of praise for the Name is a hundredfold more meritorious than that; meditation upon it is a hundred times superior to that;
the mantra is a hundred times superior to that; and the armor (kavaca) is a hundred times superior to that.
Having become pure and composed, endowed with devotion and faith,
one should establish the Śakti, who is solely devoted to her Lord, on one's left side.
Seated upon red garments, auspicious, and bearing the mantra of Śiva—
she who is Śakti is the Great Goddess, while the practitioner is the form of Hara.
O Goddess, divinity arises from mutual contemplation;
endowed with Śakti, one should worship the Goddess either in the Cakra or even with a rosary.
O beloved, one should then worship with enjoyments such as the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and well-perfumed betel leaves,
and then, with a single-minded focus, recite the divine armor (kavaca).
For him, there shall be the accomplishment of all goals; no doubt should be entertained in this regard.
This is the supreme secret, the great and ultimate source of well-being.
O Goddess, whoever should recite this even once, or listen to it with a concentrated mind,
shall obtain all desires and go to the supreme city of the Goddess.
O Goddess, whoever recites this armor (kavaca), which is difficult even for the gods to obtain, even once,
shall undoubtedly attain the fruit of all sacrifices.
In battles he shall conquer his enemies like a lion among elephants;
and those missiles and weapons shall prevail against his body.
For him, disease never arises, nor does suffering ever exist;
his movement is everywhere, and he is always like the wind.
One shall always be long-lived, a lord of sensual enjoyments, and devoted to one's guru;
oh, how great is the majesty of this armor-mantra when recited daily!
Even without the practice of yoga,
one may attain the state of a yogi by drawing a well-constructed wheel there upon birch bark.
Having inscribed the syllables of the practitioner and the person for whom the rite is performed within a triangle in the center,
one should extract the root mantra and encircle it with the letters of the Mātṛkā.
O beautiful one, O Maheśānī, this yantra composed by Laghumiśra, Candra, and Candana is difficult to obtain even for gods and asuras.
One should draw the armor (kavaca) outside that with cow-gallstone and saffron;
having wrapped it with a white thread, one should encircle it with lac.

Having bathed [the image] on an auspicious day with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should worship the pill (guṭikā), which is the embodiment of the deity and the granter of all desires.
One should enjoin the vital breath (prāṇa) into the tantra with the Prāṇapratiṣṭhā mantra;
then, having meditated upon the inner womb (antaryoni), the wise one should establish [the deity] therein.
But this pill, O Goddess, when placed upon the neck, bestows wealth;
on the head, O Goddess, it brings subjugation; and at the navel, it causes paralysis.
When placed on the left arm of the bride, she brings about the destruction of the enemy faction;
when situated in the belly, she subdues disease and bestows sons.
The goddess Yaśaskarī, who bestows knowledge upon the forehead and bestows glory upon the crest-lock,
grants all desires and brings about the destruction of all diseases.
If it always remains at the base of the right arm,
then all purposes will be accomplished, whatever resides in one's mind.
O beloved, by reciting and wearing this armor-mantra for three days, one attains all desires; this has been revealed out of affection for you.
O Goddess, just as true knowledge is obtained through the grace of the Guru’s feet,
so too is this armor, which is difficult to find in the three worlds.
And that god Hara is manifestly present there, as is his consort, the Supreme Goddess;
O beloved, he whose devotion to the Guru is constant, like that toward a deity.
Then the accomplishment of the mantra and the yantra occurs, and not otherwise;
likewise, there is the accomplishment of the armor and the beautiful pill.
O Goddess, without knowing the armor-mantra (kavaca) and without having recited the guru’s sandals-mantra (gurupādukā), one does not attain that fruit;
in the hereafter, one shall go to hell.
Truth, truth, again truth, truth, truth, again and again:
I am not able to describe the power of this armor.
O Sovereign of the Gods, this Kavaceśa, which is extremely difficult to obtain, must not be given to just anyone;
it should not be given to the disciples of others nor to those who are miserly.
To a disciple who is devoid of devotion, as well as to a libertine,
to one lacking devotion for the guru, and to one who is addicted to the wives of others.
O beautiful one, he who gives this armor spoken from my own mouth to those who are censurers, of immoral conduct, or hypocrites— to such forbidden persons— [commits a grave fault].
Elsewhere one encounters suffering, and in the next world one goes to hell;
[therefore, this] should be given to a disciple who is peaceful and devoted to the guru.
"To her who is endowed with all auspicious marks and joined with that mantra"—
thus ends the Śrī Dakṣiṇakālī Kavaca, within the *Antaratantra*, in the dialogue between Kālī and Bhairava.
Now follows the refinement of another instrument.
In the Vāmakeśvaratantra.
The illustrious Bhairavī said:
O Great God, by your grace I have heard about the schism of the wheel;
now I wish to hear the determination of the ritual for consecration.
The illustrious Śaṅkara said:
Listen, O Goddess, O Kaulinī, creator of the world; I shall explain the concluding rite (udyāpana) as an auxiliary part of that [practice], which provides a definitive determination for all castes.
Having bathed, the practitioner of mantra should form a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) and perform the worship of the Guru;
the Guru, with the mantra, should draw the yantra with a golden stylus.
Having first prepared the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) consecrated with the Śiva-mantra,
the practitioner, composed in mind, should cast the wheel there while reciting the Praṇava.
Therefore, having lifted that wheel, one should place it upon a golden lotus,
[bathing it] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), milk, and cool water.
O Goddess, one should bathe [the deity] with sandalwood, musk, and saffron,
using eight golden jars filled with water.
One should bathe [the deity] with water brought in jars while reciting the mantra;
then, having lifted that yantra, one should place it in a golden vessel.
"To the King of Yantras, to the Great Yantra in its embodied form, we meditate;
at the end of this, one should utter: 'May the Yantra impel us there.'"

Having touched the yantra with the tip of a blade of kuśa grass, one should consecrate it with the Sāvitrī mantra one hundred and eight times, O Goddess; thus the state of being the deity will be accomplished.
Then, having performed the purification of oneself, one should become the deity through meditative absorption;
there, one should worship the Goddess with offerings of betel nut, jasmine, and food oblations.
O Maheśvarī, one should offer silk thread and the like, as well as garments and ornaments, a flower bud, a fly-whisk, and a bell, according to what is appropriate.
One should offer all this with great effort, for it leads to the attainment of the earth;
thereafter, one should recite the mantra a thousand times for the sake of accomplishing every desired object.
Then, having performed the ritual offering (validāna), one should prostrate to the king of yantras;
having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one should pour the residual clarified butter (saṃpātājya) [into the fire].
The preceptor should protect [the disciple] from the impact of weapons and perform everything [for his benefit];
having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor according to one's ability, one should bid him farewell.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the Kulamuktikallolinī composed by the venerable Ādyānanda.
Now, the divisions of Kālī.
In the Tantraśekhara:
The temporal divisions of its emergence are concealed in all the Tantras;
it is firmly established from the beginning of the mouth to the end of the mouth, and is endowed with the limit of Śiva.
This Vidyā, which is worshipped by the worlds, is said to have Āsya as its crest-jewel.
The letter *ka* is at the end of its mouth; the letter *ya* is followed by *repha*; the long *ī* is at the end of *śiva*; and the *bindu* is at the end of its mouth.
The goddess, consisting of six syllables, is consecrated with the seed-syllable and accompanied by Śiva; thus, the mantra is *krīṃ kālike svāhā*.
One should discard the terminal seed-syllables of the previously mentioned king of mantras;
this sixteenfold Vidyā consists of the letters corresponding to the lunar days (tithis) and is endowed with Ramā.
The collection of seed-syllables (bīja) belonging to the Vidyā, which consists of the letters corresponding to the lunar days (tithi),
should be recited in reverse order, preceded by two *ṭha* syllables.
The Vidyā consisting of three seeds is considered by Brahmā to be worshiped by Kāma;
that which begins with vīḍā is worshiped by Śakra, while the Vaiṣṇavī ends with hūṃ phaṭ.
When deprived of three syllables, Vaiṣṇavī becomes Bhairavī;
Bhairavī is said to be Nāradī, while Hārdā bestows both wealth and dharma.
Salutation to the Heart.
The seed-syllable of the Vidyā residing in the letter Va is known as the beloved of Agni;
the Vidyā worshipped by Kuvera is Kālī—these are remembered as the divisions.
The seed, the sevenfold seed.
The seer and other details were previously stated, as before, regarding the worship during the vehicle [of practice].
In the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*.
Brahmā, joined with Sarasvatī and situated in the mouth of the Lord,
conjoined with the power of knowledge (vidyā-śakti), is declared to be the Kālī-mantra.
Brahmā is the letter *a*; Sarasvatī is the long *ī*; the mouth of the deity is the *repha* (*r*).
The power of knowledge is the bindu.
O Bhairava, having recited it once, twice, or even thrice, one may attract the entire world, both the stationary and the moving.
This ignorance is the great knowledge (mahāvidyā), remembered as secret and more secret than the secret;
the prior seed-syllable is the supreme power, and from that seed-syllable, the conceptualization of the form [is made].
One should perform the visualization of the limbs and so forth using the seed-syllable that possesses six long vowels;
all else is as described for the twenty-two syllable mantra.
In the Kālītantra.
By means of the Kālī-hṛdaya-vidyā, the Siddhavidyā, and the Mahodayā,
as well as through ancient practice, the inhabitants of the celestial realms attained accomplishment.
The syllable of desire (KĀM) situated in fire (R), together with Indirā (I) and the nasal sound and point (NĀDA-VINDU),
is known as this King of Mantras, difficult to obtain for those with sinful minds.
Accessible through devotion to those of great mind who have performed meritorious deeds, this [work],
which awakens one to all scriptures, is especially distinguished by its threefold lunar digits.
Indeed, there is no knowledge equal to this bestowed by Sarasvatī;
it includes all meditation, worship, spiritual practice, and ritual honors.
O Aniruddha, Sarasvatī has been fully glorified as equal [to the other goddesses].
Now I shall proclaim the Jewel of Knowledge, which, upon being heard, immediately becomes an ornament for the ears.
The Māyā-bīja, the pair of Kūrcas, the three ending with Indra (Ra), the three Madanas (Sa),
and the Māyā-bīja joined with Bindu and Īśvara (Ha)— this is the word "Kālike" in the south.
By means of the yoga of the sequence of withdrawal, one should utter the seven seed-syllables;
this twenty-one-syllable mantra is worshipped by the universe, beginning with Tārā.
This king of mantras consists of twenty-three syllables when ending with *svāhā*;
without *svāhā*, this mantra that grants desires consists of twenty-one syllables.
The Vidyā consists of twenty syllables, ending with "svāhā" and excluding the Praṇava. All rites such as meditation and worship should be performed according to the procedure for the Dakṣiṇā.
Also in the Kumārī Tantra:
Having extracted the twenty-two syllables, the Great Vidyā consists of the previous seed-syllable.
Likewise, there are three preceding seed-syllables.
O Maheśvarī, the pair of *kūrca*s is the Great Vidyā, as is the single *kūrca*;
the pair of *lajjā*s is the Great Vidyā, and likewise there may be a single *lajjā*.
In the south is "Kālike Svāhā"; this is proclaimed as another Vidyā.
This Vidyā is the royal Vidyā for both recitation and worship.
Now I shall proclaim the Great Vidyā, the perfected Vidyā of great prosperity,
which was formerly taught by Īśvara and is known as Devīhṛdayā.
By the power of whose knowledge I perceive the three worlds;
having first uttered the Praṇava, one should then utter the seed-syllable Hṛllekhā.
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Rati, joined with the fifth letter [Pa] and endowed with the Bhaga [Ū],
and conjoined with two Ṭha-s, she is proclaimed as the Queen of Vidyās.
A science such as this is very difficult to find within the Kālītantra;
the seed-syllable of Rati is *krīṃ*, which is by its own nature the auspicious armor (*kavaca*) of the world.
The syllable *om* is the fifth [vowel].
Bhairava is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), Virāṭ is cited as the meter (chandas),
and the deity is Bhuvaneśvarī, who is Siddhakālī and the embodiment of Brahman.
The seed-syllable of Rati is her seed; Hṛllekhā is said to be her Śakti.
One should fashion [the mantra] with Hṛllekhā preceded by the Praṇava and the six long vowels.
Then, having performed the placement of the six limbs and meditated upon the Goddess, one becomes Śiva.
Her limbs drenched by the nectar flowing from the orb of the moon split open by her sword, the three-eyed goddess, with disheveled hair, drinks blood from a skull-bowl held in her right hand.
Clad in the directions as her garment, adorned with a girdle and a jeweled crown, she possesses blazing tongues and feet licked by blue lotuses, suns, moons, and shimmering earrings.
The knower of mantras should recite twenty-one thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice with soft flowers using one-tenth of that number.
Having approached a triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one who has mastered the vidyā becomes Śiva;
the worship and the ritual application should be performed according to the form of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Or indeed, the entire ritual procedure for the Ekākṣarī Mahākālī.
In the Viśvasāra Tantra:
O Pārvatī, listen; I shall now declare the six-syllabled Mahākālī mantra.
Having extracted the three seed-syllables, one should extract the syllable of the weapon (astra).
The Vidyā known as Trailokyamohinī is said to end with the wife of Vahni (the fire-god).
In the Bhairavī Tantra.
The Vāgbhava [bīja] is the heart-syllable (HRĪM) mounted on fire (the letter RA),
conjoined with the second vowel (Ī), and joined with the bindu and the crescent moon (the anusvāra and visarga).
Having uttered [the first part] twice, then again the fourth vowel joined with the bindu;
having uttered that twice, followed by "Kālikāyai" and the wife of Vahni (Svāhā)—this is the mantra.
Also in the *Kāmākṣāpañcāśikā*:
Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme eleven-syllable Great Vidyā:
having first uttered the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], one places Prajāpati mounted upon Fire.
Again, these two seed-syllables, joined with the facial rotation (mukhavṛtta), O Goddess, are the two seed-syllables of Kālī; thereafter, one should utter "Kālikāyai."
The mantra, ending with the wife of Vahni (Svāhā), is declared to bestow all prosperity;
Dakṣiṇāmūrti is its seer, and Paṅkti is said to be its meter.
The goddess Kālikā is remembered as the power higher than the highest;
the eleven-syllable mantra of Kālikā is very difficult to obtain.
By good fortune, she bestows all sovereignty and happiness;
two hundred thousand recitations should be performed as the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
Likewise, according to the ritual procedure including all its limbs and sub-limbs, one should [meditate upon her] eight thousand times—
[her] four-armed, black-complexioned [form], adorned with a garland of severed heads.
She bears a sword in her right hand and a bow with an arrow,
while she carries, in order, a shaven head and an alms-bowl in her left hands.
She herself bears a single matted lock upon her head that reaches up to the sky,
while always wearing a garland of severed heads both on her head and around her neck.
One should visualize her arriving here as described below: possessing blood-red eyes,
wearing black garments, and having a tiger skin draped around her waist.
Having placed the left foot upon the heart of the corpse and having set the right foot upon the back of the lion, [he stands] over the corpse itself, licking his lips.
Having thus visualized the Supreme Goddess Kālikā with her devotees— possessing loud, terrifying laughter, endowed with most dreadful cries, and inspiring awe.
By those who are constantly endowed with devotion and who desire enjoyments and sovereignty.
In the independent [tantra].
Listen attentively, O beloved, to the mantra of Śmaśānakālikā:
first Vāṇī, then Māyā, then Lakṣmī, and after that the Kāmabīja.
O Goddess of gods, one should write the four seed-syllables in a combined form within the *kālika*; this eleven-syllable mantra bestows the four aims of human life.
The seer is Bhṛgu, the metre is Nivṛt, and the deity is the supreme Kālikā;
O Maheśvarī, Śmaśānādyā, Vāṅmayā, Bīja, and Śakti [are the limbs].
The *kīlaka* shall be the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*). Listen, O beloved, to the worship and the offering (*bali*):
with four, three, and four syllables, and by repeating [the sequence] twice, one performs the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa), one should, with a concentrated mind, meditate upon the Goddess Kālikā,
who resembles a mountain of collyrium and dwells in the cremation ground.
She has three eyes and loose, disheveled hair; she is extremely terrifying with her emaciated flesh, has tawny eyes, and holds in her left hand a skull-cup filled with wine.
Holding a freshly severed head in her right hand,
Śivā always has a smiling face, while she is intent on chewing the flesh of the left [hand].
Having thus meditated upon the Goddess— her limbs adorned with various ornaments, naked, intoxicated, and always [seated] on corpses— one should especially worship Her in a cremation ground.
Or even at home, a householder, having become naked and being composed in mind, should perform the great worship at night with excellent meals consisting of fish and meat.
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus within a circle, and outside of that, the ground;
it should be provided with four gates, and one should inscribe the root mantra in the center.
On the petals, one should inscribe the eight groups of consonants beginning with the *ka*-group;
on the earth [of the lotus], one should draw four gates in the four directions.
From the east to the north, one should worship the Goddess in the center.
O beloved, having worshipped the Mothers beginning with Brāhmī on the eight petals starting from the east,
one should worship the Bhairavas beginning with Asitāṅga upon the ground.
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for this consists of eleven lakh recitations of the mantra;
one should recite the mantra for one lakh syllables and perform the fire oblation (homa) with a tenth part of that amount.
In the Svatantra [Tantra].
Having written the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM), one should write the word "to Kālikā" (kālikāyai);
O Goddess of the Gods, with [the disciple's] name at the end, this is the supreme mantra of seven syllables.
The goddess Kālikā is the entire body; everything else is as previously described.
In the Bhairavatantra.
O Goddess, the two seed-syllables of Kālī, along with the long *hūṃ* syllable—
this three-syllabled great vidyā is known as Cāmuṇḍā-Kālikā.
O Goddess, the first is Vāgbhava, and likewise Kūrcabīja;
then Vedādi, which is Vāgbhava, and likewise Māyāvīja.
The mantra joined with *phaṭ* and *svāhā* bestows the accomplishment of all aims;
O Goddess, it likewise contains the two *kālī* seeds and the pair of *kūrca* mantras.
O Goddess of gods, there is a pair of *māyās* and the six-syllabled *Kālī-vidyā*.
Having first extracted one's own seed-syllable (*svabīja*), [one places] "Kālike" to the south.
One's own seed-syllable and "svāhā" constitute that ten-syllabled Kālikā;
O Goddess, [the mantra] consists of the Māyā-bīja twice, followed by the word "dakṣiṇe kālike."
The seed-syllable of Kūrca, likewise Māyā, and at the end Vahni-vallabhā—
this is the great vidyā of Kālī, which bestows all eloquence.
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Kālī, as well as the Kūrca and Māyā syllables,
[one should utter] "O Kālikā" in the south, followed by one's own seed-syllable and the Kūrca seed-syllable.
O Goddess, the auspicious fourteen-syllable mantra beginning with "māyā svāhā" belongs to you;
you are the goddess who holds a sword and a severed head, bestowing boons and granting fearlessness.
In the Rudrayāmala.
The first of all [syllables], the *kūrca* seed-syllable (*hūṃ*), and likewise the two *lajjā* syllables (*hrīṃ hrīṃ*);
then "O Kālikā" in the dative case, and after that, the pair of *kūrca* syllables (*hūṃ hūṃ*).
This supreme Vidyā, beginning with Tārā and followed by the wife of Vahni (Svāhā), has been declared;
all worship is as before, and the mantra consists of fifteen syllables.
Then, the seed-syllable of *lajjā* (hrīṃ) three times, followed by "O Kālikā" on the right;
then again the triad of *lajjā*, followed by the wife of fire (svāhā).
The ritual procedure is declared as before; the syllable *vanārṇa* has been proclaimed. O Goddess, the pair of seed-syllables of sound is "Kālike," and the word for the right side is "dakṣiṇe."
Likewise, O Goddess, the twelve-syllable mantra for the armor (*varma*) ends with *svāhā*;
one should perform all rites such as the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and worship as previously described.
O Kuleśvarī, the twelve-syllable mantra consists of the seed-syllable *carm* at the beginning of the name, followed by the name itself, then two *hrīṃ*s, and finally joined with two *ṭha*s.
The armor is the seed-syllable *hūṃ*, [and] *hrīṃ*.
One should indeed visualize all [the deities] beginning with Dhyāna as before;
first, O Goddess, the pair of Lajjās, and then Kālikā on the right.
The pair of *krīṃ* syllables, followed by the pair of *kūc*s,
and ending with *svāhā*— this is the sixteenth *alajjā*, well-guarded in secrecy.
Likewise, "lajjā" means the pair [of shame] consisting of *lajjā*.
The word *kālike* on the right is flanked by *lajjā* (the seed-syllable of Māmakī) on both sides;
this twelve-syllable mantra is joined with the wife of Fire (svāhā).
Then, on the right, [one should place] the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* encircling the beard (*kūrca*), followed by *kālike*.
These, along with the previously mentioned seed-syllables, are joined with the wife of fire (*vahnijāyā*).
This great mantra of Kālikā, consisting of thirty-two syllables, has been proclaimed;
one should perform their meditations, worship, and so forth, according to the rite of Dakṣiṇā.
In the Rudrayāmala:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim that which is difficult to obtain and heart-pleasing:
having extracted the seed-syllable of Śakti, immediately thereafter [extract] the seed-syllable of Kālī.
Then, O Goddess, one should extract the pair of *kūrca*s and the heart-mantra;
this knowledge, O highly fortunate lady, is difficult to obtain in the three worlds.
For one who masters this, what on earth cannot be accomplished?
Likewise, the seers, meters, deities, as well as recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth.

All that has been declared regarding the twenty-two-syllable mantra of the Goddess is the same [as before]. One should utter the word "Prāsāda" ending in "Ātman," and then utter the words "Kāli Mahākāli."
The syllable *ka* joined with the eye (*i*) is doubled; at its end, one utters *phaṭ* and *svāhā*. This fourteen-syllabled mantra is that of Mahākālī.
The syllables *ka* and *la* constitute the eyes; it is joined with the short vowel *i*.
Thus, the pair *ka* and *la* results in the word *kilikili*.
HOṂ KĀLIMAHĀKĀLI KILIKILI PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. Then, the three-syllable mantra consists of the seed-syllable of Lañjā (HRĪḤ), followed by the Kūrca (HUṂ), and ending with PHAṬ.
The two fires of dissolution (ha) are joined with blood (ra) and upward-pointing hair (u);
likewise, the two forms of Krodha (kṣa) are again conjoined with Nāda (the nasal bindu).
O beloved, accept from my feet this armor and weapon-mantra consisting of fourteen syllables, beginning with the word *dhruva*, which is proclaimed as Mahākālī.
*Pha-kārau*, *tuṃ*, *phreṃ*, *phreṃ*, *hūṃ*, *hūṃ*, *idaṃ gṛhāṇa*, *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This is the *Sārvajñavidyā* of Kālī from the *Viṣṇuyāmala*.
First is the Vāgbhava seed-syllable; Prajāpati mounted upon Fire (Ra), joined with Śrī (Ī) and the Bindu (M)—one should recite this seed-syllable three times.
This great vidyā has been told, the Kaulikī, the beautiful one of the Kula.
Endowed with *śrī* and joined with the vowel *ī*.
Śyāmā is the abode of all good fortune, the bestower of all happiness,
the giver of omniscience, and the increaser of poetic talent and wealth.
Free from defects such as sleep and the like, she grants all accomplishments through mere remembrance;
there is no requirement for recitation, fire-offerings, or especially for ritual conduct.
This Vidyā, worshipped by Nandikeśvara, bestows accomplishment through its grasping;
Bhairava is declared its seer (ṛṣi), and Uṣṇik is cited as its meter (chandas).
The deity Dakṣiṇakālī is the bestower of the accomplishment of all fruits.
In the Śrīvārāhī Tantra: 280a)
The Blessed One said:
Now, having paid homage to my Lord, I shall declare the *mantra* of Kālī, which bestows all human goals (*puruṣārtha*), according to the tradition of Mātsya.
Seated upon Kapila and Urghīśa, she is adorned by the Nāda and the Moon.
The form Kapila is Arghīśa, the sixth vowel.
The first seed-syllable consists of a single letter; the second is the *mayā*-seed.
The fourth syllable is joined with an arrow, beginning with the letter of speech (*vāk*), which is the color of an arrow.
The seer is Kṛṣṇaka, and the meter is proclaimed to be Anuṣṭubh;
the deity is Kālī, and one should employ this for the sake of one's desired object.
One should recite the seed-syllable (bīja) one hundred and twenty-four times; this is declared to be the deposition of the principles (tattvanyāsa).
Fifty oblations (homa) are prescribed, and by means of a sixteenth part (kalāṃśa), the Sun is manifested.
The libation (tarpaṇa) is declared to be twofold, and the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is likewise prescribed;
for indeed, without the puraścaraṇa, no spiritual accomplishment (siddhi) arises.
This yantra is described as an eight-petaled lotus adorned with the three qualities (guṇas), supported by the earth, and possessing four gates.
One should apply the Māyā-bīja along with the six long vowels to the hands and limbs;
