one should perform this together with the respective *jāti* mantras and accompanied by their own specific *mudrās*.
Facing north, one should construct a pedestal and perform worship;
alternatively, worship in the Maṇipūra cakra at the yoni-liṅga is highly praised.
Worship should be performed for the sake of prosperity upon a great liṅga, a jewel, a yantra, a white liṅga, an image, or within lotuses.
In the mantra, the merit is tenfold; in the yoni and the liṅga, it is ten times greater;
and in the heart, the yoni, and the lalanā, the fruit is twenty-fivefold.
One should worship Gaṇeśa, Rudracaṇḍa, Vārāha, and Nandin as the door-keepers (dvārapālas) in order, beginning from the north.
A vast island, thrice-threefold in extent, with a beautiful and most enchanting sound,
resounding with the cries of cuckoos and attended by gentle breezes.
Having meditated upon that jeweled pavilion, which was filled with bees, flowers, and creepers, and where the rising moon and sun were situated within its own essence; in that [pavilion], he stood.
Upon a lotus on a jeweled lion-throne, within a triangle containing a blazing knife,
one should visualize the Goddess herself, the most beautiful in the three worlds, seated upon that seat.
Resembling a blue lotus, standing in the pratyālīḍha posture,
four-armed, three-eyed, and adorned with a crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
Long-bellied and large-eyed, seated upon a white corpse,
she holds a sword in her upper right hand and a blue lotus in her upper left.
She holds a skull-cup in her right lower hand and a flaying knife;
her matted locks are bound by eight serpents, and she is worshipped by the gods.
She has red, round eyes and her gleaming teeth are clearly visible;
she is clothed in a tiger skin and anointed with the eight perfumes.
Having thus meditated upon her, whose mouth is filled with betel and who is saluted by gods and demons, one should place her within the sixteen-spoked [mandala] and worship her.
Having performed the worship of the limbs, one should then worship [the goddesses] upon the petals:
Ādyānityā, Subhadrā, Maṅgalā, and Aṅgacāriṇī.
One should then worship Kāmākṣā, Rūpadā, Tārā, and Kālī;
one should worship these in the filaments in order, beginning from the northeast (aiśānī).
One should worship Bhadrā, Bhīmā, Jayā, Māyā, Bhuvaneśī, Bhairavī,
Tripurā, Kāmadā, and Durgā with the syllable "Ṭha" at the end of each name.
In the center, within the *kālīkāra*, one should worship Rātri, Kāmeśī, Kāmanā, Kamalā, Kālikā,
and Kāntā with their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*).
All the young female messengers have two arms and are intent on playing the lute;
they are red, enchanting, well-attired, and intoxicated with passion.
The vowels, excluding the neuter ones and devoid of the first and last pairs, ending with the bindu, are the *manus* for them; and [the mantra] ends with the wife of fire (*svāhā*).
Having recited the *yamala* mantra ten thousand times, one should offer oblations of ten thousand *madhūka* flowers smeared with honey,
thereby pleasing the Guru according to one's heart's desire.
One should worship the Goddess at the Śaktipīṭha according to the method to be described;
the practitioner of mantra, established in the posture of reclining, should mutter the perfected mantra one thousand times.
Having meditated upon whichever woman one desires, she arrives at that very moment.

Having inscribed the *māyā* (the syllable Hrīḥ) in the center of the eight [petals] and the *kāma* (the syllable Kṛm) in the corners, one should place the letters of the *astra* (the syllable Phaṭ) on the outside.
Outside of that, the yantra of Kālī, surrounded by the Mātṛkā letters, is auspicious and highly praised.
One should place the armor-mantra on the forehead and the woman-mantra in the cavity of the heart;
if one writes these with saffron and kuśīta and wears them, [the protection is secured].
He becomes beloved by women, as if he were another Kāma;
having placed the Vāgbhava at the head, one should meditate upon the goddess Kālikā.
Having meditated upon Bhuvaneśvarī, one should place the seed-syllable of Śakti on the forehead;
having meditated upon the Sun and Fire, one should place the two syllables of Śava on the eyes.
One should place the letter ending in 's' (sa), joined with a half-moon and rays, upon the face-circle;
one should likewise place it on the tongue; thus, in the assembly, one becomes a lord of speech.
By offering a thousand horse-sacrifices, one is released from bondage;
by offering lotuses, one should recite [the mantra] against enemies; and with dūrvā grass, one shall obtain peace.
Through oblations of *palāśa* flowers one attains nourishment, and through grains, the prosperity of grain;
a *homa* performed with crow feathers spreads enmity among men.
By means of *marīca* oblations, the enemy will certainly meet his death;
having meditated upon the Goddess, one should destroy those who practice minor malevolent rites, spirits, and the like.
One should worship with stainless, reddish flowers that are exceedingly beautiful and fragrant,
as well as with incense, lamps, and other offerings, along with enchanting dances and songs.
Thus, the practitioner who has mastered the mantra becomes a lord of men and women;
within a year, he considers himself the conqueror of Lakṣmī and a sovereign of wealth.
Having fashioned a vulva-shaped sacrificial pit (yoni-kuṇḍa), one should then perform the fire oblation according to one's own desire;
by offering jasmine flowers, one shall bring the entire world under control.

One may pacify malevolent spells, treachery, and the like by offering stalks of sugarcane soaked in honey into the fire using the *pṛṣṭhaka* verses; by performing such oblations, one shall attain great success.
Through barley there shall be abundance of grain; with wheat, one is endowed with the fulfillment of desired goals;
through rice, there shall be success in the sciences (akṣasiddhi); and with ten thousand sesame seeds, there is prosperity and steadfastness.
By offering blue lotuses with mantras, one brings the king’s wife under control;
by offering full-blown lotuses, one brings the entire earth under control.
By offering oblations with *aśoka* flowers, one obtains a son; with *madhuka* flowers, one shall obtain what is desired;
and by sacrificing with fruits produced from the *jambu* tree, one shall swiftly overwhelm one's enemies.
By performing a fire sacrifice with *ketakī* leaves, one will certainly destroy a rival.
The number of oblations should be ten thousand (*ayuta*), and the recitation (*japa*) is prescribed to be of the same amount.
Bathing with water consecrated by those mantras is known to remove all diseases;
water over which that [mantra] has been recited, when poured into the mouth, removes poison.
One should give medicine to the afflicted person, consecrated with this mantra;
by its power, that human being shall be liberated from that disease.
A ring made of the three metals, properly purified with this mantra,
pacifies sorcery, malice, and the like, and destroys all diseases.
This [mantra] is considered the eternal bestower of all prosperity and the subjugator of all;
whatever one desires, one should accomplish that by means of this mantra.
One should worship at midnight, at the twilights, and throughout the day and night;
having offered oblations and partaken of food, one should recite the mantra, and thus one is liberated from all sins.
On the eighth day of both fortnights, and especially on the ninth,
one should offer an oblation according to the prescribed rite with human beings, goats, buffaloes, and so forth.
When the fifteenth day of the month of Āṣāḍha arrives during the fourth watch of the night,
any gift, recitation, or fire-offering performed there at that time remains inexhaustible throughout the night.
When the conjunction of Puṣya arrives, one obtains the fruit of the Gomedha sacrifice;
a favorable conjunction may occasionally occur, and it is distinguished as superior in each such instance.
To Phetkārī.
Having uttered the seed-syllable of the palace (*prāsāda-bīja*), one should extract the word *kālī*;
then, having spoken the word *mahākālī*, [one should utter] the pair of *kāli*s thereafter.
This great mantra of Bhadrakālī, beginning with "astra," "agni," "priyānta," and "toya," one should worship and constantly recite one hundred and eight times.
A bone garland consisting of one hundred and eight [bones] should be fashioned;
this great vidyā, Bhadrakālī, the remover of fear, should be meditated upon.
Emaciated by hunger, with hollow eyes and a face soiled with filth, her hair disheveled and weeping, she cries out, "I am not yet satiated;

I shall make this entire world my single morsel! Holding in her two hands a pair of nooses resembling blazing tongues of fire, and possessing teeth like the fruit of the jambu tree, may Bhadrakālī dispel all fear.
Karālā.
In the *Aśeṣakālikā-tantra*, this goddess, the Great Goddess who brings about the subjugation of enemies, is proclaimed for the sake of accomplishing all tasks.
One should perform all her worship and other rites in the same manner as those for Kālikā.
In the Rudrayāmala:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim that which is difficult to obtain in the three worlds:
having extracted the seed-syllable of Śakti, immediately thereafter [extract] the seed-syllable of Kālī.
Then, O Goddess, one should extract the mantra ending with "svāhā" preceded by the pair of *kūrca* syllables.
This knowledge, O Great Goddess, is difficult to obtain in the three worlds.
The seed-syllable of power is Bhuvaneśvarī.
The seer, the meter, and the deity, as well as the recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth—
all these for the twenty-two-syllable goddess are exactly the same.
*Namaḥ pāśāṅkuśau dvedhā phaṭ svāhā kālikālike dīrghatanucchadaṃ kāli*— this is the fifteen-syllable mantra of Kālī.
And one should perform the rites for its seer, meter, and so forth, as well as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
In the Viśvasāra:
I shall proclaim the divisions of the mantras; listen, O lotus-faced one!
By the mere knowledge of these, one becomes Gaṅgādhara himself.
I shall now proclaim that great vidyā of three syllables:
first the root seed-syllable, then the māyā, and after that the seed-syllable of modesty (lajjā).
Māyā hūṃ.
O Dear One, Mahāvidyā is considered to be Mahākālī by Mahākāla.
Now, O lotus-faced one, hear the five-syllabled vidyā:
having extracted Prajāpati (the letter *pra*), followed by that which is mounted upon fire (*ra*).
One should extract Īśāna, joined with the fourth vowel, adorned with the bindu and nāda,
and joined with the left ear (the letter ś).
Having formed a blazing mass with the *viṃdu* and *khaṇḍa*, this is known as the *kūrca* seed-syllable (*bīja*).
The syllables *ī*, *śa*, *vai*, *śva*, *na*, and *ra* are mounted [upon the vowels], adorned with the *rati* (long vowel) and the *viṃdu*.
This seed-syllable, *lajjā*, is proclaimed to be endowed with all tantras;
the three seed-syllables are to be applied in sequence, and at their end is Vahnisundarī.
The five-syllabled Great Vidyā was spoken by the Lotus-born One;
O Pārvatī, listen as I shall now describe the six-syllabled Mahākālī.
Having extracted the three seed-syllables, one should extract the vowel *a* (avarṇa);
this Vidyā, ending with the wife of fire (svāhā), is proclaimed as the Enchantress of the Three Worlds.
O Pārvatī, listen as the eight-syllabled Great Vidyā is described:
the wise one [should recite] the three seed-syllables in sequence, followed again by the three seed-syllables.
This Vidyā, ending with *svāhā*, is said to bestow the fruits of the four aims of life.
O Pārvatī, listen as the eleven-syllable Vidyā is now described.
One should utter the Vāgbhava as the heart, joined with the fourth vowel, adorned with the nasal sound (nāda) and the bindu, and [ending] with the word "vada" (speak), O Prajāpati.
Having doubled that [syllable] and then appending the word *kālikā* ending in *ṅ*,
and concluding with *svāhā*, O Dear One, this ten-syllabled Vidyā is declared to be the beloved of Iṣṭakā.
The seer is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the meter is declared to be Paṅkti,
and the deity is remembered as Kālikā, the power higher than the highest.
This eleven-syllable mantra of Kālikā is very difficult to obtain;
it is acquired only through great fortune and bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life.
One should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times for the rite of *puraścaraṇa*; for other [mantras], it is said by Padmayoni that one hundred thousand recitations per syllable is required.
I shall describe the meditation upon these; listen, O lotus-faced one, to that which was formerly proclaimed by the sage known as Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Four-armed and black in color, adorned with a garland of severed heads,
she holds a sword in her right hand and two blue lotuses.
Holding a skull-topped staff and a begging bowl in her left hand in succession,
she herself bears a single matted lock of hair upon her head that reaches up to the sky.
She always wears a garland of severed heads upon her head and around her neck, and she bears a necklace of serpents upon her chest; she has blood-red eyes.
Wearing black garments and clad in a tiger skin around her waist,
she places her left foot upon the heart of a corpse and her right foot—
Having placed upon the back of a lion a corpse that is itself licking its lips,
one should visualize her as Aṭṭahāsā, endowed with a most terrible roar and terrifying in appearance.
Thus should one constantly meditate upon Kālī, the destroyer of the impurities of the Kali age,
by those who are humble with devotion and who desire fortune, sovereignty, and happiness.
Having bowed to the Guru according to the prescribed rite, one should meditate upon the Supreme Deity.
Now I shall describe another auspicious method;
listen with supreme devotion to this [teaching] which destroys the impurities of Kālī.
The root seed-syllable, likewise the Māyā, and after that the seed-syllable of modesty;
then "O Kālikā" on the right, and at the end of that, Vahnisundarī.
The eleven-syllable Kālī mantra bestows the fruits of the four aims of life;
it begins with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) and the root-seed (*mūlabīja*), and at its end is Bhuvaneśvarī.
And then, in the south as well, that which ends with the weapon-mantra was uttered.
By virtue of the word "and" (ca), [it is understood as] "at the time of death" (kālike).
Now I shall proclaim another vidyā, that nine-syllabled one:
having extracted the root seed-syllable, there follow two words ending in "saṃbudhya."
This fourteen-syllable Vidyā of Kālikā, which ends in *svāhā*, is said to bring about the destruction of all enemies. It is now set forth.
By whose mere sidelong glance one becomes equal to the Lord of Speech (Vāgīśvara)—
her armor begins with the root seed-syllable, and at its end is Bhuvaneśvarī.
Then, "dakṣiṇe kālike ca"— these three seed-syllables followed by "svāhā" are declared to be the vidyā that bestows the fruits of all dharmas.
The fourteen-syllable vidyā is proclaimed as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Now I shall proclaim another vidyā consisting of twenty syllables,
by the mere grace of which one may become a Purandara upon the earth.
One should utter the two root-seeds, then the pair of *kūrca* mantras,
and having extracted the pair of *lajjā* mantras, [one should utter] the two words ending in the vocative case.
As before, there is the syllable *saṭ* and likewise the seed-syllable; at its end is the beautiful goddess Vahnisundarī.
Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the seer (*ṛṣi*), and the meter (*chandas*) is declared to be Paṅkti.
The deities have been described by the virtuous as Kālī preceded by Dakṣiṇā;
this eleven-syllable vidyā is now being told—listen, O Pārvatī.
The root mantra, the armor, and the illusion [mantra],
followed by two words ending in *svāhā*, are declared to be the Vidyā that bestows the fruits of the four aims of life.
The seer is Dakṣiṇāmūrti himself; the meter is declared to be Anuṣṭubh.
Now I shall proclaim another vidyā, the Mistress of the Three Worlds:
having extracted one's own seed-syllable, at its end [one places] Vahnisundarī.
The sages are declared to be the Bhairavas, endowed with all the Tantras:
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, and the one known as Unmatta.
Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra—these are the eight Bhairavas.
O lotus-faced one, hear now their great vidyās.
That eight-syllabled mantra has been proclaimed, which is hidden in all tantras;
it consists of two of its own seed-syllables, two *kūrca* syllables, and then two *lajjā* syllables.
The nine-syllable great vidyā, ending in *svāhā*, is said to be Kālī, who bestows the fruits of righteous deeds; listen, O lotus-faced one!
The three of one's own seed-syllables, followed by the pair of *kūrca*, then the pair of *lajjā*,
ending with *svāhā*— this auspicious *vidyā* is said to bestow all prosperity.
The nine-syllabled great vidyā is endowed with nine characteristics.
Now I shall proclaim another [vidyā], endowed with ten principles,
by whose mere sidelong glance one becomes the enchanter of the three worlds.
The two roots, the pair of *kūrca*s, and the two *lajjā*s follow thereafter;
again those very same [syllables] in that same order, and at the end of that, the beautiful goddess Vahni.
The fourteen-syllable vidyā bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe Kālī, the destroyer of sins,
by whose mere sidelong glance one may become another Vāgīśvara.
Wealth, grain, sons, a wife, horses, elephants, and even gold—
whatever one desires in the mind, all that shall certainly be obtained.
There is no knowledge higher than this, no supreme ford greater than this,
and no task for sages more important than this, which bestows liberation.
For both householders and ascetics,
it bestows the fruit of all desires.
A person need not perform worship or ritual adoration of her; they should merely recite the mantra.
In the Kali age, all supernatural powers (siddhis) come into the hands of such a person.
Having extracted the three Brahmās, joined with Rati and Vahni, and endowed with Nāda and Bindu,
[one places] the two supreme Lañjās and Kūrcas.
Then, having again extracted [the syllables] in sequence up to the wife of Fire (Svāhā),
this is declared to be the Sixteenfold Vidyā, which is like a wish-fulfilling tree.
O Dear One, their worship, as well as all the ritual depositions (*nyāsa*) and so forth, is as before;
[these mantras consist of] fourteen, sixteen, and thirty syllables respectively.

For those [mantras], the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) in the performance of the ritual should consist of one hundred thousand recitations; for all other vidyās, one hundred thousand recitations per syllable is proclaimed.
For all of them, however, a great worship accompanied by sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) is prescribed.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall proclaim the Great Vidyā Guhyakālī, who bestows the fruits of all desires and is exceedingly difficult to attain within the three worlds.
Having combined the term beginning with the group starting with *Indra* (i.e., *indrādi*) with *Rati* (the letter *e*) and the *bindu*,
and having tripled that, one should then extract the two *Īśas* (the letters *ī* and *ī*).
The left eye (va) conjoined with fire (ra), adorned with the nāda and bindu—
this is declared to be the double *lajjā* (hrīṃ hrīṃ), which follows as the essence of all vidyās.
Then, one should again extract the seven syllables beginning with "guhyakālike";
this vidyā, ending in svāhā, is said to be hidden in all tantras.
There is no knowledge higher than this, nor is there a more excellent sacred ford than this;
and various great sciences have been proclaimed by the Lotus-born One.
Listen to that, O Great Goddess, which has been declared by the exponents of Brahman:
the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma), likewise the Kūrca, and at its end, Bhuvaneśvarī.
Whether in the *guhya* or the *kālika*, there shall likewise be the three seed-syllables;
this vidyā, ending in *svāhā*, is declared to be the most excellent among all vidyās.
Then, having extracted two seeds at a time, one should utter them for the purpose of awakening;
again, in the same manner, the six seeds [are placed], and at their end is Vahnisundarī.
The Vidyā is proclaimed as consisting of twenty syllables,
less one; thereafter, one should utter the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja), the armor (kavaca), and Bhuvaneśvarī.
Then one should utter the invocation ending with "svāhā"; this is remembered as the other [form].
The eleven-syllable vidyā becomes ten syllables in nature.
The single-syllable is the seed of desire, and the three-syllable consists of the three seeds.
The six-syllable [mantra] consists of the six seed-syllables; it becomes three-syllabled when ending with *svāhā*.
The two-syllable [mantra] is the *kāmabīja*; it becomes three-syllabled when ending with *phaṭ*.
Then the three seed-syllables and the weapon-mantra (astra) are declared as the four-syllable [mantra];
having doubled the seed-syllables and omitted the word of address.
This Vidyā, ending with *svāhā*, is declared to be hidden in all Tantras;
by prefixing the word *dakṣiṇe*, it becomes fifteen syllables long.
Having abandoned the seed-syllable of desire, or else the sixteen-syllabled mantra—
thus are many kinds of vidyās proclaimed in various tantras.
In the Viśvasāra:
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall declare the Vidyā that bestows all fruits,
which directly grants the four aims of life and destroys even the greatest of sins.
The Goddess who bestows all accomplishments, the granter of both worldly enjoyment and liberation—
Guhyakālī, the Great Vidyā, is exceedingly difficult to attain within the three worlds.
Having likewise tripled the group beginning with Indra, which is established [in the quarters] and conjoined with the *rati* (e) and the *bindu* (m), one should then extract the syllable for Īśāna.
Joined with the sixth vowel, consisting of the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*,
one should then double it and extract the two *īśas*.
The left eye (va) conjoined with fire (ra) and adorned with the nasal sound (nāda) and the bindu;
that is declared as Kālikā in the secret place, or else one may say it is in the right [eye].
Furthermore, one should first apply the seven seeds in their proper sequence;
this mantra, ending with the wife of Fire (svāhā), is declared to be the Trailokyamohinī-vidyā.
Now, the mantra "atha vā" is indeed "dakṣiṇe vā."
Now I shall speak of the Great Vidyā, which is concealed in all tantras;
listen to that which was proclaimed by Bhṛgurāma, O lotus-faced one!

Having extracted the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma), one should utter the two words "saṃbudhyanta"; then, at the end of that, one should again place the desire-seed and the beautiful consort of Fire (Vahni).
This is the nine-syllable vidyā, endowed with the secret word;
by uttering the word "dakṣiṇe," it becomes the ten-syllable vidyā.
The Vidyā spoken by Mahākāla is divided into one hundred thousand parts;
among them, the Vidyās beginning with Kālī are now described—listen, O Pārvatī.
One should place the seed-syllables beginning with Kāmarāja according to their anterior and posterior divisions,
and likewise join Bhadrakālī, ending in the feminine suffix Ṅi, in the middle of the seed-syllables.
"O Dear One, this auspicious Vidyā consisting of twenty syllables ending in *svāhā* has been declared;
it is the goddess Bhadrakālī of beautiful countenance, the bestower of the four aims of life."
One should first extract the seed-syllables, then the word *mahākālī*, and at the end of that, the seven seed-syllables ending in *svāhā*; this is the method accepted in the Tantra.
The Mahāvidyā of Mahākālī is proclaimed to have twenty leaves;
O lotus-faced one, listen as I describe their meditation.
She has the radiance of a great cloud, is red in color, and wears black garments;
she has a lolling tongue, terrible fangs, sunken eyes, and a laughing face.
With a single matted lock, adorned with a serpent-necklace and a vine, which serves as a crescent moon for its remaining portion, she licks a corpse while painting the very sky.
Her body is adorned with a sacred thread of serpents, she is embellished with the skins of serpent-chiefs,
she wears a forest garland made of fifty human skulls, and she has a massive belly.
One should visualize Guhyakālī, whose head above is adorned with a thousand hoods at night,
and who is encircled by the hoods of nāgas in the four directions.
Her left bracelet was adorned by Takṣaka, the king of nāgas,
and her right bracelet was made by Ananta, the king of nāgas.
The Naga fashioned a girdle of tongues for Ratnagehinī;
she is Aṭṭahāsā, the greatly terrifying one who grants the desires of the practitioner.
One should meditate upon the Goddess as having two arms,
wearing a sacred thread made of a serpent, and adorned with earrings set with the nine gems upon her ears.
The consort of Śiva, with a serene countenance, gentle, adorned with all kinds of jewels,
and attended by hosts of sages such as Nārada and others.

Having thus meditated upon the goddess who laughs with a loud laugh, who is most terrifying, who grants the desires of practitioners, and who destroys the impurities of those who are pinned down, one shall conquer.
Alternatively, one should meditate upon Kālī, who is dear to Mahākāla,
possessing the luster of a great cloud, dark-complexioned, and clothed in red garments.
With a lolling tongue and a gaping mouth, possessing terrible fangs and a fearsome appearance,
she was adorned with a pair of earrings made from corpses, yet remained exceedingly beautiful.
She whose two lips are the abode of all loveliness, from which her hair falls,
who has fashioned a girdle from clusters of her own lotus-stalks, and who faces [her lover] with a smile.
O Mahādeva in the form of Śava, she stands in the pratyālīḍha posture, wearing a garland of severed heads, and is seated upon your heart.
[She holds] the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), the boon-granting gesture (vara), and a sword beautifully adorned with a [serpent's] head;
she is further embellished by various jewels upon her thousand hoods.
O Mahādeva in the form of a Śava, you have assumed a body at will;
your right hand is adorned by the king of serpents within.
It was served by various gods and gandharvas accompanied by diverse cymbals,
and frequented by many nāgas— truly enchanting to the mind.
Thus the Goddess should reflect, joined with Kurukullā and the others;
she should worship the highly exalted Guhyakālī with supreme devotion.
One should perform all [rites], such as the worship of the yantra, together with the ritual fee (dakṣiṇā).
The mantra of the seat is as follows:
One should first utter Sadāśiva, then the word Mahāpreta;
followed by Guhyakālī-pīṭhāsana ending in the letter Ṅa, conjoined with Guhyakālī.
The Vidyā beginning with *praṇava*, beginning with *hrīḥ*, ending with *hūṃ*,
and concluding with *namaḥ* was taught by the Lotus-born One for the seat of Guhyakālī.
The mantra for the offering (bali) is as follows:

Then one should say: "Come, come" (*ehi ehi*), the pair of words; likewise the word "O Guhyakālī" (*guhyakāli*); then the pair of words "Seize, seize" (*gṛhṇa gṛhṇa*); and thereafter, [one should say] "my enemies" (*mama śatrūn*).
One should utter "nāśaya" twice, say "khādaya" twice,
then the pair of words "turu turu," and thereafter "skura skura."
"Chindhi chindhi," "pada-dvandvam," "siddhiṃ dehi," and the pair of "pada" syllables;
one should utter the two armor-mantras (kavaca), and at their end, Vahnisundarī.
The mantra for the offering of the two-fold fifty-fold oblation (vali) is thus remembered;
this great vidyā should be employed for the offering of the oblation.
One should recite the Gāyatrī mantra with the word "Guhyā" joined [to it];
having uttered "Kāmarāja," one should then say "Guhye Kālike."
And at the end of that, one should indeed utter "vidmahe" with effort;
having pronounced "vidye puṇye," one should say "dhīmahi" after that.
Having addressed that *pada* to us, the Goddess shall then impel it;
likewise, O Beloved, the *gāyatrī* of Guhyakālī has been declared, O Goddess.
In the Kālīkulārṇava.
Having first taken the seed-syllable of passion (RĀ), one should then extract the seed-syllable of sound (HŪM);
likewise, having uttered HṚLLEKHĀ, one should say KĀLIKE DAKṢINE.
Furthermore, one should apply these seeds in their proper sequence;
all rites such as recitation and worship should be performed with the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) as the standard.
Kāmākṣā is in Pañcāsikā.
The pair of the Praṇava and the Aṅkuśa (the syllables *oṃ* and *phaṭ*) at the end of the mantra,
followed by the word *kāli* and *kālike*, is the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*), the leader of all mantras.
Then, having joined it with the *tāra* (om), up to the long [vowel], and then with the *hṛllekhā*,
and having reached the weapons, one should meditate on the Goddess with undistracted mind.
The meditation consists of [visualizing] the moon's orb split by a sword, and so forth;
having invoked the Goddess into the center of a six-cornered lotus, one should worship her.
Then, one should worship with the root mantra itself, using water for the feet and other offerings, as well as the six limbs;
thereafter, one should worship the hexagon of the Goddess, whose auspicious enclosures possess that same form.
And Mahābhairavī, Pūrvabhairavī, Siṃhabhairavī,
Dhūmrabhairavī, Viśvabhairavī, and Unmattabhairavī.
Then, for the subjugation [mantra] of Bhairavī and the delusion [mantra] of Bhairavī,
these [deities], beginning with *Oṃ* and ending with *Namaḥ*, are to be worshipped on the eight petals.
Having thus worshipped the Queen of the Gods with the ritual offerings, he should again perform japa;
having offered three handfuls of flowers, he should dissolve [the deity] into his own heart with the mantra "Aja Svāhā."
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is prescribed as ten thousand repetitions;
in the Kali age, the number is fourfold, whereby it yields results swiftly.
Having performed the fire-oblation with red flowers after preparing Kuṣṭha according to the prescribed ritual,
the practitioner who recites this mantra is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
What need is there for other numerous sins, such as the killing of one's father or mother,
when compared to the fruit of the gift of a Kapilā cow filled with jewels and the entire earth?
The practitioner attains that fruit through meditation on the Goddess;
the supreme practitioner obtains the great siddhis, such as aṇimā and the rest.

Having touched or seen [the object], one should recite the mantra; whomever one does so, that person will be brought under control. By reciting it one hundred and eight times and performing a fire offering (*homa*) with red flowers, [the same result is achieved].
A minister can bring even a king under his control; there is nothing in the three worlds that cannot be accomplished.
[One should perform this] in an empty house, a temple, or even a cremation ground.
A celibate practitioner who eats sacrificial food becomes equal to Indra through recitation;
for the sake of peace and likewise for nourishment, [the fire] should be established in a triangular pit.
The mantra-practitioner should offer ten thousand oblations, or three thousand;
and furthermore, having meditated upon the Goddess there in the sacrificial fire, he should perform the libation.
By offering a thousand bilva leaves smeared with ghee daily while reciting the complete root mantra, one attains the supreme goal.
By offering oblations of *mālatī* flowers smeared with clarified butter, one becomes a swift poet;
for one who knows this mantra, nothing whatsoever remains impossible at all times.
In the Mahākālasaṃhitā.
Henceforth, O my beloved, listen to my *mālā-mantra*:
having uttered the three root-seeds (*mūla-bīja*) and having uttered the three *kūrca* [seeds].
Lajjā, the triad, the seed-syllable of Ramā, the fourfold Vāgbhava,
Ḍākinī, Phetkārī, and likewise Pāśakroṭa.
Again, having extracted those very same [syllables], one should perform the salutation to the Bhagavatī with "Khecarī," "Kāla," "Kārmuka," and likewise "Caṇḍa."
The fifteen-syllable vidyā bestows the fruit of all accomplishments;
Dakṣiṇāmūrti is its seer (ṛṣi), and Virāj is proclaimed as its meter (chanda).
Bhogeśvarī Dakṣiṇakālī is proclaimed as the deity;
Phetkārī is the seed-syllable (bīja), Lajjā is the power (śakti), and Ramā is the pin (kīlaka).
The application (viniyoga) is proclaimed for the attainment of happiness and sovereignty;
therefore, listen attentively to the one-hundred-syllable mantra (śatākṣarī-vidyā).
One should utter the *praṇava* (oṃ) for the Bhagavatī, then *kālike* on the right,
and then, having recollected *cāmuṇḍe*, one should extract the seed-syllable (*vīja*) of the Yoginī.
Having uttered the three *kapālas*, one should speak the three *dānavas*;
O Goddess, one should then utter one's own three *bījas* and the three *kūrca*s.
Having addressed Madanonmādinī, one should likewise address Kālikā on the right,
as well as Cāmuṇḍā, Caṇḍakāpālinī, Bhāluṇḍā, and Śakti.
O Dear One, [the mantras] are Kūrma, Ananta, Hayagrīva, Kṣeḍa, Mānasa, Vāgbhava, Pāśa, Krodha, Mahākrodha, Prāsāda, and Gāruḍa.
Having spoken thus to the one who laughs with a terrible roar, the bestower of Śiva’s liberation,
she then addressed her who resembles the form of Brahmā and illuminates the great darkness.
Beyond that, in the abode of the discus (Cakranilaya), there is a triad of Śākinīs;
then follow Vidyut, Amṛt, Mahākāla, Bhūta, Kārmuka, and Pannaga.
Pralayāpsara, Phetkārī, and at the end Vahnisundarī—

among all, the Kaulika is the best, as is the follower of the Urdhvāmnāya and the Vāmaga.
299b) He who is endowed with devotion and serves the true guru is alone worthy of veneration by the Kaulas; others are considered mere drinkers of wine.
Remembering Him, chanting His name, beholding Him, bowing to Him, and likewise conversing with Him, yields a fruit greater than that of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Wherever that deity dwells, there shall be prosperity and victory;
there shall be freedom from disease, good rain, abundance of food, and an absence of calamities.
Having seen [the Guru], one should bow to his vision; another [who is not a Guru] should be avoided from afar.
The Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya) is of the nature of emanation (sṛṣṭi), while the Southern [Tradition] is of the nature of maintenance (sthiti).
Withdrawal occurs in the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya), while in the Northern Tradition (Uttara), there is grasping (graha).
They know Mantra-yoga to be the Eastern [Tradition], whereas Bhakti-yoga is the Southern.
The western yoga is that of action (karmayoga), and likewise the northern is that of knowledge (jñānayoga);
and another [yoga] is also mentioned in that very same place.
O Goddess, when your body was abandoned at the sacrifice of Dakṣa,
I took it upon my shoulder and prepared to enter the funeral pyre.
Wherever he went in search of the Vaḍavā fire,
there it was quickly extinguished by Śakra with waters.
As I wandered in this manner for a year, great perspiration arose within me; if even a single drop of it were to fall, the earth would be consumed by fire.
Then Viṣṇu was entreated for the protection of the earth;
thereupon, he pierced his limbs with small arrows.
Having divided him into eighty-four fragments, he cast them upon the earth;
and as I was fanned by the wind, everyone then became joyful and energetic.
And Viṣṇu, having manifested himself, fell at my feet;
having raised me up, he embraced me, and your grief was forgotten.
At that time, O Pārvatī, the gods beginning with Brahmā and the great sages beginning with Nārada praised me; then Viṣṇu spoke these words.
O Knower, how have you, who possess the sovereignty of Maheśvara, fallen into delusion as to enter the fire along with the body of Mati?
"A woman should follow her husband; she does not go to one who is arrogant. Having disregarded this scriptural injunction, O Lord, how have you been so deluded?
When the Lord of Gods had thus spoken, they, along with Brahmā,
praised Hari with words adorned by the figure of speech known as *śleṣa*.
Then we both said, "O twice-born ones, ask for a boon.
To that, those brahmins replied, "This dissolution of dharma has arrived."
The Śaivas who resorted to Dakṣa’s sacrifice were deprived of their Brahminhood;
and all the twice-born who had come to the sacrifice were likewise cursed by Śiva.
If this surface of the earth were real, it would be devoid of Brahmanical rites due to the touch of corpses everywhere, for its limbs have been severed by Viṣṇu.
Therefore, act in such a way that the purification of the earth, the purity of the Brahmins,
and the truthfulness of Brahmā’s word may all be realized.
Then, having reflected and having obtained Viṣṇu’s consent, I declared:
"Where the Vedic rites have been destroyed, there let the Tantra be set in motion."
For those Brahmins who have been consumed by curses and are devoid of Vedic rites,
this family dharma is indeed the means for both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O Prajāpati, those Brahmins who were born from seats and whose status as Brahmins was consumed by a curse— they alone have the right to this path within their lineage.
Because it is to be honored within that very family (kula), this path is called Kaula;
the Vāma-mārga is inferior to that, while the Nākṣatra and Vaiśyaka paths are not [even mentioned].
The authority for those two [rites] is declared there to belong to the sacrificers;
other than that, the Siddhāntin holds that there is no authority for Śūdras in this matter.
Those who enter the Kaula dharma without knowing its lineage will undoubtedly be destitute, deprived of progeny, and afflicted by disease.
O Goddess, he who, being unaccomplished in the knowledge of the Kaula, desires to consume that substance, is a great sinner and is excluded from all rites.

For one who is deficient in the conduct of the samaya, who acts according to his own whims, and is evil-minded, there are no spiritual accomplishments; rather, there is a fall from his lineage. Therefore, one should not associate with such a person.
He who, casting aside the injunctions of the scriptures, acts according to his own whims,
attains neither perfection in this world nor the supreme goal in the hereafter.
Those who, having resorted to [false] views, enjoy the wealth of their families,
are born among the sources of beings (bhūtayoni) as many times as there are hairs on their bodies.
And if one whose self is inflated by pride understands nothing at all—
neither meditation, nor the five sciences, nor the Dharma, nor virtuous conduct— then what?
If there is neither divine grace, nor the guru, nor self-inquiry for one in the Kaula tradition,
then being solely attached to sense objects, he surely falls— of this there is no doubt.
Or else, it is in that very same [text], in the dialogue between Hara and Gaurī.
Having slain the demon Kolāsura, Lakṣmī, intoxicated by drinking his blood,
was then laughed at at her will by the Brahmins out of anger.
O best of Brahmins, even if Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or I were to desire it,
then the enraged Mahālakṣmī would vanish into the earth.
Everything has become devoid of splendor and appears as if one were about to die;
Dharma does not waver anywhere, nor do the deities of the crossroads.
Thus, for a hundred years, they went for refuge to Brahmā as he was born;
even Brahmā there appeared devoid of splendor, like a pauper.
O Creator, the sages asked, "Whence has this lack of fortune come?
O beloved, at that time, Brahmā laughed and was then enlightened by the Brahman.
Thinking, "This is a great Brahmanic splendor," Viṣṇu remained silent;
and Śrī Śiva laughed at the obstruction of your side.
Therefore, she became enraged and departed from that place for the subterranean realm (rasātala). All those who rely on prosperity are consumed by pride; none who do not rely on it are so destroyed.
Therefore, O Śakra, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and I, as well as you who have come from the past,
the nāgas, the ancestors, the siddhas, the guardians of the quarters, the yakṣas, and the rākṣasas— [all these are one].
Then, propitiating and praising that goddess with great hymns,
they all assembled together and went to the Śrīśaila mountain.
Having seen a certain person [endowed] with splendor, they then propitiated the Cruel One (Krūra) and praised him with various hymns according to Vedic and Tantric paths.
Thus, after three years, prosperity became manifest;
and looking with a compassionate gaze, he spoke these great words.
For what reason did the Brahmins laugh, and from where did the gods arise?
Furthermore, why was worship now performed for her who is difficult to behold?
Then she was addressed by me: "The entire universe is pervaded by you;
they do not know your power and laugh at you, yet you are a performer of actions."
O sharp-hearted one, it was with this understanding that I committed this jest;
yet your power is known by all the brahmins, as well as by the gods and demons.
"Therefore, O Lord, be gracious and carry on the course of worldly affairs.
Having heard these words of mine, Śrī indeed spoke as follows at that time.
This Surā is my sister;
the deity will rejoice with those who perform her primary worship.
As long as this illusory manifestation exists, it is in vain without me;
likewise, all forms of worship are in vain without the worship of the Cakra.
If you desire enjoyments in this world, or if you desire [the state of] divinity in the next,
then the worship of the Discus (Cakra) should be performed by men.
"It is dear to all the gods; it must be guarded and concealed with great effort. Thus [it is said].

In this manner, even among the *bhūdevas* (brahmins), the worship and propitiation of deities with liquor is observed; nevertheless, it is stated that the status of a *kaula* belongs only to those who have reached the [appropriate] time-cycle (*vāra*), and not to brahmins alone. That authority is established solely by that very proof, which is found in the *Merutantra* itself.
When one who follows the left path enters the right, he is obstructed and even tormented by the gods; he does not attain accomplishment.
When the right-hand path enters the left, then those gods,
pervading both worlds, devour that left-handed one.
Therefore, having understood the path of one's own family, one should perform the worship.
In the continuation of the governing topic.
Even a piece of flesh the size of a sesame seed, or half a sesame seed, or even a single drop,
when offered as a libation just once, yields for the emitters [of semen] the fruit born of sacrifice.
Free from hesitation, fearless, steadfast, devoid of shame, and without curiosity,
one who has ascertained the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras may drink the boon-granting Varuni wine.
Through the purification of mantra-rites, the state of a deity arises for men by drinking liquor; otherwise, there is the manifestation of a preta.
It should be drunk by Brāhmaṇas during the Kaulika [observance], by all Kṣatriyas at the arrival of the Aṇu [period],
by Vaiśyas during the Golaṃbha [rite], and by Śūdras during the Anveṣaṇa rite.
Having worshipped the gods and the ancestors according to the path prescribed by one's capacity and the scriptures,
one who drinks liquor and eats meat while remembering the Guru incurs no fault.
For the sake of steadiness in the meditation on Brahman and for the purpose of satisfying the deities, one may consume honey and meat; however, if there is craving [for them], he is a sinner.
By consuming substances such as fish, meat,
and liquor, he who passes the time that ought to be spent in yoga becomes a perpetrator of a great sin.
Just as the drinking of Soma by the learned (vipras) during sacrifices is not censured,
so too the drinking of wine by the Kaulas at the conclusion of worship is not forbidden.
Having thoroughly understood the latent impressions from the Kula scriptures of the venerable Guru, one should deposit the five mudrās; otherwise, one shall fall.
A hero who worships the lineage of gurus, the *āvṛtti*, and the *vaṭukas* and so forth,
yet drinks liquor in vain, shall incur the curse of the deities.
Such is the teacher on the left-hand path (vāmamārga), according to the statement in that very same [text].
He is the illuminator of his own practice of knowledge, austerity, and dharma,
and the illuminator of the knowledge, austerity, and dharma of the social classes and stages of life.
He who is fully accomplished in the six rites, who is a giver and an enjoyer rather than a beggar—he alone is a true Kaulika Ācārya; any other is a mere hypocrite of the Kula.
He who correctly understands the *piṇḍa*, the *pada*, as well as *rūpa*, *rūpātīta*, and the stainless (*nirañjana*),
is a true Guru and shall uplift the other.
O Dear One, he who understands the noose, the pillar, piercing, initiation, and the seizing of the bound soul (paśu)— these three— is declared to be a Guru.

O Dear One, he who knows the fruit of the movement of the vital breath (jīvacāra) within the petals of the seven lotuses from the base to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra)— he alone is the Guru, and no other.
A wise man should choose only that teacher from whose very association supreme bliss arises;
he should not choose anyone else.
"By one who has consumed the entire triple world, including all moving and non-moving beings,
with apprehension— by whom even apprehension itself was consumed— that Guru is difficult to find on earth," and so forth.
Ishvara said:
Having traveled repeatedly from the mūlādhāra up to the brahmarandhra,
the arising of bliss occurs through the mudrā of the moon of consciousness and the kuṇḍalinī energy.
That which arises from the nectar of the motionless lotus of the sky is called the drinking of honey; others are sinners who drink liquor.

The knower of yoga, with the sword of knowledge, should lead the mind— which is the sacrificial animal of merit and demerit— to dissolution in the Supreme; thus he attains the state of one who has consumed the sacrificial meat.
One who restrains the group of one's own senses with the mind and applies them to the Self is called a "fish-eater";
all others are said to have the livelihood of fishermen.
The power of the beast is unawakened, while that of the Kaulika is awakened;
he who serves that power shall be a true servant of power.
Thus, I have declared the secret reality of the five mudrās;
he who, having understood it correctly from the mouth of the guru, practices it, is liberated.
In the Kālītantra:
The illustrious Pārvatī said:
O Blessed One, be gracious, O Lord of Gods, the essence that is for the welfare of all living beings;
tell us, O Bhairava, the means by which success may certainly be attained.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme reality, the most excellent among all knowledge;
by the mere realization of which, Vidyā quickly becomes propitious.
The fundamental, extraordinary power, whose form is that of a serpent, resides on that ground; this wind and water is called "prāṇa" by the wise.
Satisfied by hundreds [of offerings], they coo with indistinctly sweet sounds through the resonance;
departing via the aperture of Brahma, they enter their own abode.
One should effect the dissolution of the mind therein through the very process of coming and going;
by that, the crest of mantra arrives, which is the illuminator of all accomplishments.
Just as darkness in a house filled with it reveals nothing at all,
so too mantras devoid of the crest-syllable (śikhā) never attain success.
O Supreme Goddess, the instruction on the crest-lock (śikhā) is concealed everywhere;
without this [instruction], there shall be no accomplishment even in hundreds of millions of years.
Therefore, O Girijā, you too must guard this with great effort.
O Kuleśvara, having fully integrated that [reality] within oneself as the form of the Goddess,
there is neither worship, nor ritual placement (nyāsa), nor steadfast devotion, nor vows and the like.
I am Pūrṇāha, the self of Bhairava; I am eternal bliss, the imperishable.
I am the stainless essential nature, and I am the formless Lord.
I am devoted to all the scriptures and am a worshiper of everything herein;
there is no god higher than this, none who has been born, nor shall there ever be one.
One who knows the reality of the manifold forms and acts for the benefit of all—by meditating upon him, one becomes satisfied and attains liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Abiding in various locations within the body, such as the support (ādhāra) and so forth,
wherever one should perceive [the object], there is the eternal Brahman-nature.
Know the Self to be Brahman; abandon deluded knowledge.
By this [Self] the Goddess creates, and likewise, by this she protects.
By this, know that the One Cause of all worlds has been withdrawn;
therefore, the wise should diligently practice self-knowledge.

Salutations to you, that Supreme Goddess, who— though she is the Yami, the source of the lotus (Brahma), and the consort of the Lord of the Immortals (Indra)— is not perceived even by Agni, the god of fire, who dwells upon their heads;
she who consists of bliss, whose nature is profound as the senses,
who transcends the intellect and the organs of perception, and who is realized in the hearts of those who contemplate her through the command of the Guru.
The bees of the Kaulika tradition, who are like swarms of honeybees emerging from the thousand-petaled lotuses of awakened consciousness surrounded by gentle waves.

May those who seek the goals of the [four] classes drink [of this] incessantly with fervor; for by worshipping the lotus-feet of the Guru, even that [attainment] is obtainable here in this very world.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the Kulamuktikallolinī composed by Śrī Ādyānanda.
May it be auspicious!
